12092-the-oxford-movement-twelve-years-1:
R. W. Church, sometime dean of St. Paul and fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, wrote these papers on the Oxford Movement, covering 1833 to 1845. Friends prepared them for print after his death, from drafts he had revised in his last months.

Church traces how John Henry Newman, John Keble, Hurrell Froude, and their circle challenged routine Anglican practice, calling the Church back to older doctrine and ritual. He weighs their sermons, tracts, and quarrels with bishops, and follows Newman path toward Rome. The account is sympathetic but measured, written by a man who knew the leaders. It remains a first-hand guide to a movement that split English religion.
23060-the-unknown-masterpiece-1845:
Honoré de Balzac meditates on art in The Unknown Masterpiece, dated 1845 in this edition. No brief, fragile feeling, Balzac writes, comes closer to love than a young artist's passion for his calling. The young man stands at the start of a blissful martyrdom, a career of glory and disaster, vague expectations and real disappointments.

Balzac's tale pits a young painter against old Frenhofer, who has spent ten years perfecting a canvas no one may see. When the masterpiece is finally unveiled, art's deepest question stands on the easel. Painters from Cézanne to Picasso claimed this story as a prophecy of modern art. It is short enough to read in an hour and large enough to argue about for a lifetime.
25207-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
The June 1845 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume 57, number 356, leads with a sketch of Pushkin, the Russian poet, by Thomas B. Shaw. Shaw, a Cambridge man teaching in St. Petersburg, traces Pushkin's life and works for English readers who knew little of Russian letters.

Other pieces discuss the novel and the drama, continue Marston's memoirs, review Cennino Cennini on painting, and offer a fourth essay on the aesthetics of dress. The number also prints Suspiria de Profundis, the sequel to the Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, with stanzas for Admiral Milne and Thomas Hood.
26692-a-daughter-of-raasay-a-tale-of-the:
William MacLeod Raine published this Jacobite romance with Frederick A. Stokes at New York in 1902, copyrighted in 1901 and 1902, illustrated by Stuart Travis. Its foreword promises that where the romance touches history it agrees with accepted facts, with one possible exception. It presents the Young Chevalier as charming and gallant in bearing, whatever his later life failed to fulfil.

Chapters run from The Sport of Chance and A Cry in the Night through Deoch Slaint an Righ and Of Love and War. The Hue and Cry leads to Charles Edward Stuart, Blue Bonnets over the Border, and Culloden. The Red Heather Hills, Volney's debt, the Aftermath, a Reprieve, and the Valley of the Shadow follow. Love, loyalty, and a worthless cause, in Raine's phrase, carry the tale from London playgoing to Highland defeat.
28336-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for July 1845, volume fifty-eight, number 357, opens the second half of the year with a strong number. Its contents list Marlborough, part one, Pushkin the Russian poet, part two, and Suspiria de Profundis, sequel to De Quincey's Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, part two. Northern Lights, house-hunting in Wales, and Goethe's Torquato Tasso follow.

A tale of Wales, David the Telynwr, and North's specimens of British critics close the number. Blackwood and Sons published the magazine in Edinburgh and London. The issue shows a leading Victorian monthly mixing history, poetry, and criticism.
29605-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Number 351 of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume fifty-seven, dated January 1845 and printed by William Blackwood and Sons of Edinburgh and London, offers a full month of Victorian letters. Its contents open with Homer, Dante, and Michael Angelo, then Settled at Last, or Red River Recollections, Borodino in ode form, and a ramble in Montenegro.

Later pages treat the aesthetics of dress through a case of hats, the Three Guardsmen, memoirs of a statesman, Janus from Ovid's Fasti, and Coleridge and opium-eating. The mix shows Blackwood's range: poetry, travel, criticism, and serial fiction. Readers of period magazines will find a rich, varied issue from the magazine's mid-century prime.
32589-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
This March 1845 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine gathers eight pieces for a wide-reading public. It opens with a sequel to the Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, musing on dreams, grandeur, and the rush of modern life.

Other items weigh a book on farming, print verse, and review Lord Malmesbury's diaries. They sample German-American tales, trace British history in the eighteenth century, and judge Dryden and Pope as critics. Together they show a monthly review mixing verse, politics, and practical lore for its readers. The number also notes the press, steam, and new forces reshaping British life in 1845.
33097-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for April 1845, number 354 of volume fifty-seven, offers a full number of Victorian periodical writing. Its contents open with Virgil, Tasso, and Raphael, then Ping-Kee's View of the Stage, The Midnight Watch, and Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation. They go on to part sixteen of Marston, or the Memoirs of a Statesman, Betham's Etruria Celtica, and Suspiria de Profundis. The last is a sequel to the Confessions of an English Opium-Eater.

North's Specimens of the British Critics, on Dryden, closes the number, published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London. The issue shows Blackwood's at its most varied: poetry and art, fiction, science, memoir, and criticism in one monthly parcel. For students of Victorian letters, it is a rich single number, with De Quincey's sequel as its most famous piece.
33141-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for May 1845, number 355 of volume fifty-seven, offers a full number of Victorian periodical writing. Its contents run from Sismondi and My First Spec in the Biggleswades through German-American romances and The Rector's Daughter. They go on to A Glance at the Peninsula, Aesthetics of Dress number three, North's Specimens of the British Critics number four on Dryden on Chaucer, and Maynooth. The opening essay on Sismondi reflects on genius and imitation.

Published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London, the number shows Blackwood's range: history, fiction, criticism, and current controversy in one monthly parcel. For students of Victorian letters, it is a rich single issue. The Maynooth piece touches a live political debate and the criticism pieces show how the magazine taught its readers to read. It preserves the voice of a confident Tory review at mid-century.
7600-select-speeches-of-daniel-webster-1:
Daniel Webster's speeches, from 1817 to 1845, are gathered here in a school edition with preface, introduction, and notes by A. J. George, instructor in rhetoric and English literature at Newton High School. The volume, published by Heath in 1903, is dedicated to George F. Hoar, described as a worthy successor of Webster in the Senate. A Shakespeare epigraph praises a form where every god did seem to set his seal.

George's notes aim at more than rhetorical comparison. One who studies such authors merely to formulate a historical estimate, or to compare externals of form, has lost the true perspective of literary judgment, the preface warns. The speeches themselves, on union, law, and the Constitution, are the main matter. The edition remains a clear doorway into Webster the orator.
alchemiae-gebri-arabis-philosophi-solert:
Alchemiae Gebri, printed at Bern in 1545, is a Latin collection of the alchemical books of Geber, the Latin name of Jabir ibn Hayyan. The printer was Mathias Apiarius, publishing at the expense of the Nuremberg printer Johann Petreius, in August of that year. Around Geber's books the volume gathers other authorities, as its title page announces.

With Geber stand Roger Bacon's Speculum Alchemiae, the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, Hortulanus's commentary on that tablet, and writings of Khalid ibn Yazid. Woodcut illustrations include furnaces from the section on building them. The collection shows how Renaissance readers received Arabic alchemy: as a library of ancient masters bound in one Latin volume.
arxiv-2509-00045:
Xiang Li and five co-authors argue in 2025 that algorithm scores must count carbon cost, not just accuracy. Training deep models burns large amounts of power and emits much carbon. Past reviews rank methods by performance alone, which hides that cost and skews design toward waste.

The team builds a two-part gauge of sustainability. One score blends total energy use with performance through a harmonic mean, which punishes a weak side, to show output per unit of energy. A second score traces the full curve of performance against power across a run. Tests span many multimodal tasks to show the gauges travel well. Shared green gauges could steer labs toward models that do more with less power.
arxiv-2509-00145:
Ilja Dorsner, Svjetlana Fajfer, and Shaikh Saad explore neutron-antineutron oscillation in unified particle models in 2025. In this rare process, a neutron turns into its antimatter twin, which breaks baryon number, a conserved count in the standard model, by two units. Finding it would prove new physics and point to specific unified theories.

Next-generation experiments will sharply raise sensitivity to the effect. The team works in a unified frame that fits charged fermion masses and yields viable neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism, which explains why neutrinos are so light. Two routes to the oscillation arise in two SU(5) scenarios, each with set scalar particles. Observable rates are shown to be within reach of the planned searches.
arxiv-2509-00645:
Marco A Jimenez-Valencia leads five authors in total, with Parth Kumar, Yiheng Xu, Ferdinand Evers, and Charles A Stafford, on entropy flow at the quantum limit. Heat management matters from global energy use down to chips and quantum devices, and heat flow is traditionally found by subtracting a convective part from total energy flow.

Jimenez-Valencia and his co-authors show that in the quantum limit this classic formula implies a paradox: entropy carried by heat would be unbounded even as entropy itself tends to zero. They find the formula misses a quantum term. The corrected formula predicts far less heat produced in quantum processes than believed, with welcome consequences for the efficiency of quantum machines.
arxiv-2509-00745:
Kuniko Paxton leads five authors in total, with Koorosh Aslansefat, Dhavalkumar Thakker, Yiannis Papadopoulos, and Tanaya Maslekar, on fairness in skin lesion classification. Deep learning aids medical diagnosis, but models can be biased by skin color, and verifying fairness is hard because skin tones are tough to classify and checks are costly.

Paxton and her co-authors calculate the skewness, the asymmetry, of feature maps in a VGG network and of patches and attention heads in a Vision Transformer. Guided by those measures, their prune learning method cuts channels tied to skin tone and focuses on the lesion area. The approach lowers compute cost and model size while mitigating bias without conventional statistical methods.
arxiv-2509-00845:
Nataliya Arefyeva and Evgeny Polyakov propose a tape recorder model for quantum histories. Such histories describe coarse-grained pasts of a quantum system. The authors seek a clear recipe to build them. The recipe must work in a controlled way. It must also handle systems with memory and integrable cases.

They study a sudden local change inside an integrable bath. The bath does not interact within itself. Some modes in the bath store records of the system's past. Those records are stored for good as time goes on. The modes emerge one by one, much like a tape advancing. They define the projectors needed for the histories. Numerics show off-diagonal terms shrink fast in the key functional.
arxiv-2509-00945:
Christopher M Drupieski and Jonathan R Kujawa study Lie superalgebras generated by reflections. The groups are finite Weyl groups of classical type. Types A, B, C, and D are all covered. They view these groups as supergroups. In that view, reflections carry odd superdegree.

The complex group algebras become Lie superalgebras via the graded commutator bracket. The team determines the structure of the sub-superalgebras generated by reflections. In each case, the result has a clean form. It equals the full derived subalgebra of the group algebra. The span of the class sums of the reflections is added. The description is uniform across the classical families.
arxiv-2509-01145:
Soft robots can help patients with weak or damaged arm movement, but many designs respond slowly, move little, or push too weakly. Haiyun Zhang, with five co-authors, presents two air-driven soft actuators shaped by nature. One, for the elbow, copies a lobster form; the other, for the shoulder, copies a scallop shell.

The elbow device showed faster response, stronger force, and a straighter link between pressure and bend. The shoulder device also gave strong force and was simpler to make. Zhang and the team built math models linking pressure, bend angle, and output, then tested whether the pair could work in an upper-limb exoskeleton. The study supports soft aids that are both strong and wearable.
arxiv-2509-01245:
Linux schedulers decide which programs run when, but kernel rules cannot grasp what each application truly needs. Yusheng Zheng, Yanpeng Hu, Wei Zhang, and Andi Quinn present SchedCP, a framework that lets language model agents tune schedulers on their own, safely. The key move is a split control plane: the agent reasons about what to optimize, while the system controls how to observe and act.

Built as a protocol server, SchedCP offers a workload analysis engine, a growing store of scheduler policies, and a verifier that checks all agent-made code before it runs. A multi-agent system built on it shows the design at work. Zheng and the team argue this split, not a stronger model alone, makes autonomous scheduler tuning practical.
arxiv-2509-01545:
A binary star called ALS 8814 was recently proposed as a Be star paired with a black hole. The claim rested on the Be star's large swinging speeds. No light from any companion had been seen. Kareem El-Badry, with four co-authors, reanalyzes spectra of the system from the LAMOST survey. Their closer look finds the behavior far more complex than first reported.

Trailed spectra reveal a second set of absorption lines. Those lines move in anti-phase with the Be star, the mark of a real companion in orbit. Emission and absorption lines also vary in clashing ways. They seem to trace different stars. By untangling the combined light, the team recovers the spectrum of a fast-spinning companion. Its broad, shallow lines had gone unseen. Tests show line variability alone is unlikely to explain all the signs, though the system's traits remain uncertain.
arxiv-2509-01945:
Shafik Nassar and Ronak Ramachandran define a quantum version of witness indistinguishability for interactive proofs. In such proofs, a prover convinces a verifier without leaking which valid witness was used. The statistical form hides that choice even against strong verifiers, up to chance. Their quantum class, called QSWI, allows quantum transcripts and verifiers.

Using quantum techniques from prior work, they turn any honest verifier quantum proof of this type into a short public coin proof against cheating verifiers. No classical analogue of that upgrade is known. As a fallout, the classical class sits inside the quantum one. They also show quantum batch proofs, which pack many claims, yield such proofs with small hiding error.
arxiv-2509-02045:
Luca Locher, Mats J Stensrud, and Aaron L Sarvet study interpretational errors in instrumental variable studies across top journals. Instrumental variables estimate causal effects when direct experiments fail, under stated assumptions. They typically identify a local average effect for a narrow subgroup, not the original target effect. Many authors pragmatically swap targets, then misread results as if the original question were answered.

A systematic review covers hundreds of unique studies in economics, politics, epidemiology, and clinical medicine. Most targeted the local effect, yet few showed specific interest in that parameter. A majority of those studies made claims implying a different parameter was estimated. Since values can differ or even flip sign, conclusions often rest on shaky ground. The authors urge sharper reporting of target parameters.
arxiv-2509-02245:
C S Benson leads twenty-eight co-authors in tests of on chip filter bank spectrometers for SPT-SLIM at the South Pole Telescope. Line strength maps chart faint lines in the sky to trace how the cosmos is built. On chip spectrometers give small tools for that wave band work. SPT-SLIM is a test run placed through one south summer on site.

Band pass reads on site use a Fourier tool to scan each channel in the bank. Flaws in that tool can warp width reads for the slim passes of the bank. A new trick reads those slim passes past the base width of the scan tool. The tests ground the skill claims for the pathfinder run on site. Next line map tools will draw on the gains won here.
arxiv-2509-02745:
Marcela Best and four co-authors wrote a 2025 planetary science paper on how an outer giant planet, a cold Jupiter, shapes the growth of close-in planets. Surveys show systems with outer giants often break the neat, evenly spaced pattern seen elsewhere.

The team simulates planetesimals, kilometre-sized building blocks, colliding and moving under the giant's gravity inside a dissipating gas disk. An initially spread disk quickly grows larger bodies, then a sweeping secular resonance, a slow orbital alignment effect, drags material inward over millions of years. The outcome is compact rings holding several Earth masses of material, in Moon-sized objects near the star. Giant planets thus redistribute the raw material of inner planets early, which may explain the architectural differences surveys observe.
arxiv-2509-03345:
Yunxin Sun and Abulhair Saparov tested whether large language models follow Occam's razor in a 2025 study. The razor prefers the simplest hypothesis that fits the facts. Most tests of model reasoning ignore that preference, even though inductive and abductive reasoning, generalizing and explaining, usually admit many valid hypotheses at once.

Their framework generates reasoning questions synthetically, in a form expressible in first-order logic and extendable to many more cases. An agent must propose hypotheses explaining observations under a stated world model. A new automated metric scores whether hypotheses are both correct and simple. Top current models handled simple scenarios reasonably. They struggled as world models grew complex, and producing high-quality hypotheses stayed hard even with prompting tricks and reinforcement-tuned reasoning.
arxiv-2509-03645:
J. Piekarewicz's 2025 physics paper estimates the weak radius of argon-40, a measure of how its weakly interacting charge is spread out. Neutron and weak-charge radii are hard to predict reliably, a problem highlighted by the unresolved CREX-PREX dilemma in nuclear experiments. Those radii also feed into searches for new physics through coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, where a neutrino bounces off a whole nucleus.

Piekarewicz anchors the estimate on CREX, an experiment measuring calcium, and on a strong correlation between calcium and argon radii. The result is a robust baseline value for argon-40's weak radius, with separate statistical and systematic uncertainties stated. Argon matters because liquid-argon detectors anchor many current and planned neutrino campaigns. The weak radius also controls how coherence fades at small momentum transfers, shaping what those detectors should see.
arxiv-2509-03845:
Yang Chen and six co-authors turn to inferring reward functions for many interacting agents with different goals in a 2025 research paper. Inverse reinforcement learning works backward from expert behaviour to the rewards that would explain it. In mean field games, which model huge populations at once, existing inverse methods assume all agents share one objective, an assumption real demonstrations often break.

Their approach builds a deep latent variable model of the mean field game, with probabilistic context variables for each agent's hidden situation. The inverse method can then recover rewards from demonstrations drawn from tasks that differ yet share structure. No prior knowledge of the contexts is needed, and the game model stays unchanged. Experiments cover simulated scenarios plus a real-world pricing problem for spatial taxi rides. Across them, the method beats leading inverse methods for mean field games, handling heterogeneous, unknown objectives that defeat older tools.
arxiv-2509-03945:
Guglielmo Gattiglio and two co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to Prob-GParareal, a solver that adds uncertainty estimates to parallel-in-time solving. Solving an evolution equation step by step is serial by nature, wasting modern parallel hardware. Parareal methods split the time axis across processors and fix the seams in rounds, and GParareal uses Gaussian processes to model those fixes.

Prob-GParareal extends the idea so uncertainty travels with the answer. Gaussian processes model the fix, letting numerical uncertainty move across time segments and yielding forecasts with probabilities attached, not just one path. Uncertain starting conditions are supported too. The method still works with classical solvers, so it fits existing Parareal setups. A theory analysis derives error bounds and cost. Five benchmark systems test accuracy and robustness, covering chaotic, stiff, and bifurcation problems. A nearest-neighbour variant trades some statistical machinery for speed, shown on a PDE example.
arxiv-2509-04045:
Fengjun Zhuo and four co-authors review a young field called moiré spintronics in a 2025 paper. Spintronics builds devices around electron spin, a property tied to magnetism, rather than charge alone. Twisting two atom-thin sheets by a small angle creates moiré patterns, repeating overlaps that can change how the material behaves. Magnetic sheets only two atoms thick receive special attention here.

Chapters cover magnetism that depends on how layers stack, swirling spin patterns, and tiny magnetic whirlpools named skyrmions. Waves of magnetism called magnons get their own treatment. The authors also show how machine learning, software that learns patterns from data, can speed the search for useful new materials.
arxiv-2509-04145:
Dongliang Cao and three co-authors generate moving digital humans by dreaming up the weights of a neural network in a 2025 research paper. Photorealistic avatars usually need training on one person at a time, which blocks variety. Cartoon-like generators cover many faces but move stiffly and miss details like cloth wrinkles that shift with pose. The team's plan joins both strengths in two stages.

First, one small network is fitted per person, capturing how that body deforms while moving. Next, a diffusion model learns the pattern of those fitted networks' weights. At run time it produces fresh weights for a new person, ready for real-time rendering. Tests on a large multi-person video set beat earlier methods.
arxiv-2509-04945:
A collapsing star might bounce instead of ending in a singularity, under loop quantum gravity inspired models. Francesco Fazzini examines the fate of that bounce in a solo 2025 physics paper. In the model studied, the bounce is generally followed by shell-crossing singularities, which threaten the physical sense of the evolution.

Fazzini derives the dynamics of a thin dust shell inside the effective Hamiltonian framework. The shell's motion stays timelike throughout. After the quantum-gravitational bounce it expands again. In time it emerges from the white-hole vacuum region. The build thus extends spacetime past the shell-crossing singularity in a physically meaningful way.
arxiv-2509-05345:
Planning multi-axis printing as one continuous field problem is proposed by Jiasheng Qu and seven co-authors in a 2025 manufacturing paper. Ordinary planning splits toolpath layout and collision avoidance into separate steps, which slows work on complex shapes.

Their framework stores the part as a signed distance field, a map giving distance to the surface everywhere. Goals such as printing without supports, good surface finish, and steady material flow are built into one guidance field. Shell and filling paths come from that field, and print order plus machine motion are optimised together over a field of orientations. Against older explicit methods they report far faster runs and smaller path errors, confirmed on a robot printing system.
arxiv-2509-05745:
Maps between spaces that act like retractions cannot raise several size measures, Nursultan Kuanyshov proves in a solo 2025 topology paper. A retraction, in the sense used here, links continuous maps. It generalises the idea of projecting a space onto part of itself without stretching.

The measures include (co)homological dimensions, which gauge algebraic size. They also include the Lusternik-Schnirelmann category, a count of how many simple pieces cover a space. Motion planning difficulty, and its sequential form, are covered too. Under such a map, Kuanyshov proves matching inequalities between the measures. The results also apply to newer measures from recent work.
arxiv-2509-05845:
Counting the proper colorings of circular chord graphs is the task of a 2025 paper by Rogelio N. Lopez-Bonilla and three co-authors. These graphs start from a ring of points and add chords of fixed offset, plus diameters when the ring is even. The count of three-colorings turns out to follow striking patterns.

Using transfer matrices, tables that carry counts step by step around the ring, the authors derive exact formulas for the chord length three case. Along odd rings the counts grow at the golden ratio rate, tied to the Lucas number sequence, with extra periodic terms. Even rings need a paired-window matrix that respects the diameters. The counts show strong modular patterns, and the methods double as feasibility checks for cyclic scheduling problems such as airline gate assignment.
arxiv-2509-06045:
Extrapolating a treatment's effect from a trial to a wider population is risky when hidden factors distort observational data, and Stephanie Riley and two co-authors improve the correction in a 2025 paper. Trials are trustworthy but small and selective; records are large but confounded. Existing fixes use one trial to debias effect estimates from records through a deconfounding function.

The extension borrows strength across trials of several related treatments at once. Simulations show a single trial estimates effects poorly outside its own support, especially when the deconfounding function is nonlinear and the trial is small. Adding a second treatment's trial markedly improves accuracy beyond both trials' ranges. The work offers a practical route to fairer effect estimates for patients unlike those enrolled.
arxiv-2509-06245:
Google's newest congestion control algorithm behaves differently on managed home Wi-Fi, and Shyam Kumar Shrestha and two co-authors measure it in a 2025 paper. Their modular testbed pairs a commercial router with a live dashboard for throughput, latency, and fairness. BBRv3, which paces traffic by bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip time, faces the loss-based CUBIC under three queue management schemes.

BBRv3 improves fairness and convergence notably under active queue management, especially FQ-CoDel. The testbed and visualization tool are offered as a practical base for judging next-generation transport variants on real wireless links rather than simulations alone.
arxiv-2509-06445:
A public contest to hear the universe's faintest steady hum is reported in a 2025 paper led by Rodrigo Tenorio with thirty-one co-authors. Continuous gravitational waves from spinning neutron stars remain undetected, and the Kaggle-hosted challenge asked over a thousand participants to find simulated signals hidden in real LIGO data under realistic search conditions.

The top ten approaches are described and judged as preprocessing for standard searches. On the challenge data they cut computing cost by one to three orders of magnitude at equal false-dismissal rates, and several drove new GPU-accelerated pipelines now used elsewhere. The dataset is released as the first open standardized benchmark for continuous-wave detection.
arxiv-2509-06545:
Measuring the size of rough, thin shapes in a stretched geometry is the subject of a solo 2025 mathematics paper by Filip Fryš. Minkowski content gauges how much room a set takes up when thickened slightly, while a companion measure uses a different averaging idea. Direction-dependent, or anisotropic, versions matter when stretching is not equal in all directions.

Fryš proves that the anisotropic measures relate to each other much as their ordinary versions do, through matching inequalities. A key step shows that the associated volume function is of Kneser type, a regularity property that supports many of the proofs. He also defines anisotropic versions of two fractal dimensions and links them by inequalities. As a test case, he studies whether the famous Sierpinski gasket, a triangular fractal, has well-defined contents at its natural dimension.
arxiv-2509-07145:
Florian Lengyel, writing alone in 2025, studies a game in which players claim shares of a limited resource. Each player has an entitlement, and a claim above it counts as defection, while a claim below it leaves slack. At the end, a clearing rule hands the leftover surplus to defectors in proportion to how far each one went over.

Lengyel shows that the selfish outcome still gives every player exactly the cooperative payoff. With bounded choices, defecting is a weakly dominant strategy, meaning it never hurts a player. Within a family of power rules, only the simple linear rule stays smooth at the boundary. The outcome also holds up against group deals when money can be shared. A use case for carbon rationing with a penalty cap closes the argument.
arxiv-2509-07445:
Harrison Field and 5 co-authors present Text2Touch in 2025, a system that teaches a robot hand to rotate objects by touch, using rewards written by a language model. Reward design, specifying what counts as success, is a bottleneck in robot learning. Tactile sensing, touch feedback from the fingers, is vital for human-like dexterity but had not been paired with language-model rewards before.

The prompting strategy handles over 70 environment variables, and a sim-to-real distillation step transfers the learned skill to a real four-fingered hand with vision-based touch sensors. The hand rotates objects around several axes in both palm-up and palm-down poses. Text2Touch beats a carefully tuned human-engineered baseline in rotation speed and stability, with reward functions an order of magnitude shorter. The authors argue such methods shorten the path from idea to working dexterous skills.
arxiv-2509-07745:
Giovanni Barontini, writing alone in 2025, reports a cold-atom experiment that tests the problem of time. In the Wheeler-DeWitt picture of quantum gravity, the universe's equation has no external time variable. Time must be read from inside the system, in a relational way. The experiment asks whether an internal clock built from entropy can order events in part of an isolated system.

A Bose-Einstein condensate is the system used. It is a cloud of atoms in a single quantum state. It evolves in a trap split by a thin optical barrier into observed and unobserved sectors. Dissipation is negligible on the test timescale. An entropic time is built from a coarse-grained entropy measured in the lab. It robustly orders events in the observed sector, across repeated cycles of expansion and recollapse. An effective Schrödinger equation set by that internal time reproduces the measured evolution.
arxiv-2509-07945:
One world model that plans across many different tasks is the aim of Yuan Pu and 5 co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Tasks differ in what the agent sees, what it can do, and how hard they are. Existing multi-task world models such as UniZero shine on single tasks but lose efficiency when the suite grows broad.

Two problems stand out: gradients from different tasks conflict during training, and the model gradually loses plasticity, its ability to keep learning. The authors examine architectural choices within each learning step and changes across the whole learning process. Efficient shared world models would let one planning agent serve games, control problems, and simulations without training a separate brain for each.
arxiv-2509-08045:
Star-forming galaxies in the epoch of reionization are measured for size and merging activity by H. M. O. Stephenson and 20 co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. Data come from the JWST Emission Line Survey, which catches hydrogen emission from twenty-three galaxies at redshift 6.1 in the COSMOS field. That emission traces fresh star formation rather than older stars.

Sizes in the emission line are compared with sizes in light from established stellar populations and near-ultraviolet light. The size-mass relation matches the slope seen at later times but sits at smaller sizes. Merger fractions add evidence about how early galaxies grew, whether smoothly or by crashing together, while the young universe was being reionised by their light.
arxiv-2509-08145:
Peer effects estimated from incomplete social networks are the concern of Vincent Boucher and Aristide Houndetoungan in a 2025 econometrics paper. Researchers rarely see a whole friendship network: samples, censoring, and misclassified links all corrupt the map. The question is whether influence estimates survive that damage.

Assuming researchers can estimate the network's distribution consistently turns out to be enough for a linear-in-means model of peer influence. An application to the Add Health data on students shows network errors bias achievement peer effects strongly downward. The message for empirical work is blunt: sloppy network measurement does not merely add noise, it systematically shrinks the influence researchers report, which can mislead school policy built on those numbers.
arxiv-2509-08445:
Róbert Németh and 2 co-authors compute the resistance of an endless grid with one flawed line in a 2025 paper. Along the flawed line, each resistor changes in a repeating pattern. The flaw may stand for a crack or a seam in a conducting sheet. The grid has no end, so node-by-node maths fails at the start.

A matrix identity does the heavy lifting. It is applied to the grid's Green function in wave space. The answer shrinks to a single integral over one variable. In special cases that integral can be done exactly. The work uses the square grid, but the frame fits other grids and mixed parts. Designers of large resistor networks gain a formula where brute-force grids would grow forever.
arxiv-2509-08545:
A protein's job depends on its folded shape, and peptides, its smaller cousins, let scientists study folding in isolation. Åke Andersson and Vitali Zhaunerchyk review infrared spectroscopy of gas-phase peptides in a 2025 book chapter. A molecule's structure is written into its vibrational spectrum in the infrared range. Water hides that spectrum inside living tissue, so peptides are studied alone in the gas phase instead.

The chapter gathers recent studies that pair infrared measurements with quantum chemical calculations. Together, the two pin down molecular structures that neither could fix alone. The collected spectra also let researchers grade different quantum chemical models against experiment. Models that pass on peptides can then be trusted on larger proteins. The review serves spectroscopists entering the field and modelers who need hard experimental tests for their calculations.
arxiv-2509-08645:
Nina Beranek and 2 co-authors study time and space discretization for nonlinear parabolic equations in a 2025 paper. Such equations model heat and diffusion processes that change over time. Good numerical methods should be nearly optimal in accuracy for the work used.

By adding an extra variable, the authors rewrite the problem as a system with a well behaved inverse. Galerkin methods, which build solutions from chosen basis pieces, can then be solved with an inexact Uzawa algorithm. A condition on test and trial spaces guarantees quality. A later check can also confirm quality when the test space is large enough.
arxiv-2509-08845:
Scalar waves around magnetically charged black holes in a quintessence field are studied by Ali Hasnain in a 2025 paper. Quasinormal modes are the fading ringing tones of a black hole after disturbance. Quintessence is a field proposed to drive cosmic acceleration.

The background comes from an Einstein-Power-Maxwell action with a Kiselev type quintessence term. The wave equation is solved by high order WKB, an iteration method, and time domain integration, cross checked for accuracy. Magnetic charge generally lowers the main oscillation frequency, while quintessence changes damping times. A check confirms the correct form of the magnetic term. Data and code are shared for reuse.
arxiv-2509-08945:
Leo Hahn and 2 co-authors resolve clustering and steady states of jamming run-and-tumble particles in a 2025 paper. Run-and-tumble particles move actively and can jam when they meet. The three particle steady state is solved exactly, a first beyond two bodies.

A Markov process description plus symmetry gives the invariant measure, the long run distribution. Persistent, separated, and diffusive regimes are ruled by an activity parameter. A cascade of scales shows the separated phase dominates at finite activity. For larger systems, cluster number becomes sharply set by activity. Activity acts like a fugacity, a weight for cluster count, giving a grand canonical like structure.
arxiv-2509-09045:
Shrabani Ghosh and 1 co-author test how the choice of community finder shapes graph mining results in a 2025 paper. Large graphs show links in complex systems, and communities are tight clusters in them. Traits drawn from communities can boost tasks like link prediction and node class calls.

True communities are rarely known, and no one finder wins on all tasks. A frame lets many finders plug in so their downstream effects can be compared in a fair way. Some finders clearly suit some tasks more than others. Choice thus moves results a lot, yet users often pick with no such test. The pair urge a deliberate match of finder to task.
arxiv-2509-09145:
A battery pack's core temperature decides its safety, but the sensors and computers inside a vehicle are small and weak. Soumyoraj Mallick and 3 co-authors present KAN-Therm in a 2025 research paper. KAN-Therm estimates the core temperature of a cylindrical lithium-ion cell. It uses a Kolmogorov-Arnold network, whose learnable activation functions capture complexity with lean models.

Physics-based thermal models are too slow for the limited hardware in a battery management system. Ordinary neural networks are fast but memory-hungry. The authors compared memory use and estimation time against leading neural and tree-based models. KAN-Therm aims at the middle: accurate estimation that fits physical hardware limits. Safer electric vehicles depend on exactly this kind of unglamorous estimation. It must run in real time, thousands of times per trip, without a data center's help.
arxiv-2509-09245:
Shuocheng Li and 9 co-authors present Jupiter, a framework to enhance language model data analysis, in a 2025 paper. Models still find multi-step reasoning and tool use hard on complex analysis tasks. Real Jupyter notebooks offer authentic examples of tool based workflows.

A pipeline extracts high quality tasks and executable multi-step solutions from notebooks and data files, forming the NbQA dataset. Jupiter then treats analysis as search, using Monte Carlo Tree Search to generate diverse solution paths for value model learning. At inference, the value model guides efficient plan collection. Fine-tuned models match or surpass GPT-4o on a data analysis benchmark and generalize across tasks.
arxiv-2509-09345:
An attosecond flash can set a molecule's electrons dancing together. The dance falls apart within a femtosecond, too fast to matter. Lina Fransén, Sandra Gomez, and Morgane Vacher test that assumption in a 2025 research paper. Their subject is ethylene, a small organic molecule used as a test case. Full quantum simulations follow electrons and nuclei together after ionization and coherent excitation.

Those coherences indeed died with half-lives under one femtosecond. Yet they left vibrational coherences on the nuclei along set coupling paths. Those nuclear motions lasted fifty times longer than the flash itself. Short-lived order thus leaves a long legacy in molecular movement. The finding matters for reading attosecond experiments. It also backs attochemistry: steering chemistry by shaping those first moments before the nuclei respond.
arxiv-2509-09445:
Hussein Talib and 3 co-authors propose a new building block for photonic circuits that multiply matrices in 2025. Their programmable chip design rests on double racetrack resonators, ring-like optical parts joined in pairs. The authors first show on paper that a single block's transfer behaviour matches familiar parts such as directional couplers and Mach-Zehnder interferometers.

From those blocks they assemble a small three-by-three processor and check it with full-wave finite element simulations, then study larger versions through hybrid modelling. A low-pass filter built the same way shows the scheme also handles non-unitary tasks. Close agreement between models supports using the blocks in reconfigurable, all-optical signal processing.
arxiv-2509-09645:
Pranav Khadpe and 3 co-authors study what an AI-assistance label does to the moral reading of a message in a 2025 paper. A kind note normally tells readers something about its sender's character. Two vignette studies with 399 people show the label does not simply make senders look worse. Instead it mutes the signal in both directions at once.

An unaided thank-you or apology made senders seem warmer, and unaided bragging or blame made them seem colder. Add an AI label and both judgements softened toward the middle. The authors call this a diagnosticity effect: a labelled message is treated as weaker evidence about who the sender really is, for better and for worse.
arxiv-2509-09845:
František Bartoš and 2 co-authors introduce a meta-analysis toolkit inside free statistics software in a 2025 methods paper, the first of a series. Meta-analysis pools results across many studies to sharpen conclusions, yet strong methods often hide behind programming skill that many scientists and students never gained. The JASP module answers with a point-and-click interface over both standard and advanced techniques.

Worked examples walk through classical approaches while companion videos show each step on screen. The design goals are rigour, relevance, and results another researcher can reproduce exactly. By lowering the entry barrier, the authors hope careful evidence synthesis spreads beyond specialist circles, a theme later parts of the series extend toward newer methods.
arxiv-2509-10045:
Jan Kalina's 2025 paper rethinks shrinkage estimation through a Bayesian lens. It also takes a detour into computing with coarse numbers. Shrinkage pulls noisy estimates toward a shared centre. That pull helps when many linked values are measured at once. Kalina first links Bayes methods with inference under rounded inputs. The link ties a school of stats to a habit from engineering.

Next, means from two samples justify a shrink toward the pooled mean. The same Bayesian case is made for discriminant analysis. Several shrinkage plans are defended on those grounds. Fresh methods to compute them are also given. Trials on real and simulated data back the plans. Users gain shrinkage with a clear basis, not a rule of thumb.
arxiv-2509-10145:
Leslie A. Young and 1 co-author build a faster way to predict how starlight bends through a planetary atmosphere during an occultation in a 2025 planetary science paper. When a distant star passes behind an atmosphere, the dip and shimmer of its light reveal the air's structure, and waves in that air leave signatures observers prize. Forward models must turn a guessed refractivity profile into the bending angles that shape the recorded light curve.

Writing the profile as an exponential dressed with a wavelet expansion makes those bending profiles writable in closed form. Demanding the atmosphere stay statically stable then caps how large the waves may grow and how strongly they can mark the curve. The technique gives analysts a principled playground for testing wavy atmospheres against crisp ground-based data.
arxiv-2509-10345:
Pointing at what words describe is the skill Georgios Pantazopoulos and Eda B. Özyiğit survey in this 2025 paper on visual grounding in vision-language models. Grounding means finding the region of an image or video that matches a phrase, a talent behind question answering, detailed captioning, and robot control.

The survey maps how modern grounded models are built, what parts they combine, and where they are used, along with the benchmarks and metrics that grade them. It also traces the links between grounding, step-by-step multimodal reasoning, and chain-of-thought methods. The authors close by sorting the open difficulties, from fine spatial precision to trustworthy evaluation, and naming the research directions they judge most promising.
arxiv-2509-10445:
Shuai Liu and six co-authors report a first in this 2025 photonics paper. They made squeezed light across a whole silicon wafer, evenly. Squeezed states quiet quantum noise below the ordinary limit. They power quantum-enhanced sensors and continuous-variable quantum computing. Single chips had done it before. Squeezed light is so fragile, though, that wafer-scale consistency stayed out of reach.

The wafer is four inches of CMOS-compatible silicon nitride. Eight dies on it each produced two-mode squeezed vacuum. The squeezing measured just under or over three decibels. It varied by less than two tenths of a decibel. Three device choices made that evenness possible. The resonators lose very little light. Pump-rejection filters clean the beam. Careful fiber couplers carry the light off chip. A first-principles model matched the measurements. The result points toward quantum light sources that factories can build.
arxiv-2509-10545:
Ruwanga Konara and 2 co-authors sketch a decentralized identity system on the Ripple blockchain in this 2025 paper. Digital identity today usually sits in central databases, with known security and privacy costs. Decentralized designs move control toward users, and one family of them issues attestations about a person's attributes rather than storing the attributes themselves.

That attestation-based, attribute-based variant has drawn little research, the authors note. Most published systems sit on chains such as Ethereum or Hyperledger, and none, they argue, has been built on Ripple, whose speed and low fees suit identity transactions well. Their paper lays out a conceptual framework for such a system on Ripple, meant to guide a later working build.
arxiv-2509-10745:
Carsten A. Ullrich surveys time-dependent density-functional theory in this solo-authored 2025 perspective. TDDFT extends a workhorse method of electronic structure into motion. It treats excited states and light-driven processes. It handles coupled electron-nuclear dynamics, in gentle and violent regimes alike. Applications run from physics and biochemistry to materials science.

As a snapshot rather than a research report, the paper takes stock. Ullrich reviews recent developments and successes. He turns to the formal and computational challenges that still limit the theory. He surveys the hot topics drawing current effort. The value is orientation. A practitioner choosing tools for a photoexcitation problem gains a map. A newcomer entering the field gains one, too. The map shows what TDDFT can now be trusted with. It shows where the theory strains, and where its builders are pushing next.
arxiv-2509-11145:
Yi Wang and 8 co-authors define a standard language for operating an AI agent's memory in this 2025 paper. Agents that talk over long stretches need memory, yet most frameworks expose only a few crude actions, such as store, fetch, and delete. Richer moves like merging, promoting, or expiring memories are missing or behave differently in every system, which makes behavior unpredictable.

Text2Mem specifies a compact set of memory operations in a formal, executable way. Each command is a structured record that a parser checks and turns into a typed object before anything runs. Adapters connect it to a simple database or to real memory frameworks. The authors also outline a planned benchmark and call the design a first standard base for agent memory.
arxiv-2509-11245:
Yuxuan Shi and Hongbo Cheng ask what a black hole would look like if it sat inside a halo of Hernquist dark matter, in this 2025 astrophysics paper. The picture a telescope sees depends heavily on how the surrounding gas glows and falls, so the authors compare three accretion setups side by side.

For a Schwarzschild black hole wrapped in the halo, they model a thin glowing disk, a still spherical flow, and a spherical flow raining inward. The dark matter halo noticeably enlarges the photon sphere, so the dark central shadow grows by a few percent up to nearly a third compared with empty space. Overall brightness drops, especially for the infalling gas, where Doppler effects dim the image further. The shadow's size and brightness profile could thus constrain how dark matter gathers at galactic centers.
arxiv-2509-11345:
Azher Ahmed Efat and 3 co-authors predict which animal host a virus came from, directly from its genetic text, in this 2025 paper. Viruses that jump from animals to humans have repeatedly upended public life. Naming the likely host early can help stop spread, but laboratory identification is slow.

Their model, BiLSTM-VHP, reads nucleotide sequences with a bidirectional long short-term memory network, a design suited to patterns in long strings. It was trained and tested on three curated data sets covering orthohantavirus, rabies lyssavirus, and rotavirus A, with tens of thousands of sequences across many host classes. Reported accuracy ran high for rotavirus and orthohantavirus and lower for rabies, beating prior studies on the same task. The data and code are public.
arxiv-2509-11745:
De Zhang Lee and three co-authors attack, then defend, a watermark for AI images. This 2025 computer security paper treats latent-based watermarking. The scheme seeds generation with noise from a secret distribution. Pseudorandom error-correcting codes pair with it. Watermarked images look ordinary and survive white noise.

Looking ordinary is not the same as resisting removal. Their attack exploits boundary information. The leak sits in where watermarked content rests. Distortion needed to strip the mark falls sharply, up to fifteen-fold in some settings. Their defense hides the boundary with a secret transformation. A proof shows any attacker's tampering then matches a naive noise adversary. Tests across several Stable Diffusion versions confirm both halves.
arxiv-2509-11945:
How pulsar beams change shape with observing frequency is the puzzle P. Jaroenjittichai and nine co-authors revisit in 2025, using wideband observations from the Murriyang telescope at Parkes. More than a hundred pulsars were recorded across a broad frequency span.

The team measured profile widths at several intensity levels, broke profiles into Gaussian parts, and estimated emission heights from aberration and retardation effects. Many profiles narrow as frequency rises, but a sizable share widen instead, and the component peaks barely move while their widths shrink. That pattern points to propagation effects, not a single emission height sliding downward, favoring fan-shaped or patchy beams spread over many altitudes. The classic one-height picture, the authors conclude, cannot cover the variety seen.
arxiv-2509-12345:
Determinants built from Toeplitz plus Hankel matrices encode deep problems in random systems and orthogonal polynomials, and their large-size behavior is extracted through a Riemann-Hilbert problem. Roozbeh Gharakhloo and one co-author continue that program in 2025, in a second installment removing a restriction that had blocked the most natural case.

Their earlier framework forced the winding numbers of the symbol functions into a special pattern, excluding zero winding. The new framework admits a broader range of winding configurations. As the demonstration case, with winding numbers zero and one, they work out how the norms of the matching orthogonal polynomial system grow.
arxiv-2509-12645:
Frontier language models look like better reasoners with each release. But the gains may be bought with hidden computation. Lachlan McGinness and one co-author track three leading models across eighteen months in 2025. The test uses true-or-false logic questions. They score accuracy. They also score faithfulness to reasoning strategies taught in context.

Much of the early improvement traces to hidden chain-of-thought prompting. The later jump traces to dedicated thinking models. Their alternative is neuro-symbolic. A modest model translates each problem into a standard form. A solver then decides it. The pair reaches near-perfect accuracy at a fraction of the computing cost. Tokens and operations are honestly counted.
arxiv-2509-13645:
Damping placed only far away from the origin is the subject of Ryo Ikehata's solo 2025 paper on the wave equation in the plane. Friction near spatial infinity should still drain the wave's energy, and he asks how fast that drainage is when the damping never acts near the center.

He obtains a fast decay estimate whose rate carries a logarithmic factor. The two-dimensional setting again blocks the usual Hardy-type inequalities, so the proof uses Poincaré-type inequalities in whole space together with the finite speed at which waves travel to build the estimate. Comparing whole space with exterior domains, he notes the whole-space problem genuinely needs its logarithmic correction, a sharp contrast between the two settings.
arxiv-2509-14045:
A large ATLAS collaboration team reports reliability testing of timing detector modules in a 2025 instrumentation paper. The High Granularity Timing Detector for the High-Luminosity LHC will stack thousands of hybrid pixel modules. Each module joins low-gain avalanche diode sensors to readout chips with tiny solder bumps. They will run cold for years under irradiation. Because the bump spacing is unusually wide, the solder joints are a thermomechanical weak point.

The team combined finite element simulation with thermal cycling tests. The tests ran between deep cold and warm extremes to find how the flip-chip connections fail. The failure analysis drove a redesign of the module. The optimized version shows markedly better robustness. It is projected to survive the detector's full working lifetime.
arxiv-2509-14145:
Giovanni Inchiostro, Roberto Svaldi and Junyan Zhao study families of surfaces in 2025. Each pair carries a boundary curve and maps onto a curve. Such pairs are called log Calabi-Yau fibrations when a key curvature total cancels.

The authors prove results on stable reduction, which cleans up degenerate families. They use them to describe the edge of the KSBA compactification. Their results cover three concrete cases, including divisors on a product of two lines, K3 surfaces mapping two to one onto a ruled surface, and elliptic surfaces. Main tools include stable quasimaps, the canonical bundle formula and the minimal model program.
arxiv-2509-14245:
Zhiliang Deng, Chen Li and Xiaomei Yang tackle a heat puzzle in 2025: finding point heat sources inside a body using only heat flow measured at its edge. Guessing the sources is hard because they form a sharp, highly structured pattern that standard Bayesian methods, which weigh evidence with prior beliefs, handle poorly.

Their combined method first draws candidate sources with a level set approach, which marks regions on a grid, then thins those candidates with a filter borrowed from random point models. One part proposes sources and the other keeps only the plausible ones. Tests with simulated data showed the method could recover the true source positions and weights with good accuracy, giving a cleaner route to a hard inverse problem.
arxiv-2509-14445:
Zhe Xian Koong and sixteen co-authors achieve coherent control in 2025 of a quantum dot spin using cyclic optical transitions. Solid state spins can link stationary qubits to single photons for quantum communication. Quantum dots offer good optical coherence and long lived spins, but control and readout clash.

Most solid state emitters cannot be controlled optically and read out in a single shot at the same time. The team exploits light hole mixing to build a highly asymmetric three level system in a charged exciton. They cancel large Stark shifts from uneven control fields and cool the nuclear spin bath. An electron spin qubit then comes under quantum control with a route toward single shot readout, a step for dot based quantum networks.
arxiv-2509-14545:
Shuyao Xu and five co-authors build a framework in 2025 to control language difficulty in dialogues for second language learners. Chat practice with language models helps speaking skills, but replies at the wrong level either bore or overwhelm a learner. Difficulty must be dialled precisely.

Three feature families quantify complexity: readability scores, syntactic measures such as tree depth, and lexical measures such as simple word share. Training models on dialogue data annotated with those features enables fine modulation of output difficulty. Learner level can then guide generation turn by turn. Precise difficulty control turns a generic chatbot into a practice partner that stretches a learner without flooding them, a key need in language education technology.
arxiv-2509-14645:
Hiroaki Hanyu and three co-authors show in 2025 that final prices in parimutuel betting markets do not tell the whole information story. In such markets all stakes pool and winners share the pool, so odds move until betting closes. Analysts often read beliefs from final odds alone.

Using interim odds from horse racing, the authors find returns depend on the odds path, not only the endpoint. Horses whose odds fell in the last minutes earned higher realised returns than horses with similar final odds. A two period information model explains the pattern: informed bettors wager late on private signals. Final price sufficiency fails when timing itself carries information, a caution for market based belief measurement.
arxiv-2509-14745:
Miku Watanabe and five co-authors study agentic coding pull requests on GitHub in 2025, asking whether agent submitted code changes actually land in real projects. Autonomous coding tools now open pull requests with minimal human help. Acceptance in the wild was largely unknown.

Several hundred pull requests generated with Claude Code across more than one hundred fifty open source projects were analysed. Developers leaned on agents for refactoring, documentation and similar bounded tasks, the study finds. Acceptance patterns and review discussion reveal where agent work fits maintainer expectations. Evidence from merged and rejected requests gives tool builders a grounded view of agent usefulness, beyond benchmark scores on isolated coding puzzles.
arxiv-2509-15145:
Lorne Applebaum and four co-authors learn from group-level label shares with a low-noise fix in a 2025 paper. At times only group labels are known: the share of good cases in each bag of items, not each item's own label. Ads online drive the problem, since logs and privacy rules give group outcomes.

Their fix corrects share-based estimates while keeping noise low. It fits many loss types in both two-class and multi-class tasks. Paired with standard learning tools, it sharpens the sample bounds for a broad class of losses used in practice. Tests on many data sets show clear gains over standard baselines. Learning from shares matters where item labels are private, costly, or never logged.
arxiv-2509-15345:
J. Untzaga and seven co-authors present a catalog of hypercompact stellar systems and three new Milky Way satellites in a 2025 astronomy paper. Searching for compact stellar overdensities in survey data from the Pan-STARRS telescope, the team followed up candidates with deep imaging from a large Canary Islands telescope and with Gaia astrometry.

Three systems, named Yasone-1, Yasone-2, and Yasone-3, sit at unusually low Galactic latitudes where the Milky Way's own glare hides satellites. Their structure and colors fit old, metal-poor populations, with ages around twelve billion years and iron abundances well below the Sun's. Seventeen further hypercompact candidates await confirmation in the catalog. Each new satellite is a fossil of early galaxy assembly orbiting inside our own galaxy's disk region.
arxiv-2509-15945:
Nicola Fabiano, writing alone, argues that quantum state space can replace fuzzy metrics for modeling uncertainty. Fuzzy metrics grade how near two items are with degrees and special rules. They are used in learning, choice systems, and AI. Fabiano says they bolt doubt onto crisp items from outside. In quantum and mind like domains, doubt is built in, not bolted on.

His swap uses the Hilbert space of quantum mechanics, a century old frame. States are the points, and the norm gives distance tied to how well states can be told apart. He models AI concepts as bell shaped wave packets and sorts vague inputs by overlap. The frame handles clashes and shapes that fuzzy rules miss.
arxiv-2509-16045:
Sending one message safely to many users at once is hard when an eavesdropper may listen in. Shan Shan and three co-authors study this task for pinching-antenna systems, where antennas slide along waveguides to aim signals. They design both the sent signal and the antenna spots to raise the rate of secret delivery.

Cases with one user group and with many groups are solved with step-by-step methods of differing cost. In all tested setups, the sliding antennas beat fixed antennas on secrecy. The edge grows with larger service areas, more antennas, and more users and eavesdroppers. Placement, not just power, drives safety here.
arxiv-2509-16545:
Takao Suyama derives a set of equations for loop quantities in a 2025 theory paper. The loops, named for Wilson, are tracked inside a model known as ABJM theory. Their expected values change with a coupling strength. Suyama links those changes to equations tied to a special curve.

The curve comes from the matrix model that underlies the theory. Near set points, local solutions of the equations match known weak and strong coupling behavior. A step-by-step rule also emerges. That rule can give loop values for any chosen representation. The work gives a cleaner path through calculations that were once done case by case.
arxiv-2509-16645:
Yichen Wang and co-authors probe attacks on embodied AI agents in a 2025 paper. Such agents use vision and language to drive cars or move robot arms. Small, crafted changes to an image can fool the vision side. Past attacks tended to be blunt. The team aim for fine control over what the agent thinks it sees.

Their attack frame comes in two forms. One erases a chosen object from the scene as the agent reads it. The other plants a new object that is not there. Tests show strong attack success with that fine control. The results expose risks that builders of driving and robot systems must guard against.
arxiv-2509-16745:
Ritabrata Chakraborty, Avijit Dasgupta, and Sandeep Chaurasia test whether AI explanations point at the right spots in a 2025 paper. Heat maps can look right while missing the true structure. The team use QR codes as a test bed, since their layout is fixed and known. A good map should light the code's key parts and skip the background.

Their benchmark scores maps on that structural fit. It also ships with metrics and training recipes others can copy. The test acts as a quick check of whether a map is truly structure-aware. Such checks matter when explanations guide trust in medical or safety tools.
arxiv-2509-17045:
Alexander I. Bufetov and Yosuke Kawamoto wrote a 2025 arXiv paper in pure mathematics about boundary processes tied to Laguerre processes. The work builds on an earlier study by the same pair, where they set up a linked family of these processes with one fixed parameter. Here they ask what process appears at the boundary of that family.

To answer, the authors use a method built on operators that link one process to the next. They work out the boundary process in full, and it turns out to be a system that moves in a fixed, rule-based way with no randomness left. The same frame also fits Pickrell diffusions, so the paper derives the random boundary process for that family as well.
arxiv-2509-17145:
Forecasting what a running business process will do next is the task taken up in a 2025 arXiv paper by Amaan Ansari and two co-authors. Their field uses past event records to predict how open cases will unfold over time. The paper asks how far the neural networks used for this work can be shrunk before their forecasts get worse.

The authors test two known methods on five event logs and cut the models down in size and depth. A much smaller Transformer lost only a small share of its score. The LSTM design proved a bit more fragile, most of all when it predicted waiting times. The results suggest that lean models can stay accurate while costing far less to run.
arxiv-2509-17445:
Chaodong Tong and five co-authors built a sharper detector for made-up answers from language models. Their 2025 arXiv paper works on question answering, where a fluent answer can still be factually wrong. Entropy-based checks at the meaning level try to flag such hallucinations, but sampling noise and shaky grouping of answers of varied length weaken them.

Their method, Semantic Reformulation Entropy, attacks both flaws. On the input side, faithful paraphrases of the question widen the sampling space and cut bias from surface habits of the decoder. On the output side, a progressive, energy-based hybrid clustering keeps the meaning groups stable. On SQuAD and TriviaQA, the method beat strong baselines at spotting hallucinations. The authors argue that diversifying the input and steadying the grouping jointly give uncertainty estimates that travel better across tasks.
arxiv-2509-17645:
Andreas Hadjigeorghiou and seven co-authors built a pipeline that vets candidate exoplanets from the TESS telescope. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents RAVEN, a system for ranking and validating the signals TESS flags. Most candidates are false positives from stellar behavior or instrument noise, and human vetting cannot keep pace with the flow.

RAVEN works in a Bayesian frame, weighing the planet case against a set of false positive scenarios. Two classifiers, a gradient boosted tree and a Gaussian process, train on synthetic planets and on injected fakes across many astrophysical scenarios. A further training set holds real candidates caused by variability and systematics. The machine scores merge with scenario priors, including position-based odds. Candidates that clear a strict bar against every scenario, with a modest radius, count as validated. The pipeline aims at survey-scale triage.
arxiv-2509-17845:
Kai Zhang and 4 co-authors build a time-series model shaped like the pyramid form of classic image nets. Their 2025 paper deals with long records that vary in length, such as sensor or market data. Large attention models can waste traits and fail to travel to new data.

Their frame cuts time in patches, shrinks the time span step by step, and widens trait channels. A cross-scale step blends traits from fine and coarse views. A log-scale fix helps with records of mixed length. Tests show cleaner traits, less waste, and top scores on forecast and sort tasks.
arxiv-2509-17945:
S Abe leads a large team that seeks better models of how neutrinos hit atomic nuclei. Their 2025 paper centres on a known fit puzzle, Peelle's Pertinent Puzzle. Odd clashes between data and models block work to sharpen neutrino measures, which need high precision.

The team traces where those clashes come from and sets out fixes, with case studies. Data from two big neutrino setups are run through one shared frame to show the issues. A key plea is to make model fit tests a standard part of cross-section papers. That habit would make results more robust, the team argues.
arxiv-2509-18145:
Syed Ahmad Chan Bukhari and 3 co-authors flag several kinds of decline in intensive care patients at once. Their 2025 study uses the first day of ICU data to warn of care escalation needs. Past warning scores chase one outcome at a time, which misses how decline spans body systems at once.

Signs span lung fail, blood flow woes, kidney strain, and brain decline. Rule-based tags on the next two days set the targets to predict. Traits come from vital signs, lab values, and fixed patient facts. On a huge stay data set, a boosted tree model scored best across the four tags.
arxiv-2509-18445:
Simulating how mesh-based structures bend and stretch is slow with classic solvers. Kangzheng Liu and Leixin Ma present MeshODENet, a learning model built to speed that work up. Their 2025 paper notes that graph networks fit mesh data well, but step-by-step rollouts pile up errors over long runs. The new model pairs graph reasoning with a continuous-time equation learner.

Graph layers read the mesh layout, while a neural ordinary differential equation carries the state forward in smooth time. Tests covered elastic bodies in one and two dimensions with large, nonlinear bends. The model beat baselines on long-run accuracy and stability. It also ran far faster than classic solvers. The authors present it as a general tool for data-driven stand-ins. Such stand-ins could speed design studies that need many simulation runs.
arxiv-2509-18545:
Network slicing lets one mobile network serve many uses, each with its own service promises. Ioannis Panitsas and four co-authors present SlicePilot, a framework for placing those slices across mixed clouds. Their 2025 paper tackles a hard layout problem: cloud sites differ in power and cost, and slices differ in demand. Placement must stay cheap while keeping each slice's quality promises.

SlicePilot first profiles real traffic to estimate what each slice type needs. A team of learning agents then schedules the software functions, aiming at low cost under quality limits. On a multi-cloud testbed, the method ran nineteen times faster than exact combinatorial solvers. Its costs stayed within about eight percent of the best known. Under heavy load it breached quality promises more often, a trade the authors accept for speed. They present it as fit for live, fast-moving deployments.
arxiv-2509-18745:
Stretching a two-dimensional material changes its behavior, so measuring that strain precisely matters. Z. Mu and seven co-authors show that spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride can serve as strain sensors. Their 2025 paper uses boron-vacancy centers, flaws that respond to strain and can be read with light. The sensors resolve strain at sub-micrometer scales.

The team used the centers to measure how a Raman signal from a layered flake shifts under one-way stress. The reading pins down the strain with quantitative precision. That establishes the defects as a new metrology tool for stacked two-dimensional materials. The same centers offer other sensing modes beyond strain. The authors see them as a multi-use probe for strain-engineered materials. The work links defect physics to practical measurement.
arxiv-2509-18845:
Spin liquids are magnetic phases that refuse to order, held loose by local rules. Naïmo Davier and Ludovic D. C. Jaubert add interactions between spin clusters to that picture in this 2025 paper. In the classic case, each cluster's spins form a zero-divergence field, like a fluid that cannot pile up. Flat energy bands follow from those rules.

Their generic theory joins graph connectivity matrices with band topology. Flat bands hold at zero energy until the interaction passes a threshold. Then a dipping band steadies a spiral spin liquid whose ground states form a surface in momentum space. That surface acts like a Fermi surface that selects energies, though no particles fill it. It molds half-moon patterns in the scattering signal. The team extends half moons to higher-rank fields and exotic charges. A topology change of the surface marks a Lifshitz-style transition.
arxiv-2509-19045:
Dakota Thompson and Amro M. Farid build a tool for watching energy and raw materials flow through the whole United States energy system at once. That system joins four networks: electricity, natural gas, oil, and coal. Climate policy needs to know how these networks depend on each other, in structure and in behavior. Their work focuses on behavior, using a framework called hetero-functional graph theory.

Power grid operators have long used state estimation to infer the true state of a grid from imperfect data. The authors extend that idea to all four networks at once. Their estimator is an optimization program that weighs data errors by least squares and recovers the best-fit flows of mass and energy. It does so down to the level of single assets, a first for this combined framework. Two modeled regions show the method in action.
arxiv-2509-19145:
Hussein Cheikh Ali and Bruno Premoselli attack a celebrated equation of mathematical physics, the Brézis-Nirenberg problem, in its hardest dimension. The problem asks for bump-shaped solutions of a nonlinear equation on a bounded domain, with a parameter that shifts the spectrum. In three dimensions, the standard energy methods stumble in the non-coercive range. The authors hunt for least-energy solutions, defined by having the smallest norm among all nonzero solutions.

They build a new variational problem out of a weighted eigenvalue, minimized over normalized weights, inspired by spectral theory. Under an explicit positive-mass assumption, minimizers exist and produce least-energy solutions. This gives the first existence result on a general smooth domain for the full parameter range above the first eigenvalue. The paper also proves the problem's energy function jumps exactly at eigenvalues in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2509-19445:
Rare decays of heavy particles test whether the Standard Model of physics tells the whole story. Utsab Dey and Soumitra Nandi study decays of the Bc meson, a particle made of two heavy quarks. They look at paths where it turns into a D meson plus light particles. Shape factors that guide these decays are computed with quantum chromodynamics methods, tuned with results from lattice simulations.

The authors predict how often each decay should occur. They also predict traits that would shift if unseen physics were at play, such as gaps between decay rates for different light particles. A chained decay gets a full angular study, with forecasts for several angle-based measures. Collider teams can compare these forecasts with real events. Any clear mismatch would hint at physics past the Standard Model.
arxiv-2509-19545:
Two-legged robots need walking plans that are fast to compute yet safe on real hardware. Min Dai and Aaron D. Ames present RoMoCo, a free C++ toolbox for that job. It bundles reduced-order planners, which use simple stand-in models of walking, with whole-body controllers that command every joint. All parts share one interface, so teams can swap pieces and repeat tests fairly.

The team ran broad simulations on three robots: Cassie and two Unitree humanoids. They then ran real hardware tests on Cassie and one Unitree model. The same gait tools worked across all of them. That portability is the point: labs should not rebuild control stacks for each new robot. The toolbox gives the field a shared base for comparing walking methods.
arxiv-2509-19745:
Speech models must recognize and translate many languages without letting them blur together. Pei Zhang and five co-authors train alignment in stages, a method they call PART. Within-language alignment comes first, so each language keeps its own character. Cross-language alignment follows, with the language model itself partly unfrozen to join in.

Text tasks arrive later to deepen multilingual understanding. Older recipes froze the language model and forced all languages through the encoder at once, which capped performance. PART beat those recipes across four speech sets, including CommonVoice and Fleurs. Analysis shows a better balance between language-specific detail and shared structure. The staging idea may guide other multimodal training where one-size-fits-all alignment hurts.
arxiv-2509-19845:
Cosmology's standard model fits much, yet several measurements tug against each other in what are called tensions. A. Khodam-Mohammadi and M. Monshizadeh test whether exotic entropy rules can ease the strain. They rebuild cosmic expansion with Tsallis, Rényi, and Kaniadakis entropies, three generalizations of disorder. A modified stress-energy source carries the entropy's effect while ordinary matter density stays untouched.

For each entropy they derive the expansion history and its fingerprint numbers: deceleration, jerk, snap, and lerk. The modified route differs sharply from the traditional formal route, above all for Tsallis entropy. Such comparisons show which tweaks are real physics and which are bookkeeping. The authors offer the framework as a testbed for entropy-driven cosmology.
arxiv-2509-20045:
Small dialect differences that humans shrug off can trip language models badly. Vani Kanjirangat and three co-authors trace part of that gap to tokenization. They measure two parities: how evenly tokenizers split text across languages, and how much information the tokens preserve. Those bias measures are then correlated with downstream results.

Three tasks are tested: dialect labeling, topic labeling, and extractive question answering. Modern decoder models face older encoder models across scripts and resource levels. Tokenization parity predicts best on tasks leaning on syntax and word form. The dialect gap has social and economic roots, but this work isolates a mechanical one. Fairer tokenizers are a concrete fix that model builders control directly.
arxiv-2509-20645:
Running a benchmark is expensive, so Jungsoo Park and three co-authors ask whether its outcome can be predicted from the task description alone in a 2025 arXiv paper. They call this anticipatory evaluation. Their resource, EVALCAST, pairs natural-language descriptions of setups with the performance actually reported.
