It holds more than two thousand pairs drawn from over fifteen hundred papers.

A held-out test set uses papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff, guarding against memorized answers. Two tasks were tested: predicting the absolute score, and judging which of two benchmarks is harder. Frontier models struggled with absolute prediction. Pairwise difficulty judgments, under matched settings, recovered the true ordering much better. Streaming checks suggested the signal is not only recall of published numbers. The resource aims to help researchers prioritize which benchmarks are worth building.
arxiv-2509-20745:
Ships and other objects at sea are hard to spot in images, and labeled training photos are scarce. Yu Guo and seven co-authors address both problems with Neptune-X, a 2025 framework for maritime object detection. The approach generates synthetic training scenes and then selects the most useful ones.

A generator called X-to-Maritime creates varied, realistic sea scenes from several kinds of input. A special attention module models the boundary where objects meet water, a common source of detection errors. A task-aware selection step then picks synthetic samples that help training most. The authors report better detection and stronger generalization across object types, viewpoints, locations, and imaging conditions than training on limited real data alone.
arxiv-2509-20845:
New solar cell materials are often tested on a computer long before anyone grows them in a lab. H Laltlanmawii and six co-authors screen a family of copper-based compounds in a 2025 simulation study. The compounds pair copper and silicon with germanium, tin, or lead, plus sulfur.

Using density functional theory, the team computes structure, electronic behavior, light absorption, and mechanical strength. Molecular dynamics checks confirm the compounds stay stable at room temperature. Their band gaps fall in a range suited to harvesting sunlight. The authors report the germanium and tin variants as photovoltaic candidates for the first time. A device simulator then estimates how solar cells built from these materials might perform.
arxiv-2509-20945:
Galois points are special vantage points from which a hypersurface projects in a highly symmetric way. Taro Hayashi and three co-authors study wild Galois points in positive characteristic in a 2025 algebra paper. Wild means the symmetry group has order divisible by the characteristic, where behavior turns subtle.

The authors show that Galois groups arising from wild Galois points can be lifted to the general linear group, where they act naturally on vector spaces. They give necessary and sufficient conditions for a subgroup of the projective linear group to arise this way. They also prove that projections from wild Galois points on normal hypersurfaces are always wildly ramified. A geometric criterion, based on fixed loci of birational automorphisms, detects that ramification.
arxiv-2509-21145:
Two robot arms grasping one large object must agree on holds that are stable and do not collide. Md Faizal Karim and four co-authors present DAGDiff in a 2025 paper on dual-arm grasping. Earlier methods proposed each arm's grasp separately, leaning on region hints or heuristics.

DAGDiff generates the grasp pair jointly, denoising directly in the combined space of both gripper poses. Classifier signals guide the diffusion toward grasps that satisfy geometry, stability, and collision constraints. Enforcing those properties during generation, rather than filtering afterward, is the key insight. The framework needs no explicit region detection or object priors. Reliable two-arm grasps matter for warehouses and factories handling objects too big or awkward for one arm.
arxiv-2509-21445:
Origami surfaces can fold into many shapes, but each shape usually needs many actuators. Archie Webster and 2 co-authors present a robot that moves with just one actuator in a 2025 paper. Their platform, GeoGami, is a soft rigid design. Origami surface compliance supports shape contraction and locomotion. A geometric compliant skeleton adds repeatable motion.

The team demonstrates the robot and develops a stiffness model for it. A central gearbox mechanism drives the transformation. Alternative cable driven methods for the skeleton are also analysed. Evaluation covers shape transformation and rolling locomotion. By using one actuator, the design cuts complexity sharply. The authors argue the platform opens new options for robots that change shape for tasks.
arxiv-2509-21545:
Whether language models show metacognition, the ability to judge their own knowledge, is tested in a 2025 paper by Christopher Ackerman. Public debate about model self awareness runs ahead of measurement science. Self reports are not trusted as evidence here. Instead, two experimental paradigms from animal metacognition research are adapted. Models must use knowledge of their internal states in a strategic way.

Frontier models released since early 2024 showed growing evidence of certain abilities, the author reports. They could assess and use their own confidence on factual and reasoning questions. They could also anticipate answers they would give and use that information suitably. Behavioural findings, not self reports, support those claims. The paper frames the results as limited metacognition, with safety and policy relevance.
arxiv-2509-21845:
Answering a question that needs facts from several passages at once is called multi-hop question answering, and it stays hard for machines. Zichen Zhang, Kunlong Zhang, and two co-authors compare ways to do it in this 2025 paper. Their setup pairs Transformer models with retrieval, where the system first fetches passages and then writes an answer from them.

The team compared three ways to fetch passages: plain similarity, a diversity method, and a hybrid that mixes meaning-based matching with word overlap and re-ranking. They also adapted a known pipeline to sharpen the questions asked during search. On the HotpotQA data set, the hybrid clearly beat the plain method on both exact answers and overlap scores. Studying the errors showed better recall of key names, while tricky decoy passages and time-based questions stayed weak points.
arxiv-2509-21945:
Tuning a software system's settings for speed usually leans on a surrogate model that predicts performance, sparing costly real measurements. Pengzhou Chen, Hongyuan Liang, and Tao Chen challenge a natural belief in this 2025 paper, accepted by TOSEM: that a more accurate surrogate is always a better guide. Earlier work hinted that accuracy can lie, leaving open what a surrogate actually does for a tuner.

The authors answer through fitness landscape analysis, a view of how the performance surface is shaped. They build a theory of model usefulness for tuning that does not rest on accuracy, then test it across tens of thousands of cases. On that basis they propose Model4Tune, a tool that predicts the best model and tuner pairing for a new system without costly trials. It beat random guessing in most cases by a wide margin.
arxiv-2509-22145:
Marco Bonatto and Filippo Spaggiari classify Latin quandles in this 2025 paper. A quandle is a set with an operation that mimics the moves of knot theory. A Latin quandle is one whose operation table is a Latin square. Each element appears once in every row and column. The authors settle the classification for quandles whose size is sixteen times an odd prime.

Their result is that such quandles are almost always built from smaller pieces, in the sense called subdirectly reducible. When the prime leaves remainder one on division by three, exactly two exceptional quandles of this size appear for each such prime, reducible but not directly decomposable. For the two smallest primes, three and five, a single subdirectly irreducible example exists. The quandles turn out to be affine for most primes. The authors give explicit constructions of every case as coset quandles.
arxiv-2509-22245:
Hans Vandierendonck, writing alone, speeds up the search for the largest clique in a graph: the biggest set of nodes all connected to each other. The problem is NP-hard, so searches can run very long. Most of the work goes into proving that whole regions of the search space cannot contain the best clique, so they can be skipped. His 2025 paper presents a set of techniques built entirely around that avoidance of work.

The techniques include a graph representation built lazily, only where the search actually goes. A filtering step runs before any detailed search begins. The set intersection operations at the search's core get early exits when they cannot succeed. The algorithm also exploits freedom in choosing among strategies as the search proceeds. Together these gave large speedups over the most comparable existing algorithm, and a clear lead over another leading method.
arxiv-2509-22445:
Peter Shaw and 3 co-authors link a classic theory of simplicity to how transformers should be trained. The minimum description length principle says the best model squeezes the data into the shortest code. For neural networks, though, there was no principled measure of model complexity. The team defines objectives that are asymptotically optimal, grounded in Kolmogorov complexity.

A minimizer of such an objective compresses any data set near optimally as resources grow. They prove such objectives exist for transformers, using a new proof of transformer universality. A variational version with an adaptive mixture prior is workable and differentiable. In tests it favored simple, well-generalizing solutions, but standard optimizers often failed to find them.
arxiv-2509-22645:
Zhen-Hao Xie and 5 co-authors give CLIP-based incremental learning a sense of concept hierarchy. Plain text templates like a photo of a class ignore that some class pairs differ in coarse cues and others in fine detail. Standard CLIP features also come only from the last layer, wasting earlier layers' detail. Their method, HERMAN, asks language models to generate discriminative text descriptors at several levels of detail.

Those descriptors are matched to matching levels of visual features and routed as the task demands. The routing supports fine discrimination while easing catastrophic forgetting of old classes. Across multiple benchmarks, HERMAN consistently reached state-of-the-art scores for CLIP-based incremental learning.
arxiv-2509-22745:
Jaehan Kim and 3 co-authors defend mixture-of-experts language models against malicious fine-tuning. These models route each input to a few specialist subnetworks. Safety rests on harmful inputs being routed to safety-critical experts. The team shows that routing for harmful inputs drifts sharply after fine-tuning, opening an attack path. Defenses built for monolithic models do not stop that drift.

Their method, SafeMoE, penalizes the gap between a fine-tuned model's routing weights and the original safety-aligned model's. That keeps harmful inputs on their safe routes. Across open models from small to very large, SafeMoE cut harmfulness scores steeply. Task utility fell by under one percent, and overhead stayed near two percent.
arxiv-2509-23045:
Two schools build coding models: agents that act over many turns, and agentless flows with single checkable steps. Zonghan Yang and 20 co-authors argue the two can feed each other. Agentless training builds skill priors like localization, code editing, and self-reflection. Their model, Kimi-Dev, tops workflow methods on SWE-bench Verified. It is open source.

A light round of fine-tuning on public agent traces adapts it to agent use. The agent version scored on par with a known Claude model. The team read this as proof that structured skills transfer. Workflow training can thus seed capable coding agents.
arxiv-2509-23345:
Gamma-ray burst afterglows shine by synchrotron light, and upscattered photons reach far higher energies. Nissim Fraija and 4 co-authors derive closure relations for that self-Compton light from the reverse shock. Thick and thin shell cases both get treated. The reverse shock is adiabatic, in uniform or stratified media. Closure relations tie spectral and temporal slopes together.

The team check the relations against the second Fermi-LAT burst catalog. Thin shells in a constant-density medium fit better than the alternatives. Hard, atypical bursts also fit the scenario under varied cooling. Two famous bursts share one electron population for optical flash and GeV light. Scattered photons are needed for the highest energies.
arxiv-2509-23645:
Re-running a Jupyter notebook does not always give the same answer, thanks to randomness, library updates, and shifting machines. A S M Shahadat Hossain and 3 co-authors propose the Similarity-based Reproducibility Index, a score for how close a rerun comes. Their methods compare outputs type by type, using similarity measures built for different kinds of Python objects. Each output cell gets a number between zero and one, plus qualitative notes.

A case study applies the index to a set of notebooks. It shows how the per-type similarity scores can turn a vague sense of reproducibility into a measured one, helping teams judge whether shared computational work can be trusted.
arxiv-2509-23745:
A controller tuned for one robot body usually fails on the next, so Min Liu and 2 co-authors trained a generalist instead. LocoFormer learns locomotion for legged and wheeled robots it has never seen, even without exact knowledge of their build. Two choices drive that flexibility. Training runs massive reinforcement learning on procedurally generated robots with heavy randomization.

The second choice is memory: context windows stretch across episode boundaries, orders of magnitude longer than usual. One deployed model handled varied robots through weight changes and motor failures. In extreme trials it even learned from falls in early episodes to control better in later ones.
arxiv-2509-23945:
Sampling a three-dimensional spin glass is one of statistical physics' stubborn open problems, with rugged landscapes that freeze ordinary Monte Carlo. Tao Chen and 3 co-authors introduce Tensor Network Markov Chain Monte Carlo to break the jam. Tensor networks propose large collective updates on two-dimensional slices of the 3D lattice. Autocorrelation times plunge, and unbiased samples arrive orders of magnitude faster.

On a single CPU, the method handled spin glasses up to sixty-four cubed, work that usually needs a supercomputer. It also crossed the exponential barriers of a strong first-order transition in the three-state Potts model, where conventional sampling fails outright.
arxiv-2509-24045:
Sumit Nandi sets out a new test for true many-party quantum link. The link, called genuine multipartite entanglement, means all parts share one joint state that cannot be split into smaller groups. His test uses measures in mutually unbiased bases, sets of views that reveal quite different facts about a state.

Nandi shows that states which can be split obey a fixed bound on these measures. States with the full link break that bound, so the test can certify them. He checks the method on three-party and four-party cases. The same measures also track closely with some known scores of this kind of link.
arxiv-2509-24145:
Tom Stoiber asks when the spectra of a family of algebras vary without jumps. His setting is a continuous field of étale groupoids that share the rapid decay property, a growth condition on their elements. He works with the reduced groupoid C*-algebras built from each field member.

Stoiber shows those algebras themselves form a continuous field. That gives a new sufficient criterion for spectral continuity, and it applies in the non-amenable case where full and reduced algebras can part ways. Uses he notes include convergence of spectra in inverse systems of finite-index subgroups. Magnetic models on hyperbolic lattices are another case in point.
arxiv-2509-24545:
Counting people in fog is hard: distant figures blur, local detail fades, and contrast drops. Yuhao Wang and 5 co-authors build a crowd counting method that starts from the physics of atmospheric scattering rather than from data alone. A differentiable scattering model estimates how haze weakens targets at each depth, with parameters that calibrate themselves.

A Kolmogorov-Arnold style network with learnable edge activations strengthens features in degraded regions. A weather-aware graph network then links spatial neighbors using those deep features. On four public data sets, counting error in dense fog fell by a wide margin against mainstream methods. Physics and learning, tuned together, did the work.
arxiv-2510-00045:
Franck Vandewiele and three colleagues published this research paper in 2025 on bias in text-to-image models. Such models are AI tools that turn written prompts into pictures. The team studied hospital jobs, where gender stereotypes are strong and easy to measure. They asked whether six open models draw men and women fairly across five hospital roles.

The team made one hundred images for each mix of job and prompt wording, then counted who appeared. Every model drew nurses only as women, and most drew surgeons as men. The word corporate pushed the images toward men, while beautiful pushed them toward women. Each model also reacted to wording changes in its own way. The authors argue that builders need fairer defaults and clearer user guidance.
arxiv-2510-00145:
Nicholas DiBrita and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on preparing quantum states with today's noisy quantum computers. The task is to tune a shallow circuit so its outputs mimic a target state's pattern. The search space is huge, jagged, and noisy, which defeats standard optimizers. The team proposes CircuitTree, a guide based on Bayesian optimization with tree-shaped surrogate models.

CircuitTree splits the circuit's parameters into blocks that follow its layered design. Each block is then optimized in a distributed, sample-efficient way. The authors prove convergence guarantees for the scheme under mild assumptions. On synthetic tests and variational tasks, CircuitTree matched target states closely with much shallower circuits than rivals. The method avoids the smoothness assumptions that Gaussian process models need. It offers a practical route to state preparation on near-term hardware.
arxiv-2510-00245:
Rizul Sharma and colleagues at the University of Cincinnati published this 2025 short paper testing AI agents in online meetings. Meeting assistants increasingly listen in, summarize, and answer questions about what was shown. Charts complicate that job, since talk about data mixes speech with visuals. The team built a test suite around real spoken discussions of data visualizations.

Their corpus holds 72 recorded dialogues about charts, paired with 318 benchmark questions. A dual-axis framework sorts each question by complexity and by topic. Four pipelines were compared, mixing language-only and vision-language models with chart images, chart code, or both. The text-only language model pipeline won outright, reaching about ninety-six percent accuracy. The authors suggest meeting tools should feed agents text descriptions of charts, not just the pictures themselves.
arxiv-2510-00445:
Song-Ung Ri, Hyon-Hui Ju, and Jin-Myong Kim at Kim Il Sung University in Pyongyang wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on wild operator dynamics. A hypercyclic operator has one vector whose orbit under repeated application comes near every point. Weighted shift operators are the classic playground for such behavior. The authors study generalized bilateral shifts acting on a Hilbert module over compact operators.

They examine frequent hypercyclicity, where the orbit visits each region a positive share of the time. Disjoint hypercyclicity, where several operators share one universal orbit vector, also gets full treatment. Using Furstenberg families, they frame a strong form of topological transitivity for the shifts. Criteria in the paper say exactly when these dynamical properties hold. The module setting generalizes earlier Hilbert space results in a nontrivial way. Such work extends linear dynamics, a field linking operator theory with chaotic behavior.
arxiv-2510-00545:
Seokhun Park and five colleagues published this 2025 paper on explaining complex models by splitting their predictions into parts. Functional ANOVA breaks a high-dimensional function into pieces owned by single variables and their interactions. Neural tensor-product bases can fit those pieces, but someone must choose them in advance. High-order pieces then explode in cost and memory. The team's Bayesian variant lets the data decide which pieces exist.

A Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler explores component choices efficiently. The Bayesian machinery detects higher-order interactions at lower cost than the earlier deterministic method. Benchmark datasets showed stronger prediction accuracy alongside honest uncertainty estimates. Theory backs the practice: the posterior provably concentrates on the truth as data grows. The authors suggest letting selection odds adapt to which variables the current model already uses. Interpretable modeling gains a principled, self-pruning engine.
arxiv-2510-00745:
Laveda-Martínez and eight co-authors automate defect detection inside ceramic parts in this 2025 arXiv paper on non-destructive testing. Manufacturers inspect ceramics for pores, delaminations, and inclusions, but manual visual checks are subjective and cannot see below the surface. Optical coherence tomography images the interior at high resolution without damaging the part. The team trained a U-Net network on OCT volumes with hand-segmented defect annotations.

They compared multiple experimental configurations and added post-processing so predictions could be judged quantitatively and visually. The chosen system reached a Dice score near 0.98 for segmenting inclusion defects, which beat comparable published studies. Inference took about nineteen seconds per volume, fast enough for production quality control. The dataset was small, only thirty volumes, and only inclusions were targeted, which the authors note as limits. Horizon Europe funding supported the work.
arxiv-2510-00845:
Méloux, Portet, and Peyrard argue that mechanistic interpretability findings should be treated as statistical estimates, in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI interpretability. Circuit discovery methods claim to find the sub-network responsible for a model's behaviour, and papers usually report one circuit as fact. The authors ask how stable that answer is when anything in the pipeline wiggles. They stress-test EAP-IG, a state-of-the-art attribution method with integrated gradients, under controlled perturbations.

They varied the input sample by bootstrapping, paraphrased prompts, changed hyperparameters, and injected noise into the causal analysis itself. Discovered circuits showed high structural variance across those perturbations, and no variant stayed consistently stable. A circuit found once may be an artifact of the sample or the settings rather than the model's true mechanism. The authors recommend reporting stability metrics, such as pairwise Jaccard overlap under resampling, alongside every circuit claim.
arxiv-2510-00945:
Varadaraj and the Euclid Consortium report a hunt for bright galaxies at redshift near seven in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such galaxies shine from the universe's first billion years, and finding the bright ones guides later deep studies. The team searched the COSMOS field using the UltraVISTA near-infrared survey, adding deep optical and Spitzer space telescope imaging.

Without Euclid data, their selection found 289 candidate galaxies across the target redshift range. Adding Euclid photometry produced a cleaner sample of 140 galaxies, including 38 that the ground-based selection had missed. Euclid data also removed contamination from cool dwarf stars and image artefacts. The resulting luminosity function declined smoothly toward brighter galaxies and agreed well with earlier Hubble-based studies. The sample reaches fainter than the function's knee, a first for ground-based selection at this redshift.
arxiv-2510-01045:
Tautvaišienė and a large team use carbon and nitrogen abundances to read the ages and life stages of giant stars, in this 2025 arXiv paper based on the Gaia-ESO survey. As low-mass stars climb the red giant branch, mixing dredges processed material to the surface and shifts the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. That ratio can serve as a clock, but only if astronomers know which mixing events have already happened. The core helium flash, predicted sixty years ago, was one untested suspect.

The team measured abundances for 327 evolved stars in 44 open clusters with high-resolution spectra from the VLT. Red clump stars that had passed the helium flash showed clearly lower carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, driven by extra nitrogen. First-ascent giants matched theory less closely than expected, since their dredge-up looked weaker than models predict. The authors provide separate age calibrations for each evolutionary stage.
arxiv-2510-01145:
Imam and nine co-authors review speech recognition research for African low-resource languages in this 2025 arXiv systematic literature review. Automatic speech recognition has advanced quickly, yet Africa's two thousand plus languages remain underrepresented, which blocks digital inclusion. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, the team searched five scholarly databases for studies from January 2020 to July 2025. They screened over two thousand records and kept seventy-one studies .

Those studies cover seventy-four datasets across one hundred eleven languages, totalling roughly eleven thousand hours of speech. Fewer than fifteen percent shared reproducible materials, and dataset licensing was often unclear . Self-supervised and transfer learning look promising, but scarce pretraining data and weak dialect coverage hold them back. Most researchers report word error rate alone, which suits tonal, morphologically rich languages poorly. The authors recommend openly licensed corpora, linguistically informed metrics, and community partnerships.
arxiv-2510-01245:
Chen, Jiang, and Huang forecast city movement by reading the news and posts that explain why crowds suddenly shift. Standard mobility models miss concerts, matches, and disruptions because their inputs are only numbers. Their pipeline, SeMob, uses language-model agents to mine online text for relevant events.

Agents extract and reason over spatiotemporally related text automatically. A progressive fusion design then merges those event insights with movement data. Errors dropped notably against a strong spatiotemporal baseline. Gains concentrated exactly where intuition says they should, near each event in place and time. Error reductions reached double digits against the spatiotemporal model alone. Event priors from pretraining enrich what raw text supplies. Routing and traffic management are the downstream customers named. Multi-agent extraction divides a messy reading job into checkable pieces. Forecasts improve most where life is least routine in the city.
arxiv-2510-01545:
Cai, Peng, and Zhou stretch a single human correction so it teaches an agent about the future, not just the present. Interactive training usually fixes only the action a supervisor interrupts. The risky states an agent will meet seconds later go untaught, even though they matter more.

Their method spreads each intervention across a short horizon of predicted states. It assumes the same correction would apply there, then turns those states into preference lessons. Driving and robot-arm tests needed fewer demonstrations while learning faster. One well-timed correction, projected forward, can guard a whole stretch of behavior. Preference optimization then steers the agent away from states the expert would fix. Future rollouts come from the agent's own predictions, keeping lessons on-policy. Safety-critical regions get attention before the agent wanders into them alone. Human time stays the scarce resource being saved.
arxiv-2510-01645:
Mireshghallah and Li argue that privacy research on language models stares at memorization while larger threats walk past unstudied. Training-data extraction dominates the literature, but real harms also flow from data collection, inference-time leakage, autonomous agents, and cheap deep surveillance. Their position paper maps risks across the whole system lifecycle.

A decade of over thirteen hundred privacy papers shows the attention imbalance quantitatively. Case studies demonstrate current frameworks failing against the broader threat set. Technical fixes offer little traction on the most pressing harms. The authors call for interdisciplinary approaches as the only credible way forward. Data collection practices open the taxonomy at the lifecycle's start. Context leakage at inference time needs no training-data theft at all. Democratized surveillance scales harm beyond any single breach. Policy and design belong inside the privacy field's remit. Memorization is one room in a large house.
arxiv-2510-01845:
Takmaz, Bylinina, and Dotlačil train small language models on child-scale data in this 2025 paper. Their entry targets the BabyLM challenge, which limits training data to amounts children plausibly hear. Giant vision-and-language models learn from far more data than any child sees. The team builds both text-only and multimodal models under the same tight budget.

Their multimodal models beat earlier BabyLM baselines on the challenge's measures. A known weakness appeared too, since multimodal training hurt grammar-focused language scores. To repair that, the authors merged model weights by simple weighted averaging. Fusing a multimodal model with a text-only one recovered part of the lost language skill. Multimodal performance largely survived the merge intact. The result suggests a cheap fix for keeping language sharp inside small multimodal systems.
arxiv-2510-01945:
Muller uses measurement time itself as a dial for quantum coherence in molecular junctions in this 2025 physics paper. The devices are break junctions, where a molecule bridges two electrodes that are pulled apart. In a partially wet solvent phase, these junctions keep quantum coherence for an unusually long one to twenty milliseconds at room conditions. That longevity makes the crossover visible in a tabletop setup.

By tuning how long each current reading lasts, Muller compares it directly against the coherence lifetime. Short readings reveal quantum interference as structured bands of data points. Long readings wash those bands into a single averaged, classical-looking response. The measurement process itself thus steers how quantum the system appears. Strain on the junction adds a second handle on the effect. The work offers a controlled way to study how coherence decays, a core puzzle of quantum theory, without cryogenic gear.
arxiv-2510-02045:
Kurichin and Ivanchik rebuild the helium emission spectrum with proper radiative transfer in this 2025 astrophysics paper. Helium lines are workhorse diagnostics for nebulae, and they anchor primordial helium measurements. Older models often assumed the gas is optically thin in every line. Transitions ending on the metastable triplet state break that assumption in real nebulae.

Their new model uses up-to-date atomic data and follows how line photons scatter inside the gas. With nonzero optical depth, two prominent lines shift substantially: previous models underestimated one line's emissivity and overestimated another's by five to twenty percent. In the thin limit, the new results agree with earlier studies. The authors tabulate emissivities across the density and temperature grids typical of H II regions and planetary nebulae. Fresh fitting formulas give transfer corrections for key optical and near-infrared lines.
arxiv-2510-02245:
Zhan and co-authors argue that reasoning training wastes its own practice work. Their 2025 machine learning paper studies reinforcement learning with checkable rewards. Standard training throws away each practice attempt after one update. That habit wastes compute and makes learning unstable. The team asked which past attempts deserve reuse. They found two strong signals of value. One signal is whether the attempt reached a correct answer. The other is its entropy, a measure of spread in the model choices.

Their method, ExGRPO, stores and ranks valuable attempts for reuse. A mixed objective balances fresh exploration against that stored experience. Tests covered five base models, from small to mid sized. ExGRPO beat standard training by several points on math and general tests. Gains averaged about three and a half points on one group and more on another. Training also grew steadier across runs.
arxiv-2510-02545:
Helson, Tanre, and Veltz simplify spiking neural networks whose synapses learn from timing. Their 2025 mathematical neuroscience paper tackles a modeling problem. A fully connected network holds connections on the order of N squared. Neuron and synapse dynamics tangle together. Plasticity keeps injecting heterogeneity into the mix. Classic mean-field and slow-fast tools strain under that coupling. The authors introduce a typical neuron variable instead. It bundles voltage, time since the last spike, and weights. The weights enter through their empirical distribution. A stochastic timing based plasticity rule drives the connections.

Taking the network size to infinity collapses the description. A McKean-Vlasov style limit law governs the typical neuron. Proofs of the limit fill the supplementary material. Two hard phenomena, spikes and plasticity, meet in one analysis. Recurrent settings had resisted this treatment until now. Brain scale models become mathematically tractable. The method opens tools for complex neural systems.
arxiv-2510-02845:
Guo and a large team report the first light-based photonic time crystal. A time crystal repeats its pattern in time instead. Its optical traits pulse up and down very fast. Theory promised wild effects from such pulsing. Real devices at optical speeds stayed out of reach for years. The team built theirs from a plasmonic metamaterial. It works at terahertz frequencies, just below visible light.

Strong fields drive the material's charge carriers in cycles. The drive swings their effective mass by a huge share. That swing is deep and coherent enough to form the time crystal. Theory fitted to the experiment predicts rich effects nearby. Sound-like plasmon waves should gain energy from the drive. Paired, entangled plasmons should also appear. The platform is tunable from the outside. It opens a new lab for time-based control of light.
arxiv-2510-02945:
Rojas and Lee give lifelong learning agents a sense of risk. Continual reinforcement learning trains agents that never stop learning. Tasks and worlds keep changing over an endless run. Nearly all theory so far judges agents by average reward alone. Averages hide the chance of rare, bad stretches. The authors test whether they fit endless learning.

They show the classic tools break in the continual setting. The mismatch is structural, not a matter of tuning. They then build a new class called ergodic risk measures. These are shaped for agents that run forever. A case study puts the new tools to work. A risk-aware learner used a tail-risk rule in a shifting task. Results matched the theory and felt sound in practice. The paper lays a formal base for careful, risk-aware lifelong agents. Future systems may weigh safety beside raw score from the start.
arxiv-2510-03145:
Linton charts the subgroup geometry of mapping tori built from free groups. A mapping torus twists a free group by one of its maps. Such groups generalize the free-by-cyclic family. That family mirrors fibered three-manifold groups in many ways. Few subgroup facts were known without strong extra assumptions. Linton finds a canonical family of maximal sub-tori inside. The whole group is relatively hyperbolic against that family.

Locally quasi-convex hyperbolic groups get a full characterization. The characterization covers free-by-cyclic and one-relator groups. Older results upgrade from the tame case to the general one. Dehn functions can now be computed in this generality. The conjugacy problem gains a solution here too. The finitely generated intersection property is pinned down. Linton's frame explains where such subgroups sit instead. An open problem asks which subgroups are fully quasi-convex.
arxiv-2510-03645:
Blanc and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper giving evidence that quantum circuits are stronger than classical ones for sampling tasks. An earlier result separated the two for exact sampling only. This paper extends the separation to approximate sampling, the realistic case, relative to a random oracle. The authors exhibit a distribution that polynomial size quantum circuits sample exactly. They then bound what classical circuits of subexponential size can do against it.

No classical circuit can come loosely close to the distribution, the proof shows. The allowed error is nearly total, yet approximation fails. A hardness amplification lemma drives the argument: the chance that a family of query algorithms finds many solutions to a search problem decays exponentially in their number. Separations for uniform algorithms were known; this one covers circuit based samplers. Results like this underpin claims that quantum devices can perform tasks no classical machine can mimic.
arxiv-2510-03745:
Van Huffel and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper generating low discrepancy point sequences with a network, beating classical number theory constructions at their game. Such sequences fill space unusually evenly, and every segment must stay even, which makes them prized for numerical integration and simulation. Classical recipes come from algebra, and a learning method could make sets but not sequences. NeuroLDS trains a network that maps each index to a point, first imitating classical sequences, then fine tuning against prefix discrepancy.

The learned sequences outperformed previous constructions by a margin on discrepancy measures. The authors demonstrate wins in numerical integration, robot motion planning, and scientific machine learning. Evenly spread samples mean fewer points for the same accuracy, which compounds across simulations. Learning a construction that mathematicians refined for decades, and then surpassing it, marks a shift. Designers of sampling schemes for graphics, robotics, and uncertainty studies gain a tool.
arxiv-2510-04045:
Zhang, McKeown, and Muresan present this 2025 arXiv paper on teaching language models to adopt a requested viewpoint faithfully. Most models are trained toward one uniform set of values, which limits tasks needing a specific community's perspective. Steerable pluralism asks a model to argue from a chosen standpoint on demand. The authors test whether chain-of-thought reasoning, where the model thinks step by step, can build that steerability.

They compare four routes: prompting with reasoning, fine-tuning on human-written reasoning, fine-tuning on synthetic explanations, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Evaluation used the Value Kaleidoscope and OpinionQA datasets, which probe values and public opinions. The reinforcement learning route won consistently and learned from few training examples. The team also audited the reasoning traces for faithfulness and safety risks. The findings favor reward-based training for pluralistic alignment work.
arxiv-2510-04245:
Mehrotra and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper defending image classifiers against adversarial patches without knowing anything about the patch. A printed sticker placed on an object can force targeted misclassification in the physical world, threatening vehicles and face recognition. Existing defenses usually assume the patch's size or location, so attacks outside those assumptions slip through. The authors repurpose interpretability machinery as the defense itself.

Their method uses the CRAFT explanation technique to extract the model's most influential concept activation vectors. Adversarial patch pixels, being unnaturally influential, should concentrate in exactly those concepts. Masking the top fraction of influential concepts therefore neutralizes the patch without detecting it explicitly. On Imagenette with a ResNet-50, the defense beat the state-of-the-art PatchCleanser in both robust and clean accuracy. Concept-driven defenses turn explanation tools into security tools, a direction the authors argue scales better than patch hunting.
arxiv-2510-04745:
Lucas Sempéré, Yue Bi, Yue Wu, Pengwenlong Gu, and Selma Boumerdassi wrote this 2025 paper on taming interference in device networks. Swarms of sensors need to send sums of their readings, not each value alone. Over the air computation exploits radio physics to add signals during transmission itself. In multi cluster networks, though, clusters jam each other and corrupt the sums. The authors design an interference alignment scheme for this uplink setting.

Alignment packs interfering signals into shared corners of the signal space, leaving clean room for each cluster. Their scheme works for any number of clusters, where earlier ones did not. Each cluster can use half of the channels at once. Time sharing, the fallback, would give each cluster only a slice that shrinks as clusters multiply. The paper also handles users shared between neighboring clusters. The gains matter for smart cities, health monitoring, and other dense sensor webs.
arxiv-2510-04945:
Juan-José Guzmán-Landa and four co-authors present the first context-free grammar for Nawatl in this 2025 arXiv paper. Nawatl, also called Nahuatl, is Mexico's most widely spoken indigenous language. It has very few digital resources, and almost no text collections exist for training language models. That shortage blocks modern language technology for its speakers.

A context-free grammar is a set of rules that can generate correct sentences. The authors use theirs to grow a small Nawatl corpus they call π-yalli with artificial sentences. They then train word-embedding models such as FastText on the enlarged corpus. Early results beat some large language models on sentence-level meaning tasks. The team notes that a richer grammar would bring still larger gains.
arxiv-2510-05245:
Yue Pan and ten co-authors redesign computer memory for serving mixture-of-experts models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such models activate only a few expert sub-networks per input. That sparsity gives huge capacity at modest compute cost. The expert layers still move massive volumes of data, which strains ordinary hardware.

Their design, Stratum, stacks monolithic 3D DRAM directly on logic through hybrid bonding. Processing units sit near the memory to crunch expert and attention work locally. Because taller stacks have uneven access speeds, the system tiers its memory. A topic-based predictor guesses which experts a request will need and places them in fast tiers. Stratum delivered up to 8.29 times the decoding throughput of GPU baselines. Energy efficiency improved up to 7.66 times as well.
arxiv-2510-05445:
Zhang and colleagues address a practical puzzle in question answering with language models. Teams can now choose among many models and many agent designs for the same task. No single setup wins everywhere, and bigger models do not always perform best. Their 2025 paper, AgentRouter, learns which agent should handle each new question.

The method turns each question, its context, and the candidate agents into one knowledge graph. A graph neural network then spreads signals across that graph and assigns work to agents. Final answers blend agent outputs with learned weights. In broad tests, the router beat single agents and plain ensembles across benchmarks and model backbones. The gains show that routing works best when it reads the task context, not just past scores. The authors note the system still uses a fixed pool of hand-built agents. Cost control is left for later work.
arxiv-2510-05745:
Litvinova reviews how nuclear giant resonances fragment into many smaller peaks. Giant resonances are collective vibrations that probe nuclear forces and correlations. Their strength rarely sits in one clean peak, especially at low spin. Her 2025 contribution examines monopole and dipole responses in medium-heavy nuclei.

Fragmentation patterns encode how collective motion couples to complex configurations. Capturing them demands non-perturbative many-body methods like Green functions and equations of motion. The nucleon-nucleon interaction itself remains uncertain, which limits every calculation. Soft modes add further structure at low excitation energy. Single-nucleon propagators benchmark the theory against transfer and knock-out reactions. Pairing correlations surface through pair propagators and their residues. No current theory describes the data accurately across the nuclear landscape. A predictive framework must stay accurate yet transfer across energy scales. The review maps open problems inspired by Angela Bracco's research line.
arxiv-2510-06445:
Shahriar and four co-authors survey language-model agent security across applications, threats, and defenses in a 2025 paper. Agents now work throughout cybersecurity, enabling powerful autonomous tools. Their autonomy opens new attack surfaces. Prior surveys treated uses, attacks, and countermeasures separately.

The survey organizes over two hundred sixty papers into one taxonomy. Applications cover how agents serve downstream security tasks. Threat analysis examines entry points, targeted agent-loop stages, and threat models. Defense analysis weighs strategies by cost, trade-offs, and lifecycle placement. The authors map which defenses cover which attack classes. They chart trends in architectures, backbone models, and research growth. It also compares red-teaming agents built to attack systems with blue-teaming agents built to defend them. Their verdict is blunt: agentic systems are structurally fragile by default. Securing them requires defenses spanning the full agent lifecycle, not single-layer patches.
arxiv-2510-06645:
Zhiyuan Wei, Xiaoxuan Yang, Jing Sun, and Zijian Zhang hunt security flaws in C and C++ code. Their 2025 paper uses large language models to find vulnerabilities automatically. Big models are capable but costly to run on large codebases. Small models are cheap but usually miss subtle flaws and logical errors.

Their framework, FineSec, transfers knowledge from large teacher models into compact student models. That process is called knowledge distillation. FineSec wraps it in a four-stage workflow covering data preparation, training, evaluation, and ongoing learning. Parameter-efficient tuning and instruction alignment sharpen the student further. In broad tests on C and C++ code, FineSec beat both plain base models and larger language models. It caught complex vulnerabilities that the bigger models missed. The result points to small, specialized models as a practical choice for everyday code auditing.
arxiv-2510-06745:
Somasekhara Sontti and Arnab Atta simulate long gas bubbles moving through tiny liquid-filled channels. Their 2025 paper studies Taylor bubbles in a co-flow microchannel, using computational fluid dynamics. Such slug flows appear in lab-on-a-chip devices and small chemical reactors. The team varies surface tension, inlet speeds, and the liquid's apparent thickness.

They compare plain liquids with a thickened solution that behaves as a power-law fluid. In every case, bubble length shrank as the capillary number rose. A higher gas-to-liquid speed ratio and more thickener also shortened the bubbles. Bubbles sped up because the liquid film around them grew thicker. At high speeds, the bubble shapes changed noticeably and developed wiggles. More thickener raised the bubble formation rate while shortening each bubble. Knowing these trade-offs helps engineers tune microchannel devices. Bubble size and speed affect how reactions and heat transfer proceed inside them.
arxiv-2510-06845:
Jasem Hamoud and Duaa Abdullah pin down the range of a graph irregularity measure. Their 2025 paper studies the Sigma index, a topological index used in chemistry. For each edge of a graph, the index adds the squared difference between the degrees of its two endpoints. A regular graph scores zero, while uneven graphs score higher.

The authors establish sharp lower and upper bounds for the index. Their arguments work from a graph's degree sequence, listed from largest to smallest. They connect the Sigma index to other indices, including harmonic ones. One result gives an upper bound for trees in terms of the forgotten index and graph counts. The bounds behave differently for closed graphs than for trees, which the paper highlights. Bounds matter because they reveal how different graph measures relate to each other. They limit what values a chemist or network analyst can expect before computing anything.
arxiv-2510-06945:
Lorenzo Pastori, Veronika Eyring, and Mierk Schwabe ask when a flexible model trains better than a focused one. Their 2025 paper studies Fourier regression models, which mirror a broad class of quantum neural networks. Two quantities guide their analysis. Effective dimension measures how much of its capacity a model really uses. Bias measures how strongly the model leans toward the target function beforehand.

The authors derive an exact formula for the Fisher information matrix of these models. That formula exposes which features set the effective dimension and the bias. They then build models with tunable values of both and compare training outcomes. For a model with no prior lean, higher effective dimension usually trained better. For a model already biased toward the answer, lower effective dimension helped instead. The reversal is the paper's central lesson for model design. Quantum machine learning builders can use it when sizing their networks.
arxiv-2510-07445:
Chartab and co-authors use three-dimensional maps of intergalactic gas to ask whether environment shaped galaxies at cosmic noon. Their 2025 paper draws on the LATIS survey, which tomographs the gas between galaxies using background light. The main sample holds over two thousand ultraviolet-selected galaxies seen about eleven billion years ago. A literature sample adds another thousand with better mass coverage. Mock catalogs built from a large simulation, with the same selection filters applied, reveal what the surveys can and cannot see.

The real samples show those trends much weaker or absent. Star formation rate per unit mass shows no measurable tie to gas overdensity among the LATIS galaxies. The mocks reproduce that flatness, proving the cause: ultraviolet selection systematically misses the passive and dusty galaxies that live in dense places.
arxiv-2510-07545:
Laskar and a large team report hard lessons from making tiny vision-language models judge chart-reading systems. Their 2025 paper starts from an economics problem. Big models judge chart answers well but cost too much to run, while models under two billion parameters judge poorly. Two cost-cutting strategies are tested. Multi-criteria prompting packs several grading criteria into one instruction. Fine-tuning instead trains a tiny model on synthetic judgments in the chart domain. The result is a specialist called ChartJudge-2B, distilled from larger judges' behavior on a source dataset and transferred to new ones.

Multi-criteria prompting exposed fragility: several seven-billion-parameter judges, including a specialized critic model, dropped sharply when criteria combined. The fine-tuned two-billion model beat many larger rivals in both single- and multi-criteria settings. Analysis across chart types and question difficulty maps where the savings hold.
arxiv-2510-07745:
You and five coauthors wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on giving reasoning models more time to think. Language models often improve when they sample many chains of thought and vote. A new style reasons silently in continuous vectors instead of words. That latent style lacks a way to sample paths. It also lacks scores for picking a path. The authors supply both missing pieces.

For sampling, they add two randomness strategies borrowed from uncertainty methods. One uses Monte Carlo dropout, and the other adds Gaussian noise. Both scaled well as computing budgets grew, with exploration styles. For selection, they train a latent reward model that scores reasoning steps. The reward model learned through contrastive training on contrasting steps. Together, the pieces let latent models spend inference compute productively. The work opens test-time scaling to a class of models that could not use it.
arxiv-2510-07845:
Bhattacharya and Chen wrote this 2025 representation theory paper on the Bernstein center for p-adic groups. The Bernstein center organizes the smooth representations of a group over a local field. Depth, an invariant from Moy and Prasad, grades representations by how deep their structure runs. Earlier work by the authors described the center at integral depths. Here they extend the description to all rational depths for a split reductive group.

They present the depth-r center as a limit of standard parahoric Hecke algebras at that depth. With that picture, they build maps from stable functions on Moy-Prasad quotients into the center. They attach Deligne-Lusztig parameters to irreducible representations. The assignment agrees with restricted Langlands parameters for Moy-Prasad types from prior work. As a payoff, the representation category splits into blocks indexed by those parameters. The result sharpens a bookkeeping tool of the Langlands program.
arxiv-2510-08045:
Chernobrovkin, Sälzer, Schwarzentruber, and Troquard wrote this 2025 paper proving that verifying graph neural networks with a global readout is intractable. Graph neural networks classify graphs in chemistry, drug discovery, and social networks. Real deployments quantize their numbers, and safety rules increasingly demand proof that outputs behave. Earlier work verified quantized networks without readout. Readout, pooling the whole graph into one verdict, is essential for graph classification.

The authors build a logical language that characterizes these networks exactly. With it, they prove verification tasks are complete for a very high complexity class, far above the level without readout. In plain terms, no efficient general verifier exists. They also built a prototype verifier for bounded-size graphs as a baseline. Experiments showed quantized models stay lightweight with accuracy near full-precision versions. The result redirects safety research toward restricted cases and approximations.
arxiv-2510-08245:
Jannek Ulm, Kevin Du, and Vésteinn Snæbjarnarson explore in a 2025 arXiv paper whether fake training text can help language models learn. Models train on huge piles of real text, and some fear that supply may run short. One fix is to train on text that models write themselves. The authors test a sampling trick called contrastive decoding for making such text.

Their setup compares a strong model and a weak model trained on the same hundred-million-word corpus. Contrastive decoding boosts what the strong model favors and the weak one does not. The team mixed this synthetic text with real text and retrained new models. The mix improved language modeling scores and several downstream tasks. Gains were largest on tasks needing reasoning, while plain sampling helped more on surface language skills like grammar.
arxiv-2510-08445:
Wenxuan Wang and co-authors generate synthetic time series together with their formulas, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Foundation models for time series promise one model for forecasting, classification, and more. Scarcity and imbalance of real training data hold them back. Drawing on complex dynamic systems theory, the team built a generator with no practical size limit.

Their mechanism produces time series paired with the symbolic expressions that generated them. Such pairs are tightly correlated by construction, unlike scraped real-world data. They then pre-train SymTime, a foundation model that learns series representations using the symbolic side. Fine-tuned on downstream tasks, SymTime stayed competitive across five major time series task types. It rivaled foundation models pre-trained on real data sets, the authors report. The code is publicly available for reuse.
arxiv-2510-08745:
Karmakar and Mandal study fluid flow through a channel partly filled with a porous layer, in this 2025 arXiv paper on applied fluid mechanics. The fluid changes thickness as it moves, and the porous layer lets fluid pass more easily in some directions than in others. Part of the channel flows freely, while flow inside the layer feels drag and inertia at once.

Standard math methods solve the flow well when the layer is very open or very tight, but they fail in the middle range. To cover that gap, the pair train a neural network, a computer model that learns patterns from examples, with a fitting method that adjusts its own step size. The model also describes shear stress in artery blood flow and points to designs for tiny devices that mimic blood vessel lining.
arxiv-2510-08945:
Hildebrand and co-authors benchmark whole retrieval-augmented AI systems, not just their parts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such systems fetch documents and ground a language model's answers in them, a design meant to cut invented facts. Existing tests probe retrieval alone, leaving the full pipeline's digestion of mixed material unmeasured. Their test set holds ninety-three human-written questions spanning text, tables, images, and facts split across documents.

They score answers by phrase-level recall and flag likely hallucinations with a nearest-neighbor classifier over embeddings. Two open-source pipelines faced four closed commercial systems. The closed systems won clearly on both correctness and hallucination scores, and their lead widened on questions needing several modalities or several documents. Human judges rated both scoring metrics above four and a half on a five-point scale. The team works at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.
arxiv-2510-09045:
Chakraborty, Ghosh, and Gupta make long programs translatable by language models through a renaming trick, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Translating code between programming languages is a natural job for these models, but long files overflow their reading window and the translation degrades. Much of that bulk is identifiers, the names programmers give to variables and functions, which can be extremely long in real projects.

Their method swaps each long identifier for a short general placeholder before translation, and swaps back afterward. Freed from the names, the model can spend its limited window on the code's logical structure. The approach needs no examples or training, working zero-shot. In experiments, translations kept the code's syntax and hierarchy intact while using noticeably fewer tokens. The authors frame the savings as both an accuracy gain and a cost cut, since model providers charge by the token.
arxiv-2510-09245:
Guo and co-authors change a speaker's voice in real time by training their converter entirely on synthetic examples, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Voice conversion keeps the words but swaps the timbre, making one person sound like another. Streaming versions lag behind offline ones: they are slow, lean on speech recognition modules, or wrestle to separate content from identity, which leaks the original voice through. SynthVC sidesteps that separation problem altogether.

A pre-trained zero-shot converter first manufactures parallel training data, the same sentences in source and target voices. SynthVC learns the timbre transformation directly from those pairs, end to end. Built on a neural audio codec, it converts with low latency and high fidelity. It beat baseline streaming systems on naturalness and similarity to the target speaker, with an end-to-end delay of about seventy-seven milliseconds.
arxiv-2510-09345:
Subaru Nomoto, the sole author, studies curves in four-dimensional Lorentz space in a 2025 arXiv paper in differential geometry. A Bishop frame is a set of axes that travels along a curve, and a generalised Bishop frame lets the axes rotate by rules written as a matrix. Nomoto had earlier defined such frames for curves in ordinary four-dimensional Euclidean space and ranked their types in a hierarchy.

The new work moves to regular time-like curves, meaning curves whose direction behaves like a path through time in relativity. Four types of these frames exist once the tangent direction is fixed first. Unlike light-like or space-like curves, the time-like case mirrors the Euclidean one closely. Nomoto shows the same hierarchy of frame types holds there, and uses it to propose a fresh classification of the curves themselves.
arxiv-2510-09745:
Jakub Klencki and Brian Metzger explain a class of brilliant cosmic flashes in a 2025 arXiv paper. Luminous fast blue optical transients rise and fade in days at extreme brightness, and their engines are debated. The authors link them to binaries where a massive star feeds a black hole companion through a long phase of stable mass transfer.

In many, the transfer ends in a delayed dynamical instability. The black hole plunges into the donor, ejects about ten solar masses of enriched gas, and disrupts the helium core, accreting far above the Eddington limit. Combining evolution models, analytic estimates, and population synthesis, the authors predict the transient population. The explosion shines by interaction with the ejecta, rising over days to enormous luminosities, with radio emission over months. These would be failed gravitational wave sources, binaries that never merge.
arxiv-2510-10245:
Zenati, Bariscan Bozkurt, and Arthur Gretton study treatment effects with adaptively gathered data in this 2025 arXiv paper on causal inference. Adaptive trials assign treatments based on past outcomes, which boosts efficiency but breaks the random sampling that classical statistics assumes. Many questions are also distributional, asking how a treatment shifts the whole spread of outcomes.

Kernel treatment effects encode counterfactual outcome laws in a kernel space and compare them with kernel distances. The authors build the theory for adaptive data, where the standard limit results fail. Sound inference under adaptivity matters for clinical and online trials, which adapt by design more and more, and still need honest statements of uncertainty.
arxiv-2510-10445:
Mohd Aariyan Khan, Hemant Rathi, and Dibakar Roychowdhury compute how electric charge flows in a model black hole, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They study Taub-NUT AdS black holes, an exotic family whose rotation drags nearby space along, an effect called frame dragging. Using a holographic method with probe D-branes, they calculate the direct current conductivity, which measures how easily charge moves.

Their results split by temperature. In the low temperature regime, the conductivity responds strongly to the Misner string, the feature that causes the frame dragging. The conductivity rises near the string, and the rise is sharper close to it than at points farther away. In the high temperature regime, the picture flips. The frame dragging effects fade sharply, and heat driven transport takes over from the charge carriers. The work shows how this unusual black hole geometry shapes charge flow.
arxiv-2510-10745:
Tyler P Evans and Eden Heyen question a simplifying habit in models of ion bombarded thin films, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Amorphous films under ion irradiation are often modeled as highly viscous fluids. Their ion enhanced fluidity, the ease with which the surface relaxes, is almost always treated as constant through the layer. But the fluidity comes from radiation induced defect kinetics inside the film, so it should vary with depth and with experimental settings.

The authors build a model that couples the defect kinetics to the continuum equations of a viscous thin film. Using realistic parameter values, they show the defect kinetics can meaningfully change predictions of surface relaxation and fluidity. The fluidity ends up depending sensitively on ion energy, species, flux, angle, and temperature. They discuss what this means for aligning theory with experiment, especially for nanopatterning silicon with low energy argon ions.
arxiv-2510-10945:
Haishan Ye, Xiangyu Chang, and Xi Chen unify derivative free optimization under one sketching idea, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Zeroth order methods optimize functions using only value queries, estimating gradients from finite differences. The plain random version suffers high variance and weak guarantees. The team's framework views both classic estimators through oblivious randomized sketching: random linear compressions chosen without looking at the data. Properly chosen sketch matrices, they show, can slash the variance of random finite difference estimates.

That control delivers high probability convergence guarantees, which random finite difference analyses rarely provide. On convex quadratic problems, their query complexity depends on the trace of the Hessian matrix rather than the full dimension. When the Hessian's eigenvalues decay fast, that is dramatically cheaper than standard bounds that grow linearly with dimension. The advantages extend to strongly convex and Hessian aware settings.
arxiv-2510-11045:
Yicheng Guang and three co-authors propose analyzing ordinary software with quantum computers, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classical program analysis, techniques like symbolic execution, verifies correctness and guides compilers. But programs with huge or exponential state spaces defeat these tools. Quantum computing offers parallelism over superposed states. The team's QEX design synthesizes quantum circuits that encode many program states at once in superposition, and traces how variables depend on each other through entanglement.

As a proof of concept, QEX analyzed 22 benchmark programs successfully. To broaden language support and arrive sooner on fault tolerant hardware, the authors propose QEX-H, which mixes the quantum analysis with classical tools. They describe the work as the first proposal to use quantum computing for classical program analysis. Applications range from debugging and security checks to compiler tuning for future hardware.
arxiv-2510-11145:
Modern radio telescopes produce more data than astronomers can inspect by hand, so machine learning has become a core analysis tool. Nikhel Gupta summarizes recent studies of machine learning frameworks for large-scale radio surveys in this 2025 arXiv review paper. The work centers on the Evolutionary Map of the Universe survey, carried out with the ASKAP telescope in Australia.

Gupta reviews methods for detecting and classifying radio galaxies and for hunting down peculiar sources that do not fit known classes. The studies span supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, and weakly supervised learning, each suited to different amounts of labeled data across all four families. Large surveys now generate over 100 petabytes of data each year, which makes automated pipelines essential rather than optional. The paper draws lessons for ongoing surveys and for the even larger data flows expected from future radio facilities.
arxiv-2510-11545:
Model providers face a dilemma: showing users a model's full reasoning builds trust, but those traces are perfect training data for rivals who want to distill the model into their own. Jiayu Ding and co-authors propose PART, a reformulation method that keeps traces useful to humans while poisoning them for distillation, in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. 

PART rewrites traces in two steps: it removes the model's self-talk behaviors and reorders sub-conclusions, preserving the information a reader needs while disrupting what supervised fine-tuning feeds on. A small auxiliary model performs the reformulation with minimal computational overhead. Across student models of different sizes and types and several reasoning benchmarks, training on reformulated traces consistently degraded the students. A 32-billion-parameter student's score on the AIME 2024 benchmark fell from 54.17 to 46.88, a thirteen and a half percent degradation, when it trained on PART-processed traces.
arxiv-2510-11945:
Ethan T. Ritz and five colleagues build a bookkeeping tool that explains where a material's stiffness comes from. Standard calculations give a solid's total energy but not which electrons earn it. Their 2025 arXiv paper partitions that energy among individual electronic states, using maximally localized Wannier functions, compact orbitals centered on atoms. The split works for any property defined as an energy derivative.

The team demonstrates the method on a mystery in lead titanate, a ferroelectric material used in sensors and actuators. Under applied stress this crystal shows a curious elastic anomaly that had gone unexplained. The orbital-resolved accounts point to the s and p orbitals of the apical oxygen atoms, the oxygens sitting above and below the titanium. Those states carry the anomalous response. The authors argue the technique can expose the chemical origins of mechanical behavior generally, guiding chemists who design materials with tailored stiffness or flexibility.
arxiv-2510-12045:
Onur Eren Arpaci, Raouf Boutaba, and Florian Kerschbaum help rival organizations hunt shared intruders without exposing their logs. Collaborative intrusion detection needs the IP addresses that appear across several partners' networks. Raw addresses are sensitive, even legally protected personal data. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a private protocol for exactly this overlap hunt.

The over-threshold private set intersection protocol reveals only addresses present in at least t participants' sets, a tunable quorum. Everything else stays hidden. A novel hashing scheme slashes the computational complexity compared with the previous best protocol, making real network logs practical to process. The team tested it on joint logs from multiple institutions. Two deployment flavors trade safety for economy. One is collusion-safe, with stronger guarantees and more communication. The other is non-interactive and far cheaper, trusting the collector not to collude. The design fits how security alliances actually share intelligence.
arxiv-2510-12145:
Bibhu Prasad Tripathy and three colleagues hunt numbers belonging to two famous families at once. Padovan, Perrin, and Narayana's cows numbers grow from simple three-term recurrences, each term built from earlier ones. Thabit and Williams numbers have a different shape, built from powers of a base with small adjustments. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks which recurrence numbers also wear the Thabit-Williams form, in any base.

The team solves the resulting Diophantine equations completely for the overlapping families, determining exactly which Padovan, Perrin, and Narayana numbers qualify. For bases from two through ten, they enumerate all solutions of the governing equations. The machinery is the modern standard. Linear forms in logarithms bound the exponents, and a reduction method shrinks those bounds until computers finish. The finished catalogs close three chapters in the audit of special numbers.
arxiv-2510-12245:
Yin and colleagues present MoRA, a method that adapts a large language model to a specific molecule on the fly, in a 2025 arXiv paper on drug discovery. Linking molecular graph structures to language models is hard, and most methods fine tune the model or attach one fixed adapter for all molecules. A shared adapter cannot capture what makes each structure distinct, and fine tuning can erode the model's general reasoning.

MoRA generates a unique set of low rank adaptation parameters for each input molecular graph. The weights are injected into a frozen language model, so the model tailors its reasoning to that molecule while keeping its core knowledge intact. In experiments MoRA beat statically adapted baselines on chemical reaction prediction and molecular captioning. It improved reaction prediction exact match by a relative fourteen percent and cut error in quantum property prediction by about a fifth.
arxiv-2510-12345:
Boulite and co-authors prove new estimates that make it possible to steer a random heat like equation to zero, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. These are forward stochastic parabolic equations, where noise acts throughout space and time and the boundary itself evolves as heat crosses it.

The core tool is a Carleman estimate, a weighted inequality that quantifies how much of a solution can hide from observation. They derive one for a backward equation with general dynamic boundary conditions and weak divergence source terms in both bulk and surface equations. They refine a known estimate to track dependence on the final control time, then use duality to handle the source terms. They prove null and approximate controllability of the forward equations with reaction and convection terms. They also give an explicit estimate of the null controllability cost from the final time and the coefficients.
arxiv-2510-12645:
Gault and a large team hunt for winds driven out of a small star forming galaxy by its own stars, and find surprisingly little, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Stellar feedback should blow gas out of low mass galaxies easily, since their shallow gravity wells cannot hold it. Resolved observations are scarce because the winds are faint and transient.

This pilot study of a planned forty galaxy survey examines the dwarf galaxy NGC 3741. It uses new optical imaging and spectroscopy, radio observations of its neutral hydrogen, and star formation histories from resolved Hubble photometry. Comparing neutral and ionized gas shapes and motions, the team calculates mass loading factors, the ratio of outflowing to star forming mass. Despite a current starburst, mass loading factors are very low and strong outflow signatures are absent. The authors suggest the recent star formation surge has not produced enough massive stars to drive powerful winds.
arxiv-2510-13045:
Banerjee and Zeng use topological superconductors to test a diagnostic for gapless topological phases in this 2025 arXiv paper. Topological phases are usually identified through their entanglement spectrum, the fingerprint left when a system is split in two, but that tool was developed for systems with an energy gap. Gapless systems, whose bulk excitations cost arbitrarily little energy, are harder to characterize.

The authors work with free fermion models of bulk gapless topological superconductors in one and two dimensions. They show that the subsystem correlation spectrum, equivalent to the entanglement spectrum for such models, carries clear signatures of the ground state's topology. Both edge modes and bulk low-energy modes appear in the spectrum, though with different behaviors. The work extends the classic Li-Haldane entanglement characterization of topological edge states to two-dimensional systems with gapless bulk.
arxiv-2510-13445:
Mazuelas and Álvarez present RMBoost, a boosting method designed to stay accurate when training labels contain errors. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a known fragility: boosting often degrades sharply under label noise. Earlier robust methods guaranteed safety only for narrow noise types and ideal sample sizes. Some also gave mediocre accuracy even on clean data.

RMBoost minimizes worst-case error probabilities rather than average losses. This minimax design makes it robust to general forms of label noise. The authors prove finite-sample guarantees against two yardsticks. One compares its error with the error reached on noise-free data. The other compares it with the best achievable error, the Bayes risk. Experiments back the theory: the method resisted label noise in tests. It also delivered strong classification accuracy in its own right.
arxiv-2510-13645:
Cui, Qi, Hu, and Li pick apart odd dark current quirks in silicon sensors built for space telescopes. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies phosphorus-doped blocked-impurity-band detectors, which sense mid-to-far infrared light. These devices show strange effects, like current that resists in reverse and swings alone. Dark current, the signal a sensor makes with no light, caps how faint a source it can see.

The team traces the quirks to current paths bunching up inside the device. Messy internal structure plus the way charge moves through the impurity band drives the bunching, their tests show. Modelled curves match lab tests closely across a wide bias range. That match backs their account of how charge moves through the device. They also train a neural net on dark current data. The net forecasts dark current trends under new settings, guiding how the sensors get tuned.
arxiv-2510-13845:
Kadambi and co-authors argue that multimodal language models need bodies, both outside and inside, to truly understand the world. Their 2025 arXiv paper reviews how these models still fail at situated physical and social interaction. A rotated point-light figure of a walking person gets misread as a constellation. Such errors expose missing grounding in lived bodily experience.

The authors describe mechanisms of external embodiment: acting and sensing in the world. Internal embodiment covers interoception, the sensing of one's own states and drives. Humans fuse both streams constantly, and the paper maps each onto current model advances. Early alignment work already borrows fragments of these representations. Their dual-embodied framework proposes modelling the interaction between the two forms explicitly. Bridging multimodal data and world experience is the stated frontier. The review sets an agenda rather than reporting new experiments.
arxiv-2510-13945:
Xucheng Gan, Hyungjin Kim, and Andrea Mitridate ask whether pulsar timing arrays can detect ultralight dark matter that interacts with ordinary matter in a quadratic way, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Pulsar timing arrays track flashes from spinning neutron stars across the galaxy, and dark matter passing through would subtly shift the arrival times. Quadratic coupling means the effect grows with the square of the dark matter field.

The authors characterize two kinds of signal, coherent oscillations and random stochastic fluctuations, including how dark matter behaves inside matter of finite density. For coherent signals, they find current pulsar timing sensitivity rivals, and sometimes beats, established probes such as equivalence-principle tests and atomic clocks. Stochastic signals fare worse: both existing and upcoming pulsar data sets underperform the equivalence-principle limits. Their results map where pulsar timing genuinely adds power in the hunt for ultralight dark matter.
arxiv-2510-14345:
Ahmad Sheykhi and Leila Liravi derive cosmology from an unexpected starting point, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The starting point is MOND, the modified Newtonian dynamics invented to explain galaxy rotation without dark matter. It is combined with the idea that gravity is thermodynamic in origin. If spacetime horizons carry entropy like black holes do, Einstein's equations can emerge from thermodynamics, and changing the entropy should change the cosmology.
