Working backwards, the authors construct a general entropy expression for the horizon matching MOND, then insert the corrected entropy into the thermodynamics-gravity correspondence. They recover the modified Friedmann equation, which governs the universe's expansion, by three independent routes: the first law of thermodynamics, the entropic force scenario, and the emergence-of-gravity picture. They confirm the second law still holds for the universe inside its apparent horizon, and argue MOND may be deduced from modified horizon entropy, filling a gap.
arxiv-2510-14645:
Menon and co-authors look, in a 2025 arXiv paper, for wasted effort in streaming video encoding. Adaptive streaming needs one video encoded at many bitrates, so viewers on different connections all get a suitable version. The VVC standard compresses very well, but it is heavy to compute, and repeating the full job at every bitrate multiplies the cost.

Encoders split each frame into coding units, and deciding how to split them is much of the work. The authors reuse that decision across bitrates. Their single- and double-bound strategies take depth limits from a reference encode and constrain the other encodes, so they skip splits already ruled out. Tested with the VVenC encoder at several presets, the methods cut encoding time by up to 11.69 percent in the reported runs, with bitrate overhead under 0.6 percent and video quality essentially preserved.
arxiv-2510-14745:
Alés and co-authors examine, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how the artificial thermostat used in simulations quietly changes the transport properties being measured. In dilute gases, quantities like thermal conductivity, self-diffusion, and viscosity are set by collisions between atoms, which depend on the force law between them. Simulations often hold temperature steady with a Langevin thermostat, a friction-and-noise device, without asking what it does to the numbers.

The team ran molecular dynamics simulations for several interaction laws: soft-core and hard-core potentials, each with and without an attractive region. They paired the simulations with a theory built on an electrical analogy, in which the thermostat acts like a resistor in a series circuit. Coefficients were then derived by treating the thermostat as that resistance. Comparing across potentials and couplings shows how strongly the measurement setup itself shapes the reported values.
arxiv-2510-14845:
Abdelraheem, Favero, Bovet, and Frossard ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether a backdoor can be scrubbed from a foundation model without retraining it. A backdoor is a hidden trigger: show the model a marked input and it misbehaves, while behaving normally otherwise. Retraining huge models for safety is impractical, and fine-tuning the backdoor away tends to damage unrelated abilities.

The authors study how backdoors are stored in the model's weights. They find the backdoor's influence is disentangled from the features serving benign tasks, sitting in its own separable component. Their unlearning method isolates and erases that component. On CLIP-based vision models with common triggers, and given knowledge of the attack, the method achieved approximately perfect unlearning while keeping ninety-six percent of clean accuracy on average. It also remained effective when the attack and its presence were unknown beforehand.
arxiv-2510-14945:
Lee and co-authors present 3DScenePrompt, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a video generation framework that keeps a scene consistent while the camera moves freely. Most generators condition on one image or a short clip, so over long sequences the setting drifts and camera commands lose precision. The authors condition on the input video, split two ways.

Temporally adjacent frames guide motion continuity, while spatially adjacent content anchors the scene. The catch is that copying spatial neighbors would freeze moving objects in place. So the team builds a 3D scene memory holding static geometry. It is extracted from the input with dynamic SLAM, plus a masking strategy that strips moving elements out. This model is projected into any target viewpoint, producing warped views that serve as prompts, while dynamic regions evolve from the temporal context. The result is long-range spatial coherence and precise camera control over arbitrary-length continuations.
arxiv-2510-15145:
Xiao Li and five colleagues ask how much cold hydrogen gas truly remains in massive galaxies that have stopped forming stars. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that such quiescent galaxies are known to be gas-poor, but older surveys lacked the sensitivity to say how poor. The team used FAST, China's giant radio telescope, for far deeper observations.

They observed seventy-eight nearby massive, red galaxies chosen by mass and color, reaching a detection limit far below earlier surveys. Only about a third matched the gas levels older surveys had predicted; the other two-thirds held far less gas, often below detection even when their signals were stacked. Gas content showed no clear link to star formation, shape, or structure. The pattern closely matched a known sample of early-type galaxies, hinting that both galaxy type and environment drain gas, though neither alone explains the extreme shortage.
arxiv-2510-15545:
Sibo Xiao, Jinyuan Fu, Zhongle Xie, and Lidan Shou speed up large language models by letting a small model draft text for a big one to check. Their 2025 arXiv paper works on speculative decoding, where the checker accepts or rejects drafted tokens. The catch is that both models must share the same vocabulary, which rules out most ready-made draft models.

Their algorithm, TokenTiming, borrows dynamic time warping, a classic method for aligning two time series. It re-encodes the draft's tokens into the target model's vocabulary and builds a mapping that transfers token probabilities between them. Any off-the-shelf pair can then work together with no retraining. Across several tasks the method delivered a speedup of about one and a half times. The team presents it as a universal way to pick draft models.
arxiv-2510-15845:
M Saad Bin-Alam and colleagues report new photonic devices in a 2025 paper. They built the first microring resonators from Huygens' metawaveguides. Couplers were built the same way. These waveguides steer light through engineered resonant elements. The devices target the standard telecommunications wavelength. They aim to give chip designers finer control. Light propagation and coupling between guides are the focus.

The team demonstrated efficient evanescent coupling. Light hops between neighbouring guides this way. Coupling worked in both the same and opposite directions. The resonators showed high quality factors. They also showed unusual properties. These include a negative group index and near-zero dispersion. Such traits could serve compact optical circuits. On-chip signal processing is another use.
arxiv-2510-16245:
Antonio Gómez-Bañón, Pantelis Pnigouras, and José A Pons ask what happens if axions pool inside neutron stars. Axions are light particles dreamed up to fix a puzzle in the strong nuclear force. They might clump into a condensate, a shared quantum state, in dense star cores. That would give the star a new kind of ground state.

The team builds star models with a trusted matter recipe and solves for steady shapes with the axion field included. They then ring the stars in math and watch the tones fade. Two tone families appear: gentle fluid tones that fade slowly, and axion tones that die fast. The axion also drains the fluid tones above its own mass, with fading times of mere seconds. Such ringing is hard to catch, but the work sketches how star quakes could one day probe axions.
arxiv-2510-16445:
Chien Thai leads four co-authors in a 2025 study on finding turned objects in images. Boxes that sit straight fail on objects at an angle, like planes in air photos. Their fix draws each object as a soft oval blob, called a Gaussian box. It then scores box match with a distance that suits oval shapes.

The oval can stretch more in one direction than the other. That helps with near-square objects, where old scores blur the angle. A loss term that ignores pure spin keeps training steady. Tests on known detectors show clear gains in mean score. Better turned-object finds help air surveys, road scenes, and self-driving cars.
arxiv-2510-16645:
Zhixuan He and Yue Feng let four AI agents debate in a 2025 study on clear reasoning. Single models can be strong yet hide how they reach a call. Their frame, DiMo, splits thought into four set modes of reasoning. Each agent holds one mode and argues its case in the open. Rounds of debate let agents probe and hone each other's drafts.

The merged result is both stronger and easier to audit. Tests span six benchmarks in one open setup for all runs. DiMo beat solo models and past debate frames on scores. Maths tasks gained the most from the clash of modes. The frame can tag each claim with source links for checks. Clear chains help users trust and reuse model work.
arxiv-2510-17045:
Deepak Sridhar leads five co-authors in making video reasoning cheaper in a 2025 paper. Large multimodal models reason about video through long written chains. Training them with reinforcement learning is expensive. Their thinking length is also hard to control at runtime.

The team studied entropy, a measure of the model's output uncertainty. Good models showed cycles of brief exploration and brief settling. Later they showed a longer thinking peak and confident endings. The authors turned that pattern into an inference-time controller. The controller adjusts the model's memory cache while it answers. No retraining or fine-tuning is involved at all. Experiments showed clear gains over the base model. The approach offers cheaper reasoning control for video question answering.
arxiv-2510-17145:
Phi-Hung Hoang and three co-authors grade fish freshness from eye photos in this 2025 paper. Freshness sets price and health risk, yet human checks vary and lack a fixed scale. Spoilage signs in eyes are faint and differ by fish type. The team builds scores from hand-made traits of each photo.

Traits cover color spread, tone bands, and surface marks in the eye. The team adds trait groups step by step to test each one's worth. One tuned tree model beat a prior deep model by a wide margin. With more training photos, a neural net scored near ninety-seven percent right. The clear trait list helps shops check fish in a steady way.
arxiv-2510-17245:
Wenyu Mao and five co-authors speed up diffusion-based recommenders in this 2025 paper. Such systems guess the next item a user will pick, step by step. Each step chips noise off a draft pick in many rounds. Many rounds cost time and add step error to the pick.

Their two-stage frame smooths the chip path so one step can suffice. A time-match rule keeps close steps in line while training. A later tune step bends picks toward true user likes. The tune weight shifts with like-pair match and step time. Tests show the frame cuts step error and lifts pick quality. It thus eases the speed versus truth trade-off in such systems.
arxiv-2510-17345:
A sound scene classifier trained on one recorder often stumbles when a different device captures the sound. Peihong Zhang, joined by six co-authors, targets that device shift problem, which grows worse when labelled examples are few. Earlier fixes ordered training examples from easy to hard, but they fixed that order before training began and never updated it.

Zhang and her co-authors propose a dynamic schedule that recalculates two signals after each training round: how device independent an example looks, and how much the model is still learning from it. Early rounds favour steady examples, and later rounds give more weight to device specific ones. Under a standard contest protocol, the schedule lifted cross-device scores across several base models.
arxiv-2510-17445:
Mohd Saif Ali Khan, with Karthik RM and Samar Agnihotri, tackles signals in cell free networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. In these networks, many small access points serve users together instead of one large tower. A central unit usually merges their signals, but that needs channel data from every access point. Local merging rules can also leave too much interference, meaning unwanted signals from other users.

The team offers a merged design that needs only local channel data at each point. They also recast merging as a choice about how to split antenna freedom between blocking interference and boosting signal. Their adaptive method picks the best split at each access point. Computer tests show clear gains over older schemes.
arxiv-2510-17545:
Yichen Liu, with Yan Lin and four co-authors, presents a vehicle trajectory learning model in a 2025 arXiv paper. GPS traces record how cars move through a city over time. These traces carry clues about travel patterns and trip purposes. Two problems block learning from them: road and place details are costly to encode, and traces hold many redundant points.

Their model, called TrajMamba, reads both GPS points and road layout to capture movement. A pre training step folds trip purpose into the learned codes without slowing later use. A second step learns which points matter most and compresses the rest away. Tests on two real datasets and three tasks beat prior methods on speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2510-17745:
Lars Niedermeier, Vyom Shah, and Jeffrey L. Krichmar built software for brain-like chips at the edge. Edge devices process sensor data on site, without cloud links. Their target is spiking neural networks, which send brief pulses instead of steady signals. Such networks suit low-power neuromorphic hardware, meaning chips modeled on brains.

Their multi-threading kernel splits work across all cores of a processor. On mid-size networks it ran about four times faster than one thread. It also used up to seventy percent less energy than fixed core assignment. Balanced loading across cores explains much of that saving. The kernel may help future low-power devices that use neuromorphic chips.
arxiv-2510-17845:
Jusheng Zhang and four co-authors treat the training of an image labeler as a team job done live by software agents. In their MAT-Agent system, agents adjust data changes, the optimizer, learning rates, and loss terms while training runs. A bandit method balances trying new settings against keeping ones that already work well.

Rewards blend accuracy, rare-class results, and steady training. On three public image sets, the system beat the compared methods on the main scores the authors track. The paper gives a concrete design for readers who want training that adapts itself instead of following fixed settings.
arxiv-2510-17945:
Sandro Andric, as sole author, proves an exact link between control effort and a quantile gap in a class of linear systems with Gaussian noise. The setting asks for the cheapest control that pushes a system into a target half-space by a set time. Effort is measured with a quadratic cost over the control path.

The cheapest energy, the proof shows, equals a squared quantile gap scaled by a ratio of control reach to noise spread. A matched-filter control reaches that bound, and a discrete-time twin result is given. Links to risk-sensitive control and bridge problems follow, with Monte Carlo checks.
arxiv-2510-18045:
Gerlind Plonka and Anahita Riahi rebuild images from only a few rows of their Fourier data, a pattern driven by parallel MRI needs. The rows kept near the center of frequency space carry the broad shapes, and their width turns out to be crucial. Too few or too many central rows both hurt the recovery.

The authors prove that fixed, non-adaptive schemes cannot give satisfying results here. Their hybrid method blends an edge-preserving minimization with tricks tied to the special sampling pattern. On both natural and cartoon-like images it performed very well. Imaging readers get guidance on which frequencies are worth paying for.
arxiv-2510-18145:
Sakineh Vosoughi-nia and Michał P Nowak design a superconducting qubit that needs no magnetic field, using a new class of magnets. Altermagnets split electron behavior in ways that can shape Josephson junctions. The study computes the bound states of a narrow junction and shows how two symmetry patterns differ sharply.

One pattern splits spins, while the other keeps spin pairs whole and splits states through mode mixing instead. A sideways electric field can then tune the device into a parity-protected qubit, which the authors name altermon. Quantum hardware readers get a field-free route to a protected qubit design.
arxiv-2510-18345:
Yudong Li and his three co-authors, Hao Li, Xianxu Hou, and Linlin Shen, introduce GPTFace, a model meant to learn about human faces from material gathered on the web. Most face models are trained on sets of photos that people labeled by hand, which takes great effort and limits how far the models can grow. GPTFace learns instead from weakly matched pairs of face images and text.

During training, parts of images and text are hidden so the model must fill them in, and the model also learns to judge whether an image and a text belong together. On later tests, the finished model matched leading systems at tasks such as naming face traits and reading expressions. It could also edit faces, change expressions, remove masks, and fill in missing parts of photos.
arxiv-2510-18545:
Greivin Alfaro Miranda and his five co-authors study a phase of matter called many-body localization, where a disordered quantum system fails to settle into equilibrium. Rare resonances spanning the whole system may decide whether that phase survives, so their statistical weight matters. The team borrows a method from the theory of disordered glasses to characterize how signals travel between far-apart configurations of a disordered spin chain.

A control knob in their method, playing the role of a temperature, tunes how strongly extreme outliers count. Three regimes emerge: an ergodic phase where signals spread evenly, a middle regime where rare long-range resonances drive spreading, and a robust localized phase that resonances cannot break. Their phase diagram matches recent numerical results, and they show that even tiny interactions can destroy the non-interacting insulator at finite disorder.
arxiv-2510-18745:
Taha Binhuraib, with Greta Tuckute and Nicholas Blauch, gives transformer language models a brain-like spatial layout. In real brains, neurons are arranged topographically: cells with similar jobs sit near each other. Standard transformers instead store representations in unordered vector spaces that are hard to visualize or interpret.

Their Topoformer redesigns self-attention so that queries and keys live on two-dimensional grids, with local pools of queries tied to each key, and rewires the attention layer to connect only locally. A small sentiment model first proved the idea workable, with organization emerging in different parts of the layer. Scaled up to a BERT-style model trained on masked language modeling, the topographic version matched the ordinary model on language benchmarks while producing interpretable maps across eight linguistic test suites. The authors also compared the organization with human brain responses to natural sentences.
arxiv-2510-18845:
Ryan Teoh and his six co-authors extend a safety framework for robots facing an adversary. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability computes value functions that guarantee safety against worst-case disturbances, but exact computation collapses in high dimensions. Neural approximations scale better yet converge slowly and inaccurately, partly because the learning signal from the underlying equation is weak.

Their framework guides the neural training with model predictive control, an established technique that supplies regular supervision drawn from the structure of the control problem itself. Earlier guided approaches handled only single-player problems and simple games, while this one targets the full two-player, zero-sum setting, returning optimal strategies for both sides and safe policies under worst-case attack. Across many simulated and real robotic systems with varied dynamics, the method beat leading baselines in simulation and performed impressively on hardware.
arxiv-2510-19145:
Sanskar Amgain and four co-authors introduce HAMLOCK, an attack that splits a backdoor between a neural network model and the hardware that runs it. Third-party accelerators are now common, and ordinary backdoors hide all their logic in model weights, leaving a traceable pattern that detectors can find layer by layer.

Under HAMLOCK, the model is barely changed, with a few neurons tuned to fire unusually high values when a trigger appears. A hardware Trojan watches for that signal and completes the attack. Splitting the logic across the software-hardware boundary makes the threat far stealthier, and a warning to accelerator buyers.
arxiv-2510-19245:
Yimeng Zhang and twelve co-authors study how vision-language agents simulate online shoppers, arguing that text alone misses how web page appearance shapes buying choices. Earlier simulators improved action prediction with training on action traces and reinforcement learning, yet they read pages as text and ignore screenshots entirely.

Using a dataset of real shopping sessions, the authors ground agent decisions in both page text and screenshots. Seeing the page as users do should narrow the gap between synthetic shoppers and real ones. Better simulations help retailers test store designs without experimenting on actual customers.
arxiv-2510-19345:
Alvaro Perez-Diaz and three co-authors argue that the form of a forecast matters as much as its accuracy for time series foundation models. A forecast can be a single point, a range of quantiles, a full distribution, or an ensemble of full trajectories. Each form supports different real decisions.

Surveying recent models, they find two-thirds emit only point or simple distribution forecasts, while many practical tasks need trajectory ensembles that keep time dependence intact. Trajectory ensembles can be reduced to simpler forms freely. But the reverse needs extra assumptions. The authors prove some path-dependent risks cannot be recovered from marginal forecasts at all.
arxiv-2510-19445:
Carles Roch I Carceller and four co-authors certify quantum randomness from sequential measurements. The measurements happen one after another on the same system. Real devices reveal only partial information. Sequential access can extract more. Certification must stay honest even when attackers adapt. Their strategy can shift as results come in.

The team uses sequential maximum confidence measurements. The setting is semi-device-independent. Numerical tools bound how much randomness can be certified. A duality technique supplies key tradeoff functions. Those functions support entropy accumulation, the standard guard against adaptive attacks. The frame suits real quantum cryptography work.
arxiv-2510-19645:
The STAR Collaboration compares flow patterns in small nuclear collision systems to test whether tiny drops of quark-gluon plasma form there. Flow in such small systems is puzzling. The starting shape mixes where the nucleons sit with jitter inside the nucleons. The team measured elliptic and triangular flow in deuteron-gold hits, which are lopsided, and oxygen-oxygen hits, which are symmetric, at two hundred giga-electron-volts.

The two systems make matter of like size but with very unlike starting shapes. Elliptic flow was larger in deuteron-gold, matching its stretched shape. Triangular flow was alike in both, which points to the jitter inside nucleons as its source. A fluid model tuned on large systems matched the patterns well, backing the idea of plasma-like drops even in these small hits.
arxiv-2510-20445:
Giovanni Di Bartolomeo and three co-authors give a way to cut coherent slips in the build of stabilizer states on quantum gear. Such states back much of quantum work and are made well by Clifford gates. But small angle slips in real gates can harm their grade a lot. Their way, called VCEM, uses the stabilizer frame in a search over gate knobs to squash the slips.

Sim tests show the way works well and is near proof to stray noise. That split counts in use. Coherent slips can be pre-paid in this way, then stock tools clean the rest of the noise. The team frames the step as a strong first layer for quantum error work.
arxiv-2510-20845:
Michael Arnold Bruna, working alone, studies Schur paired curvature on folded exponential families that respect two sided symmetry on a simplex. Exponential families are a core class in stats, and folding them by symmetry creates curved shapes whose behavior was not well mapped.

Three structural results anchor the work, the curvature is convex in the log parameter, it has a single stationary point at a golden ratio value in key cases including twelve fold symmetry. It obeys a folded quadratic law whose coefficients come from an explicit projector metric. Symmetry and convexity alone thus fix both the golden lock in point and the form of the law, a neat rigidity result with echoes for signal and shape models.
arxiv-2510-20945:
Urs Frauenfelder and one co-author study the linearized Floer equation inside a chart that is not of Darboux type, a setting not treated before in this corner of symplectic geometry. The Hessian of the area functional in such a chart behaves in unusual ways that break standard assumptions.

A new structure, called an almost extendable weak Hessian field, is introduced to capture that behavior. The main result is a Fredholm theorem for Robbin Salamon operators tied to non continuous Hessians, proved by exploiting the new structure. Fredholm control is the gateway to counting solutions and building Floer theories on broader spaces.
arxiv-2510-21245:
Noah Oberweis and Semih Cayci analyze a training method that mixes gradient descent with random noise, viewed through a continuous-time equation. They focus on the lazy training regime, where a wide network barely moves from its starting values while it learns, a setting that makes the math tractable.

Under stated smoothness conditions on the loss, they show the process keeps a well-behaved kernel with high probability throughout training. They also prove fast, exponential convergence toward the best fit to the training data, in expectation, with explicit bounds tied to time and network width. Numerical examples in a regression setting match the theory, supporting the claim that noisy training stays stable in this regime.
arxiv-2510-21345:
Aymane El Firdoussi and three co-authors introduce a new family of fine-tuning methods for adapting pretrained models with little data. The best-known approach, LoRA, adds a small trainable matrix beside a frozen one, and the authors ask whether rescaling the base model itself can make such updates generalize better.

Their rescaling approach is set out as a broader class of reparameterizations that contains the usual additive style as a relative. They prove its value in a high-dimensional binary classification task, using random matrix theory to track how the tuned model behaves. They then check the findings in more realistic settings, including fine-tuning large language models, where the experiments support the theory.
arxiv-2510-21745:
Eashan Wadhwa and Shanker Shreejith trim the power hunger of FPGA chips by listening to their own simulations. Much of a chip's dynamic power burns in needless signal toggling. Classic countermeasures like gating or rewriting demand intrusive design surgery. They also fade as devices densify.

Their framework, Simopt-Power, profiles switching activity during simulation and hunts the hottest paths. It selectively reconfigures them. It duplicates small logic blocks along Shannon decomposition lines and relocates critical nets. Transitions then quiet down while the circuit's function stays untouched. On an open benchmark suite, switching-driven power falls by about nine percent on average. The cost is about nine percent more logic resources on arithmetic designs. That is a practical trade inside ordinary design flows.
arxiv-2510-21945:
Antoine Ledent, Rodrigo Alves, and Yunwen Lei ask why deep networks generalize instead of merely memorizing, focusing on a curious pattern. As networks deepen, their internal weight and activation tables settle into an approximately low-rank shape, as if the data forces a bottleneck.

Building on that observation, the trio proves learning guarantees that sharpen when the low-rank structure is present. The bounds run through a family of size measures for matrices, called Schatten quasi-norms, which stay small when a matrix is nearly low-rank. In plain terms, the number of examples needed grows with network width and depth but is discounted by the bottleneck rank. A network that compresses well needs less data to be trusted. The results connect a training habit, weight decay, to the same compression story.
arxiv-2510-22045:
Hyeonsu Kang, Emily Bao, and Anjan Goswami grade vision-language models on an everyday artifact they are increasingly asked to judge: presentation slides. As models take on critic roles in automated pipelines, slide understanding matters, yet it has rarely been tested on its own terms.

Their framework, VLM-SlideEval, probes three levels of skill. Models must extract slide elements to match ground truth pulled from real deck files, stay consistent when geometry, style, or wording is deliberately perturbed. Recover the story order of a deck whose slides have been shuffled. On public decks, the models fell short at pixel-accurate extraction and wobbled noticeably under controlled changes, while doing better at the broad comprehension tasks. The results map where slide-savvy evaluation still needs work.
arxiv-2510-22345:
David Anton, Henning Wessels, Ulrich Römer, Alexander Henkes, and Jorge-Humberto Urrea-Quintero put error bars on discovered material laws. Constitutive model discovery picks a formula for how a material deforms. The formula comes from a library of candidates. Its parameters are fit to test data at the same time. The data are noisy, so the law should carry honest uncertainty.

Earlier uncertainty methods had real limits. They forced users to choose parameter priors. They handled only models whose parameters enter linearly. Or they allowed only stiff distribution shapes. The team's partially Bayesian route enriches the stress-deformation data with a Gaussian process first. An interpretable model is then distilled from that richer posterior. Parameters that enter nonlinearly stay within reach. The prior-selection burden for them is skipped.
arxiv-2510-22845:
Testing a function for a forbidden pattern can be done with few queries. Harish Chandramouleeswaran, Ilan Newman, Tomer Pelleg, and Nithin Varma study that task in 2025. Their domain is a high dimensional grid, or hypergrid. A pattern is a small order type to avoid. Functions far from pattern free need many edits.

For two dimensions and size three patterns, they give a tester. It is adaptive and one sided. Query cost grows below linear in grid size. Lower bounds show nonadaptive testers need linear queries. Adaptive testers need at least square root queries. Monotone patterns admit far cheaper testers. That split is exponential in their results.
arxiv-2510-23045:
Guiyao Tie, Pan Zhou, and Lichao Sun survey the rise of AI scientists, systems meant to run the full research cycle on their own. Such a system would form hypotheses, run studies, and write up findings for publication. Systems have spread fast and in many forms, leaving the field fragmented and hard to compare.

The survey organizes the landscape, tracing shared methods and trends across designs. It clarifies what current systems can truly do, from idea generation to final synthesis. For researchers and funders, the map helps judge claims about automated discovery and spot the gaps that still need human judgment.
arxiv-2510-23345:
Zhen Cao and 326 co-authors of the LHAASO collaboration report the first detection of ultra-high-energy gamma rays from the binary system LS I plus 61 303. This prototypical gamma-ray binary pairs a massive star with a compact object. Data from the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory show emission above one hundred teraelectronvolts.

Two detector arrays saw the source at high significance, with sixteen photon-like events above that energy against about five expected background events. The detection proves extreme particle acceleration in the binary. Such systems become natural laboratories for how nature builds cosmic accelerators.
arxiv-2510-23845:
Grace Byun and four co-authors introduce CRADLE Bench, a benchmark for testing whether language models can spot mental health crises in conversation. The situations covered include suicidal ideation, rape, domestic violence, child abuse, and sexual harassment, where a missed flag can have grave consequences. Earlier benchmarks covered fewer crisis types and ignored how risk unfolds over time.

The benchmark spans seven crisis types defined along clinical lines and is the first to carry temporal labels. It holds six hundred clinician-annotated test examples and four hundred twenty development examples. A training set of about four thousand examples was labeled by majority vote across several models, which beat single-model labeling clearly. The authors also fine-tune six detection models on subsets split by how strongly the ensemble agreed. The result is a shared yardstick for a safety task that model builders have largely left unmeasured.
arxiv-2510-23945:
Sujay Champati and two co-authors ask whether long gamma-ray bursts really track the cosmic star formation rate across time, using a bigger sample than earlier studies. Long bursts are supposed to come from collapsing massive stars, so their numbers should mirror star birth, while short bursts follow with a delay. Doubts grew after several groups found too many long bursts at low redshift, and two nearby long bursts arrived with kilonovae, pointing at mergers instead.

The authors combine the enlarged set of bursts with measured redshifts and a second set whose redshifts come from machine learning. Non-parametric methods correct for the bias in which bursts get measured redshifts, yielding the luminosity evolution and luminosity function. The measured-redshift sample alone still shows the low-redshift excess. Adding the machine-learned redshifts, which pile up at middle distances, softens the excess rather than erasing the question.
arxiv-2510-24345:
Zikai Xiao and nine co-authors introduce LongWeave, a benchmark for long form text generation that is both realistic and objectively checkable. Producing long, informative, and factual output remains a major challenge for large language models. Earlier benchmarks either used real queries with metrics that are hard to verify or synthetic tasks that miss real world complexity.

LongWeave uses Constraint Verifier Evaluation: it first defines verifiable targets inside real world scenarios, then generates the queries, source materials, and constraints from those targets. This design keeps tasks realistic while making scoring rigorous. The benchmark aims to measure long generation quality in a way that reflects actual use.
arxiv-2510-24545:
Nicola Tuccari leads a team of five authors on visualizing huge simulations. Cosmology simulations now make more data than disks can hold. Writing all that data to disk has long slowed supercomputing. In-situ processing studies data while the simulation still runs. Nothing full is stored, so the storage bottleneck disappears.

Their tool, Hecuba, streams simulation data through a distributed database. It feeds viewing tools live, without files in between. They link Hecuba to ChaNGa, a high-performance cosmology simulator. N-body results, point clouds of stars and dark matter, appear on screen live. Viewers use ParaView and VisIVO, two known analysis tools. The work shows exascale runs can be watched as they unfold.
arxiv-2510-24645:
Zengzhuang Xu leads a team with sixteen co-authors who built a way to make training data for tool use by AI agents. Real tasks need many turns of talk and tool calls that depend on each other. Past ways to fake such data, like random picks or role play, were too weak.

Their frame, FunReason-MT, maps how tools link to each other so it can build set task paths. It also builds hard user asks in a clean way and grows a step by step thought chain. On a known tool call test board, data from this frame lifted scores for trained models.
arxiv-2510-24845:
T Dorstel, T Iadecola, J H Wilson, and M Buchhold study a hands on way to drive quantum systems into rich linked states. Their plan pairs checks on the system with small local fixes, with no need to throw runs away. The goal state is a dark state, one that all the checks leave alone.

How fast the system settles turns on how odd charges move through it, the team shows. Checks and stir steps both move those charges, so both set the clock. One base case maps to a walk that soaks in at a set rate. Chains with step like links settle far more slow, which marks the transport point.
arxiv-2510-24945:
Haoyuan Shi, Christopher J Mundy, Gregory K Schenter, and Jaehun Chun build a contact code for hard parts that are not round, with strict keep of total energy. Shape slant drives how such parts pack and move, in colloids and in grain flows. Past codes could let parts overlap or leak energy as they hit and spin.

Their frame checks hits from points, edges, and faces in two and three dimensions, in one joined form. Forces are read in a smooth way, so no overlap is let through while total energy holds. Runs on flat and solid shapes show pack acts and slant spread. The frame can grow to more hard cases of flow and self build.
arxiv-2510-25045:
Nicholas Loveday and Tracy Hertneky build a fair test to match an AI weather model with a classic fine grid model on hard rain. AI models now rival classic ones at less cost, but hard rain is where trust is won or lost. Space match counts here, and the two model grids do not line up.

Their frame joins space check tools with score rules that weight high rain lines more. Users can set how much each rain line counts for a call, to fit how a forecast desk would read it. A run of past hard rain cases shows the frame at work. It is built to test the events that hurt most, not mean days.
arxiv-2510-25545:
King Cho Wong led seventeen co-authors on super-Moire spin textures. Ruoming Peng, Eric Anderson, and Jackson Ross helped. Bowen Yang, Meixin Cheng, and Sreehari Jayaram joined. Many further collaborators in materials and microscopy joined. Their 2025 physics paper reports a new magnetic state. Stacking 2D layered materials engineers magnetic states.

Moire magnetism usually has unit cell periodicity. Their super-Moire state extends far beyond one cell. It appears in twisted double bilayer chromium triiodide. At small twist angles, texture size grows with angle. That is opposite to underlying Moire periodicity trend. Texture size reaches about three hundred nanometers maximum. It vanishes at twist angles above two degrees. Scanning quantum spin magnetometry produced vector field maps. Maps suggest antiferromagnetic Neel-type skyrmions spanning cells. Large-scale atomistic runs support the twist dependence. Magnetic competition between effects produces the topological textures. Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya effect, anisotropy, and exchange all compete.
arxiv-2510-25745:
Christodoulos Benetatos, Yongyi Zang, and Randal Leistikow separate vocal sources quickly. Their 2025 paper presents windowed sink attention for audio. leading vocal separation models use full time attention. Each frame interacts with every other frame there. Chunking and windowing methods are motivated by cost.

Time attention patterns concentrate nearby in time. Small time windows plus attention sinks are used. Fine-tuning from original checkpoint recovers most results. Ninety-two percent of original quality was recovered. Floating point operations fell by over forty times. Quick separation could run on smaller hardware. Their code and checkpoints are released openly.
arxiv-2510-25845:
Jinchao Zhao, Peizhi Mai, Gaurav Tenkila, and Philip W. Phillips argue that a key change in materials follows a simple symmetry rule. The Mott transition is the switch between a metal, which conducts, and an insulator, which does not, driven by electron repulsion. They claim the switch reflects the breaking of a two fold symmetry in momentum space, and that the energy gap in the insulator follows from that break.

Zhao and the team use large numerical runs to support the claim. Charge compressibility, how easily charge can be squeezed in, acts as the marker that is zero in the insulator and nonzero in the metal. Their scaling results also match recent cold atom simulator work.
arxiv-2510-25945:
Atsuhiro Yaginuma, Aster G. Taylor, and Darryl Z. Seligman model how heat moves inside the third known interstellar object, named 3I/ATLAS. The object, found in July twenty twenty five, follows a hyperbolic path through the solar system and shows comet like release of volatile gases. Comparing heat models with the observed onset of activity can reveal bulk traits of its nucleus.

Yaginuma and the team compute one dimensional temperature profiles with depth along the whole trajectory, trying typical comet and asteroid values for heat capacity, density, and conductivity. They benchmark the profiles against the temperatures where water, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide turn to gas. Early water activity near three astronomical units already constrains surface temperature in their model.
arxiv-2510-26245:
Juyeop Kim, Hyejin Shin, Sohee Kim, and Ilmu Byun work on locating a phone precisely from 5G signals. In 5G New Radio, a terminal position is found from the time of arrival of positioning reference signals sent by base stations. Accuracy suffers when the receiver samples the signal at a low rate, which is common in low cost hardware.

Kim and the team propose an algorithm that improves time of arrival accuracy under low sampling limits. They implement the positioning signals in a software defined modem, where radio functions run in software. They also study how flexible allocation of time and frequency resources for the signals affects accuracy, and discuss which configurations suit a given signal environment best.
arxiv-2510-26345:
Mykhailo Poliakov and Nadiya Shvai improve spotting of logical flawed claims in health false claims with made up training data. Claims that distort scientific findings are common and in a way that can do harm harmful, and flawed arguments are hard to spot. Their pipeline, MisSynth, uses lookup aided creation to produce made up fallacy samples modeled on the MISSCI data set and setup, which lists flawed claims in scientific false claims.

The made up samples fine tune a language model with lightweight methods. On the MISSCI test split, a fine tuned LLaMA model gained over thirty five percent in F1 score, an full gain over its vanilla baseline in their report. The work shows that made up adding made up data can lift performance even with limited labeled data and modest compute, and code and data are released.
arxiv-2510-26445:
Basile Husquinet, Julie Vitorino, Olli Sipilä, Paola Caselli, and François Dulieu test whether neon changes ice chemistry in space. Neon is the fifth most common element in the universe, but it is inert, so models of molecule building have ignored it. In pre-stellar cores, the cold clouds that precede stars, temperatures fall below ten kelvin, cold enough for neon to settle on dust grains.

Husquinet and his four co-authors grow carbon monoxide and hydrogen layers in a vacuum chamber, with and without neon, and also stack the layers in both orders. Neon cut the making of formaldehyde sharply: by thirty-eight percent at eleven kelvin with little neon, and by up to ninety-one percent at nine kelvin with a few layers. Methanol fell less, by up to seventy-seven percent. A gas-grain code shows where in a core this effect should matter.
arxiv-2510-26545:
Sujit K Dalui and Shantanu Desai test a claimed constant of dark matter halos. Observations suggest that halo surface density, the product of a halo's core radius and its central density, stays nearly the same across many galaxy types. The pair check this claim in the FIRE-2 simulations, which model galaxies with feedback from stars.

Dalui and Desai compute the surface density for dwarf galaxies of about ten billion solar masses. They use three setups: cold dark matter, self-interacting dark matter with baryons, and self-interacting dark matter without them. Mock catalogues from the simulations gave nearly constant surface and column densities in all three. Fits with the Burkert profile matched galactic observations within one standard step. Links between central surface density and peak speed also matched what is seen in Milky Way and Andromeda dwarfs.
arxiv-2510-26645:
Katarina Petrović, with seven co-authors, learns the hidden flow rules of natural systems from population snapshots. Flow matching models how a population moves between two distributions along paths of least action, which gives gradient dynamics. Some real systems, such as cell cycles in single-cell data, move in cycles instead, and gradient methods cannot capture that.

Petrović and the team present Curly Flow Matching, which builds a Schrödinger bridge problem with a nonzero drift reference process, made from inferred velocities plus snapshot data. That change lets the model learn non-gradient, periodic behaviour. Tests on single cells, fluid dynamics, and ocean currents showed trajectories that matched both the reference process and the population data better than rivals. The authors frame the method as a step from modelling populations to modelling known periodic behaviour.
arxiv-2510-26745:
Shahriar Noroozizadeh, Vaishnavh Nagarajan, Elan Rosenfeld, and Sanjiv Kumar report a surprising way deep sequence models store facts. The usual picture is associative memory: a lookup of things seen together. The team identifies geometric memory instead, where a model's embeddings encode global relations among all entities, even ones that never appeared together in training.

Noroozizadeh and his three co-authors show this storage is powerful: it can turn a hard multi-step reasoning task into a one-step navigation task. Oddly, the geometry arises even when it is more complex than brute-force lookup, and standard pressures do not explain it. By linking the effect to Node2Vec, a graph embedding method, they trace it to a spectral bias that arises naturally. They also point out headroom for making Transformer memory more strongly geometric.
arxiv-2510-27245:
Alik Pramanick, Mayank Bansal, and three other co-authors address a known flaw of image AI in their 2025 paper. Deep neural networks sort images well, yet tiny crafted changes can fool them into wrong answers. Such attacks matter where safety is on the line. Their defense, Trans-defense, first cleans the image, then sorts the cleaned copy.

The team found that attacks harm the fine detail of an image most. So the cleaner splits each image into broad shapes and fine detail, using a wavelet method, a math lens for that split. A transformer, an AI block that weighs parts against each other, then rebuilds a clean image. Retrained on cleaned images, the sorter scored far higher under attack on three standard image sets. The code is public.
arxiv-2510-27345:
Anders Westerkam, Amelia Struyf, Dimitri Lederer, Troels Pedersen, and Francois Quitin track low Earth orbit satellites for millimeter-wave communication from a ground station. Such satellites cross the sky in tens of minutes, and large hybrid analog-digital antenna arrays must steer beams rapidly to follow them. The team presents a variational message passing algorithm for joint localization and beam tracking.

The algorithm estimates parameters of a circular orbit model, from which pointing angles follow directly. Simulations show high resilience to missed detections, reliable tracking even near the horizon, and effective resolution of ambiguities inherent in hybrid architectures. Reliable orbit-based tracking matters because beam misalignment at millimeter-wave frequencies quickly breaks the link, and visibility windows leave little time to reacquire.
arxiv-2510-27645:
Aron Karakai, Jaap Eising, Andrea Martinelli, and Florian Dörfler offer a systems view of distributed optimization in 2025. In such problems, many units each hold part of a cost and must agree on a shared best choice. Past proofs tend to be built case by case, which makes new designs hard to check.

The team models each method as a web of linked dynamic systems. Tests for success rest on dissipativity, an energy-like balance rule, and on contraction, which means gaps shrink over time. Steps for the check fit any web shape, with rules written as matrix conditions. A numeric test on shared gradient descent shows the gain over older proofs. The frame gives designers a clear, repeatable check.
arxiv-2511-00145:
Abhishek Banerjee, Reza Ebadi, and Surjeet Rajendran propose a Rydberg-atom single photon detector for dark matter in the sub to ten millielectronvolt mass range, paired with the BREAD dish antenna experiment. Photons produced and focused by the dish are absorbed by Rydberg atoms and traded for free electrons that are easy to detect. At lower masses, photons drive transitions between Rydberg states, read out by selective ionization.

At higher masses, photons ionize the Rydberg atoms directly. Particle astrophysics readers get a detector design covering a wide, hard frequency band. Single photon sensitivity at these energies could open a dark matter window that conventional electronics cannot reach.
arxiv-2511-00245:
Iain Smears offers an introduction to checking the accuracy of computer solutions for parabolic equations, the class that includes heat flow over time. Unlike steady problems, time-dependent ones raise special difficulties. His guide uses the heat equation as the running example, so readers can see each issue in a familiar setting.

Two choices shape the whole analysis. One is the error norm, the yardstick that says what counts as a big error. The other is how the discrete solution is rebuilt into a smooth form for checking. Smears explains how each choice affects the quality of the resulting error estimators, especially their efficiency. The article suits newcomers who need a clear entry into a technical field.
arxiv-2511-00345:
Amir Ziashahabi and five co-authors introduce OSMGen, a system that creates realistic satellite images straight from OpenStreetMap data. Planners and monitors need current images of specific urban features, but curated datasets of features and their changes are scarce. Unlike earlier tools that start from flat map tiles, OSMGen reads the full map data: shapes, tags, place, and time.

That rich input gives fine control over each scene. Editing the map data produces matched before-and-after image pairs, where only the intended change appears and the rest stays fixed. Such pairs can train detectors, ease class imbalance, and let planners preview projects by editing a map. The paired map-and-image data also points toward a loop where new imagery updates the map itself.
arxiv-2511-00545:
Hang Song, Satyvir Singh, Manuel Torrilhon, and Semih Cayci teach machine learning to close the equations of rarefied gas flow, the thin-gas regime where standard fluid theory breaks down. Moment equations track averages of particle motion, but they need closure relations for higher moments, and far-from-equilibrium conditions defeat hand-built closures. Their approach learns those closures from particle simulation data instead.

High-order moments and collision integrals, both strongly shaped by non-equilibrium effects, serve as the key inputs. Training data comes from shock simulations computed with direct simulation Monte Carlo. The learned model keeps physical consistency, couples with a Galerkin solver, and reproduces normal shock shapes well. It also extends to hypersonic and some unsteady wave cases, charting a route to better heat-flow forecasts for fast craft.
arxiv-2511-01245:
Persi Diaconis, Andrew Lin, and Arun Ram exhibit a Markov chain whose speed of mixing depends curiously on how mixing is measured. The chain is the Burnside process on the hypercube, a sampling scheme built from group actions, here on binary strings of length n.

Started from the all zeros state, the chain mixes in a bounded number of steps, however large n grows, in both the l1 and l2 senses. From a general starting point it still mixes within about log n steps in l1. But in l2, most starting points need on the order of n divided by log n steps, vastly slower. The l2 results come from diagonalizing the chain explicitly, with eigenvectors valued in binomial coefficients.
arxiv-2511-01545:
Ronivaldo Ferreira, Guilherme da Silva, Carla Rocha, and Gustavo Pinto report lessons from running a machine learning pipeline inside Brazil's Brasil Participativo platform, a public participation system. Government settings add burdens private teams rarely face: extreme class imbalance, data drift, bureaucratic access to data, missing dataset versions, and weak control over provenance and monitoring.

Common shortcuts helped and hurt at once. Several shortcuts sped development. Language models did pre-labeling, models were split into routed classifiers, and synthetic data filled gaps. But each shortcut added risks in traceability, reliability, and cost, unless paired with data governance and human checking. The authors argue that responsible machine learning in the public sector is an institutional engineering problem: pipelines are civic infrastructure and must be transparent and reproducible.
arxiv-2511-01745:
Mei-Chin Pang and four colleagues release OSBAD, an open benchmark for finding faults in battery data. Missed faults can mean fires, failures, or costly downtime, in goods from phones to electric aircraft. Yet rival methods are most often compared on private data with patchy labels. That makes progress hard to judge.

OSBAD runs 15 methods head to head. The set spans statistical, distance-based, and unsupervised machine learning methods, across varied datasets. A physics- and statistics-guided change of features makes faults stand out more clearly. It breaks group faults into single-point ones. A Bayesian tuning pipeline sets each method's knobs on its own, working around the lack of labels. Tests span liquid and solid-state chemistries. The methods carry across both, a base for safer battery monitoring.
arxiv-2511-02245:
A. R. Shelke and nine co-authors settle an argument about how strongly electrons interact inside a layered material called NiTe2, short for nickel ditelluride. It had been identified as a type-II Dirac semimetal, but researchers disagreed about the role of electron correlations. The team measured core levels and valence bands with several X-ray techniques on single crystals, including soft and hard X-ray photoemission and resonant photoemission.

From the measurements they extracted the on-site Coulomb energy for nickel's d electrons and the charge-transfer energy. That energy came out negative, unlike the well-known comparison material nickel oxide, where both are larger and positive. The hybridization strength was smaller in the telluride and does not explain the difference. Their conclusion: a reduced but finite repulsion pushes the d states away from the Fermi level just enough to make the material a moderately correlated Dirac semimetal.
arxiv-2511-02345:
David Nabergoj and Erik Štrumbelj simplify a trick used to make Bayesian sampling work on awkwardly shaped probability distributions. Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers explore a target distribution faster when an invertible map, a preconditioner, first straightens its geometry. Neural normalizing flows can learn such maps, but oversized flows can in fact hurt sampling, and current approaches do not adapt the flow's size to the target.

Their architecture splits the job: a plain linear preconditioner handles the dimensions that look roughly Gaussian, judged from warmup samples, while a smaller conditional flow models only the complicated dimensions. On two difficult synthetic distributions the method gave markedly better samples in the tails. It also won consistently on a sparse logistic regression posterior and on hierarchical model posteriors with funnel shapes and weak data.
arxiv-2511-02445:
Eriks Klotins, Magnus Ahlgren, Nicolas Martin Vivaldi, and Even-André Karlsson study why many large companies cannot adopt continuous software delivery even when they want to. Continuous software engineering promises speed, quality, and responsiveness, but complex products, legacy systems, organisational inertia, and regulation all push back. The authors examined four industrial cases, in automation, automotive, retail, and chemicals, using expert interviews.

They applied and extended a current industry readiness model to judge each company's current and realistically reachable level of adoption. The updated model adds finer levels of internal and external feedback and separates constraints that come from the market from those inside the organisation. The conclusion is measured: full end-to-end continuous engineering may be out of reach for some firms, but substantial internal improvements remain possible and worthwhile, and the model helps practitioners set honest goals.
arxiv-2511-03045:
C. Murray and Z. Berta-Thompson study how starspots distort the measured size of a transiting planet. When a planet crosses a dark spot on its star, the light curve blips, and fits can misread both the planet's depth and the spot's traits. Their 2025 paper injects fake spot crossings into light curves with the starry package, then recovers them to see what can be trusted.

For strong events, spot longitudes came back tightly, most within one degree of the truth. Spot contrast, size, and latitude stayed tangled in degeneracies. Transit depths were off by under one percent on average. Fitting the crossing beat masking it when the spot strongly inflated the depth, but for faint or tiny spots, fitting overcorrected. The team also gives a method to narrow the spot search using the event's own observables.
arxiv-2511-03145:
Andre Casajus, Yukihiko Funaki, and Frank Huettner extend the Shapley value, the classic fair-share rule of game theory, to games where outside parties affect what a group can earn. In such games with externalities, fairness and consistency need fresh definitions. Their 2025 paper builds on a restriction found in earlier work to define balanced contributions and two kinds of consistency for this harder setting.

They then show those properties characterize a generalized Shapley value proposed by Macho-Stadler and colleagues in 2007. The characterization mirrors the famous ones for the original Shapley value: adopt the listed fairness and consistency demands, and this value is the only rule left standing. Such results matter for dividing gains when coalitions cannot seal themselves off from rivals.
arxiv-2511-03445:
Karoly Seller, Zsolt Szep, and Zoltan Trocsanyi compute the full leading prediction for a key asymmetry in hot early-universe decays. Leptogenesis tries to explain why matter beat antimatter, hinging on a charge-parity asymmetry when heavy Majorana neutrinos decay. Heat changes those decays, so cold formulas mislead at the temperatures where the process ran.

Their equilibrium treatment covers decays in both directions wherever motion allows them. All needed pieces for a one-loop thermal evaluation are laid out together. A numerical check compares the new formulas with older ones in print and shows where they diverge. Reliable hot values matter because small asymmetry errors grow into large errors in the predicted matter surplus.
arxiv-2511-03945:
Fu-Chun Yang and Jason Eshraghian propose letting large language models talk to each other directly through translated internal vectors instead of plain token messages. Token passing in debate, reflection, and tool-calling setups discards most latent meaning and adds computing overhead, the pair argue.

A dual-encoder translator between two seven-billion-parameter models reached a moderate average alignment in cosine terms. Injecting translated vectors at thirty percent blending steered the target model's output without destabilising its scores. Transfer proved uneven by direction, with general-purpose models giving more transferable representations than instruction-tuned ones. Careful injection kept stability while showing that cross-model latent communication is feasible in principle.
arxiv-2511-04045:
Ankush, Sangeeta Dey, Rishu Verma, Manoj Kumar, B C Chauhan, and Mahadev Patgiri study predictive neutrino mass matrices inside the scotogenic model. In that model, neutrino mass, dark matter, and neutrinoless double beta decay are linked. Their matrices carry one texture zero and one vanishing sub-trace.

Twelve viable texture structures are analysed, and every non-zero matrix entry can be written through the effective Majorana mass that governs double beta decay. Eleven textures predict dark matter near the TeV scale with correlated bounds testable in current and coming experiments. One texture is excluded for needing unrealistic couplings and no TeV dark matter solution.
arxiv-2511-04245:
G R Boroun, writing alone in the arXiv record, calculates a ratio between the reduced cross section and the proton structure function in a momentum-space approach. Catalog evidence credited an additional author; the arXiv record lists Boroun alone, and that record governs. A Block-Durand-Ha parameterization supplies the structure function.

Results are compared with H1 data and extended to high inelasticity. A fixed-energy version of the ratio is checked against HERA data and colour dipole model bounds. Adding a simple higher-twist term improves the low-momentum, low-energy-fraction description. The method, Boroun argues, can serve analyses for the Large Hadron Collider and a future circular collider programme.
arxiv-2511-04445:
Syeda Sitara Wishal Fatima and her co-author present ForecastGAN for multi-horizon time series forecasting. Forecasts guide finance, supply chains, and many other fields. Transformer models do well over long horizons but often lag on short ones and ignore category features.

ForecastGAN splits a series into seasonal and trend parts before predicting. A selection module picks the network setup that fits each forecast horizon best. Adversarial training, borrowed from generative models, then makes predictions more robust. By joining these three parts, the framework targets accurate forecasts at both short and long ranges in one system.
arxiv-2511-05045:
Alessandro Sosso, Ambrogio Maria Bernardelli, and Stefano Gualandi give a new way to compute the integrality gap for small cases of the asymmetric traveling salesman problem. That gap gauges how far a relaxed math form can drift from true tour costs.

Their method lists pairs of cycle covers, then maps them to half-integer points of the relaxed polytope, skipping copies by a set order. A fast check tests if a point is truly a corner of that shape. The flip in order beats past methods that made all corners first, and it matches known results for up to nine cities.
arxiv-2511-05345:
Michael Wilson finds a sharp threshold that governs the low-energy behavior of the Lichnerowicz operator on asymptotically flat three-dimensional spaces. That operator acts on symmetric tensors and shapes how linearized gravity scatters at long range.

If curvature falls off faster than a cubic rate, zero energy is regular and scattering stays tame. At exactly the cubic rate, spread and curvature balance, and zero enters as a singular point. Wilson's line sorts when the far field of gravity is spectrally clean, a base fact for work on gravitational waves and stability.
arxiv-2511-05545:
Swapnil Kumar Singh presents a theory of the early universe built inside supergravity, the framework that joins gravity with supersymmetry. His model mixes hybrid inflation, where a second field ends the fast expansion, with alpha-attractor models, which predict a smooth plateau in the energy landscape. A hidden sector adds a steady lift to that landscape.

Singh works out how the fields evolve and when the ending waterfall step stays stable. The model keeps the known alpha-attractor pattern, with small fixes from the lift and the end point. He tests the results against recent sky survey data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope and a galaxy survey called DESI.
arxiv-2511-06145:
Christopher Williamson ranks poker hands for decks with any number of ranks, not just the standard thirteen. Hand rankings are usually treated as fixed lore. Here the deck has r ranks, and Williamson derives the correct ranking for every r, hunting for where the order flips.

Odd things happen along the way. There is a smallest rank count where flushes drop below one-pair hands. And the ranking keeps changing until the deck reaches hundreds of ranks, a deck of thousands of cards. He also studies showdown frequency, how often a hand type is actually declared, and finds cases where a rarer hand shows down more often, a paradox without wild cards. The standard deck is the smallest that avoids that clash for all but high-card hands.
arxiv-2511-06745:
Lan Thi Ha Nguyen and co-authors ground a robot's daydreams in physics so the goals it imagines for itself stay achievable. Self-supervised robots learn skills by inventing practice goals, yet goal generators based on autoencoders often propose physically impossible targets that waste training. Their system, PI-RIG, folds physical law into the goal generator itself.

The autoencoder's hidden space splits into physics variables describing object dynamics and appearance factors describing how scenes look. Physics equations and conservation laws police that side during training. The resulting goals respect object permanence, collisions, and dynamic feasibility. Experiments on reaching, pushing, and pick-and-place tasks showed better goal quality, exploration, and skill learning.
arxiv-2511-06945:
Maria Emilia Maietti and Davide Trotta work in categorical logic, studying two major classes of toposes, abstract universes for mathematical reasoning. Localic toposes arise from geometry, and realizability toposes from computation, yet both are produced by the same tripos-to-topos construction of Hyland, Johnstone, and Pitts. The paper looks for the common geometric structure underneath both classes.

The authors develop an algebraic abstraction of localic presheaves and of localic sheafification, the process that forces a presheaf to respect locality, along with the role of supercompactification in the Comparison Lemma. The resulting system covers a broad class of toposes from the construction, including all set-based triposes. Localic and realizability toposes thus fall under one geometric account, clarifying what the tripos-to-topos machine yields.
arxiv-2511-07245:
Ruifeng Zheng and five co-authors model molecular communication channels inside microfluidic devices with a Markov chain. The method sends information by releasing molecules that drift and diffuse to a receiver, a scheme for tiny medical and lab-on-chip systems. By chopping the advection-diffusion dynamics into steps, the authors obtain a consistent state-space model whose transition matrix encodes diffusion, flow, reversible binding, and flow out of the channel.

Because the formulation is a discrete-time linear system, both short-term responses and steady behavior can be worked out in formulas rather than only simulated. Numerical results confirm the model reproduces channel behavior well across a wide range of flow conditions. The authors offer the system as a tractable base for building and studying such systems.
arxiv-2511-07345:
Roberto Morales and Javier Ramírez-Ganga solve an inverse problem for the Ginzburg-Landau equation, the model of superconductivity and related phase-ordering physics. The task is to identify a source term that varies over space and time, given only observations of the system at the final time, a severely underdetermined reconstruction. Their approach works in a weak-solution system and studies the identification through Tikhonov regularization, the standard penalty method for such problems.

They derive an explicit formula for the gradient of the Tikhonov functional using an adjoint system, and prove that gradient is Lipschitz continuous, which is what makes iterative minimization reliable. Existence and uniqueness results are established for quasi-solutions, the regularized stand-ins for a true solution. Numerical tests with iterative methods validate the theory, showing the source can indeed be recovered from final data alone.
arxiv-2511-07445:
Claire Lin and colleagues test whether retrieval-augmented generation can answer questions from Taiwanese historical archives. Their pipeline searches old documents first, then lets a language model answer from what it finds. Few earlier studies had tried the method on Traditional Chinese historical sources.

Two datasets anchor the tests: records on Fort Zeelandia and the Taiwan Provincial Council Gazette, each with open-ended questions. Adding metadata early in the pipeline improved both retrieval and answer accuracy. Problems remain, including invented details and trouble with time-based or multi-step questions. The study gives archivists and historians a first map of strengths and limits.
arxiv-2511-07545:
Raymond Cheng proves broad rationality results for shapes defined by polynomial equations. A variety is unirational when rational functions can parametrize it, a strong form of tameness. Cheng builds such parametrizations for general low-degree complete intersections using lines that touch the shape to high order.

Highly tangent lines supply the geometric engine for the construction. For hypersurfaces of degree at least six, the method works once dimension passes an explicit bound, sharply improving classical thresholds. Though the bound stays enormous, finiteness with a concrete recipe matters. Algebraic geometers gain a uniform route to unirationality for many hypersurfaces at once.
arxiv-2511-07945:
Rongjie Yin works on how evenly certain number theory sequences spread across arithmetic progressions. The sequence comes from the Hecke eigenvalues of a holomorphic cusp form, combined with the constant sequence through convolution. Knowing this spread helps mathematicians judge how far sieve style arguments can reach.

For square-free moduli, Yin proves the exponent of distribution can be as large as one half plus one forty-sixth. That value passes the familiar one half barrier by a small but meaningful amount. The result concerns smooth handling of the modulus and adds a precise new bound for these coefficients.
arxiv-2511-08245:
Jisoo Jang and co-authors improve translation from natural language questions into SQL database queries through prompt tuning with error correction. Natural language interfaces are spreading, but generated SQL often contains fixable mistakes. Their setup borrows the rhythm of medical diagnosis: spot the error type, find its cause, write fixing instructions, and apply the correction to the query.

Embedding fine tuning and retrieval augmented generation add outside knowledge and improve transparency. The error correction loop sits on top of generative pretrained language models. In comprehensive tests, the combined setup raises accuracy by about twelve percent over current baselines, suggesting a practical route to more reliable data access.
arxiv-2511-08345:
Joao Vitorino, Daniela Pinto, Eva Maia, and Ivone Amorim revisit network traffic analysis by rebuilding data set flows with one consistent tool. Machine learning detectors for cyberattacks need high quality traffic traits, yet popular data sets were processed by varied exporters whose similar looking traits behave differently. Internet of things attack patterns are above all hard to represent faithfully in prebuilt spreadsheet files.

The team reanalyzed raw packet files from Bot-IoT, IoT-23, and CICIoT23 with the HERA tool, producing new labeled flows and traits. Models tuned on the rebuilt versions, above all bagging and gradient boosting tree ensembles, generalized better than those using original files. Consistent extraction makes cross data set comparison more trustworthy.
arxiv-2511-08545:
Sriram Srinivasan and Gautam Ramachandra present RePose-NeRF, a setup that rebuilds three dimensional scenes as editable meshes even when camera poses are noisy. Robots need exact reconstructions for navigation and manipulation, but real world camera positions are hard to pin down, and standard neural radiance field methods depend on precise poses. Their implicit scene volumes also clash with the polygonal meshes that common graphics and robotics tools expect.

The method refines camera poses jointly while learning an implicit representation with fine geometry and realistic appearance. Converting that representation to a mesh bridges neural reconstruction and practical software. Benchmarks show exact, robust reconstruction under pose uncertainty, supporting downstream robotic use without perfect calibration.
arxiv-2511-08645:
Ujunwa Mgboh and three co-authors automate a slow step in prostate cancer radiotherapy: drawing the fluence maps that shape radiation beams. In intensity-modulated therapy these maps decide how much dose hits the tumor versus healthy tissue, and hand optimization depends heavily on planner skill.

A 3D Swin-UNETR network, a transformer design, reads CT scans and anatomy outlines and predicts nine-beam fluence maps directly. Training used ninety-nine prostate cases, with twenty held out for testing. Predicted maps, recalculated in a clinical planning system, correlate very strongly with the originals and pass gamma checks at high rates. Dose-volume measures show no significant differences from clinical plans. The authors present the system as a fast, consistent route to automated planning.
arxiv-2511-08845:
Sarp Er and Marcello Meldi let the flow itself decide how an Ensemble Kalman Filter should localize its updates. Data assimilation blends simulations with measurements. Localization limits how far a measurement's influence reaches. It is usually drawn from fixed formulas that ignore what the fluid is actually doing.

The proposed localization function evolves with the instantaneous features of the ensemble members. It shrinks the regions that must be assimilated. That cuts the cost of coupling the filter to fluid dynamics solvers. Two test cases probe different physics: flow past a two-dimensional square cylinder at low Reynolds number, and turbulent flow around a three-dimensional circular cylinder at a Reynolds number of thirty-nine hundred. In both, accuracy holds while computational demands drop, which the authors call an excellent trade-off.
arxiv-2511-09345:
Shiyu Ji and four co-authors make test-time scaling of language models cheaper by estimating the sampling budget before spending it. Letting a model generate many answers and vote improves accuracy, but wastes tokens and adds latency. Their framework, SeerSC, splits the work between fast intuition and slow deliberation.

A quick System 1 pass first computes the answer entropy for a query, gauging how much extra sampling could help. System 2 then runs dynamic self-consistency sized by that estimate, generating in parallel to cut waiting time. The authors report token savings up to about 47 percent and latency cuts up to about 43 percent against existing methods. Accuracy, they say, drops only insignificantly.
arxiv-2511-09545:
Etienne Dallaire argues that retrieval-augmented generation systems are being measured with the wrong yardsticks. Language models consume a set of passages, not a ranked list a user browses. Classic metrics like nDCG therefore discount the wrong thing. What matters is whether the retrieved set, cut at size K, contains the decisive evidence for the answer.

Dallaire proposes a rarity-aware, per-query set score, plus oracle ceilings that separate retrieval headroom from ordering headroom. A companion pipeline builds auditable golden test sets, with listwise refinement beating single-shot model ranking. A large benchmark on a scientific-paper corpus spans retrievers, embedding models, rerankers, and quantization. Diagnostics also probe how embedding models handle proper names and conversational noise, guiding practical cost-latency-quality choices.
arxiv-2511-09645:
Michel Pannier defines a mathematical object called the Wilson spool for three-dimensional gravity with no cosmological constant. The Wilson spool arose in work at nonzero constant, where it packages the one-loop partition function of a massive spinning field. Extending the idea to flat spacetime had been missing.

Pannier's definition builds on constructing that one-loop partition function from a fixed background holonomy, with the background taken as a flat-space cosmology. He expects the definition to hold independently of the underlying geometry, not just for that chosen background. Comments in the paper point toward connections with the object's two-dimensional versions at nonzero cosmological constant. The work continues a program of computing quantum gravity partition functions exactly in three dimensions.
arxiv-2511-09845:
Cac Phan and Kai Wang give the first finite-time convergence guarantees for stochastic bilevel optimization with linear constraints using only first-order information. Bilevel problems, where one optimization sits inside another, get much harder with random noise and constraints together. Earlier methods needed second-order derivatives, handled only unconstrained cases, or promised convergence only in the limit.

Their framework approximates the hypergradient with smoothed penalty functions, using approximate primal and dual solutions to handle the clash between constraints and noise. They bound the bias and variance of that estimator explicitly and prove the algorithm reaches a Goldstein stationary point with a stated number of gradient evaluations. Experiments aside, the headline is the theory: a first finite-time complexity result for this problem class.
arxiv-2511-10145:
Bao-Xi Sun, Qin-Qin Cao, and Ying-Tai Sun solve the Schrödinger equation for pairs of mesons bound by one-pion exchange, hunting for states that match puzzling particles. For the kaon and vector antikaon system in the S-wave, they recover the known f1(1285) and predict another bound state just below threshold, provisionally labeled f1(1378). Coupling constants are fixed from those binding energies.

Under outgoing-wave conditions, two resonance states appear near 1400 MeV, and the authors argue both plausibly correspond to the single catalogued particle f1(1420). The same method applied to the charm system, treating a known particle as a bound state, yields three further catalogued states as solutions. All of them come out with spin-parity one-plus.
arxiv-2511-10245:
Rizal Khoirul Anam, writing alone, compares three ways to hide a watermark inside a digital image for copyright protection and authentication. One works in the spatial domain by flipping least large bits, one in the frequency domain through a Fourier transform.
