One hybrid combines both with redundant embedding and a fallback extraction route. All three were implemented in one MATLAB approach for a fair comparison.

Standard image sets were attacked with compression, Gaussian noise, and salt-and-pepper noise at several strengths. The spatial method looked cleanest but broke easily; the frequency method survived attacks at the cost of visible quality. The hybrid balanced both, keeping high fidelity while resisting every tested attack best, as scored by standard imperceptibility and recovery measures.
arxiv-2511-11045:
Wenrui Li, Yidan Lu, and their colleagues present a network that matches written queries to 3D objects while keeping rank and part structure intact. Flat embedding spaces tend to crush layered links, from broad class down to fine part, and noisy fragments can drown the few cues that matter. Both flaws make hard near-matches tough to tell apart.

Their network places text and 3D data in a curved hyperbolic space, where volume growth keeps layered gaps open. A cone-based loss forces each matched object to sit inside the cone of its query text. A weighting step scores each local feature by relevance before merging, which protects key cues from noise.
arxiv-2511-11845:
K. A. I. N Jayarathne, R. M. N. M. Rathnayaka, and D. P. S. S. Peiris design an underwater vehicle with a cognitive layer. Deep-sea work brings hard problems. Crews face disorientation, lost contact, and shifting surroundings. Plain navigation tools often fail there.

The system couples mapping and localization with a Soar-based cognitive layer. That layer handles perception, attention, planning, and learning. Sonar, inertial, and Doppler velocity data are fused together. The cognitive side separates moving objects from static ones. This cuts false loop closures. Maps stay consistent over long missions. Vehicles that adapt when the ocean moves are the goal.
arxiv-2511-12345:
Matéo Ghezal proves that certain smooth surface maps can have only finitely many measures of maximal entropy that are ergodic. The setting is infinitely smooth local diffeomorphisms of closed surfaces whose topological entropy exceeds the logarithm of their degree. Maximal entropy measures describe the most chaotic statistical behavior a system can sustain, and whether there are finitely many is a basic structural question.

To prove finiteness, Ghezal builds families of rectangles with clean geometry that display a Markov property, so the dynamics moves between them in a controlled way. He then follows how unstable curves crossing those rectangles evolve under iteration, using tools from Yomdin theory to control their growth and shape.
arxiv-2511-12445:
Jing-Juan Qi, Zhen-Yang Wang, Zhen-Hua Zhang and Xin-Heng Guo address a normalization problem in a refined way of measuring CP violation, the matter-antimatter asymmetry, in multi-body decays of heavy hadrons. Partial-wave asymmetries carry rich interference information between decay channels, but their overall scale is not fixed by the usual definitions, which blocks fair comparison.

The authors rescale the asymmetries with extra factors chosen so that all of them share the same statistical error, rather than fixing the factors by a normalization demand alone. The result is a set of quasi-normalized measures close to the ideal ones. They apply the method to a three-pion decay of B mesons, studying interference among several resonances using LHCb data.
arxiv-2511-12645:
Junwei Li and four co-authors look at how a large beauty company checks new generative AI tools for legal and ethical risks. Biometric and personal data sit at the center of beauty technology, so the stakes of a bad review are high. The team first interviewed six experts, four IT managers and two legal managers, and found reviews that were manual, fragmented, and reactive. Guidance arrived late, and past cases were hard to reuse.

In response they built BeautyGuard, a roundtable of role-specialized AI agents that handle legal reading, checklist review, precedent search, and risk advice, then merge their views into structured guidance. The same experts rated the prototype highly for usability and low workload. The authors draw three lessons: such systems preserve expert know-how, people accept information support more readily than automated decisions, and enterprise AI works best when it mirrors how the organization is built.
arxiv-2511-12845:
Jericho Cain explores whether machine learning can pick individual gravitational wave sources out of a crowd. The future space detector LISA will not face LIGO's problem of rare signals in loud noise. Its data will hold millions of unresolved galactic binaries blended into a confusion background, and the task is to find sources that stand out from that population. Cain trains a convolutional autoencoder on the background alone, so unusual signals show up as reconstruction errors, and adds a term based on the geometry of the model's latent space.

The combined score beat the autoencoder alone by about thirty-five percent on injected test sources. Tuning showed the latent-space geometry carried more discriminating power than reconstruction error by itself. The results are early but suggest manifold learning could assist LISA pipelines. The paper appeared in Classical and Quantum Gravity after revision.
arxiv-2511-12945:
Yujie Li and six co-authors improve time series forecasting when the data's distribution drifts. Forecasters usually normalize each series by its recent mean and variance, which captures local level but misses global shifts in the distribution. Standard fixes struggle with missing values, noise, and channels that need their own treatment. Their module, Affine Prototype-Timestamp, is a plug-in that learns prototypes indexed by timestamp and generates the scaling and shifting parameters used to normalize both inputs and outputs of a forecasting model.

Because the prototypes come from clustered, self-supervised instances, the normalization adapts to the regime the timestamp implies. The module adds little computation and works with arbitrary forecasting backbones and normalization schemes. Across six benchmark datasets and many backbone combinations, it clearly improved scores under distribution shift. The work targets real pipelines, where drift is routine.
arxiv-2511-13045:
Mayur Abhisheki and Prasanta Kumar Das test an inflationary potential shaped like a squared inverse tangent. Cosmic inflation models live or die by their predictions for the scalar spectral index and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, measured by Planck and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. For their potential, governed by one free parameter, the authors derive the slow-roll parameters, the number of e-folds. The spectral observables, then confront them with Planck 2018 and recent ACT data to constrain the parameter.

They extend the analysis to reheating, the era when the inflaton's energy became ordinary matter, using entropy conservation to bound the reheating temperature and duration. Their closing claim is pointed: the inverse tangent potential can serve as an alternative to standard favorites like the Starobinsky model, which the latest ACT release excludes at two sigma.
arxiv-2511-13145:
Cesar Portocarrero Rodriguez, Laura Vandeweyen, and Yosuke Yamamoto aim computer vision at America's crumbling roads. The civil engineers' society grades United States infrastructure a C and its roads a D, yet inspection still leans on manual surveys and laser rigs that are slow and costly. With vehicles now streaming visual data constantly, the authors test whether modern segmentation models can map road distress, cracks and damage, automatically, and whether synthetic training data helps.

They first generate road images with generative adversarial networks and measure their value for training, then compare a convolutional network against MaskFormer, a transformer-based mapping model. The synthetic data improved results, and MaskFormer beat the rival model on both mean average precision and intersection over union. The practical pitch is triage: continuous, cheap detection from ordinary road imagery would let repair agencies spend repair budgets where the damage is.
arxiv-2511-13545:
Md. Iqbal Hossain and 3 co-authors defend multimodal contrastive models such as CLIP against backdoor attacks without retraining from scratch. A backdoor poisons the model so a hidden trigger forces a chosen wrong answer, while normal inputs still behave. Older defenses need huge clean datasets and never name the labels under attack.

Their method uses an image segmentation oracle as a supervisor and compares its knowledge with the poisoned model's output. That contrast reveals the trigger, the victim samples, and the affected labels. A compact fine-tuning set built from those findings then repairs the model. Tests on visual recognition benchmarks showed the repair removed backdoor effects effectively.
arxiv-2511-13845:
Xin Guan, Bernhard Mistlberger, and Michael Ruf compute a hard correction in a highly symmetric theory of particle physics. They study a three-point form factor, a quantity that links a simple operator built from scalar fields to three outgoing particles, in the theory known as N=4 super Yang-Mills. Their work pushes the calculation to three loops in the quantum expansion.

Unlike most past results, theirs holds beyond the leading-color limit, where only the strongest color terms are kept. The final formulas turn out to be strikingly compact, built from weight-six polylogarithm functions with integer coefficients. The result will feed efforts to extend the amplitude bootstrap program past its usual approximation.
arxiv-2511-14045:
Yule Liu, Heyi Zhang, and seven co-authors audit whether private training prompts leaked into a language model's reinforcement learning stage. Modern models are tuned with verifiable rewards on valuable, non-public prompt sets, raising fears of unauthorized data use. Standard membership tests look for fitting to one fixed answer string, which does not fit training that rewards the model's own successful replies.

Their framework, DIBA, compares a tuned model against its earlier checkpoint on each query. It combines reward-side evidence, changes in task success, with policy-side evidence, drift in behavior for the same prompt. Averaging over repeated sampled replies gives a stable signal that beat strong likelihood-based baselines in white-box tests.
arxiv-2511-14345:
Gábor Korchmáros, Federico Romaniello, and Valentino Smaldore study error-correcting codes built from the Hermitian curve, a favorite source of algebraic geometry codes because those codes perform well and enjoy large symmetry groups. Their focus narrows to the codes arising from the Singer cycle of that curve, a particular cyclic symmetry acting on its points.

The paper investigates these Singer-related Hermitian codes as a family in their own right. Work of this kind matters because a code's automorphism group shapes how it can be encoded, decoded, and analyzed, and the Singer cycle is among the richest structures the Hermitian curve offers. The authors develop the theory of this special subfamily.
arxiv-2511-14445:
Trishala Jayesh Ahalpara presents Tell Me, a mental well-being helper built on large language models. The tool is a calm space for working through feelings. It is not a stand-in for a trained therapist, and it says so. Its first part is a chat helper that pulls from a stored set of well-being facts, so its talk stays grounded and tuned to the user.

A second part makes fake client and therapist talks, shaped by client profiles. That eases the lack of private therapy data for study and for training. A third part, a crew of helper agents, builds weekly self-care plans and guided calm-down audio. The paper lays out the build and tests the chat part on set tasks.
arxiv-2511-14545:
Haorui Ma, Dennis Frauen, and Stefan Feuerriegel present DeepBlip, a neural method to estimate treatment effects that unfold over time. Structural nested mean models split a full treatment sequence effect into local blip effects at each time. That split aids interpretation and fast policy evaluation. Past versions could not be trained end to end with neural networks.

A double optimization trick lets all blip functions learn at once. Sequence networks like LSTMs or transformers capture complex time patterns. The method adjusts for time varying confounding by design. Its orthogonal loss adds robustness when nuisance models are imperfect. Experiments test the approach on time based treatment data.
arxiv-2511-14945:
Fan Yang, Quanting Xie, and six co-authors open a new benchmark for finding long, repeating workflows in human activity. Factory routines, sports drills, and daily habits all repeat with a hidden step structure, but their patterns are faint and stretch over long spans. Short, crisp repeating motions have been studied for years, while these long workflows have not.

The benchmark gathers several hundred multimodal activity sequences and sets three tasks: spotting the workflow without labels, tracking task completion, and flagging procedural mistakes. A light, training-free baseline is included to start the field. Early results show the tasks are genuinely hard for current methods, which leaves clear room for progress.
arxiv-2511-15045:
Kirsten Landsiedel and three co-authors propose a targeted estimator for survival under resampling designs in HIV care research. In low resource settings many patients are lost to follow up, so deaths are undercounted. Tracking a subset of lost patients corrects much bias. Standard weighted survival curves ignore rich covariate data from clinic visits, though.

Their hazard based targeted maximum likelihood estimator uses baseline and longitudinal covariates for greater efficiency. It is a plug in estimator that stays consistent even if the initial hazard model is misspecified. That robustness comes from known properties of the initial estimator. Better survival estimates can change judgments about standards of care. The method targets settings where follow up is incomplete by necessity.
arxiv-2511-15245:
Chuanlei Li and three co-authors uncover cross chain sandwich attacks against liquidity pool based blockchain bridges. Cross chain messages enable asset transfers between blockchains, yet their transparency leaks trade details. Events on a source chain can reveal a pending transaction on the destination chain early. Attackers can exploit that preview before normal monitoring bots see the trade.

With that head start, attackers place front and back running trades around the victim transaction. Their front run is guaranteed to land first in the studied setting. Value is extracted through classic sandwich manipulation, now across chains. The work exposes a critical design flaw in bridge protocols. Defenses must hide or protect cross chain event information.
arxiv-2511-15745:
Beatriz Machado, Douglas Lautert, Cristhian Kapelinski, and Diego Kreutz use large language models to turn messy security scanner reports into structured data. Reports from the OpenVAS and Tenable WAS scanners list vulnerabilities in unstructured text, which is slow to use for risk management. Their automated method extracts each weakness and rewrites it in a standardized format.

In a test on a report containing thirty-four vulnerabilities, two leading models produced output closest to a human baseline, scoring high on a standard text overlap measure. The authors conclude the approach is feasible for turning complex reports into usable data sets. Structured output enables clearer prioritization and opens the door to anonymizing sensitive details later.
arxiv-2511-15845:
Shaon Mandal Chakraborty, Bibhut Sahoo, Peter Sollich, and Rituparno Mandal explore what happens when coupled oscillators act on each other unequally. Basic forces are reciprocal, but in the living and engineered world, one-way pull is common. The Kuramoto model, a classic for synchronization, is their test bed. They focus on chimera states, where oscillators split into synced and unsynced groups.

Non-reciprocity reshapes the map of where chimera states live. It also creates new states not seen in the reciprocal model. These include traveling chimeras that move through the system, run-and-chase patterns, and phases where different behaviors coexist. The findings clarify how one-sided coupling enriches collective dynamics.
arxiv-2511-16545:
Loïc Fernandez and Jean-Loïc Kneur review recent progress on the pressure of cold, dense quark matter, a quantity needed to model the cores of neutron stars. It is hard to compute because the strong coupling grows at low energies. Perturbation theory alone leaves a large dependence on the arbitrary renormalization scale.

Two improvement strategies are discussed. One resums soft modes to all orders; the other uses renormalization group optimized perturbation theory, which builds the scale dependence into the expansion itself. Both approaches shrink the residual scale dependence markedly compared with the state-of-the-art perturbative pressure. The note, a conference contribution, explains where the gains come from and why they matter for dense matter predictions.
arxiv-2511-16645:
Francesco Albarelli, Dominic Branford, and Jesús Rubio give a full Bayesian treatment of multiparameter quantum estimation, where several unknown quantities must be measured at once. The best measurements for each may be incompatible with each other. The question is how much precision that incompatibility actually costs.

Combining the pretty good measurement from hypothesis testing with the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound, the authors prove a limit. Incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss compared with an idealized case where individually optimal measurements could be performed jointly. In practice, then, the idealized benchmark is a safe and cheap stand-in for the full optimization. Applications cover discrete phase imaging, phase with dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, and an open-source package computes all the bounds.
arxiv-2511-16745:
Thomas R Beauchamp, Scarlett Gauthier, and Stephanie Wehner write a white paper on the computer science problems behind a future quantum internet. Their starting point is a network that can create shared quantum links between end points on request, so that distant machines can run quantum tasks together. Good control of such a network is needed if users are to trust the service.

Earlier work by the group proposed a layered control design and tested a first version of it. That test raised hard open questions, and the white paper lays them out for the wider field. The issues cover how control should be split, how requests should be handled, and how a quantum network can run beside normal operating systems while staying reliable.
arxiv-2511-16845:
Zijian Zhang and five co-authors give conformal prediction sets for ordinal classification that are provably as short as possible. Conformal prediction wraps any model with coverage guarantees, a prized property in high-stakes settings such as medical diagnosis. Earlier ordinal methods were heuristic or forced the model to predict a single-peaked distribution.

The authors recast the problem as minimum-length covering at the level of each individual instance. A sliding-window algorithm solves it optimally on each calibration point in time linear in the number of labels, and a length-regularized variant shrinks sets further while keeping coverage. On four benchmark datasets from varied domains, the methods cut prediction set size by about fifteen percent on average against baselines, with model-agnostic, distribution-free guarantees intact.
arxiv-2511-17145:
Robert V. Harlander, Jonas T. Kohnen, and Andrea Shindler compute a set of matching coefficients needed to connect lattice simulations of quantum chromodynamics with the standard scheme used for parton distribution functions. Parton distributions describe how a proton's momentum is shared among its quarks and gluons, and lattice calculations using the gradient flow method can now determine their moments directly. Converting those results requires coefficients from the short-flow-time expansion, computed in perturbation theory.

The authors determine the coefficients for the first six non-singlet moments, carrying the expansion to next-to-next-to-leading order in the strong coupling. That is one order beyond routine calculations, and it sharpens the accuracy of the conversion. The result is a technical but necessary ingredient for extracting precise parton distributions from lattice data.
arxiv-2511-17445:
Faheem Gul and four co-authors ask why the antiferromagnet EuCd2Sb2 shows a large topological Hall effect, an extra Hall signal that signals swirling spin textures or momentum-space Berry curvature. The compound orders antiferromagnetically at about 7.4 kelvin. Magnetoresistance and Hall measurements reveal anomalies that evolve with temperature and field, tracking the magnetization closely. The authors pull apart three mechanisms behind the enhanced Berry curvature.

Above and below the ordering temperature, Weyl states supply most of the momentum-space curvature, though they form differently in the two regimes. Below, the mechanism is symmetry breaking and field splitting of Dirac points; above, it is strong spin fluctuations. A third contribution, active below the transition, comes from scalar spin chirality inside antiferromagnetic domain walls, generating real-space curvature. The study maps how several topological effects share one material.
arxiv-2511-17545:
Frederik Koch and four co-authors cut the resource cost of quantum optimization by changing how problems are encoded. The standard encoding, quadratic binary optimization, inflates circuits with penalty terms, demanding qubits and gates that near-term devices cannot spare. Higher-order encodings keep the problem's natural multi-variable interactions instead of flattening them. The authors show how to construct the corresponding quantum Hamiltonians systematically.

Benchmarked on gate assignment, maximum colorable subgraph, and integer programming problems, the higher-order formulation needed far fewer qubits. It also cut total entangling gate counts by at least about ninety percent on every tested instance. They release an open-source Python library that automates the construction and reaches beyond their examples. The pitch is practical: many optimization problems fit today's quantum hardware only if the encoding stops wasting its scarcest resources.
arxiv-2511-17645:
Sandro Andric builds BlockCert, a framework for taking transformer language models apart with receipts. Mechanistic interpretability tries to reverse-engineer networks into explicit algorithms, and model editing tries to change specific behaviors. Both usually rest on informal evidence, with no bound on how far the extracted or edited model can drift from the original. BlockCert instead extracts structured surrogate versions of single residual blocks, each shipped with a machine-checkable certificate bounding its error, logging coverage, and hashing the artifacts involved.

A combining theorem, proved in the Lean 4 prover, lifts the per-block guarantees into a global deviation bound. Applied to GPT-2 small and two Llama-family models, the framework achieved high per-block coverage with small errors, and a fully stitched TinyLlama matched baseline perplexity almost exactly on stress prompts. The work bridges interpretability and formal proof.
arxiv-2511-17845:
Hiroto Odaka, Luke Smith, and Kunihiko Taira simulate what happens when a strong swirling gust, moving faster than a small aircraft's cruise speed, hits a square wing. Such extreme encounters matter for miniature aircraft, yet they have rarely been studied in detail.

Direct simulations show that the sign of the gust decides whether a leading edge vortex forms on the upper or lower surface, and tip vortices strengthen or reverse. Tip vortices both drive large lift swings and damp them, with the damping winning overall. Flying on the right side of a gust can also reduce lift swings, a useful hint for design.
arxiv-2511-18345:
Luca Ornigotti, Darren W. Moore, and Radim Filip show that a basic force can give a prized quantum effect for free. Nonlinear links between quantum parts are sought for new quantum tools, but they cost much to build by design. The push and pull between charged parts, the Coulomb force, is the most plain such link.

Once the plain spring part of that force is nulled by an added force, a bent part stays. That part makes the noise in one part boost the clear signal of a shift in the other, a one way effect. The sign holds across wide ranges of trap rate and mass, in both chance based and quantum regimes. A natural force may thus supply what labs now build at cost.
arxiv-2511-18545:
Matthew Magin studies separating morphisms of real algebraic curves, maps to the projective line whose real points come only from real points of the curve. Such a map covers the real projective line by the curve's real components, and the degrees on each component form a vector of natural numbers.

Collecting those vectors over all separating morphisms gives the curve's separating semigroup, a notion defined by Kummer and Shaw. Magin proves that for any fixed non negative genus, only finitely many separating semigroups can occur among curves of that genus. The result limits the possible covering patterns that real curves of a given complexity can realize.
arxiv-2511-18645:
Raoul H. Kutil, Georg Zimmermann, and Christian Borgelt build a recommender that guides diagnosis of cognitive disorders by symptoms. Diagnosis is delicate: disorders share symptoms, and the next most telling symptom to check is hard to pick from memory alone. Their system rests on a binary matrix that maps each disorder to its symptom set.

As a patient's known symptoms come in, the matrix filters rows and columns to the live candidates. The system then names the next symptom whose answer splits the field most. A Python prototype was tested on synthetic and some real cases. The aim is decision support, not a verdict: a guide for which question to ask next. Such a guide could steady a hard, overlap prone task.
arxiv-2511-18945:
German Gritsai, Megan Richards, Maxime Méloux, Kyunghyun Cho, and Maxime Peyrard train a network to estimate mutual information, the shared signal between two variables. Classic estimators lean on theory that can cramp odd data. Their MIST estimator takes the fully data driven route: a network reads a sample pair and outputs the value.

Training uses a vast meta set of synthetic joint distributions with known true values, in the hundreds of thousands. A two way attention scheme keeps the net blind to sample order and fit for varied sizes and dimensions. A quantile loss lets it return a spread, not just one point, so doubt shows. The trade is plain: broad guarantees yield to flexibility and speed.
arxiv-2511-19245:
Claude Duhr and Sara Maggio compute a family of Feynman integrals known as three-loop banana integrals, with three of the four particle masses equal. Such integrals appear in precision particle physics and are tied to deep geometry: their maximal cuts live on a K3 surface. That surface splits into two elliptic curves in this case.

The split lets the authors write the governing differential equations using modular forms, a classical kind of symmetry-rich function. They prove the forms have only simple poles and give explicit results for all master integrals as iterated integrals of these forms. It is a first for K3-type integrals depending on two ratios.
arxiv-2511-19345:
Juan A. Aledo and three co-authors combine conflicting rankings into one consensus ranking that allows ties. Forcing every item into a strict order is often too rigid, so their output is a weak order: items sit in ordered buckets, sharing a rank inside each bucket. Binary variables encode whether one item precedes or ties another.

The framework handles fixed bucket counts, given bucket sizes, top-item rankings, and fairness rules for groups near the top, all through added linear constraints. As a case study, the Optimal Bucket Order Problem is cast as a mixed-integer program for the first time. Benchmarks from PrefLib and MovieLens test the approach.
arxiv-2511-19745:
Yassine Afif, Mohammed Almekhlafi, Antoine Lesage-Landry, and Gunes Karabulut Kurt jointly tune power use and satellite handovers in low Earth orbit networks. Fast-moving satellites must hand users off often, and each handoff costs signaling and power. As constellations grow, that burden grows with them.

The team formulates power allocation, user-satellite matching, and a handoff penalty as one mixed-integer program that standard solvers can handle. Users in remote areas with no ground networks are the target case. Monte Carlo simulations beat the naive rule of joining the closest visible satellite, showing better control of total rate and power.
arxiv-2511-20045:
Hui-Jia Zhao, Jie Lu, Yunqing Jiang, Xiao-Ping Lu, and Kaichang Di present HAC-MoE, an unsupervised method for sharpening planetary images. Blind super-resolution of remote sensing pictures is ill-posed: the blur is unknown and no ground-truth images exist for supervision. Older unsupervised methods suffer unstable training and shifting distributions, and they blur distinct surface features.

The framework separates blur kernel estimation from image reconstruction with no outside kernel priors. A contrastive sampling step builds plausible kernels, and a history-augmented contrastive strategy uses past model states as negative self-priors, which the authors show steadies training. A morphology-aware mixture of experts then rebuilds varied planetary terrain. Their new Ceres-50 benchmark supports the tests, where the method leads in reconstruction and kernel accuracy.
arxiv-2511-20145:
Jiao, Shang, Li, and colleagues teach vision-language models to write PET/CT reports. Their 2025 paper tackles automated reporting for cancer scans. PET/CT demand outgrows the supply of trained specialists. Whole-body 3D context matters more than local patches here. Reporting styles also vary between hospitals considerably.

Their framework, PETRG-3D, encodes PET and CT in separate branches. Style-adaptive prompts absorb each hospital's reporting habits. A new lymphoma dataset, PETRG-Lym, anchors the work. It holds 824 reports from four hospitals. Over 245,000 paired scan slices accompany them. A public benchmark, AutoPET-RG-Lym, adds 135 expert-checked cases. Their PETRG-Score grades reports region by region. Language quality jumped by about thirty-one percent in ROUGE-L terms. Clinical efficacy scores rose by roughly eight percent. Dual-modality volumetric modeling drove the gains. The authors admit diagnostic depth still lags clinical needs. Longitudinal change modeling is future work.
arxiv-2511-20445:
Padidar, Huang, Giuliani, and Spivak generate fusion reactor designs with AI. Their 2025 paper trains a diffusion model to design stellarators. Stellarators confine hot plasma with fully three-dimensional magnetic fields. Designing one means solving costly design problems for hours. Large databases of finished designs now exist for learning. The team poses design generation as an open inverse problem.

Their conditional diffusion model trained on the QUASR database. It targeted quasisymmetric designs with chosen aspect ratio and rotational transform. The model produced designs with traits unseen in training. Many generated stellarators performed solidly in testing. Deviations from targets stayed under five percent in most cases. The field's ambition is to push below one percent. Test protocols accompany the case study. Several further avenues for generative modeling are sketched. Fast AI design could speed up the whole fusion program.
arxiv-2511-20545:
Kalpada, Vijayvargia, Day-Roberts, and Erten add new measurements to a quantum magnet and redraw its phases. Their 2025 paper studies the measurement-only Kitaev model. Quantum circuits there evolve by measurements, not gates. Entanglement settles into area-law, critical-law, or volume-law phases. Extra check operators can tune which phase wins.

A single-qubit check acts like a magnetic field term. At high strength it forces a plain product state. A volume-law phase appears at middle strengths on the way. A three-qubit check that commutes with the fluxes does the opposite. It shields the critical phase against the area-law phase. A four-qubit plaquette check makes its own volume-law phase. Topological order survives because plaquette fluxes stay intact. The memory of the area-law phase coexists with heavy entanglement. Stabilizer simulations placed the phase borders with numbers. Shared information measures marked each transition.
arxiv-2511-20845:
Nathan X. Roth and colleagues report in 2025 the chemistry of 3I/ATLAS, the third interstellar object caught crossing our solar system, using ALMA's Atacama Compact Array. They detected methanol and hydrogen cyanide as the comet fell sunward from 2.6 to 1.7 astronomical units between late August and October 2025. The two gases behaved oppositely: hydrogen cyanide was depleted on the sunward side of the coma, while methanol was enhanced there.

Methanol also came partly from sources within the coma itself, with production extending beyond 258 kilometres at 99 percent confidence, whereas hydrogen cyanide was consistent with sublimation from the nucleus. Methanol production surged as the comet approached, ticking up near 2 astronomical units, the inner edge of the water sublimation zone. The methanol-to-HCN production ratios, 124 on September 12 and 79 on September 15, rank among the most enriched ever measured in a comet. Only the anomalous solar-system comet C/2016 R2 has scored higher.
arxiv-2511-20945:
Steven Chen and colleagues report in 2025 a non-detection: the James Webb Space Telescope stared at the centre of Omega Centauri, the Milky Way's biggest globular cluster, hunting an intermediate-mass black hole. Such black holes, between stellar and supermassive in size, are the missing link of black hole growth. Fast-moving stars near the cluster centre, tracked by Hubble, suggest one may lurk there. It would feed on cluster gas, glowing faintly.

The team measured every source in Webb's NIRCam and MIRI cameras and built ultraviolet-to-infrared energy profiles using Hubble photometry. None matched the profiles predicted for a slowly accreting black hole. The silence still constrains: for black holes below about 20,000 solar masses, the Webb limits are tighter than radio limits. The result does not contradict the mass range from the fast stars, and the authors note a nearby star's light could be swamping any glow.
arxiv-2511-21045:
Jionghao Han and colleagues open in 2025 a new task: making machines sing in voices no human could produce. Games, films, and virtual characters want cartoonish, robotic, or creature-like singing, from Splatoon's underwater vocals to sped-up chipmunk songs. The authors name the task Non-Human Singing Generation, covering synthesis from a score and conversion of a performance. Data scarcity, missing annotations, and the wide timbral gap from human voices make it hard.

Their CartoonSing framework splits the problem in two. A score encoder, trained on annotated human singing, predicts content tokens and pitch contours from the musical score. A timbre-aware vocoder then rebuilds the waveform for human or non-human timbres alike, trained jointly on both kinds of audio. Experiments show the system generates non-human singing and generalises to timbres never seen in training. Conventional singing tools, the authors argue, should stretch beyond the human range.
arxiv-2511-21145:
Jiaming He and colleagues build in 2025 TEAR, an automated red-teamer that attacks text-to-video models through time. A video can be harmful only in sequence: each frame innocuous, the unfolding story a violation. Image-era safety tests miss such temporal attacks entirely. TEAR generates innocent-looking prompts so the video's temporal dynamics cross policy lines. Its generator is trained in two stages, then refined by online preference learning, while a refine model cycles prompts toward stealth and punch.

The framework was tested on two open-source systems, Wan2.2 and Hunyuan-Video, and three commercial ones, Veo-3.1, Hailuo-2.3, and Ray 2, plus three safety filters. Across six unsafe categories, TEAR's attack success rate exceeded 80 percent. The best earlier red-teaming result stood at 57 percent, so the jump is large. The authors publish the method, with warnings about offensive outputs, so developers can patch blind spots before attackers exploit them.
arxiv-2511-21245:
Chen Ling, Henglin Shi, and Hedvig Kjellström aim to make computer-rebuilt faces actually feel something, in a 2025 computer vision paper. Reconstructing a 3D face from one photo is now routine, but subtle emotional details are often lost because training leans on flat 2D images without true 3D expression data. Their system, FIELDS, adds direct supervision from real expression parameters captured in spontaneous 4D facial scans.

Ling and his coauthors pair that direct signal with an intensity-aware emotion loss, a penalty teaching the model to match how strong a feeling is without exaggerating it. The dual supervision closes the gap between flat images and 3D geometry and reduces intensity bias. From a single photo, FIELDS builds emotion-rich faces that look natural, and it improves expression recognition on in-the-wild photos, both for named emotion categories and for continuous valence and arousal scores.
arxiv-2511-21345:
Chin-Hung Chen, Yan Wu, Wim van Houtum, and Alex Alvarado design a radio receiver that calibrates itself with no help, in 2025. Digital Audio Broadcasting style systems encode data differentially and can decode it iteratively for big gains, a scheme called turbo demodulation. The catch is estimating the channel, its phase twist, gain, and noise level, without pilot signals to measure from, which broadcasting scenarios rarely provide.

Chen and his coauthors build a fully blind receiver that extracts all three channel properties from the received signal itself. A two-dimensional trellis decomposition, a grid tracking phase across time and frequency, handles phase estimation, while power measurements supply gain and noise estimates. Simulations across code lengths, phase quantization levels, and block sizes show the blind receiver nearly matching one with perfect channel knowledge, and staying robust under realistic transmission conditions.
arxiv-2511-21845:
Yonetsu and colleagues report first science tests of a new receiver on Mexico's Large Millimeter Telescope. The instrument, called B4R, listens at wavelengths near two millimeters. The team pointed it at Orion-KL, a dense star-forming cloud, and scanned across a 10 gigahertz band. They used both maps of the region and single-point scans. Receivers like this one turn faint radio signals from space into data astronomers can study.

Even with a short observing run, the receiver picked up nearly 400 separate emission lines. The lines came from 29 kinds of molecules. They included rare heavy-isotope variants, deuterated molecules, and molecules in excited vibrating states. The team also caught two hydrogen recombination lines. Such line surveys help astronomers read the chemistry of cold gas where stars are born. The haul shows the receiver works well and is ready for regular science use.
arxiv-2511-21945:
Tai tackles rebuilding a complete 3D object from a few photographs with no recorded camera positions and parts hidden. Traditional multi-view methods need many carefully calibrated views and produce holes or misaligned shapes from such sparse, blocked inputs. Simply completing each 2D image first and then lifting to 3D gives inconsistent results between views.

Tai's framework, AmodalGen3D, treats reconstruction as generation. It completes each view in 2D, fuses features across views with a view-wise attention module. Conditions generation on partial geometry from multi-view stereo through a second, stereo-conditioned attention module, so visible and hidden regions are modelled jointly. On synthetic and real-world datasets it beat existing sparse-view and amodal baselines in fidelity and completeness under heavy occlusion in the reported experiments. The caveat: hallucinated parts may look plausible without matching true geometry.
arxiv-2511-22345:
Chen, Xu, Wang, and colleagues from Alibaba improve normalizing flows by teaching the generation direction, not the analysis direction. Flows are invertible generative models: one pass turns images into noise for exact likelihood training, the reverse pass creates new images. Training by likelihood alone leaves their internal features semantically poor, which caps image quality. Because the architecture is invertible, the authors align the features of the reverse, generative pass with representations from a pretrained vision foundation model, a trick with no analogue in ordinary generators.

Flow training accelerates by more than 3.3 times in their experiments, while generation quality and classification accuracy both improve, setting new state-of-the-art flow results on ImageNet at two resolutions. A training-free test-time classifier, optimizing a label token by the flow's own loss, probes the semantic knowledge instilled.
arxiv-2511-22745:
Dong, Taghvaei, and Georgiou recast network routing's oldest problem as a regression. Finding a graph's shortest path is classically Dijkstra's algorithm, a greedy procedure from 1959, but for very large networks a reasonably short path often suffices and distributed computation matters more. The search becomes an l1-regularised regression, the lasso of statistics, whose sparsity penalty plays the role of path length, turning route-finding into convex optimisation.

Through the LARS solver, they prove it replicates a defining feature of bidirectional Dijkstra: growing two shortest-path trees, one from each endpoint, until they connect, giving Dijkstra's method a wholly new interpretation. ADMM and an inexact variant split the problem for distributed implementation, accept warm starts, and update efficiently when the topology changes. The result suits huge, evolving networks where classical algorithms are awkward to parallelise.
arxiv-2511-23345:
Ghaemi and colleagues simulate what happens when a bubble bursts at the surface of a viscoplastic fluid. A material like a gel that flows only once pushed past a yield stress, using the Herschel-Bulkley model. Bubble bursting in liquids is a contest between viscosity, surface tension, and gravity. But yield stress and shear-dependent thickness rewrite the contest, and the team explores it with numerical simulations checked against experiments.

Across more than 800 simulations spanning the parameters over orders of magnitude. Viscoplasticity proved to control how capillary waves interact inside the collapsing cavity and whether a jet forms at all. Shear-thinning fluids produced tall, slender jets where a stronger yield stress arrested the surface instead. And at high viscosity-like settings the free surface froze into a non-flat equilibrium once internal stresses dropped below the yield stress, behavior with relevance to foams, coatings, and aerosol formation.
arxiv-2511-23445:
Ciardo and colleagues bring a classical idea into quantum complexity theory: polymorphisms. In constraint satisfaction problems, a polymorphism is an operation that combines solutions into new solutions, and they largely decide which problems are easy or hard. The quantum version concerns non-local games, where separated players share entanglement, a quantum link, and win or lose together.

The team defines quantum polymorphisms and uses them to settle when commutativity gadgets exist. Such gadgets, introduced by Ji, let classical hardness proofs stay valid when players use quantum strategies. The answer is a clean test: gadgets exist exactly when every quantum polymorphism of the problem is already classical. Applying the test, the authors show that all odd cycles admit gadgets, so the entangled problem built on odd cycles is undecidable. They also establish a quantum version of the Galois connection that ties problems to their polymorphisms.
arxiv-2512-00045:
Hung-Ming Huang and co-authors assess language models that write design specifications from RTL code. As chip design grows more complex, documenting existing register-transfer code by hand is slow and error-prone. Models have been studied for generating code from specifications, but the reverse task is underexplored.

The missing piece is a reliable way to evaluate generated specifications. The authors tackle that assessment problem for hardware description code. Trustworthy auto-documentation would help teams maintain and reuse large legacy chip designs. Reliable evaluation methods are the stated gap, since generated specifications cannot be trusted until they can be graded.
arxiv-2512-00145:
Dark matter halos are the vast structures that host galaxies, and their centers hold clues to what dark matter is. Vinh Tran and co-authors study prompt cusps in a 2025 study of self-interacting dark matter. Prompt cusps form when dense spots in the early universe collapse directly.

These cusps sit at the center of every dark matter halo and are denser than the classic profile predicts. The authors examine the role prompt cusps play in driving the core collapse of self-interacting halos. The results matter for astronomers who use halo behavior to test dark matter theories against telescope observations. Core collapse changes what telescopes should see when they look at dark matter dominated systems.
arxiv-2512-00445:
Controlling a system of parabolic equations means steering its state to zero with a limited input. Juan Límaco, Rafael Martins Lobosco, and Luis Yapu study controllability of a semilinear parabolic system with nonlocal terms in 2025. The work extends their earlier results for a coupled linear system.

Nonlocal interactions were motivated by applications in finance, such as generalized Black-Scholes models. The authors establish local null controllability at a fixed time using a single internal control acting on one component. The proof combines a fixed-point theorem with estimates for the linearized dynamics, a template useful across control theory. A single control acting on one component is the economical setup engineers prefer.
arxiv-2512-00745:
Md Abdullah Al Kafi and Sumit Kumar Banshal present FastPOS in a 2025 paper on language technology. Part-of-speech tagging labels each word in a sentence as a noun, verb, or other type. It is a basic step for many language tools, but low-resource languages often lack the data such tools need.

Their framework is built on transformers and is designed to work across languages. Bangla and Hindi serve as the test cases. Adapting the system from Bangla to Hindi took only a few lines of framework code, the authors report. A tagger that moves this easily could help bring language tools to many underserved languages.
arxiv-2512-00845:
André Soares, Christos Tserkezis, and N Peres study waves in graphene in a 2025 physics paper. Graphene is a single sheet of carbon atoms with unusual electronic behavior. Plasmons are waves of electron density that ripple across such a sheet, and they can carry light-like signals at tiny scales.

The team forms a one-dimensional plasmonic crystal by modulating a graphene sheet in a repeating pattern, placed over a metallic substrate. They develop the theory for quantizing the screened acoustic plasmons that arise there. Topological effects in these waves could lead to signals that resist defects, useful for future nano-optics.
arxiv-2512-00945:
Thibault Damour, Tamanna Jain, and Ulrich Sperhake compare theory with simulation for colliding boson stars in a 2025 paper. Boson stars are dense clumps of scalar field matter, held together by their own gravity. When two such stars pass each other, gravity bends their paths by a scattering angle.

The authors include three effects: point-mass gravity, tidal distortion, and short-range scalar-field interaction. They compare their analytic results with the scattering angle from four sets of numerical relativity simulations. The runs share a fixed energy and vary the impact parameter. Agreement between formulas and simulations builds trust in both.
arxiv-2512-01045:
Shenxi Liu and five coauthors present Med-CRAFT in a 2025 paper on medical video data. Progress in medical multimodal models is slowed by a lack of high-quality, logically annotated video datasets. Hand annotation is too costly to scale, while synthetic methods often hallucinate and lack clear logic.

Med-CRAFT builds interpretable, multi-hop video workloads automatically by traversing a knowledge graph. Multi-hop means each task chains several facts or observations together. Graph traversal keeps the chain explicit, so the reasoning behind each task can be inspected. Trustworthy synthetic data could help train medical video models without inventing fake clinical logic.
arxiv-2512-01345:
Hyun Keun Lee and Hyunsuk Hong study swarms whose parts both move and tick in sync. Such parts are called swarmalators. Each has a place in space and a phase, like a clock hand. The two traits affect each other.

The pair change the base model in one key way. They swap phase terms in the move rule for a simpler drive. That drive rests on phase and on a fixed center point. With it, the swarm forms turning currents while in sync. Work like this helps explain rings and spins seen in cells, bots, and other swarms.
arxiv-2512-01845:
Pericle Perazzo and co-authors add croppable signatures to JPEG images to fight deepfakes. Deepfakes use AI to swap faces and voices into media. The fakes can look fully real. Provenance marks must survive normal edits like cropping, or they fail in real sharing.

Their signatures stay valid after an image is cropped. A cropped photo can still prove its source. That trait matches how images are actually shared online. Croppable proof could help newsrooms and courts trust photos that have been trimmed for layout. JPEG is the web's default photo format, so a signature that lives inside it needs no new file type for platforms to adopt.
arxiv-2512-02245:
Next-wave wireless gear may use large holographic antenna sheets. Such sheets can shape radio waves with great skill. Ashutosh Prajapati and three co-authors stretch a scheme called wavenumber-division multiplexing in 2025. They take it from clean, direct paths to the messy case where waves bounce first.

The scheme splits streams by the slant of the wave, much as older schemes split them by tone. Real rooms and streets rarely give a clean path, so proof in the bounced case counts for much. Holographic rigs are a prospect for sixth-wave networks. Each new kind of path they can handle widens their use.
arxiv-2512-02745:
Qinling Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, and Fang Fang pin down when a Fourier based option pricing method can be trusted. The COS method prices options by expanding a density in cosine terms and cutting the sum short. That truncation creates error, and users need simple checks that guarantee the method converges.

In one dimension, the note gives verifiable conditions on the density. It must sit in two function spaces and hold a finite weighted moment above a stated order. Clear conditions help practitioners in finance apply the fast COS method without silent pricing errors. Plain tests that a desk can run by hand, with no black box in the loop, are worth their weight in trust.
arxiv-2512-02845:
Yalda Keivan Jafari and Krishno Dey build hate speech detection for Bangla, a language technology has largely skipped. Bangla is spoken by more than two hundred thirty million people in Bangladesh and India. Automated moderation for it lags because datasets are thin and spelling varies widely.

The authors fine tune transformer models for Bangla hate speech classification. Low resource languages need methods that learn well from little, messy data. Better tools could make Bangla social media safer, and the lessons may transfer to many other underserved languages. Tools for big tongues came first by habit, so each gain for a skipped tongue helps right a long slant in the field.
arxiv-2512-03045:
Minkyung Kwon and eight co-authors uncover how multi view diffusion models keep their views consistent. Such models synthesize an object from new angles, a paradigm growing in power. The mechanism behind their view consistency had stayed unclear until now.

The team verifies that attention maps pick up geometric correspondence during training. Attention lands on matching regions across reference and target views, guiding consistent generation. Building on that correspondence, their alignment method strengthens it. Understanding the mechanism lets builders improve 3D aware generation on purpose, not by trial and error. Maps that line up by shape, not by chance, are the clue. The tool sees the thing, not just its shades and tones in a flat frame of light.
arxiv-2512-03145:
Galaxies in groups can lose their gas over time. Jinsu Rhee and a large team study that loss in this 2025 work. They use the NewHorizon2 simulation to model small groups of galaxies and their satellite members.

The team tracks how the group setting shapes the gas content of satellites above a set mass. Stripping gas can slow star formation and change a galaxy's look. Knowing which forces strip gas helps explain why group galaxies differ from lone ones. The work adds detail to models of galaxy evolution. Group galaxies are common, so stripping helps explain why many satellites look gas-poor and red today.
arxiv-2512-03545:
Industrial drives must keep power safe even when parts fail. Nicolas Kirsch, Catalin Arghir, Silvia Mastellone, and Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate study resilient drive control in this 2025 work. Active front-end drives deliver power while holding electrical setpoints in safe ranges.

Their method uses neural networks with tracking guarantees. Guarantees matter because a learned controller in a factory must not drift off target. Resilient drives keep production running through faults. The work blends machine learning with the rigor that heavy industry demands. Tracking guarantees separate this approach from black-box controllers that industry cannot certify.
arxiv-2512-03645:
Some physical theories contain a redundant freedom: rescaling everything changes nothing about the real behaviour. Callum Bell and David Sloan study how to remove that freedom in a 2025 preprint spanning gravity, field theory, and mathematical physics. Earlier work covered ordinary particle and field models, and the reduced theory that remains behaves as if friction were present.

The new work extends the reduction method to singular Lagrangians, a class where the usual machinery breaks down. To keep the phase space finite in size, field theories are handled through the De Donder-Weyl formalism, which equips field bundles with a multisymplectic structure. Bell and Sloan then apply the construction to several physically motivated examples. A closing discussion considers what the results mean for classical general relativity, where scale symmetry plays a quiet but important role.
arxiv-2512-03845:
Around every massive galaxy hangs a halo of gas whose cool part records how galaxies feed and recycle material. Yu-Ling Chang, Ting-Wen Lan, and colleagues trace that gas around luminous red galaxies in a 2025 preprint. They use first-year DESI data, pairing galaxies with background quasars whose light filters through the halos.

From about eight hundred thousand such pairs, the team measures how magnesium absorption traces cool gas between redshifts where the universe was younger and today. The fraction of sightlines hitting cool gas grows with redshift, echoing the cosmic history of star formation. Near galaxy centres, that fraction falls as stellar mass rises, hinting that heavy galaxies suppress their inner cool gas. The gas splits into narrow and broad velocity components. The broad part strengthens outward and in massive galaxies, shaping debates about where this cool material originates.
arxiv-2512-03945:
Knowing whether a museum visitor enjoyed talking to a robot is normally gathered by handing them a questionnaire afterwards. Michael Schiffmann, Sabina Jeschke, and Anja Richert test an automatic alternative in a 2025 human-computer interaction preprint. Their data comes from a field trial at Bonn's Deutsches Museum, where a Furhat robot head served as an information point for real visitors.

The trial recorded dozens of single-user interactions, each with questionnaire answers and video. From the video, the team extracted time series of body pose, facial expression, and the visitor's distance from the robot. Classifiers trained on those social signals, under three different feature designs, learned to flag interactions with low satisfaction. The method worked without any hand-labelled training data. The authors see automated satisfaction sensing as a feedback channel that could steadily improve social robots and the experiences they offer.
arxiv-2512-04145:
The Rubin Observatory will soon image nearly twenty billion galaxies, far more than astronomers can inspect one by one. Alexander T. Gagliano, Yunyi Shen, and V. A. Villar present Minuet in a 2025 preprint, a diffusion autoencoder compressing a multi-band galaxy image into just five numbers. Those latent values are meant to be interpretable where ordinary embeddings are not.

Minuet trains on six million galaxy cutouts from a legacy survey. It learns to rebuild each image from its five-number summary with a conditional diffusion model. Classifiers on the latent features recover Galaxy Zoo morphology labels. A companion model turns the features into estimates of redshift, stellar mass, and star formation rate, with uncertainties. Nearest-neighbour searches in the tiny latent space also work well. Galaxy images, the authors conclude, have low intrinsic complexity.
arxiv-2512-04445:
Yanbin Zhang, Hanhui Ye, Yue Bai, Qiming Zhang, and Liao Xiang introduce AutoDW, a framework that automates long document workflows step by step. Office work runs on multi-step document tasks that stretch across a whole session. Earlier agent systems handle single commands well but lose control over long chains. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives the agent a tighter grip on the process.

AutoDW plans one action at a time, based on the user's words, a filtered list of fitting tools, and the document's current state. If a step goes wrong, rollback tools can undo it at the level of a single argument or a whole action. That safety net keeps long runs aligned with user intent. The team built a broad benchmark to grade such systems. AutoDW's stepwise control and recovery scored well, pointing toward office agents that finish real paperwork rather than fragments.
arxiv-2512-04645:
Mizna Ashraf, Jessy Jose, Gregory Herczeg, and co-authors examine young low-mass stars growing up in a cluster unusually poor in heavy elements. A star-forming region's metal content shapes how disks evolve and planets form, yet its role stays poorly pinned down. The cluster Dolidze 25 holds about a fifth of the Sun's metal share. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses the MUSE instrument on the Very Large Telescope to study its smallest members before they settle onto the main sequence.

Gaia positions plus youth markers such as lithium lines picked out well over a hundred members. Low-metal model fits gave each star's temperature, dimming, and glow, and from those its mass and age. The team then measured how fast gas still falls onto the stars. Such accretion rates show how long disks live in a metal-poor cradle, a clue to how planets formed in the young universe.
arxiv-2512-05145:
Inna Wanyin Lin and seven co-authors show how a vision-language model can be trained to judge other models' answers without any human preference labels. Automatic judges are essential for improving multimodal models, but human annotations are expensive and go stale as the models improve. Their framework instead manufactures its own training data and improves the judge in rounds.

Each round generates instruction-and-answer pairs at varied quality, writes reasoning and a judgment for each, and throws away judgments that disagree with the quality they were built to have. Training on the survivors steadily sharpens the judge. Starting from a mid-sized open model, the method lifts accuracy on standard judge benchmarks past that of several much larger systems. The strongest gains come in general quality, hallucination spotting, and reasoning. The authors argue a self-improving judge could keep pace with the models it grades.
arxiv-2512-05245:
Mehmet Efe Akça, Gökçe Uludoğan, Arzucan Özgür, and İnci Baytaş present STAR-GO, a transformer framework for predicting what a protein does. Proteins are annotated with Gene Ontology terms arranged in a hierarchy, each with a textual definition — but experiments lag behind sequencing, so most proteins lack labels. Models that lean on only the hierarchy or only the text generalize poorly, especially to terms the ontology gains as it grows.

STAR-GO learns unified representations of the terms by fusing their definitions with the ontology's graph structure. It processes them in hierarchical order, so information flows from general terms to specific ones. These are aligned with protein sequence embeddings to capture how sequence relates to function. The framework reaches state-of-the-art accuracy and keeps working for terms it never saw in training — zero-shot generalization that keeps pace as the ontology evolves.
arxiv-2512-05545:
Enrique Alvarez, Luis Alvarez-Gaume, Jesus Anero, and Carmelo Martin compute, for chiral fermions moving in a curved gravitational background, the part of the Weyl anomaly that is odd under parity. Anomalies — quantum breakings of classical symmetries — are tightly constrained. For fermions that come in only one handedness, the question is whether the Weyl anomaly can contain a part that flips sign under mirror reflection. The answer matters for the consistency of chiral theories coupled to gravity.

Starting from a form of the Lagrangian that is manifestly real, rather than real only up to a boundary term, the authors regulate the theory with Pauli-Villars spectator fermions. In the calculation, every parity-odd term cancels already in the integrand, before any integration is performed. The Weyl anomaly for chiral fermions is therefore necessarily parity-even — a clean negative result that removes a possible source of inconsistency from chiral gravitational theories.
arxiv-2512-05845:
Sibibalan Jeevanandam and Neera Jain model how drivers decide whether to rely on a car's automation. Their hybrid model tracks three mental states that drift smoothly over time: trust in the system, perceived risk, and mental workload. A fourth, discrete state records reliance itself, flipping when the smooth states cross set thresholds. Only twelve parameters govern the whole machine.

The model was fitted to data from sixteen people driving in a simulator. Their reliance choices and occasional self reports were enough: eight minutes of one person's driving can pin down that person's parameters. Fits were good for several participants. For some, trust drove reliance; for others, perceived risk; for many, both. Readable parameters expose personal differences in time scales and in how task complexity moves the states. Automation can then be tuned to the human, not just the road.
arxiv-2512-06145: Alex Degtyarev and Sławomir Rams settle a counting problem on K3 surfaces in algebraic geometry. A K3 can carry smooth rational curves. Miyaoka's bound caps how many curves of a given degree can coexist. The question is sharpness: when is the cap achieved? The authors answer for surface degree large against the curve degree. They find the maximal number. They characterize the sharp configurations, when the product of degrees is odd. Such extremal arrangements are rare and rigid. Cataloguing them feeds K3 classification.
arxiv-2512-06445:
Zhentao He, Chao Ji, and Yifan Tao study a wave equation posed on a network of edges, a metric graph, with defects at some corners. The equation is of Schrodinger type, the workhorse of quantum mechanics, here in a regime where the nonlinearity is strong. The defects act only at chosen vertices, where the flow of the wave bends by a rule tied to its own size. Solutions are sought with a fixed total mass, a normalization that adds a free multiplier to the problem.

The authors first prove that a positive solution with this fixed mass exists for every choice of mass and every nonempty set of defect corners. They then prove that many solutions exist when the mass is small and enough half lines fan out from the defect corners. Such graphs model thin wires and junctions, so knowing when standing waves exist guides work on them.
arxiv-2512-06645:
Muyang Fan studies what makes crashes more likely where human drivers and robot vehicles mix under learning based traffic control. Multi agent reinforcement learning can run traffic lights across a network, learning from trial and error. Safety, though, is not guaranteed by smooth flow, and the collision rate is the most direct measure of risk in such a system.

Through controlled simulations, Fan varies three factors one at a time: how many vehicles crowd the network, whether intersections are signalized or not, and how turning moves are handled. Collision rates proved sensitive to all three: density, the level of signal coordination, and turning design each moved the risk. The findings give practical guidance for building mixed traffic control that pursues efficiency and safety together, rather than trading one for the other blindly.
arxiv-2512-06745:
Jorge Ibanez Marcos, Pedro Tradacete, and Ignacio Villanueva study valuations on convex bodies, functions that assign a number to each shape in a way that adds up when shapes are glued. Volume is the classic example. Their question is about continuity: when a valuation is bounded and respects translations, must it vary smoothly as the shape varies, without anyone assuming so?

For valuations restricted to stretched boxes aligned to a fixed basis, they prove an automatic continuity theorem: boundedness alone forces continuity. Joined with a counting argument, that yields a stronger form of Hadwiger's classical characterization of volume. As a byproduct, they pin down exactly which degrees of homogeneity such valuations can have in each dimension, a short list with a gap in it. The result tightens the foundations of convex geometry, where volume like measures are classified.
arxiv-2512-07545:
Balázs Endre Szigeti, Imre Ferenc Barna, and Gergely Gábor Barnaföldi wrote this 2025 relativity paper. Gravity has no built-in scale, in Newton's version or in Einstein's. That freedom allows self-similar solutions, whose shape stays the same under rescaling.

Self-similarity turns hard partial differential equations into far simpler ordinary ones. Such solutions act as attractors that govern how broader solutions settle down. Sometimes the symmetry holds only in part, giving kinematic self-similar solutions. The authors take up that partial case in a broad setting. Their stage is the most general spherically symmetric spacetime they can write. Bulk viscous flows run through the matter filling that space. Viscosity adds friction-like behavior to the fluid. The paper sorts these solutions into a systematic classification.  Asymptotic behavior, the long-run fate of such systems, is the prize.
arxiv-2512-07645: Azeddine Baalal, Mohamed Berghout, and El-Houcine Ouali wrote this 2025 paper on a hard equation problem. The equation is nonlocal and singular, with a fractional Musielak operator whose order can vary. The authors work in fractional Musielak-Sobolev spaces with variable order, under a Dirichlet boundary rule. Their main tool is the variational method. Help also comes from nonlinear analysis, convex analysis, and critical point theory. Together, those tools prove that positive weak solutions to the problem do in fact exist for the cases the authors study here.
arxiv-2512-07845:
Shuaihang Yuan, Congcong Wen, Muhammad Shafique, Anthony Tzes, and Yi Fang wrote this 2025 computer science paper. Sound carries rich information, yet most audio datasets float free of any space. A noise without a place tells a robot little about its world.

The authors build two datasets that bolt audio onto three-dimensional scenes. AudioScanNet and AudioRoboTHOR pair sound clips with spatially aligned indoor environments. Each object-event sound is tied to where it belongs in the scene. Large language models supply the commonsense links between sounds and places. Human verification then checks those links for accuracy and diversity. Agreement measures confirm the annotation quality holds up under scrutiny. Two benchmark tasks test what the datasets make possible. One grounds spoken or heard events in a 3D scene. The other navigates a robot by sound alone, with no prior training. Current audio-centered methods fall short on both tasks, they find.
arxiv-2512-07945:
Sergio Martínez-González, Santiago Jiménez, and Casiana Muñoz-Tuñón wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a puzzle from the young universe. Some super-early galaxies, nicknamed Blue Monsters, shine extremely blue. Their faint far-infrared glow suggests far less dust than theory expects.

Where did their dust go? The authors blame clustered supernovae blowing the nursery apart. Explosions in stratified, self-gravitating clouds drive mechanical blowout and venting. They combine full three-dimensional dust-survival yields with thin-shell scaling laws. The result predicts how much dust a cluster keeps after the blasts. Confined blasts retain dust; venting ones expel both. Across typical traits, venting removes much of both. Retained dust falls well below the supernova yield in their accounting. Gas concentration, not metal content, is the lever that matters most. Folded over a whole galaxy, the prediction matches the Blue Monsters.
arxiv-2512-08045:
Kester Wong, Feng Shihui, Sahan Bulathwela, and Mutlu Cukurova, education researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025, accepted for a learning analytics conference. Their topic is collaborative problem solving in school classrooms, and how much guidance students should get. They compare a maximal scaffold, with strong step by step support, against a minimal one.

Using network analysis and sequential pattern mining, the team tracked how students talked and acted across phases of group work. Students with the maximal scaffold showed more dialogic engagement in more phases, but also heavy scripting behavior, a sign of overscripting. The minimal group showed more true problem solving, yet repeated behaviors and drifted into socializing more. In both groups, problem solving rarely led to more problem solving. The findings offer concrete lessons for scaffold design and classroom teaching practice.
arxiv-2512-08145:
Haoran Wang, Zhuohang Chen, Guang Li, Bo Ma, and Chuanghuang Li, engineers in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about talking to drones. Today, human drone interaction is mostly designed by engineers around fixed commands. The team wants user driven control, where people describe tasks in plain words and the drone plans around their personal needs.

Their framework uses two large language model agents that work as a pair. One agent handles understanding and task planning, while the second handles execution, each shaped by its own prompt design. They built a task database covering four common drone uses, from farming to aerial photography, logistics, and environmental monitoring. User study results showed smoother interaction and more flexible task handling than single agent designs. Different language models were also swapped in to compare how well each one controlled the drone.
arxiv-2512-08445:
Madhav Gupta, Vishak Prasad C, and Ganesh Ramakrishnan, computer scientists in India, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is explaining vision models by selecting the image regions that drive a prediction. Such subset methods work well on familiar data, but the authors show their explanations fall apart on out of distribution images, turning redundant, unstable, and shaky.

Their framework adds uncertainty awareness to the selection process. Layer by layer gradient based estimates, obtained by gently perturbing the model weights, measure how unsure the model is about each region. Those estimates guide a submodular optimization that picks diverse, informative regions, with no extra training and no helper models. Across many in and out of distribution test pairs, the method fixed the weaknesses under shift. It even improved explanations on familiar data. The authors argue that trustworthy visual explanations must know what the model does not know.
arxiv-2512-08645:
Young Kyung Kim and coauthors tackle a core problem with image generation models: their inner process is hard to watch or steer. Even when the final picture looks good, users cannot easily see why it came out that way or fix a step that went wrong. The authors propose Chain of Image Generation to make the process open and step based.

A large language model first breaks a prompt into a short sequence of simple steps, each adding one clear element. An image model then builds and edits the picture step by step, so each stage can be checked. The team defines two measures for clarity and for the effect of each step on the final image. Tests show better monitoring and strong composition, and the method works with many base models.
arxiv-2512-09145:
Lauren Ajax and coauthors introduce inhomogeneous branching random walks as a model for growth such as bacterial colony growth. Standard stochastic models often assume each agent behaves independently in the same way, or allow variation only in space and time. That misses genealogy: descendants of one ancestor may branch and move differently from those of another, shaping long time patterns.

Their method lets branching rates and displacement rules depend on time, space, and genealogy together. Several two dimensional models are proposed, each stressing a other source of inhomogeneity. A combined model then averages positions across those separate models with chosen weights, to study the shape of the growing pattern. Computer studies tune the genealogical and spatiotemporal parameters. The resulting structures are compared with images of real bacterial colonies. The work aims to show how family history, not just location and time, governs the form that a growing colony takes.
arxiv-2512-09345:
Qi Zhang and colleagues present Eunomia, a framework for dividing control duties among controllers in layered satellite networks. Mega-constellations of low Earth orbit satellites are becoming a backbone of 6G coverage. Controllers manage the satellite switches in their assigned domains, but satellites move fast, and a controller can only see part of the sky at once.

That limit is costly: reaching a satellite outside a controller's view takes extra hops and multiplies response time. Eunomia partitions domains in three steps, using movement-aware splitting that respects what each controller can see, inside a hybrid control plane of ground stations and medium-orbit craft. It balances traffic with spectral clustering and assigns controllers with a classic matching algorithm. On an emulation platform with constellation settings, Eunomia cut request loss, control overhead, and computation time sharply compared with leading alternatives, while keeping signaling to a single hop.
arxiv-2512-09445:
Nico Groenenboom computes scattering amplitudes in the eikonal regime around a black hole. That is the high-energy, small-deflection limit where particles graze past each other and the physics simplifies into phase shifts. Earlier calculations covered the two-to-two case, with gaps: contributions from transverse separation were missing and masses were handled incorrectly in the poles.

Using covariant quantization in a spherical harmonics basis on the Schwarzschild background, Groenenboom resums the amplitude over partial waves. As a check, the machinery in flat space reproduces the flat-space eikonal amplitude. He then extends the result, for the first time, to scattering with many incoming and outgoing particles. That covers both flat space and the black hole background, for leading interactions through scalar and electromagnetic vertices. The black hole amplitude matches the S-matrix derived by 't Hooft, and concludes it gives the general elastic contribution in the eikonal phase.
arxiv-2512-09645:
Steve Prabu leads a team reporting that the jet from the black hole X-ray binary Cygnus X-1 is visibly bent by the wind of its companion star. Jets from accreting black holes carry kinetic energy into their surroundings, and galaxy formation models fail without that feedback. Yet jet power had never been measured at the moment of emission, forcing models to assume how much accretion power becomes jet power.

Using eighteen years of high-resolution radio imaging, the authors detect the jet curving under the pressure of the companion's stellar wind. Modeling that jet-wind interaction pins down the jet's kinetic power. The value comes out comparable to the accretion energy inferred from the system's X-ray brightness. The team presents this as the first empirical footing for assumptions about black hole jet energetics used both in galaxy formation simulations and in scaling models of black hole accretion.
arxiv-2512-09945:
Bob van der Vuurst, Jiří Kosinka, and Cristóbal Bertoglio speed up a key step in heart valve simulation. Simulating a valve's full interaction with blood flow is expensive. A cheaper approach treats the valve as a resistive obstacle inside the flow, updated as it moves, with no remeshing. The authors start from a parametric surface model of the valve, defined by a set of curves. Adaptive sampling turns the curves into polylines and then into a surface of points, against which distances are cheap to compute.

Three algorithms compute the needed distances: minimization, sampling, and triangulation. Two mesh traversal strategies are compared: visiting every node, or searching recursively through neighbors. The neighbor search cuts the number of distance calculations sharply. The pipeline is demonstrated on a published aortic valve model and a new mitral valve model. The point is rapid shape updates for interactive simulation work.
arxiv-2512-10045:
Helaman Flores and colleagues design a device that converts single photons between the visible and infrared worlds in one step. Quantum networks need to connect color centers, defects in diamond that store quantum information and emit visible light, to fibers that carry infrared light best. Usually spatial and spectral conversion are separate, lossy interfaces. Their framework uses four wave mixing inside ring resonators, phase matched across free space. The process merges the spatial and spectral interfaces into a single nonlinear optical step, with a wide operating bandwidth.

The design fits current heterogeneous integration techniques.
