The authors outline a fabrication ready diamond on insulator route toward modular unit cells that natively bridge visible color centers to the infrared. They also analyze the full chain of coupling efficiency from a color center into a network. By treating conversion and coupling together, the work aims at practical building blocks for quantum networks.
arxiv-2512-10345:
Shuo Li and colleagues extract stars' physical properties from the blurriest spectra a major telescope will soon produce. The Chinese Space Station Telescope will gather huge volumes of ultra low resolution spectra, far too coarse for the traditional template matching used on high resolution data, which is also noise sensitive. The team instead trains a fully connected residual network to read them. Training data were manufactured by degrading real LAMOST spectra to the new telescope's resolution, with reference labels from the APOGEE survey. In one pass the network estimates temperature, surface gravity, and overall metal content, plus carbon, nitrogen, and magnesium abundances.

Against traditional machine learning methods and a convolutional network, the residual network predicted most precisely. It is fast and tiny, processing a million spectra in under a minute.
arxiv-2512-10445:
Francesco Freni and co-authors tackle prediction when the test data come from a different environment than the training data. A model that shines at home can fail abroad, so one school of work trains for the worst case, minimising the maximum risk across environments. Their paper brings that principle to random forests, a workhorse method that had no such variant.

The team defines forest variants built on maximum risk minimisation, supplies efficient algorithms, and proves statistical consistency for the main one. The method can use squared error, negative reward, or regret, the excess over the best possible predictor, as its risk. For the regret version they prove a fresh guarantee covering unseen test distributions. Simulations and real-world data round out the study, which runs to forty-seven pages.
arxiv-2512-10545:
Iñaki Lacunza and co-authors work on the language imbalance inside large language models. Training text comes overwhelmingly from a few big languages, and performance in mid- and low-resource languages suffers for it. Their answer is to rebalance the training mix itself, using a small proxy model to learn how much text each language should contribute.

Their method, XDoGE, extends an earlier domain reweighting algorithm to many languages at once. They target six languages with varied family ties, from English and Spanish down to Galician and Basque, and test with the Salamandra model family under the IberoBench evaluation. The team also releases IberianLLM-7B-Instruct, a model centred on Iberian languages and English, pretrained from scratch and then improved with continued training using the learned language weights.
arxiv-2512-10845:
Kuang-Ru Wu works on RC-positivity, a curvature condition Xiaokui Yang introduced to attack Yau's conjecture linking positive holomorphic sectional curvature to projectivity and rational connectedness of Kähler manifolds. Some of Yang's key theorems need only a weaker version of the condition, which raises a natural question. Does the weak form secretly imply the strong one, at least in the uniform versions of both?

Wu answers partway. If a vector bundle is uniformly weakly RC-positive, then its symmetric powers tensored with its determinant bundle are uniformly RC-positive at every order. And the symmetric powers alone become uniformly RC-positive once the order is large. He also lays out an approach that might settle the full question of whether weak RC-positivity implies RC-positivity for the bundle itself. The stakes include understanding how rational connectedness of a space relates to positivity of its tangent bundle.
arxiv-2512-11045:
Shota Komatsu, Yuya Kusuki, Marco Meineri, and Hirosi Ooguri answer a basic question about conformal field theories, the scale free theories central to modern physics. Some families of these theories can be tuned smoothly from one to another, forming a conformal manifold. The authors ask whether such a family always comes with special operators that generate the tuning.

They prove the answer is yes, under the assumption that a suitable boundary, called a conformal interface, connects nearby theories in the family. The tuning operator can be rebuilt from the interface's displacement operator, which measures how the boundary can bend. The argument is general and does not depend on any specific model. It rests only on conformal symmetry, giving a firmer footing to the study of continuous families of theories.
arxiv-2512-11245:
Zikang Chen and colleagues built Breast-Rehab, a low cost phone based system that guides breast cancer survivors through arm rehabilitation exercises at home. Shoulder and arm problems after surgery are common, yet patients often skip home exercises and nursing support is scarce. Virtual reality systems exist but their hardware burden blocks wide clinical use.

The system recognises and segments exercise movements from ordinary home videos by fusing visual data with three dimensional skeleton tracking, beating standard models on messy home recordings. A retrieval augmented language model then turns the segments and a specialist knowledge base into clinical assessment reports, which reduces invented content and computing cost. Delivered through a WeChat mini program with a nurse dashboard, the system passed a preliminary clinical study, with patients exercising regularly over two weeks and accepting the tool well.
arxiv-2512-11545:
Sheng Feng, Shuqing Ma, and Xiaoqian Zhu recognise underwater targets from their sound signatures by treating the data as a graph rather than a flat picture. Ships radiate distinctive noise, but ocean variability and the signals' non stationary, non-linear character make spotting hard. Most deep learning models quietly assume the data live in normal flat space, which clashes with that complex topology.

Their UATR-GTransformer first cuts a Mel spectrogram, a standard sound picture tuned to frequency perception, into overlapping patches. A transformer encoder captures relationships among the patches to form graph embeddings, and a graph neural network then refines them using local neighbourhood structure before classification. On two widely used benchmark data sets the model proved competitive with the best current methods. Interpretability analysis showed it extracting rich frequency domain information, supporting use in ocean engineering.
arxiv-2512-11845:
Wenbo Du and co-authors present DTSFormer, a forecasting model for airport passenger flows. Accurate flow forecasts keep airports staffed and calm, but flows mix daily rhythms, shocks, and holiday surges. Patch based transformers are strong forecasters, yet fixed patch sizes fit such mixed patterns poorly.

DTSFormer cuts the series into patches of varying lengths that match local rhythms. Within each scale, a frequency domain attention step reads both fast wiggles and slow cycles. The parts are then fused back in the time domain. On Beijing Capital airport data from January 2023 to March 2024, the model beat top rivals at every forecast horizon. The flexible patches proved key to catching sudden spikes.
arxiv-2512-12145:
Mostafa M Rezaee and co-authors release an open source toolkit for modeling heat inside a laser crystal. The crystal, potassium titanyl phosphate or KTP, doubles light frequency in continuous wave setups. Absorbed light heats it unevenly, which can bend the beam and cap power, so designers need the temperature field.

Modules cover geometry, materials, boundary and cooling models, and steady and transient solvers on a finite difference grid. Users set beam and crystal values and cooling profiles; the tool returns temperature fields and radial and axial profiles as data files. Scenario sweeps vary conductivity rules and cooling strength. Fortran kernels report built in benchmarks, and published KTP results are reproduced for validation.
arxiv-2512-12245:
Anika Sharma, Tianyi Niu, Emma Wrenn, and Shashank Srivastava test sound symbolism across languages in a 2025 paper. Sound symbolism means word sounds hint at meaning, as in the bouba kiki effect. Most past proof came from small tests, not large scale checks, and this study looks at words for size.

The team built a set of 810 adjectives, 30 words in each of 27 languages, checked with native speaker audio. Simple classifiers guessed size meaning from sound alone above chance, even across unrelated languages. A scrubber tool then hid which language a word came from, and the size signal stayed. That points to a bias shared across language families.
arxiv-2512-12645:
Salman Sajad Wani and Saif Al-Kuwari study quantum reference frames inside quantum circuits in a 2025 paper. Quantum reference frames treat observers as quantum systems, describing physics from within. Frame change maps are understood in theory, but their effect on circuit based quantum computing was largely unexplored until now.

They turn frame transformations into circuit compilation rules for systems with finite Abelian symmetry. Gates that commute with the symmetry stay local, up to phases, while generic gates become controlled entangling operations using the old frame as a control register. Gate counts thus depend on the observer's frame. In a three qubit model run on IBM Quantum hardware, the frame unitary converted local coherence into entanglement, preserving their sum up to device noise.
arxiv-2512-12845:
Davor Dragicevic studies how a split in the behavior of a dynamic system holds up when the system is slightly changed. Such splits, called exponential dichotomies, can be uniform or nonuniform. Past work found a new class of changes under which the nonuniform kind survives.

Dragicevic shows that this class of safe changes can be made wider still. His result also goes beyond the earlier work in scope. It covers general families of linear operators that move a system forward in time. Those operators do not even need to be reversible. The result widens the range of systems where this kind of stability can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-13445:
Alexander Guterman and Andrey Yurkov complete their two-part study of linear maps preserving the Cullis determinant, the extension of the determinant to tall rectangular matrices. Part one handled the case where the row and column counts sum to an even number. This second paper treats the odd case.

For matrices of size n by k with k at least four and n at least k plus two, they describe all preserving maps when n plus k is odd. Unlike the even case, singular maps can now occur. Every preserving map splits into a two-sided matrix multiplication plus a map whose outputs have all rows equal.
arxiv-2512-13645:
Nadav Kunievsky examines how to read linear regression results when the true data process is nonlinear. Textbook readings of a coefficient rely on the mean outcome being a linear function of the inputs. In many real cases, that premise fails, and the plain reading can mislead.

Kunievsky shows that when links between the key variable and other covariates are linear, the coefficient is a weighted average of local derivatives. When those links are nonlinear, the coefficient is biased away from that average. He shows the bias has a clear form, much like biases from measurement error or omitted variables. The paper gives applied users a firmer way to state what a regression coefficient means.
arxiv-2512-13845:
Lars T. Kyllingstad studies an unexpected error source in co-simulation, where two simulation units run together and exchange a variable. When both units keep an internal state equal to the time integral of a shared variable, extrapolation errors make those two states drift apart. One normally expects smaller macro time steps to shrink that gap.

Kyllingstad shows that step size changes can, under certain circumstances, make the discrepancy grow instead. That happens even when the change is toward smaller steps, the direction meant to improve accuracy. The paper runs 17 pages with 10 figures, and code to run the simulations and plots is public. The result is a caution for coupled simulation setups in engineering.
arxiv-2512-14045:
Omar Abusabha and co-authors study the security effects of function inlining on machine learning based binary analysis. Inlining is a compiler step that replaces a call site with the callee's body. It improves performance but changes static features such as instructions and control flow graphs, which binary analysis tools depend on.

The authors dissect the inlining decision pipeline in LLVM's cost model and craft compiler options that push inlining far past standard levels, which they term extreme inlining. They test five ML-assisted security tasks with 20 unique models. Inlining shifted model behavior enough to evade discriminative and generative models, and static-feature models were highly sensitive. Subtle compiler settings could craft evasive binaries on purpose, and inlining ratios varied widely across applications.
arxiv-2512-14245:
Gideon Chiusole and Christian Kuehn study traveling fronts in the two dimensional renormalized Allen Cahn equation in a 2025 paper. The Allen Cahn equation models phase change, and its stochastic version needs renormalization, a method that removes infinite terms. The authors study the deterministic skeleton beneath it.

For all small enough regularization values, they construct monotone traveling wave fronts that connect the renormalized equilibria. They describe the profile and speed of those fronts as the parameter shrinks, and find the leading order terms. Linearizing around the wave, they prove a spectral gap after the zero mode tied to symmetry. That gap grows linearly in the renormalization constant as the parameter tends to zero.
arxiv-2512-14345:
Baruch Meerson and Ohad Vilk develop an age structured hydrodynamic theory in a 2025 paper. They study large groups of particles that diffuse anomalously, meaning their spread does not follow the normal pattern, and that reset to a start point under renewal rules.

Age here means the time since a particle last reset, and the theory treats it as a full dynamical variable. The diffusion model is scaled Brownian motion, with a power law diffusion coefficient. They apply the theory to three resetting protocols, including one based on the Brownian bees model. All reach non equilibrium steady states, whose densities they compute. For coupled protocols the steady densities have compact support, unlike the single particle case.
arxiv-2512-14745:
Edward Lue Chee Lip and coauthors test a safety setup for strong AI models that cannot be fully trusted. In their 2025 design, Factor(U,T), an untrusted but capable model splits a big task into small child tasks, and trusted models carry out each part alone. Earlier schemes let only trusted models do the splitting, which weakens the setup on hard tasks.

The team red teamed the design on BigCodeBench, a set of Python coding tasks. Monitors that saw only the task plans barely beat chance, with an AUROC of 0.52, while monitors that saw finished code scored 0.96. A flipped setup with a trusted planner reached 0.96 and a 1.2% attack success rate. Watching real work, it turns out, beats watching plans.
arxiv-2512-14945:
David Wittman and five coauthors dissect a rich galaxy cluster caught in the act of merging. The cluster, RXC J0032.1+1808, looks stretched from north to south in visible light and in gravity based mass maps. New X-ray views show two clumps, the sign of two subclusters passing through each other.

From archived XMM-Newton data the team measured a global X-ray temperature of 8.5 keV and a luminosity of 1.04 times 10^45 erg per second. A redshift survey of member galaxies put the speed gap between the subclusters at 1002 to 1785 kilometers per second. Matching the scene to public simulations, they rule out a head on crash. The blow was offset by 0.5 or 1 megaparsec, and the closest pass came roughly 315 to 550 million years ago.
arxiv-2512-15245:
Gordon Blower and a coauthor connect control theory machinery to a famous nonlinear wave equation. Their starting point is a linear system in continuous time, with input, output, and a state space. The system's impulse response defines a Hankel integral operator, and when that operator is trace class, its Fredholm determinant yields a tau function.

From there the paper builds algebras of operators tied to the system and obtains solutions of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation, a partial differential equation for shallow water like waves. Pöppe's semi additive operators are identified with orbits of a shift action on integral kernels, and his bracket operation is expressed through the Fedosov product. The authors also show a Fredholm determinant formula gives an effective way to compute KP solutions numerically. The work links linear systems, determinants, and soliton mathematics in one frame.
arxiv-2512-15345:
V. A. Checha leads fifteen authors studying the rhythmic flickering of rho Leo, a blue supergiant star. How massive stars evolve after the main sequence is poorly understood, and blue supergiants vary in brightness and spectrum in quasi periodic ways. The team combines long term data from TESS, Kepler, and a 1.5 meter telescope in Estonia to pin down the star's properties.

Period searches and line profile fits reveal cycles from about 0.8 to 35 days, some steady across seasons and others shifting. A period near 11 days is tied to the star's rotation, and one near 17 days to radial pulsations, where the star breathes in and out. Synthetic spectra fitted with the FastWind code give the star's basic parameters. The pattern of timescales suggests rho Leo is on a blue loop, evolving back after a red supergiant phase.
arxiv-2512-15545:
Amit Haldar, Shriganesh Prabhu, and Shovon Pal probe nonlinear behavior in a terahertz metamaterial that mimics induced transparency in a 2025 paper. Electromagnetically induced transparency here comes from coupling between a bright radiative mode and a dark subradiant mode. How those modes exchange energy controls the transparency window.

Using nonlinear two dimensional terahertz spectroscopy, the team reads pump probe and photon echo signals from a platform of two coupled resonators. The bright mode relaxation time is almost twice the coherent energy exchange time between the modes. Multi peak photon echo signals directly show interference between dressed states. A time resolved density matrix model matches the observed features well.
arxiv-2512-15645:
Wissam Karroucha and co authors review machine learning for RNA targeting drug design in a 2025 paper. Small molecules that bind RNA could treat diseases that protein targeting cannot reach. Machine learning could speed the search, from first hits to lead optimization, yet protein tuned tools transfer poorly to RNA.

RNA differs from proteins in structure and in how small molecules bind, so RNA specific methods have grown up around binding site finding and virtual screening. The review compares tools by task, method, and relevance to RNA work. It also sets guidelines for standard drug design benchmarks and tests how well current models predict specific drug RNA interactions.
arxiv-2512-15945:
Jai Kruthunz Naveen Kumar and co authors study privacy talk and emotional dynamics in mental health communities on Reddit in a 2025 paper. Reddit hosts much peer support for mental health, and privacy worries increasingly surface in those discussions. The team asks how privacy themes and community sentiment move together.

They analyze 10,119 posts and 65,385 comments from 14 mental health and regulatory subreddits, gathered with a custom scraper. Sentiment distributions align closely between some community pairs, reaching 0.989 similarity for MentalHealthSupport and MentalIllness. Keyword dictionaries tag themes such as HIPAA and GDPR. Privacy discussion rose 50 percent from 2020 to 2025, with spikes around regulatory events.
arxiv-2512-17045:
Alejandro Ranchal-Pedrosa and coauthors present Sedna, a protocol for sending transactions in blockchains with many concurrent proposers. Multi-proposer consensus kills the single-leader bottleneck, but users still face a trilemma among censorship resistance, low latency, and cost.

Copying full transactions to many proposers wastes throughput and exposes payloads to front-running. Sedna instead ships coded symbol bundles to subsets of proposers in private, with execution in a set order once enough symbols finalize to decode. Proofs give liveness and privacy until decode. Bandwidth overhead nears the theoretical floor, a two to three times gain over plain copying, and no consensus change is needed.
arxiv-2512-17145:
Josh Barber and coauthors rank hypotheses for prediction under uncertainty with a Solomonoff-inspired score, which favors hypotheses that are both simple and predictive. Sparse-data tasks force a balance that plain accuracy contests handle poorly.

Large language models propose the candidate hypotheses, and the method weights them by simplicity and fit into a mixture forecast per cell on Mini-ARC tasks. Against Bayesian Model Averaging, Solomonoff scoring spreads weight more evenly across rivals, while the Bayesian route piles weight on one likely but possibly flawed pick. The outputs stay conservative and uncertainty-aware even when hypotheses are noisy, a case for algorithmic priors in multi-hypothesis reasoning.
arxiv-2512-17545:
Yunqi Gao and coauthors present ClothHMR, a method that rebuilds a 3D mesh of a person from a single photo, even when loose or varied clothing hides the body shape. Standard mesh recovery tools lean on tight clothing cues, so draped garments often throw them off.

ClothHMR works in two stages. A clothing tailoring module first estimates body semantics and predicts body edges under the cloth, and a mesh recovery module built on the FHVM model then fits the full body mesh. The method beats prior state of the art systems on standard benchmarks and on photos taken in the wild. The team also built a web app on top of it for online fashion and shopping, where a shopper's body shape drives fit and size advice.
arxiv-2512-17745:
Adam R Lamson, Mohammadhossein Firouznia, and Michael J Shelley simulate how DNA strands gather into droplets inside the cell nucleus. Cells switch genes partly by parking DNA and proteins in condensates, blobs that form like dew. Theory explains the blobs' final size well, but the route they take to get there, minute by minute, was murky.

Their 3D simulations follow one long chain, anchored at its ends, as fleeting crosslinks tug it together. Clusters appear by two routes: ripening, where big clusters grow by stealing from small ones, and merging, where clusters drift together and fuse. Protein density, link lifetime, and stiffness steer which route wins. A stripped-down energy model then reproduces the timing laws the simulations found.
arxiv-2512-18145:
D. L. Flannery and A. E. Zalesski bound a rare class of matrix groups. Their setting is the special linear group over a finite field, with the size set by a prime degree. Inside it, some subgroups sit only in one hard class from the Aschbacher scheme, the non geometric class, which resists the usual tools.

For such groups, the authors cap the group size by a rule that depends on the degree and field power, but not on the prime itself. The count of such groups, up to a change of basis, is capped by the degree alone. The caps feed a computing version of a deep number theory result about dense subgroups, where firm bounds make searches end.
arxiv-2512-18445:
Amirreza Abbasi and Mohsen Hooshmand survey what is known about the transformer, the neural network design behind most modern AI systems. Their review, posted to arXiv in December 2025, asks a basic question. In what sense are transformers universal, able to represent any computation or function? And how much attention do they really need?

The authors review recent progress on structural minimality, asking which parts of the design can be trimmed. They also cover approximation rates, which measure how well a transformer of a given size can mimic a target function. They sort solid guarantees from fragile ones and flag open problems. The result is a map of transformer theory for researchers who build or study these models.
arxiv-2512-18545:
Gui-Qiang G. Chen, Jiawen Zhang, and Shengguo Zhu settle a question about when compressible fluid flows break down. For round, symmetric flows of a compressible gas, it was unknown whether smooth solutions can break down into cavitation or implosion in finite time. With constant viscosity, recent results showed implosions do occur. Their 2025 paper proves the opposite when the viscosity is degenerate, depending on density, as in the shallow water equations.

For large initial data with bounded positive density, solutions stay globally regular, with no cavitation or implosion, in two and three dimensions. It covers every adiabatic exponent above 1 in two dimensions, and the range 1 to 3 in three. No smallness condition is needed. The proof rests on weighted radial estimates, built through a region segmentation method controlling density and effective velocity. The authors expect the technique to help other nonlinear equations facing the same singularity at the origin.
arxiv-2512-18745:
Kaican Li and nine co-authors build an AI agent that can search inside images the way people scan a map or a dense chart. Open multimodal models still reason weakly about such tasks, leaning on perception without checking details. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, introduces a benchmark, O3-Bench, and a two-agent system, InSight-o3.

O3-Bench asks models to piece together subtle clues from separate image regions over several steps; even OpenAI's o3 scores only 40.8 percent. InSight-o3 pairs a reasoning agent with a search agent trained by reinforcement learning to find regions described in free-form language, including fuzzy or relational targets. Plugged into frontier models, the searcher lifts performance across many benchmarks. The design is a concrete step toward open systems that think with images.
arxiv-2512-19145:
Yuan-Yuan Huang, Xu Cao, Taifu Feng, and Krešimir Kumerički estimate what a planned Chinese electron-ion collider would add to the study of the proton's inner structure. The probe is deeply virtual Compton scattering, where a scattered electron reveals generalized parton distributions of the proton. Current data leave wide uncertainty bands on those maps.

The team fits world data with a neural network that parameterizes the key Compton form factors, using replica methods for honest error bars. Adding simulated collider measurements, from single and double polarization setups, shrinks the errors sharply. The gain is strongest in the sea-quark region, where present knowledge is weakest.
arxiv-2512-19645:
Martin Kreuzer, Anja Moldenhauer, and Gerhard Rosenberger study the subgroups of glued groups. Their groups join two smaller groups over a shared cyclic subgroup. The shared part sits in a special, tight way inside the whole. The core question is simple to state. How much of the parts' subgroup structure survives the gluing?

The team uses the Nielsen method, reshaped for glued products. They prove that key traits of the parts carry over to the whole. The work covers groups whose small subgroups split into few cyclic pieces. It gives sharp options for subgroups built from four generators. They also revisit a known conjecture on groups whose large subgroups are all free. For these glued groups, and for some HNN extensions, they give fresh proofs. The conjecture says any such group must be a surface group.
arxiv-2512-19845:
Harry Greatorex and five co-authors mine fifteen years of solar data for a flare afterglow. The Solar Dynamics Observatory has watched the Sun since 2010. It found the EUV late phase, a second rise in warm coronal glow. The rise comes tens of minutes after a flare's main peak. Its role in space weather is known, but its stats and causes were murky.

The team scanned 5,335 lone flares from 2010 to 2025. They confirmed 467 late-phase events, a rate near nine percent. The rate barely tracks the solar cycle. A typical event starts about nineteen minutes after its flare. It lasts about ninety-three minutes. Rise and decay rates track each other well. Yet no firm link ties the flare's traits to the late phase's traits. A factor study split the spread into near-free axes.
arxiv-2512-20445:
Milko Estrada builds black holes in two related gravity theories that add an æther, a preferred cosmic frame. The theories are Hořava gravity and Einstein-æther theory. His procedure reverses the usual order: he fixes the matter's equation of state first, then solves for the black hole that it supports.

Three linear equations of state are studied, mimicking a charged black hole, an extremal black hole, and an ultra-relativistic stiff fluid. The æther terms break the usual density-pressure relation and produce exotic behaviour. One case yields a horizon with odd-fold degeneracy. Another forms a remnant whose horizon encloses a plain singularity rather than a smooth core. Thermodynamics of the solutions is as unusual as their geometry.
arxiv-2512-20645:
Matthew Mark Romano, Zhengzhi Liu, and JungHyun Bae sharpen particle tracking in a segmented detector. Cosmic ray muons crossing an eight-by-eight scintillator array deposit energy in blocks; the traditional centroid method estimates position from those deposits, wasting information. The team compares four reconstruction methods on Geant4-simulated data.

Transformer networks win outright. Their angular error and position error improve on the centroid method by factors of more than two and more than six in turn. Convolutional networks and linear regression fall between the two extremes. Finer positions mean finer angles, and finer angles mean better muon tomography, where scattered muons image the insides of containers, volcanoes, and structures. Learned methods squeeze resolution the hardware never provided.
arxiv-2512-20845:
Onat Ozer and five co-authors try to fix a failure of self-correction in language models. A model that reviews its own mistakes can improve, but reviewing itself repeatedly often loops: it repeats the same error while knowing it is wrong. The authors call this degeneration of thought.

Their method, MAR, replaces the lone reviewer with several debating personas that generate reflections together. Debate produced more varied feedback, and the acting model used it better. Scores reached forty-seven percent exact match on the HotPotQA questions and about eighty-three percent on HumanEval coding tasks. Both beat single-model reflection, suggesting that outside perspectives, even simulated ones, keep reasoning honest.
arxiv-2512-21045:
Siyuan Wang, Qing Xia, and Qiong Ye measure what happens to homework when a capable AI sits next to every student. Across two terms of Business Calculus, Linear Algebra, and Calculus III, they compare homework done without a proctor against proctored exams. They use score gaps, homework-exam correlations, and distribution distances. The pattern is an integrity gap. It widens as courses move from step-by-step drills toward ideas and spatial material.

Homework format made little difference. Handwritten, assistant-graded work showed the same offloading signs as online work, so paper is not safer by itself. In drill-based courses homework still partly predicts exam mastery. In upper-level courses the match collapses. Strong homework there more and more reflects fluent output without real understanding behind it. The authors close with a call to redesign assessment for the AI era.
arxiv-2512-21345:
Asked a question the database cannot answer, a text-to-SQL system usually invents plausible SQL anyway, and the output looks correct. Jasmin Saxer, Isabella Aigner, Luise Linzmeier, Andreas Weiler, and Kurt Stockinger build Query Carefully to catch those cases. Their testbed is biomedical, where a wrong answer carries real risk.

The pipeline pairs language-model SQL generation with explicit no-answer rules, schema-aware prompts, and few-shot examples of both kinds. They built OncoMX-NAQ, eighty unanswerable questions across eight categories, from out-of-domain requests to missing columns. Balanced prompting detected the unanswerable best, near-perfectly on structural cases, though missing values and ambiguous columns stayed hard. A small interface shows users the SQL, the results, or the refusal.
arxiv-2512-21545:
Sanghyun Jo, Kyungsu Kim, and their co-authors tackle object removal in images: erasing an object and rebuilding the background behind it. Recent dataset-free methods steer a diffusion model through its attention so it cannot look at the masked region. That approach fails two ways, mistaking other objects for background and blurring textures by treating all background alike.

Their method, EraseLoRA, replaces attention surgery with explicit background reasoning and needs no training data. First, a multimodal large language model separates the target object, other foreground objects, and clean background. Then the system optimizes at test time, treating background subtypes as pieces that must join consistently. EraseLoRA plugs into different diffusion backbones as an add-on. In tests it rebuilt backgrounds at least twenty-three percent more faithfully than earlier dataset-free methods. It also nearly halved unwanted reappearance of removed objects, beating even methods that use training data.
arxiv-2512-21845:
Chuangxin Zhang, Kaiyang Liao, and their co-authors tackle class-incremental learning, where a model must absorb new categories over time without forgetting old ones. Freezing the old network and bolting on new modules avoids forgetting, but the modules' features drift apart and the classifier misaligns as the class distribution evolves.

Their method, SCL-PNC, grows the backbone only as needed, through a small adapt layer, keeping expansion costs minimal. The classifier is a parametric version of an equiangular tight frame, a geometric arrangement inspired by neural collapse, the phenomenon where trained features settle into a highly symmetric pattern. The frame becomes dynamic, reshaping itself as classes arrive. To fight feature drift between old and new modules, a parallel expansion layout uses knowledge distillation to align their features. On standard benchmarks, the method proved effective and efficient.
arxiv-2512-22045:
Artificial networks learning from non-stationary data forget old tasks and lose plasticity, yet animal brains keep learning while their neural representations drift beneath stable behavior. Suzanne van der Veldt, Gido M. van de Ven, Sanne Moorman, and Guillaume Etter review representational drift across species and brain regions and ask what it means for continual learning.

They propose drift reflects a mix of homeostatic turnover and learning-related synaptic plasticity, with new-task learning itself inducing drift in older representations that accumulates across regions. For artificial systems, drift is compatible only with approaches that do not freeze parameters against forgetting. The authors argue drift is a byproduct rather than a solution, but studying it could reshape how continual learning balances stability and plasticity.
arxiv-2512-22245:
Bhaktipriya Radharapu and five co-authors make AI judges report how unsure they are, accurately and cheaply. Language models increasingly grade other models' work, but their stated confidence is often poorly calibrated, and sampling many answers to estimate uncertainty costs a lot of computation. The team's fix is a linear probe, a small readout trained on the judge's hidden states with a Brier-score loss.

Across objective tasks like reasoning, mathematics, factuality, and coding, plus subjective human preference judgments, the probes calibrated better than verbalized confidence or multi-generation methods at about a tenth of the compute. They generalized to unseen domains and were more accurate on their high-confidence calls. Their estimates run conservative, suiting safety-critical settings where false positives hurt most.
arxiv-2512-22545:
Jesen Zhang and seven co-authors present SR-MCR, a label-free method for making multimodal models reason more honestly about images. Such models often sound fluent while their step-by-step reasoning wanders and loses touch with the picture, because training usually grades only the final answer. SR-MCR instead scores the reasoning process itself using five self-referential cues drawn from the model's own outputs.

The cues measure semantic alignment, lexical fidelity, non-redundancy, visual grounding, and step consistency, combined into a reliability-weighted reward. A critic-free reinforcement objective with confidence-aware cooling steadies training and discourages trivial or overconfident answers. Built on Qwen2.5-VL, the seven-billion-parameter version reached state-of-the-art average accuracy among comparable open models across visual benchmarks, and ablations credited each reward term and the cooling module.
arxiv-2512-22645:
Alex Chan proves a divisibility test for a generalized family of repunits. Usual Mersenne numbers are one less than a power of two. Generalized Mersenne numbers here are repunits, strings of ones. They are written in two different bases, a-to-the-m and a-to-the-k, sharing the same length. Chan's theorem gives a criterion determining when one such number divides the other.

The main proof handles the general case across all choices of the bases' exponents and the length. Chan also supplies a second, alternative proof specialized to one case of the theorem, giving readers two routes to the same criterion. The note is a compact contribution to elementary number theory's long study of repunit divisibility.
arxiv-2512-23245:
Shin Seong Kim, Minjung Shin, Hyunin Cho, and Youngjung Uh present ASemConsist, a method for keeping a character's identity steady across a series of generated images. Text-to-image models draw beautifully, but asking for the same person in a new scene trades identity against obedience to each prompt. Their fix works without training, by editing text embeddings selectively rather than retraining the generator.

The key observation concerns padding embeddings, the filler slots in text encodings. In multi-encoder models, only padding slots that carry prompt-related meaning can serve as containers for identity information. ASemConsist injects per-image semantics into those slots while suppressing irrelevant components. An adaptive feature-sharing step measures how specific each identity prompt is and applies constraints only when identity is ambiguous. A new metric, SeeSaw, scores the balance between the two. Built on two generator backbones, the method beat existing competitors.
arxiv-2512-23945:
Ruiqing Sun and eight co-authors improve evolutionary algorithms for engineering problems with several objectives and several constraints at once. Real constrained multi-objective problems couple their constraints in complicated ways, and recent methods decouple them, chasing the best front for each constraint separately along the search direction. The authors show that reasoning misses something: parts of the true constrained optimum may touch no single-constraint front at all, being shaped instead by the boundaries of infeasible regions.

They name that missing piece the independent constrained Pareto front, and pin down the informative infeasible boundaries as reverse fronts. Their algorithm, DCF2D, identifies whichever constraint currently blocks the main population and dispatches helper populations to search forward or in reverse as needed, inside a three-stage framework. Across eighty-seven benchmark instances and twenty-eight real engineering problems, it achieved the best overall performance among nine algorithms.
arxiv-2512-24145:
Udit Sharma studies a subtle statistical point in how machine learning systems are compared. These systems look random, but their randomness comes from seeded generators, so the same seed replays the exact same run. Standard evaluations ignore this and treat runs of rival systems as independent, throwing away a free source of precision.

Sharma analyzes what happens when competing systems are instead evaluated on identical seeds, so their runs are matched pair by pair. Whenever outcomes under the same seed move together, this pairing strictly reduces the variance of the comparison. Using an extended learning-based multi-agent economic simulator, the paper shows paired evaluation exposing clear differences in both overall and distributional outcomes that stayed statistically inconclusive under independent runs at the same budget. The lesson is practical: seed pairing sharpens comparisons without extra computing.
arxiv-2512-24445:
Akash Samanta and Sheldon Williamson build learning systems that watch their own errors. Deployed learners face nonstationary, safety-critical settings. Instability, slow convergence, and brittle adaptation follow. Modern optimizers adapt to gradient statistics. They mostly ignore the time structure of the error signal itself. This paper makes that structure the control signal.

Every error trajectory is split into three diagnostics. Bias captures persistent drift. Noise captures random variability. Alignment captures repeated push in one direction, the seed of overshoot. The statistics are light and computed online. They work for any architecture or domain. Three systems instantiate the idea: a supervised optimizer, an actor-critic reinforcement learner, and a meta-learned learning policy. Bounded updates and stability hold under standard smoothness assumptions. Error evolution becomes a first-class object in adaptive learning.
arxiv-2512-24945:
Eduardo Sontag argues that biological systems encode function mainly in transient responses, not steady states. Overshoots, two-phase dynamics, adaptation speed, fold-change detection, and entrainment often decide what a cell or organism actually does, yet steady-state dose-response analysis captures them poorly. An input-output perspective on these dynamic phenotypes is developed.

Qualitative features of transient behavior constrain which network architectures could produce them, independently of detailed parameter values. Systems biology readers get a way to rule out models from response shape alone. Synthetic biologists can use the same ideas to design circuits whose timing, not just final level, carries the function.
arxiv-2601-00245:
Osvaldo Simeone, writing alone, reviews how modern AI quietly absorbs brain inspired design ideas. AI growth has driven energy costs sharply upward. Neuromorphic computing promises brain like efficiency in return. Its tools include sparse, discrete spikes and feedback loops. Newer AI models already echo those traits. Quantized activations and state space dynamics are two examples.

His lens splits work inside one token from work across tokens. Early spiking networks handled the inside token case. They remixed channels of a single input vector. Recent work pushes the same ideas across tokens. Sparse attention and state space memory pick what to combine. Associative memory sits at the core of that shift. Training methods get a full review as well. They range from surrogate gradients to local reinforcement rules. The paper maps one field onto another.
arxiv-2601-00545:
Varun Agrawal and Frank Dellaert give roboticists an exact way to reason about problems that mix yes-or-no choices with continuous quantities. A robot may need to decide which landmark it saw while also estimating positions, and hybrid factor graphs can model both together. Existing solvers for such graphs, however, rely on approximations.

The authors introduce a new hybrid Gaussian factor and a hybrid conditional that can hold several continuous hypotheses at once, each tied to a discrete choice. From those pieces they derive a variable elimination algorithm that produces a hybrid Bayes network. That network supports exact best-estimate computation and exact marginal probabilities over both kinds of variables, a firmer foundation for estimation in robotics.
arxiv-2601-00745:
Demerson N Gonçalves and three co-authors give, in 2026, a way to bound the error of quantum regressors without training them. A regressor guesses a number, not a class. Their bound is built from Pauli values, the basic readouts of quantum states. They weigh simple predictors that use one readout axis at a time. The best such predictor caps the error of any fancier model on the same quantum map.

The catch is that the exact cap needs a scan of all readout axes, which is far too many. So the team sample a small set of axes by chance instead. They prove bounds on how far that sample can stray, for a set read budget. Labs can thus rank quantum maps before they build big models. The work turns a rule of thumb from classification into a proven tool for regression.
arxiv-2601-00945:
Kareem El-Badry, Antonio Rodriguez, Matthew Green, and Kevin Burdge use the James Webb Space Telescope to catch the hidden donor stars in three ultra-compact binary systems. AM CVn binaries pair a white dwarf with a helium donor in orbits of fifty to sixty-two minutes. At these long periods the donors are cool and invisible in ordinary light, so they had never been seen directly.

Infrared spectroscopy over two full orbits of each system shows strong double-peaked helium emission from the accretion disk, with moving sub-components where the gas stream strikes the disk. In two systems, sodium lines in emission track the donor's irradiated face, the first direct detection of donors in long-period systems of this class. No donor absorption lines appear.
arxiv-2601-01245:
Yiyuan Huang, Ling Zhou, Min Zhang, and Peter Song tackle a subtle bias in medical studies of repeated events. When a treatment is judged by how often a problem recurs, patients who live longer naturally rack up more events, which can unfairly count against a treatment that keeps people alive. An existing while-alive test fixes that bias but assumes the event rate stays constant over time.

When the rate changes, that test can cry wolf too often and misstate the effect. The authors propose a new test on a proportional rate model, in a causal framework separating recurrence from survival effects. Simulations show it keeps false alarms at the right level while matching the older test's power. They apply it to heart-support devices in a national registry, comparing gut bleeding risk after surgery.
arxiv-2601-01345:
Mathias Nthiani Muia studies copula models, which describe how variables move together while keeping each variable's own behavior separate. In practice, the strength of that linkage often shifts with outside factors such as age or income. His work examines local estimators that fit the linkage near each value of those factors, weighting nearby data most.

Muia proves uniform results: across a whole range of factor values at once, the local likelihood, its slope, and its curvature all settle at stated rates. Those results yield consistent estimates of both the local fit and the linkage function it implies. The proofs lean on empirical process tools for shrinking neighborhoods. The theory matters because covariate-dependent copulas are used in finance and risk work, where unstable local fits can mislead. A uniform guarantee says the whole estimated curve, not just single points, can be trusted as data grow.
arxiv-2601-01945:
Heat carried by light between nanoscale objects can be choreographed if the materials change in time. Philippe Ben-Abdallah studies what happens when a material's permittivity changes in time. The change is periodic. It creates elastic and inelastic scattering channels for thermal photons. The relative phase between modulations decides the outcome. The channels either reinforce or cancel.

That interference control produces directional heat currents and splits heat flow even when everything sits at thermal equilibrium, where no net flow is normally possible. Modulation strength and frequency further tune how much energy moves and where. The mechanism suggests thermal routing and logic steps built from photons. It offers a general platform for heat control at the nanoscale. The platform can be reconfigured as needed.
arxiv-2601-02045:
Compilers are being rebuilt around large language models, and Shuoming Zhang and six co-authors survey the emerging stack. Their taxonomy sorts the work in several ways. One is design outlook: the model may select among existing passes. It may translate code. Or it may generate new artifacts. Other axes are method, level of code detail, and task.

Three benefits recur. Compiler development becomes accessible to more people. Models discover tuning strategies humans missed. The compiler's scope broadens beyond its old borders. The hard problems are correctness and scale. A wrong optimization silently corrupts programs. Real codebases are huge. Hybrid systems marry model flexibility with classical guarantees. They strike the authors as the most promising direction. The survey is offered as a roadmap for the field.
arxiv-2601-02245:
Eight researchers led by Michiel Van Kenhove present MOZAIK, a system for storing and studying data from Internet of Things devices without exposing private values. Sensors produce large amounts of sensitive data, and normal cloud storage gives scale but forces users to trust the cloud provider. MOZAIK aims to keep data encrypted at every step.

The design keeps information encrypted while it travels, while it is stored, and while it is processed. It does this with two tools for computing on encrypted data, secure multi party computation and fully homomorphic encryption. A working test version and speed measurements show what the privacy costs compared with a plain system, and all parts were released as open source software.
arxiv-2601-02645:
Samarth Kalluraya and Yiannis Kantaros give a robot a way to complete a task that looks impossible. Standard planners find collision free, dynamically feasible paths, but they assume the goal can be reached at all. In their setting, a known three dimensional workspace holds surfaces at different heights, formed by objects such as tables that cannot move and boxes that can. The surfaces are disconnected by height gaps, holes, or sideways separations. The goal sits on an elevated surface the robot cannot reach.

Instead of declaring failure, the robot rearranges movable objects to build new traversable connections, a problem family called navigation among movable objects. The planner must decide both where to move each block and how to travel across the changing layout. The work extends earlier navigation among movable objects methods toward genuinely three dimensional, dynamically grounded planning.
arxiv-2601-02845:
Kai Li and eleven co-authors present TiMem, a memory system for chat agents that must stay coherent over very long conversations. Large language models can only hold a limited amount of text at once, so growing chat histories overflow their context windows. Older memory tools often store facts in a flat, fragmented way, which weakens personal responses over time.

TiMem organizes chats in a Temporal Memory Tree, steadily merging raw exchanges into more abstract summaries of the user. It recalls memories with an eye to how hard each question is, balancing accuracy against cost. On two public benchmarks it beat all compared systems, reaching about seventy-five percent accuracy on one while recalling far less stored text.
arxiv-2601-02945:
Xinyi Wei and six co-authors build VTONQA, the first dataset made specifically for judging the quality of virtual try-on images. Online fashion tools that dress a shopper's photo often produce warped garments or bodies that do not match the clothing. The dataset holds more than eight thousand images made by eleven representative try-on models, each scored by human raters.

Raters scored every image on three dimensions: clothing fit, body compatibility, and overall quality, giving more than twenty-four thousand mean opinion scores in total. The authors benchmark both try-on models and many standard image quality metrics against these human judgments. The comparisons expose limits in current evaluation methods and give future work a solid, perception-based foundation.
arxiv-2601-03145:
Sofía Garzón Mora and Christian Haase classify a spectrum of numbers arising in Fine polyhedral adjunction theory, a framework that measures how a polytope interacts with the lattice points inside it. Their work mirrors a recently solved spectrum conjecture of Fujita in algebraic geometry. The central objects are the largest values the Fine spectrum can take, first in low dimensions and then in general.

Computational results for lower-dimensional polytopes lead the authors to a complete classification of the highest numbers of this spectrum in any dimension. They also classify the full Fine spectrum in dimensions one and two, and almost completely in dimension three. A general framework is provided for pushing the classification further in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2601-03245:
Rémi Goerlich and six co-authors rebuild the thermodynamics of systems held away from equilibrium. They use transitions between steady states, rather than the states alone. Far from equilibrium, temperature and free energy grow vague when read off steady-state traits only. The team works with an optically trapped microparticle, driven by a tunable correlated noise. They create active-like steady states, then abruptly change the trap stiffness.

During those jumps, they measure the stochastic work, heat, and entropy produced. A state-dependent effective temperature emerges. It restores the second law for such transitions and supports a generalized notion of work. With it, they derive a Crooks-like fluctuation relation and verify it in the lab. They also establish a fluctuation theorem for the entropy production itself.
arxiv-2601-03545:
Thomas Meier and eight co-authors introduce a new nuclear magnetic resonance method for samples squeezed to extreme pressures inside diamond anvil cells. Such experiments probe how matter changes deep inside planets and under crushing loads, but crowded signals often blur together, hiding chemically similar parts of a sample. Their method, called muT2-NMR, works in the time domain and sorts signals by how fast they relax.

The team benchmarked the method on three hydrogen-rich molecular solids at pressures up to seventy-two gigapascals. The approach separated individual molecular units in relaxation space, where older spectra overlapped. That separation opens a path to sharper high-pressure studies of molecular solids. Better resolution under pressure helps physicists track structural and electronic changes that were previously smeared into one signal.
arxiv-2601-03845:
Akihiro Takemura, Masayuki Otani, and Katsumi Inoue build formal accounts for decision tree models using answer set programming. Trees, random forests, and boosted trees predict well, but their tangled structure resists interpretation, a real problem when decisions need formal justification in safety-critical settings. Earlier work derived logical and abductive accounts with automated reasoning, often through SAT solvers.

The authors' answer set approach yields several account types: sufficient, contrastive, majority, and tree-specific. Encoding user preferences is more flexible than in SAT approaches, and all possible accounts can be listed rather than just one. Tests on varied datasets show where the method shines and where it struggles compared with current tools. For regulated uses of tree models, an explanation that is provably tied to the model's logic carries real weight.
arxiv-2601-04045:
Derek Egolf and Stavros Tripakis present a method to build recursive programs from logical rules that mix quantifiers. Their method starts from a sketch, an outline of the wanted program, and fills it in by search. Counterexamples guide the search away from wrong candidates.

The pair's algorithm learns syntax limits from each counterexample, which prunes the space of candidates. A second pruning trick blocks invalid candidates before they are even listed. Their tool, Cataclyst, solves nearly all of a suite of sixty test cases. Versions without either pruning idea solve fewer. The only other tool that handles such mixed rules lacks sketching and solves far fewer cases in the suite.
arxiv-2601-04145:
Stephon Alexander, Lawrence Edmond, and Cooper Niu propose a way to grow halos made of dark photons during the matter-dominated era. Dark photons are hypothetical partners of ordinary light. In their setup an ultralight axion field couples to dark photons through a parity-breaking Chern-Simons term, and its steady oscillation feeds them through a tachyonic instability.

The dark photons carry a net helicity, which twists the surrounding metric and can seed chiral substructures. For axion masses in the stated ultralight range, the lumps collapse into halos spanning a wide mass range, from galactic dwarf scale up to large galaxy scale. During collapse the induced swirl could move angular momentum efficiently. That would allow single-piece collapse and give early seeds for supermassive black holes, the three authors argue.
arxiv-2601-04245:
Goshi Aoki and Navid Ghaffarzadegan place an AI agent in the role of a city mayor during a simulated epidemic. Agents are used more and more as stand-alone workers, yet rarely as models of human decision-making. Their generative agent works inside a SEIR simulation, the standard model that moves people through susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered states.

Each week the agent reads updated case data and sets business restriction levels. A memory that weights recent events more heavily guides its choices, in single-agent and group settings and across scenes of varied complexity. The agent behaves in human-like reactive ways, tightening as cases rise and loosening as risk falls. Giving it brief systems knowledge about feedback between spread and behaviour improves decision quality and stability a lot, the pair report.
arxiv-2601-05045:
YeongHyeon Park and 5 co-authors investigate hidden settings inside radiotherapy planning software in a 2026 paper. Inverse optimization algorithms plan high-dose-rate brachytherapy for gynaecologic cancers, placing radiation sources to hit tumours while sparing healthy tissue. Commercial planning systems embed user parameter choices that are not visible on the surface, and the team asks how much those hidden inputs change the delivered dose.

They implement three algorithms in-house and compare them against commercial plans across cervical cancer cases with two applicator types. Each algorithm is tested across many combinations of the hidden parameters. If invisible settings swing the dose, clinics need to know, because two planners using the same software could otherwise produce meaningfully different treatments.
arxiv-2601-05345:
Sphiwe B. Skhosana and Najmeh Nakhaei Rad build a way to group data when the thing to be called is an arc, not a line, in a 2026 paper. An arc answer turns up in life science, in rock work, and in the study of winds and waves: a trend, a time of day, a slope's face. The stock model for such data leans on the von Mises law, the arc form of the bell curve. That law fails when the answer has more than one hump.

The pair put forth a mix of arc fits: a set of hid-den groups, each with its own fit of the arc answer on arc or line inputs. The fit finds the groups as it fits them. Arc data with more than one hump are the norm in beast tracks and wind logs, where one mean trend can match no group at all.
arxiv-2601-05545:
Hongjin Kim and 2 co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether automated essay scoring and language models can tell harmful essays from merely argumentative ones. Scoring systems may reward fluent writing while missing racist or otherwise harmful content. That failure could give high marks to essays spreading damaging views.

The team built the Harmful Essay Detection benchmark, containing essays on sensitive topics such as racism and gender bias. Several language models were evaluated on recognizing and scoring that material. Results showed models still struggle to separate harmful from argumentative writing, and scoring systems largely ignore ethical content. The authors call for scoring tools designed with ethical sensitivity built in from the start.
arxiv-2601-05845:
Eric Weine and 3 co-authors introduce in 2026 a new family of Poisson non-negative matrix factorization methods that let data parts combine multiplicatively as well as additively. The method decomposes count data into interpretable parts. Standard versions assume parts simply add, which fits some datasets but not others.

A shifted-log link function, controlled by one tuning parameter, interpolates between additive and multiplicative combination. The authors provide a maximum-likelihood fitting algorithm and a faster approximation whose cost scales with the number of nonzero entries, suiting large sparse data. Examples on varied real datasets show the link choice can change results substantially. In some settings the shifted-log version produced more interpretable decompositions than the standard additive model.
arxiv-2601-06045:
Félix Mortas measures what turning a camera off during video calls actually saves in a 2026 paper. Popular claims say cameras off greatly cut the carbon footprint of virtual meetings. Emissions come from the data transferred, so data use is the thing to measure.

The experiment ran over a 4G phone connection and compared data transfer with video on and off. Turning the camera off could halve data use and the linked emissions, especially on mobile networks. That is a real saving, but the paper frames it against the larger claims in circulation. It ends with recommendations to trim data use and lower the environmental impact of calls without giving up meetings.
arxiv-2601-06445:
A tale is more than a chain of cause and effect. It has pulse, strain, and arc. Mingzhe Lu and 10 co-authors test if AI can grasp that shape in a 2026 paper. Their test, LitVISTA, rests on real works of prose and verse, marked up by form.

A frame called VISTA Space scores two things at once: what a beat does in the tale, and how the tale is built. Top AI models took the test with gold marks for key beats in hand. All fell short in the same ways. None held role and build in one view. When the marks were cut, most faults came from missed or misplaced beats. Modes that claim deep thought helped in a mixed, thin way. The work says prose craft is a live gap in AI skill.
arxiv-2601-06845:
Ping Guo, Chao Li, Yinglan Feng, and Chaoning Zhang wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on control for self-run systems. Their work grows control code by means of a search that tests and keeps the best code. Large language models help drive that search.

Control rules for such systems are hard to design well. Teams often train them by trial and error, or build them by hand. Trial and error can need a huge number of tests. It can also yield rules no one can read or check with ease. Code that comes from the search stays open to view. A reader can trace what the code does and why it acts as it does.
arxiv-2601-06945:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Kevin Hughes and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers wave packet systems and connections to spectral analysis of limiting operators. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. We discuss the design of “wave packet systems” that admit strong concentration properties in phase space.

We make a connection between this problem and topics in signal processing related to the spectral behavior of spatial and frequency-limiting operators. The results have engineering applications in medical imaging, geophysics, and astronomy. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07145:
Ruhi Sayana and nine co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on new dye-like molecules that glow. Such molecules are called fluorophores. Teams use them in sharp imaging work in the life sciences. To find new ones, teams must search a vast space of forms a molecule can take. AI tools can draw new dye frames at speed.

Past tools drew frames that labs could not build in real life. The frames broke the rules of how bonds form in a lab. The flaw came from a lack of reaction rules in the design step. The team built SyntheFluor-RL to fix that gap. It draws on known reaction sets and on blocks that labs can buy or make. It learns by reinforcement, with rewards for frames that a lab can build. The aim is new dyes that are both fresh in form and real to make.
arxiv-2601-07245:
Pranav Kallem and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers learning to trust the crowd. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong average performance yet remain unreliable at the instance level, with frequent hallucinations, brittle failures, and poorly calibrated confidence.

The authors study reliability through the lens of multi-model consensus : given responses from several heterogeneous LLMs. Can we learn which answer is most likely correct for a given query. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07345: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Ze-fan Wang(王泽凡) and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers new h ⁡ ( z ) h(z) measurement at redshift = 0.12. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The Hubble parameter ( H ( z ) H(z) ) is a function of. The redshift and a reliable measurement is very important to understand the expansion history of the Universe. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07445:
Francesco Marcolli, Martin James, and Agnese Seminara ask a counterintuitive question in their 2026 preprint: can noise help find a smell? Their subject is odor source localization, meaning how to infer where a scent comes from. The setting is a turbulent plume, where wind breaks the odor into scattered patches.

Many sensors spread through the plume supply the data for the inference. The authors draw on distributed chemosensation in biology, where living systems sense chemicals across many receptors at once. Their focus is proprioceptive noise, the error in sensing one's own position or state. Rather than assume noise only harms accuracy, they test whether it changes how well the source can be located. Readers get a fresh angle on a classic search problem.
arxiv-2601-07545:
Private linear regression is the subject of this 2026 preprint, which proposes a new method called iterative Hessian mixing. The task is ordinary least squares under differential privacy, using bounded data. Privacy noise must be added so no single person's data can be recovered. The standard approach, adaptive sufficient-statistics perturbation, perturbs the key matrices of the regression.

That standard method is known for near-optimal accuracy and strong results in practice. A new contender must therefore match a high bar. Iterative Hessian mixing offers a different route to the same goal. The Hessian captures curvature of the fitting problem, and mixing steps may spread privacy noise more efficiently. The paper speaks to scholars who need regression on sensitive data with formal privacy guarantees.
arxiv-2601-07845:
Shree Charran R and Rahul Kumar Dubey design an edge AI system to help enforce road safety in fast-growing economies. Rapid motorization in India created a sharp imbalance: over eleven million recorded violations in 2023, against roughly one officer per four thousand vehicles. Traditional surveillance and manual ticketing cannot scale to that volume. Their 2026 preprint proposes an autonomous, cooperative, energy-efficient perception node at the edge.

Edge processing means cameras analyze scenes locally instead of streaming everything to a cloud. Connected-vehicle integration lets the node share findings with vehicles and authorities. Energy efficiency matters for roadside hardware that runs all day. The system aims to close the enforcement gap without hiring at impossible scale. Transport and smart city engineers are the readers. The paper grounds its design in real violation and staffing numbers.
arxiv-2601-08145: Qi Meng and Chang Xu study how light atomic nuclei form and dissolve inside nuclear matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a microscopic in-medium few-body approach. The clusters covered are the deuteron, tritium, helium-3, and the alpha particle. Clustering of nucleons shapes both nuclear physics and astrophysics, from lab reactions to stellar matter. As density rises, clusters can break apart in what is called a Mott transition. The authors track formation and dissolution across medium conditions. Their results help model matter in neutron stars and heavy-ion collisions.
arxiv-2601-08245: Hao Liu, Jin Lei, and Zhongzhou Ren study absorption in reactions of weakly bound nuclei. Their 2026 arXiv paper works within the continuum-discretized coupled-channels framework. Untangling reaction mechanisms in such nuclei has long been hard. A common habit treats absorption as an incoherent sum of channel contributions. The authors apply the generalized optical theorem to test that habit. They find a dual role for off-diagonal couplings in coherent absorption dynamics. The result may change how theorists model breakup and fusion in halo nuclei and other fragile systems.
arxiv-2601-08445:
Guan-Ting Lin and four co-authors apply multiobjective model predictive control to home energy management. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies residential users in demand response programs under real-time pricing. Households must balance electricity costs against user dissatisfaction when prices shift.

The system includes battery storage and must handle uncertainty in prices and demand. Laguerre functions parameterize the control signals, turning the problem into one with linear inequalities. That form allows efficient exploration of trade-offs between cost and comfort. For utilities and smart home builders, the method offers a principled way to shift home energy use without angering residents.
arxiv-2601-08545:
Zhenlong Dai and co-authors introduce learner-tailored program repair for programming students. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that large language models have pushed intelligent programming coaching forward. Most research repairs learners' buggy code without explaining the underlying causes of the bugs, though.

The new task, LPR, asks for repairs tailored to the learner, not just correct code. Their generator uses iterative edit-driven retrieval to improve its fixes. A repair that shows why code failed can teach, while a silent fix cannot. For education platforms, tailored repair could turn each bug into a small lesson matched to the student's own code.
arxiv-2601-09445:
Minh Vu Pham, Hsuvas Borkakoty, and Yufang Hou look inside language models for clashes in what they know. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies intra-memory knowledge conflict, where one model stores inconsistent facts about the same event. Earlier work mostly handled clashes between a model's knowledge and outside sources.

Fixes like fine-tuning or knowledge editing target that outside-facing problem. Far less is known about conflicts baked in during pre-training, inside the model's own representations. The authors study how to localize such conflicts mechanically. Knowing where a contradiction lives is a first step toward models that can catch their own mixed-up facts.
arxiv-2601-09745:
Antonio Abu Nassar and Eitan Farchi report a case study on writing exact software specifications with AI help. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether recent AI advances can rescue formal specification. Formal specs catch errors early and state invariants plainly, yet industry rarely uses them.

The barriers are notation overhead and the rare expertise the languages demand. The case study shows AI assistance keeping many benefits while cutting those costs sharply. If specs become cheap to write, more teams could prove key properties before code ships. The study offers evidence from practice, not just promise.
arxiv-2601-09845:
Sergio Suárez-Dou and five co-authors test a machine-learned force field against quantum chemistry on proteins. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies protein stability and vibrations in vacuum and water. Predicting energies and spectra of biomolecules needs quantum accuracy at force-field speed.

The SO3LR learned force field is checked against PBE0+MBD density-functional theory. The authors report fidelity beyond anything seen before, across molecules larger and more complex than its training set. What matters most are the energy gaps between metastable states and the surface's local curvature. A field this faithful could speed drug and enzyme studies sharply.
arxiv-2601-10245:
Vansh Kapoor and co authors route hard steps of a task to a large model, and easy steps to a small one. Multi step tasks can fail from one bad step. That one step can wreck the whole chain. Past route plans send the full task to one model.

That treats all steps as the same. The team made TRIM, a step wise route plan. It spots the steps most apt to wreck the chain. Those steps go to a large model. Plain steps stay with a small model. The aim is high grades at a lower cost than all large runs.
arxiv-2601-10345:
Yunyi Liu and Taketo Akama fix songs that were pitch shifted with crude tools. Pitch shift is a base tool in song work. Crude shifts can move the tone of the voice. They can add a robot like hue. The harm grows as the shift grows.

The team recast the task as a fix up job. They take the shifted track as a spoiled form. A shallow diffusion model then cleans it. Melody and time stay as they were. What changes is the hue of the voice. The aim is a shifted song that still sounds like a true voice.
arxiv-2601-10445:
Glenna Nightingale and co authors track mental health paths through the COVID years in UK data. The health hit of the pandemic is well known. Less is known about how it moved in time. It may have hit groups in unlike ways and at unlike times.

The team use data from the whole UK. They track paths by age, sex, and place based traits. Such paths show who bore the worst load and when. They also show who got well fast and who did not. The work can guide where care funds should go when a next shock hits.
arxiv-2601-10645:
Yuxi Xia, Loris Schoenegger, and Benjamin Roth study the training data behind a language model's stated confidence. Models often say how sure they are in words. Users may trust those words, yet models tend to sound more sure than they should be. Stated confidence often fails to match real accuracy.

The authors retrieve the training examples that most shaped a model's verbalized confidence. Finding those examples helps explain why a model sounds sure or unsure on a given answer. That kind of audit can guide fixes for overconfidence. It matters for any setting where users act on what a model claims to know.
arxiv-2601-10845:
Myriam AbiHabib and Ayman Badawi introduce the n-total graph of an integral domain. Graph constructions turn algebra into pictures: elements become vertices, and a rule draws the edges. Here the base is a finite product of integral domains, with a chosen union of prime ideals. A positive integer n sets the rule's strength.

The paper defines the graph and begins its study. Such graphs reveal how zero divisors and units sit inside a ring. Patterns in the picture can point to algebraic facts that are hard to see in symbols alone. The work joins a lively line of research that reads rings through the graphs they cast.
arxiv-2601-11445:
Juan Garrido, Nabil Kazi-Tani, and Emilio Vilches add noise to a sweeping process. Their 2026 preprint studies existence of solutions in that setting. A sweeping process models a point dragged by a moving set. Think of a load pushed along by a shifting constraint.

Here the moving set takes prox-regular values throughout. It shifts continuously in Hausdorff distance, with no smoothness asked. Random perturbations then shake the process as it runs. The team asks when solutions still exist in that noise. They weigh several geometric assumptions for the moving set. Links between those assumptions are set out with care. The work sits where stochastic analysis meets geometry.
arxiv-2601-11545:
Houhao Liang and six coauthors fuse data on how older adults move in cities. Their 2026 preprint studies micro-scale features of the built environment. Safe, inclusive mobility for vulnerable older adults is a rising priority. Urban planning needs to know what helps or hinders them.

Surveys and GIS audits give only a limited view today. They miss how small features shape real behavior and perception. A low curb or poor light can change a whole trip. The team fuses multimodal data to catch those dynamics. Dynamic interaction between people and places is the target. Better data can guide age-friendly street design.
arxiv-2601-11645:
Ujjwal Jain and three coauthors segment brain cells in microscope images. Their 2026 preprint names the frame IMSAHLO, on outlining nerve cells. Measuring cell shape needs accurate cell outlines first. Different neuronal datasets call for different model architectures.

IMSAHLO adds attention at many scales into the outlining net. Attention at several scales catches cells of unlike sizes. A hybrid loss optimization steadies training across cases. Robust outlining must hold up on varied microscope data. Cell shapes differ by type, stain, and imaging rig. The frame aims at one robust tool for many sets. Better outlines feed studies of brain cell form and health.
arxiv-2601-11845:
Justin Young, Muthoni Ngatia, and Eleanor W. Dillon test how well causal tools work when the truth is known. New machine learning tools make it easier to model links between traits, treatments, and outcomes. That makes causal claims from plain data look more safe.

They use a rare data set with two parts. One part is a true trial roll-out of a new product trait at a large tech firm. The other part is users who chose the trait on their own. By matching tool calls to the trial truth, they can grade each tool fairly.
arxiv-2601-12445:
Cosmin Pohoata proves a result about dot products formed by permuting one of two sets of real numbers. Take two sets, each with n numbers. Pair them up in some order and add the products to get one sum. Each new pairing, or permutation, can give a new sum, and the question is how many distinct sums must arise.

Pohoata shows that the count is always large, on the order of n cubed. That bound holds for any choice of the two sets at all. Results of this kind sit in additive combinatorics, where one counts how rich a set of sums must be. A cubic floor is a strong pledge about that richness.
arxiv-2601-13145:
S. Spiridon Kasapis and a large team built a data set to help spot new active zones on the Sun. Active zones are the spots where flares and storms are born. To guard space craft and grids, teams must spot zones before they form on the face we can see.
