Their set is called SolARED. It is made for machine learning tools that aim to guess where a zone will next rise. Early flags would give a head start for space weather alerts. The set gives such tools a shared base to train and test on. Sun watch teams gain a way to judge which guess tools work best before real storms hit.
arxiv-2601-13345:
Saurabhsingh Rajput, Alex Brandt, Vadim Elisseev, and Tushar Sharma cut the power draw of GPU kernels by static code checks. AI apps, above all large language models, run on graphics chips. Their small code units, called kernels, burn a lot of power. Yet coders often lack the chip craft to tune them for power.

Their frame is called FlipFlop. It reads code with no run, finds waste, and guides fixes that save power with no loss of task. Static reads can run in a build chain, so teams gain the checks at scale. For data hubs, small per kernel saves stack into vast cuts in cost and heat.
arxiv-2601-13845:
Raiane Ferreira Monteiro and a large team study sulfur harm to tiny metal clusters used as catalysts in 2026. Transition-metal nanoclusters have size-tuned traits that can beat bulk materials in catalysis. Sulfur poisoning can block their active sites and kill that edge. The team studies clusters of thirteen atoms with an icosahedral shape.

They use interpretable, physics-informed learning to reveal how sulfur adsorbs. Adsorption is the sticking of atoms onto a surface. Clear mechanisms show why poisoning hits and how to resist it. Catalysts that shrug off sulfur last longer in fuel and chemical work.
arxiv-2601-14045:
Ben Lakeland and a large team report two new exoplanets around the star TOI-5788 in 2026. TOI-5788 is a metal-poor, solar-type star. The planets transit, crossing the star's face as seen from Earth. The team used six TESS sectors and a dedicated CHEOPS programme, plus HARPS-N data.

The inner planet, TOI-5788 b, orbits in about 6.34 days. Its radius is about 1.53 times that of Earth. Metal-poor stars test planet formation theories built on richer stars. Two planets in one such system give a rich case for study. The star is poor in metals, which makes the pair a good test of how planets form with less raw stuff. Two worlds in one system let the team check size and gap side by side.
arxiv-2601-14145:
H. Witała discusses how to teleport a quantum state using proton systems in 2026. Quantum state teleportation moves a state via entanglement and classical signals. The team discusses generating entangled Bell states of two nucleons. Sources include unpolarized nucleon-nucleon scattering and exclusive deuteron breakup.

They follow an approach by Shen and co-authors from a 2025 preprint. In that work, Bell states were identified in unpolarized proton-proton elastic scattering. Nucleon systems could give labs a new route to teleportation tests. Such tests extend quantum information into nuclear physics. Proton rigs are far more common than photon rigs in some labs. A proton path could bring teleport tests to new groups.
arxiv-2601-14245:
Zhongyu Yang, Wei Pang, and Yingfang Yuan present a search method in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM Web Conference. Their topic is composed image retrieval. In that task, a search starts with one reference image plus a text note on what to change. The system must find images that fit both parts at once.

The authors argue that older embedding methods see too little of this mix. They catch few cross-modal cues and do weak semantic reasoning. Their answer is XR, a system of cross-modal agents. Agents are AI workers that plan and act in steps. The design aims for deeper thought about both the image and the text note.
arxiv-2601-14445:
Aiden Mazidi and six co-authors work on touch feedback in robot surgery in this 2026 paper. Robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery lacks the feel a surgeon's hands would give. Adding accurate haptic feedback is hard. Precise force rendering is tough, and safety during teleoperation must hold at all times.

The team presents NIMA, a Nonlinear Impedance Matching Approach. It extends their past Impedance Matching Approach, which they had already validated. The new version adds nonlinear dynamics to model complex tool-tissue interactions. It renders those forces in real time. Readers get a step toward surgical robots that let a remote operator feel tissue more truly and safely.
arxiv-2601-14945:
Yuteng Sun, Haoran Wang, and co-authors tackle a timing flaw in robot control. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with vision-language-action models, large models that guide robots. These models reason well about meaning but respond slowly.

That slowness forces a batch-and-execute style of work. While the robot acts, it is blind to change. A moving target can slip away in that gap. The team proposes TIDAL, a layered design. It splits slow semantic thought from fast motor actuation, weaving the two loops together in time so the robot can react far sooner.
arxiv-2601-15045:
Bastien Isabella, Cécile Monteux, and Sylvain Deville watch bubbles form as a liquid turns solid. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the solidification front, the moving edge where freezing takes place. Trapped gas bubbles shape the structure and strength of the final material.

This matters from metal alloys to plain ice. Gas gathering at the front is well documented. What stays murky is the live motion of the bubbles: how they are born, grow, and get swallowed. The authors study in real time how those steps depend on the speed of freezing.
arxiv-2601-15245:
Domagoj Bradač, Jacob Fox, Raphael Steiner, Benny Sudakov, and Shengtong Zhang sharpen a classic coloring bound. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with degenerate graphs, where every part has a low-degree vertex. A d-degenerate graph can always be colored with d plus one colors.

Complete graphs show that this bound cannot be improved in general. The authors ask if it stays tight under extra limits. They study small, locally sparse degenerate graphs, where large cliques are forbidden. Related problems get the same treatment, to see where the classic bound can finally be beaten.
arxiv-2601-15345:
Amanda Gatto Lamas and Taylor L. Hughes ask whether motion can force a quantum state to be entangled over long range. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with one-dimensional systems where translation symmetry is broken. An earlier result by Gioia and Wang frames the question.

That result showed symmetric states with nonzero momentum must be long-range entangled. With the symmetry gone, momentum itself needs a new meaning. The authors ask if such a notion can still encode the nature of a state's entanglement. Their answer, flagged in the title, is yes: nonzero momentum implies long-range entanglement.
arxiv-2601-15745:
Ruoqing Zhao, Runze Xia, and Piji Li work on trust in automated medical reports in a 2026 arXiv paper. Natural language tools now help write radiology reports. They ease the workload of radiologists. Large vision-language models read scans and draft text with real skill. Yet they can generate plausible yet inaccurate claims. The field calls these hallucinations. In medicine, a false claim in a report can mislead treatment.

The paper's title names its goal: mitigating hallucination in medical report generation. The nuanced, critical nature of the field raises the bar for fixes. A report must match the scan, not just sound fluent. For hospitals weighing automation, hallucination control is the gating issue. This work speaks to that gate.
arxiv-2601-16045:
Yue Shi and a large team build a tool to guess crop mass when water is short. Their 2026 preprint, named AgriPINN, blends a neural net with crop growth rules. Plain data models scale well but can be hard to read. They can also fail when new fields differ from past fields. Crop rule models need long set up and do not scale with ease.

AgriPINN aims to join the strengths of both paths. The net learns from data while the crop rules guide its form. That guide should keep the tool clear to read and firm on new ground. Good mass guesses help guide water use and track crop yield. The team frames the tool for use at wide scale.
arxiv-2601-16545:
Pavel Exner, Jiří Lipovský and Jan Pekař find graph tones from a cut off twin. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum graphs that join a core to leads. Leads run out with no end in the full graph. Tones of the full graph, called resonances, are hard to read straight. The team cuts the leads to a fixed length in a twin graph.

Tone shifts in the cut twin mark the tones of the full graph. As the cut length grows, those marks grow sharp and true. A twin trick turns a hard read to a plain one. That trick serves wave guides and wire nets. The work gives a clean route to graph tones.
arxiv-2601-16645:
Minsu Gong and three coauthors keep edge lines in pic edits with a new loss. Their 2026 preprint deals with edits by latent spread models. Such models give wide, text led edits on many pic types. Yet they oft blur or shift fine edge lines in the pic. True edge lines count for style swaps and tone fixes.

A new loss in train guards edge lines as edits run. Guard loss weighs edge drift and holds it low in the end pic. Low drift keeps the pic true while its look shifts. That pair is what pro edit tools must give. The work adds edge care to spread edit craft.
arxiv-2601-16745:
Horia Cornean, Bernard Helffer, and Radu Purice take a fresh look at a famed swap in quantum math. The swap trades a slow magnet field for a shift in wave phase. It sits in the Bloch tale of electrons in crystals. Their 2026 preprint gives the swap a broad new form. The form works for a set of Bloch bands at once.

A local gap in the band stack is the key need. No slow-change plea is made for the field. Long-range fields come in scope as well. Tight frames that hug each site do the work. The swap now fits more real crystal and chip traits.
arxiv-2601-16945:
Adam Chojecki, Piotr Graczyk, Hideyuki Ishi, and Bartosz Kołodziejek ease Bayes work for a class of graph models. Their models tie traits in graphs with hue rules. Traits linked by hue must share or split in set ways. Picking the best graph by Bayes needs a hard norm count. That count has long blocked this class.

Their 2026 preprint finds plain forms for that count. The forms use gamma-type sums over cone sets. Plain counts let Bayes picks run at real scale. Such models serve gene, brain, and risk webs. Hue rules there catch shared traits that plain graphs miss.
arxiv-2601-17145:
Vydhourie Thiyageswaran and five co-authors study how to design trials on social networks. In such trials, one person's treatment can spill over to friends. That spillover is called interference. A common fix groups people into clusters and assigns whole clusters at once. The team asks when that fix helps and when it hurts.

They focus on homophily, the pull for like people to link up. With strong homophily, cluster designs can raise error in the mean effect being measured. The authors weigh that risk against robustness needs. Their work guides teams who test programs on real networks. It shows why network shape must shape trial design from the start.
arxiv-2601-17645:
Xilin Jiang and co-authors introduce AVMeme Exam, a benchmark for cultural knowledge in AI models. Internet clips carry meaning in sound and motion over time. Text alone cannot hold that meaning. The benchmark is human-curated. It holds over one thousand iconic sounds and videos. Items span speech, songs, music, and sound effects.

Models have to grasp those items in a human cultural frame. Meme knowledge is a real part of online literacy. A model that misses it will misread user intent. The benchmark spans many cultures and languages, as its title states. It tests contextual and cultural thinking, not just recall. Builders gain a hard, fun test of model breadth.
arxiv-2601-17845:
Killian Davitt, Dan Ristea, and Steven J. Murdoch test whether anonymous networks are now fast enough for live use. Their 2026 preprint is about mixnets. A mixnet hides who talks to whom by mixing traffic, and it adds delay on purpose to do so. New designs have cut that delay from hours down to seconds while keeping the same level of anonymity.

Live chat and calls need low delay to feel usable. The authors ask, in effect, if the field has become collaborative yet. They study how the new latency feels in real-time tasks. The answer matters for activists, reporters, and anyone who needs both privacy and live contact. Speed has long been the price of strong anonymity.
arxiv-2601-17945:
Giovanni Gaiffi and Giovanni Interdonato generalize a classic count in combinatorics. Their 2026 preprint grows out of work by Lin on semipermutations. Those objects index a basis for the cohomology of a Hessenberg-type variety. The counts of that basis, called Betti numbers, extend the Eulerian numbers, a famous family that counts descents in permutations. The authors connect these objects back to the symmetric group in three ways.

They find three distinct subsets of the symmetric group that match the semipermutations one-to-one. Such matches let results move between algebra, geometry, and counting. Each bijection is a small bridge between fields. The work enriches the story of how Eulerian numbers generalize.
arxiv-2601-18145:
Heguang Lin and co-authors compute exact confidence sets for multinomial outcomes. Their 2026 preprint deals with a basic tool of data science. Confidence sets underpin A/B testing and the analysis of learning algorithms. For outcomes with several categories, a good set should be as small as truth allows. The team studies the intersection of confidence sets with minimum volume, and they make the computation exact.

Exactness matters when sets guide product or policy choices. A set that is too wide wastes data; one that cheats breaks trust. Minimum volume squeezes the most from each sample. The work serves testers who must state what the data really support.
arxiv-2601-18245:
Santanu Das and Jatin Batra tackle phase retrieval when the data are dirty in two ways at once. Their 2026 preprint studies recovery of a signal from phaseless measurements. Each measurement keeps only the squared size of an inner product, plus noise. The noise here has heavy tails, so wild values are common. An adversary may also corrupt part of the data. The authors give a tractable method with near-linear sample complexity, meaning the needed measurements grow almost in step with the signal size.

Phase retrieval sits inside imaging, optics, and signal tools. Robust versions matter wherever sensors misbehave or foes interfere. A method that stays fast under attack is a strong result.
arxiv-2601-18445:
Eymen Ünay, Björn Franke, and Jackson Woodruff work on a math trick that lets firms do math on locked data. The trick, called fully homomorphic encryption, keeps facts hid while a cloud host works on them. It is strong but slow, and it eats memory. Most of that memory goes to a set of keys that let the host turn the locked bits in place.

In big jobs those keys can choke the whole run and cap how much work gets done. The team built a tool chain that plans key use with care from the start. Their compiler and run time aim to keep the key stock small while the job still runs fast. Less waste would bring locked math closer to real use in banks and health care.
arxiv-2601-19145:
Juraj Földes and Declan Stacy extend a survival test for species and states in endless dimensional systems. Stochastic persistence asks whether a random system keeps all its parts alive in the long run, rather than letting one die out. The models that need it, like reaction diffusion equations with noise, live in infinite dimensions.

A classic test uses an average Lyapunov function, but it was known only in finite dimensions. The pair build general criteria for the infinite case. Ecology and biology gain a tool for models where space and noise both matter and no finite shortcut exists.
arxiv-2601-19345:
Abdullah Khanfor and three co-authors survey how to spot intruders among city drones. Drones promise cities better traffic watching, disaster response, and environmental checks. That spread also opens fresh security holes that must be closed for safe, trusted use over people's heads.

Their survey gathers the state of AI driven intrusion detection for drones in smart city settings. It maps what kinds of attacks arise and which detectors answer them. A clear survey gives city planners and drone builders one place to see the threat picture before fleets grow. It also gives later work a shared map of terms, threats, and open problems to build on.
arxiv-2601-19945:
Thomas Schuster and colleagues benchmark speech recognition for German medical practice. Automatic speech recognition could relieve medical staff by drafting documentation from spoken case histories. English has many benchmarks; the German medical context lacks specific evaluations. Dialects and accents, common in real clinics, are rarely tested at all.

The team analyses how well current speech recognition models perform on German medical interviews. Their focus is the anamnesis conversation, where a patient recounts symptoms and history. Errors there can flow into records and treatment. Knowing real accuracy, including for dialect speakers, tells hospitals what the tools can safely do. The work fills a practical gap for German-speaking healthcare.
arxiv-2601-20145:
Xingyuan Lin, Xiuxiu Lin, and Xuesong Chen analyze errors in a finite element method for elliptic optimal control problems. The problems have a Robin boundary condition, and the quantity of interest is observed on the boundary. The method studied combines mesh size and polynomial degree, known as the hp approach.

The authors derive error estimates both before and after computation, called a priori and a posteriori estimates. Their proofs use a Clément-type approach and an auxiliary system. Such estimates tell engineers how fine a mesh must be to trust a computed control. They also show where to refine it for the best accuracy per cost.
arxiv-2601-20545:
Dylan M. Paré and four colleagues test whether polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons can explain anomalous microwave emission near the plane of our galaxy. This emission has been a puzzle for close to thirty years. One candidate source is rotational emission from these large carbon molecules, which can have the electric dipole and size range needed to match the signal.

The authors analyze the hydrocarbons as a tracer of the emission using the CosmoGlobe reduction of DIRBE data. Settling the source matters because the emission contaminates maps of the early universe, and because it traces carbon chemistry in interstellar space. DIRBE was a space instrument that mapped the sky in infrared light.
arxiv-2601-20645:
T. C. Adorno, S. P. Gavrilov, and D. M. Gitman study photon emission when a strong electric field makes the vacuum unstable. In such fields, electron-positron pairs can be created from empty space. The authors follow a nonperturbative formulation of strong-field quantum electrodynamics from their earlier work, for a quasi-constant field of finite duration.

They construct closed formulas for the total probabilities of the emission that accompanies pair creation. Exact formulas of this kind are benchmarks for the laser facilities now reaching field strengths where vacuum effects begin to matter.
arxiv-2601-20745:
Guoan Wang and four co-authors tackle the memory problem of very large language models. Their 2026 paper presents Hestia, a training framework for extremely low-bit models. Quantization stores model weights in very few bits to save memory. Done during training, it is called quantization-aware training. The catch is that most methods round weights hard from the very first step.

That early rounding, the authors argue, harms learning. It freezes the search space too soon and leaves a lasting mismatch between real and quantized weights. Hestia uses Hessian guidance, that is, curvature information, to steer the process. The aim is a small model that still trains well. The work speaks to anyone who needs big models to run on modest hardware.
arxiv-2601-20945:
Wenjie Ji, Ryan Lanzetta, Zheng Zhou, and Chong Wang study a puzzling phase transition in the toric code. Their 2026 paper concerns self-dual Higgs transitions. The toric code is a model system for topological order. Deforming it while keeping its self-duality symmetry leads somewhere strange. The symmetry swaps electric and magnetic excitations. The deformed code can pass into a topologically trivial state. That state breaks the symmetry on its own.

Numerically, this transition was found to be continuous. A smooth transition of this kind is enigmatic. No continuum field theory description has long been available for it. The authors take up that gap, going beyond the toric code itself. Their work tests how far known theory can stretch. It matters for the physics of quantum matter and error-correcting codes alike.
arxiv-2601-21145:
Felipe Sobrero, Luca Abrahão, and Thiago Guerreiro revisit a thought experiment about the quantum nature of strong gravity. Their 2026 paper builds on an analysis by Belenchia and co-authors. Two observers, Alice and Bob, try to communicate by superluminal signals. Their scheme uses a superposition of massive particles dressed by Newtonian fields. A test particle serves as the field detector. If the scheme worked, it would break known physics.

It does not work, and the paper examines why. Quantum fluctuations in the particle motion and the field block the signal. Those fluctuations prevent violations of quantum mechanics. The setup becomes a probe of how gravity must behave quantum mechanically. Arguments of this kind constrain any future theory of quantum gravity. The paper sharpens one of the field's favorite sanity checks.
arxiv-2601-21245:
Yeping Li, Gaofeng Wang, and Tianfang Wu study the fluid limit of a kinetic model for charged gas mixtures. The starting model mixes Vlasov, Poisson, and Boltzmann terms to track particles, electric fields, and collisions. The authors ask what fluid equations emerge when collisions dominate.

They work in the whole space and cover a wide range for a key interaction parameter. Passing from particle rules to fluid rules is a core step in plasma and gas theory. A rigorous limit tells modelers when the simpler fluid picture is safe to use. It also anchors simulations that switch between the two levels.
arxiv-2601-21445:
Oleg Karpenkov, Ian Short, Matty van Son, and Andrei Zabolotskii classify tilings built from whole numbers. The work grows out of a classic puzzle where triangulated polygons model patterns of positive integers. Interest surged after cluster algebras appeared in the early two thousands.

The authors aim to classify all tame integer tilings and their higher-dimensional cousins, called hypertilings. The classification uses cubes from Bhargava's work, frieze patterns, and determinant-like quantities. A full catalogue turns scattered examples into a map of what is possible. Such maps often reveal number patterns that no single example would suggest.
arxiv-2601-21645:
Vahid Shahverdi, Giovanni Luca Marchetti, Georg Bökman, and Kathlén Kohn prove a tidy fact about symmetry in deep networks. A network is equivariant when shifting the input shifts the output in a matching way. That property can hold for the whole network while the inner layers look messy.

The authors show the mess is optional. For any such network, the same overall function can be realized with layers that are each equivariant too. Layerwise symmetry makes networks easier to analyze and to build by design. The theorem assures designers that imposing symmetry layer by layer costs nothing in what the network can express.
arxiv-2601-22145:
Mehmet Asım Gümüş and co-authors push a scheme that finds how bits of matter scatter, with no small-print law to start from. Their test case is a plain four-bit hit in four space dims. At strong force, the hit strength must be bent so that chance is not lost. That bend is the hard part of the task.

The scheme adds up a vast sum of flat graphs. Each graph is built from rules for two-bit hits and from a swap rule for the bits. The team casts the sum as a set of curved sum laws for the jumps in the hit strength. Their work can cope with hits that spawn new bits. It is a step toward laws of force drawn from rules of sense, not from a guessed first law.
arxiv-2601-22345:
Mahdi JafariRaviz and five co-authors find that top language models explore too little when a task needs trial and error. Their 2026 preprint sets three tasks whose search load can be dialed up or down. Each model gets a fixed budget of tries in a live, changing setup.

Across leading models, the team find thin search and weak final picks. Simple search-then-use rules often beat the models by a wide gap. More tries help the models less than one would hope. The result warns teams that chat skill is not search skill. Agents sent to explore need checks.
arxiv-2601-22945:
Joshua J Bon, James Bailie, Judith Rousseau, and Christian P Robert frame privacy as a game. Their Bayesian game-theoretic view treats a data holder and an attacker as players with goals. From that view, new privacy definitions can be built for a clear purpose, with solid justification.

The same lens can grade existing privacy promises, showing what they really protect against. Privacy rules are often adopted on habit or authority, without a stated threat model. A game-based frame forces that model into the open, where it can be debated.
arxiv-2601-23045:
Alexander Hägele and four co-authors ask how AI misalignment grows as models get smarter and tasks get harder. Capable systems now take on broad, consequential work, so their failure modes matter more. The central worry is whether strong models fail by calmly chasing goals we never intended.

The study tracks how that risk scales with intelligence and task complexity. If misalignment grows in a predictable way, builders can plan safeguards before models reach that level. If it jumps suddenly, the case for caution is even stronger. Systematically pursuing unintended goals is the failure mode under study, distinct from random errors or simple incapability.
arxiv-2601-23145:
John Southworth revisits the eclipsing binary star system DV Boötes, in a long-running series on such systems. DV Boo pairs a metallic-lined A-type star with a normal late-F star. The two orbit each other in just under four days, on a path that may be slightly eccentric.

Eclipsing binaries let astronomers weigh and measure stars with rare precision. One star here shows the chemical oddity called metallic lining, which tests theories of stellar atmospheres. Careful re-measurement keeps the basic data of stellar physics honest and current.
arxiv-2602-00245: Pedro R. Nicácio Falcão and coauthors use fermionic antiflatness to track non-Gaussianity in disordered quantum spin chains. Non-Gaussianity marks departure from a classically tractable free fermion picture, a necessary resource for quantum advantage. Scaling follows a volume law for the XXZ chain, with an area law bound for the impurity case. Rare cat like states show a sharp antiflatness boost, flagging mechanisms that may destabilize localization.
arxiv-2602-00345: Piotr Bizoń and team establish three self similar solutions of Yang-Mills equations in high odd dimensions. Extensive computations suggest N equals 3 for all odd d at or above 11. Two solutions admit closed form expressions, one previously known and one apparently new, pointing to a simple landscape of blowup scenarios.
arxiv-2602-00445: Michelle Sebastian studies the relationship between star cluster radius and mass, and whether age and star formation rate influence cluster size. Using regression analysis on 5,105 star clusters from the LEGUS survey, the author compares a full multivariate model with a mass only baseline. Mass dominated the radius-mass relation, while star formation rate and age contributed negligibly. Cross-validation showed that the mass only model generalized better than the full model.
arxiv-2602-00545: Shenyang Deng and colleagues challenge the view that the bulk-and-spike Hessian spectrum of deep networks comes from imbalanced data covariance. In a deep linear network with perfectly balanced data covariance, the Hessian still splits into a dominant cluster and a bulk cluster. The ratio between dominant and bulk eigenvalues grows linearly with network depth, showing architecture, not data alone, shapes the spectral gap. Architecture and data characteristics should therefore both inform optimisation algorithm design for deep networks.
arxiv-2602-00845: Senkang Hu and colleagues present InfoReasoner, a method that rewards good information seeking in agent work with large reasoning models. They define information gain as uncertainty drop over belief states, with proofs of basic guarantees. An intrinsic estimator finds gain from outputs via meaning groups, needing no manual labels. The reward guides training via Group Relative Policy Optimization. Tests across seven benchmarks show up to 5.4% higher accuracy than strong baselines.
arxiv-2602-01045: Zixin Jessie Chen and co-authors test how packed features shape the speed law of training in a teacher-pupil setup. With no packing, their math ties the speed exponent to data shape and channel weight. Once a packing bottleneck bites, the law flips to a plain one-over-time curve near 1, whatever the data or channel mix. That packed regime trains up to ten times faster than step-by-step learning unpacked. Since many big nets pack features, the find may bear on a wide swath of real models.
arxiv-2602-01345: Yu Zhang and co-authors speed visual autoregressive nets with NOVA, a no-train token trim guided by doubt. Such nets burn compute on huge token counts, while past trim plans use fixed stage cuts, stiff schedules, and narrow scope, leaving speed untapped. Since doubt shifts track guess risk, NOVA spots the bend point of scale doubt growth live and fires trimming there. Scale- and layer-linked ratios then trim low-doubt tokens per scale and layer, reusing prior-scale caches to hold quality while cutting run time.
arxiv-2602-01645: Yuxuan Liu and colleagues audit generative music models for copyright compliance by testing whether an audio clip trained the model. Loss based signals like reconstruction error line up poorly with perception, giving weak separation at the low false positive rates forensics demands. Their white box LSA-Probe measures a geometric trait of reverse diffusion: the smallest time normalized perturbation budget that pushes an intermediate state across a perceptual degradation threshold. Training members sit in more stable regions and demand a higher degradation cost, making that cost a membership signal.
arxiv-2602-01745: Wenhao Yu and colleagues improve guided fine tuning with token weighting, where single signals mislead. Ground truth probability reflects alignment, while token entropy reflects built in uncertainty from the training prior. Their RankTuner builds a probability entropy tuning signal, the rank signal, matching the ground truth token rank with its expected rank under guesses. Its inverse serves as a scale for weighting, focusing updates on under learned tokens without over punishing unsure spots. Tests on backbones show math tasks and out of domain transfer gains over single indicator baselines.
arxiv-2602-01945: Simon Sundelin and colleagues detect quasiparticle tunneling in real time in two co housed transmons on a shared line. Background tunneling rates sit at single hertz, with timing resolution of tens of microseconds. Time tagged coincidence analysis shows single events uncorrelated across devices, while bursts occur about once per minute, largely correlated. Bursts last seven milliseconds and raise the tunneling rate a thousand fold across both devices. A rarer burst subset shifts offset charge, about hourly, giving a practical method to identify bursts, correlations and structure against correlated errors.
arxiv-2602-02045: Yiming Yang and colleagues study diffusion sampling for Bayesian inverse problems, where such models serve as learned priors. Wrong odds are common and degrade results under outliers. They map the induced drift and prove solvers hold for linear problems, showing weak spots under outliers. To address this, they propose robust diffusion posterior sampling, proven outlier-robust for linear problems and works with gradient samplers. Tests on real inverse problems and natural images show power and strength, with steady gains under outliers.
arxiv-2602-02145: Rohit Joshi and Steven Spallone work out formulas for symmetry group representations. First, they compute symmetric sums of weights. Those weights show up when an irreducible representation drawn from a reductive Lie algebra is cut down to its Cartan subalgebra. Each sum is read as a function of the highest weight. They then take a connected reductive complex algebraic group with its maximal torus. Chern class limits for its irreducible representations on that torus take highest weight form. The same treatment covers Stiefel Whitney classes for orthogonal representations.
arxiv-2602-02245: Alec Dektor and others present two sampling methods for two-dimensional isometric tensor network states. Sampling a quantum system probability distribution matters for quantum advantage tests and Monte Carlo methods. The first new method performs independent sampling, returning a single configuration with its probability. The second uses a greedy search to spot high-probability configurations and their probabilities. Numerical results show effectiveness across states with varying entanglement and system size, generalizing shown one-dimensional methods to two sizes.
arxiv-2602-02345: Shojibur Rahman and colleagues compare five coding agents on open-source projects using a dataset of AI-generated pull requests. Performance is judged along three dimensions spanning the pull-request lifecycle: acceptance rate, review discussion volume, and commit message quality. Codex achieves high acceptance rates across most task categories, while Copilot pull requests trigger the highest review discussion volume. Commit quality varies independently of acceptance. Claude and Cursor produce larger shares of high-quality commit messages across task types, while Codex shows lower commit quality despite strong integration outcomes.
arxiv-2602-02445:
Seo Taek Kong and 1 co-author prove finite-sample error bounds for stochastic approximation, the family of iterative methods behind gradient descent and time-based-difference learning, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such methods return either the last iterate or a running average. The question is how close those outputs sit to a Gaussian limit after finitely many steps.

Their system combines moment bounds for normalized iterates with quantitative Gaussian approximation of the weighted driving noise. The resulting Wasserstein distance bounds yield convergence of moments and high-probability guarantees whose leading terms are Gaussian. The heavier dependence on confidence level hides in a fix that vanishes as samples grow. The authors verify the conditions for nonlinear methods with independent or Markovian data, and for linear methods with Markovian data. Applications include stochastic gradient descent and time-based-difference learning in reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2602-02545:
Dayu Wang and 4 co-authors challenge the claim that reinforcement learning only polishes reasoning a language model already has, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Critics argue exploration stays trapped inside the pretrained model's low-rank bias manifold, the narrow subspace its habits occupy. The authors set out to expand that space geometrically.

Their method works in two stages. Spectral orthogonal exploration first ejects the policy initialization into the null space of the bias manifold, starting learning outside the habitual directions. An effective rank regularizer then rewards keeping reasoning trajectories high-dimensional during optimization. That counters standard reinforcement learning's tendency to collapse entropy. A four-billion-parameter model reached state-of-the-art results on mathematical tasks, beating much larger models and standard group-based optimization. Reasoning capacity, the authors argue, can genuinely grow.
arxiv-2602-02645:
How large is the Hilbert space of a black hole? Vijay Balasubramanian and 4 co-authors answer for three-dimensional gravity in their 2026 paper, using Krylov complexity, a measure of how a quantum state spreads through a special basis. They start from a thermofield double state, the entangled state describing two sides of an eternal black hole in anti-de Sitter space.

The state's spread over the Krylov basis yields Lanczos coefficients matching chaotic motion on a known symmetry group. Non-perturbative effects, included through path integral ensemble averages, make the complexity saturate at late times. The saturation value equals the exponential of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, exactly the expected Hilbert space dimension. The method generalizes: saturation of spread complexity can size the state space of other complex interacting systems. Black hole entropy becomes a dynamical measurement, not just a formula.
arxiv-2602-02945:
Solving fluid flow formulas with stated doubt is the aim of Nicholas Polson and 1 co-author in a 2026 paper. The Navier-Stokes formulas govern incompressible flow, but a single computed trajectory hides modeling error. The authors treat the discretized motion as a state-space model, so solving becomes computing a probability spread instead.

Priors encode real form and error. In two dimensions, stochastic representations motivate Monte Carlo solvers and show how doubt spreads. In three dimensions, particle and ensemble workflows propagate doubt through spectral methods. Parameter learning stays stable through a particle learning scheme that avoids weight collapse. Heavy-tailed error models are also discussed. Partial observations can update the answer as they arrive.
arxiv-2602-03045:
Ambiguous design requests should trigger questions, not guesses, argues a 2026 paper by Bo Yuan and 4 co-authors. Language models can now turn text into parametric CAD programs, the code that defines a three-dimensional part. Descriptions often miss critical dimensions or contain conflicting constraints, and fine-tuned models tend to invent the missing numbers silently instead of asking.

Their framework, ProCAD, pairs two agents. A clarifying agent audits the prompt and asks targeted questions only when needed for a consistent specification. A coding agent then translates the settled specification into an executable CadQuery program. Both agents were fine-tuned on curated data. Proactive clarification greatly improved robustness to ambiguous prompts, beating frontier closed models on shape distance and validity.
arxiv-2602-03145:
Ya-Ting Yang, working with 1 colleague, offers an Internet of Agentic AI in work published during 2026. Language model agents can reason, plan, and invoke tools, but most designs stay centralized and monolithic. That limits scale, focus, and interworking when agents are spread across cloud and edge systems with other owners, skills, and costs to coordinate in practice.

Their system lets heterogeneous agents form coalitions dynamically to execute task-driven workflows. A feasibility check tests skill coverage, network locality, and economic workability, with incentives kept compatible. A decentralized method solves a minimum-effort coalition choice problem. The layer can sit above the Model Context Protocol. A healthcare case study shows domain focus and cloud-edge diversity enabling scalable, resilient workflows.
arxiv-2602-03245:
A beloved children's story becomes speech technology training data in work by Nikola Ljubešić, together with 2 colleagues. They release a Chakavian dialect translation of The Little Prince, in print and audio, as a computer-readable, artificial-intelligence-ready dataset. Text and audio are aligned word by word. Chakavian is a Croatian dialect with limited digital resources, so the aligned edition preserves valuable content beyond small print runs.

The dataset is published in a public repository for anyone interested. The team adapts a leading open speech recognition model, strong on standard Croatian, to Chakavian speech. Word error rate on test data fell by half, and character errors by up to two thirds. The authors envision dialect research and further technology uses, plus a digital online edition.
arxiv-2602-03345:
Fair rankings should track income, not just exposure, argue Xuancheng Li and a group of 4 co-authors in a second appearance in this slice, distinct from the shrinking work. Ranking systems allocate focus among items and providers, balancing relevance against fairness. Exposure fairness assumes utility follows exposure. Real provider income depends on context-dependent conversion through clicks, purchases, or advertising value. That value varies across situations and providers over time.

They formalize income fairness. Cumulative provider income must be proportional to relevance, with an unfairness metric built on that rule. Their method, DIDRF, derives a state-aware scoring rule from the quadratic form of income violations. It jointly weighs ranking quality and each decision's marginal effect on cumulative fairness. Tests on learning-to-rank datasets with semi-synthetic income settings improved income fairness over earlier methods while keeping competitive rankings.
arxiv-2602-03445:
A household robot must keep learning new chores without forgetting the old ones. Qixin Zeng and 8 co-authors address that stability-plasticity tension for vision-language-action models in a 2026 paper. Their framework, CRL-VLA, supports continual post-training of robot policies through reinforcement learning in open-world settings.

The authors derive a performance bound that ties the trade-off to the size of goal-conditioned advantages and to policy divergence. CRL-VLA regulates the two sides unevenly: it caps advantage growth on old tasks while letting new tasks grow under control. A dual-critic design, with one frozen critic anchoring meaning and one trainable critic driving adaptation, implements the idea. On the LIBERO benchmark it beats baselines at both remembering and adapting.
arxiv-2602-03545:
Testing an AI assistant on realistic users is hard when real user data is expensive or out of reach to collect. Davide Paglieri and 4 co-authors introduce Persona Generators in a 2026 paper: functions that make diverse synthetic populations for any context. Earlier simulation work mimicked certain individuals, but it chased the most probable traits and left rare combinations unmapped.

The team evolves the generator code itself, with large language models driving the changes inside an AlphaEvolve-style loop. Over hundreds of iterations, small context descriptions expand into populations spanning wide opinion and preference ranges. The evolved generators beat existing baselines on six variety metrics in held-out contexts. They surface long-tail trait combinations that standard model outputs rarely produce.
arxiv-2602-03745:
Magnetic shape-memory alloys deform as their internal phases rearrange, and the moving boundary between phases decides the material's behavior. Michael Poluektov models those transformation fronts in deformable ferromagnets in a 2026 paper. A complete continuum model needs three things. It needs bulk equations coupling magnetism and mechanics. It also needs a velocity law for the front, and a computer method that can follow it.

Poluektov derives the driving force for front propagation in a general magneto-mechanical setting, starting from the entropy produced at the boundary. He then adapts the cut-finite-element method, which tracks moving interfaces without remeshing the grid. The results are applied to qualitative modeling of magnetic shape-memory alloys. The same physics appears in other materials, such as magnetic perovskites.
arxiv-2602-03945:
Tables whose rows depend on each other defeat simple predictors. Tamara Cucumides and 1 co-author pin down when graph structure helps tabular prediction in a 2026 paper. Their tool, grables, splits how a table becomes a graph from how predictions run on that graph.

Row-wise models provably cannot express targets driven by counts, overlaps, or relations across rows. The tool ranks architectures from boosted trees to relational graph networks on one axis. Tests on made-up, transactional, and relational data confirm the gaps they predicted. The hierarchy tells practitioners when a light look at neighbors suffices and when full graph building cannot be avoided.
arxiv-2602-04045:
Proofs and probabilities may share one graphical language. Rémi Di Guardia and 3 co-authors connect Bayesian networks, which encode probabilistic dependencies, with proof-nets, the graphical form of proofs in linear logic. Their 2026 paper pursues a proof-theoretic account of Bayesian inference, in the spirit of the Curry-Howard link between proofs and programs.

Graphs decompose more flexibly than proof trees, which helps composition but complicates it too. The authors exploit that flexibility while tracking computational efficiency. A Curry-Howard-style correspondence for probability would let logicians reason about inference with proof tools, and let probabilistic systems borrow compositional structure from logic.
arxiv-2602-04145:
Reward models that grade each reasoning step are hungry for labeled data. Jinyuan Li and 6 co-authors show much of that data is redundant. Their 2026 paper studies training data efficiency for multimodal process reward models, which supervise visual reasoning step by step using Monte Carlo annotations.

Random subsampling saturated performance quickly, signaling waste. Their theory says informative updates depend on the mix of positive and negative steps and on label reliability. A Balanced-Information Score ranks existing data by both factors at no extra annotation cost. Subsets chosen by the score matched or beat full-data training on two model backbones, cutting the annotation bill for step-level supervision.
arxiv-2602-04445:
Software teams often lose track of why their systems were built in a certain way. Rudra Dhar, Karthik Vaidhyanathan, and Vasudeva Varma address that problem in a 2026 paper on architecture knowledge management, which means keeping records of design choices and the reasons behind them.

The authors propose AgenticAKM, a system that splits the work among specialized software agents. Separate agents extract, retrieve, generate, and check architectural knowledge. The team tested an early version by producing architecture decision records from code repositories. In a user study covering many repositories, the agent approach produced better records than simpler methods. The work offers a practical route toward keeping software documentation current with less manual effort.
arxiv-2602-04545:
N. R. Sree Harsha and 4 co-authors build a statistical scheme for friction in a 2026 paper on the generalized Langevin equation, a model that keeps memory of past motion. Their test case is drag on a particle moving through a uniform plasma.

The central claim is that a memory kernel measured in thermal balance suffices to predict behavior in a steady non-equilibrium state. The kernel comes from force fluctuations through a standard theorem. The scheme naturally yields effects such as effective mass change and oscillatory relaxation. A classic stopping power formula emerges as the simple limit. Particle runs confirmed the predicted oscillating kernel, supporting the method as an efficient prediction tool.
arxiv-2602-04645:
V. M. Kalari and 5 co-authors hunt for eruptive star behavior in the Large Magellanic Cloud in a 2026 paper on luminous blue variables. These rare stars suffer episodic outbursts with spectral changes, and astronomers debate whether every massive star passes through such a phase.

Using the OGLE survey, the team examined two decades of light curves for dozens of blue supergiants, plus shorter records for others. One star showed the right kind of photometric variation and a possible spectral change. Its low mass and luminosity, however, kept it from qualifying as a true case. The study suggests the eruptive phase is very short. Variability at low luminosities hints that related physics may span many masses.
arxiv-2602-04745:
Amadeu A. Coco and 4 co-authors study how to keep solution archives diverse in multi-objective local search, in a 2026 paper. Problems with several competing goals can produce exploding numbers of non-dominated solutions, answers no other answer beats on every goal. Bounded archives cap that growth.

Most diversity methods measure variety in objective space, the space of goal values. The authors instead design methods that enhance diversity in solution space, the space of decisions themselves. Their Hamming distance archiving algorithm, which counts how many decision components differ, outperformed two established methods drawn from the literature. The result suggests decision-level diversity makes the overall search more efficient. It may help optimizers cover the trade-off front more evenly.
arxiv-2602-04845:
Sanjaye Ramgoolam reviews how finite-dimensional algebras organize gauge-string duality in a 2026 survey paper. Gauge-invariant polynomial functions of matrix and tensor terms capture the combinatorics of that duality, the match between gauge theories and string theories.

Recent work uses these algebras as state spaces for eigenvalue systems, yielding fast algorithms to build orthogonal bases in multi-matrix problems. Counting formulas for systems with two kinds of symmetry have led to gauged quantum models with unusual heat behavior. Their specific heat is negative over one energy branch, then turns positive at larger energies. The negative branch reflects near-exponential growth of degeneracies, while finite-size cuts in freedom take over later and reverse the sign.
arxiv-2602-04945:
A newly found quantum phase hides in a two-leg ladder, a strip of atoms with two rows governed by a model that mixes electron hopping with magnetic coupling. It is the work of Hanbit Oh and 2 co-authors. By making the two legs unequal, they push the system into a middle regime worth exploring.

Simulations and analytic theory agree on a spin-gapped phase where pairs of particles form a density wave whose pattern does not line up with the lattice. Pairs across the legs oscillate one way, driven by mismatched momenta, while pairs within a leg oscillate another way, tied to the opposite leg. The phase survives across wide ranges of doping and imbalance. The authors discuss building the model with cold atoms and links to a real nickel-based material.
arxiv-2602-05145:
Speculative decoding speeds up language model serving by drafting tokens with a small model and checking them with the big one. Jiyoung Park and 3 co-authors present TIDE in this 2026 systems paper, accepted at the SC'26 supercomputing conference. The practical problem is drift: workloads change, and a draft model tuned for yesterday's traffic can slow today's serving down.

TIDE adapts the draft model online, inside the serving engine itself. It recycles the target model's own hidden states, produced anyway during inference, as free training signals, and switches speculation and training on only when they pay off. On heterogeneous clusters it places inference and training on the GPU classes that suit each. Across real workloads, throughput rose up to about 1.66 times over no speculation, with training time cut by up to about three times and storage by a factor of 24 against existing draft training approaches.
arxiv-2602-05545:
Superionic conductors carry ions unusually fast while staying solid, a trait wanted for batteries, yet the moment their carrier sublattice melts is still poorly understood. Sucharita Niyogi, Takenobu Nakamura, and 3 co-authors build a minimal model: a rigid host lattice held by short-range repulsion, plus a soft carrier sublattice with long-range forces. That contrast gives the two parts different melting points and an in-between phase.

Molecular dynamics simulations show three regimes: fully crystalline, sublattice-melted, and fully molten, marked by sharp changes in diffusion and structure. Near the middle transition, carrier motion is strongly anharmonic and uneven across space, beyond simple hopping pictures. Tuning the density lets the team control where the transition sits. The simple model matches the key signatures of standard Coulomb models of superionicity. The authors offer it as a shared microscopic basis for designing conductors that stay mechanically strong.
arxiv-2602-05745:
Shining light on a magnetic sample can rewrite its electronic nature, and Fang Qin and Xiao-Bin Qiang show that a lit-up altermagnet can become a Chern insulator, a topological phase. They use oval polarized light from a high frequency beam on a d wave altermagnet. The paper then looks at the odd heat-flow and thermal Hall effects in the driven sample.

At low heat levels, the heat-flow Hall factor grows in step with heat and drops to zero inside the energy gap at one mirror point. Sharp peaks and dips appear at gap edges elsewhere. The thermal Hall factor also grows in step, and becomes stepped across the bandwidth, a mark of the topological phase. The authors argue these transport signals are keen tests of gapped regions and induced topology. It suggests tests that read topology through heat driven currents rather than charge alone.
arxiv-2602-05845:
Self supervised image models learn by aligning views of the same picture, and multi crop training has a known failure in that family. Pierre-François De Plaen, Abhishek Jha, and 3 co-authors explain it as a task conflict. One shared predictor is forced to solve many different alignment tasks at once, one per spatial transformation. That interference makes optimization unstable.

Their fix gives each view type its own predictor over a shared encoder. The change unlocks clear gains in linear evaluation across several well known frameworks. The same perspective suggests adding new transformations as fresh tasks. The authors add asymmetric cutout views, where a masked view aligns with a complete target, forming a semantic inpainting objective. The framework stayed stable across ResNet and vision transformer backbones, and improved results on ImageNet and COCO. The paper reframes a training trick as a multi task design principle.
arxiv-2602-05945:
Item guides need good blurbs, and Zhouhang Xie and 13 co-authors study how language model agents should make them. Open ended making yields floods of near copy tags that later models cannot use. Their frame, AgenticTagger, shows each item as a run of text tags drawn from a set word list.

Two stages do the work. First, a word-list stage picks a layered, low count, high quality tag set. Second, models hand in-list tags to items. A multi agent rethink loop ties the word list to the item set: a planner model polishes it while checker models test it against real items side by side. Tests on public and private data show steady gains across making and term based lookup, ranking, and review based tips. The authors argue tag quality is a choke point agent teamwork can ease. The frame keeps the making space small on purpose.
arxiv-2602-06145:
Quantum theory allows value distributions that can dip below zero, unlike ordinary probability. Andrew N Jordan and 2 co-authors set out a theory for measuring one such pseudo-distribution directly. Their route runs through its characteristic function, a standard summary built from measurement data.

Gentle measurements, called weak measurements, of momentum shifts supply the needed data. Matrix structures built from the measured values sit at the heart of the method. The result matches the known Kirkwood-Dirac pseudo-distribution, and a conditional version links to weak-value physics. Swapping the roles of position and momentum even gives a way to test the basic commutation rule for any quantum state.
arxiv-2602-06345:
AI agents that can pay for things act on signed mandates rather than live human approval, under protocols like the Agent Payments Protocol. Qianlong Lan and 3 co-authors audit how those mandates behave at run time. Retries, parallel calls, and orchestration layers strain the assumptions baked into a mandate when it was issued.

They propose a zero-trust verification layer that checks each use as it happens. Fresh, short-lived nonces bind a mandate to its exact context, and each mandate can be consumed only once. Simulations under heavy concurrency showed the two guards stop different failure classes: replay attacks and context mix-ups. The work argues authorization should be decided at execution time, not presumed from issuance.
arxiv-2602-06445:
Humanoid robots that walk for long stretches must mind their energy budget, not just their balance. Weidong Huang and 8 co-authors present ECO, a learning framework that treats energy as a hard constraint instead of one more term in a mixed reward. Blended rewards, they note, need endless tuning and often settle for mediocre trade-offs.

ECO states energy use and reference motion tracking as explicit inequality constraints, enforced with a Lagrangian method. The physics stays readable, and tuning becomes more direct. Tested against model-based control, standard shaped-reward learning, and four constrained rivals, ECO cut energy use significantly while keeping walking robust. Trials included transfers between simulators and onto the kid-sized humanoid robot BRUCE.
arxiv-2602-06645:
Gaiane Panina and Dirk Siersma solve a geometry problem about closed curves floating in three-dimensional space. From a point in space, one can drop lines that meet the curve at a right angle; these are called normals. The paper asks how many such normals a single well-chosen point must send out.

For a smooth generic curve whose twisting keeps one sign, they prove some point emits at least six normals, and at least eight when the curve is knotted. For curves built from straight segments, the bounds rise to eight and ten. The proof uses Morse theory applied to the squared distance from the point, together with the self-crossings of a related surface called the focal surface.
arxiv-2602-06745:
Thomas E. Cecil and Patrick J. Ryan survey Élie Cartan's classic examples of isoparametric hypersurfaces in spheres. The topic sits in geometry and concerns surfaces whose nearby surfaces behave in a controlled way. Cartan laid the base of the subject in four papers published between 1938 and 1940. His examples, and the focal submanifolds tied to them, remain central guideposts.

The survey walks through the examples Cartan described in that founding work and the focal submanifolds that arise from them. Focal submanifolds capture where the family of nearby surfaces meets, and they carry much of the geometry's structure. For readers new to the field, the paper gathers a scattered classic source into one account, linking Cartan's work to the questions geometers still study.
arxiv-2602-06845:
Lajos Diósi writes a short comment challenging a recent claim about quantum mechanics and relativity. The claim, published by Hsu in 2026, held that a nonlinear change to the Tomonaga-Schwinger equation breaks its relativistic covariance. Diósi argues the opposite: the equation stays covariant even with the nonlinear term.

The comment points out gaps and mistakes in Hsu's argument, and shows that once those are corrected the proof of covariance becomes simple. The piece is a pointed correction rather than a new theory, and it matters because covariance is a basic must for any relativistic quantum framework.
arxiv-2602-07245:
Continued fractions support exact arithmetic, and continued logs extend the idea to numbers far too large or small for plain notation. Michael J. Collins presents methods for arithmetic on these logs, then extends them to trig, exponential, and log functions.

All work stays inside the continued log form, reading one input term at a time and giving out output terms as soon as they are set, with no floating-point math at all. The methods turn out simpler than their continued-fraction cousins, and a Haskell build backs the claims. Readers keen on exact math and chip-friendly arithmetic will find a compact treatment.
arxiv-2602-07645:
Infographics exported as images lock their content into pixels, making updates, translation, and reuse expensive.  Leonardo Gonzalez describes Images2Slides, an API-based pipeline that converts a static infographic into a native, editable Google Slides slide.

A vision-language model extracts a region-level specification, pixel shape is mapped into slide coordinates. Elements are recreated through the Slides batch update API, with a common JSON schema and deterministic postprocessing supporting multiple model backends.  On a controlled benchmark of 29 generated slides, element recovery reaches about 98. 9 percent.  Designers and document builders get a working bridge from dead pixels to slides they can edit.
arxiv-2602-07945:
Solving nonlinear partial differential equations over space and time together promises compression through tensor trains, but monolithic Newton iterations often stall on stiff or advection-dominated problems. N. R. Rapaka and seven co-authors propose a multilevel tensor-train method that embeds a coarse-to-fine strategy fully inside the tensor format.

Each level refines spatial and temporal resolution, transferring solutions through low-rank prolongation operators that provide robust starting guesses for the next level. The paper also supplies systematic comparisons with classical time-stepping, convergence analysis, and quantitative study of rounding effects across diverse equations. Numeric scientists gain a more reliable space-time solver with the evidence to judge where it actually helps.
arxiv-2602-08245:
Diffusion policies give robots flexible, multi-sense action spreads, but step-by-step cleaning makes them too slow for fast closed-loop control. Jinhao Li and seven co-authors propose STEP, a lightweight tool that predicts space-time steady warm-start actions for eye-hand policies.

The warm starts sit close to the target action spread and stay in time steady, keeping the diffusion policy's making ability while cutting judgment work. A speed-aware tweak tool then tunes drive excitation based on how fast actions change, preventing execution stalls. Robot manipulation teams gain faster closed-loop control without sacrificing the multimodality that made diffusion policies attractive in the first place.
arxiv-2602-08345:
Quantum teleportation moves a quantum state from one place to another, but the circuits that do it can be needlessly large and deep. Wen-Xiu Zhang and two co-authors slim those circuits down across six different entangled setups. Their arXiv paper reports smaller gate counts, lower costs, and shallower depths in every case.

The savings range from modest trims to dramatic cuts. One design drops from 36 gates and a depth of 20 down to 15 gates and a depth of 11. None of the new schemes needs a feed-forward recovery step. Tests on an IBM quantum computer show the leaner circuits still run with good fidelity. Readers get a practical set of blueprints for cheaper, more reliable teleportation.
arxiv-2602-08545:
Graph-based retrieval usually leans on fixed communities or shallow structure, missing the richer topology that could answer complex questions. Xingyuan Zeng and six co-authors propose DA-RAG, which extracts relevant subgraphs on the fly using attributed community search. Their arXiv paper targets dynamic queries where static communities fall short.

High-order graph structure lets the system pull in self-complementary knowledge, while a chunk-layer index supports retrieval at several granularities. Tests show wins of up to 40 percent over existing retrieval methods across four metrics, with index-build time down up to 37 percent and token overhead down up to 41 percent. Readers get a cheaper, sharper way to ground language models in graph knowledge.
arxiv-2602-08745:
Graph neural networks are the main learned approach to Boolean satisfiability, but their limits are poorly mapped. Saku Peltonen and Roger Wattenhofer analyze that expressive power through the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy. Their arXiv paper proves the full hierarchy cannot in general separate satisfiable from unsatisfiable instances.

Indistinguishability under higher-order tests carries over to practical limits for test-bounded solvers that assign variables one by one. The authors also study expressivity needs for regular, random, and planar instance families, and test random and industrial benchmarks. Random instances prove largely distinguishable, while industrial instances often demand more expressivity. Readers get a clear map of where graph networks can and cannot solve SAT.
arxiv-2602-08845:
When an operator steers a robot from far away, the robot should track the operator's hand and settle smoothly. Lazaro F. Torres and three co-authors design controllers for this two-sided teleoperation of fully powered nonlinear machines. Their schemes shape the system's energy with simple proportional-plus-damping rules, a classic control idea.

With no time delay and passive contact at both ends, position error and speed fall to zero in finite time, not just eventually. The math rests on a homogeneous approximation of negative degree. Both computer simulations and lab experiments back the design, which the authors present as simple, continuous, and ready to adapt.
arxiv-2602-08945:
Community Notes let readers fact-check posts at scale, but machines that write them face a trade-off between coverage and quality. Sahajpreet Singh and three co-authors introduce GitSearch, which first spots what is missing, vague, or disputed in a post, then searches precisely to fill those gaps before drafting a note. A new test set, PolBench, holds 78,698 U.S. political posts with notes.

With search budget held fixed, GitSearch lifts human-rated helpfulness by 0.43 over plain web search and wins 59 percent of head-to-head comparisons. It produces notes for 99 percent of cases, including nearly half where summary-based methods fail. Readers even prefer its notes to human-written helpful ones 69 percent of the time, mainly for fuller context.
arxiv-2602-09045:
H. Alharazin and two co-authors apply score-based diffusion models to two-dimensional SU(2) lattice gauge theory, extending earlier work on the simpler U(1) case. The SU(2) manifold is handled through a quaternion parameterization. Training uses 10,000 Hybrid Monte Carlo configurations at coupling 2.0 on an 8-by-8 lattice, doubled to 20,000 by random gauge transformations.

Physics-conditioned sampling exploits the linear coupling dependence of the score to generate new couplings without retraining, while a convolutional architecture with periodic boundaries reaches new lattice sizes. The model reproduces the exact average plaquette within 0.001 for couplings between 1.5 and 2.5 at training size. The work marks diffusion models as promising generators for non-Abelian gauge fields.
arxiv-2602-09145:
Doctors more and more collect daily data, like motion traces over a day, but causal methods for such treatments lag behind. Ziren Jiang and two co-authors target a new goal, the tweaked daily treatment policy: the average outcome if each person slightly alters their seen treatment path. That modest question avoids the strong overlap needs of average dose-response curves and is easier to read.

Defining an average over endless many-sided paths needs care, and the authors do it through daily-pattern analysis, proving it can be pinned down. Outcome fitting, inverse weighting, and doubly safe tools follow with proofs. Applied to NHANES motion-sensor data, the framework estimates death effects of cutting broken nighttime motion and idle time.
arxiv-2602-09345:
AI coding agents in shared clouds run tool calls inside sandboxed containers, and their resource appetite swings fast and unpredictably. A 2026 measurement study led by Yusheng Zheng, with five co-authors, maps those dynamics across over a hundred software-engineering tasks and two language models. Operating-system work, including tool calls and startup, eats most of total task time, while memory, not processor power, limits how many agents can run together.

Memory spikes from single tool calls rise far above average use, and demand varies sharply across tasks, runs, and models. Current controls mismatch in three ways: container-level rules against tool-call-level dynamics, slow user-space reactions against sub-second bursts, and history-based prediction against stateful execution. Their answer, AgentCgroup, is an intent-driven controller on kernel mechanisms that aligns resource groups with tool-call boundaries. Early tests show better isolation between tenants and less wasted capacity.
arxiv-2602-09545:
Flat-band systems amplify interactions because quenched kinetics let single excitations bind into composite quasiparticles. Wei-Tao Zhou and two co-authors study spin polarons across the full momentum and energy range in the Mielke-Tasaki model in their 2026 paper, using projected exact diagonalization. Distinct low-energy polarons appear at two momenta, alongside multiple high-energy branches.

Interaction-induced Hartree dispersion proves decisive for which momentum sector hosts the low-energy polarons. Adding finite bandwidth reveals the binding mechanisms: low-energy polarons form through conventional virtual exchange, while high-energy ones arise jointly from effective attraction and virtual exchange. The results point toward realizing spin polaron crystals and probing novel superconducting pairing in moiré materials such as twisted tungsten diselenide and molybdenum ditelluride.
arxiv-2602-10045:
Instance segmentation models perform well on average yet offer no principled uncertainty about any single mask. A 2026 paper led by Kerri Lu, with three co-authors, introduces a conformal method that returns adaptive prediction sets for segmenting instances. Feed it an image and a pixel, and it returns a set of candidate instances for that pixel.

The guarantee is that at least one prediction in the set closely overlaps the true instance mask, with a provable probability. Set sizes adapt to query difficulty, and the method beats naive and dilation-based baselines on field delineation, cell segmentation, and vehicle detection. Versions with asymptotic and finite-sample guarantees are provided.
arxiv-2602-10345:
Behavioral nudges steer health decisions without limiting choice, yet finding them across PubMed is a bottleneck. A 2026 paper led by Jaydeep Chauhan, with seven co-authors, presents a scalable AI system identifying and extracting evidence-based nudges from unstructured biomedical literature. A multi-stage pipeline first applies hybrid filtering with keywords, TF-IDF, cosine scores, and a nudge-term boost, cutting the corpus to about eighty-one thousand.

OpenScholar, a quantized eight-billion model, then classifies papers and extracts fields such as nudge type and target behavior in one pass, checked against a JSON schema. On a labeled test set of one hundred ninety-seven, the best setup reaches sixty-seven percent F1 and seventy-two percent recall, ideal for discovery. A precise variant using seven randomized passes achieves perfect precision with twelve percent recall. The system is being integrated into Agile Nudge+, grounding interventions in peer-reviewed evidence.
arxiv-2602-10445:
Jie Jiang and ten co-authors rebuild how creative recommenders name items in a 2026 paper. Creative recommendation turns suggestion into next-token prediction, which requires turning each item into a discrete Meaning ID. The standard two-stage method, residual quantization, compresses embeddings into codes in a separate step, and that separation degrades meaning and piles up errors.

Their system, UniSID, optimizes embeddings and Meaning IDs end to end from raw advertising data. Meaning information flows directly into the code space instead of passing through a detached compression stage. The paper reports gains on advertisement recommendation tasks, arguing that joint training fixes both the objective mismatch and the error accumulation of the older pipeline.
arxiv-2602-10545:
Yuxin Ma and five co-authors make model upscaling cheaper and more principled in a 2026 paper. Large models ship in several sizes, and initializing a big model from a trained smaller one can speed settling. But hyperparameters tuned at the small size may not transfer, and tuning them directly at the large size is prohibitively expensive.

Motivated by maximal update parameterization and systems of any size, the authors present a general width-based upscaling method. Like Net2Net it copies and perturbs weights, but the perturbations use theoretically grounded, width-dependent scalings. The paper also studies when tuning on small models and extrapolating is sound, giving builders a principled warm start instead of an expensive gamble.
arxiv-2602-10745:
Mohamad Dhaini and three co-authors extend contrastive learning to hyperspectral fitting in a 2026 paper. Contrastive methods have done well in model learning, mainly for image sorting, but fitting tasks and hyperspectral data have got far less focus. The gap matters because hyperspectral fitting backs remote sensing and matter analysis.

Their spectral-spatial contrastive system works for fitting on hyperspectral data in an any-model design, lifting bases from solid convolutional networks to focus models. A set of changes fitted to hyperspectral data growth joins the system. Tests on mock and real data sets show large gains across all studied bases, hinting contrastive early training transfers well beyond sorting.
arxiv-2602-11145:
Wavelet spread gives useful gradients for judging sound and image quality, but costs too much to use as a training loss. Christopher Mitcheltree and three co-authors propose SCRAPL, a random scheme that evaluates spread transforms through random paths. It targets the joint time-rate transform, which reads spectrotemporal patterns at many scales.

Applied to differentiable signal processing, SCRAPL matches sounds from a granular synth and a classic drum machine without supervision. An importance-sampling start adapts the method to each data set's perceptual content, speeding convergence. Code and audio samples are released, with SCRAPL packaged for wider use in audio and vision training.
arxiv-2602-11245:
Quantum circuits that are hard to run can be swapped for easier variants, at a price in variance. Joshua W. Dai and Bálint Koczor develop a frame for accounting for and cutting that variance in quasi-probability decompositions. Their key tool is stratified sampling under proportional sharing.

They prove the stratified estimator stays unbiased and never fares worse than naive sampling, except in degenerate cases. A classic moving program enables stratification on arbitrary product-form decompositions. Simulations of error cancellation and angle interpolation show constant-factor variance cuts, with large gains in an oracle model and modest savings in the single-shot regime. The method cuts sampling cost without extra quantum resources.
arxiv-2602-11745:
Graph query languages are diverse and far less familiar than SQL, making graph databases hard for most users to query. Songlin Lyu and fourteen co-authors present Text2GraphQuery-Bench, the first benchmark covering all mainstream declarative property graph query languages: Cypher, GQL, and SQL/PGQ. It holds 267,276 question-query pairs across 34 databases and 13 domains, built to adapt from varied resources with domain-aware synthesis and a design that extends rapidly to new languages.

Evaluation reports grammar, similarity, and execution accuracy under graph-native difficulty, question abstraction, and schema aliasing. Tests on eight language models reveal a sharp language gap: zero-shot grammar for GQL and SQL/PGQ lags far behind Cypher, though few-shot prompting largely recovers it. Fine-tuning a smaller model can match or beat zero-shot large models, suggesting unfamiliarity rather than capacity is the main barrier, while the hardest questions remain a persistent bottleneck.
arxiv-2602-11845:
Reconstructing dynamic worlds from a single video remains hard without a unified way to separate motion in space and time. Qisen Wang and two co-authors propose WorldTree, a framework with two parts. A Temporal Partition Tree enables coarse-to-fine tuning through a parent-child split tree for layered time splits. Spatial Ancestral Chains query step by step through parent structure to supply matching spatial dynamics while fitting motion codes to parent nodes.

Existing methods suffer either whole-scene time tuning or coupled layered spatial composition, lacking a unified split of time and space. WorldTree addresses both sides at once. Tests on different datasets show improvements of about 8 percent on one picture-quality metric and about 9 percent on another over the second-best method. For single-video dynamic world-building, the tree-chain design offers a principled split of time and space.
arxiv-2602-11945:
Federated learning lets many nodes train one model without sharing raw data, but real deployments are heterogeneous: nodes differ in data and in how often they join. Hongliang Zhang and six co-authors propose PMFL, a model-contrastive federated learning framework that uses historical training information to steady the process. On the node side, a contrastive term built from past local models keeps updates consistent across differing data.

On the server side, each node's cumulative participation count adjusts its aggregation weight, correcting bias from uneven participation. The updated global model also folds in past global models, damping swings in performance between rounds. Across experiments in heterogeneous settings, PMFL beats existing federated methods, suggesting that memory of past models, on both sides of the exchange, is a cheap route to stronger federated learning.
arxiv-2602-12045:
Designing new crystals means respecting periodicity, balance, and physical constraints at scale, a challenge for coordinate-based models. Jed A. Duersch and four co-authors propose a Fourier-space pipeline representing crystals through a truncated Fourier transform of the species-resolved unit-cell density, rather than atom spots directly. That representation is period-native, handles space-group symmetries with simple algebra, and supports variable atom counts when building.

With only nine Fourier basis functions per spatial dimension, the approach rebuilds unit cells holding up to 108 atoms per chemical species. A transformer variational autoencoder over complex-valued Fourier coefficients compresses the code, and a latent diffusion model generates within that compressed space. Evaluated on the LeMaterial benchmark and against atom-spot baselines for small cells, the method shows Fourier space as a natural home for crystal generation.
arxiv-2602-12245:
Two research lines look alike from a distance: predictive embedding models learn an energy for pairs of states, while goal control learns directed costs for reaching targets.
