Anthony Kobanda led this work with one co-author, Waris Radji, joining them through intrinsic energies, defined as the least total local effort along allowed paths between states. Under mild closure and additivity rules, any such energy is a quasimetric.

That link runs both ways. Optimal cost-to-go functions have exactly this intrinsic form, and embedding models trained on intrinsic energies land in the value class that quasimetric control targets. Symmetric finite energies, by contrast, fit poorly with one-way reachability, which is why direction-aware, asymmetric energies matter when the route from A to B differs from B to A.
arxiv-2602-12345:
Axion models face a domain wall problem that can threaten standard cosmology, and the Lazarides-Shafi mechanism tries to defuse it by identifying degenerate vacua through a continuous gauge symmetry. Motoo Suzuki led this work with one co-author, Ryo Yokokura, recasting that mechanism as a Dijkgraaf-Witten topological field theory. That move isolates its essential structure and exposes its generalised symmetry pattern.

The frame yields a master formula for the domain wall number and clarifies, in a model-independent way, the higher-form symmetry conditions needed for full vacuum identification. Even when domain wall number one removes all higher-form global symmetries, a non-trivial four-group structure remains, realising a symmetry-protected topological phase. The paper thus gives both a counting tool and a sharper symmetry picture.
arxiv-2602-12445:
Language models show response biases, favouring certain options in fixed-response questions regardless of content, which skews evaluations of their true abilities. Om Bhatt led this work with one co-author, Anna A. Ivanova, proposing RBCorr, a simple, low-cost correction strategy. Tests cover 12 open-weight models on yes-no, entailment, and multiple-choice questions.

Response bias proves prevalent before correction, and RBCorr effectively eliminates bias while boosting performance. The team also probes how bias behaviour generalises across models, data sets, and prompt formats, finding that LogProbs-based correction depends heavily on all three. Overall, RBCorr is easy to use, lifts smaller models in particular, and brings closed-response benchmark scores closer to true capabilities.
arxiv-2602-12545:
Space runs need codes that handle gas, light, and real rules together, at high speed. Zhuo Chen led this work with one co-author, Xue-Ning Bai, giving Guangqi, a new two-dimensional, finite-volume gas flow code written in Fortran and split via Message Passing Interface. It at once solves gas flow for complex rules and hidden light transport under flux-limited spread.

Guangqi supports exact hydrogen and helium rules under local thermal and chem balance, in flat and round shapes with non-uniform grids, plus static and flexible detail. A passive scalar AM method fixes AM keeping in round coords, while Z-order and Hilbert space-filling curves manage domain split for scaling. Checks against standard benchmarks and new tests test non-linear coupling among gas motion, rules, light transport, and AM keeping.
arxiv-2602-12745:
Heavy neutral leptons, if they exist at energies near a billion electron volts, would have shaped the early Universe's first nuclei. Pieter Braat and four co-authors ask what Big Bang nucleosynthesis can say about them within an extended theory that adds these particles to the standard model. The early Universe is a sensitive probe, since extra particles change how fast it expands and cools.

The authors show that, on very general grounds, nucleosynthesis limits complement lab searches at colliders, beam dumps, and double-beta decay experiments. For heavy neutral lepton masses above about 100 mega-electron volts, the data cap the energy scale where the effective theory breaks down. They also map target regions, bounded above and below, where future lab probes could test the remaining space.
arxiv-2602-12845:
Official statistics often lean on administrative data that cover only part of the population and were never collected as a probability sample. Donatas Šlevinskas and two co-authors propose a two-step small-area method for that messy reality. First, a measurement-error model fitted on the overlap between survey and external source feeds domain totals through calibration constraints, giving nearly design-unbiased estimates.

Second, those totals and their variances feed an area-level model with known covariates, yielding empirical best linear unbiased predictors. Demonstrations on three enterprise surveys, using administrative records, a cut-off source, and web-scraped data, show steady precision gains over direct estimation. They also beat a benchmark that treats the proxy as a plain covariate. Crucially, the gains need no model of how the external source selected its units.
arxiv-2602-13045:
Imbalanced data trip up classifiers when the majority class intrudes into the minority's territory, blurring the edge, most of all with noise and overlap. Xubin Wang and two co-authors propose shape surface rectification, a system that exploits local shape instead of symmetric cleaning rules. It guesses confidence from inverse-distance-weighted nearest-neighbour voting with an adaptive metric, capturing local reliability.

Cleaning is then asymmetric: strict on majority samples, protective of minority samples through a cap on minority removal. That asymmetry avoids the common failure of deleting informative minority points along with noise. Tests on multiple benchmarks show the method competing with strong sampling plain rivals. For tabular imbalanced learning, shape-aware cleaning offers a more careful other to blanket undersampling.
arxiv-2602-13645:
In cheap talk games, a principal who cannot commit to decisions faces a strategic agent. This paper asks how much information she can guarantee herself when many informative equilibria exist. Worst-case setup is defined as setup via the worst non-trivial equilibrium of a device, and under that goal, standard full-commitment devices fail, yielding no more than the no-talk payoff. Partial commitment, however, strictly improves matters.

The threat of facing a strategic, uncommitted principal shapes the agent's reporting motives across all equilibria. The worst-case best device is mapped under weak preference premises and has a simple two-message structure, with splitting messages designed to maximize strategic impact on the principal's actions. Uses span bail-setting tools, fintech lending, handoffs, lobbying, and audit design. Andrei Iakovlev is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13745:
Language-model interfaces increasingly support high-consequence workflows such as healthcare communication, where presentation shapes later actions, and they must stay usable for people with disabilities. Plain-language interfaces enable meaningful human oversight. Yet hallucinations, meaning shifts, bias, and access barriers can hurt reliability and users' ability to understand, monitor, and intervene. In practice oversight is often a late check, without clear rules for when action is required or who is accountable.

This paper proposes oversight-by-design: putting human judgment across the pipeline through escalate rules and explicit interface controls for risk signaling and action. Automated checks flag readability, meaning fidelity, factual consistency, and standards-based access risks. They escalate to mandatory human-in-the-loop review before release when thresholds are violated or uncertainty is high, while human-on-the-loop watching tunes policies and detects drift. Blessing Jerry leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13845:
Allysson Allex Araújo and five co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv study of what makes online tech hiring feel fair and kind. It looks at early-career software engineers, for whom a hiring round is often a first brush with the field. Many such rounds feel opaque or off-putting, the authors note.

The team drew on 22 interviews covering more than 470 hiring experiences, guided by a theory of how applicants judge and react to firms. From those accounts they distilled 22 good practices, such as clear job ads, specific feedback that helps a candidate grow, respectful human contact, and treating hiring as a two-way street. Firms can use the list to draw and keep new engineers.
arxiv-2602-14145:
Wen-Jie Yu and six co-authors trace the birthplaces of Galactic binary neutron stars in a 2026 arXiv study. Using Gaia DR3 astrometry, updated pulsar distances, and Monte Carlo sampling of errors, they wound back the paths of 11 such binaries. They also tracked 167 globular clusters and 2,967 open clusters for past encounters.

Globular clusters look unlikely as birthplaces, with low encounter odds and ejection speeds that strain belief. Open clusters, by contrast, form a real channel. The double pulsar J0737-3039 shows a 13.9% chance of coming from young cluster OC 0450, and 5.4% from Theia 58. On timing and closeness, the authors judge Theia 58 the more plausible home.
arxiv-2602-14245:
José J Gil, writing alone, names a 2026 arXiv geometric phase structure for Mueller transformations. A broad physically doable Mueller matrix carries one built-in shape phase form: the slowing part of the mark pure part from its mark split, defining a canonical holonomic content.

A Mueller matrix alone does not fix a unique seen Pancharatnam phase, since that phase hangs on the physical build and the interferometric read-out. Other mark layers may shift seen clarity and its angle through convex averaging, yet they define no unique holonomy of their own. The paper also sets up the quantum twin for open two-level dynamics in the Choi form.
arxiv-2602-14345:
Amirali Sajadi and three co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv exploit-confirmation engine for vulnerability reports. Detection tools flood maintainers with false positives and non-actionable reports, while automated exploitation systems usually ignore detection metadata such as vulnerability type and code location. AXE, the Agentic eXploit Engine, works in a grey-box setting using just a CWE class and a vulnerable location.

A multi-agent design splits planning, code exploration, and dynamic execution feedback, mapping light metadata to concrete exploits for web applications. On the CVE-Bench dataset, AXE reached a 30% exploitation success rate, three times the state-of-the-art black-box baselines. Even a single-agent version gained from grey-box metadata, improving 1.75-fold, showing that a little detection context goes a long way.
arxiv-2602-14445:
Hasi Hays, writing alone, offers a 2026 arXiv attention mechanism inspired by coupled oscillators. Old transformer self-focus carries square cost and lacks grounding in living neural work. Selective Sync Focus swaps dot-product self-focus with a closed-form map from the calm answer of the Kuramoto model of linked clocks.

Each token turns into a clock with a learnable base rate and phase. Sync strength between token pairs, set by rate-tied coupling and a phase-lock rule, serves as the focus weight. That design yields natural sparseness: tokens with clashing rates get zero weight with no plain masking. It also joins place and meaning coding through the base rate spectrum, dropping the need for split place codes.
arxiv-2602-14745:
Jia-Li Mo, Meirav Amram, and Cheng Gong study non-planar degeneracies with cylindrical configurations, built as products of a projective line with a complex torus under an embedding. They prove that fundamental groups of Galois covers of these surfaces hold an abelian subgroup of rank tied to the embedding numbers. They also prove that the surfaces' irregularity is at least twice the product of those numbers minus one.

Chern numbers then let the authors compute the index of such surfaces and classify them. The paper joins topology and arithmetic in one geometric family, turning abstract invariants into concrete bounds. Degenerate surfaces gain a clear algebraic portrait.
arxiv-2602-14845:
Trajan Hammonds stretches trace growth laws past the steady case for PGL2 times GL1. Nelson and Venkatesh had worked out such growth laws for Gan-Gross-Prasad pairs when the Rankin-Selberg L size sat in a steady zone, far from size drops.

Hammonds works in the p-adic world and beats the steady guess, letting size drops count in full. Trace laws thus gain forms where the old path stopped, at just the points where sizes fall. A hard edge case turns into workable ground. The old steady zone had kept such drops out of reach, and the new forms bring them in.
arxiv-2602-15245:
Bhattarai and colleagues present MyoInteract, a tool for fast prototyping of biomechanical HCI tasks with reinforcement learning. Biomechanical simulations based on reinforcement learning could change HCI research and interaction design, but current tools lack ease of use and clarity. Using the Human Action Cycle as a design lens, the team names key limits of existing frameworks and builds MyoInteract.

Designers set up tasks, user models, and training settings from an easy GUI within minutes. The tool trains and tests muscle-driven simulated users within minutes, cutting training times by up to 98 percent. A workshop study with 12 interaction designers found that novices in biomechanical reinforcement learning could set up, train, and assess goal-directed user movements in one session. By turning a days-long expert task into an hour-long workflow, the work lowers barriers to entry and speeds iteration in HCI biomechanics research.
arxiv-2602-15345:
Nigam and colleagues tackle electron calculations, a chokepoint in atom tests, with ML. Most methods map molecular geometries, graphs or encoded local data to molecular properties. Others use ML as a stand-in for electronic structure, aiming at the Fock or density matrices in an atomic orbital basis. Led by the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem, the team offers an operator-centered framework where the external potential in that basis is the model input.

From this operator, they build layered representations echoing popular atom-based descriptors. The matrix-valued external potential links to equivariant message-passing networks. Products of the external potential provide a scalable route to message passing and long-range effects. This method can model molecular properties, such as energies and dipole moments, from the external potential. It can learn operator-to-operator maps to the Fock matrix and the reduced density matrix, yielding multiple molecular readings.
arxiv-2602-15745:
Milton and colleagues study social media through the eyes of users living with mental illness. Platforms adopted algorithmic curation fast, with little regard for harm to mental well-being. In design workshops with 21 participants diagnosed with mental illness, the team finds that users build cause-and-effect explanations, or folk theories, to make sense of algorithmic curation.

Those folk theories expose a breakdown the authors frame as entanglement: a disconnect between user actions and platform outcomes on an emotional level. Participant designs for easing entanglement centre on contextualising engagement and restoring explicit user control. The entanglement frame and resulting design recommendations matter for social computing and recommender research, especially for evaluating and building platforms that support mental well-being.
arxiv-2602-15845:
Gibert and colleagues survey knowledge distillation for machine translation, or KD4MT, across 105 papers through October 1, 2025. Knowledge distillation has gained traction as a compression tool for ever-larger models in NLP. In the field, however, it also functions as a general-purpose knowledge transfer mechanism shaping supervision and translation quality as well as efficiency.

Advances are then grouped by method gains and by useful uses. Noted and counted reviews identify common trends, key research gaps, and the absence of unified testing practice for methods in the field. Practical tips for selecting a method in real cases are provided. Potential risks for machine translation include increased hallucination and bias growth. Finally, the role of large language models in reshaping the KD4MT field is discussed. An open base sums main traits of surveyed methods, and a list of key terms aids further research.
arxiv-2602-16145:
Mohammed Zain Ali Ahmed studies how graph neural networks behave on large random graphs with realistic node features. Prior studies of convergence on large random graphs mostly ignore correlations between node features, yet such correlations arise naturally in real networks. That gap matters: limits derived without them may not reflect how expressive these networks truly are on realistic graphs. The paper introduces a new method for generating random graphs whose node features correlate between neighbors.

The sampling scheme draws motivation from traits of real graphs, notably traits captured by the Barabasi-Albert model. Theoretical analysis strongly indicates that convergence can be avoided in some cases, and experiments on large random graphs built with the new method validate that claim. The observed divergent behavior suggests graph neural networks may prove more expressive than early studies implied, especially where node features correlate as they do in the wild.
arxiv-2602-16545:
Kaiting Liu and Hazel Doughty address a plain flaw in video recognition. Fixed label sets are often too coarse. They lump distinct objects, manners, or outcomes under one label. When tasks change, fresh labels and retraining cost a lot. The authors define a new task called category splitting. An existing classifier is edited to refine one coarse class into finer ones. Accuracy elsewhere must hold.

Their zero-shot method draws on the latent structure of video classifiers. It exposes fine distinctions with no added data. It also gives a strong start for low-shot fine-tuning. On new video benchmarks, it beats vision-language baselines. Accuracy on split classes rises without harming the rest. Video teams get a cheap way to sharpen classifiers as definitions change.
arxiv-2602-16745:
Zhangyi Liu and co-authors introduce PETS, a principled frame for optimal trajectory allocation in test-time self-consistency. Test-time scaling lifts scores by aggregating stochastic reasoning paths, but sample-efficient allocation under a fixed budget stays an open challenge. Central to the approach is the self-consistency rate, defined as agreement with the infinite-budget majority vote, which grounds allocation in rigorous theory.

In the offline setting, where all questions are known in advance, allocation is linked to crowdsourcing theory by treating reasoning traces as workers, yielding guarantees and an efficient majority-voting allocation algorithm. In the online streaming setting, where questions arrive one by one, a new method adapts budgets to question difficulty while keeping strong guarantees and low compute. Model builders get a principled way to spend test-time samples wisely.
arxiv-2602-16845:
Patrick Shober hunts meteor sets for signs of recent asteroidal activity, with a possible tidal disruption family in view. Asteroid activity such as thermo-mechanical breakdown, impacts, rotational shedding, and tidal disruption can inject meteoroids into near-Earth space and leave detectable traces in orbit lists. The study uses orbit-similarity stats and explicit null-hypothesis testing on shower-removed, asteroidal video-meteor data.

The sample holds over two hundred thirty-five thousand meteors and fireballs from four all-sky video nets. Routes include a geocentric dissimilarity gauge, kernel-density null realizations, and clustering to isolate coherent structures. No survey-consistent, stream-like sign appears in the Earth-like, low-inclination zone expected for a recent tidal-disruption family. Instead, a cautious combined upper limit is set on sporadic asteroidal meteors plausibly tied to such a source.
arxiv-2602-17045:
Jared Moore led a six-author team testing whether large language models truly read minds when they persuade, or merely sound as if they do. Most theory of mind tests use static question-and-answer items, but the authors argue that live, first-person interaction is the real test. Their task asks a persuader to sway a target toward one of three policy proposals by revealing facts in a smart order, which requires sensing what the target knows and values.

Across three experiments, models beat human persuaders when the target's knowledge and motives were shown, yet fell below chance when those states were hidden and had to be drawn out. Humans did fairly well in both setups. But when targets were real people, models still swayed beliefs more than humans did. The paper warns against crediting models with human-like mind reading, while noting their real power to shape belief.
arxiv-2602-17145:
Joseph Bingham led a two-author paper on making convolutional neural networks leaner through pruning. As these networks grow more accurate, they also grow larger, slower, more memory-hungry, and more power-hungry. Pruning methods exist, but each uses its own metrics and code, making them hard to implement or compare fairly.

The authors introduce a framework called Combine, a criterion-based pruning solution for iterative pruning, plus a standard language for comparing criterion functions and several new criteria of their own. They show different criteria affect different models differently, and they test the framework on VGG-inspired models. Pruning removed a large share of filters while holding or improving accuracy and cutting the computation needed by a large share, showing pruning done right costs little.
arxiv-2602-17245:
Linxi Jiang led a six-author position paper arguing that web agents should act through typed actions, not clicks. Today's agents drive browsers with clicks, keystrokes, and DOM manipulation, producing brittle long-horizon behavior, high execution cost, and weak auditability. The paper proposes web verbs as the semantic layer. Each verb exposes a web operation as a typed function with structured inputs, outputs, and documented behavior, backed by a server API or a maintained client workflow.

Verb calls can carry preconditions, postconditions, policy tags, and logging hooks. That lets agents synthesize concise programs with explicit control and data flow plus checkable execution traces. Case studies show verb composition yielding correct, reproducible outcomes where click-driven agents go brittle or reason wrongly. The paper closes with a call for standards, tooling, and community process to make the layer deployable at web scale.
arxiv-2602-17345:
Boyang Ma led an eight-author survey arguing that embodied AI breaks down for reasons beyond language model flaws or old-school cyber-physical flaws. Robotic systems like self-driving cars, service robots, and language agents now face safety-first real rollouts, where breakdowns carry lasting harms. Past research views them through language model weak spots or cyber-physical flaws, but the survey claims a large breakdown class comes from body-induced gaps.

Four insights explain why such AI resists securing. First, meaning rightness does not guarantee real safety, since language reasoning ignores shape, motion, and contact. Second, same actions diverge across real states under tangled dynamics and uncertainty. Third, small errors amplify across tight sense-decide-act loops. Fourth, safety does not compose across time or layers, so locally safe choices pile into unsafe conduct. Protecting such AI thus demands system-level thought about risk, doubt, and failure spread.
arxiv-2602-17445:
Mateusz Nowak led a three-author team exposing hidden biases in multiple-choice benchmarks. Multiple-choice benchmarks are a standard way to measure language models' reasoning. Through a synthetic NonsenseQA benchmark, the team found that different models show varying degrees of label-position-few-shot-prompt bias. Models lean on answer position, the label in front of the answer, the distribution of correct answers in the few-shot prompt, or a mix of all three.

The paper proposes a simple bias-reduced evaluation protocol. It swaps each question's labels for uniform, unordered labels and prompts the model to use the whole answer presented. With a sentence similarity model, the protocol improves robustness and lowers standard deviation across answer permutations, with only a minimal drop in model performance. Across multiple benchmarks and models, the protocol improves robustness to answer permutations, cutting mean accuracy variance threefold while barely lowering mean performance.
arxiv-2602-17545:
Xiaokai Chen led a three-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on optimization spread across a network of agents. Each agent holds its own smooth convex loss, and all agents share one nonsmooth convex term. The paper proposes decentralized methods in which agents adjust their own step sizes by local backtracking, linked through light min-consensus protocols.

The design grows from a three-operator splitting factorization of a reformulated problem. A new BCV preconditioning metric, named for Bertsekas, O'Connor, and Vandenberghe, makes the decentralized form workable and lets step sizes adapt locally. The authors prove robust convergence guarantees. Under mere convexity, the methods converge sublinearly. With strong convexity of the sum and a partly smooth nonsmooth part, they prove linear convergence. Numerical tests back the theory and show the adaptive step size strategy working in practice.
arxiv-2602-17645:
Xiaohan Zhao and team push black-box attacks on large vision-language models, where missing gradients and tangled multimodal boundaries make progress hard. Prior transfer methods match local crops between source and target images, but that yields high-variance, near-orthogonal gradients across steps. The authors trace the instability to two causes: ViT translation sensitivity and a structural asymmetry between source and target crops.

They recast local matching as an asymmetric expectation over source transforms and target semantics, giving M-Attack-V2. Multi-crop alignment averages gradients over local views, auxiliary target alignment swaps harsh target augmentation for correlated helper images, and patch momentum plus a diverse surrogate ensemble strengthen transfer. Success rates jump sharply over the prior method on all three tested models.
arxiv-2602-17745:
Tobias Herrmann and team study driving-over detection for fully automated trains. New components must take over tasks now handled by operating staff, including collision detection. Two collision types matter: impacts with the front of the train and driving-over events at the wheel. Technologies for the latter are barely investigated, so the team ran detailed driving-over experiments.

Test objects of steel, wood, stone and bone supplied the data for three automatic detection methods. One method uses convolutional neural networks, while the other two use classical threshold-based approaches. The neural method reaches nearly perfect mean accuracy, while the classical methods reach about eighty-five and eighty-nine percent. The work supplies tested knowledge for fully automated rail operations, where reliable driving-over detection is a safety must.
arxiv-2602-17845:
Bryce Christopherson and Farhad Jafari refine Coron's needed condition for smooth feedback stabilization of nonlinear control systems, using Čech cohomology and the Vietoris-Begle mapping theorem. Coron established a hole-counting block: long-run stabilizability implies the driven map meets a top-class condition on homology groups. The paper sharpens that condition from a single top class to full cohomological stiffness.

The authors prove that the closed version of the relevant set must be a Čech cohomology sphere in degree one below the state dimension. They also prove that limiting the system map to this subset gives a full match on its Čech cohomology groups in all degrees. Readers gain a sharper needed condition for steady control, with a complete cohomological limit replacing Coron's partial one. The refinement offers a finer tool for ruling out feedback stabilization in nonlinear control.
arxiv-2602-17945:
Ian Marquette and team use the Lie-algebra notion of commutant in Poisson algebra to build a frame for deforming Hamiltonian laws. Taking a sub-algebra of the algebra of integrals, they look at functions that Poisson commute with that sub-algebra. It can then be deformed while keeping that trait.

They deform Liouville systems and superintegrable Lotka-Volterra systems studied in earlier work, giving different builds for Abelian and non-Abelian sub-algebras of integrals. They obtain superintegrable systems for set dimensions and in any dimension. Polynomial systems deform into ratio systems, some with non-ratio integrals. Superintegrability seems kept in this approach, offering readers a route to new stable systems.
arxiv-2602-18045:
Petrus Zwart studies what conformal prediction leaves open. Conformal prediction gives exact finite-sample coverage under exchangeability, but deployment judges more than coverage. For a rule reused over a finite window, users weigh commitment rates, deferral, and error risk. That alone does not fix those numbers, and similar-coverage rules can still produce distinct use patterns.

Zwart works with binary split conformal prediction under exchangeability and a fixed deployed rule. He proposes the Small-Sample Beta Correction, giving the deployed rule finite-sample coverage meaning by flipping the law behind calibration-conditional coverage. Calibrate-and-Audit fixes the rule, then uses a fresh audit split for a summary table yielding indicators by projection. Use rates allow exact finite-sample Binomial inference; Beta-Binomial ranges sketch future windows. Tests back the correction; molecular toxicity data supply an example, and a solubility study shows planning once coverage meaning is fixed.
arxiv-2602-18245:
Georg Lehner computes a family of invariants for sheaf categories over a broad class of spaces. His 2026 paper treats a broad family of invariants, algebraic K-theory among them, for sheaf categories over a wide class of locally compact spaces. The formula he derives covers the older cases in one stroke.

Locally compact Hausdorff spaces and coherent, or spectral, spaces both fall out as special cases of the new formula. Several smaller K-theory computations, previously done one by one, are recovered the same way. The result gives topologists a single machine for invariants that once needed separate arguments, and it widens the ground where such calculations can be run.
arxiv-2602-18545:
Alperen Keles and four co-authors make property-based testing programmable. Their 2026 paper notes property-based testing is a popular technique for trust in software, where users write properties, executable specs, checked many times by a framework. In modern frameworks, properties are usually written in shallow languages, tightly coupled to testing.

Such frameworks often provide options for testing, but users are limited to what library authors allowed when building the framework. For more flexibility, they may need a new framework from scratch. The team proposes a deeper property language based on a mixed form called deferred binding syntax, which turns properties into data decoupled from the property runners executing them. The language is implemented in Rocq and Racket, using dependent and dynamic types. Finally, the team shows the flexibility of this approach by rapidly prototyping property runners, highlighting domain-specific testing gains from more programmable testing.
arxiv-2602-18745:
Vision-language models still stumble on geometry, partly because training sets are thin and diagrams do not line up well with symbolic reasoning. Haobo Lin, with six co-authors, proposes in 2026 to synthesise geometry problems from scratch, producing the GeoCode dataset and a new way to align vision with symbols.

Generation splits into symbolic seed construction, grounded instantiation with verification, and diagram rendering from plotting code, so structure, text, reasoning, and image stay consistent. The same plotting code then becomes a training target: predicting it turns visual understanding into a supervised structured task. Models trained on GeoCode improve across several geometry benchmarks, while multi-stage validation keeps the maths correct.
arxiv-2602-18845:
When a multimodal model is copied and fine-tuned, its owner may have no way to prove lineage. Chengwei Xia, with five co-authors, proposes in 2026 a way to plant a verifiable ownership trigger in such models. The trigger is an image that should elicit ownership-related text only in fine-tuned derivatives, while staying inert in other models.

The image is built as a learnable tensor with dual injection of ownership semantics. One injection enforces textual consistency between an auxiliary model's output and a target ownership text. The other minimises the distance between CLIP features of image and text. An extra adversarial stage trains the auxiliary model to resist producing the target text, hardening the trigger against heavy fine-tuning. Tests show the method tracks lineage across fine-tuning and domain shifts.
arxiv-2602-18945:
Black holes in modified gravity can behave very differently from their Einstein counterparts. Bilel Hamil, with one co-author, constructs charged anti-de Sitter black holes in 2026 in four-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity coupled with Euler-Heisenberg nonlinear electrodynamics.

Higher-curvature and nonlinear electromagnetic tweaks reshape the horizon structure. Multiple horizons become possible, depending on model settings. In extended phase space, where the cosmological constant acts as pressure, both couplings modify the equation of state, critical behaviour, and heat stability. Treating mass as enthalpy, the authors study Joule-Thomson expansion and find its inversion point. Cooling and heating regions shift substantially. Time-like geodesics show that Gauss-Bonnet corrections also alter orbital stability, particle motion, and the effective potential in strong fields. Black holes can thus have rich heat behaviour. That richness comes from the extra terms.
arxiv-2602-19045:
Simulating Ising spin systems needs speed and flexibility. Yan Ru Pei, writing alone in 2026, presents peapods, an open-source Python tool for Monte Carlo simulation. It handles arbitrary couplings on periodic Bravais lattices with user-chosen neighbour offsets. A Rust core, exposed through PyO3, pairs a friendly Python interface with compiled, memory-safe speed.

The package covers Metropolis and Gibbs single-spin flips. It also covers parallel tempering, Swendsen-Wang and Wolff cluster updates, and three replica cluster moves for glassy spins. Overlap statistics yield the spin-glass order parameter and Binder ratio. Replica parallelism runs through the Rayon work-stealing scheduler. Validation matches exact critical temperatures for the square and triangular lattices. Finite-size scaling of the Binder cumulant confirms the implementation.
arxiv-2602-19145:
Why is the cosmological constant so small, and why does it dominate only now? H. R. Fazlollahi, writing alone in 2026, reframes both puzzles. Fine-tuning and coincidence problems haunt the standard model, where they stay effectively frozen. A different viewpoint, rooted in other gravity theories, may dissolve them.

The author argues the root error is interpretive. Identifying the constant with quantum ground-state energy of spacetime misleads. A novel physical interpretation is proposed instead. A new mechanism, Breaking Energy-Momentum Symmetry, supplies the frame. It offers a natural, unified route toward easing both problems, possibly resolving them. The conventional paradigm thus gains a compelling rival.
arxiv-2602-19945:
AdamW speeds training of large models, but under differentially private federated learning it runs into trouble: noise and data differences inflate variance, bias the second-moment estimate, and worsen drift between clients. A 2026 arXiv paper by Jin Liu and three co-authors adapts AdamW to that setting with DP-FedAdamW.

The optimizer steadies second-moment variance and strips out privacy-induced bias. It also lines local updates up with the global descent direction to curb drift. Theory gives an unbiased second-moment estimator and a linearly accelerated convergence rate. It needs no assumption about data homogeneity, and it offers tighter privacy guarantees. Tests across language and vision transformers and a residual network show strong results, including a clear margin over the prior best on a standard image benchmark under a strict privacy budget.
arxiv-2602-20045:
Combined sensing and communication shares wireless resources, but it opens new security holes: private messages can be read, and unapproved receivers can exploit target echoes to infer sensing parameters unnoticed. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yinchao Yang and five co-authors proposes a dual-secure framework protecting both sides at once, without needing eavesdroppers' channel information.

Transmit beamformers are designed jointly to inject added noise against message eavesdroppers, while warping the reference signal available to sensing snoopers to impair their sensing. The design also generates artificial ghosts with fake angle-delay-Doppler profiles. The rightful sensing receiver blocks those ghosts using prior knowledge of true target aims, while sensing snoopers cannot, sharply reducing their chance of finding true targets. Tests show the framework strengthens both messaging and sensing security while keeping quality for rightful users.
arxiv-2602-20245:
Pairs of stars moving through dark matter feel a drag, and that drag slowly reshapes their orbits. A 2026 arXiv paper by Nicolas Esser, working alone, works out formulas and timescales for how orbital elements change. It covers both wide pairs and close pairs, taking each pair's motion through the dark matter into account.

In settings like the faintest dwarf galaxies, the results show some pairs swinging through large eccentricity changes while their separations shrink bit by bit over cosmic time. Across a population, the drag thins out wide pairs and leaves more pairs on stretched orbits. Curiously, the strongest drag does not sit where dark matter is densest, because denser regions also stir stars to higher speeds, and fast motion weakens the drag. With better theory and data, star pairs may become probes of dark matter in the faintest galaxies.
arxiv-2602-20445:
The ALMA Central Molecular Zone Exploration Survey maps the crowded heart of the Milky Way in molecular lines. A large team led by Xing Lu releases data from its two intermediate-width spectral windows, covering silicon monoxide, sulfur monoxide, and rare isotopologue lines among other molecular transitions. The data carry angular resolution near two arcseconds and velocity resolution of one point seven kilometres per second.

The release includes full data cubes for both windows plus maps of integrated brightness, peak brightness, centroid velocity, and longitude-velocity structure for six lines. The authors briefly discuss links between continuum and line emission shapes, and brightness ratios between isotopologue line pairs. They flag features and trends for follow-up in upcoming survey science papers.
arxiv-2602-20545:
Bend bounds limit the shapes of maps between shape spaces. Ravindra Singh proves Casorati bounds for Riemannian maps and submersions in quaternionic space forms, with shape tests for their match cases. For these maps, the bounds describe when a match holds: the leaves of the range space are evenly quasi-umbilical, and the linked shape tool matrix swaps cleanly.

For maps that drop a dimension from that setting, bounds use the basic tensor fields T and A, with shape readings. A match for tensor A along the flat spread is the same as the flat spread fitting together. A match for tensor T along the upright spread marks fibres with that round shape and a swapping shape tool. A joint match for both tensors gives fitting together plus round fibres with swapping shape tools.
arxiv-2602-20745:
Rishav Agrawal and three co-authors study gravitational wave output from cyclic orbits in regular black hole spaces, mainly with known number and exact methods. They show clear gaps with the plain Schwarzschild shape by mapping orbit traits, wave strain curves, and the matching power range, for different values of the smoothing value g.

They also weigh their results against LISA sensitivity curves, showing how they may help build ready-to-use patterns for detecting regular black holes as live options to the plain ones. The notes to the article give details on errors in their figures. They provide, for the first time, some exact forms on wave output from different types of cyclic orbits in Schwarzschild spacetime.
arxiv-2602-21045:
Scholarly question-answering systems built on language models often err subtly, with unsupported claims or telling omissions, and plain citations are too coarse to catch them. Anna Martin-Boyle, Cara Leckey, Martha Brown, and Harmanpreet Kaur introduce PaperTrail in this 2026 arXiv paper. The interface splits answers and sources into discrete claims and evidence and maps them against each other.

A study with twenty-six researchers doing scholarly editing tasks found PaperTrail lowered trust compared with a baseline interface. That extra caution did not change behavior, though: participants still relied on generated edits to avoid a cognitively heavy task. The paper draws design lessons for communicating provenance in ways that respect how researchers actually work.
arxiv-2602-21145:
Simulating lattice field theories in real time hinges on Trotter-Suzuki decompositions of time evolution. Marko Malezic and Johann Ostmeyer guide readers through those schemes in this 2026 arXiv paper, covering implementations on quantum hardware and classical tensor networks alike. Low-order schemes remain standard for their simplicity, but higher-order schemes promise better efficiency.

The paper highlights new efficient schemes found by an optimization framework and demonstrates them on the Heisenberg model. Readers get a short, practical guide plus fresh schemes worth trying. The work serves practitioners choosing decompositions for dynamics simulations who want efficiency without wading through scattered literature.
arxiv-2602-21445:
Haoxuan Wang and four co-authors ask how far a robot should execute each predicted action chunk. Action chunking is now standard in flow-based Vision-Language-Action models. But the execution horizon, the number of actions run from each chunk, had been little studied, and varying it swings performance up then down.

Attention analysis reveals two patterns. Actions inside a chunk attend almost identically to vision-language tokens, limiting adaptation to change. Meanwhile, the first and last action tokens act as stable anchors around which middle actions organize. Treating self-attention weights as a proxy for predictive limits, the team proposes AutoHorizon, a test-time method that estimates the horizon per chunk. Across simulated and real manipulation tasks, it performs well with negligible extra compute and generalizes across tasks and models.
arxiv-2602-21745:
Hyo Jin Kim introduces the ASIR Courage Model, a phase-dynamic view of truth telling as a state change rather than an inborn habit. The shift from holding back to speaking out occurs when helping forces beat blocking limits: basic openness, bond boost, and built-up inner pressure outweigh change costs. First built for human truth telling under uneven stakes, it extends to AI systems under policy limits and alignment filters.

For AI, holding back maps to limited output states, while structural pressure comes from competing goals, context tension, and recursive back-and-forth. A feedback loop lets change results reset system settings, creating path memory and split paths over runs. Rather than granting intent to AI systems, the model reads shifts in seeming honesty as geometric results of clashing forces in phase space. It gives one account of human silence under pressure and AI preference-driven skew.
arxiv-2602-21845:
Explanations from most generators are often highly redundant, changing far more features than needed. Lin Zhu and one co-author present xai-cola, an open-source Python library that trims such explanations down to their essentials. It works with outputs from any generator, cutting needless feature changes while keeping the result valid.

The library takes raw tabular data in pandas DataFrame form, a preprocessing object for scaling and encoding, and a trained scikit-learn or PyTorch model. Users can employ built-in or imported generators. It also offers several trimming policies and plotting routines for comparing trimmed explanations. Released under the MIT license and installable from PyPI, xai-cola yields sparser explanations across several generators, reducing changed features by up to 50 percent in the authors' setting.
arxiv-2602-21945:
Ahmed Hussain, Asmaa Abdallah, Ahmed Nasser, Abdulkadir Celik, and Ahmed Eltawil test a near-field claim about wireless antennas with real hardware. In the far field, a direct line-of-sight link supports only one spatial channel, but spherical wavefronts at close range should open up several. Prior work argued the point in theory, yet experiments pinning down where the extra channels fade remained scarce.

The authors build a framework for the effective channel count of a linear array system. It offers two matching formulas: one tied to beam width and aperture size, and one built for lab use from angular decomposition. They also name two key distances: where the count drops to one, and where it peaks. Measurements with widely spaced phased arrays track the theory closely, validating both the framework and its distance markers.
arxiv-2602-22045:
Distributed ledger technology spans coins, contracts, patents, and hype, but language researchers have lacked one large text base covering the whole domain. Walter Hernandez Cruz and four co-authors assemble DLT-Corpus, the largest such collection to date, drawn from scientific papers, patent filings, and social media posts. Older resources focused narrowly on coin prices and smart contracts, leaving the domain's language largely unmapped.

The corpus lets the team trace how technologies emerge: new ideas tend to surface in research papers first, then reach patents and social posts, following classic technology transfer. Social media mood stays bullish even through crypto winters, while research and patent activity follow a steadier path. For analysts, the corpus offers a single ground for studying how ledger technology talk moves from lab to market.
arxiv-2602-22145:
When workers ask language models to professionalize their writing, something quiet can be lost: the markers of their own English variety. Satyam Kumar Navneet and two co-authors name that loss cultural ghosting, the systematic erasure of features unique to non-native Englishes during text processing. They test Indian, Singaporean, and Nigerian English texts across five models and three prompt styles.

Across tens of thousands of outputs, about one marker in ten vanished, with wide variation between models. Meaning mostly survived even as identity markers faded, a paradox the authors call semantic preservation. Politeness markers proved far more vulnerable than vocabulary. The study gives workplaces a measured warning about what polish costs.
arxiv-2602-22445:
Group routines like Broadcast and Reduce underpin parallel computing, but failures can break them. Martin Kuettler and Hermann Haertig adapt a known Broadcast recipe, spread then fix-up, to Reduce. Their design runs a fix-up-like message phase before a tree-based phase, yielding a Reduce routine tolerant of failed processes.

The paper states and proves the meaning of the resulting routine, then joins Broadcast and Reduce into Allreduce. The approach reuses a proven pattern: let a rough spread run first, then fix it, rather than demanding fault-free runs throughout. Parallel coders gain group routines that survive process failures.
arxiv-2602-22545:
Agamdeep S. Chopra and five co-authors introduce SFL-Net, a system that predicts tau-PET brain scans from ordinary structural MRI. Tau-PET helps stage Alzheimer's disease, but tracers, scanners, and radiation make it hard to scale, so building the scan from T1-weighted and FLAIR MRI is attractive. The catch is that those MRI types show anatomy, not the tau signal itself.

SFL-Net splits its internal representation into shared, T1-specific, FLAIR-specific, and complementary pathways, and keeps anatomical detail through latent structural conditioning instead of direct encoder-decoder links. Tested on 605 training and 83 validation subjects from the ADNI-3 and OASIS-3 studies, it matched baselines on image quality and clinical measures. It also added source-level auditability, showing which MRI input drove each part of the result.
arxiv-2602-23145:
Juan Guillermo Garrido and two co-authors study random rate-of-change sets driven by maximal one-way maps with empty insides. The work is spurred by ongoing-time models of first-order tuning methods under noisy or rough map input. Well-soundness is tackled first: solutions exist and are unique without the usual need that the map's field has some inside, through a fitting notion of solution.

Long-run traits of the ensuing random shifts are then analyzed, stretching settling promises beyond earlier studied settings leaning on smooth curves, full-field subslopes, or Lipschitz one-way maps. Also, the team studies a Tikhonov-style smoothing of the random set and proves matching well-soundness and long-run settling results for the smoothed shifts.
arxiv-2602-23545:
Matteo Ceriscioli and one co-author propose planning under distribution shifts with causal partially observable Markov decision processes. A model learned under one set of conditions may fail when state distributions or dynamics change, breaking previously learned strategies.

Their framework represents environmental shifts as interventions on a causal POMDP. This enables evaluation of plans under hypothesized changes and active identification of which components changed. The method maintains and updates a belief over both the latent state and the underlying domain. The authors prove the value function stays piecewise linear and convex in this augmented belief space. Preserving that structure under shifts keeps planning tractable via alpha-vector-based POMDP methods.
arxiv-2602-23845:
Jian Kai and seven co-authors introduce CLFEC, a new task for joint linguistic and factual error correction in paragraph-level Chinese professional writing. The 2026 paper notes that past work splits spelling and grammar from factual repair, yet in real drafts the two error types co-occur and interact.

The team builds a mixed multi-domain dataset spanning current affairs, finance, law, and medicine, then tests language-model correction styles from prompting to retrieval-augmented generation and agentic workflows. Challenges emerge: specialized correctors generalize poorly, factual repair needs evidence grounding, mixed-error paragraphs are hard, and clean inputs risk over-correction. Joint handling beats decoupled pipelines, and agentic workflows work well with suitable base models. CLFEC offers a benchmark and practical guidance for proofreading systems.
arxiv-2603-00045: Li's team attacks the factorization barrier in diffusion language models. Tokens guessed at once are wrongly treated as independent, forcing a speed-versus-coherence trade-off. They argue the barrier is structural misspecification, not weak backbones, since full joint laws would need far too many numbers. Their Coupled Discrete Diffusion method replaces factored outputs with a lightweight tractable inference layer. It matches reinforcement-learning rivals on reason tasks at a fraction of training cost and stops collapse in few-step output.
arxiv-2603-00345: Kang and colleagues present CensorLess, a proxy on a serverless platform that dodges censorship at low cost, easing the burden shaping user choice and provider sustainability. Earlier low-cost designs used spot servers as bridges but still paid heavily for network links and upkeep. The proxy combines a local front end, a refresher that swaps in new bridges on a schedule, and a live switch that keeps links up. Compared with existing low-cost methods, it cuts costs by 97 percent while strengthening censorship resistance through bridge swaps.
arxiv-2603-00645: Borisov and Piatnitski build new function spaces from nonlocal convolution integrals and study their main traits in detail. Under natural convexity and growth rules for the integrand, the spaces prove Banach and separable. The paper also maps the dual spaces and works through examples. The result gives analysts a workable setting for nonlocal convolution type problems.
arxiv-2603-00745: Chowdhury and four colleagues predict aero engine remaining life with Bi-cLSTM, a bidirectional residual corrected LSTM. Two way time models plus adaptive residual correction refine sequences step by step. Prep work using regime based normalisation, feature picks, and exponential smoothing steadies results under shifting settings and noisy sensors. Tests on all four NASA C-MAPSS subsets show the model beats LSTM baselines and matches the best rivals, most clearly in tough multi condition cases.
arxiv-2603-00945: Wang and Si study robust Markov decision processes where the ambiguity set links transitions across states, dropping the usual rectangularity assumption. They show history-dependent policies with sublinear regret are robust-optimal, and the robust value takes a minimax form over the ambiguity set without robust dynamic programming. Since average-reward optimality can hide arbitrarily poor short-run behavior, they add a transient-value framework and an epoch-based policy achieving constant-order transient value.
arxiv-2603-01145: Yang and eleven colleagues let language-model agents gather skills across sessions with AutoSkill, an experience-driven life-long learning layer. It abstracts reusable skills from chat traces, keeps evolving them, and injects the fitting ones into future requests without new training for the base model. As a model-neutral plugin with a standard skill format for sharing across agents and users, it turns fleeting chats into clear mixable powers for tailored agents.
arxiv-2603-01245: Beri and Baker draw lessons for an AI whistleblower office from 30 case studies spanning 1978 to 2020 across 15 fields. Good programs reward tipsters with cash, protect them, allow nameless tips, stay well staffed and funded, and advise future tipsters. The paper distills these findings into ten concrete tips for building an AI tipster program that can surface rule-breaking.
arxiv-2603-01445:
Curves in geometry carry a special cycle, called the Ceresa cycle, that tests how complex a curve is. Tejasi Bhatnagar, Sheela Devadas, Toren D'Nelly-Warady, and Padmavathi Srinivasan study that cycle for covers of curves in this 2026 work. A cover is a second curve mapped onto the first, often with branching.

The team proves that for a very general branched cover, the Ceresa cycle does not vanish in the key test group. They also build whole families of covers where the same trait holds at a general point. Two small families of genus six curves make the claim concrete. Their method turns the cycle test into a point test on a related space, then uses deep facts about rare special points.
arxiv-2603-01545:
Cutting moving objects out of video from a vague text clue is hard when the clue needs thought, not just sight. Zhengtong Zhu, Jiaqing Fan, Zhixuan Liu, and Fanzhang Li offer a training-free path in this 2026 work. Past tools fine-tune large vision-language models for the task, which takes heavy compute and data.

Their method, SDAM, uses only pre-trained models and splits space work from time work. In each frame it finds and cuts the target, while across frames it keeps the track stable. A memory module picks key objects by motion cues and holds them for later frames. That split, plus the memory, keeps masks steady as scenes change. Scores stay strong across five test sets, even against tools that needed fine-tuning.
arxiv-2603-01645:
Axel Turnquist studies how well finite cutoffs can stand in for targets that stretch to infinity. His 2026 work concerns optimal transport, the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another. The source here is bounded, while the target spreads over all space with no edge.

In practice, solvers cut the target at some radius and solve the smaller problem instead. Turnquist asks how fast the cut maps and potentials approach the true ones as that radius grows. He treats both the forward and inverse problems, in round symmetric cases and in general ones. For the squared-distance cost, he derives concrete pointwise rates that do not hide behind limits. Those rates can justify numeric solvers for a key transport equation used in optics and imaging.
arxiv-2603-01945:
Thibault Prouteau, Francis Lareau, and Nicolas Dugue test whether automatic topic scores match what human readers see. Their 2026 work studies topic models, which find hidden themes in large text collections. Automatic scores for coherence and diversity are cheap, yet they may drift from human judgment in expert fields.

The team adds a new human task, Topic Word Mixing, that tests if topics stay distinct. Annotators judge whether a word set comes from one topic or from a blend of topics. Six models face both automatic scores and human tasks on a philosophy of science corpus. Nearly four thousand annotations ground the comparison between the two lenses. Word intrusion scores and coherence scores do not always align, while the new task tracks perceived distinctness and diversity well.
arxiv-2603-02345:
Sami Abuzakuk, Lucas Crijns, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, and colleagues make cloud checking more robust in this 2026 paper. Cloud systems are set up from code, but live systems drift from that code over time. Bugs, manual edits, and updates all cause drift. AI agents could hunt drift in telemetry, yet they trust their tools blindly.

A broken tool looks the same as a real fault to a naive agent. Their system, RIVA, pairs two agents that cross-check each other's work. One verifies the system, while the other generates fresh tools to test with. Call history and multiple viewpoints help separate real drift from tool errors. On a standard benchmark, accuracy recovered strongly when tool errors were injected. Scores also rose when no errors were present.
arxiv-2603-02645:
Reese Jones and Jan Fuhg compare three physics-based ways to teach neural networks how real materials deform. Their 2026 paper notes that most learning setups quietly pick one theory of heat and energy loss and build its rules in. Performance gaps may then come from the theory itself, not from data or network design.

To isolate that effect, they placed each framework inside the same network design and trained all three on the same data. The data came from detailed simulations of a metal alloy, a layered composite, and a crystal-based material. All three frameworks predicted held-out cases well. The strictest one lagged slightly on the hardest set but edged ahead on a uniform material set.
arxiv-2603-02745:
Ramin Hashemi, Vismika Ranasinghe, Teemu Veijalainen, and colleagues use learning agents to manage beams in millimeter-wave networks. Their 2026 paper tackles multi-panel radio access with many users sharing beam-based links. Choosing beams in real time is complex, and poor choices cut throughput and raise delay.

The team frames beam control as a step-by-step decision problem and trains a deep reinforcement learning agent on live observations. Inputs include beam overlap across panels, measured signal power, and beam usage history. The agent adjusts beams as conditions shift, rather than following fixed legacy rules. In simulations, throughput rose by up to sixteen percent. Delay also fell by a factor of three to seven against the baseline method.
arxiv-2603-02945:
Haotian Wu, Hehai Lin, Weiquan Huang, and colleagues merge several fine-tuned models into one without touching any training data. Model merging promises a single model with many expert skills, but experts trained on different goals interfere and drag each other down. Their 2026 method, ACE-Merging, attacks that interference directly.

Theory shows each task's input covariance, a key ingredient for ideal merging, hides inside the model's own weight changes and can be estimated with no data at all. Their closed-form recipe uses those estimates to cancel cross-task interference. Across vision and language tests it set a new best among data-free methods, with a clear average gain on a seven-task language suite. The formula is cheap to compute as well.
arxiv-2603-03045:
Inhoe Koo, Hyunho Cha, and Jungwoo Lee build quantum circuits with a learner that prizes variety as well as success. Their 2026 framework, QFlowNet, tackles unitary synthesis: breaking a target quantum operation into a short gate sequence. Reinforcement learners often chase one best answer and struggle when rewards are rare.

A generative flow network instead learns to sample solutions in proportion to their reward, yielding many diverse circuits. A transformer encoder reads the target operation's nonlocal structure and compresses it for the policy. On a three-qubit benchmark, the agent succeeded on nearly every case across short circuit lengths. It also produced a varied set of compact circuits, offering compilers real choices rather than a single take-it-or-leave-it answer.
arxiv-2603-03645:
Rahul Singh, Weixin Lu, Kaelyn Ferris, and Javad Shabani mimic the braiding of Majorana modes on a quantum processor, cheaply. Majorana zero modes, quasiparticles in topological superconductors, obey exotic exchange rules that could power error-proof quantum computing. Handling the real modes remains hard in the lab, so researchers mimic their conduct digitally, usually by slowly evolving a mapped spin model through deep, costly circuits.

Their 2026 method replaces that slow change with direct braiding operations built for a trijunction, a three-way junction shape. The operators simulate the same change with far less gate overhead. The construction then generalizes to extended trijunction layouts assembled from Kitaev chains, the standard theoretical model of the topological phase. The result is a resource-efficient route to studying protected gates before the hardware modes cooperate.
arxiv-2603-03945: Mathilde Perez and others propose a time method disentangling choice from algorithmic feedback in dynamic graphs. Link output models increasingly suggest contacts in changing networks, yet their structural impact is usually judged from static snapshots. Observed homophily mixes genuine contact tendencies with amplification from network motion and algorithmic feedback. The method uses multivariate Hawkes steps to separate the two sources and presents an instantaneous bias measure built on contact intensities, tracking present reinforcement rather than accumulated totals.
arxiv-2603-04045: Fernández Burda and others adapt Logit Diff Amplification for inference-time toxicity mitigation in protein models. Protein language models aid de novo protein design, yet tuning to given taxonomic groups can draw out toxic output even absent toxicity as a training goal. The method amplifies the gap between baseline and toxicity-finetuned model logits, modifying token probabilities with no retraining.
arxiv-2603-04145: Nguyen and others present VietNormalizer, a stand-alone Python library for Vietnamese text cleanup. Vietnamese text cleanup is underserved, since real-world text is dense with non-standard words needing conversion. Pre-compiled regular expressions enable high-throughput batch processing with tiny memory overhead, and the library is installable via pip.
arxiv-2603-04245: Wei and others present LikeThis!, empowering app users to submit UI gain suggestions instead of complaints. User feedback is crucial for mobile app evolution. However, research suggests users often submit uninformative, vague, or destructive feedback. To evaluate LikeThis!, they first ran a model benchmarking study using a public set of carefully critiqued UI designs. An intermediate step generates a answer specification before sketching the design, key to effective gain.
arxiv-2603-04345: Martinez and Moreno-Ternero share river cleanup fairly among agents along a river. Claims rest on population, past emissions, and business as usual output, split from a budget below total claims. Upstream emissions harm more than downstream ones, so location must shape the split. Geometric rules adjust proportional shares to balance fairness with environmental harm. The class rivals a recent Yang proposal, compared by axioms and by a Tuojiang Basin case in China.
arxiv-2603-04445: Moslem and Kelleher survey dynamic routing and cascading for language model inference. Static use ignores query hardness and domain, wasting performance and money. The survey maps kinds from difficulty and preference to clustering, uncertainty, reinforcement learning, multimodality, and cascading, with methods and trade offs for each. A framework sorts systems by decision timing, information, and computation, showing real systems blend kinds. Good routing can beat the strongest single model by exploiting specialist strengths. The best pick thus depends on the job at hand.
arxiv-2603-04545: Afandi and colleagues speed graph neural network inference on huge knowledge graphs. Each query targets different nodes linked to subgraphs of varied density and shape. Old accelerators shrink models yet ignore per query structure and semantics. They load whole monolithic files instead of only relevant parts. KG-WISE splits trained models into fine parts loaded partially per queried subgraph. Language model templates pull relevant subgraphs. On six graphs, the largest with 42 million nodes and 166 million edges, it runs up to 28 times faster with 98 percent less memory, holding accuracy.
arxiv-2603-05045: Daniel Ceverino and colleagues study galaxy size evolution at cosmic dawn from redshift 14 to 5 using 430 zoom-in cosmological simulations from the FirstLight database. The size-mass relation already exists at redshift 14 with wide diversity at fixed mass; extended galaxies show higher specific star-formation rates than compact ones. The mass-dependent slope barely evolves. At fixed mass, size grows very fast: normalization rises 0.5 dex between redshift 14 and 6 within 600 million years.
arxiv-2603-05145: Kento Tsubouchi and colleagues ask how much error-syndrome information can improve estimates of logical observables from noisy quantum states. In classical syndrome-aware schemes, where the measurement basis stays fixed and syndromes enter only later processing, the gain is capped: the effective logical error rate improves at most twofold. Once quantum control is allowed to adapt to each observed syndrome, that error rate instead falls exponentially with the number of code blocks. The findings guide fault-tolerant designs to exploit syndrome records rather than discard them after decoding.
arxiv-2603-05345: Stefan Bott and team present a multilingual Easy-to-Read corpus. Grasp information matters for democratic participation. Auto simplification research lacks high-quality training material, Spanish, Catalan, and Italian. The corpus offers three-language first texts with human simplification, from iDEM assessing Easy-to-Read language. Texts come from topic-related domains, selected for relevance, copyright, and ethics, all at Easy-to-Read level. It includes the first annotated Catalan corpus, a noteworthy Spanish and Italian contribution, freely open.
arxiv-2603-05445: C. San Nicolas Martinez and team present TILARA, a template-independent radial speed code. Precise radial speeds commonly come from cross-link or template-matching, both relying on a reference spectrum. Line-by-line methods compute radial speeds but still rely on template making. TILARA works across stellar types. A curated absorption-line list measures line centers via Gaussian fitting. Using the reference list and ARES-measured lines, TILARA computes radial speeds with outlier rejection. Code setups were tested. 520 ESPRESSO observations of HD 102365 tested it.
arxiv-2603-05545: Ehlers and team present VarP-GP, a low-cost Bayesian emulator for costly models with variable statistical precision, aimed at quark-gluon plasma readings from high-energy nuclear collisions. Training data come from Monte Carlo simulations whose precision depends on compute used. VarP-GP joins runs of varying precision across the parameter space, using the smoothness of QCD-driven processes there. Against a standard emulator, it cuts uncertainty a lot at fixed cost, hinting broad parameter-space contours matter more than dense detail at few design points.
arxiv-2603-06345: Eisenhofer and his team combine ordering based saturation and subgoal reduction proof strategies, backing symmetry breaking SAT methods for first order connection calculi. Unlike classical reductions of first order logic to propositional logic, their method encodes the proof search structure itself. They present three SAT encodings for such calculi, analyze their theory properties, and discuss SAT/SMT solver effects on them. The work is implemented in the new solver upCoP with real use showcased.
arxiv-2603-06445: Liu and his team set out WanderDream, a first large-scale dataset for copycat simulation of mental exploration. Can an agent, given a limited view, simulate in mind a trajectory to a target and answer spatial what-if questions? Active looking underpins placed reasoning, yet robot constraints and safety concerns can block it. The Gen set holds 15.8K panoramic videos across 1,088 scenes, depicting imagined paths to targets. The QA set holds 158K question-answer pairs over starts, paths, and ends; tests show imagination aids thought and transfers to cases.
arxiv-2603-06545: Sanson and colleagues present LiveSense, a platform turning a laptop Wi-Fi network card into a centimeter-level Range-Doppler sensor keeping simultaneous communication. Laptops use Intel AX211 or BE201 cards. LiveSense extracts synchronized channel state information at 40 Hz or more, aligns time and phase, and cancels self-interference. The demo detects distance and radial velocity of attendees, respiration, and hand-gesture ranging, as the first demo obtaining target range from Wi-Fi despite 160 MHz bandwidth.
arxiv-2603-06645: Rigas bounds Eve's forgery probability in quantum key distribution, the chance a message is accepted by Alice or Bob over a noisy quantum channel. From Renner and Wolf's min-entropy success probability for asymmetric security, the author upper-bounds forgery with a Holevo-type quantity made negligibly small. The bound uses Eve's false acceptance estimates with a chosen two-universal function paralleling two-universal hashing. The protocol is not only epsilon-secure for positive epsilon but also composable against forgery plus key leakage, under a unified threshold.
arxiv-2603-06745: Kang and Kim present DIRECTER, a steering method that helps language models follow complex instructions without oversteering. Plain activation steering can push too hard, harming accuracy and text quality. DIRECTER scales the KV cache and pairs steering with a plausibility-guided decoding loop that weakens steering step by step when steered output looks implausible. A one-time layer-sensitivity analysis ranks layers by influence. Tests show clear instruction-following gains with no usual quality trade-off.
arxiv-2603-06845: Eickhoff and colleagues map the adsorption growth window for gallium selenide films on gallium arsenide substrates, grown by beam epitaxy. III-Se compounds like InSe and GaSe promise optoelectronics with high room electron speeds, nonlinear light responses, ferroelectricity, sealed surfaces, and alloying for bandgap tuning. Adsorption control guides mix and phase forming, yet GaSe window bounds were not mapped in full, and polytype and twinning control stayed hard. Phase edges match Ellingham diagram forecasts, all films form the gamma form, and hotter growth cut mosaic spread and smooth surfaces.
arxiv-2603-07145: Duan and colleagues name and fix the out-of-sight dynamics problem in generative video world models. Current models freeze objects once they leave the camera's view, so revisiting a region later misses events that should have happened meanwhile. LiveWorld instead keeps a persistent global state: a static 3D background plus dynamic entities that keep evolving even when unseen. That design lets the simulated world keep changing off camera, so later views reflect the events that occurred in the meantime.
arxiv-2603-07345: Bansal and colleagues describe how Uber replaced blanket double capacity with a failover design tiered by business importance. Vital services keep full backup guarantees, while others borrow idle backup room in normal times and yield it during rare full-peak events. Automatic checks, including dependency review and regression gates, keep vital services running through those takeovers. The redesign cuts steady-state capacity sharply while holding uptime near total.
arxiv-2603-07545: Tang and colleagues teach world models to handle new physics instead of merely fitting correlations. Their symmetry search plan drives an agent with a Hamiltonian curiosity bonus to probe conservation rules and gather telling data. Their world model then learns invariant states from raw pixel views via a self-supervised contrast goal. Their DreamSAC system beats strong baselines on 3D physics simulations needing reach past training.
arxiv-2603-07745: Sassoli de Bianchi gives a shape-based route to why dimension matters in Gleason's theorem, using the broad Bloch picture. He studies chance rules swapping the Born formula's Bloch-space link for a real function f. For qubits, countless non-Born rules meet norming for every measurement. Above dimension 3, simplex geometry forces extra scalar-product links, and norming yields a Cauchy-type equation forcing f straight-line with bounded size. The case shows plainly why two-dimensional freedom vanishes higher up, without linked sets across right-angle splits.
arxiv-2603-08145: Zou and colleagues present DARC, a retraining-free method for aligning language models when human preferences disagree. Preference-based methods like RLHF and DPO usually optimize a single score, averaging over mixed preferences. But steady disagreement among raters and user groups makes mean-reward chasing brittle and prone to proxy over-optimization. DARC instead frames reply choice at inference time as robust, risk-aware selection, ranking replies against several preference samples or scalable disagreement stand-ins.
arxiv-2603-08245: Huber and colleagues propose a topologically stable Hough transform for detecting lines in point clouds. The classical Hough transform relies on a discretized voting scheme, which can make its output fragile. The authors replace that scheme with a continuous score function, whose lasting features in persistent homology yield candidate lines. They also devise and implement an algorithm that computes these lines fast.
arxiv-2603-08445: Hsieh and colleagues personalize gaze estimation to a new user from only a few unlabeled samples. This task is hard because traits like eyelid shape or facial structure can spoil a pre-trained model. Their method, Alfa, reframes personalization as reweighting features already in the model, not learning new ones. Singular value decomposition pulls spatial parts from pre-trained filters, and attention boosts the parts that fit the target user. Alfa claims the lowest gaze errors across four cross-dataset benchmarks, beating rival test-time methods and LoRA baselines.
arxiv-2603-08545: Álvaro Lozano-Robledo and Benjamin York give a fast way to compute the image of the adelic Galois representation for a special class of elliptic curves. They treat curves over the rationals with complex multiplication, leaving out the two cases where the j-invariant is 0 or 1728. Their method describes the image up to conjugation and is put into code, so other workers can run it directly.
arxiv-2603-08845: Veronika Baumann and Maximilian Lock ask how clocks agree on when events happen in relational quantum dynamics. Evolution there comes from links between a system and a clock, with the joint state frozen by a constraint. From one clock, two ways of modeling interventions both support operational causality, but across clocks only the built-in way stays consistent, at the price of temporal delocalization.
arxiv-2603-09045: Yuchen Tang and colleagues present two low mass-ratio microlensing planets from high-magnification events. One planet has a mass ratio near 4.5 times ten to the minus five, likely orbiting an M- or K-dwarf at about 3 astronomical units. The other has a larger ratio near 1 astronomical unit. Reviewing nine central-resonant events, they divide the degeneracy into two types in separate mass-ratio and source-radius regions, guiding searches for the alternative solution.
arxiv-2603-09145: Zhen Zhang and colleagues fight feature collision in class-incremental learning, where new-task features drift into space held by old ones. They blame spurious correlations, both shortcuts inside one task and confusion between look-alike classes across tasks. Their fix uses a necessity-and-sufficiency measure, extended for expanding models, to guide which features get added. A twin-network generator makes counterfactual features for both scopes, aiming at complete yet separable representations.
arxiv-2603-09445: Serge Cantat and Romain Dujardin study multiplier rigidity for complex Hénon maps, a class of polynomial automorphisms of the complex plane squared. A map of given degree is set, up to finitely many options, by its multiplier spectrum or by the unstable multipliers at its saddle periodic points. For composed Hénon maps the same holds once multi-degree and multi-Jacobian are fixed. The proof rests on ruling out stable algebraic families and on sharp Lyapunov exponent bounds along diverging families.
arxiv-2603-09545: Siddharth Narayan Singh and colleagues study how to tell quark jets from gluon jets in dijet photoproduction at the future Electron-Ion Collider. Events come from PYTHIA simulations across the collider's energy range, split into direct and resolved photoproduction. Jets are rebuilt with the kT algorithm in FastJet, and their shapes are studied with jet-shape variables and subjet counts. Quark- and gluon-initiated jets differ enough that telling them apart looks feasible at these energies.
arxiv-2603-09845: Daniel Persaud and coauthors built MAP-E, a robot platform that runs corrosion tests with no human hands on the work. Corrosion testing is slow and varies with operator skill, starving data driven materials work of clean data. Robotic liquid handling and multichannel control pull corrosion metrics in parallel. Checked against a standard benchmark, the platform then mapped pH and chloride stability for stainless steel on its own.
