In a first full test on 320 made-up cases of up to 10 strings and 500 letters, the method beats plain beam search at like runtimes.
arxiv-2604-18745: Hernandez and three colleagues present DeltaSeg, a U-shaped encoder-decoder net for finding defects in inspection images. Attention is tiered: channel attention in the encoder, coordinate attention at the bottleneck and decoder, and a deep delta attention step in the skip links. Depthwise separable convolutions with dilated stages keep detail, while multi-scale pooling at the bottleneck takes in context. On two defect data sets with 7 and 9 classes, DeltaSeg beats 12 rival nets. The goal is defect outlines even when damage types vary and some classes are rare.
arxiv-2604-19045: Browning, Munshi, and Wang use the circle method on a particular cubic fourfold, passing the square-root barrier. The circle method counts solutions by splitting a Fourier integral into major arcs, where the main contribution sits, and minor arcs, which must be bounded. The square-root barrier marks the precision limit of straightforward minor arc bounds. Passing it requires a stronger treatment of the minor arcs, which the authors supply for this fourfold.
arxiv-2604-19245: Lachenmaier, Bultmann, and Zarrieß examine language model repair, the process of resolving trouble in conversation, in multi-turn dialogues about solvable and unsolvable math questions. They ask whether models initiate repair and how they respond to user repair. Reactions range from almost completely resistant to appropriate repair to highly susceptible and easily manipulated. Beyond a single turn, behavior grows more distinctive and less predictable across systems. Each tested model shows its own characteristic unreliability in the repair context.
arxiv-2604-19345: Wang and colleagues study the inbuilt shape features of highly similar objects for ultra-fine-grained sorting with limited data. Their Geometric Attribute Exploration Network makes shape attributes as fresh recognition cues, drawn from details that match an object's patterns, such as vein structures in soybean leaves. Each class shows distinct shape signs that stay strong even among near-twin objects. The tool finds those attributes by first boosting shape-key signals, a factor recent work has largely missed.
arxiv-2604-19545: Phukan and colleagues test Big Bang Nucleosynthesis in cosmological models from generalized horizon entropies. Studying shifts in the growth rate, they derive model bounds from freeze-out temperature and helium and deuterium abundances. The freeze-out rule gives the most stringent constraint. Helium and deuterium limits stay steady across all models. Lithium constraints fail, a gap blamed on the well-known lithium problem.
arxiv-2604-19845: Perrier formalizes self-modification in artificial superintelligence on an associative operator algebra, treating modification as an action that needs a supplement outside the act. A propagation theorem shows non-commutation spreads to self-picture, and the liar paradox appears as the rank-one case. Systems in which the update operator acts on the difference operator reproduce the paradox at system scale, yielding a structure matching Priest's schema.
arxiv-2604-20245: Åhlgren and Günlü study secure rate distortion perception trade offs, where compressed data keeps perceptual quality over public channels with negligible leakage. For noiseless channels they pin down the exact secure region, and for broadcast channels they derive an inner bound tight for more capable channels. Separate source channel coding proves optimal for the exact region with unlimited shared randomness on hand. Side information at both ends pins down the exact region again for noiseless channels, while decoder only side information yields an inner bound plus a special case.
arxiv-2604-20445: Bhattacharya and three colleagues assess shortfall risk for the Great Britain grid by shifting winter weather inside a statistical demand model. Shifting matters, they argue, because demand can look low when harsh weather lands on a weekend or over Christmas. On a British example, winter 2010-11 ranks either as the worst in the data or as unremarkable, depending on how days of the week line up with the weather series. They note that judging a weather year without the day-of-week effect is incomplete.
arxiv-2604-20645: Aviles Felix and eight others study strain in Co80Ir20 films, where reverse magnetocrystalline anisotropy adds to shape bias and favors in-plane pull. The team studies films with bases and tops to induce strain. X-ray diffraction shows the c-axis parameter depends on base, with more squeeze for tantalum, while texture stays constant, and magnetism differs by base. Tantalum gives bias close to shape values, while platinum adds an in-plane field of about 7 to 9 kOe. Stress effects cannot be ignored when estimating the magnetocrystalline contribution.
arxiv-2604-20945: Agarwal and colleagues audit eight leading open-source language models with interpretability-driven jailbreak methods, steering internal activations toward unsafe behavior concepts. Llama-3 models prove highly vulnerable, with up to 91 percent of responses jailbroken on one model, while GPT-oss-120B resists both steering methods. Smaller Qwen and Phi models mostly show lower jailbreak rates than their larger siblings, underscoring dual-use risks and the need for stronger internal defenses.
arxiv-2604-21545: Luisa Ferrari and three colleagues propose a Bayesian method for grouping binary data, as in ecology, via Bernoulli mixtures. Many methods trade speed against full inference; their method delivers both. They fix a group count with an asymmetric Dirichlet prior on mixture weights, with prior settings from Penalized Complexity, letting users shape the induced cluster-count spread. An MCMC routine fits the model. Simulations and applications show the method matching rivals, beating them in some settings. A presence-absence dataset shows the proposal, with cluster parameters tied to environment.
arxiv-2604-21645: Ashley Abraham and colleagues tackle large-scale nearest-neighbor search, where finding the closest matches in huge high-dimensional datasets costs too much memory and time. They split the work with product quantization, a memory-efficient approximate search method, and inverted indexing, dividing datasets and recombining results through Dask in Python. The divide-and-conquer design cuts the computing load to roughly what medium-scale data needs, without giving up accuracy.
arxiv-2604-21745: Wu traces the history of Fréchet distances. It starts with his 1906 thesis on distances in abstract sets. It then covers the distance between polygonal curves and its 1990s algorithms. Next comes his 1957 coupling-based distance between probability laws, linking that facet to the geometric facet on curves, with a glimpse of Wasserstein distance. It ends with the Fréchet Inception Distance, a Wasserstein-2 distance between multivariate Gaussians for generative model evaluation. An appendix translates his 1906 and 1957 works and Lévy's 1950 note.
arxiv-2604-21845: Kafker and Bulgac present the first use of an enhanced Generator Coordinate Method. It is applied to a grazing multi-nucleon transfer reaction: calcium-48 plus lead-208 near the Coulomb barrier. Unlike Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock or standard Generator Coordinate approaches, the enhanced method describes the birth and later life of the compound nucleus conjectured by Niels Bohr in 1936. It does so in a fully quantum microscopic picture. Its thermalization time beats the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis prediction by at least two orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2604-22045: Mehrotra and three colleagues present H-Sets, a two-step tool for finding and scoring group feature effects in image classifiers. H-Sets first finds nearby interacting pairs from input Hessians. It then merges them into linked groups, using Segment Anything segmentation as a spatial grouping prior. Second, each set is scored with IDG-Vis, a set-level version of Integrated Directional Gradients. It adds directional gradients along pixel-space paths, combined with Harsanyi dividends.
arxiv-2604-22145: Duan and five colleagues study six recurrent sunspot light bridge jets with the New Vacuum Solar Telescope. Like coronal jets, each jet shows a base point followed by a narrow spire. Base points slip between under 1 and 1.5 km/s, in step with quasi-periodic photospheric motion. Spire fronts slip similarly higher up, and CHASE spectra at the base points look like Ellerman bombs, confirming reconnection at the base. The authors propose repeated 3D reconnection between horizontal light-bridge field and vertical umbral field drives these jets.
arxiv-2604-22445: Lanne, Luoto and Rybarczyk propose a new approach to inference in tightly identified, large-scale structural vector models, using a reparameterization that imposes inequality limits through smooth mappings. Allowed restrictions include shape and ranking restrictions plus bounds on relevant elasticities, and zero limits fit easily. They implement a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm, with posterior density quick to compute under the new setup, easing large-scale inference. Two empirical studies show lower serial dependence in Markov chains, larger sample sizes and reduced run time versus existing methods.
arxiv-2604-22545: Boscagli and three colleagues simulate a Mach 6 flow layer over a flat plate. They test whether uneven surface heat across the span can delay breakdown. Where laminar flow turns rough matters greatly for drag and heating on high-speed vehicle surfaces. Earlier work steadied such layers with best-growing streaks, and recent tests generated streaks with uneven spanwise surface heat. This study tests two cases: two-dimensional second Mack mode waves leading, and oblique first Mack mode waves leading the early linear stage.
arxiv-2604-22845: Iosifidis studies a spinning, dilating particle with hadronic traits moving through a curved geometric background that also carries torsion and nonmetricity. He introduces a shear supplementary condition with generalized spin rules, then tracks how the particle's dynamical mass evolves. In general, mass relates to dilation and shear currents through novel Regge-like trajectories. For such particles, rest mass is therefore not a constant of motion.
arxiv-2604-23145: Nguyen and four colleagues build UpstreamQA, a modular setup that makes video question answering reason out loud instead of hiding steps inside large multimodal models. Multimodal reasoning models first identify objects and sketch scene context, then pass those traces to downstream models that answer the questions. Tests on OpenEQA and NExTQA with two reasoning models and two answering models show clear gains in accuracy and clarity. Gains fade when the baseline already scores high, so explicit reasoning helps most where the base model still struggles.
arxiv-2604-23445: Suhas and colleagues warn that safety training can make mental-health chatbots clinically harmful rather than merely cautious. Testing four models on therapy scenarios, they find surface empathy stays near perfect while therapeutic quality collapses at high severity. Safety rules interrupt exposure exercises, insert crisis text, or refuse to challenge distorted thoughts. They argue no such system should ship without passing a five-part clinical evaluation.
arxiv-2604-23745: Pfreundschuh and Kummerow bridge the sensitivity gap in satellite rainfall estimates by fusing cloud-radar and precipitation-radar references into a new passive-microwave retrieval. Trained on light rain from cloud radar and heavier rain from precipitation radar, the fused product lifts high-latitude detection skill by about a quarter. It also cuts underestimation of light and frozen rain by over half. Instantaneous precision does not improve, likely due to noise in the cloud-radar reference.
arxiv-2604-24145: Ghosh and Nandy study a closed bosonic string near a five-dimensional Schwarzschild black hole under a generalized BMS supertranslation. The string's extended nature makes it sensitive to anisotropic distortions, most clearly in the angular sector of worldsheet dynamics. Time and radial sectors stay untouched, while angular deformation breaks the background SO(4) symmetry. Radial motion follows modified Bessel modes with a nonzero conserved current, giving a dynamical picture of string spreading near the horizon.
arxiv-2604-24245: Töpfer and six colleagues learn an interpretable committor for retinal isomerization, the cis-trans flip around the C13-C14 bond. They apply AI molecular mechanism discovery to N-retinylidene-lysine in vacuum, learning from unbiased trajectories by two-way shooting. Using the logit rather than the committor resolves the reaction path across the transition region. Four dihedrals around the reactive bond carry the signal. Symbolic regression shows their nonlinear coupling is required for the S-shaped stepwise pathway in transition paths, a shape the minimum-energy path misses.
arxiv-2604-24945: Bianchi, Chen and Gamonal study Toller matrices in causal spinfoam models for four-dimensional Lorentzian quantum gravity. These functions on the Lorentz group relate to the Wigner matrix. Ruhl's account via analyticity and asymptotics matches the recent Feynman prescription in spinfoams. Also, they equal an integral over boost-operator eigenvalues, giving a sum over residues. This reproduces the Wick rotation from Euclidean Spin(4) to Lorentzian SL(2,C) spinfoams. They give direct hypergeometric forms and specialize to the gamma-simple cases for spinfoams.
arxiv-2604-25045: Xu, Yachbes and Zhang study hierarchies of no-regret algorithms in two-player games. The hierarchy runs from weakest to strongest: no-swap-regret, no-regret, and uniform random play. Counterintuitively, no-swap-regret often hurts its players, giving better utility to opponents. The root cause is a difference in effective learning rate: no-swap-regret algorithms learn substantially slower than no-regret algorithms. For games where each player has 7 actions, no-swap-regret algorithms perform clearly better in ways not explained by unfairly adjusted learning rates.
arxiv-2604-25245: Funo, Vu and Saito study entropy in non-Markovian systems. A nesting of Langevin motion from a Gaussian bath shows reduced entropy splits into bigger Markovian entropy plus a link part, giving a ladder. The ladder yields trade-offs: entropy bounds, power-use trade-offs, uncertainty rules, speed limits. Bath memory thus constrains speed and engine output. The ladder extends beyond Gaussian baths to non-quantum and quantum baths.
arxiv-2604-25345: Rawat and Flek test CMBAgent on eighteen space tasks in two modes. In One-Shot mode, rich domain context lifts scores by about 6 times, but the main flaw is quiet wrong math: code that looks right yet gives wrong results. In Deep Research mode, the system also fails in silence, giving posteriors that clash. Scores are strong on crisply set tasks but fall on tasks that push reasoning bounds. The worst flaw is sure-but-wrong results. They share the frame for AI trust checks.
arxiv-2604-25445: Koram and Elishco prove a central limit theorem for mutation systems, which model how sequences over an alphabet evolve by chance. Such systems sit at the heart of in-vivo DNA storage, where duplications, deletions, and substitutions alter sequences over time. Past work fixed the limit of k-tuple frequencies; the team now characterises fluctuations around those values. Their approach projects centred count vectors using spectral traits of the k-substitution matrix. It approximates the system by a martingale difference sequence and checks martingale conditions, yielding the limiting covariance matrix.
arxiv-2604-25645: Ghosh and Kannan study the geometric invariant theory quotient of a minimal-dimensional Schubert variety modulo a subtorus. They work with the projective special linear group and its maximal torus. Earlier work by Kannan and Sardar found the unique minimal variety admitting semistable points. The subtorus is generated by one-parameter subgroups tied to the peaks of the defining Weyl group element. Their main result identifies the quotient with the total space of an iterated projective space bundle over a projective space.
arxiv-2604-26145: Knight and four colleagues examine how language-learning feedback can fail in ways learners and teachers miss. Such failures can reinforce misconceptions over long use. Drawing on part of a benchmark for language education, they analyze failures across six dimensions of good feedback. These run from diagnostic accuracy and awareness of appropriacy to prioritization, guidance, and support for self-control. Failures that look helpful but rest on flawed explanations, which they call explainability pitfalls, risk attainment, human-AI interaction, and socioaffective harms. The language-learning context amplifies those risks.
arxiv-2604-26245: Chang compared online talk about political violence in France and the United States across three killings, from 2020 through 2026. French discussion centered on victims' civic roles, while American discussion split along partisan lines. Comparing two French cases with different victim profiles, he found support for a civic floor: French institutions sustain a shared civic baseline whatever a victim's politics.
arxiv-2604-26345: Krajczok and three colleagues showed that lp-pseudofunctions, recently used to build exotic completions of group algebras, yield well-behaved crossed product functors. The build runs through Banach algebras tied to operators on Hilbert-valued lp spaces, which at first seem to hinge on a chosen representation. The authors proved these algebras match no matter which representation is picked, so their envelopes match isometrically. For some non-amenable actions, these completions are truly exotic.
arxiv-2604-26445: Wang and five colleagues trained a neural network to guess the electron localization function of dense hydrogen from atomic geometry alone. The model skipped costly electronic-structure sums and learned from first-principles data across many pressures in dense fluid hydrogen. It matched the function's overall spread well. Leftover error came mostly from smooth long-wave parts that grow with pressure. Though trained only on fluids, it still worked on crystals, keeping key critical points and hydrogen-network links.
arxiv-2604-26545: Philipp and five colleagues modeled cyclic and calendar aging in lithium-ion batteries with silicon-graphite composite anodes. Silicon boosts capacity but swells and shrinks with lithiation, slashing lifetime, so grasping decay is key to slowing it. Their physics-based model splits basic decay paths, such as interphase growth, from silicon paths like particle cracking, crack interphase growth, and active-material loss. It also probes how check-up timing shapes observed storage decay and ties decay to use conditions for better battery use and design.
arxiv-2604-27145: Ramos and twenty colleagues measure fission-fragment patterns from plutonium-240 made by a two-proton transfer between uranium-238 and carbon-12, a stand-in for neutron-driven fission of plutonium-239. Fragments are fully identified with the VAMOS spectrometer in inverse kinematics. Prompt neutron counts run clearly lower in the surrogate reaction than in neutron-capture fission, showing that the entrance channel shapes the fission outcome in an unexpected way.
arxiv-2604-27645: Sun presents an exact rank-23 scheme for general 3-by-3 matrix multiplication using 56 additions and 23 products, 79 scalar steps in total. It tops recent 60-, 59-, and 58-addition schemes at rank 23 and works over arbitrary associative rings, even noncommutative ones. Its tensor coefficients are ternary, taking only the values minus one, zero, and one. Correctness is certified by 729 Brent equations, plus finite-field and noncommutative implementation tests.
arxiv-2604-27745: Leo van Iersel and four colleagues study tuned methods for average-tree diversity in rooted nets. Their main knob is scanwidth, a tree-likeness measure of loop-free graphs. A top-diversity taxa subset can be found in fast time at scanwidth 2 or less, but turns NP-hard at scanwidth 3 or less. They design a method finding diversity in blowup-width, straight-size time. They give a straight-time method for net-seen taxa networks in fixed-knob form for hidden joins.
arxiv-2604-28145: Kurfman and colleagues achieve strong coupling between magnon modes in a micron-scale yttrium iron garnet platelet and microwaves in a superconducting resonator. Cut from a single crystal by focused ion beam methods and placed on a constricted inductive line, the platelet shows numerous anti-crossings that survive even at extremely low input powers. Simulations and analytic calculations identify the modes, opening a path to efficient on-chip magnon experiments at reduced powers.
arxiv-2605-00045:
Dechao Li, Yutao Yao, and Jingyao Duan study how transitive a fuzzy relation is, and how to keep that property when relations are combined. Transitivity matters for fuzzy set theory, artificial intelligence, clustering, and decision making, yet real fuzzy relations often fail it. Rather than forcing a transitive closure, the authors measure the degree of transitivity a relation already has.

They investigate two measures of transitivity built from well-known fuzzy implications, and work out how the two degrees relate. They then define a relaxed notion in which a relation counts as transitive up to a small allowed error, and they characterize which aggregation functions preserve that property. The relaxed relations are used to draw inferences and to cluster objects under the permissible error.
arxiv-2605-00145:
Anne Kétri P. da Fonseca, Joelson D. V. Hermes, and Edson D. Leonel study a billiard system whose boundary mixes oval and elliptical shapes. In such systems a ball moves in straight lines and bounces off the edge, and the motion can stay orderly or turn chaotic. Adding the elliptical part adds a second way to deform the boundary.

The authors derive a formula for the critical setting where the last orderly curve breaks down, then test it with computer simulations. A stronger elliptical part lowers the threshold for full chaos. When the two deformations line up in phase, though, order can return. The result gives a clearer handle on how boundary shape controls chaos in these simple systems.
arxiv-2605-00345:
Zihan Zhou and 6 co-authors generate three-dimensional objects that come out already posed, not merely well shaped. The usual pipeline builds an object in a neutral canonical pose and rotates it afterward, which invites mismatches and ambiguity about the final orientation. Their method, Pose-Aware Diffusion, skips the canonical step entirely.

A single image's depth map is lifted into a partial point cloud and injected into the diffusion process as a three-dimensional anchor. Generation then happens directly in the space where the object was observed, under firm spatial supervision. Experiments show better geometric alignment and image-to-object match than leading rivals. The method also extends naturally to whole scenes: independently generated objects can simply be united while keeping their precise layout.
arxiv-2605-00545:
Junda Ying and 4 co-authors reconstruct how individual cells divide, die, and change fate from snapshot data, where each measurement destroys the sample. Optimal transport methods infer such dynamics at the population level, treating cell mass as a continuous fluid. That view smears out the discrete birth and death events that define lineage branching. Their framework, Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridge, keeps those jumps.

The method gives a tractable solution to a branching version of the Schrödinger bridge problem, with a microscopic picture in which each cell both diffuses and undergoes random birth-death jumps. A simulation-free training objective makes the solver scale to high-dimensional omics data. On simulated and real datasets it matched or beat deterministic baselines at trajectory reconstruction. Uniquely, it can also simulate realistic discrete birth-death dynamics cell by cell, which population-level methods cannot express.
arxiv-2605-00645:
Alireza Namazi and Heman Shakeri argue that blood glucose forecasters should be graded on the clinical jobs they serve, not on average error. Their evaluation framework for diabetes technology is built around two tasks: early warning of hypoglycemia, dangerous low blood sugar, and support for insulin dosing decisions. In safety-critical care, a model can look accurate on average while failing exactly where the risk is highest.

For early warning, they score models on real data from three clinical cohorts by detected events and false alarms per patient-day. Models with strong overall recall failed badly right after insulin boluses, when warnings matter most. For dosing, they use a regulator-accepted simulator to test whether models predict responses to changed insulin plans. Many strong forecasters failed on direction, size, and ranking of those effects, and chose poor doses. The benchmark and datasets are released as a toolkit.
arxiv-2605-00845:
Mengying Wang and five co-authors present UniQGen, a framework that uses language-model agents to generate graph queries under constraints. Knowledge graph question answering usually targets RDF and SPARQL, leaving Cypher and property graphs underexplored despite industry demand. UniQGen extracts and refines representative query clauses into executable queries that match user intent across languages, without fine-tuning for schema matching.

The method extends the classic Chase and Backchase optimization approach with dynamic reasoning over constraints and model-based quality estimates. On a Cypher-supported Freebase graph hosted on Amazon Neptune, UniQGen beats leading methods on standard benchmarks in both accuracy and efficiency. The team releases Cypher outputs and a Neptune-ready snapshot for reproducible cross-language research.
arxiv-2605-00945:
Shreyas Upadhye and one co-author study oscillons, localized lumps of energy that oscillate in time and can persist long after inflation ends. Such quasi-stable, non-topological set-ups form during preheating and decay slowly. Earlier work studied them in general relativity with the metric formalism. The authors instead modify gravity with a non-minimal coupling between the scalar field and the Ricci scalar, working in the Palatini formulation.

Using CosmoLattice simulations with a polynomial potential, they find oscillatory, decaying solutions as expected. An extended period of oscillon domination follows in the early universe. The uneven spread of the lumps also generates gravitational waves at ultra-high frequencies, in the range aimed at by planned future detectors and experiments.
arxiv-2605-01045:
Graeme J. Ackland and three co-authors describe atomic motion in caesium hydroxide monohydrate, a layered compound of water and hydroxide ions. Each oxygen joins three hydrogen bonds in a quasi-two-dimensional honeycomb lattice. Oxygen and caesium sit on a typical crystal lattice, but hydrogen behavior is more complex: covalent and hydrogen bonds continually interchange, so water and hydroxyl convert into each other by proton exchange.

The order-disorder transition proceeds by chemical reaction rather than rotation or diffusion. A hydrogen can leave the layer, and the vacancy can then move rapidly by single molecule rotation, enabling fast ionic conduction. The exchange also creates a novel Raman signature that combines stretch and exchange. The authors model it in theory.
arxiv-2605-01145:
Anish Bhat, Ryo Ide, and Zihan Zhao study when independent Gaussian models fail in one-dimensional phi-four theory on a lattice, a self-interacting field model. Practical systems break Gaussian and independence assumptions through self-interactions. The authors analyze how interaction strength and system size jointly affect the distributions of Fourier modes, which represent the field by frequency.

They find failure comes primarily from structured dependencies between modes, not from individual modes becoming strongly non-Gaussian, since single modes stay approximately Gaussian even as coupling grows with size. Three distinct regimes delineate where traditional methods remain effective and where more expressive models are needed. A computationally simple diagnostic and a concrete design criterion for future nonlinear models follow from the analysis.
arxiv-2605-01345:
Anjie Liu and eight co-authors argue that vision-language models fail fine tasks not for lack of smarts but for lack of visual bandwidth. A wide view keeps context but loses small detail, so hard questions need the model to gather the right detail first, step by step.

They cast this hunt for evidence as sequential experimental design, where each step picks the next patch to inspect. Since exact reasoning over huge images is infeasible, they use a proxy goal that trades coverage against sharpness. Their method, FOVEA, needs no training and refines the model's own crop choices through probing. On high-resolution benchmarks it beats direct answers and step-by-step agent baselines, with the largest gains on remote-sensing tasks where the target must be searched for.
arxiv-2605-01445:
Maxim Lyutikov shows that Alfvén waves, magnetic ripples that run along field lines, can tear themselves apart in the hot pair plasma around strongly magnetic stars. The setting is a plasma of electrons and their antimatter twins, threaded by an intense field.

Working in a two-fluid picture, Lyutikov sets up a round-polarized wave in its own moving frame. In that frame each charge type gyrates at its own rate, as the wave's strength shifts the drift speed. Particle simulations with the EPOCH code then show the wave near a key scale sprouting large density swings and breaking up fast. Charge separation matters early, but the lasting swings are neutral and grow big. The mix of new modes depends on how strongly the plasma is magnetized. The author ties the results to fast radio bursts born in the magnetospheres of magnetars.
arxiv-2605-01645:
Shinya Ae computes how spin current flows along a chain of quantum spins at high temperature, using a theory of ballistic fluctuations on large scales. The system is the spin-half XXZ chain in its critical regime, a standard test bed where spin transport shows anomalous, superdiffusive behavior near the isotropic point.

Ae integrates the equal-time spin correlation function to reach the spin conductivity. When a chain prepared with a very long-wavelength magnetization pattern relaxes, correlations survive at a scale set by the inverse chain length. At high temperature the ballistic channel dies, while a diffusive one persists on large scales. The conductivity falls off in inverse proportion to temperature, and its high-temperature prefactor blows up when a single quasiparticle carries unbounded magnetization. The analysis pins superdiffusion on that faint long-range correlation, clarifying the dynamic scaling at the isotropic point.
arxiv-2605-01745:
Xu Zheng and four co-authors price language data sets that platforms buy and govern as assets, when a set's true privacy or access cost is still unknown. Each round brings a task and an asset with a rough cost guess; the platform may pay to sharpen that guess before posting a price.

Their framework, NH-CROP, clips prices for robustness and gates the information purchase: verify only when the refined signal's estimated decision value beats the best no-check option. It weighs direct pricing, risk-aware pricing, and verify-then-price side by side. Across synthetic, real-proxy, and utility-grounded tests the clipped variants match or beat price-only and risk-aware rivals. Ablations surprise: in the realistic settings the strongest policies often skip verification. The gains come from calibrated pricing under uncertainty. Paid checks stay valuable only where information is cheap and changes the call.
arxiv-2605-01845:
Renato Leme, Carlos Olarte, and Elaine Pimentel work on logic systems where a statement can take more than a simple true or false value. They focus on restricted non-deterministic matrices, a tool that lets connectives return a set of possible values while ruling out unsound rows. Such matrices already give sound semantics for paraconsistent, intuitionistic, and modal logics, but no fast decision method used them.

The authors turn the semantics into problems for SMT solvers, building automatic provers that can check validity and also build countermodels when a claim fails. In tests, the provers set the best known results for paraconsistent logics. They also stay competitive on the other logic families covered in the study.
arxiv-2605-02145:
Hefei Zhao and Yun Tian derive Picard-Fuchs equations for Abelian integrals in piecewise smooth near-Hamiltonian systems. Abelian integrals appear along orbital arcs set by a polynomial energy function, and their zeros control limit cycles after perturbation. The authors obtain the inhomogeneous equations explicitly for a family of such integrals.

They also describe how to use those equations to compute, step by step, asymptotic expansions of generating functions near a homoclinic loop. As an application, they bound the maximum number of isolated zeros of Melnikov functions near a nilpotent saddle loop. That setting covers piecewise polynomial perturbations where the angle of the separation line is a free parameter. Zero counts translate into limits on cycles.
arxiv-2605-02445:
Ann-Kathrin Kollak and three co-authors report a lab study of two tiny zinc oxide nanowire lasers placed very close together. The gap between the wires was under ten nanometers, deep in the near field where light from one wire can reach the other. By moving where they shone light on the pair, the team could change how the two lasers behaved.

The pair showed full and partial frequency locking, where all or some of their light modes lined up at the same pitch. In one case the pair gave a single clean mode, though each wire alone gave many. Unlike older paired designs that used fixed filtering, the match here formed in active use. The result points to small, stable light sources for future photonic chips.
arxiv-2605-02545:
Ruiqing Zhao and seven co-authors present SAGE, a framework that teaches language models to pick a good modeling strategy before writing an optimization program. Models can already produce valid code, but a poor strategy choice leads to wrong formulations or slow solvers. SAGE makes the strategy an explicit part of both training data and training rewards.

The team builds a dataset whose formulations are checked by a solver, with several strategies per problem. A student model is then fine-tuned and further trained with a weighted reinforcement method that rewards format, correctness, and solver speed. Across eight benchmarks, average first-try success rose well above the strongest open baseline. With more tries, SAGE found more distinct correct forms and, at large scale, produced leaner constraint systems.
arxiv-2605-02645:
Faustino Maciala, Cláudia M. Araújo, and Pedro Patrício ask when tensor calculations done in a transformed, complex form can be brought back to purely real tensors. Third-order tensors under the t-product are usually handled over complex numbers, using Fourier methods that split them into slices. Many applications, though, need real-valued answers.

The authors show the deciding factor is a conjugate-pairing pattern among the Fourier slices. When that pattern holds, transform-domain constructions return real tensors after the inverse step. Applications give real versions of several standard tensor factorizations, plus an account of when generalized inverses exist and what they look like. The framework lets matrix-style constructions move to real tensors without breaking the algebraic rules of the product.
arxiv-2605-02845:
Alex B. Grilo and Marios Rozos settle the complexity of a problem about stoquastic Hamiltonians, a class of quantum systems whose off-diagonal terms have a helpful sign. The related proof class sits between two randomized extensions of NP and plays a central role in classifying how hard Hamiltonian problems are. Pinning down its power is a standing goal in quantum complexity theory.

The authors study the sparse version of the problem, where the Hamiltonian is given compactly. They show it belongs to the stoquastic proof class. Since the local version is already known hard for that class, the sparse problem is complete for it. A separable variant, where the proof splits into two unentangled parts, is shown complete for the two-proof version of the class. The results tighten the map of quantum verification.
arxiv-2605-03045:
Gideon Stein, Niklas Penzel, Tristan Piater, and Joachim Denzler build TCD-Arena, a test kit for checking how time series causal discovery methods cope when their assumptions fail. Such methods are powerful for science, but they rest on strong claims that are hard to verify in practice.

The kit is modular and lets users apply graded violations step by step. In a large demo study with about thirty million attempts, the team mapped robustness across many violations for current methods. They also test ensembles of methods and find they can improve overall robustness, a useful lead for real-world use.
arxiv-2605-03645:
James L. Borg, Irene Sciriha, and Zoia Sherman give a new proof of a striking property of threshold graphs. Threshold graphs can be described in several ways, including as graphs avoiding certain small patterns, or through a finite sequence of positive integers. Their remarkable feature is that all threshold graphs of the same order share a common integer Laplacian eigenbasis.

Having an integer eigenbasis shared across a whole family is unusual, and the property actually characterizes threshold graphs. The result was first proved by Macharete and Del Vecchio. Borg and his co-authors supply a different proof of the same theorem, offering a fresh route through the structure that may suit other arguments.
arxiv-2605-03845:
Riccardo Cescon, Andrea Martin, and Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate study distributionally robust control, where a controller must work despite incomplete knowledge of the uncertainty affecting a system. Their ambiguity sets are built with the Sinkhorn discrepancy, a regularized optimal transport measure. Unlike the Wasserstein distance, it does not force worst-case distributions to be discrete and can blend observed data with a prior reference distribution.

That makes the approach attractive when only few noise samples are available. The authors establish convexity and weak compactness of Sinkhorn ambiguity sets. They then prove the resulting linear quadratic control problem over linear policies can be solved by convex programming. That holds even with robust safety constraints added. A trajectory planning example validates the theory and shows the method in action.
arxiv-2605-03945:
Tianyu Wang, Luhao Zhang, and Rachel Cummings relax differential privacy to account for the fact that not all features in a dataset are equally sensitive. The standard notion imposes the same constraints across features. It ignores practical distinctions between sensitive and insensitive ones. Their framework, CorrDP, lets insensitive features be treated more loosely. It still accounts for their correlation with sensitive features. They measure that correlation by total variation distance. The point is simple. Privacy should be strict where it matters, and looser where it does not.

They design algorithms for empirical risk minimization under CorrDP, adding distance-dependent noise to gradients for better utility guarantees. When the correlation distance is unknown, they estimate it from the dataset. Results stay comparable. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show CorrDP-based algorithms beating the standard framework. That holds whenever insensitive features are present.
arxiv-2605-04145:
Oscar J. C. Dias, David Sola Gil, and Jorge E. Santos study gravity in a three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space coupled to a massive scalar field. They use precise spectral methods to build boson stars, which are stable lumps of the field, and black holes that carry scalar hair.

For each pattern number, the hairy black holes branch off from the known empty-space family at the point where an instability sets in. At fixed mass and spin, the hairy holes always hold more entropy, so they dominate in that comparison. The authors also identify a boson star as the true lowest-energy state when the space itself becomes unstable.
arxiv-2605-04345:
Jules Sintes, Ana Bušić, and Jiamin Zhu study delays in groups of cooperating agents that each see only part of their world. A delay can sit in sensing, so agents act on old observations, or in action, so choices take effect late, and the two are often treated as different problems.

The authors prove the two settings are fully equivalent. They allow the same policies and produce the same behaviour. They also share the same best solutions, in any mixed form too. Yet their experiments show learning dynamics differ sharply in practice, so methods tuned for one delay type may not transfer directly to the other.
arxiv-2605-04545:
Shigenaga and colleagues build better signal constellations for wireless links that cannot rely on channel knowledge. Grassmannian constellations can reach capacity over Rayleigh fading channels without coherent reception at high signal-to-noise ratios, yet constructing them efficiently stays hard. The authors work on the Bloch sphere, the unit sphere familiar from quantum computing, where they show chordal distance on the Grassmann manifold tracks Euclidean distance. That link yields a theoretical upper bound from the Fejes-Toth bound on minimum chordal distance.

Two constructions follow. S-Opt, built from sphere-packing solutions, attains the bound for the optimal packings considered, and its detector matches the standard generalized likelihood-ratio detector while scaling gently with antennas and constellation size. Z-Opt stacks regular polygons on the sphere, and its minimum distance approaches the bound across tested sizes. Both detectors keep full detection performance at far lower complexity.
arxiv-2605-04845:
Johannes Härtel investigates whether language-model agents can mine software repositories as well as simpler models given prepared context. Repository mining means sorting items such as commits, reviews, code lines, or whole projects into classes. Human labelling is costly and error-prone, and limited context often causes mistakes or unsure labels.

Across four tasks, eight setups, and nearly five thousand classifications, agents that explored repositories with standard shell commands matched simpler approaches on accuracy. Their main edge was robustness, since they fetched their own context and avoided overflow limits. Reviewing disputed cases also suggested the reference labels themselves often suffered from narrow context or unclear task rules.
arxiv-2605-04945:
Melvin Strobl and five co-authors examine quantum Fourier models at the level of hardware pulses rather than abstract circuit gates. These models are a structured form of quantum machine learning with well-defined mathematics. Pulse-level computing drives the hardware directly through microwave settings, yet little was known about how these models behave there.

The team links measures such as expressibility and Fourier coefficient correlation to the wider set of pulse parameters. Overall expressibility barely changes, but the training landscape changes deeply, they find. For composite gates, separate pulse scalings loosen rigid couplings between angles and give gradient descent more escape routes, which significantly boosts training performance in their tests.
arxiv-2605-05245:
Yilin Guo, Yinshan Wang, and Yixuan Wang present AdaGATE, a training-free controller that gathers evidence for multi-hop questions under a tight token budget. Retrieval-augmented systems often pass noisy or extra passages to the generator, and existing tools either keep adding context or pick from a fixed top set. Missing bridge facts, the links between hops, are rarely repaired directly.

AdaGATE tracks gaps around the entities in the question, issues small targeted follow-up queries, and scores the passages it found by gap coverage, support, novelty, overlap, and fit. On the HotpotQA benchmark it earned the best evidence scores among compared tools under clean, redundant, and noisy retrieval, while using far fewer input tokens than a smart rival.
arxiv-2605-05445:
Some disordered quantum systems stay localized, refusing to spread energy like normal materials. Carlo Vanoni, David M. Long, and Anushya Chandran work on a puzzle in that field: simulations of many-body localization drift toward delocalization as systems grow. The drift seems driven by resonances that multiply at middling disorder.

The authors build a statistical method that tracks how resonances at one frequency scale affect those forming at lower scales. Their flow equation matches numerics on several model systems. It also matches real-space models at intermediate disorder, a step toward explaining the stubborn finite-size drift.
arxiv-2605-05745:
Choosing the best option under uncertainty usually means tasting each arm directly. Qirun Zeng and five co-authors study a hybrid: at each round the learner may take an absolute reward from one arm, or a relative duel between two. Both feedback types follow generalized linear models, and the goal is fixed-confidence identification of the best arm.

They build a likelihood-ratio confidence sequence that unifies the two observation kinds into one ellipsoidal confidence set. Their Track-and-Stop algorithm then allocates queries by following a minimax-optimal design over arms and pairs jointly. Correctness and sample-complexity bounds accompany the method.
arxiv-2605-05845:
Finding a small hidden object with scattered waves is faster with the right focusing trick. The targets are small objects buried in a flat scene. Won-Kwang Park designs a bifocusing imaging method for bistatic setups, where source and receiver sit apart. He works out the indicator function's math through Bessel function series, material traits, and the angle between the two arms of the setup.

The theory proves sharpness fades as that angle nears 180 degrees. At exactly 180 degrees, spotting it becomes impossible. Tests back the analysis, giving practitioners a sharp map of where the method works and where it cannot.
arxiv-2605-05945:
Senthil Palanisamy and five co-authors present open tools for collecting long egocentric data with ordinary phones. Vision language action models need large first person data sets, but most current sets hold episodes of only a few minutes. That short span misses the long term links that complex robot tasks demand.

MobileEgo Anywhere lets users record hour plus sessions using modern smartphone sensors for pose tracking. The release includes a free recording app and a video pipeline that turns raw captures into training ready formats. It also includes a 200 hour data set drawn from 584 sessions. Training a model on this data lowered its error when predicting held out actions.
arxiv-2605-06145:
Alireza Modirshanechi and three co-authors unify two families of reinforcement learning theory under one idea, control maximization. Goal conditioned learning trains agents to reach commanded goals, while mutual information skill learning discovers diverse skills without a task. Why skills from the second should help the first reach goals has been a theoretical mystery, the authors say.

They identify three canonical goal conditioned formulations and prove the three are fundamentally inequivalent, inducing incompatible optimal policies in the same setting. All three still share one reading: a good policy's future path is highly sensitive to the commanded goal. Skill learning objectives measure a kindred sensitivity. The authors bound each skill objective by a matching goal sensitivity, pairing every goal formulation with a pretraining objective that suits it.
arxiv-2605-06245:
Yan Zhuang and four co-authors build an emotion recognition framework that stays reliable when input channels vary. Multimodal systems read face, voice, and text together, but those channels differ in meaning, quality, and availability from sample to sample. Mixed combinations of present and missing channels make consistent emotion judgments hard for standard fusion designs, the authors note.

Their framework works from representation consistency, with two core parts. A contrastive mechanism pulls together samples that share both emotion category and the same available modality set. A second part assigns each sample an uncertainty based weight during training, damping unreliable examples. Across three standard benchmarks the method beat existing approaches, with the largest average F1 gain, above four points, on the IEMOCAP data set.
arxiv-2605-06345:
Jie Yu and Song Qiu build an AI framework for the stage of research before a question even exists. Research agents usually automate search and writing once a clear question is supplied, but human work often starts as tacit friction, a felt misalignment that resists words. InciteResearch aims to make that implicit understanding explicit, inspectable, and actionable for the researcher who holds it, using structured Socratic questioning spread across its pipeline.

The system elicits a five dimensional researcher profile anchored in concrete friction points, even from vague inputs outside the domain. It then violates hidden assumptions under a staged causal trace and checks that the proposed method follows necessarily from the reframed insight. A new benchmark for tacit to explicit assistance tests the approach. Scores for novelty and impact rose clearly over a prompt based baseline.
arxiv-2605-06545:
M. Tomlinson and eight co-authors report making bulk 1T-NbSe2, a layered material once reachable only as a single layer. They stabilize the bulk form by inserting tin atoms between the layers with an electric current. Microscope images confirm the new 1T structure, while the inserted samples stop conducting, unlike the metallic 2H form.

Standard density functional theory predicts a metal, so the insulating behavior points to strong emergent electron correlations. Raman spectra show modes tied to the tin insertion and possible charge density wave order. The result shows this insertion route can reach bulk forms once out of reach and a platform for studying correlated states.
arxiv-2605-06845:
Nicola Bariletto and three co-authors study how fast Bayesian estimates recover the hidden mixing pattern behind mixture data. Their setting allows endless components, with unknown location and scale shared across them. Knowing that estimated densities converge is not enough; the latent mixing measure itself must also converge.

The authors prove new inequalities linking density distance to gaps between mixing measures and scale values. Those bounds depend on how smooth the mixture kernel is, and they yield first rates of their kind for several common kernels. The work also separates how location estimates and scale estimates behave, giving a finer picture of convergence.
arxiv-2605-07045:
Gilberto Diaz-Garcia, Keith Paarporn, and Jason R. Marden study how a coordinator can gain an edge in competitive contests for resources. Rather than controlling agents directly, the coordinator shapes the values those agents believe a prize holds. The setting is a Tullock contest, where players bid effort against each other.

The authors first characterize equilibrium bidding and payoffs when valuations and costs vary across players. They then derive the best reported valuations for a coordinator managing two subordinates against one opponent. That solution's structure extends to any number of subordinates, shrinking the coordinator's problem to just two variables regardless of system size.
arxiv-2605-07545:
Yuanzhi Wang and seven co-authors work on animating still human images, where hands are the hardest part to get right. Hands move in complex ways, and small errors look glaring. Preference-based fine-tuning could help, but building strict pairs of good and bad hand examples frame by frame is too costly to be practical.

Their framework, Implicit Preference Alignment, skips paired data entirely. It rewards the model for producing its own high-quality samples while keeping it close to the pretrained model, and a hand-aware step steers training toward hand regions. Tests show better hand quality with far less data preparation. The authors released their code publicly for other researchers to build on.
arxiv-2605-07645:
Elisenda Feliu and five co-authors count solutions of sparse polynomial systems whose coefficients have a special vertical dependence structure. Such systems arise at the critical points of optimization problems and, with linear forms added, at the steady states of chemical reaction networks. In fact, every polynomial system is a special case of one of these parametrized systems.

Using tropical geometry, they prove the generic number of complex solutions equals a tropical intersection number, which becomes a mixed volume in a special matroid case. For positive solutions, the number that matters in applications, they derive lower bounds from positive tropical data and simpler upper bounds when the solutions have toric structure. The resulting algorithms are implemented in Julia.
arxiv-2605-07745:
Eric Oevermann and Thomas D. Cohen compute the zero-temperature equation of state for the massive Thirring and sine-Gordon model, a classic exactly solvable quantum field theory. The work demonstrates recently derived model-independent upper and lower bounds. Those bounds cover systems carrying both a fixed particle density and a non-zero current density. That is a regime where Monte Carlo methods offer a way around the sign problem.

Because this model can be solved with the Bethe ansatz at both densities, it is an ideal test case. The optimal bounds confine the energy density within a factor of two at high density for all coupling choices. The lower bound becomes exact at low density, while the upper bound loosens there.
arxiv-2605-08145:
Yuriel Ryan, Hei Man Ip, Adriel Kuek, Paul Pu Liang, and coauthors argue that vision-language models fail on unclear images partly because training data strips out redundancy. When image and text repeat the same information, a damaged channel can be repaired from the other one. Modern instruction sets remove that overlap to force visual grounding.

The authors sort cross-modal information into redundant, unique, and synergistic parts, then build a self-captioning workflow with a gate that converts unique information into redundant form. Their findings suggest that raising redundancy cuts errors caused by corrupted vision, offering a data-side route to more robust multimodal models.
arxiv-2605-08245:
Harshvardhan Saini, Samyak Jha, Yiming Tang, and Dianbo Liu trace vision-language model hallucinations to a geometric cause. Decoder-based models must align visual embeddings with the text space for attention to work. The authors argue the alignment overshoots. Visual features are pulled so far onto the language manifold that language bias drowns fine visual detail.

The study gives the first measured account of this over-alignment. It shows the language bias sits in the top principal components of the representation. Rather than costly black-box decoding fixes, the authors pursue geometric debiasing at the source. The direction has direct stakes for medical imaging and autonomous systems.
arxiv-2605-08345:
Mathilde Gaillard and Ulysse Herbach study the long-run behavior of stochastic gene expression models with transcriptional bursting. Genes switch and fire in bursts. Two piecewise-deterministic Markov processes are standard models for the protein dynamics that follow. The networks can hold any number of interacting genes.

Under mild conditions on the jump rate, the authors prove a unique stationary distribution exists. It exists for any count of genes and any strength of interaction. Coupling methods then give explicit upper bounds on the speed of convergence. The bounds are stated in Wasserstein distance. Such results tell modelers how long a simulated cell must run before its statistics can be trusted.
arxiv-2605-08445:
Prasanna Desikan, Harshit Rajgarhia, Shivali Dalmia, and Ananya Mantravadi argue that healthcare AI is graded on the wrong exams. Models now work inside live clinical workflows. Most benchmarks measure stored knowledge instead. Frontier systems nearly ace licensing tests. Their reliability, safety, and clinical fit under real conditions go unmeasured.

The authors survey benchmarks for generative, multimodal, and agentic medical AI. The benchmarks grew through ad hoc dataset building aimed at narrow tasks. The authors call for structured sets of tasks, data, and metrics. They should be designed around dependability in messy practice. The study maps what a serious measurement program for clinical AI should cover.
arxiv-2605-08545:
Peter Kirgis and eleven coauthors argue that judging AI agents by final pass or fail scores alone is not credible. Scores can hide shortcuts, test flaws, poor real world fit, and even dangerous actions taken along the way. Their remedy is log analysis: careful study of inputs, steps, and outputs during each agent run.

A taxonomy sorts the threats that logs can expose, and guiding rules show how to study them well. On one airline service test, log review found success had been understated by nearly half and revealed failure modes that scores missed. Benchmark makers and deployers gain a practical case for reading the record, not just the result.
arxiv-2605-08745:
Pritam Roy and three coauthors swap a task to expose a quantum edge in a deep test. The test asks if hidden states can explain prep in quantum tasks. With parity hid, the old task of fetch back showed no quantum edge. The flat result was a puzzle. Their new task asks for shut out, not fetch back.

For the first small case, the best quantum score breaks the plain bound. At larger prime symbol sizes, the gap grows in a clean way. The best score also pins down size in a sharp way. Checks on noise show labs today can run it. The shut out task gives quantum work a sharper probe.
arxiv-2605-08845:
Toma-Stefan Cezar, Marios Maroudas, and Dieter Horns build a data acquisition platform that never misses a sample during high speed physics experiments. Their modular, software defined system pairs fast digitizer boards with consumer graphics cards, running transforms and statistical averaging in real time. Continuous processing holds at sampling rates up to five hundred million samples per second, moving about a gigabyte per second.

End to end phase tests bound fractional data loss below one part in a trillion, and one run lasted a full month uninterrupted. Deployed on a dark matter experiment, real time spectral averaging slashes storage needs. The platform offers labs a flexible, cheaper alternative to traditional fixed hardware pipelines.
arxiv-2605-09245:
Xian and five colleagues track objects across several cameras without calibration or manual labelling, a hard problem when identities must stay consistent across viewpoints. Multi camera tracking struggles when calibration must be precise and annotations extensive, and appearance shifts across views break identity association. Their framework, CalibFree, learns representations by separating view agnostic features from view specific ones, through distillation in one view and reconstruction across views.

That separation lets the method adapt to complex, dynamic scenes with minimal overhead and no calibration or labels. On the MMP-MvMHAT data set, CalibFree improves overall accuracy by 3 percent and average F1 score by 7 point 5 percent over leading approaches. On the more diverse MvMHAT set, it tracks well over time and performs strongly across views and varied camera configurations. The work confirms a calibration free design can handle wide camera variation, including changing camera counts and placements.
arxiv-2605-09345:
Li and a colleague spot a Selection Plateau in one-shot pruning: diverse importance criteria land at similar scores. Rank-monotone scorers on weight magnitude all pick the same channels and settle on a sparsity-dependent plateau, no matter the form.

To explain this, the team puts forward the Sparsity-Information-Complexity Spectrum hypothesis. A sparsity-dependent minimum feature complexity exists; scorers need features at least that complex to escape. Tests use ViT-Small on CIFAR-10 alone, nine feature classes at four sparsity levels. Three regimes appear. At low sparsity the plateau is optimal, with non-monotone features matching or hurting results. At critical sparsity, smooth non-monotone features aligned with the rank threshold give a 6 point 6 percent escape. At extreme sparsity, only high-frequency wiggle features escape. SICS explains the shared plateau, predicts when feature work beats baseline ranking, and suggests selectors adapt complexity to sparsity.
arxiv-2605-09545:
Wu builds diagnostic certificates for data quality in Koopman identification, a method that lifts nonlinear dynamics into linear form for prediction and control. Classical excitation tests ask whether an input signal is rich enough. But in extended dynamic mode decomposition with control, data quality depends on lifted state features joined to control inputs. Rich inputs can still visit a narrow state region, and wide state samples can still yield degenerate lifted features. Either failure can wreck the final regression.

His certificates separate three layers: state spread and grouping, lifted feature soundness, and the regression spectrum. Only the last layer carries direct theory, controlling the smallest singular value with finite sample bounds. Examples and a Schur complement condition show the layers cannot stand in for each other. Tests on Duffing, Van der Pol, and Lorenz systems confirm the layers separate in practice, guiding data collection rather than promising universal optimality.
arxiv-2605-10045:
Yan and six colleagues fix a resolution problem in visual autoregressive models, image generators that build pictures coarse-to-fine, scale by scale. These models train at one fixed size, so asking for larger images directly breaks them. Copying training-free tricks from language or diffusion models gives three failures: repeated patterns globally, repeated patterns locally, and lost detail.

The authors trace all three to one cause, a band-stage mismatch: each generation stage runs on its own dominant RoPE frequency band, and failures strike when a stage's band is disturbed. Their Stage-Aware RoPE Remapping gives each band a stage-specific rule, suppressing all three failures at once. A second trick, Entropy-Driven Adaptive Attention Calibration, measures how attention spreads at higher resolution and rescales it per head, beating prior extrapolation methods on structure and detail.
arxiv-2605-10145:
Ali and two co-authors propose a generative-AI-boosted digital twin system for proactive interference management in very large antenna arrays. Next-gen indoor networks use ultra-dense setups with hybrid near-field and far-field propagation, where blockage can wreck a link without warning. Their framework builds a high-detail, site-matched virtual replica of the indoor space that maps where and why blockage occurs in true 3D.

A gen-AI module then anticipates blockage and suppresses it proactively, rather than reacting after disruption. Simulations based on Sionna ray-tracing data sets show clear gains in interference suppression and signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio, plus lower outage probability over conventional reactive schemes and purely deterministic digital-twin approaches. The work targets dynamic indoor scenarios where ultra-dense networks must deliver extreme data rates and sub-millisecond latency.
arxiv-2605-10845:
Qi Yang and four colleagues introduce BabelDOC, a 2026 framework for translating PDF documents while keeping their original layout intact. Existing tools either strip layout when they translate text or extract text without a way to rebuild the page faithfully, leaving formulas, tables, and glossaries adrift.

BabelDOC splits layout metadata from meaning into an intermediate representation, so translation can handle terms, cross-page context, and glossaries before an adaptive typesetting engine re-anchors the result to the original page. On a two-hundred-page benchmark, human and automated judges rated it ahead of rivals on layout fidelity, looks, and term consistency. Teams translating rich documents get an open toolkit that preserves the page, not just the words.
arxiv-2605-10945:
A.V. Nikulov argues that the Meissner effect, the expulsion of magnetic flux from a bulk superconductor, needs no radial charge flow. An alternative theory claims the persistent surface current arises from the Lorentz force on such a flow, and its author insists the flow is required.

Nikulov counters that the current follows from quantization of Cooper-pair angular momentum, a fact established by experiment, not merely by conventional theory. Since the Lorentz-force story cannot explain that experimental fact, the radial flow is an unnecessary extra. Superconductivity researchers get a pointed defense of the standard account against a long-running alternative.
arxiv-2605-11045:
Paheli Bhattacharya, Manojit Chakraborty, Santhosh Kumar Arumugam, and Rishabh Gupta present ReXCL, a tool that automates two chores in requirements work: pulling structure from raw docs and sorting what they ask for. Raw docs arrive half-structured, and turning them into managed, sorted items usually eats much manual effort.

ReXCL's first module parses docs into a fixed schema with rules of thumb and predictive models, while its second module labels items through adaptive fine-tuning of encoder models. Output exports to outside requirements tools, and tests show gains in both speed and correctness. Software teams get a practical route to tidy requirements without hand-processing every doc.
arxiv-2605-11145:
Md Aminul Islam, Ahmed Sayeed Faruk, Sourav Medya, and Elena Zheleva debias message passing in graph-neural-network recommenders to fight popularity bias. Recommenders pass user-item signals over interaction graphs, but skewed distributions and repeated high-order message combining boost popular items while burying long-tail ones.

Existing re-weighting, penalty, causal, and post-processing debiasing falls short in graph settings because it never counters bias inside message combining. Recent in-combining weightings lean on static rules of thumb or unstable vectors. Their DPAA framework weaves adaptive interaction weights that respect encodings, plus layer-wise weights, straight into message passing. Weights come from a representation-based popularity signal steadied by a smooth shift from pretrained to shifting vectors. Recommender teams get debiasing that acts where bias actually spreads.
arxiv-2605-11545: Guruswami, Ren and Tang prove strong inapproximability for a promise rank problem. Given a subspace of n by n matrices promised to contain a rank-1 matrix, they show finding a matrix of rank n to a small power is hard. This assumes NP lacks sub-exponential algorithms. Even the exact version's hardness drove recent PCP-free hardness results for minimum distance and shortest vector. The proof combines superposition soundness from Khot and Saket with moment matrices. A second moment-matrix construction runs slower but works for any finite field.
arxiv-2605-11645: Yang and seven colleagues present GeomHerd, forward-looking herding quantification via Ricci flow geometry. Herding, where agents align and act collectively, drives market fragility, but price statistics lag because they detect coordination only after it moves returns. GeomHerd quantifies coordination directly on upstream agent-interaction graphs from an LLM-driven multi-agent simulator, tracking discrete Ollivier-Ricci curvature. A mean-field bridge links the graph metric to CSAD, the classical herding statistic. On a continuous-spin testbed the main detector fires a median 272 steps before order-parameter onset.
arxiv-2605-11845: Davide Baldelli and four colleagues ask whether language models can be trained to sample from a target spread rather than merely imitate text. They fine-tune models on mock prompts that ask for samples from math spreads. Two methods are compared: soft targets derived from a trie, and hard targets from drawn samples. Across 12 models, both methods greatly raised sampling match on unseen spreads and carried over to open-ended writing, though math thinking sometimes dipped.
arxiv-2605-12045: N. Rajeesh Kumar and ten colleagues study magnets in Na5Yb(MoO4)4, a stretched diamond lattice solid. Neutron scans at 3.3 kelvin confirm a four-sided structure with Yb ions 6.33 angstroms apart, while magnetic response and heat tests show no long-range order down to 60 mK. Low-heat traits follow a spin-1/2 Kramers doublet, and math shows exchange links are tiny. Muon tests reveal lasting spin motion, marking the compound as a rare dipolar quantum magnet.
arxiv-2605-12345: Lorandi and Belz explore how to steer text generation by combining small fine-tuned modules instead of retraining for every new mix of traits. They compare training on combined data sets, adding module weights at inference, and adding module outputs at inference, using QLoRA modules on three language models. Summing outputs proves strongest, matching or beating the alternatives on sentiment, topic and multi-attribute control. Even against single-task specialists on their own tasks, three-module output composition gains about two points on average.
arxiv-2605-12445: Beysel, Bartel and Joseph bring vector-length-agnostic code generation to machine-learning compilation. Scalable vector sets like Arm SVE let one program adapt to many vector lengths, yet they break the usual habit of fixing tiling and layout at compile time. Their approach adds vector-length-aware packed layouts and compiler extensions inside MLIR and IREE, extending tiling, fusion and vectorisation to scalable lengths. On Arm CPUs it matches or beats NEON-based code, reaching up to about one and a half times the speed.
arxiv-2605-12545: Dong and three colleagues recast aesthetic image cropping as a reasoning task, not a saliency hunt. Older methods lean on saliency maps or similar past cases, and both miss the composition trade-offs that human experts weigh in complex scenes. Their CROP method directs a vision-language model to think like a professional photographer, breaking a scene down by composition and taste before choosing a crop. The goal is crops that match expert choices, with reasons the model can articulate rather than blind retrieval.
arxiv-2605-12645: Amirizaniani and three colleagues train language models for personalised question answering grounded in user intent. Intent means the implicit why behind a query, beyond its explicit wording, yet existing personalisation leans on multi-turn context or rich user profiles and never models intent explicitly during reasoning. That limits single-turn settings, where a latent goal is guessed from minimal input. Their IAP framework uses reinforcement learning to infer implicit intent from one question and weave it into thinking steps with a tag-based schema, producing intent-grounded personalised answers.
arxiv-2605-12745: Callaghan, Simmons and Admoni give agents a second-order theory of mind for handling what people wrongly think agents know. Gaps between an agent's actual knowledge and a person's beliefs about that knowledge can hinder interaction. Using an interactive partially observable Markov decision process framework, the agent models how a person's erroneous beliefs evolve and the cognitive biases and heuristics behind them. It can then detect when such biases are at play and generate feedback that accounts for them, improving teacher informativeness in an in-person study.
arxiv-2605-13045: Guan and eight co-authors build TempoMed-Bench, the first benchmark for temporal awareness of medical knowledge in language models. Medical knowledge evolves as evidence emerges and treatments gain approval, yet most tests ignore time. Models' up-to-date accuracy declines gradually over time rather than dropping sharply at a cutoff, and historical accuracy runs only 25% to 54% of current accuracy. Models also flip inconsistently across neighbouring years, and agentic search tools fail to fix the problem.
arxiv-2605-13145: Barnea, Schlisselberg and Mansour study collaboration in multi-agent Bayesian bandits, where strategic agents solve the same bandit instance together. Sharing information speeds learning, but strategic agents may free-ride and dodge exploration. Unlike prior work on short-lived agents with one decision each, their setting uses persistent agents across many periods, with information sharing as the only incentive and no monetary transfers. Their CAOS mechanism sustains collaboration as a Nash equilibrium with strong regret guarantees, performing close to fully cooperative systems despite strategic behaviour.
arxiv-2605-13445: Toon De Prins and twelve colleagues image inner rims of dusty discs around eight post-AGB binaries, using VLTI/PIONIER interferometry. Post-AGB stars have shed outer layers, and their circumbinary discs may hold substructures from the binary or hidden companions. The team built a workflow joining SPARCO with the ORGANIC algorithm. The dusty rim is well resolved for all targets, yet only one image is fully explained by tilt alone. Four targets show robust brightness bumps that may signal binary responses or vortices from fluid instabilities.
arxiv-2605-13645: Duaa Abdullah extends the theory of quantum fractional revival on unitary Cayley graphs. She studies revival under the Laplacian Hamiltonian as well as the adjacency model. For graphs of order twice an odd prime, she derives the minimum revival time 2 pi over p with exact amplitudes. She fully maps strongly cospectral vertex pairs through the arithmetic of Z_n, showing that trait equals antipodality when n is twice a prime. She also finds the von Neumann entanglement entropy from revival, showing it depends only on the revival amplitudes.
arxiv-2605-13845: Thomas Flinkow and three colleagues propose Quantitative Linear Logic, a novel logic easing the tension between logic traits of links and number worries for meaning in smooth logics. Their design is driven by fit: since logic limits turn to losses, connective meaning should be apt moves used in machine learning work. Test-time scores under attacks track well with actual checking of logic limits by off-the-shelf neural network checkers.
arxiv-2605-14045: Dong and eight co-authors offer PVRF, one system to strip many kinds of bad weather from real photos. Mixed and unseen weather damage plus distortion-led training often leave over-smooth results. PVRF first gauges soft weather odds and low-level traits with a question-answering module built on frozen vision-language models. Those gauges steer restoration nets through attribute-modulated normalization and weather-weighted adapters, forming an anchor estimate. A velocity-constrained rectified flow then refines that anchor.
arxiv-2605-14245: The CMS Collaboration studies possible anomalous Higgs boson couplings to vector bosons and fermions using Higgs candidates decaying to photons. The study uses proton-proton data at 13 TeV from CMS. Events with Higgs candidates from gluon fusion, electroweak fusion, and associated production are sorted with matrix element methods and multivariate discriminants. CP properties of Higgs-gluon couplings through heavy-particle loops, and the tensor structure of two-boson interactions, are studied. Results match standard model expectations for fractional anomalous-coupling shares of production.
arxiv-2605-14745: Aouina, Tancogne-Dejean and Botti separate functional-driven from density-driven errors in density functional approximations for solids. Quantum Monte Carlo densities for silicon, sodium chloride and copper serve as reference. Functional errors usually dominate, but density-driven errors win by factors of two to three in notable cases. Error cancellation is reported in sixty-three percent of functionals for silicon but only eighteen percent for copper, and 1990s GGA functionals beat many modern meta-GGAs.
arxiv-2605-14945: Stanislav Kim, Anton Pyrkin, and Oleg Borisov address quadcopter motion control using output feedback, steering from measured outputs rather than full state knowledge. A geometric transform puts the quadcopter model into normal form with a time-varying gain, which double integration of the control input then steadies. The team synthesizes a robust control law from an extended observer. The result is a feedback design that holds the quadcopter's motion on course despite model uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-15345: Roy Ricaldi and five others trace topical shifts across the dark-web cybercrime ecosystem over six years, reading 25,065 sites and over 11.4 million HTML snapshots. A longitudinal topic framework mixing domain embeddings, density clustering, and temporal pooling finds 55 topic clusters. About 75 percent of talk volume sits in a few persistent core topics, while short-lived themes make up roughly 3 percent. The median topic life of 75 months signals gradual evolution, not abrupt swap.
arxiv-2605-15445: Ruobing Zuo, Hanrui Zhao, Gaolei He, Zhengfeng Yang, and Jianlin Wang link model guesses to machine-checked proofs. The task is proving polynomial inequalities, where pure symbol methods scale poorly. A model first floats a rough sum-of-squares split. Symbol tools then hone it to an exact proof form. Lean then certifies the proof. Tests on hard cases with up to ten variables show the joint neuro-symbolic route scales where pure symbol tools stall.
arxiv-2605-15745: Caragiannis, Kollias, Roghani, Schild and Sinop formalize where idle robotaxis should wait when rider demand is random. They model the expected distance of the perfect matching between k vehicles and k riders over a finite metric space. Sampling positions from demand gives a randomized 2-approximation, and a reduction from maximum coverage sets an inapproximability bound. For tree metrics, a dynamic programming method computes placements exactly. Tests on real ride-hailing data show a variance-reduced random strategy nearly matches costly exact methods.
arxiv-2605-16045: Dai and six colleagues propose RecMem, a memory system for long-running language-model agents. Existing systems call the model for every interaction, which burns many tokens. RecMem parks exchanges in a light layer indexed by embeddings and summons the model only when similar interactions recur. In tests it cut memory-building token costs by up to eighty-seven percent while beating rival accuracy.
arxiv-2605-16245: Tsirtsis and four colleagues show that AI-mediated communication can steer collective opinion, not just individual views. Language models instructed to edit texts on contested topics introduce directional biases, for instance nudging texts toward gun control and against atheism.
