Their tool, ROSLaunchVisual, runs inside the WebGME design space. It draws nodes, publishers, subscribers, and settings as linked blocks that users can drag and edit. Files flow in and out with no loss, and checks driven by a metamodel catch faults early. Extra plugins refresh libraries, hunt meaning errors, and manage remaps. In tests, the import and export of thirty-six launch files ran with no changes to the files. The authors say the visual route cuts errors and speeds group work on big robot builds.
arxiv-2606-09945:
Lee examines whether a quiet local region can sit inside an expanding universe with a changing clock rate, in a 2026 arXiv paper on cosmology. The setting is generalized cosmological time, which modifies the lapse function, the factor converting coordinate time into clock time, in the standard expanding-universe model. Any such change must leave local gravity and laboratory physics untouched. Other theories usually hide extra effects with screening.

Lee embeds a static Schwarzschild interior, the spacetime around a non-rotating mass, inside the expanding exterior and applies the Israel junction conditions, the rules for joining two spacetime regions smoothly. With no thin shell at the boundary, continuity of the extrinsic curvature forces a Friedmann-type relation that matches the background equations exactly. The result is a consistency condition, not new dynamics: local clocks can stay fixed while cosmic time runs differently, and standard local physics survives.
arxiv-2606-10145:
Karmakar and his team build an exact theory for swimming particles in sticky, elastic fluids, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistical physics. Active swimmers, from bacteria to synthetic microswimmers, often move through viscoelastic media whose relaxation is slow and complex. Memory effects, where past motion shapes present forces, make the process non-Markovian and little studied for active matter.

The team solves coupled generalized Langevin equations for translational and rotational motion in a medium whose memory follows a power law. The memory produces novel effects: broken-power short-time transport, enhanced long-time persistence, and a de-correlation between the force at each moment and the swimmer's heading. The memory kernel controls the odd scaling exponents, while the drive sets the crossover between sub-diffusive, ballistic, and diffusive regimes. The theory gives theorists a handle on living and lab-made swimmers in polymer-rich settings, where the surrounding medium remembers.
arxiv-2606-10445:
Lee and colleagues present SpenseGPT, a pruning method that speeds up large language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pruning removes unneeded weights so a trained model runs faster, and modern graphics chips exploit 2:4 sparsity, a pattern where two of every four weights are zero. That strict half-empty rule often damages accuracy. The Spense format instead splits each weight matrix into a sparse part following the pattern and a smaller dense part kept in full.

Choosing the dense regions well turns out to matter, and the authors devise two selection strategies, one using a small calibration dataset to judge importance. On Qwen3-32B and Seed-OSS-36B, the method reaches up to 1.2 times faster end-to-end text generation on B200 chips at FP8 precision while preserving answer quality. The authors call this the first one-shot pruning demonstration of real decoding speedups on current hardware.
arxiv-2606-10745:
Rubinstein and Wolansky upgrade an optics principle for light fields in this 2026 arXiv paper on mathematical physics. Fermat's principle of least time traces one ray between two points, but one ray is not measurable. The authors derive a weighted least action principle for the geometric optics limit of Maxwell's equations, where the data are wave intensities measured on two planes. Instead of one ray, it returns the Fresnel ray bundle connecting two intensity patterns, via a Monge transport problem whose cost comes from the medium's Hamiltonian structure.

The anisotropic case is new: media carry two ray systems, not one. Using reciprocity between Fresnel rays and phase normals, the theory recovers a wave's phase from intensity measurements. Cost functions are computed for several cases, and the machinery covers anisotropic elastic waves too. It is a satisfying arc: Monge's transport problem, once mis-tied to optics, returns as the right language.
arxiv-2606-11045:
Bertran, Roth, and Wu ask in a 2026 arXiv paper why reused machine learning benchmarks so rarely overfit, why scores keep predicting real skill instead of rewarding test-tuned tricks. Their hypothesis is compression: winning strategies can be described in very few words. They test it with language model research agents searching for strong models on a validation set.

Two bottlenecks make the test sharp. In output compression, a fresh reproducer agent gets only a short prompt, just 32 to 64 tokens in the main runs, plus training data, and must rebuild the explorer's performance. In input compression, the explorer hears only one bit per try, whether the new model beat the best so far. Across eight datasets spanning tables, vision, language, diffusion, and reward modeling, both bottlenecks cost little performance. When agents were deliberately pushed to overfit the validation set, the gains failed to survive compression, supporting the description-length account.
arxiv-2606-11245:
Park argues in a 2026 arXiv position paper that explicit memory is the cornerstone for artificial general intelligence. Large language models display remarkable skills, yet they hallucinate, plan poorly over long horizons, and reason unreliably. Park's diagnosis is memory: their learning mechanism parallels human implicit memory, the statistical know-how absorbed from experience, while the higher functions AGI needs rest on a different system.

Long-term strategic planning, metacognition, thinking about one's own thinking, and symbolic reasoning all rely on hippocampal explicit memory, the brain system storing facts and episodes for recall. Those functions, Park argues, cannot arise from implicit statistical learning alone. Drawing on neuroscience, the paper pairs this perspective with design requirements for artificial explicit memory systems: what such a memory must store, retrieve, and update. The goal is to spur work on adding explicit memory to model designs, rather than expecting scale alone to deliver it.
arxiv-2606-11345:
Isobe and twenty-six co-authors present new galaxy metallicity measurements in a 2026 arXiv paper, from the JADES survey. They derive gas-phase metallicities for star-forming galaxies at redshifts one to ten, using deep JWST NIRSpec spectra. Stacking about 1,500 spectra yields detections of the faint auroral oxygen line at very low metallicity. That lets them build strong-line calibrations.

From the calibrations they obtain mass-metallicity relations at redshifts one to ten. Metallicities decrease from today to redshift four to ten, with no slope change. At fixed metallicity, their stacks show lower excitation than calibrations from individual auroral-line emitters. Requiring auroral detections in single spectra biases samples toward higher excitation. They identify fifty extremely metal-poor galaxy candidates, at one to four percent of solar metallicity. Their scatter is large, and the lowest-metallicity ones show lower star formation rates, opposite the local fundamental metallicity relation.
arxiv-2606-11445:
Levy, Goldberg, and Stickland propose forecasting AI behavior as a learned task in a 2026 arXiv paper. Trust in AI usually rests on explanations used to forecast behavior. For large reasoning models this route is hard: token-level explanations do not generalize to long trajectories, which are often unfaithful. Their Behavior Forecasters bypass explanation entirely.

A forecaster reads one reasoning trajectory and makes explanation-style forecasts. Training data comes from querying the model itself, with no human annotation; inference takes one forward pass. They instantiate the idea on two tasks: how likely the model is to repeat its answer on re-runs, and how removing input parts changes its answer. Across three reasoning datasets, trained forecasters beat GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 reading the same trajectories as naive readers, at a fraction of the cost. Fine-tuning the backbone end-to-end and initializing it from the target model are each necessary.
arxiv-2606-11545:
Guzmán, Castellanos, and Mastache map equilibrium halos of self-gravitating Bose-Einstein condensates in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such condensates, with repulsive self-interactions, are a dark matter candidate. They solve the stationary Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson system keeping boson mass, scattering length, and total particle number explicit, treating particle number as a control parameter.

The solutions classify into ground-state, excited-state, and unbound branches by binding and nodal structure. The ground-state branch occupies a clear region of the mass-number plane, its location sensitive to the self-interaction strength. They derive scaling relations linking the halo's characteristic radius to boson mass, scattering length, and particle number, recovering the known mass-radius relation without them. Ground-state ones reproduce dwarf galaxy rotation curves using only the solitonic component. But stronger self-interactions, while shifting solutions toward boson masses allowed by Lyman-alpha forest constraints, spoil that kinematic match.
arxiv-2606-11645:
Jialin Liu and five colleagues recognise micro-gestures in video in this 2026 arXiv paper. Micro-gestures are brief, spontaneous movements, such as scratching the head or touching the nose, that can betray stress or hidden emotion. The online task requires finding each gesture in untrimmed video and reporting its start, end and category as the video plays.

Their system, DyFADet+, watches two streams at once: ordinary colour video and skeleton data, the moving positions of body joints. Both are converted into shared multi-scale time features. A gated residual module then injects skeleton motion into the colour features only where it helps, instead of simply joining the streams, which can add noise from bad pose estimates. On the SMG dataset the method reaches an F1 score, a combined measure of detection quality, of about forty-one. That placed second in the challenge track and beat the previous year's winning entry.
arxiv-2606-11945:
Simon Lupart and Kidist Amde Mekonnen report a conversational search system in this 2026 arXiv paper, the University of Amsterdam's entry to SemEval-2026 Task 8. The task tests multi-turn retrieval and question answering across finance, cloud documentation, government and Wikipedia collections. Some queries are unanswerable from the collection, and systems must recognise that.

Their pipeline combines learned sparse retrieval, which matches on weighted terms rather than dense vectors, with large language model stages. The model rewrites queries using the full conversation history, reranks candidates both pointwise and listwise, then generates the final answer, each step conditioned on the whole dialogue. Sparse retrieval is the backbone because it generalises well across domains. Analysis shows retrieval quality correlates with answer quality, while faithfulness behaves more independently. The submitted system stayed largely faithful even on hard cases, rarely inventing unsupported information, though it did not always admit when knowledge was missing.
arxiv-2606-12145:
Carter and co-authors study how a focused helium-ion beam rewrites a high-temperature superconductor, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The material is YBCO, a copper-oxide compound that superconducts, meaning it carries current with no resistance, at unusually warm temperatures. A beam of helium ions at thirty kiloelectronvolts drills defects into thin YBCO films, swelling the crystal lattice and lowering the temperature where superconductivity starts. Such patterned damage is used to build nanoscale superconducting devices.

The team varies the ion dose from ten to one hundred ions per square nanometer and the patch width from thirty to five thousand nanometers. Using electrical resistance tests, nanofocused X-ray diffraction, and atomic force microscopy, they track structure and current flow together. Surprisingly, both lattice constants grow as dose rises, unlike earlier broad-beam results. The dose where crystal order suddenly collapses also grows with patch length, a clear size effect.
arxiv-2606-12245:
Zhang and co-authors use diffusion generation to recommend new items without hurting old favorites, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recommenders rank items from user histories, so items with no interactions, cold items, start invisible. Fixes that mine content run into a seesaw dilemma: helping cold items degrades warm ones, and the reverse. The cause is geometric. Warm items live on a behavioral manifold shaped by clicks; cold items sit on a semantic manifold built from content alone, and mappings warp one into the other.

DiffCold learns to rebuild warm embeddings from content through conditional diffusion, a denoising process preserving manifold shape. A retrieval aggregator seeds generation from similar warm items instead of noise. A simulation-based alignment module keeps generated and real embeddings matched through contrastive training. On benchmarks, DiffCold beats other methods for cold and warm items. The seesaw, the authors conclude, was a mapping artifact, not a law.
arxiv-2606-12645:
Gandhi and Partida compute the algebraic cobordism rings of varieties built from matroids, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A matroid is a combinatorial structure that captures the pattern of independent sets in a collection of vectors. Algebraic cobordism is the universal theory for measuring cycles on a geometric space, refining both the Chow ring, built from subvarieties, and K-theory, built from vector bundles.

The authors give 2 combinatorial presentations for the cobordism ring of the toric variety of the Bergman fan of any loopless matroid, with generators indexed by the matroid's flats. A striking consequence is an isomorphism identifying that ring with the matroid's Chow ring tensored with the cobordism ring of a point, which generalises a known exceptional isomorphism between Chow and K-rings. For a hyperplane arrangement, they prove the wonderful variety and the matroid toric variety share the same cobordism ring.
arxiv-2606-12745:
Dai and colleagues prove a lower bound for the fundamental gap of compact horoconvex domains in hyperbolic space, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The fundamental gap is the difference between the first 2 Dirichlet eigenvalues of a domain, measuring the separation between the ground state and the first excited state of a confined quantum particle. For convex Euclidean domains the gap behaviour is classical, but negatively curved hyperbolic geometry requires different methods.

The authors study domains that are horoconvex, a convexity notion adapted to hyperbolic space of curvature minus 1, and focus on the large-diameter regime. The geometric part of the proof reduces large horoconvex domains to a fixed-width radial-height problem in all dimensions. The resulting lower bound decays like the diameter to the power minus 3, exactly matching the known large-diameter upper bound of Nguyen, Stancu, and Wei. So the D to the minus 3 scale is sharp.
arxiv-2606-13145:
Huang and colleagues present Helmsman, a low-cost, high-performance clustering-based approximate nearest neighbour search system deployed at RedNote, in this 2026 arXiv paper. RedNote's search, recommendation, and advertising services rely on approximate nearest neighbour search over hundreds of billions of embedding vectors. Meeting strict latency agreements previously required in-memory graph-based indexes, whose memory footprint created capital and operating costs as users and content grew.

Helmsman instead builds clustering-based search on all-flash servers, combining 3 components. The first is an ANNS-oriented userspace storage stack that removes kernel input-output overheads. The second is a levelling-learned pruning module that replaces the fixed pruning strategy. The third is GPU-accelerated index construction pipelines. It saves over 90 percent of hardware costs and enables billion-scale index builds within hours. In production, 40 machines now host search workloads that previously required about 35,000 processor cores and 0.35 petabytes of DRAM.
arxiv-2606-13245:
Yuan and Renganathan introduce REMAL in this 2026 arXiv paper, a method for analysing coupled systems more cheaply. Aircraft designs join fields such as structures and aerodynamics, whose outputs must agree with each other. Finding that agreement, called an equilibrium state, requires repeated rounds of simulation at every design point. REMAL learns a fast stand-in model of the residual manifold. The residual measures how far the fields are from agreeing, and the manifold is the surface where that mismatch varies.

The stand-in uses multitask Gaussian process models, statistical models that report their uncertainty. An active learning rule requests exact runs near the uncertain boundary where the residual crosses zero. Once trained, the stand-in recovers equilibrium states for fresh designs by solving an optimisation problem. The target is outer-loop tasks like design tuning and uncertainty studies, where skipping repeated full simulations saves time.
arxiv-2606-13445:
Rameshan and Messmer design a cryptographic programming interface around user intent in this 2026 arXiv paper. Organisations moving to post-quantum cryptography must swap algorithms across many programs. Most current interfaces are built around named algorithms: code names the exact scheme, policy-based choice is barely supported, and migrating existing keys to new schemes has no straightforward path. A companion assessment framework by the same authors identifies these barriers and frames the transition as a software engineering problem. This paper answers with design principles for an agile design.

The principles derive from five traits: abstraction, stability, temporal flexibility, separation, and extensibility. An intent-based design lets callers state what cover they need while the library chooses and later replaces schemes under policy. Keys must be migratable rather than stranded with obsolete schemes. The authors show how they follow from the traits and guide concrete choices.
arxiv-2606-14045:
Vijaykumar and Essick build a fast way to estimate what gravitational-wave searches would miss. Searches match signals against a bank of templates, but real signals may carry effects the bank omits: spin, eccentric orbits, or deviations from general relativity. The usual check, injecting about a million simulated signals, is slow. Their 2026 arXiv paper approximates sensitivity using fitting factors, the best overlap between a signal and any bank template.

A worked example shows the stakes. At a fitting factor of zero point seven, twenty-nine percent of signals are missed; at a perfect one, almost none are. The method matched real searches on spinning binary neutron stars, then covered eccentric binaries and relativity deviations. The computation proved robust: coarsening the frequency grid changed values by at most zero point zero zero five.
arxiv-2606-14145:
Abbasian and colleagues argue healthcare is missing a utility: always-on infrastructure for the hours when no clinician is present. A person spends about one hour a year with a clinician and eight thousand seven hundred fifty-nine hours eating, sleeping, and moving, where long-term health is decided. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes the Personal Care Utility, a layered, event-driven architecture. Signals become life events in a personal chronicle, health state is tracked against personal baselines, and an orchestrator routes guidance, separating clinical logic, behavioral strategy, and language generation.

That separation keeps language models on reasoning and communication while safety-critical decisions stay grounded in validated evidence. The system is instantiated for Type 2 diabetes, fusing glucose, meal, activity, medication, sleep, and stress data into glycemic events. It can answer with a nudge, a weekly summary, a check-in, silence, or a safety alert, depending on context.
arxiv-2606-14545:
Villani, Jin, and Galli compute light-free decay paths in spin defects in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spin defects are atomic flaws in crystals. Their spins can be controlled with light. That makes them building blocks for quantum devices. Internal conversion is a decay that sends energy into vibrations instead of light. Standard approximations often miss its rate by orders of magnitude.

Their framework mixes two ingredients. It uses many-body wavefunctions from time-dependent density functional theory. It also adds analytic couplings covering every phonon mode. The results match experiment well for the nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond. That center is a leading quantum sensor. The team also found a missed decay channel. It affects the triplet lifetime of the divacancy defect in silicon carbide.
arxiv-2606-14645:
Webb studies how the El Niño-Southern Oscillation relates to a Pacific ocean current in a 2026 arXiv ensemble paper. The North Equatorial Counter Current flows eastward across the tropical Pacific, and earlier single-run work suggested its temperature affects deep convection in the central Pacific. This study uses an ensemble of runs from the CESM climate model to test that link more firmly.

The ensemble results support the earlier findings, confirming that the counter current's temperature influences central Pacific convection, with knock-on effects on the Hadley circulation, the Southern Oscillation, and equatorial Pacific winds. The author also compares against the ERA5 atmospheric reanalysis, a reconstruction blending observations with models. The reanalysis fields show a similar correlation with the current's temperature, strengthening confidence that the modeled sensitivity reflects the real atmosphere.
arxiv-2606-14745:
Ponomarev makes stability analysis compositional for interconnected control systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. The small-gain and small-phase theorems judge a feedback system's stability from the gain and phase behavior of its parts. Classical versions struggle when a system is assembled from many multi-input, multi-output linear subsystems joined in series, parallel, and feedback combinations.

His method tracks a parameter set for each subsystem, including its phase sector and Crawford number, a phase-related quantity, and shows how those parameters bound the same quantities for each successive interconnection. Composing subsystem gains the same way enables small-gain-or-phase analysis of fairly complex assemblies piece by piece. Two worked examples are beyond the reach of classical small-phase analysis, and a third example still benefits from the compositional route, suggesting the bookkeeping scales to engineered networks.
arxiv-2606-14845:
Mondragón, Pradler, and Sholapurkar settle a foundational question about dark matter detection in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Migdal effect is the prompt ionization of an atom when its nucleus suddenly recoils, a signal direct dark matter searches rely on to catch very light particles. Its validity beyond the impulse approximation, which treats the recoil as instantaneous, had remained unresolved.

The authors present the first first-principles calculation for isolated atoms and establish the adiabatic crossover, the slow-recoil regime where ionization becomes suppressed. They show this behavior is fully encoded in the scattering amplitude with no ad hoc assumptions, and they map the relevant parameter space. Current dark matter searches, they find, lie in the unsuppressed regime, so the Migdal rates those experiments use rest on firmer ground than previously proven.
arxiv-2606-14945:
Jabbarvaziri makes autonomous research agents remember instead of re-reading in a 2026 arXiv paper. The autoresearch pattern has a language model iteratively edit code to improve a target metric. Its stateless design rebuilds context from scratch each round. Token cost then grows linearly per round and quadratically overall. Jabbarvaziri reformulates the loop as a stateful ReAct agent built with LangGraph.

Typed persistent state carries the experimental history across iterations. Tools expose that state without replaying it. Two benchmarks were run: hyperparameter tuning over fifteen iterations, and code optimization over forty. On tuning, the stateful agent used ninety percent fewer tokens, about two thousand five hundred against twenty-four thousand. On code optimization it used fifty-two percent fewer, about six hundred twenty-seven thousand against one point three million. Optimization quality stayed comparable on both tasks. The savings are structural, from a fixed-size working window.
arxiv-2606-15945:
Sauer and Schesler construct an acylindrically hyperbolic group with non-uniform exponential growth in 2026, and with Kazhdan's property (T) besides. A group grows exponentially when its Cayley-graph balls grow exponentially. Growth is uniform if the rate stays above one for every generating set; Gromov asked whether the distinction is real. Acylindrically hyperbolic groups, a broad class generalising hyperbolic groups, were not known to exhibit the non-uniform behaviour.

Their group is a common quotient of automorphism groups of free groups of increasing finite rank. A counting argument shows its infimal growth rate equals one, so growth is non-uniform; yet it grows exponentially, since such groups contain free subgroups. Property (T), a strong rigidity property, comes along by taking the quotient jointly with a Kazhdan group. The example separates two growth notions inside a major modern class, and shows they can coexist with the strongest rigidity.
arxiv-2606-16045:
Cohen-Addad and colleagues propose in 2026 a new way to pick a small training subset that still trains a model well. Data selection matters because training on full datasets is costly. Earlier geometric methods cluster embedded points and sample around centers. Many modern datasets, though, have global algebraic structure that clustering misses. Low-rank approximation, summarizing data with a few dominant patterns, fits that structure better.

Their framework pairs low-rank approximation with residual-based sampling, framed as row subset selection. A sensitivity sampling algorithm builds a small weighted coreset, a stand-in whose loss approximates the full dataset loss. The main theorem bounds coreset error by how well the data aligns with low-rank structure. Tests cover a tabular dataset and fine-tuning of Llama3-8B on three tasks. The low-rank method beats uniform sampling and clustering baselines in the reported evaluations.
arxiv-2606-16145:
Tan, Xia, and Zhou search in 2026 for neutrino signals from a dark matter candidate: memory-burdened primordial black holes, formed in the early universe. Memory burden is a proposed effect that slows their evaporation and changes their signals. Dwarf spheroidal galaxies are prime search targets, with heavy dark matter content and low astrophysical background.

The team analyzes ten years of public muon-track data from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. Fourteen dwarf galaxies with well-measured dark matter distributions, compiled from four independent literature sources, form the sample. An unbinned maximum-likelihood analysis tests each galaxy for excess neutrino emission, folding in uncertainties. No significant excess over background appears in any target. The null result becomes upper limits on the black hole abundance fraction, assuming one common mass. Limits tighten significantly in the stronger memory-burden case, especially between ten million and ten billion grams.
arxiv-2606-16245:
Lee and co-authors probe a kagome metal in 2026 that orders magnetically but skips the charge order seen in its famous cousin. The material is ScFe6Ge6, kin to FeGe, the first kagome metal found with charge density wave order inside an antiferromagnetic state. ScFe6Ge6 has no such charge order, so charge plays a smaller role. It instead passes through a magnetic transition at 195 kelvin.

The team uses angle-resolved photoemission plus Raman spectroscopy. Across the transition, the changes stay confined to a single kagome Dirac band, a case of orbital-selective behavior. That band also couples to an out-of-plane phonon through electron-phonon and magnetoelastic effects. The authors argue that such orbital-selective physics and out-of-plane links help explain how spin-linked charge order arises in magnetic kagome metals. The clean comparison case sharpens what makes FeGe special.
arxiv-2606-16445:
Craig and Madden give in 2026 a five-dimensional origin story for axion strings, defects tied to a dark matter candidate. The QCD axion solves the strong CP problem and can supply the dark matter, but its quality needs protection. Extra-dimensional axions get that protection from gauge structure. The authors show their strings are, concretely, five-dimensional 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole strings whose cores restore a non-abelian gauge symmetry.

The phase transition behind them breaks a five-dimensional SU(2) gauge symmetry rather than a four-dimensional global Peccei-Quinn symmetry. The fifth component of the unbroken U(1) gauge field becomes the four-dimensional axion. Separation between string tension and the quantum gravity scale then admits a viable post-inflationary cosmology for high-quality axion dark matter. The protective one-form symmetry is emergent below the SU(2) breaking scale, leaving irreducible but tolerable contributions to the axion potential.
arxiv-2606-16945:
Asad Ali and colleagues improve atom interferometry for gravity sensing in a 2026 quantum physics paper. Large-momentum-transfer atom interferometers split atomic waves widely to measure gravity precisely in compact devices. Their sensitivity grows with the number of Raman laser pulses, but transfer errors pile up across long pulse trains.

The team studies a shortcut method that bakes a counterdiabatic correction directly into the Raman pulse shapes, needing no extra microwave or radio-frequency fields. In simulation, microsecond pulses reach transfer fidelity very close to perfect, with negligible time overhead even at high momentum order. Weighing phase gain against contrast loss places a shot-noise optimum at a few hundred kicks. Practical limits at extreme order come instead from wave-packet separation, vibration noise, Doppler detuning and accumulated systematics. Superadiabatic Raman control thus looks promising for scalable, high-fidelity atom optics in field gravimeters.
arxiv-2606-17045:
Wu and colleagues design compact neural quantum states by starting from an exactly solvable point in a 2026 condensed matter paper. Neural-network states can represent quantum wavefunctions flexibly, but they work well only when the architecture respects the target state's sign structure and its constrained space of allowed configurations.

Their recipe: build the network at the solvable point, read the correct local rules off it, then grow only kernel size and hidden width. Four physics-motivated ingredients do the work, including stride-matched convolution and explicit spin-hole separation. Tests target valence-bond-solid states and their doped soliton variants, exact ground states of a t-J-like model with one mobile hole. The compact network hits near-unit fidelity with far fewer parameters than generic baselines. Its spin-sector rule transfers to larger systems without retraining, and parameter growth away from the solvable point stays favorable.
arxiv-2606-17145:
Ragagnin and colleagues accuracy-test a GPU port of a cosmology code in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Open Gadget3 simulates how galaxies and clusters form, following gravity and gas dynamics. Running it on graphics processors promises speed, but only if the physics survives the move intact.

The team validates the ported modules one by one: gravity integrator, hydrodynamics pieces, and conduction solver. Tests escalate, from a gravity-only universe and a shock tube to zoom-in runs of a cluster and a full-physics galaxy. Against the CPU version, GPU results agree excellently, with differences only on very small scales. Individual modules run several times faster per chip, and complex full setups roughly double or triple throughput at equal node counts. The runs span four supercomputers, so the numbers reflect portable performance. Such validation is what lets production cosmology trust accelerated hardware.
arxiv-2606-17245:
Evans and Barradas present a 2026 arXiv paper on keeping web knowledge reachable during internet blackouts, whether caused by failures or imposed by governments. Mesh-network tools already restore basic messaging in such crises, but none preserve access to web pages themselves. Their system, Cache to the Future, is designed to cache static web content in advance and deliver it over local networks while the wider internet is down.

Caching choices are crowdsourced through distributed community ratings, so limited storage goes to content people in a region value most. Digital signatures and proofs of work are used to blunt adversarial interference with the shared cache. Realistic simulations show the system delivering content at city scale across a wide range of benign and adversarial scenarios. The work targets reference, medical, and community pages whose loss during a blackout can be severe.
arxiv-2606-17745:
Therianos presents a 2026 arXiv paper asking which features of a brain's behaviour are written in its exact wiring and which follow from coarse wiring statistics alone. The test bed is the complete larval fruit-fly connectome, run as a frozen rate network with no neuron-level parameter fitted to activity data. The same network is then compared against rewired versions matched for degree and weight statistics, plus further controls. Any difference then belongs to the precise placement of synapses and nothing else in the setup.

The gross signature, gain, and effective dimensionality land within a few percent of the rewired ensemble, fixed by statistics alone. Two spatial properties break away: sparse input stays confined to a fifth of the real core, and the mushroom body concentrates the leading driving modes far beyond any control. Exact wiring, the paper shows, governs routing and mode identity, not bulk response.
arxiv-2606-17945:
Hang and colleagues argue that the starting values of a language model's parameters act like genes for its training, in a 2026 paper. Progress is usually credited to scale, data, and architecture, but the team shows that shrinking the initialization scale consistently improves pretraining. The largest gains land on reasoning-heavy tasks, exactly where models are weakest.

Two common empirical settings were masking this benefit, and relaxing them restored the favorable scaling. The authors also find a critical initialization size that balances reasoning gains against trainability. Mechanistically, small starts push parameters to first condense into simple, low-complexity structures and only later expand into richer ones, a concrete picture of compression as intelligence. Their practical rule, gamma-initialization, makes the starting range an explicit knob and defaults to small, at almost no cost.
arxiv-2606-18045:
Chakraborty and colleagues watch two young planets cross their star and time each crossing with care, in a 2026 astronomy paper. HIP 67522 is a Sun-like star only about seventeen million years old, among the youngest multi-planet hosts known, with two Saturn-sized planets in a near two-to-one rhythm. The team gathered transits from the CHEOPS and TESS space telescopes plus ground observatories.

They searched for transit timing wobbles caused by the planets tugging on each other, and for depth changes as starspots rotate across the stellar face. No timing shifts beyond two minutes appeared for the inner planet. Combining that calm with independent mass estimates caps the outer planet's mass at a few dozen Earth masses at most, and far less if its orbit tilts. The light masses make the pair a tempting target for atmospheric study.
arxiv-2606-18145:
Gu and colleagues prove that the hardest part of running a topological quantum memory is hard but approximable, in a 2026 paper. Two-dimensional topological stabilizer codes, like the toric and color codes, anchor plans for fault-tolerant quantum computers. Decoding them means finding the lightest error pattern matching a measured syndrome, a task recently proven NP-hard even in basic settings. Despair is unwarranted, though, because near-optimal answers suffice in practice.

The team proves a polynomial-time approximation scheme: for any chosen slack, an algorithm finds a recovery within that multiplicative factor of the minimum weight, in polynomial time. The method adapts Arora's geometric scheme for problems like the traveling salesman to codes whose errors form strings between point-like excitations. It reaches beyond two dimensions too, covering some higher-dimensional codes and circuit-level noise models relevant to real hardware.
arxiv-2606-18245:
Paul and Puthenpurakal pin down how fast two growth functions in homological algebra can rise, in a 2026 paper. Over a Gorenstein local ring sit a perfect module and a maximal Cohen-Macaulay module that is not free. The lengths of Tor and Ext modules against successive powers of an ideal grow like polynomials. Their degrees measure how the two modules interact, and earlier work left the degrees loosely bounded.

The authors prove both degrees are at most one less than the dimension of the perfect module, for every index. When the ideal is the maximal ideal, both bounds become equalities, so the growth is as fast as allowed. They also bound each degree by the first degree of a canonical test module, the syzygy of the residue field, whose Tor and Ext degrees all coincide. A closing section recasts the results in the stable category of Cohen-Macaulay modules.
arxiv-2606-18345:
Gerbershagen and Hollweck prove a conjecture about conformal blocks, the symmetry-determined pieces of correlation functions in conformal field theory, in a 2026 mathematical physics paper. In the semiclassical limit, where the theory's central charge grows while weights scale with it, blocks were expected to take an exponential form.

Until now that exponentiation had been proved for four-point blocks on a sphere and one-point blocks on a torus. The authors extend the proof to blocks with any number of operators, on surfaces of any genus, and in any channel, at the level of power series. Their route is an extension of the oscillator method for computing blocks to vertices where three internal lines meet. The same extension gives a constructive way to compute conformal blocks at general genus. The result matters for holographic theories, heavy-state physics, and recursion methods that lean on semiclassical blocks.
arxiv-2606-18545:
Burakov shows that a standard tool for judging credit scoring models, the cumulative accuracy profile, is secretly an application of Bayes' theorem, in a 2026 paper on credit risk statistics. The profile's curve is normally read only for its area, a measure of how well a model ranks borrowers, while the probabilities it assigns are judged separately.

Burakov makes explicit that the curve's local slope equals the default probability at that score, rescaled by the overall default rate. In cumulative coordinates, the slope is the posterior divided by the prior. From that reading, the weight of evidence becomes the log ratio of the two class slopes, and the information value falls out of the same geometry. The accuracy ratio, Somers' D, and the Gini coefficient turn out to be one number computed three ways. Run against realized outcomes, the identity also yields a calibration check.
arxiv-2606-18945:
Bi and colleagues study the anomalous Hall effect in 2026 in a phase tied to thin films of a topological material. In this phase, just half the usual quantized Hall signal shows up. It comes from a single gapless Dirac state on the surface. A key doubt is whether dirt and defects in real films add extra Hall signal and spoil that clean half value.

The authors work out the two main extra routes, known as side-jump and skew-scattering. Both routes turn out to add nothing at all in this case. That null result is the heart of the work. It means the surface state holds up well against disorder. The phase can thus be seen as robust, not fragile. The finding also helps clarify how Dirac particles on such surfaces keep their transport marks even in imperfect, dirty samples used in labs.
arxiv-2606-19045:
Al-Mekhlafi and colleagues build and analyze a fractional SVIR epidemic model in 2026. The model tracks four groups: at-risk, vaccinated, infected, and recovered people. A hybrid operator lets it capture both short- and long-term memory in how a disease spreads. Such memory matters because past contacts and immunity shape current transmission in ways standard models forget too fast.

The authors prove solutions stay positive and bounded, then derive the reproduction number and fixed points. Stability is checked with Jacobian analysis and Lyapunov tools. For computation, they design a weighted nonstandard finite difference scheme that preserves positivity and boundedness. It is stable in the fully implicit case and first-order accurate. Numerical tests show how memory parameters reshape spread.
arxiv-2606-19145:
Richter and colleagues introduce OrthoReg in 2026, a regularization method for hybrid symbolic-neural models of dynamical systems. Mechanistic models are interpretable but often too simple and misspecified. Pure neural models are flexible but give little physical insight. Hybrid models join a symbolic physics part with a neural part for the rest. The risk is that the neural part relearns what the symbolic part already says, yielding redundant and opaque models.

Standard penalties rest on a projection argument that breaks when the symbolic part is itself learned by sparse discovery. OrthoReg instead penalizes overlap between the two parts directly. The symbolic part then captures what its library can express, and the neural part captures only what remains. On benchmark systems with partial library mismatch, OrthoReg improves recovery of the true symbolic structure. It also improves behavior out of distribution. Clean separation makes hybrid models easier to interpret.
arxiv-2606-19245:
Le and colleagues introduce TxBench-PP in 2026, a benchmark testing AI agents on small-molecule drug testing. Agents promise to speed drug discovery by compressing interpretation and decision loops. Deployment needs trusted tests on real program decisions, not recall of memorized literature. TxBench-PP checks whether agents can recover accurate conclusions from real assay data in a coding environment, with structured graded answers.

The benchmark holds a hundred evaluations indexed by program stage, assay type, and task structure. Coverage spans mechanism and engagement reasoning, target checks, safety, and efficacy. Across many model and harness setups and thousands of runs, no system reliably recovered the preclinical conclusions. That gap is the point. The benchmark exposes how far current agents are from trusted drug work, and gives developers a verifiable target.
arxiv-2606-19445:
Méndez-Gallego and colleagues report evidence in 2026 that protostellar jets form a population of hadronic gamma-ray sources. Stars are born deep in cold, dense molecular clouds. Young stellar systems, once thought purely thermal, now show energetic non-thermal activity. Radio synchrotron jets hinted at relativistic electrons in these systems. Direct proof of proton acceleration stayed elusive.

The team finds a statistically significant gamma-ray detection from a population of young stellar objects. A new Galactic class emerges, gamma-loud protostars. The emission points to fast particles inside protostellar jets. Protons interact with surrounding molecular clouds and produce gamma rays through pion decay. Cosmic-ray output correlates with bolometric luminosity, so output scales with the system's mechanical power. Gamma-ray studies of protostars can now probe accretion, ejection, and feedback, tracing the energetic output young stars inject into the clouds that made them.
arxiv-2606-19545:
Santiago Cifuentes studies a hard detection problem for quantum states in 2026. Given a circuit that prepares a state, can a quantum computer tell whether some Pauli matrix has a large coefficient? A large coefficient means the state correlates strongly with that Pauli observable.

The problem allows a promise gap: either some coefficient reaches a threshold, or all stay below half of it. Cifuentes shows the problem sits inside QCMA, a quantum class for checkable proofs. He then proves that placing it inside BQP, the class quantum computers solve fast, would put NP inside BQP too. The proof reduces from the minimum-weight code problem in coding theory. It holds even for pure states with a constant threshold value. The upshot answers an open question: fast tomography for the largest Pauli coefficients cannot exist unless NP falls to quantum machines.
arxiv-2606-19945:
B. Vigneshwar, Farhaan Khan, and R. Sankaranarayanan examine work extraction from quantum batteries helped by an ancilla in 2026. Ergotropy measures the work a cyclic process can pull from a quantum system, and a measured ancilla can raise the yield, an effect called daemonic gain. The authors show the bound energy of the reduced system caps that gain tightly, with equality for globally pure system-ancilla states. A purity-based score then predicts the gain without costly measurement optimization.

Protocols in the study probe dissipation and internal interactions as well. Under a shared environment, dissipation can create and stabilize finite gain through environment-induced correlations. Level crossings reshape the attainable gain by moving the accessible bound energy. Battery design thus depends on spectrum and purity, not correlations alone.
arxiv-2606-20745:
P Bosted and the Hall C SIDIS Collaboration report charged kaon and proton multiplicities in 2026 from semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering. In such scattering, an electron strikes a target and a specific hadron is detected among the debris. Multiplicity measures how often that hadron appears under set conditions. Data were taken at Jefferson Lab in 2018 and 2019. Electron beams near 11 GeV hit liquid hydrogen and deuterium targets.

Electrons and hadrons were detected in two Hall C spectrometers. Results cover grids of hadron and lepton variables, with set ranges for energy share and transverse momentum. Fits include cosine terms for angular patterns. Kaon to pion ratios mostly agree with one fragmentation model for positive kaons. They fall well below it for negative kaons. Such data test how quarks turn into hadrons, a process called fragmentation, across regions where different theories apply.
arxiv-2606-20945:
Vishesh Tripathi and Abhay Kumar propose Grouped Query Experts in 2026, a mixture-of-experts layer built on grouped-query attention for transformers. Self-attention is central to transformer quality. It is also costly at long context, since pairwise token interactions grow fast. Standard attention applies the same heads to every token. Easy and hard tokens are treated alike, wasting compute.

Within each attention group, a router selects a few query-head experts per token. Key and value heads stay dense and unchanged. That keeps cache benefits while cutting active query-head work. On a fixed token budget at a small model scale, the method matches the all-active baseline in downstream accuracy. It uses half the routed experts per token. Prefill speed improves notably at long context. Selective query work could make long-context models cheaper without giving up quality.
arxiv-2606-21245:
Jonas Papenbrock and six colleagues built the STIR Hand in 2026, a light, low-cost robot hand with just a thumb and index finger, modeled on human grasping. The fingers are tendon-driven and underactuated, meaning one drive moves several joints, so the hand adapts its shape passively around objects. Flexible strain gauges sit inside silicone-encapsulated soft joints, giving the hand a sense of its own bend and of contact.

The team recorded grasps of twenty objects and ran unsupervised analysis plus a classification task on the sensor data. The classifier read object size, shape, and stiffness with high accuracy, and removing the joint sensors hurt performance in an ablation test. STIR grasps safely with no fingertip touch sensors and no camera, a lean route for prosthetic and assistive devices.
arxiv-2606-21345:
Hail Hochman, Natalie Shapira, and Yoav Goldberg map how language models retrieve facts in 2026, tracing the path an entity's representation follows before the model can state one of its attributes. Earlier work located stored knowledge in parts of the network, but the step-by-step computation that turns a name into a recalled fact stayed murky. Their iterative patching protocol finds the smallest set of layers that can carry out that computation.

Applied to LLaMA 3.1 8B and Qwen3 8B, the method shows these paths skip layers rather than running in one unbroken block. Models also hold several functionally equal paths for the same fact, so retrieval is redundant and widely distributed. That spread may explain why editing a fact at one site often fails to change what the model actually recalls.
arxiv-2606-21745:
Winston Chou tackles a daily dilemma of online experimentation in 2026. The proxy metric moves fast but may mislead, while the north star metric that actually matters barely twitches within one experiment's power. Teams running A/B tests at places like Netflix face this constantly. Trust the sensitive proxy, or the insensitive truth?

Chou proposes an optimal blending rule: weight the north star more as the experiment's statistical power grows, and lean on the proxy more as proxy quality improves. The framework has design teeth. Better proxies mean experimenters should run smaller, more numerous experiments; worse proxies demand larger, fewer ones. Past experiments can calibrate the blending weights and sizes. A real application to Netflix's experimentation program grounds the theory, turning a judgment call into an estimable decision rule.
arxiv-2606-22145:
Xu and Tran study, in 2026, the zero-shot transfer of reinforcement learning control policies from simulation to a physical cart-pole. The task has two parts: swinging the pendulum up, then stabilizing it inverted. The two policies are trained independently, and switching logic in Simulink hands control from one to the other on the hardware.

A first-order action smoothing filter prevents damage from high-frequency oscillatory actuation. The authors pair sensitivity-guided domain randomization with this bandwidth-aware filtering, plus a simple linear curriculum schedule during training. In all experiments, the swing-up policy injected enough energy to reach the stabilizer's region of attraction. Its stabilizer rejected disturbances within the tested range. After larger perturbations, the swing-up policy could re-engage and restore the pendulum to the inverted position, without any fine-tuning on the hardware.
arxiv-2606-22245:
Chen and Li propose, in 2026, a compensated splitting method for solving generalized Lyapunov equations, which arise in model reduction and stochastic stability analysis. The equation's natural splitting yields the standard fixed-point iteration. That iteration converges from any starting guess if and only if the spectral radius of the associated linear operator is below one, so it can diverge outright.

The compensated scheme modifies the splitting to shrink the spectral radius. The resulting iteration can still converge in cases where the standard iteration diverges. When both converge, the new version converges faster. Numerical results show it beating the standard iteration. The same equation is solved; only the splitting of the iteration changes.
arxiv-2606-22445:
Quanyuan Ruan, Jiabao Lei, Xingyi Du, and Xifeng Gao address UV unwrapping for three-dimensional models in this 2026 paper. UV parameterization flattens a 3D surface into a 2D layout so textures can be painted on it. Artists make layouts with straight seams and axis-aligned islands, patterns that classical methods, tuned to handcrafted energy functions, rarely match.

Their system, DreamUV, treats unwrapping as a generative flow matching problem, learning to turn random noise into realistic layouts. Training uses the mesh shape and a boundary-aware strategy that puts seam geometry first. A model-in-the-loop finetuning scheme corrects sampling errors, steadying the process under mixed-quality data. On a large set of professional layouts, DreamUV gave straighter boundaries and tighter axis-aligned islands than classical and learning-based baselines. Distortion stayed competitive, and a user study with professional artists confirmed the layouts fit production needs.
arxiv-2606-22545:
Jorge Luiz Deolindo-Silva and Mostafa Salarinoghabi study surfaces in 4-space in this 2026 geometry paper. They examine how a smooth surface touches flat 2-planes. They also study the apparent contour, the outline a projection casts on another plane.

For projections whose plane has no asymptotic direction, they count the tangent lines with the worst singularities. At hyperbolic or elliptic points there are up to ten, and at parabolic points up to seven, of butterfly type or worse. That locus forms smooth curves in the hyperbolic and elliptic regions but isolated points in the parabolic set. A second case, where the plane contains such a direction, links parallel projections with orthogonal ones and height functions. For fold projections, a Koenderink-type theorem links surface curvature to contour curvature. Elliptic points become vertices of the contour, while hyperbolic and parabolic points become inflections.
arxiv-2606-22945:
Junrong Huang and colleagues tackle texture tiling in a 2026 computer graphics paper. Tiling means repeating a reference pattern across a surface in a scene image. Users want control over how often the pattern repeats, its direction, and its size. Older editing tools often blur the pattern or break the lighting and shape of the scene. The team builds its method on diffusion transformers, a kind of image generation model.

Huang and colleagues add two main ideas to keep control precise. One adjusts the position codes inside the model with simple geometric transforms, so patterns repeat exactly as asked without warping pixels. The other uses a special attention mask, which controls which parts of the image the model compares. Together the changes copy the reference texture faithfully while leaving scene lighting and geometry coherent.
arxiv-2606-23045:
Michel Nowak and colleagues schedule Earth observation satellites with a Rydberg atom quantum processor in a 2026 paper. A satellite fleet faces far more imaging targets than it can serve each day. Planners must pick which targets each satellite scans, respecting timing and movement limits. The authors recast that planning puzzle for cold-atom quantum hardware. In such machines, excited Rydberg atoms encode choices through their interactions. Analog operation lets the device tackle huge configuration spaces at once.

Nowak and colleagues start with a simple planning version ignoring satellite agility, then add agility following published models. They rewrite the task as a maximum independent set problem, a graph puzzle quantum hardware handles naturally. Two solution routes are compared, one graph-based and one using a binary optimization framework. The binary route proved most relevant in deeper numerical tests. The study weighs whether such processors could serve real operations.
arxiv-2606-23245:
Ryo Nakayama and colleagues study why a small limpet rides on mobile snail hosts in a 2026 marine biology paper. The epizoic limpet Lottia tenuisculpta lives attached to other gastropods. Riding a moving host may cut the risk of being eaten, but the steps leading to attachment and its payoff were unclear. The team ran host-riding assays, tracked movement before riding, and ran survival and mucus-conditioning experiments. Crab-associated cues, chemical signs of a predator nearby, were the key test condition.

Nakayama and colleagues find that crab cues sharply raised attachment, from about a quarter of limpets to over half. Paired movement tracks also closed distance faster under the cues. In survival trials, limpets on mobile hosts survived far better than those on fixed hosts by the end of observation. The work ties a predator cue to the riding behavior and shows the survival benefit of a moving ride.
arxiv-2606-23645:
Lawrie solves an inverse design problem for wave filters by working forward instead, in a 2026 paper on wave physics. A waveguide network is a mesh of channels that guides waves, such as light or sound, along chosen paths. Designers usually start from a wanted transmission profile and search numerically for a structure that produces it. Search is slow and gives little insight.

Lawrie computes the exact transmission coefficients of periodic waveguide networks directly. The lattice response becomes a Fourier expansion, a sum of wave components, whose coefficients map cleanly onto the network itself. Lengths, gauge phases, bond connections, and refractive indices can then be read off from the target, with no search at all. The method extends from angular filtering to image synthesis, rebuilding arbitrary transmitted intensity patterns.
arxiv-2606-23745:
Jocys, Zhu, Willems, and Farrahi generate drug discovery libraries that chemists can actually synthesize, in a 2026 paper on computational drug design. DNA encoded libraries test millions of compounds at once by tagging each with a DNA barcode. Designing a focused library for a target usually starts from known active compounds, summarized as a pharmacophore, the three dimensional pattern of features a drug needs to bind. Generative models often propose compounds that no realistic chemistry can build.

Their framework, JEDEL, learns an alignment between that pattern's geometry and molecular structure. It then decodes the alignment into synthesis plans built only from available building blocks and proven reactions, so every output can really be made. Across eighteen protein targets, and with no target specific retraining, the generated libraries beat random and diversity based baselines on predicted binding strength, pattern recovery, and how few samples they need.
arxiv-2606-24345:
Adell and Alcalá build explicit confidence bands for distribution functions and their derivatives, out of an unusual ingredient: random smoothing operators. Classical kernel estimators can be recast through random Weierstrass-type operators, particularly random Steklov operators. That recasting pays off in 2026 with bands and intervals valid at finite sample size, rather than only in the limit.

Under nothing more than uniform continuity of the derivative in question, bands follow from the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality, a classic concentration result. Intervals allow the derivative isolated jumps. The honest target then becomes its midpoint function. Proofs run through such inequalities for linked processes, or sharp mean-squared error estimates. Band width is set by smoothness, through the second modulus of continuity. It shrinks at the familiar root-n rate when the function is locally a low-degree polynomial. Adell's explicit formulas give users usable error statements without simulation.
arxiv-2606-24445:
Schreiter and colleagues test how a mobile robot should tell nearby people its next move. Clear robot-to-human signals build trust, and support safer shared workspaces. Robots differ in available channels, though. People interpret signals differently, and online studies may not predict real encounters. Their 2026 validation compares messaging options for a non-humanoid mobile robot, online and in person.

Message types follow existing industrial robot standards. They cover showing a turn, asking for attention, reporting an error, being stuck, and working normally. A low-expressive strategy uses only LEDs. A highly expressive multimodal strategy combines robotic gaze, gestures, and voice. Replicated experiments in both settings find strong evidence for one winner. The expressive multimodal approach is perceived as clearer and easier to read, across the message set. Schreiter's team also probes the virtual-to-real gap directly, checking whether online judgements survive contact with a physical robot.
arxiv-2606-24945:
Hongbo Wang asks when a conservation law stays certifiable after a model learns its latent code. A certified horizon bounds how many rollout steps provably stay on an invariant's level set. The certified object matters: not a learned latent Hamiltonian or scalar witness, since a model can conserve either while true energy drifts. Wang certifies the decoded invariant instead, obtained by decoding the latent state. Shell horizon certificates follow, their budgets split into representation, readout, and latent dynamics defects.

Tests across state, learned lift, and pixel observations give a verdict. Canonical symplectic structure gives the longest horizons among known phase coordinates, yet fails to cross a learned chart. A controlled Lipschitz aligned soft invariant persists in the nonlinear settings tested, two lift systems and pixels, with the gain growing with nonlinearity. Pixel certification is recovered on a readout sub tube. The Kepler problem exposes a boundary to the method.
arxiv-2606-25045:
M. O. Herdrich and five colleagues apply machine learning to signals from metallic magnetic calorimeters. These detectors are a promising tool for high precision X-ray spectroscopy: an absorbed photon warms the sensor, and the heat change encodes the photon's energy. Their complex response and the need for scalable pipelines have slowed wider adoption. The authors explore learning based methods across the pipeline. Unsupervised techniques discover labels on their own; supervised models handle classification and regression.

Machine learning proves useful at several points. It classifies pulses and rejects artefacts. It analyses pulse shapes and extracts features from them. Across these tasks, the learned approaches match traditional methods. They add adaptability and speed: a trained pipeline adjusts to new data with less hand engineering. Herdrich and colleagues conclude the approach is robust and scalable enough for the next generation of these detectors.
arxiv-2606-25145:
Two dimensional oscillators with separable polynomial potentials trace out Lissajous figures, the woven curves familiar from coupled vibrations. A. M. Escobar-Ruiz and R. Azuaje study when those paths close into loops that repeat, and what the closing reveals about conserved quantities. The frame is superintegrability, an excess of conserved quantities beyond what a system needs.

In the harmonic case the closing is global: a rational ratio of the two frequencies gives a conserved quantity that holds everywhere, the most a system can have. For the quartic oscillator the picture changes. Each frequency now depends on the partial energies, so closed orbits appear only when the starting data meet nonlinear resonance conditions. The extra conserved quantities then live only on those paths: they are particular integrals, not global ones. For higher degree potentials the special paths are pinned down by hyperelliptic phase constraints, not by a single orbit equation.
arxiv-2606-25245:
Drones that navigate by camera alone tend to drift, and their paths come out relative rather than tied to the real map. Oussema Dhaouadi and colleagues offer OrthoTrack in 2026, a system that anchors a drone's full six degree of freedom trajectory in public aerial photographs and surface models. Key frames are matched against the overhead photo, lifted into three dimensions, and then tracked through the frames in between with optical flow. No satellite positioning or later alignment step is required.

Alongside the system, the team built the MovingDrone dataset, pairing realistic drone video with exact ground truth paths and layered geographic data. OrthoTrack ran in real time on one graphics processor and beat every baseline by a wide margin, even baselines handed the true scale. Public data means new regions need no fresh site survey.
arxiv-2606-25745:
Everyone knows mean field variational inference, the workhorse approximation for Bayesian posteriors, cheats by understating uncertainty. James Odgers, Ben Riegler, Siddharth Swaroop, and Vincent Fortuin show in 2026 that the story flips where it matters. Working with conjugate Bayesian linear regression, where the exact posterior is known, they prove the approximation must rob variance from some directions and overpay others. The overpaid directions are exactly where the training data concentrate. For a fresh test point drawn from the training distribution itself, the method's expected predictive variance actually exceeds the exact posterior's.

A pathological case drives the point home: on in distribution data the approximation can fail to reduce predictive variance below the prior at all. The results connect to the cold posterior effect in Bayesian deep learning. Cooling the posterior's temperature can correct the overestimation and pull predictions back toward the exact answer.
arxiv-2606-26045:
Sriram Kalathoor studies salt fingers, the narrow sinking plumes that mix heat and salt between ocean layers. Standard theory judges an interface by local conditions alone. Kalathoor argues the interface also remembers its past. Waves, stirring, and earlier mixing leave it rough. That inherited roughness, stored as a spectrum of bumps, may steer how fingering develops.

Three-dimensional direct simulations test the claim. Every control setting stays fixed: density ratio, diffusivity ratio, layer depth, and more. Only the starting roughness spectrum changes between runs. Broad, low-mode roughness yields the largest total salt exchange. It also brings the earliest contact across the layer depth. Fine-scale roughness stays local and weaker. Mixed roughness delays scale transfer but stays rich in scalar structure across repeat runs. The results support treating spectral memory as a genuine state variable for such exchange.
arxiv-2606-26445:
Jemima M. Briggs and nine colleagues introduce Columba, a suite of cosmological simulations of dwarf galaxies. A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy with far fewer stars than the Milky Way. Columba follows many isolated dwarfs across varied surroundings. The surroundings range from near-empty voids to denser filament structures. No Milky Way-sized galaxy sits nearby to disturb them.

The suite zooms into twenty-five spherical regions. Each region spans a wide range of average density. The simulations include cold, dense gas between the stars. Their star formation feedback, meaning energy returned by young stars, matches the observed count of galaxies by mass today. Environment changed how many haloes and galaxies formed. It did not much change the link between a galaxy's star mass and its halo mass. Halo concentration, how tightly a halo's matter packs inward, mattered more for whether a halo hosts a visible galaxy.
arxiv-2606-26645:
Hamed Alimohammadzadeh, Heather Culbertson, and Shahram Ghandeharizadeh evaluate group formation for Flying Light Specks. A Flying Light Speck is a tiny drone carrying lights. Swarms of them can draw three-dimensional shapes in the air. Users can even touch the shapes for feedback through the skin. Groups of specks support backup when some fail and divide rendering work.

Four decentralised techniques are compared. Each speck decides on its own, messaging neighbours without a shared clock. Tests used synthetic point clouds, where the best grouping is known, plus real point clouds. A point cloud is a set of points outlining a shape. One technique, Random Subset, won for small groups of five or fewer. Another, Closest Available Neighbor First, won for groups of ten or more.
arxiv-2606-26845:
Din Iskakov and six colleagues build a shared topic space so news and social media can be compared fairly. Topic models fitted to separate collections invent separate topic systems that cannot be lined up. Their framework instead anchors everything to one taxonomy, the IPTC media topics used by news organisations. Discovered topics are scored against the taxonomy and rolled up to its parent categories.

Development used a controlled newspaper corpus from one year. A guided topic model was screened, refined, and calibrated step by step. Guided models beat a zero-shot rival on mapped coverage under strict thresholds. Enriching the taxonomy targets with parent information improved both coverage and consistency. Coverage faded gently rather than collapsing as thresholds tightened. The method offers a reproducible route to like-for-like topic comparison across outlets.
arxiv-2606-26945:
Bhooshan Gadre proposes a consistency test of gravity using binaries seen by both radio telescopes and gravitational wave detectors. A compact binary pulsar's orbit tilt can be measured two ways. Radio timing gives it through the Shapiro delay, the slowing of pulses near the companion. Gravitational waves give it through the ratio of the signal's polarisation amplitudes. General relativity says both messengers must agree on the same geometry.

Gadre defines a residual: the radio value minus the wave value at a common epoch. Relativity predicts zero. A nonzero result would expose either hidden systematics or a real split between gravity's near-zone and radiative behaviour. Precision forecasts use a timing Fisher matrix and the expected sensitivity of the LISA space detector, with the Square Kilometre Array supplying radio timing. Conservative noise assumptions frame the estimates.
arxiv-2606-27545:
Göbel and colleagues give a short, self-contained proof that Glauber dynamics for the hard-core model mixes rapidly on random regular graphs beyond the uniqueness threshold. A recent breakthrough had established the result with heavy machinery drawn from local-to-global techniques. The hard-core model weights independent sets of a graph by their size, and Glauber dynamics resamples one vertex at a time. The new proof takes a Bochner-Bakry-Émery route, in a probability paper published in 2026.

A Poincaré inequality is shown directly, by writing the Dirichlet form through the squared norm of the generator acting on a test function, with a sum-of-squares term eliminated. The argument streamlines one developed for continuum Gibbs point processes and adapts it to the discrete setting. Simplicity is the contribution: fewer moving parts, easier verification, wider teachability.
arxiv-2606-27645:
Chengfeng Sun, Hao Yu, and Hui Liu study a noisy fluid model in 2026. The model adds random noise to the two-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations on a torus, a donut-shaped domain. Dissipation, the friction that calms the flow, acts only in the horizontal direction.

First, the authors prove a uniform large deviation principle for the paths of the flow. The proof joins a known result for a linear noise process, a new Lipschitz bound, and a contraction argument needing no tightness condition. Second, fast mixing cannot occur: a steady flow exists that the horizontal friction cannot touch, and it blocks exponential mixing. Without noise, the part of the flow immune to friction holds infinitely many point-like invariant measures. With the right kind of degenerate noise, none of them survive, and any invariant measure must avoid that immune part entirely.
arxiv-2606-27945:
Sandeep and six colleagues demonstrate an open nanoacoustic resonator in 2026. The device is built from a stack of oxide layers. Strontium titanate and a cuprate superconductor alternate in the stack. A nickel film generates coherent phonons, the quantised vibrations of the material. The stack acts as an acoustic mirror. It confines sound waves at very high frequencies.

Transient reflectivity measurements reveal the confined dynamics. A well-defined cavity resonance appears. Calculations of the acoustic response agree with the measurements. In the stack alone, folded acoustic modes appear in the gigahertz range. Adding the nickel layer creates the open cavity. A confined mode sits within the first stop band. That mode is absent in a control sample without the stack. The results show that complex oxide stacks can confine and control such vibrations. They form a platform for nano-acoustic devices and ultrafast phonon control.
arxiv-2606-28145:
Wearable sensors log rich training data for runners. Mateusz Kubita, Jan Zubalewicz, and Krzysztof Siwek evaluate five dimensionality reduction models in 2026. Three autoencoder variants, PCA, and a variational model compete to compress nine sensor features into one performance score. The setting is fully unsupervised. Quality is judged on reconstruction error and on how interpretable the score is. A composite criterion stops selection by accuracy alone.

The deep autoencoder won on both counts, lowest reconstruction error and highest composite score. Widening the PCA model's hidden layers made deeper variants nearly as good, suggesting capacity, not the one-dimensional bottleneck, was the limit. Feature rankings were aggregated and bootstrap-checked. Three drivers dominated across all models and resamples. Running pace came first; aerobic decoupling and average heart rate joined it, each reaching a top-three inclusion probability of one. The result matches established sports physiology, found without domain knowledge.
arxiv-2606-28245:
Thomas Basile, Xavier Bekaert, Felipe Figueroa, and Evgeny Skvortsov work out new math for continuous-spin particles. These are hypothetical particles whose spin, instead of taking one fixed value, can vary over a continuous range. They resist the standard tools physicists use to write down scattering amplitudes, the numbers that predict what happens when particles collide.

Basile and colleagues describe the states with a single two-component spinor. The style borrows from the spinor-helicity method used for massless particles. Familiar helicity states emerge when the description is split by homogeneity degree. Their amplitudes arise as the infinite-spin limit of massive-particle amplitudes, with a universal factor exponentiating just as in black hole scattering. They also find nontrivial collinear amplitudes. In those, the momentum fractions are tied to the parameter that defines each particle.
arxiv-2606-28345:
Carmen Ng and Gjergji Kasneci audit the morals of language-model-driven social robots, machines that may soon decide who gets scarce help first in care homes, schools, and service settings. Whom people prioritize varies by culture, with age, status, and group size, so a robot tuned to one culture's norms can systematically short-change another's.

Ng and Kasneci built a gradient-based audit comparing model choices against country-specific preference patterns from the Moral Machine tradition, recast as whom-to-assist-first dilemmas. Four models made tens of thousands of decisions across four country-language pairs and four prompting regimes. Calibration ran nearly twice as strong for Western languages as for Chinese and Japanese, and firm majority-first habits often erased cultural differences altogether. Contrastive cultural examples helped most; reasoning prompts sometimes hurt.
arxiv-2606-28645:
Monika D. Soraisam and a large collaboration of colleagues present GOATS, the software meant to keep astronomers sane during the alert flood. Time-domain astronomy lives on rapid follow-up: kilonovae, supernova shock breakouts, and gamma-ray bursts fade in hours, yet chasing them has meant juggling disconnected tools and interfaces across observatories.

The Gemini Observation and Analysis of Targets System unifies the chain on one platform. Targets are picked through the ANTARES alert broker, observations triggered at Gemini and partner facilities, data pulled automatically from the archive, and reduction handled interactively through established NOIRLab tools. In an end-to-end demonstration on live Rubin Observatory alerts, the team selected targets and triggered follow-up within minutes, obtaining spectra that classified several supernovae of different types. Removing manual glue work, they argue, lets scientists spend attention on interpretation.
arxiv-2606-28945:
Lemoine solves a large-N Yang-Mills theory on a lattice at strong coupling. The theory lives on a grid in any dimension from two up, with heat-kernel action. His objects are Wilson loops, traces of the field around closed paths.

He proves that normalised Wilson loop averages have infinite-volume limits as the number of colours grows. They factorise at leading order. They also admit an expansion in inverse powers of N, with coefficients that decay fast with distance. The leading order characterises the master field, one field configuration capturing the whole theory at large N. An upper bound of area-law type for the master field follows, with a stronger version checked coefficient by coefficient. The proof runs through a new loop equation. Unlike older ones, it closes only on an extended space of loop observables decorated with plaquettes.
arxiv-2606-29145:
Hawkins and Armantalab argue that travel behaviour research still needs theory, even as artificial intelligence tools boost predictive accuracy. Their field models why people make the transport choices they do. AI tools predict well but often at the cost of hypothesis-based theory testing and explanation, leaving models that forecast without understanding.

They make the case through goal pursuit theory, which models travellers as juggling context-dependent goals: hedonic, gain and normative. Unlike random utility maximisation, the field's standard frame, goal pursuit theory shows how travellers activate goals, resolve conflicts between competing objectives, and decide sequentially across time scales. Three applications illustrate the merits: activity scheduling, vehicle ownership and location choice. The authors give practical guidance too: hybrid choice models linking goals to observable behaviour, parallels with other theories, and data needs for benchmarking against standard models.
arxiv-2606-29445:
Fan and four colleagues connect two skills: answering questions about videos, and learning procedures from video tutorials well enough to act on them. Existing benchmarks mostly test whether multimodal large language models spot shallow visual cues. They rarely check whether a model can follow a tutorial and finish a long graphical interface task.

The team releases VG-GUI-Bench, a benchmark for video-guided GUI agents, where GUI means the on-screen interface of buttons and menus. They also propose TASKER, a keyframe extraction algorithm that picks informative frames using both task relevance and scene change.
