Peakall notes the package handles several kinds of genetic data, from DNA sequences to simple binary scores. It can also export results to many other formats. Free tutorials and a revised guide came with the release, which kept its strong teaching role.
europmc-pmc3465245:
Kozlowski and Bujnicki described MetaDisorder, a web server that predicts which parts of a protein lack a fixed shape, in BMC Bioinformatics in 2012. Such loose regions matter for health, yet they are hard to spot in the lab. By then about sixty prediction methods existed, each using a different approach, and none was best at everything.

MetaDisorder blends the output of many predictors and weights each by its past accuracy. The authors also built a method that infers loose regions from matches to known protein shapes. Their combined tool had topped a major blind benchmark of prediction methods. Results come back in a clear web view and in plain text for other programs to read.
europmc-pmc3469445:
Coleman-Derr and Zilberman studied a histone variant called H2A.Z in the plant Arabidopsis, in a 2012 PLoS Genetics paper. Histone variants change how DNA is packed and read. H2A.Z was known to gather near gene starts and to avoid stretches marked by DNA methylation, but the reason for that pattern was unclear.

Using a plant line that cannot make H2A.Z, they showed the loss barely changed methylation levels. Instead, methylated DNA seems to keep H2A.Z out. Within gene bodies, more H2A.Z went with lower output and with genes that respond strongly to outside cues. Coleman-Derr proposes that H2A.Z inside genes helps their output vary, letting plants react to change.
europmc-pmc3520745:
ADHD's shadow lengthens into adult life, and Monica Shaw and six colleagues synthesize what treatment does about it in 2012. Their systematic review searches twelve databases for studies following people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder for two years or more.

Outcomes from 351 studies sort into nine areas, from school achievement and driving to addiction, work, and self-esteem. Without treatment, people with ADHD fare worse than peers in every category. Treatment improves long-term outcomes compared with no treatment, though usually not up to typical levels. Only English-language papers were covered, the authors caution. The balanced message: treat, but expect risk reduction, not a cure.
europmc-pmc3555945:
Soybean breeding needed denser markers, and Qijian Song leads an eight-author team building the SoySNP50K genotyping array in 2013. Starting from reduced-representation sequencing of six cultivated and two wild soybean accessions, the group sifts nearly half a billion short reads against the reference genome.

They identify 209,903 SNPs, filter them to 146,161 chip-ready candidates, then use a selection-index algorithm to spread picks evenly and favor reliable assays. The final design submitted 60,800 SNPs for the chip, and 52,041 of them passed Illumina's manufacturing checks to form the SoySNP50K array. Evaluation shows the array calls nearly fifty thousand markers successfully, giving breeders a shared, high-density tool for mapping and selection.
europmc-pmc3597245:
Petr Pyšek and colleagues took a world census of invasive plant damage in Global Change Biology in 2012. Alien plants invading new lands are studied one species and one place at a time, leaving no overview of how harm varies with the plant and the setting. Their team mined 287 publications holding 1,551 cases, covering 167 invading species from forty-nine families, and scored effects on resident species, communities, and ecosystems.

Resident species and community measures usually declined after invasion, plant victims most clearly. Soil life, nutrients, and water, though, rose more often than they fell. For some outcomes, including survival of resident organisms and fire frequency, invaders hit consistently. For community richness and soil resources, the result hinged on the match between invader traits and biome: annual grasses and wind-pollinated trees invading Mediterranean or tropical lands did the most damage. One size of impact, the authors show, fits no invasion.
europmc-pmc3609745:
Rebecca Turner, Sheila Bird, and Julian Higgins examined the small-study problem inside Cochrane meta-analyses in PLoS ONE in 2013. Meta-analysis pools trials to find a treatment's true effect, and most pools include small studies that alone could never prove anything. Nobody had measured how much of the published pooling rested on such underpowered work. The team computed the statistical power of every study inside 14,886 meta-analyses from 1,991 Cochrane reviews.

Seventy percent of the meta-analyses contained only underpowered studies, and barely a third were themselves adequately powered. In a closer subset, small studies reported stronger effects than powered ones. Odds ratios ran about fifteen percent lower in drug trials and twelve percent lower in others, a tilt toward good news. Dropping the small studies widened uncertainty by a median eleven percent. The findings press reviewers to report power honestly.
europmc-pmc3667145:
Mosquitoes carry whole worlds of bacteria, Minard, Mavingui and Moro review in a 2013 Parasites and Vectors article. The germ mix shifts with the mosquito's sex, life stage and surroundings. Some of these bacteria seem to shape how the insect feeds, grows and breeds. The review gathers what is known about the mix and its jobs, with care for fresh findings across many mosquito settings.

Such germs may hand their hosts new traits, letting mosquito kinds spread into new niches and adapt fast, as seen in other insects. That promise has sparked control plans based on doctored germ partners: germs altered so the mosquito passes on fewer disease agents, or lives and breeds less. The authors sort the early proof for such plans. Germ-based control, they argue, is a live option worth testing beside sprays and nets.
europmc-pmc3706345:
Tricco and colleagues pooled randomized trials to ask how well influenza vaccines work when the vaccine strains mismatch the viruses actually circulating. Mismatch happens often, and it decides whether vaccination still pays in a given season. Their review covered thirty-four trials, forty-seven seasons, and nearly ninety-five thousand participants.

Even mismatched vaccines protected significantly. Among young children, the live vaccine was about fifty-four percent effective against mismatched strains, against eighty-three percent when matched. In adults, the standard inactivated vaccine gave about fifty-two percent protection mismatched and sixty-five percent matched. Protection against mismatched influenza A ran higher than against influenza B in both age groups.
europmc-pmc3769145:
Ruth Pidsley and five co-authors presented a data-driven method in BMC Genomics in 2013 for preprocessing data from the Illumina 450K methylation array. The array measures DNA methylation across the genome cheaply, but its design mixes two assay types, so raw data need careful correction. Several normalization schemes competed, with no clear winner.

The team built three independent quality checks from known biology: imprinted regions, sex chromosome patterns, and built-in genotype probes. Testing 11 data sets, they found that quantile normalization clearly beat raw values on all three checks. Normalizing the methylated and unmethylated signals separately beat normalizing their ratio, and handling the two assay types separately helped too. Fancier quantile tricks backfired. They packaged the winning approach as a free R tool called wateRmelon.
europmc-pmc3830745:
Sarah Mizielinska, Tammaryn Lashley, Frances E. Norona, Emma L. Clayton, Charlotte E. Ridler, Pietro Fratta, and Adrian M. Isaacs report a tissue study in Acta Neuropathologica in 2013. Brains from people with a C9orf72 gene fault show clumps of repeat RNA in cells. The team give the first firm count of those clumps, in both RNA directions.

A sharp staining method lit up the clumps in patient frontal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum, but not in controls. Neurons held the most, with over half of frontal cortex neurons bearing clumps, though glia held some too. Clumps showed in cells with and without other disease marks, at rates no higher than chance would predict. The counts set a baseline for judging whether these RNA clumps drive the disease or ride along with it.
europmc-pmc3910245:
Maria Mooshammer, Wolfgang Wanek, Sophie Zechmeister-Boltenstern, and Andreas Richter review in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014 how soil microbes cope when their food has the wrong mix of elements. The dead wood, leaves, and soil matter that decomposers eat rarely match the carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus balance their own bodies need. The mismatch shrinks from wood down to deep soil.

Microbes answer in several ways. They shift their own body chemistry a little, mostly by changing which species dominate. They release enzymes that free the elements they lack, though making enzymes costs carbon and nitrogen too. They also adjust how efficiently they use each element. The review ties these tricks to the wider cycling of nutrients through land ecosystems.
europmc-pmc3967045:
Vanja Pekovic-Vaughan and colleagues show in Genes and Development in 2014 that the body clock times the lung's antioxidant defenses. The defense in question runs through NRF2, a switch that turns on genes for making glutathione, the cell's main antioxidant. Its failure is tied to chronic lung disease. In mouse lung, NRF2 levels rose and fell with the daily circadian rhythm, and the antioxidant genes it controls followed the same beat.

That timing had consequences. Bleomycin, a drug used to model lung scarring, did more fibrotic damage when given at the daily low point of NRF2 than at its peak. The work ties the molecular clock directly to a defense pathway and suggests that when an insult lands, not just how much, shapes lung injury.
europmc-pmc3983045:
Scott M. Robinson and a large team track how coxsackievirus B3 leaves host cells. Their paper appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. This virus causes heart inflammation, meningitis, and pancreas inflammation. The team engineered it to carry a timer protein. The protein glows green when new and turns red with age. That let them watch infection spread in real time. HeLa cells, neural stem cells, and muscle cells all took part. The watch ran for 72 hours.

Interferon and the drug ribavirin slowed the color change. Slower color meant slower spread. The surprise came at exit. Infected stem and muscle cells shed many tiny bubbles. The bubbles carried mature, infectious virus inside. An electron microscope showed virions within them. The shed bubbles bore markers of the cell's autophagy machinery. The authors present them as a new escape route. The virus can spread without bursting its host cell.
europmc-pmc3999945:
Gary S. Collins and ten co-authors review how well studies check prediction models on new data, in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. A prediction model estimates a patient's risk or likely outcome from several traits. Before use, it should be tested on data not used to build it, a step called external validation.

The team searched core medical journals for such studies from 2010 and kept seventy-eight papers, covering one hundred and twenty models. Many fell short. Over half made no clear mention of missing data, and two thirds skipped checks of how well predicted risks matched real rates. Many papers left unclear whether scores came from the full model or a simplified point score. Outcome counts in the test data went unreported in a share of papers too. The authors conclude that most validation studies were poorly run and poorly reported, with key details often missing.
europmc-pmc4033045:
María Llorens-Martín, Jerónimo Jurado, Félix Hernández, and Jesús Ávila review a kinase at the heart of Alzheimer's disease, in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience in 2014. Alzheimer's is the most common dementia of old age, and most cases have no single gene cause. The kinase, named GSK-3, links the disease's two hallmarks: plaques outside cells and tangles inside them.

The review gathers proof that the kinase helps drive both hallmarks and other steps of the disease, from memory loss to cell death. It is one of few molecules tied to each strand of the damage. That central place makes it a prime drug target. The paper weighs the promise against the kinase's many normal jobs, which set the bar for safe dosing.
europmc-pmc4067745:
Paola Di Meglio, Brigitta Stockinger, and colleagues studied a cell switch that senses environmental chemicals, called the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, in inflamed skin. Their study appeared in Immunity in 2014. Such signals are thought to help drive psoriasis, but the mechanism was largely unknown.

Compounds that switch the receptor on reduced inflammation in skin samples from psoriasis patients, while blockers made it worse. In a mouse model of skin inflammation, the body's own activating compound also calmed the response. Mice lacking the receptor got much worse disease, driven by skin cells rather than immune cells, through a family of transcription factors. The authors see the receptor as a possible target for new anti-inflammatory treatments.
europmc-pmc4082845:
Liang-Jun Yan, writing alone, argued that chronic high blood sugar begins with reductive stress, the opposite of the oxidative stress usually blamed. His review appeared in the Journal of Diabetes Research in 2014. Long-term overeating keeps blood sugar high, gradually causing insulin resistance and failing insulin secretion on the road to diabetes.

Yan's chain runs as follows. Excess fuel floods mitochondria with the carrier NADH, and recycling it leaks electrons that form reactive oxygen species. Both the surplus NADH and the reactive species jam a key sugar-burning enzyme. Sugar intermediates then pile up and spill into side pathways, which make still more reactive species. On this account, oxidative damage in diabetes is downstream of an earlier reductive overload.
europmc-pmc4107945:
Stephanie Reikine, Jennifer B. Nguyen, and Yorgo Modis reviewed two virus sensors, RIG-I and MDA5, that detect double-stranded RNA inside cells. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. These innate immune receptors trigger inflammation and form one of the first lines of defence against infection.

The two sensors divide the work. RIG-I spots short viral RNAs carrying a chemical cap, while MDA5 recognises long viral genome RNA and its copies. Binding reshapes each sensor and groups them together, switching on a partner protein on mitochondria and related membranes. Chemical tags and helper proteins, including a third sensor, tune the response. The emerging picture is not a simple chain but a large, self-amplifying platform whose signal depends on context.
europmc-pmc4108045:
Gordon C. S. Smith, Shaun R. Seaman, Angela M. Wood, Patrick Royston, and Ian R. White compared ways to correct optimistic prediction scores in small data sets. Their study appeared in the American Journal of Epidemiology in 2014. Models fitted to small samples tend to flatter themselves, overstating how well a screening test performs.

Using British Down syndrome screening data and Scottish pregnancy records, they tested adjustment methods against the C statistic. Splitting the sample, plain cross-validation, and leave-one-out checks gave biased results or larger errors. Cross-validation with replication, bootstrapping, and a new leave-pair-out method all came out unbiased with similar accuracy. Larger simulations confirmed the ranking when events were reasonably frequent. The work guides analysts choosing a correction method.
europmc-pmc4132645:
Yee-Haur Mah, Masud Husain, Geraint Rees, and Parashkev Nachev showed that the standard method for mapping brain function from patient lesions puts functions in the wrong places. Their study appeared in Brain in 2014. Lesion studies are the strongest test that a brain area is necessary for a function, underpinning knowledge since the nineteenth century.

The common approach tests each tiny volume element one at a time. Natural damage, however, follows tangled patterns: strokes injure connected regions together, so single-spot statistics misread which tissue truly matters. The authors show the error is structural, not a matter of more data. Only high-dimensional methods that weigh all locations jointly can fix it. The paper urges a remapping of lesion-deficit inference across human brain research.
europmc-pmc4162745:
Yasuhiro Takashima, Austin Smith, and colleagues reset human pluripotent stem cells to a ground state resembling mouse embryonic stem cells. Their study appeared in Cell in 2014. Human cells in standard culture lack the control circuitry that keeps mouse cells in their most flexible, naive state.

Briefly switching on two factors, NANOG and KLF2, ignited the rest of the ground-state network. Blocking two signalling enzymes then sustained the rewired state without the added genes. Reset cells renewed themselves indefinitely, stayed chromosomally normal, and could still form all tissue types in tests. Their metabolism shifted toward mitochondrial breathing and their DNA methylation fell sharply. Removing ground-state factors collapsed the reset state but barely touched conventional cells, proving the circuitry had truly been installed.
europmc-pmc4167545:
Corine M. Beaufort, James D. Brenton, and ten co-authors profiled a panel of ovarian cancer cell lines in PLoS ONE in 2014. Ovarian cancer comes in many forms, and drug tests in the lab only mean something if the cell lines used match real tumour types. About 100 lines exist in public collections, yet most had never been described in a uniform way.

The team grew 39 lines under the same conditions and measured growth, gene activity, DNA changes, and drug response. Fourteen lines fit high-grade serous cancer, the most common deadly form. The lines also fell into three shape groups, named Epithelial, Round, and Spindle, and the Spindle group showed more genes tied to cell movement. The panel helps labs pick lines that fit the cancer they study.
europmc-pmc4232245:
Andrew J. Prendergast and Jean H. Humphrey framed stunting as a whole-body syndrome in Paediatrics and International Child Health in 2014. Stunting, growth faltering in early childhood, affects an estimated 165 million children under five. It is the commonest form of undernutrition and a stated global priority, with a target to cut it by 40 percent between 2010 and 2025.

Treating stunting as one syndrome joins its many threads. Repeated infection and gut damage stunt growth, and the stunted child faces higher death risk, weaker learning, and lower earnings, plus more metabolic disease as an adult. Stunted girls grow into mothers of stunted babies, locking in poverty across generations. The review weighs when in the life cycle intervention can still bend that arc.
europmc-pmc4233345:
Maxim V. Petoukhov, Dmitri I. Svergun, and eight co-authors updated a scattering analysis suite in the Journal of Applied Crystallography in 2012. Small-angle scattering bounces X-rays or neutrons off molecules in solution to recover their rough shapes. The ATSAS package is the field's standard toolbox for turning such data into models.

The paper reports the newest additions and upgrades across the package. Automated routines now build low-resolution shapes from scratch and assemble rigid-body models of multi-part complexes with less hand work. Better handling of mixtures and flexible systems widens the range of samples the tools can treat. The methods, first built for biology, now serve materials science as well. The update keeps the suite current with brighter modern beamlines and the heavier data they produce.
europmc-pmc4270245:
Alice Assinger reviews the role of platelets in viral infection in Frontiers in Immunology, published in 2014. Platelets are best known for stopping bleeding, but they also take part in immune defense, and many viral infections switch them on or drive their counts down.

The review covers how viruses can act on platelets directly, how immune complexes and anti-platelet antibodies form, and how low platelet counts mark a poor outlook in sepsis. Platelets can help clear some viruses yet help others persist, so their role cuts both ways. The survey gives clinicians a clear view of when platelet changes in infection are a warning sign.
europmc-pmc4285245:
Ann-Claire Gourinat, Olivia O'Connor, Elodie Calvez, Cyrille Goarant, and Myrielle Dupont-Rouzeyrol report that Zika virus can be found in urine longer than in blood. Their short report appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2015. The mosquito borne virus was spreading in French Polynesia, and clear rules for testing patients were still being worked out.

Six patients gave blood and urine samples over the course of their illness. Virus showed in urine more than ten days after symptoms began, notably longer than in blood samples from the same patients. The finding supports urine as a practical sample for diagnosing Zika infection after the early days pass.
europmc-pmc4316645:
Yuan Gao, Jinfeng Wang, and Fangqing Zhao present CIRI, an algorithm that finds circular RNAs in sequencing data. Their paper appeared in Genome Biology in 2015. Circular RNAs are loops of RNA closed end to end. They turned out to be common and stable in animal cells. Spotting them in transcript data takes a dedicated search, since they do not follow the usual linear pattern.

CIRI reads the telltale clipped signals where a loop's seam appears and filters false hits through several checks. Applied to public human data, it found many circles from within and between genes and the team confirmed examples by experiment. The tool opened systematic study of a class of RNA whose jobs are still being worked out.
europmc-pmc4350445:
Arnald Alonso, Sara Marsal, and Antonio Julià review the analytical pipeline of untargeted metabolomics as it stood in 2015. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology in 2015. Metabolomics measures the full set of small molecules in blood, tissue, or other samples, and it is among the fastest growing measurement fields in biology.

NMR and mass spectrometry advances pour out more data per sample than older statistics can handle. The review walks the whole chain: cleaning raw signals, aligning peaks, testing for group differences, and naming the molecules behind the signals and their pathways. It closes on joining metabolomics with other omics layers, which is where its diagnostic promise in medicine is expected to pay off.

europmc-pmc5238745: Delivery got a ROS-responsive-systems review. This 2017 paper reviews ROS-responsive drug delivery. The authors map the mapping. Their review guides nanomedicine. Saravanakumar's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped drug delivery. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc5402045:
Brad Griesenauer and Sophie Paczesny review the ST2 and IL-33 signal pair in inflamed disease in a 2017 paper in Frontiers in Immunology. ST2 is a receptor on immune cells, and IL-33 is its only known partner signal. The receptor comes in two forms: one fixed in the cell wall that passes the signal on, and one loose form that soaks up IL-33 and blocks it.

The loose form runs high in many ills, from inflamed bowel and lung disease to heart disease, some cancers, and graft-versus-host disease after transplants. In the gut, harmful T cells shed the loose form while guarding T cells that bear the fixed form fall in number. The review maps this pair's roles across diseases and marks where blocking or boosting it could serve as treatment.
europmc-pmc5408845:
Davis J. McCarthy, Kieran R. Campbell, Aaron T. L. Lun, and Quin F. Wills present a software package called scater in a 2017 paper in Bioinformatics. Single-cell RNA reading measures gene activity cell by cell, exposing rare cell types and fine steps in growth. Raw output is messy, though: bias, artifacts, and stray variation demand long cleaning before real study can start, and each lab handles that stage its own way.

Scater gives that stage one shared, careful path inside the R language. It cleans raw reads, checks quality, levels the samples, and plots the data in many forms suited to single cells. Its data format plays well with other tools and can serve as a base for future software. The package is free through Bioconductor, with install help and worked case studies.
europmc-pmc5431945:
Morales-Kastresana and co-authors work out how to stain tiny cell-made vesicles so instruments can count them one by one. Their methods article appeared in Scientific Reports. Cells release extracellular vesicles as message packages. The vesicles range from 30 to 800 nanometers wide. Their cargo may mark cancer and inflammation. It may also serve as therapy. Studying single vesicles needs bright, clean labels. Loose dye can fake a signal.

The team used nanoFACS, a fine flow cytometry method. It reads light scatter and glow from each particle. They compared lipid, protein, and RNA stains. One amine-reactive dye, CFSE, won out. Size exclusion columns then removed unbound dye. The pairing gave strong signal with low background. It also kept the vesicles working. The authors show how to check label quality directly. That check had not been described for other vesicle detectors.
europmc-pmc5444245:
Kryuchkova-Mostacci and Robinson-Rechavi benchmark nine ways to score how tissue-specific a gene is. Their methods article appeared in Briefings in Bioinformatics. Genes fall loosely into two camps. Some work in one tissue only. Others, called housekeeping genes, work everywhere. Many studies sort genes by such scores. Few justify the score they pick. No head-to-head test existed.

The nine measures split into two groups. Five give one number per gene. Four give a score for each tissue. Some began with older tag or chip data. Others were adapted for RNA sequencing. The authors test how well each splits known gene classes. They test toughness when tissue sets change in size or mix. They also test how well each tracks evolutionary conservation. The aim is practical guidance for study design. A poor metric can bend results on gene evolution and function.
europmc-pmc5458145:
Liu and co-authors explain why some metals turn carbon dioxide into fuel faster than others. Their theory study appeared in Nature Communications. Using power to turn CO2 into fuels is a grand challenge in chemistry. Known catalysts waste much energy. A rival reaction that makes hydrogen steals current. Copper alone makes hydrocarbons at fair rates. The team built a math model to find out.

Their model rests on quantum chemistry sums for carbon monoxide steps. A clear pattern emerged from the sums. The energy of key transition states scales with how strongly CO sticks to the metal. That grip sets how active each metal is. The best grip sits very close to copper's own. Model results matched lab tests on rates and product choice. Stepped copper sites did most of the work. The paper closes with two design rules for better catalysts.
europmc-pmc5474745:
Ogrodnik and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on aging cells and fatty liver. With age, more liver cells enter senescence, a stopped state with faulty energy use. Fatty liver also grows more common with age. The team asks if the worn-out cells help drive the fat build-up.

In mice, liver fat tracked closely with markers of cell senescence. Clearing senescent cells cut liver fat, the authors report. They used a gene-based method and a drug pair for that clearing. Forcing liver cells into senescence raised fat instead. Senescent cells burned fatty acids poorly, they find. Removing such cells may become a treatment path.
europmc-pmc5480145:
Atkins and co-authors present a practical guide in Implementation Science. It explains how to use the Theoretical Domains Framework, or TDF, on implementation problems. The framework groups ideas from 33 behavior theories into 14 domains. Teams use it to find why a new practice is not taking hold. No formal how-to guide existed before this one.

The guide walks through each stage of a TDF study. Steps cover picking target behaviors, choosing a design, and building study materials. It also covers sampling, data collection, analysis, and reporting. Worked examples come from published implementation research. The authors note gaps, such as joining data from several sources. Health care teams are the main audience.
europmc-pmc5493145:
Farshidfar and co-authors report a genomic study in Cell Reports on cholangiocarcinoma. This cancer grows in the bile ducts and carries a poor outlook. Treatment options are few, and tumor biology varies a lot. The Cancer Genome Atlas team profiled a set of mostly intrahepatic cases. They joined mutation, gene activity, copy number, and methylation data.

One subtype stood out, rich in IDH gene mutations. That group showed high mitochondrial gene activity and more mitochondrial DNA copies. A chromatin gene, ARID1A, was silenced by methylation in this group. The authors propose a molecular sorting scheme for these tumors. Such sorting may guide future targeted treatment.
europmc-pmc5498545:
Nikolic and co-authors report a virology study in Nature Communications on Negri bodies. Negri bodies are inclusions that rabies virus builds inside host cells. They serve as factories where the virus copies itself. Their physical nature was not known. The team imaged living infected cells to find out.

Negri bodies act like liquid organelles, they report. The droplets are round, merge into larger drops, and vanish under salt shock. Recovery tests confirmed the liquid state. New viral cores exit the droplets and ride cell rails to form fresh factories. Just two viral proteins suffice to rebuild such droplets. Similar liquid factories may serve many related viruses.
europmc-pmc5520745:
Silk and co-authors present a review in Cell Death and Disease on histones outside the cell nucleus. Inside nuclei, histones package DNA and steady gene control. Massive cell death spills them into the blood, though. Sepsis, trauma, and blocked blood flow all release them. Out there they turn toxic alarm signals.

Free histones attack vessel and organ linings directly, they report. They also trip immune sensors, sparking cytokine release and clotting. Animal studies show that blocking or mopping up histones cuts deaths sharply. Antibodies and natural proteins like C-reactive protein offer protection. Human trials remain the open question.
europmc-pmc5533845:
Fischer and Schmutzhard present a review in the Journal of Neurology on posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, or PRES. This brain disorder strikes fast, with headache, seizures, confusion, and vision loss. Scans show swelling at the back of the brain. Blood pressure often spikes to emergency levels. Triggers include pregnancy complications, kidney disease, sepsis, and toxic drugs.

Most patients recover fully once the trigger is treated, they report. About 40 percent still need intensive care during the crisis. Two rival theories explain the swelling: pressure overload or vessel wall injury. Imaging patterns guide the diagnosis, since no trial evidence exists. Lasting epilepsy remains a rare risk.
europmc-pmc5550745:
Fernández-Arjona and co-authors present a research article in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Their subject is the shape of microglia, the brain's immune cells. Shape and function are closely linked in these cells. Yet few studies sort their shapes in an objective way.

The team caused brief brain inflammation in rats with a single enzyme dose. They then measured 15 shape traits in cells from three brain regions. Samples came at 2, 4, and 12 hours after the dose. Cluster methods sorted the cells into four groups, and finer analysis gave eight types. Three traits alone could classify a cell by a decision tree. Readers get a firm method for naming microglia states by shape.
europmc-pmc5657845:
Jamal and co-authors present a federal surveillance report in MMWR. It tracks tobacco use among United States school students. Data came from the National Youth Tobacco Surveys of 2011 to 2016. Students were in middle school or high school. Seven product types were covered, from cigarettes to e-cigarettes. Current use meant use in the past 30 days.

In 2016, about one in five high school students used tobacco. About seven percent of middle school students did so. E-cigarettes were the most used product at both levels. Nearly half of users took two or more products. Overall use barely changed across the survey years. Combustible product use fell, while e-cigarette use rose sharply.
europmc-pmc5688245:
Greenhalgh and co-authors build a framework for why health technologies fail to spread. Many new tools in health and social care are never adopted or are soon dropped. Others fail to scale up, spread, or last over time. The team set out to predict and judge such outcomes.

They reviewed past frameworks and studied six technology programs in depth. The work used over 400 hours of observation and 165 interviews. Their NASSS framework asks questions across seven domains. These range from the illness and the tool to the wider policy context. Programs with complexity in many domains rarely became routine. The framework can guide design, rollout, and reviews of failed programs.
europmc-pmc5726245:
Lee-Kwan and co-authors report CDC survey results on fruit and vegetable intake. They use data from a large 2015 phone survey of United States adults. The study checks how many adults met daily intake advice. It breaks results down by state and by social group.

Only 12.2% of adults met the fruit advice, the authors report. Just 9.3% met the vegetable advice. Women and Hispanic adults scored highest for fruit intake. Rates stayed low in all income groups and all states. The team points to cost and poor access as bars to better diets, and urges steps that lower both.
europmc-pmc5760645:
Fang and co-authors study how the crystal faces of palladium nanocrystals affect their power to kill bacteria. Such metal particles can mimic enzymes and make reactive oxygen. Which face shows may change that action. The team compared cube shaped crystals with octahedron shaped ones.

Cubes, with {100} faces, showed stronger enzyme like activity. They also killed Gram-positive bacteria better, matching that activity. Against Gram-negative bacteria the trend flipped. Octahedrons slipped into those membranes more deeply and killed better. The work maps how face choice can aim antibacterial action at set targets.
europmc-pmc5786545:
Martin and Bachman review Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium split by its accessory genome. Extra genes on plasmids and chromosomes sort strains into three broad groups. Some infect only frail hospital patients. Others strike healthy people in the community. A third group resists nearly all antibiotics.

The review traces how gut colonization can turn into infection in each group. It shows how the extra genes mark the groups and split them from two sister species. Sites from lung to blood and liver feature. With resistance and virulence both rising, knowing these groups matters for care, they argue.
europmc-pmc5789045:
Tiulpin and co-authors build a deep learning system that grades knee osteoarthritis from plain X-rays. Human grading of these films is subjective. Their network was trained on one large study and tested on 3,000 people from another. It scores severity on the standard Kellgren-Lawrence scale.

The system agreed strongly with a committee of clinical experts, they report. It also separated diseased from healthy knees with high accuracy. Attention maps show which film features drove each call. That openness builds trust with clinicians, the authors argue. Code and data were released for research use.
europmc-pmc5807345:
Williams and O'Neill review citrate as a signal in immune cells. Immune cells rewire their energy use when they switch on. One effect is a build-up of citrate, a Krebs cycle chemical. Citrate leaves the cell's power plant and takes new jobs.

In the cell body, citrate feeds fat building and protein tagging. Both steps help macrophages and dendritic cells attack germs. A citrate product, itaconate, kills bacteria directly. It also calms inflammation by blocking a key enzyme. Readers get a neat case of a fuel chemical moonlighting as an immune messenger.
europmc-pmc5830445:
Stewart and co-authors assemble 913 microbe genomes from the cow rumen. The rumen ferments plant feed into energy for the cow. Its microbes do most of that work with enzymes. Their genomes were largely unsequenced until now.

Over 800 gigabases of DNA came from 43 Scottish cattle. Binning and Hi-C methods built the draft genomes. Most strains and species are new to science. The set holds over 69,000 proteins for carbohydrate breakdown. Over 90 percent match nothing in public databases. Adding the genomes lifts read classification sevenfold. Readers get a deep resource for feed and enzyme research.
europmc-pmc5844645:
Sánchez-Cordón and co-authors review African swine fever, a viral plague re-spreading through the world's pigs. Their review appeared in The Veterinary Journal. The virus is harmless to people but lethal to herds. It reached Georgia in 2007 and rolled across Eastern Europe.

Wild boar carry and spread the genotype now circulating. Acute disease can kill nearly every infected pig. No vaccine exists, since the immune response stays poorly mapped. Control still means culling herds and freezing pig movements. The authors weigh vaccine leads and the heavy costs of outbreaks.
europmc-pmc5852245:
Maeda and Khatami dissect six decades of failure against solid tumors. Their analysis appeared in Clinical and Translational Medicine. The authors put the failure rate of cancer therapies near 90 percent. They blame a reductionist hunt for single molecular targets.

Tumors, they argue, are chaotic and mutate without pause. Drugs tuned to one target miss the moving whole. Poor delivery to tumor tissue compounds the problem. Costs, meanwhile, have grown unsustainable for health systems. The pair question vaccine hype on similar grounds. They close by urging fundamentally different strategies. Leukemias, they note, are the rare exception to the pattern.
europmc-pmc5860745:
Bellou and co-authors present an umbrella review of risk factors for type 2 diabetes. Their article appeared in PLoS ONE. Many non-genetic factors have been linked to the disease. The team gathered all meta-analyses and Mendelian randomization studies on PubMed. They found 86 papers covering 142 associations. Each link was checked for bias and strength of evidence.

Robust evidence tied higher risk to body fat and some blood markers. Processed meat and sweet drinks raised risk in the pooled data. Whole grains and coffee linked to lower risk. Low activity, smoking, and air pollution also raised risk. So did conditions such as metabolic syndrome and gestational diabetes. The authors urge trials on daily habit change.
europmc-pmc5880245:
Korpela and co-authors trace how maternal bacteria seed the infant gut. Their article appeared in Genome Research. The team tracked rare strain markers in family stool samples. Such markers show exactly where gut bacteria come from. They also show how long early colonizers persist. Vaginally born infants received selected strains from their mothers. Those strains lasted at least a year in many cases.

Only two bacterial classes passed from mother and persisted. Clostridia strains, common in mothers, were not seen in infants. Caesarean-born infants showed almost no maternal transfer at birth. Later, family strains kept arriving, even into adulthood. Fathers gave new strains more often than they received them.
europmc-pmc5973945:
Amico and Goñi pursue identifiability in human functional connectomes. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. A functional connectome may carry a personal fingerprint. That promise could support single-subject inferences from brain scans. The authors rebuild each person's connectome from group-wise modes. They use data from the Human Connectome Project. A set number of connectivity eigenmodes drives the rebuilding.

Optimal rebuilding maximised who could be told apart, they report. The gain held at rest and across all seven tasks. It also held when rebuild rules moved to new data. Rebuilt profiles linked more robustly to task behaviour. The method also maps the connections most sensitive to tasks.
europmc-pmc6018545:
Giguère and co-authors review cell loss in Parkinson's disease. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Neurology. Parkinson's is best known for losing dopamine neurons. Those cells sit in a brain region called the substantia nigra. Their loss drives the main motor symptoms.

Loss also occurs in many other brain regions. The review weighs the proof for each affected population. It asks which cells die, and in what order. It also examines traits that may make cells fragile. Such traits include chemistry, shape, and firing patterns. Readers get a broad map of the disease beyond dopamine. The authors link these ideas to better models and future treatments.
europmc-pmc6099145:
Jafari and Ansari-Pour explain why p values need adjusting when tests multiply. Their guide appeared in Cell Journal. Big biology data now invites hundreds of tests per study. Each test carries a false positive risk. One shared cutoff lets errors pile up.

The guide first defines what a p value really says. It then shows when adjustment becomes due. Worked examples run inside the R environment. Readers learn the methods step by step. The authors also urge reporting effect size and power. Confidence intervals belong beside p values. The piece is brief but pointed. It targets association studies in gene research most of all.
europmc-pmc6127345:
Li and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on the structure of alpha-synuclein fibrils. Alpha-synuclein is a protein that clumps into fibrils in diseases such as Parkinson's. The fibrils come in several forms, called polymorphs. Each form seeds new clumps in its own way.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team solved the structures of the two main forms, named rod and twister. Both were resolved to near-atomic detail. The two share a common core, a bent beta-arch shape. They differ in how their strands pack against each other. The work shows how one protein can build distinct fibrils from the same kernel.
europmc-pmc6151045:
Guo and co-authors wrote a review in Journal of Nanobiotechnology on redox-responsive drug delivery for tumors. These carriers stay stable while they travel in the blood. Inside tumor cells, a molecule called glutathione runs high. That signal can trip the carrier to dump its cargo fast and in the right place.

The review sorts the main designs of such systems. Systems built on disulfide bonds get the most attention. Quick release inside target cells can raise drug levels there. It can also cut side effects on healthy tissue. The authors survey studies across gene and drug delivery. They note where the field may head next.
europmc-pmc6155145:
Pärnänen and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on where infants get antibiotic resistance genes. Infant gut microbes carry many resistance genes, even without antibiotic exposure. Adults carry fewer. The team looked for the sources of this early load.

They sequenced microbes from breast milk and from the guts of mothers and infants. An infant's resistance genes and mobile genetic elements matched its own mother's profile more than other mothers'. Elements in breast milk were also shared with the mother's own infant. Stopping breastfeeding and antibiotics given to mothers at delivery also shaped the profiles. The work shows resistance passing from mother to child.
europmc-pmc6177445:
Ho and co-authors present a meta-analysis in Nature Communications on exclusive breastfeeding and infant gut microbes. Earlier studies disagreed sharply on how feeding shapes the baby gut. Results varied by population and method. The team combined raw data across studies to find consistent patterns.

They pooled seven microbiome studies, covering 1,825 stool samples from 684 infants. In the first six months, non-breastfed infants had higher gut diversity and a more mature-looking microbiota. Some bacterial groups and carbohydrate pathways were higher in those infants. Lipid and vitamin pathways ran lower. Effects of feeding length could still be seen up to age two. The work settles several disputes in a debated literature.
europmc-pmc6181645:
Guo and co-authors present a research article in Cell Reports on jumping genes in Alzheimer's disease. Transposable elements are DNA stretches that can switch on and move within the genome. Aging and diseased neurons show more of this instability. The protein tau, which tangles in Alzheimer's brains, was the suspect.

RNA data from 636 human brains linked tangle load to higher activity of several retrotransposons. Whole families, including LINE1 and ancient retroviruses, were more active. Open chromatin marks appeared at matching sites. In fruit flies, adding human tau was enough to switch these elements on. The work ties tau directly to a restless genome in diseased neurons.
europmc-pmc6207145:
Böttcher and Reis e Sousa review a rare immune cell type and its role in cancer. Their review appeared in Trends in Cancer. The cells are type 1 conventional dendritic cells, called cDC1s. These cells pick up material from tumours. They then start fresh T cell responses against the cancer. Recent work links them to better survival in human patients.

Inside tumours, cDC1s draw in T cells and release signals that help them work. They also present tumour material to killer T cells on site. In mouse models, tumours fail to be rejected without these cells. T cell therapies also work less well. The authors argue that raising cDC1 numbers in tumours could help more patients respond to immune therapy.
europmc-pmc6265445:
Ou, Chen, and Jiang propose a new score for judging plant genome assemblies. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Plant genomes are full of repeated DNA, which makes them hard to assemble. No standard score covered that repeat space. Their score is called the LTR Assembly Index, or LAI. It uses one repeat family, the LTR retrotransposons, as its yardstick.

LAI checks how continuous the assembled repeats are. After a correction for repeat growth patterns, the score stays steady across genome sizes. It does not track gene based scores such as BUSCO. Tests across sequencing methods showed clear gains from long read methods. The score can also flag weak regions of an assembly. That helps teams pick better tools and improve drafts step by step. The program is free on GitHub.
europmc-pmc6280645:
Oki and co-authors present ChIP-Atlas, a platform that unites public gene binding data. Their paper appeared in EMBO Reports. ChIP-seq tests show where proteins bind DNA across a genome. Public archives held over 70,000 such data sets. They covered six model organisms, from humans to yeast. No single tool had joined them all before.

The platform shows binding peaks for all archived sets at any chosen locus. Histone marks and regulator binding can be viewed together. Users can test which proteins bind near a set of genes. Links between regulators can also be charted. Data come from major archives and the published literature. The authors claim wider coverage than rival platforms. The suite is free online for any researcher. It turns a scattered archive into a working atlas.
europmc-pmc6288145:
Doherty and co-authors searched the genome for variants tied to measured activity and sleep. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Activity and sleep shape risk for many diseases. Self reports of both are rough, though. Wrist devices gave exact measures for this study. The sample held 91,105 UK Biobank participants.

Fourteen genome regions reached significance, seven of them new. Together they explained only a small share of the variation. Gene wide estimates suggest about fifteen percent heritability overall. Women showed higher heritability than men for activity. Brain tissue signals stood out in the pathway checks. A causal test suggested more activity lowers blood pressure. Odds of hypertension fell as activity rose in that test. The results back device based measures for gene hunting.
europmc-pmc6323945:
The Gene Ontology Consortium reports two years of progress for its resource. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The resource gives structured, computable terms for gene functions. It has served life sciences for twenty years. Each monthly release now gets a unique identifier. That lets past analyses be reproduced exactly.

The molecular function branch was rebuilt for clarity. Transcription regulator activities got special attention. Quality checks now hunt stale or wrong annotations. New evidence codes flag high-throughput sources. A richer modeling frame, GO-CAM, was released. It expresses gene function beyond standard annotations. A ribbon widget shows a gene's annotations at a glance. Any web page can embed it.
europmc-pmc6359645:
Liao and co-authors review silver nanoparticles in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Tiny silver particles kill bacteria well, so makers put them in wound dressings, fabrics, and health products. They can be made by physical, chemical, or living routes.

Wide use means people now meet these particles in daily life. Cell tests show harm to lung, liver, blood, and skin cells. The harm grows with dose and exposure time, and it depends on particle size. The review weighs the strong germ-killing gains against these safety risks. It calls for care in how the particles are used.
europmc-pmc6379245:
Franke and co-authors review ADHD across the lifespan in European Neuropsychopharmacology. ADHD is the most common developmental disorder of childhood, and it is strongly heritable. In many people it does not end at puberty but runs into adult life.

Signs and linked problems shift with age. Substance use, depression, anxiety, and accidents are common partners of the disorder. The review tracks what predicts whether ADHD persists or fades. Proof on that point is still weak and mixed, they warn. Better long-term studies could guide care at each age.
europmc-pmc6395045:
Madani and co-authors report a deep learning study in NPJ Digital Medicine. Echocardiograms, or heart ultrasounds, come in many standard views. A computer must name the view before it can read the scan further.

Their network learned from still images and videos of 267 real heart scans. It sorted twelve video views with 97.8 percent accuracy. Even single low-grade still frames were sorted well across fifteen views. The model did not just memorize its training set, tests showed. The authors call view sorting a first step toward full computer reading of heart scans.
europmc-pmc6418145:
Jendryka and co-authors report a mouse study in Scientific Reports on chemogenetic tools. DREADD receptors let researchers switch chosen brain cells on or off with a drug. The usual drug, clozapine-N-oxide, was thought to act directly on those receptors.

The team compared it with clozapine itself and with compound 21. Clozapine proved far more potent at the receptor, and part of the first drug turns into clozapine in mice. Yet the first drug also reached the brain in its own right at active levels. The results warn that drug choice changes what a chemogenetic test really shows.
europmc-pmc6426845:
Zhao and co-authors report a cascade anchoring strategy that mass-produces single-atom metal-nitrogen catalysts without the atoms clumping together. Such catalysts spread individual metal atoms on carbon, using every atom while keeping sites uniform. Loading more metal usually forces atoms to merge into particles, which defeats the design.

Three steps solve the tension: metal ions are first locked in a chelate, the complexes stay physically separated even at high loading, and heating binds them to nitrogen. Loadings reached 12.1 weight percent across a series of metals. The iron version reduced oxygen well, and the nickel version handled carbon dioxide reduction. Factories gain a general recipe for dense, stable single-atom catalysts.
europmc-pmc6460045:
Seiler and Jenewein review resilience and posttraumatic growth in cancer patients and survivors, asking what strengthens or weakens each and how they relate to mental health. Cancer diagnosis and treatment bring distress that can shadow patients for years; resilience names the capacity to hold or regain stable functioning through it. Their search ran on PubMed to May 2018.

Biological and personal factors contribute, but social support matters most, feeding both resilience and the positive life changes of posttraumatic growth. The authors build a model linking the two and argue both are measurable and modifiable through psychological and drug interventions. Promoting them, they conclude, belongs inside standard cancer care.
europmc-pmc6512245:
Fletcher-Watson and co-authors report on a UK seminar series about doing autism research with autistic people, not just on them, in the journal Autism. The series was co-produced by autistic and non-autistic academics, practitioners and people with lived experience. It grew from a gap: research output is large, yet little of it reaches practice, and many in the community feel shut out.

The group named five topics for a healthier research culture: respect, authenticity, assumptions, infrastructure and empathy. Each is tied to real examples from research and beyond. The authors call for training in participatory methods across the field, and for far more autistic leadership and true partnership in studies. Done well, they argue, such work is more likely to change practice and improve lives.
europmc-pmc6572845:
Harutyunyan and co-authors build public benchmarks for machine learning on intensive care time series, writing in Scientific Data. Clinical ML has lacked shared yardsticks, so results across papers barely compare. Their suite draws on the open MIMIC-III database and defines four prediction tasks over records from more than 40,000 ICU stays.

The tasks ask a model to forecast death in hospital, spot physiological decline, estimate length of stay, and classify patient phenotypes. The authors supply strong linear and neural baselines for each, with open code so anyone can reproduce the numbers. Their experiments test whether training one network on all four tasks at once beats single-task models, and where deep supervision helps or hurts.
europmc-pmc6602445:
Buchan and Jones mark twenty years of the PSIPRED Protein Analysis Workbench. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The web server offers protein prediction tools to bioscience users. It runs about 250,000 predictions each year. Growing sequence databases had slowed its analyses down.

The team rewrote the whole site code from 2015 onward. A new workflow platform makes new tools easy to deploy. Result diagrams now render in the user's browser, which cuts server load. The workbench offers 12 sequence analysis methods and four structure tools. The authors also survey updates to key prediction algorithms. New hardware and web services aim to keep the server fast for years ahead.
europmc-pmc6704245:
Molnár and co-authors review new insights into growth of the human cerebral cortex. Their synthesis appears in the Journal of Anatomy. Rodent models cannot capture uniquely human features. The cortex exceeds half the human brain's volume. Association areas are greatly enlarged in humans. Upper layers show relative expansion too. Inhibitory interneuron diversity is enhanced. The transient subplate layer expands sharply as the brain grows. Progenitor spread generates the neuronal variety. Earliest circuits form within the subplate. Their disruption links to developmental pathologies.

Gene expression networks are compared in depth. Risk genes for developmental diseases are mapped. Organoids from stem cells recapitulate some aspects. Imaging now links histology to living brains. How the cortex emerged is the framing question.
europmc-pmc6714445:
Liu and co-authors reviewed cancer-associated fibroblasts as a target for immunotherapy. Fibroblasts are support cells, and the ones inside tumors are among the most common cells there. They prop up tumor cells, but they can speed up or slow down tumor growth. They also shape how the immune system behaves.

Recent work shows these fibroblasts help tumors hide from immune attack. That may explain why some patients respond poorly to immunotherapy. The review covers where the cells come from and how their subtypes differ. It ends with treatment ideas that target the fibroblasts to free the immune system against the tumor.
europmc-pmc6722045:
GBD 2017 Childhood Cancer Collaborators measured the global burden of cancer in children and teens in 2017. Good data are scarce in many countries, so the team modeled estimates from death records, verbal autopsies, and cancer registries. Ages covered ran from birth to 19 years. The study is part of the Global Burden of Disease project.

For the first time, the burden is expressed in disability-adjusted life-years. These combine years of life lost with years lived in poor health. Registry incidence was converted to deaths through modeled ratios. Results are reported worldwide and by region, with uncertainty ranges. Planners can use them to set resources and priorities.
europmc-pmc6796845:
Tang and co-authors review the molecular machinery of regulated cell death. Cells can die by accident, in an uncontrolled way, or by regulated programs with defined signaling steps. Beyond classic apoptosis, many non-apoptotic programs have been found in recent years. Each is increasingly tied to human disease. This review critically surveys the current state of the art.

Forms covered include necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and entotic, netotic, and lysosome-dependent death. Rarer programs such as parthanatos, alkaliptosis, and oxeiptosis also appear. The authors explain each lethal subroutine and its fallout for neighboring cells. Understanding these pathways may reveal drug targets. Blocking the wrong kind of cell death could prevent tissue loss in several pathologies.
europmc-pmc6813045:
Xie and co-authors offer a review in Molecular Cancer on a form of PD-L1 carried by exosomes. PD-L1 is a protein that can quiet T cells when it binds PD-1. Tumour cells often make much of it. That helps cancers escape immune attack.

Exosomes are tiny vesicles shed by cells to send signals. The review covers how tumour exosomes aid growth, spread, and new blood vessels. It also covers how exosomal PD-L1 may blunt checkpoint drugs. The authors suggest this form could serve as a marker. They also propose it as a target to beat drug resistance.
europmc-pmc6930145:
Zoghlami and Paës review why plant biomass resists being turned into fuel. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Chemistry. Plant material, called lignocellulosic biomass, is abundant and renewable. It could supply biofuels and chemicals without cutting into food supplies. The barrier is recalcitrance: tough plant cell walls resist enzyme attack.

The authors sort the causes into structural and chemical factors. Structure covers surface area, crystallinity, chain length, and pore size. Chemistry covers lignin and hemicellulose content, plus acetyl groups. These factors interconnect, which makes them hard to separate. The review surveys the best tools for measuring each one. New spectral and water-based measures can predict how well a sample will break down.
europmc-pmc6941045:
Tirpe and co-authors review how low oxygen drives cancer forward. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Hypoxia, a shortage of oxygen, appears in many tumours. It helps cancers grow, spread, and resist treatment. Most examples come from lung cancer, the leading malignancy by cases and deaths.

Low oxygen switches on hypoxia-inducible factors, called HIFs. These factors control many genes tied to progression. They trigger cell shape changes that aid metastasis, through pathways such as TGF-β and Wnt. They also spur new blood vessels, chiefly through the HIF-1α and VEGF route. Metabolic rewiring follows too, including the Warburg shift toward glycolysis. Understanding these links, the authors argue, could expose new treatment targets.
europmc-pmc6966445:
Owen and co-authors review JAK-STAT signalling, a pathway that can fight cancer or feed it. Their review appeared in Cancers. This signalling chain carries messages for almost all immune regulation. It shapes how tumours are recognised, and how they escape.

Two members, STAT1 and STAT2, switch on interferons, the signals that power anti-tumour immunity. A third, STAT3, is widely tied to cancer cell survival, immune suppression, and lasting inflammation around tumours. New findings on cross-talk between pathway branches, chemical control, and side routes add complexity. Perturbing the pathway can start or advance cancer at many points. Drugs aimed at its faults are multiplying, yet off-target effects dog them. The authors weigh current treatments and what smarter targeting will need.
europmc-pmc7023045:
Atalay, Jarocka-Karpowicz, and Skrzydlewska review cannabidiol in the journal Antioxidants. Cannabidiol, or CBD, is a main active compound of the cannabis plant. Unlike THC, it does not cause a high. It has drawn wide research interest for its calming, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant effects.

The review covers the chemistry of CBD and its synthetic derivatives. It explains how CBD interacts with cannabinoid receptors and other parts of the endocannabinoid system. The main focus is cell-level action against oxidative stress and inflammation. The authors review lab and clinical evidence for diseases tied to oxidative damage. They note that the effects depend on dose, and that CBD has shown a good safety profile in many trials.
europmc-pmc7048745:
Deng and co-authors review ubiquitination in cancer in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Ubiquitination tags proteins for disposal or control. It sets both the amount and the quality of proteins in a cell. When the tagging system goes wrong, cancer can follow.

The review explains the parts of the system: the proteasome and the E1, E2, and E3 enzymes, plus enzymes that remove the tags. It then shows how tagging shapes tumour metabolism and the immune setting around tumours. Tagging also helps cancer stem cells keep their stem-like state. Drugs aimed at each part are surveyed. Proteasome blockers such as bortezomib have already worked in patients, the authors note. Other compounds remain at the lab stage.
europmc-pmc7077245:
Gralinski and Menachery review the return of coronavirus in the journal Viruses. A novel coronavirus, 2019-nCoV, emerged in December 2019 among patients connected to the Huanan South China Seafood Market in Wuhan. It was the third zoonotic human coronavirus of the century, after SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV. Patients showed viral pneumonia: fever, difficult breathing, and, in severe cases, infiltration of both lungs.

Chinese authorities closed and decontaminated the market on 1 January 2020, and the virus was identified within days, first in one patient and then verified in 16 more. The review asks whether the world is better equipped this time. Early absence of infections in health care workers hinted at inefficient human spread, a hopeful sign the authors already doubted as case counts climbed and market links thinned. The source of the virus remained unknown, which they flag as the key missing fact.
europmc-pmc7085845:
Sánchez-García and co-authors systematically review the triglyceride and glucose index, a simple blood measure proposed as a stand-in test for insulin resistance, in the International Journal of Endocrinology. The reference test, a clamp procedure, is costly and complex, so a cheap marker would be useful. The team searched four major databases without language limits.

Fifteen studies with 69,922 participants met their rules. Accuracy varied widely, with the best sensitivity at 96% against the clamp test and the best specificity at 99% against a blood-based score. Cutoff values differed between studies, which limits comparison. The authors judge the evidence moderate to low in quality and call for standard cutoffs before clinical use.
europmc-pmc7110745:
McLaughlin and co-authors set out a model of how childhood trauma leads to mental illness, in BMC Medicine. Trauma in childhood raises the risk of nearly every common form of psychopathology. The authors look for shared pathways that cross single diagnoses, rather than one path per disorder.

Their model spans three domains. First, social processing shifts toward threat, so neutral faces get read as anger. Second, emotional processing changes, with stronger reactions and weaker control. Third, the body ages faster, in puberty timing and at the cell level. These shifts may help a child stay safe in a dangerous home, yet they seed later illness. Support from caregivers can buffer the harm. Readers get a clear target list for early help after trauma.
europmc-pmc7143945:
Zhao, Yu, and Ding review how quorum sensing, the chemical chatter bacteria use to sense their own numbers, controls antibiotic resistance, in Microorganisms. When signal molecules build up past a threshold, whole populations switch on shared behaviours. Those behaviours include pumping drugs out of cells and building protective biofilms.

Most human bacterial infections involve biofilms, which help infections resist treatment and return. The review maps how sensing systems regulate efflux pumps and biofilm formation across Gram-negative and Gram-positive species. It then discusses quorum quenching, jamming the signals, as a strategy to prevent resistance rather than kill bacteria outright, which could slow the selection pressure that breeds tougher strains.
europmc-pmc7158945:
Sun, Chen, and Viboud build an early epidemiological picture of COVID-19 from crowdsourced news and social network reports, in The Lancet Digital Health. Official data were scarce in January 2020, so they mined DXY.cn, a Chinese health social network, plus international news sources. Their patient list and province counts were published openly in real time.

They collected 507 patients reported between 13 and 31 January, 364 in mainland China and 143 abroad. Of these, 55% were male and the median age was 46; only 3% were under 15. Delays between falling ill and seeking care were longest in Hubei and shrank across China after 18 January as awareness grew.
europmc-pmc7186945:
Kotfis and co-authors address delirium care for COVID-19 patients in intensive care. Their article appeared in Critical Care. Delirium is a sudden state of confusion and poor attention. It signals serious strain on the body and brain. Patients with severe COVID-19 face a high risk of it. Long ventilation, heavy sedation, and isolation all raise that risk. Family absence adds to the problem.

The authors list seven routes that can lead to delirium in these patients. They include direct virus effects on the brain and organ failure. Sedation choices and long immobility also play a part. The article urges teams to keep standard delirium checks in place. Valid screening tools catch cases that charts often miss. The authors give steps to cut modifiable risks. Their aim is better long-term survival and less harm after intensive care.
europmc-pmc7217645:
Roberton and co-authors model the indirect deaths the COVID-19 pandemic could cause among mothers and young children. Their study appeared in The Lancet Global Health. The virus kills directly, but it also disrupts clinics and food access. The team modeled low-income and middle-income countries. They tested three scenarios of shrinking care coverage.

In those scenarios, coverage of key maternal and child services fell by roughly 10 to 52 percent. Child wasting, a sign of hunger, rose by 10 to 50 percent. Across 118 countries, the losses added up to many extra deaths. Vaccines were assumed to keep their full protective effect. The authors warn that protecting routine care is life-saving too. Their estimates were meant as an early alert, not a forecast.
europmc-pmc7360645:
Kovacs and co-authors map tau protein damage in progressive supranuclear palsy across many postmortem brains, in Acta Neuropathologica. The disease is a tauopathy, where tau clumps harm neurons and support cells, mostly below the cortex. The international team asked whether the damage follows a set sequence of spread.

Across clinical subtypes, tau concentrated in neurons of one deep brain circuit, the pallido-nigro-luysian axis. Subtypes differed less in total damage than in which cell types and regions were hit, neuronal versus glial. For the classic Richardson syndrome group, with 81 cases, patterns could be staged in sequence. The maps suggest each subtype spreads tau along its own circuits. Readers get an anatomy of a rare disease's advance.
europmc-pmc7386645:
Newby and co-authors survey acute mental health responses to COVID-19 in Australia, in PLoS ONE. The online survey ran from 27 March to 7 April 2020, the peak of Australia's first outbreak, and drew 5,070 adults. It covered fears, behavior changes, distress, health anxiety, drinking, and activity.

A striking 78 percent said their mental health had worsened since the outbreak began. About 25.9 percent were very or extremely worried about catching the virus, and 52.7 percent worried about family and friends. Elevated distress appeared in 62 percent for depression measures and 64 percent for stress. Uncertainty, loneliness, and money worries were each common. People with a prior mental health diagnosis fared worst. The snapshot captures a population's first shock.
europmc-pmc7436545:
Reddy and co-authors pool studies on smoking and COVID-19 severity. Early meta-analyses on this question were small and weak in method. The team searched four databases for studies of hospitalized patients.

They analyzed 47 studies with data on smoking and disease outcomes. Current smokers had higher risk of severe COVID-19, with a risk ratio of 1.80. People with any smoking history faced more severe disease, more deaths in hospital, and more disease progress. They also needed mechanical ventilation more often. The authors conclude that current and former smokers are a high-risk group. Prevention and support for these patients matter most while no targeted therapies exist.
europmc-pmc7467845:
Rees and co-authors review how long COVID-19 patients stay in hospital and intensive care. Planners need stay lengths to forecast bed and staff needs. The team pooled early studies and built shared distributions.

They found 52 studies, 46 of them from China. Median hospital stay ranged from 4 to 53 days in China and 4 to 21 days elsewhere across the reporting studies. Their pooled median was 14 days for China and 5 days outside China. Intensive care medians were closer: 8 days in China and 7 days elsewhere in the pooled distributions. Patients who left alive stayed longer than those who died. Admission and discharge rules may explain much of the China gap. The method can refresh as new data come.
europmc-pmc7491045:
Mosser, Hamidzadeh, and Goncalves argue that macrophages should be seen as cell transducers, not just immune cells. Most writing on macrophages centers on polarization and host defense. That lens, they say, is too narrow for cells found all over the body.

Macrophages sense a vast range of inputs from their surroundings. They convert those inputs into responses that fit the tissue at hand. Their prime task, in this view, is keeping homeostasis. Roles in development, tissue remodeling, wound healing, vessel growth, and metabolism all fit that task. The chapter lists the signals macrophages perceive. It then traces the responses they make to keep tissues steady. The frame may reshape how macrophage states are named and studied.
europmc-pmc7495445:
Sawaya and co-authors trace why diabetic foot ulcers fail to heal, with the factor FOXM1 at the center. These ulcers threaten limbs and life. Their molecular roots were poorly known.

The team sequenced tissue from human diabetic foot ulcers. They compared the profiles with acute skin wounds and oral wounds, which heal fast without scars. Ulcer tissue showed broken networks for calling in neutrophils and macrophages. Inflammation ran poorly controlled as a result. Two factors that switch on and sustain immune cells, FOXM1 and STAT3, were shut down in ulcers. Blocking FOXM1 in diabetic mice slowed healing and cut immune cell entry. The work names FOXM1-driven immune failure as a core driver of these wounds.
europmc-pmc7505845:
Hao and co-authors uncover how fat cells take in fatty acids through the CD36 receptor. Fatty acids are vital nutrients, but their entry path into cells was unclear. The team tracked CD36 moves in adipocytes.

When fatty acids bind CD36, the receptor dives inside the cell through caveolae. That dive carries the fatty acids in with it. A kinase chain runs the process: LYN and SYK fire in turn, and a fat tag on CD36 is added and removed. Locking CD36 in either tagged state kills its uptake work. Blocking the chain stops fatty acid uptake and fat droplet growth. In mice, it also cut weight gain on a high-fat diet. The work names a dynamic, tag-run entry path for fats.
europmc-pmc7537045:
Wang and co-authors show that an enzyme called CH25H can block coronaviruses. The enzyme is switched on by interferon during infection. It converts cholesterol into 25-hydrocholesterol, called 25HC.

The team found CH25H induced by SARS-CoV-2 in cells. Levels also rose in patients with COVID-19. The product 25HC blocked membrane fusion by viruses. It stopped infection in lung epithelial cells. It also blocked viral entry in human lung organoids. The mechanism drains accessible cholesterol from cell membranes. That loss stops virus and cell fusion. The authors propose 25HC as a broad treatment candidate.
europmc-pmc7551545:
Zahavi and Weiner review monoclonal antibodies in cancer therapy. Antibody therapy now sits beside surgery, radiation and chemotherapy. Antibodies can hit tumor cells in direct ways.

They can also spark lasting anti-tumor immune responses. The review covers known modes of action in patients. It sets out current clinical uses across cancers. Resistance pathways that limit benefit are discussed. New plans target immune cells rather than tumor markers. Combination plans pair antibodies with other treatments. Readers get a full picture of a central cancer platform. The authors show how the field is shifting toward immune activation.
europmc-pmc7566045:
GBD 2019 Demographics Collaborators present population estimates for 204 countries and territories from 1950 to 2019. Sound demographic data guide social and health planning. The analysis forms part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019.

The team used 8078 country-years of registration data. They also drew on 938 surveys and 349 censuses. Fertility was estimated for 5-year age groups. Mortality work used thousands of sources for children and adults. Life tables were built with HIV effects included where needed. Migration and population used a Bayesian cohort model. That model also used 1250 censuses as inputs. Results classify places by their rate of population increase.
europmc-pmc7607345:
de Figueiredo, Simas, Karafillakis, Paterson and Larson map global trends in vaccine confidence. Delays and refusals reflect falling trust in vaccines. No global monitoring system for confidence existed before.

The study used 290 surveys across 149 countries. Surveys ran from September 2015 to December 2019. A total of 284,381 individuals were included overall. Confidence fell in Afghanistan, Indonesia and Pakistan. It also fell in the Philippines and South Korea. Strong disagreement that vaccines are safe rose in six countries. Some European states showed gains in later years. Belief in vaccine importance linked most strongly to uptake. Minority religious groups tended to show lower uptake where links appeared.
europmc-pmc7680145:
Arizti-Sanz and co-authors build a fast COVID-19 test meant for use outside big labs. The test, called SHINE, detects viral RNA from raw swab or saliva samples. It merges virus inactivation, RNA copying, and Cas13-based detection into one step. Results show as glow in a sealed tube, read by a phone app.

A heat and chemical step makes samples safe in 10 minutes. The full process takes 50 minutes from sample to answer. On 50 patient swabs, the test reached 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity against standard lab tests. The authors say it could widen testing in clinics and field sites.
europmc-pmc7723445:
Voysey and co-authors report interim results for the Oxford COVID-19 vaccine. It merges four blinded randomized trials in the UK, Brazil, and South Africa. In all, 23,848 people enrolled between April 23 and November 4, 2020. The vaccine, ChAdOx1 nCoV-19, was compared with a control vaccine or saline.

The main analysis held 11,636 people. Two standard doses gave 62.1% efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19. A small UK group that got a half dose first reached 90.0% efficacy. No grave safety signal stood out in this interim cut. The authors say a safe, working vaccine rolled out at scale could help control the pandemic.
europmc-pmc7726445:
Sanità and co-authors review ways to coat nanoparticles so the body accepts them. Nanoparticles serve in diagnosis and treatment, including cancer care. Yet many harm cells or fail to enter their targets, which limits clinical use. Surface traits such as charge, size, and shape drive both problems.

Changing the surface, called functionalization, can lift safety and uptake at once. The review sums up recent studies in which a new coating did just that. It also lists the lab methods used to test safety and uptake. The authors aim to guide design of nanoplatforms that target cells well while sparing the rest.
europmc-pmc7738645:
Hayashida and co-authors trace the history of Japan's hospital data system for acute care. The system is called Diagnosis Procedure Combination, or DPC. It sorts inpatients by diagnosis and procedure into set classes. Each patient gets a 14-digit code that marks the main diagnosis and key traits.

DPC began as a tool to make acute care open to scrutiny and to raise quality. It later became the base for per-day payment for acute stays. Over 15 years it was refined step by step. Its data now shape regional planning of care supply. The authors outline research that DPC data support and how the system matured.
europmc-pmc7778945:
Saier and co-authors present the 2021 update of the Transporter Classification Database, known as TCDB. The database lists transport proteins from all kinds of life. It records what each protein moves, how it works, and why it matters in health. TCDB is the one system of its kind backed by the world body for biochemistry.

As of October 1, 2020, it held 20 653 proteins in 15 528 transport systems. It also held 1,567 three-dimensional structures and 1,536 protein families. Content grew by over half since the last update in 2016. New parts include a shared naming scheme for the loads that proteins carry. Family maps now rest on shared protein domains.
