The update adds 11 new types of channels and 3 types of group translocators. Man-made pores and carriers are in the database too.
europmc-pmc7845645:
Crits-Christoph and co-authors show that sewage sequencing can spot the SARS-CoV-2 variants in a region. Virus genomes are usually read from patient nose swabs. That route tracks spread one person at a time. Sewage gathers virus from a whole community at once.

The team sequenced virus genomes from sewage samples. The variants found matched those common in the area. Sewage thus gives a cheap picture of local viral diversity. It needs no testing of single patients. Changes in variant mix can be watched over time. The method suits places with thin clinical testing. It also adds an early warning layer for new variants.
europmc-pmc8289845:
Mathieu and co-authors track how cells release exosomes versus small ectosomes. Both are small vesicles that carry messages between cells. Their release routes were not fully mapped.

The team followed the markers CD63 and CD9 inside living cells. CD9 settles at the cell surface, CD63 in late endosomes. The two met briefly at both sites, then parted. More CD9 left the cell in vesicles than CD63 did. In HeLa cells, surface-born ectosomes proved more prominent than exosomes. The work sharpens how vesicle types should be told apart. Live tracking, not fixed snapshots, made the routes visible.
europmc-pmc8494645:
Zhang and co-authors make a spatially resolved cell atlas of the mouse primary motor cortex with MERFISH. This imaging method reads gene activity in single cells where they sit. It keeps the spatial layout that sequencing loses. The motor cortex was their test region.

They profiled about 300,000 cells in the motor cortex and nearby areas. The work found 95 cell clusters, both neuronal and non-neuronal. Most clusters, excitatory and inhibitory alike, sat in clear layers. One neuron class formed a smooth gradient along cortical depth. In those cells, gene activity tracked with their place. The atlas joins molecular identity to exact position.
europmc-pmc8666445:
Shah and co-authors review T cell receptor signaling in health and disease. When this receptor meets its target, signals spread through the T cell. Kinases, phosphatases, and other enzymes carry the message. Transcription factors then switch genes on to activate the cell.

Adaptor proteins link the early and late signal steps. They hold other proteins in place but do no enzyme work themselves. The review gives a full snapshot of these parts. Enzymes and adaptors each get a careful account. The authors then trace faults in this system in human disease. Blood cancers form a key case. Readers get one map of a core immune switch.
europmc-pmc8763645:
Lohoff and co-authors combine spatial and single-cell transcript data to map how mouse organs form. Standard single-cell work breaks tissue apart and loses place. Place is key to how cells choose their fate. The team used an image-based method that reads 387 target genes in embryo tissue slices.

Data came from embryos at the 8 to 12 somite stage. Merging with two cell atlases let them name cell types across the embryo. They could also infer genes that the spatial method did not measure. The map revealed early splits in gut tube cells that plain cell data missed. The work offers a route to study fate choices in place.
europmc-pmc8943045:
Zhang and co-authors rank the global health risk of antibiotic resistance genes found across habitats. Thousands of genes can confer resistance. Not all threaten patients equally. The team analyzed metagenomes from 4,572 samples. Six habitat types were covered. They detected 2,561 resistance genes in all. Those genes spanned 24 antibiotic classes. Risk scoring joined four factors: human access, mobility, presence in pathogens, and clinical relevance.

About 23.78% of the genes posed a health risk. Multidrug resistance genes ranked most dangerous. The team also scored samples from four main habitats. Machine learning mapped marine resistance threats worldwide. Its accuracy topped 75%. The method offers quantitative surveillance of a diffuse danger. Managers can target the riskiest genes and places. The authors frame it as a tool for one of medicine's gravest threats.
europmc-pmc8983045:
Lövestam and co-authors grow tau filaments in a test tube that match those from diseased human brains. Tau clumps mark more than 20 brain diseases. Each disease folds tau its own way. Lab systems could not copy those folds. That gap blocked study of how the diseases work. The team found assembly conditions using plain recombinant tau. Cryo-electron microscopy checked the products. The filaments matched Alzheimer's disease folds. They also matched chronic traumatic encephalopathy folds.

Small details fell into place. Extra densities seen in brain filaments may be simple salts. Phosphates and sodium chloride are the suspects. Chemical edits to tau seem to steer assembly. The authors offer the system as a workbench. Disease mechanisms can now be probed directly. Drug hunters can screen binders against true folds. Blocking filament birth is another testable aim.
europmc-pmc9168645:
Wang and co-authors overview the role of microglia in depression, in both cause and treatment. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. They shape inflammation, synaptic plasticity, and neural network growth. Recent work even frames depression as a microglial disease.

The review first describes microglial activation in animal models and in patients. It then sets out how these cells sense stress linked to depression. A third section covers how antidepressant drugs, both standard and natural, affect microglia. Some common pain drugs also ease symptoms by calming these cells. The authors suggest that steering microglial action could yield new therapies. Readers get a cell-level view of a major mental disorder.
europmc-pmc9226045:
Lopez-Leon and co-authors systematically review long COVID in children and adolescents and pool the results. Most long COVID research had focused on adults. The team searched for studies of patients aged 0 to 18 with at least 30 cases each. Studies had to meet a standard national definition of the condition.

They included 21 studies with 80,071 children and adolescents in all. Pooled prevalence of long COVID was 25.24%. Mood symptoms were most common at 16.50%, then fatigue at 9.66% and sleep disorders at 8.42%. Infected children faced higher risk of lasting breathlessness, loss of smell or taste, and fever than controls. The authors note weak definitions and high variation across studies.
europmc-pmc9279145:
Chen and co-authors build Sei, a sequence-based global map of regulatory activity in the human genome. Most disease-linked variants sit in noncoding regions, where their effects are hard to read. Sei uses deep learning trained on 21,907 chromatin profiles from over 1,300 cell lines and tissues. It groups sequences into classes that capture diverse regulatory roles.

The classes quantify how any sequence or variant affects activity, such as cell-specific enhancer function. Tests against expression data and evolutionary constraint support the predictions. The team used the map to split trait heritability by regulatory activity. It also suggests mechanisms for single harmful mutations. Sei is offered as a resource for genetics and disease research.
europmc-pmc9367945:
Kolimi and co-authors review new strategies to speed wound healing and regrow skin. Chronic wounds resist normal repair and invite infection. They burden about 8.2 million people and carry heavy care costs. Five-year death rates for diabetic foot ulcers reach 30.5%, close to cancer's rate.

Standard options include cell therapy, gene therapy, growth factors, dressings, and grafts. None works for every wound type. Newer options use nano-sized drug carriers and stem cells. Bioengineered grafts and 3D-printed skin are advancing fast. Matrix-based and platelet-rich plasma methods also feature. Cold plasma treatment closes the list. The authors weigh each option's gains and flaws. They call for combined regimens matched to wound type.
europmc-pmc9380445:
Katz and co-authors present Mashtree, a tool for fast comparison of whole bacterial genome files. Public genome counts have exploded, and full family-tree math is too slow at that scale. Mashtree leans on the Mash sketching method, which shrinks each genome to its top hashed fragments. A bigger sketch of 10,000 fragments sharpens the sorting.

Pairwise distances from the sketches feed a neighbor-joining tree builder. The result is a dendrogram that groups related genomes in minutes. Resampling adds confidence values to each branch point. The authors stress that the tree is a clustering aid, not a true family history. For outbreak work, that speed lets investigators spot relatives first. Finer methods can then focus where they matter most.
europmc-pmc9526145:
Arias, Saxena, and Verguet quantify the global burden of mental disorders and its economic value. Old estimates put the health and welfare losses as large. New data and new methods now allow a fresh count. A sound count matters for the investment case in mental health.

The study built a composite method on 2019 burden data. It counted early death from mental disorders more fully. It also added morbidity sources that past counts missed. The team put the toll at 418 million disability-adjusted life years for 2019. That is 16% of all global DALYs, over three times the standard figure. The linked economic value came to about USD 5 trillion. Regional losses ran from 4% of GDP in Eastern sub-Saharan Africa to 8% in high-income North America.
europmc-pmc9531345:
Fang and co-authors review the AMPK pathway in fatty liver disease. Faulty lipid handling drives both non-alcoholic and alcoholic forms of the disease. High-fat diets and ethanol are the classic triggers. AMPK is a cell energy sensor that can correct lipid balance.

Switching AMPK on eased fatty liver in mouse studies. It cut new fatty acid and cholesterol making in the liver. At the same time it raised fat burning and breakdown genes. The review walks through each signaling axis of the pathway. The Sirt1-LKB1-AMPK axis is one named route. The AMPK-ACC and AMPK-mTOR axes follow. Natural activators of AMPK get close study as well. Most such compounds also calmed inflammation and oxidative stress. The authors back AMPK activation as a drug target for liver care.
europmc-pmc9853945:
Agüero and co-authors report an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in farmed minks in Spain. The event took place in Galicia in October 2022. It affected a single farm holding more than 50,000 minks. The report covers the field, clinical, and genetic work on the outbreak.

Mortality rose sharply in the first week of October, and tests confirmed H5N1. The viruses belonged to clade 2.3.4.4b, then spreading widely in Europe. Sequencing found a T271A change in the PB2 gene with possible public health relevance. The authors state that onward spread among minks may have occurred on the farm. They discuss what mammal infection means for surveillance and control.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: Nearly five hundred pages were withheld in release 45 of the Special Counsel Mueller investigation records: the count on this Federal Bureau of Investigation sheet is 494. The log opens with runs marked Duplicate, pages treated as copies freed elsewhere. It then turns to the b5 mark, tied to the Justice Department, at times alone and at times beside the privacy pair b6 and b7C. Later runs rest on that pair alone. No report text is in the part. It maps the cuts in this release, page by page.
fremont-report-rocky-mountains-1845:
John Frémont, an army topographer, led surveys to the Rocky Mountains in 1842 and again in 1843 and 1844. His Report, published by Congress in 1845, made him famous as the Pathfinder. His wife Jessie helped shape the narrative, and Kit Carson guided the march.

The report maps the Oregon Trail, South Pass, and the Great Basin, and it describes California's valleys. Settlers used it as a guidebook for the wagon roads west. Frémont's claim that the Basin had no outlet to the sea fixed a key fact of western geography. Few government reports have moved so many people to pack and go.
frus-1861-d145:
On 19 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton for the third time in three days. The letter is document 145 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two days after the paired letters, Seward wrote to Paris yet again. The density of the August file shows where his worry lay. France, with its restless emperor, needed the steadiest hand Washington could keep on it. Worry, in Seward's world, was best met with work, and the file shows him working. Work was his answer to worry, and the posts abroad felt the good of it. Worry, for Seward, was best answered with work.
frus-1861-d245:
Writing home was James Shepherd Pike's duty, and his letter of 12 July 1861 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 245 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d45:
From London on 17 May 1861, Charles Francis Adams wrote his first report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 45 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams had just reached London, the hardest post in the service. His father and grandfather had both served there before him. His first reports show a calm, exact man taking the measure of Lord John Russell and the British cabinet in a perilous month. His cool head in those first weeks set the tone for seven years of service in London. Cool heads were the rarest goods in London that spring, and Adams had one.
frus-1862-d145:
Document 145 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume is a dispatch dated 15 September 1862 from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It belongs to the near-daily mail between the State Department and its most watched post abroad.

Britain was the one power that could change the war by backing the Confederacy, so Adams's post carried great weight. Mail on the London channel bore orders, news of the war, and the Union case against foreign help for the South. Read in sequence, the letters show how Washington worked to keep Britain neutral, week by week, in the fall of 1862.
frus-1862-d245:
William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 December 1861, in a letter printed as Document 245 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

December 1861 was the Trent month, when Britain and the Union stood near war over seized Confederate envoys. France's stance mattered because Napoleon III often moved with London on American questions. Dayton's reports from Paris told Washington whether France would back Britain, stay quiet, or use the moment for its own plans in Mexico. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d345:
Document 345 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 10 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to Paris in one mail.

Paired letters late in the year carry a different mood from September's: the questions are the same, but the urgency has ebbed. France, left alone by Britain, chose to send its truce idea to Washington and Richmond directly, where it failed. This letter belongs to the quieter work of watching that failure unfold. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d445:
Norman B. Judd, the American minister in Berlin, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 December 1861. It is Document 445 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, among the first Prussian papers in the volume.

Judd wrote in the month of the Trent crisis, when war with Britain seemed possible and every European court's attitude counted double. From Berlin he could report how Prussia and the smaller German states read the American conflict. Prussian sympathy leaned to the Union, and German volunteers were crossing the Atlantic to enlist. His early report helped Seward map the friendly ground in Europe at the end of the war's first year.
frus-1862-d45:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 April 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 45 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d545:
On 10 September 1862 Roest van Limburg sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 545 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Van Limburg wrote in the week between Lee's invasion of Maryland and the battle of Antietam, when every legation in Washington was waiting. His own business was the durable Dutch agenda of commerce and neutral right, which did not pause for campaigns. The note is one of the September pieces of the Netherlands file. It was framed in Washington. Meanwhile its writer's colleagues abroad, Pike among them, reported the same crisis from the other side of the ocean. The two Dutch files together give the volume's most balanced small-power record.
frus-1862-d645:
Townsend Harris, the first American minister to Japan, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 December 1861. Harris had opened the American legation in Japan only a few years before, after long talks led to a trade treaty in 1858. His letter is document 645 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Reports like this one carried word from a distant post back to Washington. Harris wrote about the state of ties with Japan's rulers and the day-to-day work of a small legation far from home. Read now, the letter shows how the United States kept a foothold in Japan while the Civil War raged back home.
frus-1863p1-d145:
A lone sheet between clusters, this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 7 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 145 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams wrote days after the British seized a Southern-built raider at Liverpool, a win the Union had sought for months. His mail that week told Washington how the act was taken in London. It is a lone sheet between clusters, and it catches the file at a turn. The ship fight, long a dread, had begun to break the Union's way. The calm tone is Adams's own.
frus-1863p1-d245:
The State Department's mail for London dated 23 July 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 245 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Union victories in July 1863 let Washington speak with more confidence. Orders sent after Gettysburg and Vicksburg carry a firmer note than those of the spring. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d345:
A note dated 29 December 1862 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 345 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d445:
On 4 April 1863 a formal note passed from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d45:
Judah P. Benjamin wrote this letter to James M. Mason on 26 September 1862. Benjamin was the Confederate secretary of state; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 45 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mason and Slidell were the twin heads of the South's push in Europe, one in London and one in Paris. Benjamin wrote to both in the same week of September 1862. His letters fed them the South's case at the moment its armies stood near their peak. This one, printed in the Union's own volume, lets a reader weigh that case in the words of the man who made it.
frus-1863p1-d545:
Secretary of State William H. Seward received a letter dated 30 May 1863 from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d645:
A 23 October 1863 dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London reached William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d145: Roosevelt wrote to Ambassador Steinhardt in Turkey on November 20, 1943, one of two letters to Steinhardt in this series that day. It is Document 145 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Turkey's choice, to join the war or stay out, hung over the Cairo talks, and the president worked the question by letter as well as in person. The record names the two men and the date.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d245:
The Log of the President's trip opens with its full itinerary, covering 11 November to 17 December 1943, and a foreword sketching the war situation that November. Kept by Lieutenant William Rigdon, the log tracks Roosevelt's journey to the Cairo and Tehran conferences and back, stop by stop.

The table lists each arrival and departure. The route runs from Washington and Quantico out through Oran, Tunis, and Cairo, then Tehran, a second Cairo stay, Malta, Sicily, and Dakar. It ends home at Cherry Point and Washington on 17 December. The total comes to 17,442 miles. The foreword notes Italy's surrender, German delaying battles west of the Dnieper and south of Rome, and Axis losses in the air and at sea.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d345:
Alexander Kirk, the American minister in Egypt, sent Harry Hopkins an immediate and urgent telegram from Cairo on 28 November 1943. Hopkins was at Tehran, and Kirk held the Cairo communiqué under seal, awaiting release instructions.

Kirk has learned this from Ryan of the Ministry of Information. The British have already sent the text in code through their Cairo embassy to the Foreign Office in London. It waits there, ready for release on a flash from the Tehran party. Worse, Ryan says that release will be immediate, without the twenty-four hours' notice Kirk was promised, and that the Cairo handout will serve for background only. Kirk asks for immediate, detailed instructions, so the legation makes no slip and he can notify the Chinese as Hopkins had requested.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d445: Readers who reach Document 445 meet the editors rather than the wartime leaders. The entry is an editorial note in the Cairo-Tehran volume. State Department historians inserted notes to explain, connect, and cross-reference the papers. That help matters in a record spanning two conferences in two cities. Cairo and Tehran both hosted summit talks in late 1943. Big decisions on strategy and postwar plans fill the nearby pages.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d45: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 16, 1943, and the message is Document 45 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. By then the British, American, and Soviet foreign ministers were about to open their meeting in Moscow, the first of its kind in the war. The catalog record supplies the date and the names. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' account of the weeks when the Tehran summit took final shape.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d545:
Minutes record a meeting of the Pacific War Council on January 12, 1944, marked secret. The Council brought the nations fighting Japan together in Washington under President Roosevelt's chairmanship to consult on the Pacific war. The minutes appear in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Council meetings let smaller Pacific allies, from the Netherlands to the Philippines' government in exile, hear plans and state their interests. Minutes of such a body show coalition warfare being coordinated at the political level while the Cairo-Tehran decisions reshaped the global war. For readers, the record widens the frame beyond Europe to the Pacific, where the war would run longest.
frus-1944-quebec-d145:
In telegram 774, on August 31, 1944, Churchill brought Roosevelt up to date on Italy's decisive battle. General Alexander's Eighth Army was in contact with the Gothic Line along twenty miles of the Adriatic flank. General Clark's Fifth Army had advanced from Florence. Churchill said he had pressed Alexander to destroy the enemy's forces, not merely turn his line.

Churchill no longer asked for American reinforcements beyond the 92nd Division, but he assumed no more troops would be withdrawn from Italy. Looking ahead, he saw the Eighth and Fifth Armies moving first to Istria and Trieste, and ultimately on Vienna. The two leaders would talk it over fully at Octagon.
frus-1944-quebec-d245:
Hopkins added this handwritten note to Hull's French lend-lease memorandum on September 12, 1944, and sent both to Roosevelt at Quebec by pouch. His judgment is compressed into two sentences. The proposal was acceptable, he wrote, because it gave the final decision to the president, and in the present situation that was essential.

"If you will initial this, the matter will be handled that way," Hopkins concluded. Roosevelt did not initial it. Instead, on September 14 at Quebec, he referred the memorandum to Morgenthau. His covering note read: "Will you handle this with Harry Hopkins and Cordell Hull?" The editors note one more referral. Morgenthau was also to discuss Soviet lend-lease with Hull and Stimson.
frus-1944-quebec-d45:
Roosevelt answered Churchill on September 1, 1944. The reply appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It sits in the last section of pre-conference letters.

Early September found Roosevelt preparing to receive Churchill at Quebec. American armies pressed into Belgium and toward Germany. His replies kept American terms clear. The conference would decide Germany's postwar treatment. It would also decide continued aid to Britain. For readers, the message shows the host at work. He set his table in writing before the guest arrived. The guest would reach Canada within days. The full exchange between them is printed in the volume.
frus-1945-50-intel-d145:
Formal minutes cover the Third Meeting of the National Intelligence Authority, held on 2 April 1946. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 145 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

The pages give the meeting in the plain form staff used at the time: a topic, the sense of the talk, and the result. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d245:
A memorandum from the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) reached Secretary of Defense Forrestal on 24 October 1947. It stands as document 245 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d345:
Formal minutes cover the 10th Meeting of the National Security Council, held on 22 April 1948. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 345, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Minutes trade color for proof: they may skip the tone of a talk, but they pin down its outcome. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d45:
Minutes dated 14 November 1945 record another meeting in the long autumn round on intelligence. By then, committees at State, War, and the Budget Bureau had all drafted plans. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Mid-November was the season of sorting: too many plans, one president, and a need to blend them. Meeting minutes from such weeks often hide drama in flat prose, recording outcomes without the argument that produced them. Readers should read these minutes between the papers around them. The memoranda supply the voices; the minutes supply the score. Together they show a government converging, slowly and with friction, on the central system it would announce in January.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d145:
Stettinius offered the President a Polish letter to sign on 15 November 1944. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, answers Premier Mikolajczyk's appeal of 26 October. It assumes the Big Three will not meet before the year ends, so Washington must speak on its own.

The Polish issue is so acute, Stettinius writes, that a statement of the American position is due. A draft letter to Mikolajczyk is attached. Harriman, returning to Moscow by way of London, would hand it over in person and take up the question of Lwów. If the talk convinced him, Harriman might also be cleared to plead with Stalin for Lwów and its oil fields to stay Polish.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d245:
Keeping China in the war is the first short-range aim in this briefing book paper of 13 January 1945. “Outline of Short-Range Objectives and Policies of the United States With Respect to China” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It lists what Washington is already doing to that end.

China's full strength, military and economic, is to be mobilized against Japan. The means are direct. War materials go to the Chinese armed forces. An effective air force flies in China, and an American force based in India fights in northern Burma beside Chinese units. Munitions fly in over the mountains in substantial quantity, and American officers are training Chinese troops. Cooperation has grown stronger, the paper notes, since General Wedemeyer took command of the China area.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d345:
A bomb line across Europe was the first business of the second tripartite military meeting at Yalta, February 6, 1945. General Antonov had proposed a line from Stettin through Berlin, Vienna, and Zagreb. West of it, Allied planes could bomb freely; east of it, Soviet forces held sway. Brooke asked the American chiefs for their views, since the matter touched them most.

General Kuter read a set statement of the American position. Antonov had asked Admiral Leahy to chair, but Leahy stepped aside for Brooke, who had chaired before. The minutes show air power being fenced by geography so allies would not bomb each other.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d445:
A potential powder magazine: so this British paper of February 10, 1945, describes Venezia Giulia, in Italy's northeast. As the war drew to a close, clashes there between Yugoslavs and Italians seemed likely. The paper urges that the allies prevent such outbursts as best they can.

The old plan was Allied military government over the whole province, up to the 1937 frontier. Now London doubted that course. Tito had made fairly clear he would not agree to it. He meant to administer the areas his forces held himself. The notes, written for Eden's colleagues, foresee the Trieste crisis of May 1945 in plain words.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d45: The president also used 6 January 1945 to write Ambassador Harriman in Moscow, his third message that day in this record. Filed as document 45 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, it keeps the Soviet channel current alongside the Churchill letters. Harriman needed the president's latest thinking before the delegation reached the Crimea in early February.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d145:
Acting Secretary Grew passed the British agenda list to President Truman in a memorandum dated May 30, 1945. The memo and its enclosure form document 145 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Grew offers to prepare American comments on the British list if the President wishes.

The enclosure is blunt. Poland heads the list as the main question, with Russia handing German land to Poland before any peace settlement. Germany follows: zones, feeding, displaced persons, and reparations, with a jab at the Russian habit of stripping bare the lands they control. Austria, Yugoslavia's frontiers, and Soviet behavior in the Balkans round out the printed part. The list is a frank catalogue of the young Cold War's opening disputes, drawn up before the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d245:
Ambassador Kirk forwarded a Rome newspaper story about Soviet courtship of Italy in a telegram dated July 15, 1945. The message is document 245 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It translates an article from the newspaper Il Secolo of July 13.

The article reports that the Soviet ambassador, Kostilev, told Prime Minister Parri that Russia would take the lead at Potsdam in supporting Italy's admission to the United Nations, without conditions. It recalls that Russia was first to restore full diplomatic relations with democratic Italy in 1944. It also anticipates Soviet help in reviving trade, including coal from Poland and from Russia's own Donetz basin. The clipping shows Moscow competing with Washington for Italy's friendship on the eve of the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d345:
General Clay sent the War Department a first political report on Germany on July 5, 1945, prepared with Ambassador Murphy's help. Based on reports through the end of June, it surveys the chief political questions of the moment. Similar reports, Clay said, would follow at intervals. Denazification heads his list of topics.

Removing Nazis from public office, he reported, moved at very different speeds. In Aachen and Cologne the screening was nearly complete. Less progress had been made in Württemberg and Bavaria, and the program ran slowest in the areas supreme headquarters had occupied. The report gave Washington an early, uneven map of the purge.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d445:
Allied supervision of Greek voting is endorsed in a State Department aide-mémoire to the British Embassy dated July 5, 1945. The Department answers a British note of June 16, which had asked American views on supervising a plebiscite and elections in Greece under Article 9 of the Varkiza Agreement. Washington agrees with the Foreign Office: allied supervision would raise the chances of success.

The signatories of the Crimea communiqué, the note recalls, promised jointly to help liberated countries build stable governments by democratic processes. In Greece, it says, America's responsibility cannot be counted discharged until Greek voters are assured fair elections, free of undue pressure from embittered factions. Details of polling supervision are left for the ambassadors in Athens.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d45:
President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on June 1, 1945, answering the Prime Minister's telegram about the coming Big Three meeting. The brief message is document 45 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. By then Stalin had already agreed to Truman's proposed date, and Churchill was waiting for word from Washington.

Truman tells Churchill that Stalin is agreeable to meeting near Berlin around July 15, and that the date also fits his own duties at home. He says he looks forward to seeing Churchill then. He adds that he trusts the meeting will produce results of great value for the future of the world. The reply closed the date question on the American side.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d545:
Aboard the cruiser Augusta on July 12, 1945, Secretary of State Byrnes wired Secretary of War Stimson a second answer. It is document 545 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The subject was the President's July 5 order on lend-lease arms.

Byrnes reports that the President agrees to a broad reading of his order. Supplies and gear may still go out, within the limits of past pledges. They may go to forces that free U.S. troops to move from other fronts to the war against Japan. The wire eased the strict reading that had alarmed Stimson a day before.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d645:
An extract from James Dunn's Potsdam memo of July 14, 1945, covers the Levant. It is document 645 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers, drawn from his report of a talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan. Dunn was reporting to Secretary Byrnes on the conference agenda.

Cadogan said the British team was ready to answer questions on the Levant if the Russians raised them. France's Bidault had refused a London meeting and asked that talks be held in Paris instead. London, he said, was urging the French and Syrians to settle the matter directly between them. On the special forces, only the time limit for transfer was left to settle. France, he added, would seemingly settle for consular and trade pacts with Syria and Lebanon, leaving the question of bases aside.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1045: Sir David Waley added this note to the British suggestions on reparations, dated July 23, 1945. Only an extract is printed here; the rest appears earlier in the volume. The note floats a request to the Soviet government. Moscow might undertake to make foodstuffs and coal from its zone of Germany, within the 1937 borders, available to the rest of Germany. Detailed terms would be drawn up by the Control Council, after full inquiry into the effects. Any such agreement would run twelve months, then be open to fresh review.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1145:
Moscow's team put this proposal on the table on 20 July 1945, in the middle of Potsdam's first week. Soviet papers at the summit set out demands on the postwar order for the Americans and British to answer. Each one tested how far the other two would bend.

A formal proposal is a move in a game played in writing. It claims ground, forces a reply, and leaves a record of who asked for what. This paper is one such Soviet move, kept word for word in the American files. Read in sequence with the replies it drew, it shows the bargaining as it actually moved.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1245:
Britain's team tabled this proposal on 24 July 1945. It came from the summit's second week, two days before the election count changed the British leadership. The paper set London's stand on its point in formal words.

By then the talks had moved past first positions. A proposal at this stage was built to be traded against, line by line. This one shows the British hand in that process. It also gains point from its timing. The men who wrote it were about to leave the table. Their successors would own whatever it won or lost.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1345:
Loy Henderson, director of the Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs, wrote to the acting secretary of state on 30 July 1945. Henderson spoke for the State Department's Middle East and Africa desk at the close of the Potsdam talks. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A bureau chief writing to the acting secretary shows a question rising to the top of the home office. The end of July 1945 brought no rest for regional desks, even as the summit wound down in Germany. Readers get the view from Washington. The problems of the Near East are arriving on the desk of the man running the department while Byrnes was abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-145:
Philip Mosely, political adviser to the American representative on the European Advisory Commission, wrote this memorandum on July 30, 1945. The Commission, based in London, had planned the terms for beaten Germany since 1944. Its work fed straight into Potsdam. Mosely knew the plans and the people behind them. His memo entered the second Potsdam volume.

A Mosely paper bridges two stages of planning. It links the London drafts to the choices made in Germany. Readers see how earlier staff work held up under pressure from the leaders. The memo shows the long fuse of the settlement: papers prepared for months meeting their test in days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-45:
A brief memorandum by President Truman, written July 20, 1945, at Babelsberg, records two things he told Churchill. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The note is Truman's own manuscript jotting on a memo from Admiral Leahy.

Told Churchill about it, Truman writes, without naming the subject in the note itself. The editors trace it to Leahy's memo on French pay policy. France, adjusting the franc's exchange value, was paying seventeen dollars a month to U.S. soldiers serving in France. Truman's second point was a request of his own. He asked Churchill to let no proclamations be issued by the Control Council while the leaders were in session at Potsdam. The talk, the editors judge, took place just before or just after that day's plenary meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d745:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 17, 1945, the first day of the Potsdam Conference. Document 745 stands near the front of the volume's numbered papers. Opening texts set the terms of debate. The American team arrived with drafts ready, a habit formed at earlier summits. The proposal entered the second Potsdam volume.

First-day proposals show a side before it has heard the others. Their confidence is part of the record. Readers can track which opening lines survived two weeks of talk. The document also reveals agenda power: the side that writes first frames what follows. Potsdam's paper war began with texts like this one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d845:
The Acting Secretary wrote again to Kennan in Moscow on July 19, 1945, in document 845. Grew kept the Moscow channel warm through the conference's first week. His second letter in this run went out two days after the first. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Repeated guidance to one post shows where Washington's mind was. Moscow's reading of the summit mattered to every other file. Readers see Grew managing that sensitivity in writing. The document deepens the volume's quiet subplot: a home office and an embassy, exchanging care and candor while the leaders bargained in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d945: Edwin Pauley answered William Clayton's memorandum on July 29, 1945, from Berlin. The subject is a set of recommendations on the restitution of art objects, drawn up by Control Council staff in Germany. Pauley says he has prepared the joint memorandum Clayton suggested. He has signed it to show his approval. If Clayton also approves, Pauley presumes he will send it on to General Clay for action. The memorandum itself appears later in the volume as an enclosure to document 964.
frus-1961-63v11-d45:
A telephone talk of October 22, 1962, between President Kennedy and Prime Minister Macmillan lays out the quarantine choice. A secret build-up allowed to stand would unhinge Washington across Latin America, Kennedy argues. It would also cast doubt on every word said about Berlin.

An air strike or invasion could still come, but each invites a move on Berlin. Invasion needs seven days to mount. The blockade starts the climb slowly, to bar a third world war. Kennedy notes the Cuba missiles would double Soviet strike power. He promises to speak again before any landing.
fuller-woman-nineteenth-century-1845:
Margaret Fuller published Woman in the Nineteenth Century in 1845 in New York. Fuller, editor of The Dial and a leading figure among the Transcendentalists, expanded an earlier essay for the book. It became the founding text of American feminism in its full book form.

Fuller called for women's self-dependence: the freedom to think, learn, and act without asking leave of fathers or husbands. She surveyed myth, history, and marriage law to show how women had been stunted and what they might become. Her style is dense and allusive, her demand plain. Later suffragists built on her case. The book still reads as a brave, searching plea for women's intellectual equality.
gao-gaoreports-b-296245:
TransAtlantic Lines protested an Army award for cargo runs to Cuba in GAO decision B-296245, dated July 14, 2005. The winner was Strong Vessel Operators. The runs linked Jacksonville, Florida and Guantanamo Bay. The firm said the winner failed a term on chilled cargo boxes. It also hit a missing term in the call.

GAO denied one claim and cut the other as late. The winner took no bar to the box terms. Its bid gave fair proof it could meet them. The missing term claim came after award. That was too late to raise a flaw in the call itself. Timing rules for call flaws are strict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299145:
Sikorsky Aircraft Company and Lockheed Martin Systems Integration-Owego protested an Air Force award to The Boeing Company. The contract covered the Combat Search and Rescue Replacement Vehicle. That aircraft recovers downed aircrew and stranded staff. GAO ruled in the B-299145 series on February 26, 2007.

The terms set cost on a most probable life cycle basis. That count was to weigh upkeep needs for each design. Firms had to send deep facts on upkeep tasks. The agency then leveled upkeep costs across bids. That step erased the edge of low-upkeep designs. An agency must hold to the tests it states. The scoring broke that rule. GAO sustained the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-299545:
Basic Concepts protested a Defense Logistics Agency award for hazardous spill containment units. The sole-source deal went to Bowhead Manufacturing Company. It ran through the section 8(a) business development program. GAO decided B-299545 on May 31, 2007.

A small-firm contest for the same units was still in play. The firm said the agency had to hold a fresh contest first. GAO found the two paths could run side by side. The agency met a near-term need through the 8(a) path. That step broke no statute or rule. Use of the program while a contest runs is not barred. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-303145:
GAO ruled on Defense Department use of emergency funds in B-303145. The plea grew from talks on about $178 million in projects. Those projects tied to the global war on terrorism in fiscal year 2002. GAO issued its legal ruling on December 7, 2005.

Shifts of funds need a clear legal base. Two 2002 laws gave the Defense Secretary that base here. Funds could move from the Defense Emergency Response Fund to other accounts. Once moved, the funds took on the use of the new account. The second law said so in plain terms. GAO traced the sums, the projects, and their funding roots. The transfers stood on that grant of power.
gao-gaoreports-b-303845:
GAO ruled on Education Department grant extensions in B-303845. The plea grew from a review of grants to low-income and minority serving schools. Those grants run under Titles III and V of the Higher Education Act. GAO issued its legal ruling on January 3, 2006.

The agency had added 4 years to some 5-year grants. GAO found that step improper in two ways. For graduate schools in the class, the law caps grants at 5 years in plain words. For the wider class, agency rules set the same 5-year cap. A 4-year add-on broke that rule with no sound waiver. Both sets of extensions failed.
gao-gaoreports-b-305945:
Top pay at the Architect of the Capitol is the subject of this GAO opinion, B-305945, dated September 30, 2005. The office had raised pay for some senior staff past a key mark. That mark is Level III of the Executive Schedule. The House Appropriations Committee asked if the office could do so. The office claimed its pay power had no limits.

GAO did not agree with that claim. The office may pay past Level III only with a certified review system for staff work. No such certification was in place here. So pay must stay at Level III or below for now. The opinion shows that a set pay cap binds even an office with broad pay power. It guides pay choices for senior staff.
gao-gaoreports-b-400345:
Frontier Transportation, Inc. protested the loss of a chance to rent mobile cold storage trailers to the Department of Agriculture. GAO decided B-400345 on September 9, 2008. The request for quotes No. AG-0343-S-08-9004 covered fire and incident work in the Northern Rockies. Awards were open to all small firms with fair prices.

The agency cut Frontier's quote as too high in price. GAO found the price sat well above the government's own cost view. It also sat well above the prices other small firms gave in the same round. On that record, the cut was fair, and GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-245:
Food Stamp Program, GAO-05-245 of May 5, 2005, grades a long push to cut wrong payments in food aid. In fiscal year 2003, errors hit about $1.4 billion. That was about 7 percent of $21.4 billion in aid to a monthly mean of 21 million low-income people. Wrong sums waste public cash and shake trust in the plan.

GAO breaks down what counts in the national error rate and how it has moved. It names the main causes of the errors, drawn from data for fiscal years 1999 through 2003 and talks in nine states. It lists the steps states and the food aid agency have taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-345:
Defense Logistics, GAO-05-345 of September 12, 2005, tracks a bid to tag war goods so none go lost again. The Pentagon has lost track of stock for years, most keenly in Iraq. Radio tags on gear let gates read each crate as it moves. Live tags have served since the early 1990s. Still tags, read at close range, began their roll on January 1, 2005.

By January 1, 2007, all goods but bulk loads must bear still tags. The full build will cost hundreds of millions of dollars. GAO tells how far the roll has got. It weighs the grand plan and the snags the Pentagon sees ahead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-645:
Community health centers and their grant contests fill GAO report GAO-05-645 (July 13, 2005). A White House drive aims for 1,200 grants by fiscal 2006. Money for brand-new sites fell 53 percent from fiscal 2002 to 2004, while applicants rose 28 percent. The win rate dropped from 52 percent to 20 percent. In all, 334 new-site grants and 285 expansion grants were made in those years.

The agency doubts its need test steers sites to the neediest towns and is rethinking it. Its count of actual clinic sites is unreliable, GAO adds, even as checks on center performance grow stricter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-945:
Airline bankruptcy and pensions get the full-report treatment in GAO-05-945, dated September 30, 2005. The industry has lost over $30 billion since 2001. Four big carriers filed for bankruptcy. Two ended their pension plans and passed them to the federal insurer. The net claim on the insurer was $9.7 billion. Plan members lost $5.3 billion in benefits, in constant 2005 dollars.

GAO found bankruptcy is endemic to the field. High fixed costs, cyclical demand, and fierce rivalry mark its structure. Since 1978, 162 airlines have filed, 22 in the last five years. Most bankrupt carriers cut costs, but few survive. GAO found no clear evidence that bankrupt rivals harm the industry on fares or capacity. The pension plans left standing are underfunded by $13.7 billion. That raises the risk of more losses to the insurer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-145:
Amtrak's deep management flaws are laid out in GAO-06-145, a report GAO issued on October 4, 2005. The railroad has never covered its costs from revenue. A new president began reform efforts in June 2002. Still, Amtrak needs a federal subsidy of over $1 billion a year. Its capital backlog stands near $6 billion, mostly on the Northeast Corridor. GAO reviewed planning, financial reporting, cost control, purchasing, and accountability.

GAO found no real strategic plan with clear goals and measures. Financial data were weak and at times wrong, with key costs left out of reports. Losses topped $1 billion a year and were set to grow 40 percent in four years. Food and beverage service alone lost over $160 million in fiscal years 2002 and 2003. Big departments bought goods outside the rules, with poor spending data. GAO made detailed recommendations across all five areas.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-445:
Antennas on three continents keep spacecraft in touch with Earth. The report numbered GAO-06-445, issued April 27, 2006, reviews NASA's Deep Space Network. The network supports missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Over two decades, NASA may spend $100 billion on new craft and facilities that need reliable ground contact. Three antenna sites around the world provide that contact now.

GAO describes the big operational challenges the network faces. It asks how well NASA folds the network into future plans. GAO found the current management structure is not well suited to the task. It does not match resources with future needs well. Readers see a quiet system under strain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-45:
Leaking fuel tanks can foul soil and groundwater for years. GAO wrote GAO-06-45 on November 30, 2005, about the Environmental Protection Agency's underground storage tank program. Tank owners must install leak detection gear and take steps to prevent leaks. A federal trust fund set up in 1986 helps states pay for cleanups. By early 2005, cleanup had not yet begun for over 32,000 tanks.

GAO counted leaking tanks and their cleanup status. It traced funding sources for cleanups. It studied processes in five states with many leaking tanks. More complete data and steady focus on leak prevention could improve the program, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-645:
United States aid for Caribbean disaster recovery is reviewed in GAO-06-645, a report GAO issued on May 26, 2006. The Agency for International Development ran recovery work after storms battered island nations in the region. Its projects rebuilt homes, schools, and public works, and helped local economies restart. GAO checked how many activities were finished and what slowed the rest.

GAO found that the agency completed many recovery efforts within one year. But many construction projects needed time extensions. Weak local capacity, funding delays, and other factors slowed the work. GAO also found that a lack of formal guidance, a clear time frame, and staffing problems hurt the effort. GAO urged firmer planning for future disaster programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-745:
The Army's shift to a modular force is examined in GAO-06-745. GAO issued the report on September 6, 2006. The Army called the change its most extensive restructuring since World War II. Divisions would give way to modular brigades that can deploy on their own. The Army put the cost at over $52 billion from fiscal years 2005 through 2011, including $41 billion for equipment. GAO checked the pace of the change and its equipping plans.

GAO found that the Army was well under way in creating active modular brigades. But it was not meeting its equipping goals for those brigades. Its overall equipping strategy was still unfinished. That gap raised real uncertainty about how fully brigades would be equipped, and at what final cost. GAO urged more visibility for defense leaders and Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-945:
How often gas pipelines must be rechecked is the question in GAO report GAO-06-945, dated September 8, 2006. A 2002 law told operators to test lines in crowded areas, about 20,000 miles, by 2012. They must fix flaws and retest at set spans.

Rules set retests for rust at least every 7 years, and for all threats at longer spans. GAO asked what early test results say about the 7-year span. It also asked if enough skilled crews and tools exist to do the work. It spoke with 52 operators. Risk-based rules, GAO argued, would let firms match retests to real threats.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1045:
A new education benefits system for veterans needs better planning, GAO finds in report GAO-07-1045, dated July 31, 2007. The Department of Veterans Affairs pays study aid to veterans, troops, reservists, and some family members. Since 1999 it has built a system, called TEES, to process those claims with far more automation.

GAO reported what TEES has yielded so far, and what work is left. It set out the agency's plans to finish and launch the system. It asked if TEES can land before a linked finance system is done. Site visits to regional offices feed the findings. Planning must improve, GAO said, to guide the build.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-145:
Contractors now cook, haul, and guard beside U.S. troops in war zones. GAO revisited how the Pentagon manages them in report GAO-07-145, dated December 18, 2006. GAO first mapped these problems in a June 2003 report. This follow-up asked how much had improved since then. GAO reviewed defense policies and spoke with officials at deployed sites and at home.

The department had issued new guidance, GAO found. An October 2005 instruction was its first departmentwide rule on deployed contractors. But no office clearly owned the job of making units follow it. Commanders still could not see how many contractor staff sat on each base. That blind spot hurt planning for housing, food, and protection. GAO cited about $43 million lost yearly on free meals for contractor staff who also drew food allowances. Training and lessons learned also lagged, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-245:
When floods or quakes wreck highways, a small federal fund helps states rebuild them. GAO found the fund out of balance in GAO-07-245, a report dated February 23, 2007. The Emergency Relief program has had $100 million a year since 1972. Real needs have run far past that sum. GAO traced funding from fiscal years 1997 through 2006. It studied who got the money and what work qualifies.

The program sent over $8 billion to states in that decade, GAO found. Five states took 70 percent of it, led by disaster-hit Florida and Louisiana. Since 1990, extra appropriations paid 86 percent of program costs. The $100 million yearly sum is worth about one-fourth its 1972 value. Unpaid claims hit a $740 million backlog in 2004. Eligibility rules had also crept wider over time. GAO urged tighter rules and a fresh look at funding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-445:
Airport baggage screening costs at Los Angeles and Ontario are disputed in GAO-07-445, a GAO report from March 30, 2007. To screen every checked bag by the end of 2003, the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) parked bulky scanners in lobbies. In-line systems, built into conveyor lines, work faster and need fewer staff. In 2003, TSA agreed to cover up to 75 percent of a $341 million project at both airports.

The city's airport arm soon said the design would not work as drawn. In April 2005 it sent a new estimate and asked for about $122 million more. TSA held to the old deal. By February 2007 it had pledged the full $256 million share and paid back about $26 million. GAO explains why the two cost views split.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-645:
The federal home loan insurer lost ground to nimble rivals, and GAO-07-645, a GAO report released June 29, 2007, charts the slide. The Federal Housing Administration (FHA) insures mortgages for buyers who struggle to get prime loans. From 1996 through 2005, its share of home purchase loans shrank. GAO used FHA files and Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data to trace the fall.

Other lenders changed the game in those years. Prime lenders sped approvals and widened their reach. Subprime lenders courted the very buyers FHA served, with looser terms. FHA's own process stayed slow and paper-bound by contrast. GAO weighs what the shift means for buyers: more choice, but also more risk in the loans that replaced FHA cover. It also weighs the agency's future role. The report is a market study more than an audit, built to inform bills that would let FHA fight back.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-745:
A mini submarine for Navy SEALs is examined in GAO-07-745, dated May 24, 2007. The Advanced SEAL Delivery System carries SEALs and gear in secret into high-threat areas. The first boat cost over $885 million to date. It has had major performance problems. Congress asked GAO in May 2006 to review the program. GAO checked how the Navy managed risk through its contracts. It also checked key technical flaws and the program's reshaping.

The Navy took the boat in "as is" shape to get it in service. It then failed to watch the builder's repair and upgrade work closely. The contract type gave the builder little reason to curb costs. Work often began before scope and price were set. The boat can serve only in limited ways due to reliability flaws. In April 2006, the Defense Department halted buys of more boats. GAO urged clear cost, schedule, and performance bars before any move ahead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-945:
Required audits of Medicare Advantage plans are panned in GAO-07-945, dated July 30, 2007. The program cost over $51 billion in fiscal year 2006. Private plans bid each year to serve Medicare members. A 1997 law orders audits of at least one-third of plans. GAO must watch how the Medicare agency runs them. The agency could not show it met the one-third mark. For contract years 2001 through 2005, the mark was missed. The 2006 bid audits were not designed to meet it either.

Other reviews are planned to fill the gap someday, GAO found. They would finish nearly three years after each bid round. Late audits lose their power to fix bids. Findings from the audits done were put to little use. Follow-up on problems found was weak. GAO made five recommendations on the audit duty. They cover the one-third rule, follow-up, and bid audit design. The agency agreed with all five.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-145:
Army force redesign and growth are overseen in GAO report GAO-08-145, issued December 14, 2007. The modular force plan is a multiyear redesign of Army units costing $52.5 billion. The Army also plans to spend $70 billion through fiscal year 2013 to add 74,200 troops. Congress requires GAO to report on the effort each year through fiscal year 2012.

GAO found weak links between funding requests and real progress in staffing and equipping units. That gap hampers oversight of a vast effort. GAO set out four actions, led by a full strategy and funding plan. It also gave Congress a case for demanding a broad test plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-245:
College costs keep rising in GAO report GAO-08-245, issued November 28, 2007. Nine in ten of the fastest-growing jobs in the knowledge economy call for schooling past high school. A graduate can expect to earn about $1 million more over a working life than a nongraduate. Yet most families pay more for college each year. Many fear the price shuts out low-income and minority students.

Congress asked GAO for the trend lines. The report tracks enrollment shifts across types of schools. It follows tuition and fees over time. It also traces what schools spend on teaching and related services. The title notes the key caveat: patterns vary widely by school type.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-345:
Dated January 31, 2008, GAO report GAO-08-345 looks at the Office of Personnel Management's retirement systems modernization. The program aims to replace paper-heavy processes and old systems used to retire civilian federal workers. New parts were set to go live in February 2008.

GAO credited OPM with better contractor selection, risk management, and oversight, plus new targets for accuracy and speed. But early test results had not met quality goals, so OPM could not be sure a key part would work as intended at launch. Testing was squeezed and set to run in parallel, adding risk. GAO recommended stronger testing, defect fixes, and better cost estimating. OPM said it was acting on the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-45:
Fund-raising stamp proceeds are tracked in GAO report GAO-08-45, dated October 30, 2007. The Postal Service has issued three semipostal stamps, sold above face value to fund set causes. One aids breast cancer research, one aids families of emergency workers killed or disabled on September 11, and one aids children exposed to domestic violence.

As of June 2007, the stamps had raised more than $68 million in all. The Breast Cancer Research stamp brought in about $54.6 million, the Heroes of 2001 stamp about $10.6 million, and the Stop Family Violence stamp about $3.2 million. All four named agencies have paid out their shares as grants and programs. GAO repeated its call that the Department of Health and Human Services report each year on the health institutes' use of the breast cancer funds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-645:
Paper checks cost more and arrive slower than electronic benefit payments. A 1996 law pushed food aid onto payment cards, with good results. GAO-08-645, dated June 23, 2008, asks how far other federal benefit programs have moved to electronic payment and what could move the rest.

Of 42 programs surveyed, 34 used at least one electronic method. For the five largest programs with data, 54 to 100 percent of payments went out that way. Agencies weigh cost, fraud risk, and the burden on people who get the money. GAO listed options such as making electronic payment the default, plus more outreach by the Treasury.
german-instrument-of-surrender-1945:
Germany's Instrument of Surrender was signed in May 1945, at Reims and Berlin. The Third Reich capitulates without conditions to the Allied powers. Six years of carnage on the continent come to a formal close.

German officers sign for an army and a state already in ruins. A second signing in Berlin satisfies Soviet demands for full honor. Guns fall silent across Europe within hours of the final act. The text is short, stark, and total in its surrender terms. Unconditional, complete, and final: the European war's full stop in ink and seal. Victory in Europe Day followed within hours of the Berlin signing.
giorgi-de-harmonia-mundi-1545:
Francesco Giorgi sang the harmony of the whole world in De harmonia mundi totius, printed in 1545. The Franciscan friar builds three canticles on one claim: the world hangs together by number and music. Christian Kabbalah, the music of the spheres, and the concord of great world and small man weave through the Latin text.

Giorgi advised princes and churchmen, and his vast synthesis shaped Renaissance thought on architecture, music, and the soul. Later readers mined it for the hidden math of beauty. The book stands as the great Renaissance statement of universal harmony, learned, devout, and bold in its reach.
grand-jeu-de-societe-pratiques-secretes-:
Printed at Paris in 1845, this French volume sells the secret practices of Mademoiselle Le Normand, the famed fortune-teller of the Revolution and Empire. Its author hides behind the name Madame la Comtesse de two stars. The full title promises a complete treatise of chiromancy, old and new: the reading of fate in the lines of the hand. A short treatise on faces and skulls follows, after Lavater and Gall.

The Grand Jeu itself was Le Normand's great card game of fortune, played with a full pack of pictured cards. The book teaches the meanings of lines, mounts, and fingers, with a high-flown opening discourse. Its claims are occult, not proven, and its tone is sure of itself. As a record of how fortune-telling was sold and studied in the 1800s, it is rich and curious.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-2-1845:
Volume two of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job appeared in 1845, in the Rev. James Bliss translation for the Library of the Fathers. It holds Parts Three and Four of the Moralia, the commentary Gregory wrote in the late 500s on the Bible's great book about suffering.

Gregory keeps moving through Job verse by verse, turning each scene into teaching on pride, temptation, repentance, and hope. He treats Job's friends, who blamed the sufferer, as a warning against smug religion. The middle parts deepen the portrait of the patient man as a figure of Christ. For centuries, priests and monks mined these pages for sermons and counsel.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol1-1845:
Hahnemann's second pillar beside the Organon is The Chronic Diseases, and Volume I reached English readers in Hempel's translation of 1845. Here Hahnemann sets out his psora doctrine, the claim that one deep taint underlies most long illness. The volume pairs that theory with the first of his antipsoric remedies.

Psora, in his telling, begins with the itch and spreads through the body over a lifetime. Cure means matching the case to a drug proved against that taint. The book changed homeopathic practice, turning many doctors toward deep, slow cases they once called incurable. Volume I lays the ground the other four build on.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol2-1845:
Volume II of The Chronic Diseases, in the 1845 Hempel translation, moves from theory into the remedy records. Hahnemann's psora doctrine, his root-taint theory of long illness, fills the first volume. Here the antipsoric materia medica takes over, and drug follows drug in long, patient lists of proved symptoms.

These pages were working tools, meant to lie open on the desk during long and stubborn cases. Every line traces back to a proving, a test on a healthy person watched with care over days. Readers who work through the volume see Hahnemann's method at its most patient: observe, record, compare, then prescribe.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol3-1845:
Psora theory gives Volume III of The Chronic Diseases its reason to exist, but the content is pure materia medica. In Hempel's 1845 English, Hahnemann's remedy records roll on in the same spare, steady style. A drug's signs appear in fixed order, from the mind through the whole body, section by section.

Chronic cases, Hahnemann taught, yield slowly and need remedies chosen for depth, not speed. The antipsoric drugs in these volumes were his chosen weapons against that deep taint. Doctors of his school kept the five volumes near the Organon itself, and Volume III holds the middle of that working library.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol4-1845:
Volume IV of Hahnemann's Chronic Diseases, Englished by Hempel in 1845, nears the end of the antipsoric remedy list. The form stays plain: remedy after remedy, symptoms in their set order, no ornament. Behind each entry stand provings run under Hahnemann's own strict rules.

He demanded that provers note every change, however small, and these pages honor that demand. For modern readers the volume shows how homeopathy built its knowledge in its first age, one watched symptom at a time. As part of the five-volume whole it helped fix the psora doctrine in the school's mind.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol5-1845:
With Volume V in 1845, the Hempel translation of The Chronic Diseases stands complete at last. Five volumes carry Hahnemann's late system: one root taint, psora, and a family of deep-acting remedies to meet it. The last volume rounds out the antipsoric materia medica and closes the remedy lists.

Taken with the Organon, the set forms the second pillar of classical homeopathy, as its readers have long called it. The symptom lists look dry, yet each line was a tool for matching a suffering patient to a single drug. Volume V closes an English edition that served the school for generations.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
The second part of chapter seven in John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands reads Leicester's letters to his friends. Motley calls the Earl's conduct paltry toward the men who served him. Leicester's own words, printed at length, plead his case to the Queen. He protests that God knows the spirit in which he served her.

He complains that the Queen conceived against him, though bound by no covenant of his. He has spent two or three thousand pounds of his own, he says, likely to be ill spent. Motley lets the favourite condemn himself in his own hand. Flattery, self-pity, and blame for subordinates fill the despatches. This slice of the history works like a documentary: the editor's comments are brief, and the evidence voluminous. Leicester emerges neither monster nor hero, only a courtier out of his depth.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
Deception kindly meant fills Volume 3 of In the Fire of the Forge, the Nuremberg romance by Georg Ebers. Ebers shows the young knight Boemund Altrosen watching Cordula with proud delight. He alone, besides Seitz Siebenburg, sees that she invented her tale, and he honors the kindness behind the invention in this volume.

Chapter X sorts the room by what each person believes. Cordula spoke up to shield a reckless Swiss knight, and her bold move has also tangled her future sister in law. Siebenburg twists his mustache and hides open scorn behind forced silence. Around them the company crowds Heinz Schorlin with jokes and questions, while Count von Montfort warmly clasps the hand of Els. Jealousy, rank pride, and a protective lie share one merchant's hall.
japanese-instrument-of-surrender-1945:
Japan's envoys signed the Instrument of Surrender in Tokyo Bay in 1945. The ceremony took place aboard the battleship Missouri that September. With those signatures, the Second World War formally came to an end.

Japan accepts the Potsdam terms and the Emperor's new, bound place. Allied officers from many nations watch the short, grave rite unfold. MacArthur presides over the deck in a plain, open-collar uniform. The bloodiest conflict in history closes on a few signed lines. The document ends the Pacific war and opens the atomic age in one act. Its signed original rests today in the National Archives in Washington.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-isaac: Aaron ben Isaac Sason, an author and Talmudist born in Constantinople in 1629, is treated in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He was grandson of Aaron ben Joseph Sason, an eminent Talmudist, and cousin of Hayyim Benveniste. At twenty he was already holding Talmudic controversies with Moses Benveniste, who thought them worthy of publication. Judah Rozanes referred with respect to his unpublished work Hen Yeshallah. Whether the work Sefat Emet belongs to him or to his grandfather is uncertain, the entry concludes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-judan-or-j: Abba Judan was a man famed for giving, who lived in Antioch in the early part of the second century. Once Rabbis Eliezer, Joshua, and Akiba came collecting gifts for schools. Rather than send them away empty, he sold half of his property. His wealth had already shrunk much through his giving. The rabbis blessed him, and soon after, by luck, he found a treasure. For centuries after, the name Abba Judan was used in Palestine for any man of rare kindness in giving.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abensur-daniel-: Daniel Abensur was a Portuguese Jew who died in Hamburg in 1711. At one time he advanced a large sum of money to the Polish Crown. Later he became minister resident of the King of Poland at Hamburg. That post made him the Polish king's standing envoy in the city. He was buried in the cemetery of the Portuguese congregation at Altona. The short entry names no birth date, family, or other act from his life beyond the loan and the post.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abodah-divine-s: 'Abodah, meaning divine service, was first the benediction said during the morning sacrifice in the Temple. After the Temple fell, it became the prayer for the Temple service to be restored. People also used the word for morning and evening prayer. The entry adds that folk swore by the 'Abodah as they did by the Temple itself. In later use, people swore by the Bible in the same way. The notice is brief and gives the term's main senses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-sol:
Italian scholar Abraham ben Solomon Akra lived at the end of the sixteenth century and edited scientific works. At Venice in 1599 he brought out Meharere Nemerim. The book gathers method essays and comments on several Talmudic treatises.

Akra also wrote a method treatise on the Midrash Rabbot. Isaiah Horwitz put it in Shene Luhot ha-Berit without giving him credit, and the Wilna Midrash Rabbot copied it from there.
