It first appeared with Arze Lebanon at Venice in 1601. In it Akra states that he saw the Midrash Abkir manuscript in Egypt, the last known trace of that work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-nahmias: Mention of Abraham Nahmias inside Joseph Caro's Berit Joseph is the setting for this short notice. Its content is a cross-reference plus one achievement: he rendered into another tongue the commentary Thomas Aquinas wrote on the Metaphysics of Aristotle. Anyone seeking detail must turn to the main Nahmias entry, first in its series. Dates and place go unstated, so the translation stands alone as his documented act.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abtalion-pollio:
Abtalion, also called Pollion or Ptollion, led the Pharisees in the middle of the first century B.C. By custom he was vice-president of the great Sanhedrin of Jerusalem. His partner Shemaiah was its president. Though of heathen descent, both men were loved by the people. One tale says a crowd left the high priest to follow them after a Day of Atonement.

In 37 B.C. Abtalion urged the men of Jerusalem to open the gates to Herod. Herod thanked him with great honors. The entry sorts out a later oath story in Josephus. It argues that the Pollion in that tale can not be Abtalion, who had died by then. Abtalion had learned under Judah ben Ṭabbai and Simon ben Sheṭaḥ. He may have fled for a time to Alexandria, in Egypt. His school charged a small daily fee to keep out crowds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acqui-745: Acqui is a city on the Bormida, in the province of Alessandria, Italy. It is known for hot springs and old Roman ruins. Town records show Jews there since 1400. Early in the nineteenth century they numbered about 700. By 1899 the count had fallen to 220. Many had moved to Turin and Milan. In 1881 the old synagogue and ghetto were torn down. A new synagogue rose on a street named for its donor. The rabbi in 1899 was Adolfo Ancona.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adonijah-yah-is: Adonijah was the fourth son of David, by Haggith. After Absalom's death he claimed the throne as rightful heir. He called court men to a grand rite of offering. Bathsheba and the prophet Nathan won the crown for Solomon instead. Later Adonijah asked to wed Abishag, David's mate of old. Solomon read the ask as a bid for the throne. He had him put to death for it. Rabbinic notes pair him with Absalom in kind. Both kept fifty runners at their heels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-ahai-b-miny: Aha b. Minyomi was a Babylonian amora of the fourth generation, in the fourth century, a disciple of Nahman b. Jacob and a contemporary of Abaye. The entry adds that he was probably a brother of Adda b. Minyomi. Beyond these links of teacher, generation, and family, it records no further detail of his life or teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-lione:
Lionel Lindo Alexander was a political and communal worker in London. He was born there on May 14, 1852. He died on January 31, 1901. He was schooled at St. Marylebone's and the City of London schools. For nine years, from 1884 to 1892, he served as honorary secretary to the Jewish Board of Guardians.

He sat on the committees of many Jewish schools and charities from the 1870s on. He led the Jewish Workingmen's Club and Lads' Institute as its president. He was vice-president of Jews' College and had sat on its council since 1877. Men counted him an authority on questions of work and society. He gave evidence before select committees of both Houses. The subjects were the sweating system, and emigration and immigration. He compiled the Jewish population statistics. As honorary secretary he also wrote the Board of Guardians' yearly reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alypius-of-anti: Alypius of Antioch was a famed map maker of the fourth century. He was a close friend of the emperor Julian. Julian is known as the Apostate. Alypius ruled Britain from 355 to 360. The emperor then called him back east. His new task was to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem. At first he threw zeal into the work. In time his zeal cooled, the entry says. He saw how little help the Jews gave him. He left the field to the foes of the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amulet-1445:
Amulet is a charm worn to ward off harm. The word is an old Latin word of lost root. In Talmudic speech the charm is called a kemia. That word comes from a root that means to bind. Charms guarded men, homes, and herds from dark powers. They were used to cure ills as well.

All peoples of the old world used such charms. Jews shared that wide and old belief. All gems worn on the body may have begun as charms. Women and babes wore them more than men. The long entry runs through three ages of use. Bible, Talmud, and later ages each get a full part.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ankava-abraham-:
Abraham ben Mordecai Ankava was a North African Talmudist, author, and liturgical poet born at Fez, Morocco, early in the nineteenth century. He came from the Alnaqua family and died after 1860. His special field was the law of ritual slaughter.

For that work he traveled through North Africa and Italy, asking living experts and hunting old manuscripts. At Tlemcen in Algeria he stayed three years and founded a Talmudic academy to lift Jewish schooling there. His dietary-law work Zekor le-Abraham came out at Leghorn in 1839, in verse with a commentary. A second book for slaughterers followed in 1858.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apolant-eduard-: Eduard Apolant was a German physician born at Jastrow in West Prussia on August 21, 1847. He studied at the gymnasium of Deutsch-Krone and at the University of Berlin, taking his medical degree in 1870. He served as an assistant surgeon in the Franco-Prussian war of 1870-71. Back in Berlin he practiced medicine, and in 1896 he received the title of Sanitatsrath. He wrote many papers for leading medical journals, among them studies on white and red blood cells in suppuration and on carbolic acid dressings for smallpox.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apple-of-sodom-:
Apple of Sodom, also called the Dead Sea apple, is a fruit that Josephus and Tacitus describe near the site of Sodom. Fair to look at, it turned to smoke and ashes when a hand plucked it. Travelers cited here identify it with the fruit of a tree the Arabs call osher.

That tree, ten to fifteen feet high with gray, cork-like bark, grows in Palestine only along the Dead Sea shore. Its fruit looks like a large smooth apple or orange, in clusters of three or four. Press it, and it bursts with a puff, the entry quotes Robinson as saying. Only rind shreds and fibers stay in the hand, plus a small pod of fine silk that Arabs twist into gun matches.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ardotial-andrut:
Shem Tob ben Isaac Ardotial, whose name is often miscopied, was a Spanish poet who flourished at Soria at the start of the fourteenth century. Steinschneider ties his name to the Ardot family. His works cross several kinds, the entry shows.

He wrote a book of short literary and poetic pieces called Wars of the People and the Numbers. An ethical story of his reached print in a Metz collection of 1849. His Sea of the Preacher is a prayer of two thousand words, every one beginning with the letter mem. He also wrote liturgical poems for the Spanish rite. Under the title Temporary Injunctions he turned an Arabic ritual work by Israel Israeli of Toledo into Hebrew, still in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auspitz-heinric:
Heinrich Auspitz was an Austrian skin doctor. He was born at Nikolsburg, Moravia, on Sept. 2, 1835. He died at Vienna on May 23, 1886, about two years after taking Zeissl's place. He trained at the University of Vienna under Brücke, Skoda, Rokitansky, and others. In 1863 he became a lecturer there on skin diseases and syphilis.

In 1872 Auspitz took charge of the general clinic of Vienna. In 1875 he rose to associate professor, still teaching his two subjects. He founded and edited a quarterly journal for his field in 1869. His chief book, "System der Hautkrankheiten," came out at Vienna in 1881. It was later translated into French at Paris in 1887. The entry credits him with fresh, striking views that stirred debate, and with lasting gifts to the study of skin disease. He became a convert to Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-meon-beth-: Baal-meon was a city east of the Jordan. The Bible counts it in some places as Israelite, of the tribe of Reuben. In Jeremiah and Ezekiel it appears as Moabitish. The Moabite Stone tells how King Mesha took the city back after it had passed to Israel under Omri. Eusebius put the place nine Roman miles from Heshbon. Its site is marked by the ruins of Ma'in. Houses there are cut in part from the rock, and the building remains show Roman style.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baerwald-herman:
Hermann Baerwald was a German educator born at Nakel, in Posen, on Nov. 7, 1828. He studied at Konitz and Breslau, then at the University of Berlin, where the historian Leopold von Ranke took an interest in him. In 1859 he took a post at the Jewish Teachers' Seminary in Berlin. Nine years later the Jewish community of Frankfort called him to head its school, the Philanthropin.

Baerwald led that school for thirty-one years before he retired, amid wide praise and thanks. The entry stresses his drive to spread light and ease want, and his place on the central committee of the Alliance Israélite Universelle in Paris. Hardly a charity in Frankfort, it says, missed his good influence. It closes with his few published works, among them a history of Jewish schools in Frankfort.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bankruptcy-2445:
Bankruptcy, in modern law, is the court process for a debtor who cannot pay in full. Its two aims are fairness among creditors and a fresh start for the debtor. Rabbinic law, this entry says, has no trace of the second aim. No discharge exists there. Hillel even found a way, the prosbul, to undo the Bible's own year of release for poor debtors.

On fairness the Talmud leans the other way: a sealed bond acted from its date as a mortgage on all the debtor's land, so earlier bonds beat later ones. Where several creditors of one rank share a fund, the rabbis divide by heads, not by claim size. The entry works an example: a fund of 300 dinars split among claims of 300, 200, and 100 gives each man 100. Rules on interest between two Jews holding bonds against a Gentile close the account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bassin-eliezer-:
Eliezer Bassin was a missionary at Jassy, Rumania, born about 1840 in the government of Mohilev, Russia. He went to Constantinople in 1869, met English missionaries there, and embraced Christianity. His book on the modern Hebrew and the Hebrew Christian came out in London in 1882.

That book opens with his own life story and the hardships he faced after being sent back to Russia as a deserter. Later parts describe Jewish religion and ritual, with detail on views held by Jews in Russia and by the Ḥabad sect. In 1881 he also issued a German paper defending Jews against attacks in Germany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-max-josef-:
Max Josef Beer was an Austrian pianist and composer born at Vienna on Aug. 25, 1851. He studied with Dessoff and was still very young when state grants rewarded three of his works. The entry lists him as living at Vienna in 1901.

His stage works include five operas and an operetta that won a prize. A one act opera on a strike of smiths, staged in 1897, is judged his best here. It played with success in Berlin as well. Songs, a cantata, and a piano suite round out the list, plus a piece on Wagner.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belovar-2845: Belovar is a town in Croatia, in Austria, whose Jewish community was founded about the year 1877. Some fifty Jewish families settled there at that start. While in Belovar, Moritz Grünwald published a Jewish literary journal from the town. By 1902 the community had grown to about 300 families. It formed the seat of a district rabbinate, whose holder at the time is named in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benisch-abraham:
Abraham Benisch, a journalist and theologian, was born in Bohemia in 1811 and died near London on July 31, 1878. As a student he caught a bold aim, the restoration of Jewish independence in the Holy Land. A secret society formed around that plan and sent him abroad as its envoy. London Jews rejected the scheme when he laid it before them in 1841.

He stayed in London and turned to Jewish journalism. From 1854 he edited the Jewish Chronicle for long stretches, backing a moderate orthodoxy. He helped found learned societies and aided the start of the Anglo-Jewish Association in 1871.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berendson-marti: Martin Berendson, a German publisher, was born at Hamburg in 1824 and died on June 24, 1899. He headed the well-known bookselling and publishing firm of his home city, Gebrüder Berendson. Much of his free time went to Jewish communal affairs. He filled several honored offices in the Hamburg Reform congregation. He was also a leading Freemason and held a high place in the councils of that brotherhood. The entry rests on a notice in the Jewish Chronicle after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-josep: Joseph Bernstein, a Polish physician, was born at Warsaw in 1797 and died there in 1853. He finished at the Warsaw Lyceum in 1815 and studied medicine at Berlin, taking his degree in 1822. Back in Poland he worked a year at the university clinic of Warsaw. In 1829 he became house physician of the Warsaw Jewish Hospital. Four years later he rose to chief physician there, in 1834. His one named work, printed in 1818, treats consumption of the lungs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezek-3245: Bezek is a place named twice in the Bible. First, Judah and Simeon fought there. They battled the Canaanites and Perizzites. Judges tells that story. Second, Saul gathered his forces at Bezek. He was preparing to fight the Ammonites. First Samuel tells that mustering. The entry gives a modern identification. Moore linked Bezek to Khirbet Ibzig. That site lies 14 miles southwest of Beisan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bittoon-isaac-s: Isaac Bittoon was an English pugilist and fencing master. He was born in 1778. He died in February 1838. He taught "the noble art of self-defense." His first fight beat Tom Jones of Paddington. That bout fell at Wimbledon in 1801. A drawn battle with George Maddox followed. It lasted seventy-four rounds in 1802. Another draw came against William Wood in 1804. Officers stopped that fight in the thirty-sixth round. Bittoon then worked as a second only. He later ran an athletic school in Whitechapel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brasch-moritz-3:
Moritz Brasch was a German philosopher and man of letters born at Zempelburg on Aug. 18, 1843. He died at Leipzig on Sept. 14, 1895. He studied at Berlin, Greifswald, and Jena.

Brasch settled first in Berlin, then moved to Leipsic. There he chiefly edited Brockhaus' Konversations-Lexikon from 1874 to 1879. His own books treat Spinoza, Mendelssohn, and the classics of philosophy. A three-volume work on those classics ran from 1883 to 1886. He also wrote a history of Leipzig University in 1890. As an editor he issued works of Mendelssohn, Schopenhauer, and Aristotle in German dress for new readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brothers-richar:
Richard Brothers was an English visionary and the founder of Anglo-Israelism. Born Dec. 25, 1757, at Placentia, Newfoundland, he entered the British navy in 1771. He left as a half-pay lieutenant in 1783. In 1790 he refused his pension because of the oath it required.

Two years later Brothers began claiming a divine mission to announce fulfilled prophecy. He called himself a prince of the Hebrews and expected to be revealed on Nov. 17, 1795. Instead he was placed in a lunatic asylum. There he wrote works on prophecy and a description of the New Jerusalem. The entry credits him as the first to claim the English descend from the Lost Ten Tribes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burning-bush-38:
Burning bush is the common name for the tree from which the angel of Jehovah appeared to Moses in flame. Exodus stresses that the tree burned yet was not consumed. The entry treats the scene first in rabbinical literature. Midrash answers why an angel appears in one verse and God speaks in the next.

Rabbis read the thornbush as a sign that no place is empty of God's presence. Its fire, burning without consuming, pictured Israel enduring Egypt's sorrows. A critical section then takes up the rare Hebrew word for bush and the holy ground around it. It argues the fire showed God's holiness as saving, not destroying, for Israel. The sacred tree itself, it says, held no lasting holiness of its own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calvor-casper-3: Casper Calvor was a Lutheran theologian born Nov. 8, 1650, at Hildesheim, in Prussia. He took his master's degree in 1674 and became a deacon at Zellerfeld in 1677. Posts rose step by step: superintendent in 1684, consistory councilor in 1708, and general superintendent at Clausthal in 1710. He did missionary work among the Jews. He also handed them Christian books that he printed in Hebrew and German. He died at Clausthal on May 11, 1725.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carmel-4045: Carmel, in the brief hosted text, is the title of a German Jewish weekly and also of a Hungarian Jewish weekly. The hosted text gives that identification in a single line and sends the reader on to the entry on Periodicals for more. It names no editor, place, or date for either paper. Readers should treat the line as a pointer, not a history of the two weeklies, since no further facts about them are stated here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catalan-solomon: Solomon Catalan was, in all probability, a grandson of Gerson b. Solomon Catalan. The hosted entry gives one fact beyond that link: he served as rabbi in the city of Coimbra in 1360. A single source, Kayserling's history of the Jews in Portugal, is cited for the statement. No work by Solomon Catalan is named. No dates for his birth or death appear. Readers get a brief placement of the man in place, year, and family line, and nothing more from this text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chares-4245: Chares was a leader of the Zealots in the Judæo-Roman war. Josephus calls him one of the most eminent men of Gamala. When men of Bathyra, who backed Agrippa and the peace party, stood at Gamala without their leader Philip, the Gamalians attacked them. Chares, a relative of Philip, was killed in that attack, and so was his brother Jesus. The short entry adds that Chares' name is found in inscriptions. A Syrian inscription collection is cited as its source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chiun-4345:
Chiun is a puzzling word paired with Siccuth in Amos v. 26, and scholars long debated whether the pair are common nouns or proper names. The entry leans toward names. Siccuth is matched to the Assyrian Sakkut, an epithet of Ninib and Anu. Chiun is tied to Kaiwan, a name linked with Saturn.

Much of the piece weighs how the words entered the Hebrew text. It cites the Septuagint and Syriac readings and a shared list in Assyrian inscriptions. Some scholars treat the verse as a later gloss shaped by Babylonian influence. Others defend it as genuine, a split the entry reports without fully settling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coen-graziadio-:
Graziadio Vita Anania Coen, an Italian rabbi and scholar, was born at Reggio nell' Emilia about 1750 and died on March 28, 1834. He studied under Sansone Nahmani and Isaiah Vita Carmi. In his home city he founded a school that trained several rabbis. In 1825 he was called as chief rabbi to Florence, where he set up a Hebrew printing-press.

Teaching fills his long book list. Instruction for the Boy ran through six editions by 1880. He wrote a Hebrew grammar in 1808, a Hebrew-Italian dictionary in 1812, and handbooks for young students in both tongues. Songs of Israel appeared at Leghorn in 1793. Two volumes on rabbinic poetry, printed at Florence in 1828, close the entry's account of his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-collar-4545:
Collar, as an English rendering, rests on two Hebrew words, and the entry pulls both apart. In Judges viii. 26 and Isaiah iii. 19 one word lists ornaments, of Midianite kings in one place and of Jewish women in the other. Its root means to drop, so it may mean drops or pendants. The Targum reads wreaths, and Rashi follows. Kimhi reads a perfume bottle that drips.

The second word, in Job xxx. 18, is rendered collar with little warrant, the entry says. It means only the head opening of a garment, the same word used in Psalm cxxxiii. 2 for a robe's top edge. Exodus xxviii. 32 stands behind that plain sense. The piece is a warning that one English word hides two unlike things.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coral-4645: Coral here means the hard growth made by a sea polyp. It was prized in the ancient world for ornaments, charms, and amulets. Red coral came from the Mediterranean. The entry questions whether the ancient Hebrews knew it at all. Much of the piece weighs one Hebrew word in Job, Ezekiel, and Proverbs. Greek, Latin, and Targum renderings are compared. Some readers took the word as coral, others as a stone or pearls. Modern scholars split as well, leaving a doubtful term rather than a settled identification.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremieux-hanane: Hananeel Crémieux was a French Hebraist and judge, born in 1800. He died in 1878, a son of Mordecai Crémieux. Trained as a Talmudic scholar, he taught Hebrew to Jewish children at Aix. He also served there as slaughterer, circumciser, and reader. From 1821 he built a business career. For seventeen years he sat as judge in the Aix tribunal of commerce. He helped win a bankruptcy law with new rights against unpaid stockholders. He also helped found the Archives Israélites and wrote for it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cresson-warder-:
Warder Cresson was a religious enthusiast and a convert to Judaism. He was born in Philadelphia on July 13, 1798. He died in Jerusalem on Nov. 6, 1860. Raised a Quaker, he spent his youth on religious and social questions. In 1830 he published a pamphlet urging Quakers to a better life. He then passed through sect after sect, each seeming to him the true faith.

About 1840 he met Isaac Leeser and grew deeply attached to Judaism. On May 17, 1844, he was made consul at Jerusalem, the first so commissioned. His family later won a finding of lunacy against him in 1849. A famous six-day trial in May, 1851, reversed that finding. The entry follows his Jerusalem years after the verdict.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daggatun-4845:
Daggatun is a nomad tribe of Jewish origin living near Tementit, in the oasis of Tuat in the Moroccan Sahara. The first account of them came from Rabbi Mordecai Abi Sarur of Akka. He crossed the Sahara to Timbuctu in 1857, and his travels were printed in 1895. The Daggatun live in tents, he reports. In language, religion, and customs they resemble the Berber Tuaregs around them. They are fairer than most African Jews and still aware of their origin.

Their settlement is dated to the end of the seventh century. Exiled to the desert for resisting conversion, they slowly lost their Jewish practice. They became Mohammedans in name while cut off from their brethren. The Tuaregs hold them subject and do not marry into them. Traditions of Jewish blood among the Sahara Berbers close the article.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ibn-hin-4: Ibn Hin David was a cabalist who lived at Salonica at the end of the sixteenth century and the start of the seventeenth. Although he was blind, he devoted himself to cabalistic studies. He published other men's works: the "Sefer Gerushim" of Moses Cordovero at Venice in 1600, and the "Sodot" of Joseph Gikatilla. His own book, "Liḳḳuṭe Shoshannim" (Collections of Lilies), printed at Venice in 1602, explains Bible passages using five earlier writers, among them Jacob Berab and Obadiah Sforno.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-joel-51:
Joel Deutsch was a Hebraist and teacher of deaf-mutes born in Nikolsburg, Moravia, on March 20, 1813. He knew rabbinical literature deeply and collected Hebrew books with energy. His life's work was the schooling of deaf children. When an institute for Jewish deaf-mutes opened at Nikolsburg in 1844, he joined it as teacher.

The institute moved to Vienna in 1852, and Deutsch became its director, retiring in 1888. Austria decorated him in 1859 and gave him an imperial title in 1869. His pupils went on to teach in New York, London, and Budapest. He wrote textbooks in religion, Bible history, and first lessons for deaf children. He died in Vienna on May 1, 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dubnicza-5345:
Dubnicza is a Bulgarian town, 22 miles south of Sofia, on the Jerma's left bank. Family names there point to French, Spanish, Arabian, and Hungarian roots. Jews are known at Dubnicza in 1536. Brigands called the Kirjali seized the town more than once.

In 1793 and 1794 the town paid tribute, 3,000 piasters the first time and 300 the second. Abraham Alkalai, chief rabbi there for twenty years, set the rich Jews' shares. His tomb later drew pilgrims. The entry counts 8,000 people, about 1,150 of them Jews. Carpet-weaving rests wholly in Jewish hands, and the synagogue dates from 1825.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-efrati-amram-be:
Amram ben Nathan Efrati was rabbi of Valencia in the later fourteenth century. He held that post for more than forty years. Contemporaries like Nissim of Barcelona consulted him on rabbinic law. He ranked high among them as a Talmudist and a mystic. He also knew secular sciences well.

Efrati disliked casuistry and leaned on Maimonides in his rulings. Early on he attacked powerful townsmen whose acts had caused public offense. Late in life a rival casuist, Hasdai ben Solomon, came to Valencia. He set out to defame Efrati and attacked him openly. Only a few of Efrati's responsa survive, kept in Isaac ben Sheshet's collection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-be-er-fo: Elijah be'er Fonte was an Italian doctor of note. He was born in Germany late in the fourteenth century. He settled in Italy and won civic rights at Viterbo. Rome gave him the same rights in 1405. He was freed from tolls, forced service, and the Jewish garb. He might even carry arms, a rare grant. Pope Martin the Fifth made him his own doctor. He kept that post under the next pope as well. In 1443 he signed a pact on Jewish freedom with the pope.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-emden-jacob-isr:
Jacob Emden was a German Talmudist famed for zeal. Men know him by the short name Yaabez in print. He was born at Altona on June 4, 1697. He died in that town on April 19, 1776. His father, called Hakam Zebi, taught him Talmud till he was seventeen. He wed in 1715 and kept up his studies at his new home. In time he ranged across Cabala, grammar, and philosophy too. He held that a Jew should touch worldly learning only at dusk.

He mostly turned down posts as a town rabbi. In 1728 he took the pulpit at Emden for a time. From that town he drew the name he is known by. In 1733 he came back to Altona for good. The entry marks him as a foe of the Shabbethaian sect. That hidden movement drew his fire for years on end. His trade in jewels let him stay free of patrons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-en-mishpat-5745: En Mishpat is another name for the place called Kadesh. Genesis gives the name in its tale of an old war. The place is most likely Kadeshbarnea of later texts. There Chedorlaomer and his three allies won a fight. They struck down the Amalekites and the Amorites in that field. The entry is only two lines in length. It gives no more facts than that name, place, and fight. No people, customs, or later events are tied to the spot here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esar-haddon-heb:
Esar-haddon ruled Assyria from 680 to 668 B.C., as son and successor of Sennacherib. His father was murdered, and rebels rose at Nineveh. The entry says he crushed the rising in about six weeks, then beat his brothers in an eight-month campaign. He was crowned in 680. Unlike his father, he rebuilt Babylon and honored its old gods.

His armies pushed southwest farther than Assyria had reached before. Sidon was destroyed and a new town built in its place. A first attack on Egypt in 676 failed, but a second in 671 took Memphis. King Manasseh of Judah is named among his vassals. Esar-haddon died on the march in 668, after naming Assurbanipal coregent for Assyria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fear-of-god-604:
Fear of God is the Hebrew equal of religion itself, the entry opens, and the spring of morals and wisdom. It does not mean shrinking from God like a tyrant or a wild beast. It draws a person nearer, filling him with reverent awe. Self-seeking fear is judged unworthy of God's child. Isaiah sets it against the fear of man: let God be your dread, not the crowd.

Fear of God matches love and service, the entry argues from Deuteronomy. To fear God is to walk in his ways and serve him with heart and soul. It also means hating evil: not cursing the deaf or tripping the blind. Abraham pleaded that no fear of God ruled Gerar. Job is praised as one who feared God and shunned evil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischell-a-6145:
A. Fischell was a rabbi and historian who lived in New York in the middle of the nineteenth century. He served for a time as assistant to Dr. Raphall at the Shearith Israel congregation. Little is known of him beyond that, the entry says. He is thought to have died in Holland in the last quarter of that century.

In 1859 he read a paper before the New York Historical Society. Its subject was the history of the Jews in America, set out in date order. In debate he held that early Jews had full liberty under Dutch rule in New Amsterdam.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fortis-leone-62:
Leone Fortis was an Italian critic, journalist, and dramatist born at Triest on Oct. 5, 1828. He died at Milan in 1895. He was baptized as a child and schooled at Padua. In his youth he wrote poems and a story. In 1848 he was exiled to Triest for a drama he had written.

He moved on to Venice and then to Milan. There he founded two papers, one of which was suppressed. In 1859 he was exiled again and went to Switzerland and Turin. He founded two more papers, in 1866 and in 1870. Three of his dramas are named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fraud-and-mista:
Fraud and mistake, in Jewish law, concern the loss one party suffers through the other's lies or silence. The law gives relief by undoing the deal or by payment of damages. The written law is severe against false measures and false weights. Two sets of weights, one great and one small, are called an abomination. This rule holds in dealings with Gentiles as with Jews. Courts must name inspectors of scales and punish cheats.

A seller must tell the buyer of a hidden flaw in the goods. Bad grain must not be mixed with good and sold as good. Water must not be put into wine at all. A seller's promise to bear no blame for faults does not hold, the entry says, unless the buyer knew what he waived. Other parts treat sales set aside for a price too high or too low.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frenkel-israel-:
Israel Frenkel was a Russian physician born at Rypin on June 29, 1857. Until he was twelve he had only a religious schooling. One of his teachers, a plain schoolmaster who later became a noted doctor, fired him with a wish for worldly knowledge. He went through the gymnasium at Plotzk and studied medicine at Warsaw. He took his degree in 1885 and settled in Warsaw.

He had long been drawn to Hebrew studies. At school he wrote for Jewish papers. At the university he wrote on new finds in medicine and biology for Hebrew papers of science. In 1889 he printed a Hebrew book on nervous and venereal diseases. Its title means the guardian of health.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gabbai-6445:
Gabbai names a family found in Spain in the fifteenth century and later in Italy and the Levant. Members appear as rabbis, printers, officials, and scholars across several lands. Abraham Gabbai served as hakam in Amsterdam and then in Surinam. He died before 1757. His wife Sarah had his cabalistic poem printed after his death.

Other kin ran a press at Leghorn and then at Smyrna, issuing thirteen works between 1659 and 1680. Ezekiel Gabbai founded an early Judeo-Spanish paper at Constantinople. The best known member, Meir ben Ezekiel ibn Gabbai, wrote a cabalistic account of prayer in 1507. His chief work, finished in 1530, made him a forerunner of later cabalists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gebini-b-harson: Gebini ben Harson stands in Midrash as a rich man used to gloss Ecclesiastes iv. 8. The verse speaks of one who is alone, with no child or brother, and no end to his labor. The tale says Gebini was his mother only son. His father left him a heap of coins so tall that mother and son could not see each other across it. He was blind in one eye. The day he died, Belshazzar was born, and later took all that wealth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gezer-6645: Gezer was an old Canaanite city named in Egyptian carvings and in the Amarna letters as the seat of a local prince. Israel failed to take it, by Joshua and Judges alike. Solomon gained it as a gift from the Egyptian king, who had razed it, and rebuilt it. It stood as an Ephraim border town and a Levitic city. Simon the Maccabee took it, drove out its people, and settled it with loyal Jews. Its site was found in 1873 at Tell al-Jazar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldenberg-john: John Goldenberg was a Russian merchant born on the border of Russia and Rumania, and he died in 1895. He followed the army in the Crimea in 1856-57 as a sutler and made money there, later adding greatly to it in Burma. Settling first in Turkey after the war, he reached Burma through Persia and supervised large timber-cutting deals for King The-baw. After time in Vienna and Wiesbaden, he left by an English will most of his £160,000 fortune to six London charities and hospitals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gunzburg-also-s:
Günzburg is also the name of a wide family, spelled many ways. The family came from the town of Günzburg. It is thought to have reached that town from Ulm. Its best-known early members called themselves "Ulma-Günzburg." The Ulm, Ulma, and Ullman families are held to be branches of it. Kaufmann showed that "Gunz" and "Gaunz" are mere variants of the name.

When Russia and Austria ordered Jews to take family names, many chose this honored one. A lawsuit followed at Grodno under the decree of 1804. Baer Günzburg sued a family that had taken his name. The court held that any family might choose any name. Günzburg families then grew in number.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hammedatha-7145: Hammedatha is known only as the father of Haman. Esther names him at iii. 1 and 10, viii. 5, and ix. 10 and 24. He is generally called the Agagite. Only once, at ix. 10, does the text name him without that label. The entry adds one point about the name itself: it comes from the Persian and means "given by the moon." Nothing else about Hammedatha's life is recorded here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hararite-7245: Hararite is an epithet attached to some of David's heroes, and the entry's point is that the books disagree on how many men it covers — two or three. II Samuel xxiii. 11 makes Shammah, son of Agee, a Hararite, and verse 33 names Shammah the Hararite again; the parallel list in I Chronicles xi. calls the one Shammoth the Harorite and the other Jonathan, son of Shage. The name also falls on Ahiam, son of Sharar in Samuel, son of Sacar in Chronicles. The entry leaves the count unsettled.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hasidim-hasidis:
Hasidism is a religious movement that rose among Polish Jews in the eighteenth century. It won over nearly half of the Jewish masses in eastern Europe. Its name comes from a word for the pious. The movement put feeling and faith first, ahead of dogma and ritual form.

The long article sets the rise in the Ukraine, in Volhynia, Podolia, and Galicia. There Jews lived scattered in villages, far from study centers. War and ruin in the years after 1648 left them poor in goods and in learning. Dry book-based rabbinism, the entry argues, met neither the common folk nor seekers after living faith. Mystic stirrings filled that gap.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-havoth-jair-the: Havoth-jair, the tent villages of Jair, were towns east of the Jordan in Bashan and Gilead. They took their name from their conquerors. Jair, son of Manasseh, seized the whole tract of Argob. His towns numbered sixty. Despite their name, they were strong places with high walls and gates. In Solomon's day they fed into a royal supply district. A second set of thirty villages in Gilead bore the same name. Those belonged to Jair the Gileadite, named in the Book of Judges.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ben-solo: Hayyim ben Solomon of Moghilef, also called Hayyim of Czernowitz, was a rabbi and cabalist. He was a Hasidic follower of Israel Baal Shem. He served as rabbi in five towns before settling in Jerusalem. He died there in 1813. His books include cabalistic talks on the Sabbath and on prayer. He also wrote new readings on the Pentateuch and sermons on the prophets. Several of his works were printed years after his death, at towns across eastern Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hebrew-hebr-ibr:
Hebrew, from the word Ibri, is the name outsiders used for the Israelites. Egyptians use it in the tales of Joseph and Moses. Philistines use it in the stories of Saul and Samuel. Abram is called the Hebrew in one Genesis verse. The term marks Israelites off from the foreigners around them.

Later ages changed the word's work. In Greek times it came back into use when speaking to foreigners. New Testament writers use it for the tongue of Palestine, Hebrew or Aramaic. It could also mark those who kept old customs against Greek ways. The entry derives the name from a word meaning beyond, as in land beyond a river.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hess-ernst-frie: Ernst Friedrich Hess was a German convert to Christianity and an anti-Jewish writer of the sixteenth century. His book, first printed at Fritzlar in 1589, is named in full in the entry. Later editions appeared at several cities through 1703 and beyond. In Latin works it was cited under a Latin title. The entry states one charge against him plainly. He was the first to spread a slander about Jews soiling meat they sold to Christians. No birth or death dates are given for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-fund-bar:
Baron de Hirsch Fund was a fund of $2,400,000 to better the lot of some Jewish immigrants to the United States. It was set up under New York law on Feb. 12, 1891. Baron Maurice de Hirsch created it after hearing of New York conditions. Trustees from New York and Philadelphia are named.

The deed aimed at relief, schooling, English teaching, and trade training for Jews from Russia and Rumania. It also paid travel to places with work or kin. First relief met urgent needs. Later work centered on schooling and settlement. A trade school, English classes for 500 to 600 children, and the Woodbine farm colony and school are described at length.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-solomon-:
Solomon Hirsch, born in Württemberg on March 25, 1839, was an American merchant, diplomat, and politician. He came to the United States at fifteen and lived in New York, Connecticut, and New Hampshire. In 1858 he moved to Oregon. By 1864 he headed a large Portland trade house.

Oregon voters sent Hirsch to the state legislature in 1872. He then served three terms as state senator for Multnomah county, from 1874. He presided over the state senate in 1880. A United States Senate bid in 1885 failed only through a tied process, the entry notes. President Harrison made him minister to Turkey in 1889. He served until 1892 and led Portland's Jewish congregation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hurwitz-adolf-7: Adolf Hurwitz was a German mathematician born on March 26, 1859, at Hildesheim. He studied at Munich, Berlin, and Leipsic. In 1882 he became a lecturer at Gottingen. In 1884 he was made assistant professor at Konigsberg, and in 1892 professor at the Polytechnicum of Zurich. He published in the chief math journals of his day. The Gottingen Society of Sciences elected him a corresponding member in 1892. The entry gives no account of his theorems or fields of work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibrahim-ibn-ya-:
Ibrahim ibn Ya'kub, called the Israelite, was a Jewish merchant and traveler of the tenth century. He traded in slaves and may also have carried a diplomatic task. His home was most likely North Africa. In 965 he crossed the Adriatic, reached the West Slavs, and visited Prague and eastern Germany.

At Magdeburg he met Bulgarian envoys at the court of Otto the First. He traveled along the Elbe to Schwerin. His short sketch of the Slavs is a prized source for their early history. He notes Jewish merchants carrying flour, tin, and skins out of Bohemia. His report survives inside a later book by al-Bakri and was printed with notes in 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jedidah-8545: Jedidah was the mother of Josiah, king of Judah. The short entry gives her line in a few lines only: she was a daughter of Adaiah of Boscath and the wife of Amon, Josiah's father. It also gives the sense of her name, which means beloved. The entry cites Second Kings for these facts and adds no story or further detail about her life. Readers get a name, a family place, and a meaning, and nothing more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jekuthiel-ben-s: Jekuthiel ben Solomon, also called Maestro Bonsenior, was a French physician who lived at Narbonne in the second half of the fourteenth century. The brief entry records a single work. In 1387 he turned the Lilium Medicinae of Bernard of Gordon into Hebrew, under a title meaning lily of healing. That version still exists in manuscript, the entry notes. No birth or death dates and no other writings are given for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-morning-: Jewish Morning Journal, or Morgen Journal, was the first Yiddish daily morning newspaper. Jacob Saphirstein started it in New York on July 2, 1901, and still ran it in 1904 for the Jewish Press Publishing Company. Named staff men include city editor Jacob Magidoff and the writer Peter Wiernik. The entry calls the paper Orthodox and Zionist in name, yet the most worldly of the Yiddish papers in America. It pushed hard for Russian newcomers, the bulk of its readers, to become American in habit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joinville-old-f: Joinville is a French town in the Haute-Marne district. Its name shows up in old Talmud comments in several spellings. The counts of Champagne drew rich income from its Jews, who were in effect their serfs. When Philip the Fair took Champagne in 1284, those Jews had to pay 25,000 livres as a gift on his happy coming. Named scholars of the town include Samuel ben Aaron, a commentator, and his son Simeon, a noted commentator on both Talmud and Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-jacob-88:
Jacob Joseph was a Russian-American rabbi born at Krozhe in 1848 who died at New York on July 28, 1902. He studied at Volozhin under Hirsch Leib Berlin and Israel Salanter. His quick mind won him the title harif, the sharp-witted one. He served as rabbi at Vilon, Yurburg, and other towns, and his fame as a preacher grew.

In 1883 Wilna chose him as its maggid, or preacher. Called by New York congregations, he crossed to the United States and on July 8, 1888, became chief rabbi of the Russian Orthodox communities of New York. His funeral drew more than 50,000 Jews and was marked by a public disturbance. He published Le-Bet Ya'akob, a set of sermons and new readings, at Wilna in 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judas-iscariot-:
Judas Iscariot, the man of Keriot, was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus. He betrayed his master and handed him over to the priests for judgment. The entry notes that the Gospels tell the betrayal in partisan ways that do not agree. Luke says Satan entered Judas at the Passover table; Matthew gives the price as thirty pieces of silver.

The entry doubts that greed was the true motive and reads John as a later push to make Judas a type of greed. One view holds that Judas, a man of Judah among Galileans, never shared the group's faith in Jesus. Matthew's tale of his remorse and hanging is then traced, with the priests refusing the blood money. Later legend made him a standing figure of wickedness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaufmann-isidor:
Isidor Kaufmann was a Hungarian painter born on March 22, 1853, at Arad. He was meant for trade and came to art late. He studied first at Budapest, then at Vienna. Shut out of the Vienna Academy at first, he learned from the portrait painter Aigner. He later entered its painting school and worked with Professor Trenkwald.

Kaufmann gave himself to genre painting above all. His scenes of Polish Jewish life won the most notice. One canvas, "Der Besuch des Rabbi," is held by the emperor Francis Joseph. Another, "Der Zweifler," took a gold medal at Vienna. The entry lists more honors from Berlin, Munich, and Paris. His chess players also rank among his known works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kirk-kilisseh-9:
Kirk-Kilisseh is a city in Thrace, in European Turkey. It lies 102 miles north of Constantinople. Its name signifies in Turkish "forty churches." The city contained no Jews when Sultan Murad II conquered it in 1436. In 1674 Sultan Mohammed IV brought a large number of Jews there from Kaminiec. Their descendants are called "Eskenazi." The oldest epitaph in the local cemetery, dated 1663, is that of a rabbi from Uskup.

During the Turco-Russian war of 1877-78, the Jews helped defend the city. They fought beside their fellow citizens against Circassian pillagers. The community now numbers about 1,000 Jews in a total population of 15,000. It has an ancient synagogue and two schools with 200 pupils. The Jews are busy with wine-making in autumn. The rest of the year they follow different trades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kolin-9445:
Kolin, a town in Bohemia, had one of the oldest Jewish communities in the country, with Jews present in the fourteenth century. Expulsion came in 1541 under Ferdinand I, and the departing Jews were robbed on the road to Poland. Permission to return came in 1551, yet unrest followed for years. By 1618 the community was the largest in Bohemia after Prague.

Hard limits marked daily life for long stretches. Jews faced bans on trades, on owning more than a house and one horse, and on moving freely outside their street. A ruling of Feb. 3, 1655, gave the community its own court under imperial watch. The entry ends with schools, relief work in the famine winter of 1846-47, and a list of rabbis down to the present holder.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kulisher-mikhai:
Mikhail Ignatyevich Kulisher, a Russian lawyer and author born on July 7, 1847, in a Jewish farm colony near Sophiefka, reached St. Petersburg law work by 1872. Ill health had cut his schooling more than once. He served briefly as assistant district attorney, then gave most of his time to writing. Stays in Vienna and Berlin followed from 1875.

Editing and ethnography fill the long record. Kulisher wrote on Odessa riots in 1871, on the history of the family, and on artisan guilds. He edited papers that defended Poles, Ukrainians, and Jews against anti-Semitic attack. A paper he owned was taken from him in 1886 by a claim from its nominal editor. From 1888 he returned to legal practice in St. Petersburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-las-leyes-jacob: Jacob de Las Leyes was a Spanish compiler hired to make an ethics book for a royal pupil. The son of Alfonso X the Wise gave the order, for the teaching of the infante Don Alfonso Fernandez. Jacob copied out Flores de Derecho, a careful set of extracts from many ethical works in three books. The real author, the entry says, is thought to have been Moses Ẓarfati. No dates for Jacob's own life are given, and no other works are listed under his name in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leghorn-italian:
Leghorn, called Livorno in Italian, is a seaport city of Tuscany. Its Jewish community was the youngest among the large communities of Italy. For a time it ranked first among them, thanks to the wealth, learning, and political rights of its members. The first traces of Jewish settlement date to about 1583.

Medici efforts to grow the port drew new settlers, and Spanish Maranos fleeing Ferdinand II found refuge there in 1590. Charters in 1591 and 1593 promised settlers wide rights, and in 1597 the community gained self-rule. The article traces its Jewish court, its taxes, and its power to admit new citizens. Full citizenship came only in 1859.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lemon-hartog-ca:
Hartog Lemon, a Dutch physician, was born about the mid-eighteenth century and died at Amsterdam on Dec. 5, 1823. In 1788 the leaders of Amsterdam's Ashkenazic community made him physician for the poor. When the French took Holland in 1795, he led the Felix Libertate Society, which sought equal civic rights for Jews.

The community leaders dismissed Lemon in April 1795 for that work, but he pressed on. Dutch Jews won emancipation on Sept. 2, 1796. He helped found the new Adath Jeschurun congregation and sat in parliament from 1797. Arrested in 1813 on a plot charge, he served prison time in France until April 1814. He also wrote medical works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-jacob-984: Jacob Levin, a Galician Hebraist, was born at Brody in 1844. In 1865 he became coeditor, with Werber, of the Hebrew paper "Ibri Anoki." In that paper he ran a series on the place of the Jews in Russia before Alexander II. In 1880 he brought out a teaching poem, "Hitpattehut Tebel." It treats the growth of religion and philosophy. Years before, he had turned Schiller's "Die Braut von Messina" into Hebrew. That version came out at Brody in 1868.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenfeld-leopo:
Leopold Löwenfeld, a German physician, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Munich on January 23, 1847, he studied at the gymnasium and university in his home city. He took his medical degree in 1870. During the Franco-Prussian war he served as an assistant physician in a Bavarian field hospital.

The article follows his path after the war. He practiced for several years in the United States, then settled back in Munich in 1875. His publications show a turn toward the nervous system and mental treatment. They include studies of brain hemorrhage, a textbook of psychotherapy, and a handbook on hypnotism printed in 1901. Later work covered obsessive mental symptoms and modern treatment of nervous weakness. The entry captures a doctor working at the meeting point of neurology and early psychology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machir-ben-juda:
Machir ben Judah, a French scholar of the tenth and eleventh centuries, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Metz, he was a brother of Gershom, called the Light of the Exile. His fame rests on a dictionary, the Alfa Beta. The book itself is lost.

The article reconstructs its worth from quotations. Rashi cites it often in his Talmud commentary for hard words and passages. RaSHBaM, Eliezer ben Nathan, and Jacob Tam also quote it. The dictionary dealt mainly with difficult Talmudic terms, set in alphabetical order. Machir mostly followed his brother's readings, yet sometimes differed from him. In such cases Nathan ben Jehiel often took Machir's side. Rapoport gathered the scattered quotations in his biography of Nathan. The entry honors a work that survives only inside the books of others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manasseh-ben-is:
Manasseh ben Israel, the Dutch scholar who pled for the Jews' return to England, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at La Rochelle about 1604, he came to Amsterdam as a child of refugees from Lisbon. He succeeded his teacher as rabbi of the Neveh Shalom congregation at sixteen. He died at Middleburg in 1657.

The article joins his pulpit fame to a printer's trade. A Spanish priest quipped that Manasseh said what he knew, while Aboab knew what he said. Preaching and teaching could not feed him, so he founded Holland's first Hebrew press in 1627. His great work, El Conciliador, reconciled Bible passages that seem to conflict. Written in fluent Spanish, it won him readers across learned Europe. Grotius, the Vossii, and Anna Maria de Schurman corresponded with him. The entry, cut short here, opens the life of Amsterdam's most famous rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martyrdom-restr:
The limits Jewish law sets on martyrdom are the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Solomon Schechter and Julius H. Greenstone wrote it. Its starting point is a rabbinic rule drawn from Leviticus. A person should live by the commandments, not die by them. During the persecutions under Hadrian, the rabbis worked to restrain believers who were eager to die for the faith.

The article sets out the cases on both sides. Akiba chose death rather than stop teaching, while R. Ishmael allowed almost any transgression, short of public idolatry, to save a life. The meeting at Lydda settled the rule: every commandment may be broken under threat of death. The exceptions are the bans on idolatry, adultery, and murder. But public forced transgression in a time of persecution changes the answer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medina-10545:
Medina, the second sacred city of Islam, is given a Jewish history in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Mary W. Montgomery. Set in the Hijaz about 250 miles north of Mecca, it was the goal of Mohammed's flight, his capital, and his burial place. Arabic tradition peopled it first with Amalekites, then with Israelites, and the article allows that Jewish colonies may have come in waves after Nebuchadnezzar, Pompey, Titus, and Hadrian.

Three great Jewish tribes, the Banu Kainuka, Banu Kuraiza, and Banu al-Nadir, held strongholds at Yathrib, the city's older name. Yemeni Arab clans, Aus and Khazraj, encroached from the fourth century and by treachery and a banquet massacre gained the upper hand. The article follows the tribes into the war of Bu'ath, fought a few years before the Hegira, and notes that Jewish presence helped prepare the way for Mohammed's teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-b-solom:
Menahem ben Solomon ben Isaac was a twelfth-century Italian scholar. Joseph Jacobs and A. Biram treat him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, chiefly as the author of two books. His "Sekel Tob," Good Sense, was written at Rome in 1139. It retells the old midrashim on the Pentateuch in smooth, ornate Hebrew, drawing on the Targums, the geonic mystics, Alfasi, and Hananeel. Whole in the Middle Ages, it now survives only from Genesis 15 to Exodus 11, in two Bodleian manuscripts.

His second work shows the teacher. The "Eben Bohan," the Touchstone, was finished at Rome in 1143, in five months. It was written to prepare his three young sons for Bible study. The article calls it the first full Hebrew manual of the language and of exegesis: fifty parts, the first and largest a dictionary. Only fragments remain, in a Munich manuscript, analyzed by Bacher and partly translated by Dukes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metzler-lowy-pa:
Pauline Metzler-Löwy was an Austrian contralto born at Theresienstadt in Bohemia on August 31, 1853. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn trace her career in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry published in 1906. She entered the Prague Conservatorium at seven and studied there four years. She graduated with honors and took an engagement at Altenburg.

Her leading roles included Orpheus in Gluck's opera. She also sang Azucena in Il Trovatore and Nancy in Martha. From 1875 she sang for twelve years at the Leipsic Stadttheater, under three managers. She also gave concert and oratorio work in Hamburg, Bremen, and other cities. She married the piano teacher Ferdinand Metzler in 1881. She left the operatic stage in 1887, and from 1897 she taught singing only.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-money-10945:
Money in ancient Israel began as weighed metal. A Jewish Encyclopedia article published in 1906 works out the arithmetic. Its authors are Emil G. Hirsch, Wilhelm Nowack, and Isidore Singer. The shekel was the standard unit for money as for weight. The pieces were its fractions and multiples. Behind the system stood a contest between Egypt's decimal reckoning and Babylon's sixty-based one.

The Phoenicians, the article argues, likely mediated the compromise: a mina of fifty shekels. Gold stood to silver at ten to one. Then it drifted to forty to three as silver grew plentiful. The writers show why the silver shekel could not simply match the gold one's weight. It had to be made as a smaller piece. That dry calculation is what the biblical economy rested on.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosen-moses-jul:
Julius Mosen, born Moses, was a German poet who lived from 1803 to 1867. Isidore Singer wrote his entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Marieney in Saxony, he studied law at Jena, but his father's death broke off his studies. He worked in law offices, became a judge in 1831, and practised in Dresden.

In 1844 Mosen became dramatic writer to the Court Theater at Oldenburg. Soon his health failed, and within a few years he was fully paralyzed and pensioned. He kept writing anyway, producing poems, novels, and historical plays such as Heinrich der Finkler and Cola Rienzi. His collected works filled eight volumes in 1863, and a new edition followed after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mussafia-hayyim:
Hayyim Isaac Mussafia was a Talmudist born at Jerusalem in 1760 and dead at Spalato in 1837. Gotthard Deutsch and Isidor Warsaw wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied under David Pardo of Sarajevo and advanced so fast that he was a rabbinical authority as a boy. At seventeen he became rabbi of Spalato.

Mussafia held that pulpit for sixty years, until his death. His Hayyim wa-Hesed, printed after he died, discusses Jacob ben Asher's Turim, and his Hiddushe Dinim treats points of law. Sermons and notes of his stayed in manuscript. His son Jacob followed him as rabbi of Spalato and edited the responsa of the Geonim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-11345:
Nathan names a New York family active in city and Jewish life. Joseph Jacobs, Elvira N. Solis, and Cyrus Adler wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The family had lived in New York since the late 1700s. Simon Nathan was its first member in America. His descendants worked in law, business, and public service.

One section follows Benjamin Nathan of the New York Stock Exchange. He helped lead the Jews' Hospital, now Mount Sinai Hospital. Jonathan Nathan was a lawyer known for will and equity cases. Gratz Nathan also practiced law in the city. Maud Nathan led the Consumers' League in New York. She spoke for limits on work by women and children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nero-11445:
Nero was Rome's emperor during Judea's slide to revolt. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Antium on Dec. 15, 37 C.E. Adopted by Claudius, he took the throne in 54. He gave Lesser Armenia to a Herodian prince.

Nero added Tiberias and Tarichea to Agrippa's realm. Rome's Jews fared well, and a Jewish actor served his court. Yet at Caesarea he ruled against the Jews in 60. His wife Poppaea, drawn to Judaism, won another case for them. Bad procurators still drove Palestine into revolt in 66. Nero sent Vespasian, then killed himself in despair. Talmud legend makes him flee, convert, and father Rabbi Meir's line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nikolsburg-1154:
Nikolsburg is a town in southern Moravia. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there probably in 1420, fleeing Austria. The princes of Lichtenstein protected the fugitives then. Cardinal Dietrichstein later shielded them for their taxes.

Vienna's expelled Jews swelled the town in 1670. Under Maria Theresa it held 620 Jewish families. That was about 3,000 Jews, half the town. Its yeshivah drew three to four hundred disciples. Mordecai Benet gave that school its greatest fame. A dozen synagogues once served the community there. Two remain, the Alt-Schul and the Neu-Schul. Freedom after 1848 drained the town's Jews away. Only 749 remained in Nikolsburg by 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-obadiah-ben-dav: Obadiah ben David ben Obadiah was a writer of notes on Maimonides, the great Jewish thinker. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1325 by one count, or in 1341 by another. His notes dealt with the Jewish calendar and with the stars. They were first printed at Amsterdam in 1702.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppert-jules-11:
Jules Oppert was a French scholar of the East from Hamburg. Isidore Singer and Louis H. Gray wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hamburg on July 9, 1825. He died in Paris on August 19, 1905. He read law at Heidelberg in his youth.

Love of the East drew Jules from law to old tongues. He read at Bonn, at Berlin, and at Kiel. He took his degree in the year 1847. That year he left Germany and settled in France. Great scholars there took note of his first works. His early book treated the sounds of old Persian. In 1851 France sent a team to the East. Jules went as its man for the old Assyrian tongue. There he first fixed the site of a lost town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-padua-jacob-mei:
Jacob Meir Padua was a Russian rabbi of Brest-Litovsk. The board and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in that town and died there in 1854. His kin, the Katzenellenbogen line, led there for ages. His father and grandfather both lived in that town.

In 1837 the town chose Jacob as its new rabbi. He was then rabbi of Pinsk-Karlin, in Minsk land. He did not take up the new post till 1840. In 1852 a great dearth struck the folk of Brest. In that want, he let Jews eat peas at Passover. He let them eat beans at that feast as well. That act broke with the strict rule of his faith. He made his case for it in a reply of his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-patricius-11945:
Patricius led a Jewish revolt against Rome in the fourth century. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Greek sources call him Patricius. Jewish sources call him Natrona, a name with a messianic ring.

In 351 the Jews of Palestine rose under harsh Roman rule. His men seized Sepphoris and a few nearby towns. The general Ursicinus crushed the revolt soon after. Sepphoris, Tiberias, and Lydda were destroyed in the fighting. The article thinks Patricius likely died in the war. It also notes two later rabbis of the same name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-persia-from-old:
Persia was one of the great kingdoms of the ancient world. Joseph Jacobs and A. V. W. Jackson wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its story touches Jewish history from the Captivity onward. The name can mean the whole empire or one province.

The empire ran from the Caspian Sea to the Persian Gulf. It stretched from the Tigris to the Indus River. The province alone matches the modern Fars. Persian speech grew through three clear stages. Its oldest form lives in the Avesta. Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism during the long Persian rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pi-hahiroth-121:
Pi-hahiroth was a camp of Israel on the Exodus road. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It lay between Migdol and the sea. The camp faced the shrine of Baal-zephon. Pharaoh's host overtook Israel at that camp.

Israel turned back from Etham to camp there. The name seems Egyptian, but its sense is disputed. One old version renders it as sheepfold or farm. The Mekilta links the place with Pithom. It reads the name as the mouth of freedom. Later scholars placed it by beds of reeds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-a-m-ritt:
A. M. Pollak, later Ritter von Rudin, was an Austrian match maker and giver to good causes. Isidore Singer and Emil Jelinek wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Bohemia in 1817, he trained for work in trade and craft. In 1836 he set up a match factory at Prague.

The factory did so well that Pollak sold matches abroad within ten years. He opened branch offices in London, New York, and Sydney. He later traded with Japan and Russia as well. Many new steps in match making came from his works. His giving went mostly to schools and science. He founded the Rudolphinum at Vienna, where poor students live and study free. The emperor made him a noble in 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prerau-12345:
Prerau is a town in Moravia with an old Jewish past. Gotthard Deutsch and Jacob Tauber wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jew street is named as early as the days of Charles the Fourth. The settlement stayed small for a long time, though. Growth came from sorrow elsewhere in the year 1454.

In 1454 Jews were driven from Olmütz and Breslau. Many found shelter at Prerau and made it grow. They settled in a suburb with its own synagogue. They kept a burial ground of their own there. Digging in that ground still turns up old tombstones. The entry follows the town's Jews through taxes and change.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rakowski-abraha:
Abraham Abel Rakowski was an Austrian author born in December 1855. Herman Rosenthal and Isidor Warsaw wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Maryampol in Austrian Galicia. His father, a rabbi, taught him Talmud.

The article lists many Hebrew works from 1875 onward. Rakowski translated novels by Philippson and Disraeli into Hebrew. He also wrote tales set in the Prague ghetto. Other pieces covered money, wise sayings, and Semitic history. He wrote often for the Hebrew journal Ha-Zefirah. By 1895 he had become a merchant at Zambraw. The entry shows a Hebrew writer with a very wide range.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reggio-leone-12:
Leone Reggio was an Italian rabbi born at Ferrara in 1808. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Ferrara on September 23, 1870. His father Zaccaria was chief rabbi of Ferrara.

The article says Leone taught at the Talmud Torah at age twenty. When his father died, he took the rabbinical chair. His books all serve the study of Hebrew. One is a reasoned grammar of the language, from 1844. Another treats correct Hebrew speech that same year. A later manual aids practical study of Hebrew. He also wrote rules on ritual slaughter and inspection. The entry presents a rabbi whose teaching lived in textbooks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ricius-augustin: Augustinus Ricius was a Jewish convert and astronomer of the fifteenth century. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was a disciple of Abraham Zacuto. His work treats the motion of the eighth sphere. The article says a Latin version appeared at Paris in 1521. Ricius quotes Ibn Ezra and Abraham ben Hiyya. He also cites other Jewish authors in his work. He mentions the epoch year 1477 in it. Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue supports the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenblatt-mord:
Mordecai ben Menahem Rosenblatt was a Russian rabbi known as Der Butener Zaddik, the righteous man of Buten. Isidore Singer and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born at Autopoli, in the Grodno region, in 1837.

Rosenblatt studied the Cabala and lived a strict, ascetic Hasidic life. As rabbi of Buten from 1870, he gained fame as a miracle worker. Jews, and even Christian nobles, came from far away for his advice and blessing. He later served at Korelitz and Oshmyani, and from 1904 at Slonim. His Hadrat Mordekai, printed in 1899, gathers his legal replies and sermons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rustchuk-12945:
Rustchuk is a city of Bulgaria on the southern bank of the Danube. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews first came there for trade early in the eighteenth century.

The settled community dates from 1792, founded by refugees from Belgrade. Their first chief rabbi, Abraham Graziani, drew up communal rules about 1800. He also secured land for a cemetery for the growing congregation. Trade flourished until war and blockade broke the town's prosperity. In the sieges, Russian troops used the synagogue as a stable, then burned it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shem-tob-ben-is:
Shem-Tob ben Isaac of Tortosa was a Spanish scholar and physician born in 1196. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He first worked in trade, traveling widely by land and sea. A rebuke at Acre changed the course of his life.

Acre's rabbi shamed him for knowing so little of Judaism. In 1226 Shem-Tob quit commerce for rabbinic and science study. He trained at Barcelona, then turned to medicine for twenty years. He became a skilled physician, practicing chiefly at Marseilles. His first work rendered Averroes on Aristotle's soul into Hebrew. At fifty-eight he began translating a great Arabic medical work. The entry follows a merchant remade into a doctor and translator.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siesby-oskar-13:
Oskar Siesby was a Danish philologist born at Ebeltoft, Jutland, in 1833. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was brother to Gottlieb Siesby, the poet and editor. Oskar graduated from the University of Copenhagen in 1850.

He then took up philology, the study of language and texts. In 1856 he passed the examination for teachers in his field. From 1853 he taught Latin and Greek at a Copenhagen school. He stayed at that institute for forty full years. Copenhagen made him lecturer in classical philology in 1871. He refused reappointment to that post in 1876. In 1882 he returned as an unsalaried university lecturer. His writings were few, mostly grammatical treatises in journals. The entry profiles a steady classical teacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-testame:
The Testament of Solomon is a pseudepigraphic treatise on demons. Crawford Howell Toy wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It deals with the forms and acts of demons. It also gives charms that work against those demons. The full Greek text was first printed in the nineteenth century.

The work claims to be Solomon's own account of events. During the building of the Temple, a demon plagued his overseer. God sent a magic seal ring through the angel Michael. With it Solomon forced the demon to summon Beelzebub. Demon after demon then appeared before the king in turn. Each had to name his home, origin, and ruling angel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-specific-perfor:
Specific performance is a court order forcing a contract to be carried out. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In English-American law it applies mainly to land contracts. The losing party must convey the land, not just pay damages. Rabbinical law knew ways to compel men to obey decrees.

Compulsion could come by excommunication, prison, or flogging in rabbinic law. A man could even be forced to give a divorce bill. But no compulsion could enforce a contract to convey land. Such future contracts were held void under rabbinic rules. Unless title passed by the proper act, either party could withdraw.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-staff-shebet-ma:
The staff, called shebet or matteh in Hebrew, was in universal use. Emil G Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Herodotus says every Babylonian man carried a ring and a staff. The staff top was carved with a flower or like figure. Ancient Hebrews likewise carried a staff as a daily custom.

The custom may date from their days as nomadic herdsmen. The staff kept the flock together for the herdsman at work. Its long upper end was bent, as Egyptian pictures show. It served as a weapon and as a plowman's goad as well. Wanderers needed it, and the weak leaned on it for support. In overseers' hands it became a badge of office and punishment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stettin-14045:
Stettin is a district of Pomerania and its capital city. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. In 1261 Duke Barnim the First granted local Jews Magdeburg-style rights. Less than three years later, Greifswald won leave to expel its Jews. Glückel of Hameln once lived in the city.

Since the mid-1800s the city held a Hebrew printing press. It issued Buxtorf's Concordance in 1856 and a law code in 1862. The district counted 6,416 Jews among over 1.6 million people. The capital itself held about 3,000 Jews. Its community ran an orphan asylum and an infirmary. Seven other benevolent societies served local Jews. The entry gives a snapshot of Jewish life in Pomerania around 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-swan-14145:
The swan enters the Bible through a disputed Hebrew name. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Authorized Version renders tinshemet as swan twice. It appears in Leviticus and Deuteronomy among unclean birds. The Revised Version reads horned owl instead.

Two swan species have been found in Palestine. The whooper, or wild swan, is one of them. The mute swan is the second kind recorded. Both kinds are fairly rare in the land. A Talmud phrase about fattened birds may mean swans. Most readers take it as fattened hens instead. The short entry shows one word can shift a species. It warns translators to weigh each rendering with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tappuah-14245: Tappuah is a place name shared by several sites in Joshua. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. One Tappuah was a city in the Shefelah lowland. Another marked Ephraim's western border. The land of Tappuah belonged mostly to Manasseh. A southern Tappuah bounded Manasseh as well. One Tappuah was also a son of Hebron.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tet-14345: Tet is the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé treat it in a brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The meaning of its name is uncertain. Its sound is a hard, emphatic t. The letter appears only as a root letter, seldom as a word-forming part. It sometimes swaps with other dental sounds and with a sibilant. In later use, tet also served as the numeral nine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tophet-isa-xxx-:
Tophet was a place of child sacrifice just outside Jerusalem's walls. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jeremiah names the spot most often in his book. Kings places it in the valley of Hinnom's son. Scholars debate which of three valleys held it.

All agree the valleys meet below the pool of Siloam. The favored site lies southwest of the city. There children were burned for Baal and other idols. King Josiah defiled the place to end the rite. Two kings of Judah had offered such sacrifices. Jeremiah renamed it the valley of slaughter. In later times it became a burning rubbish heap. That fate fed the image of Gehenna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-turin-14545:
Turin, an Italian city on the Po, first admitted Jews in 1424. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews likely won entry by lending at lower rates than Christians. Elia Alamandi was the first Jew to settle there with family. A 1430 statute forced a red shoulder badge.

That statute also barred Jews from living among Christians. New synagogues were forbidden under its terms. A renewable ten-year treaty governed Jewish rights instead. It promised freedom of residence in Turin itself. The duke also banned attacks on Jewish residents. Emmanuel Philibert decreed expulsion in 1560 at one point. Pleas and payments won repeated reprieves after that.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiss-isaac-hir:
Isaac Hirsch Weiss was an Austrian Talmudist and historian. He was born at Gross Meseritsch, Moravia, on February 9, 1815. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this long Jewish Encyclopedia entry. It appeared in 1906, the year after his death at Vienna. He began Talmud study in childhood schools. At age eight he entered a yeshibah.

Weiss moved from school to school seeking broader learning. Yeshibot gave him Hebrew grammar but not secular science. Krochmal, Rapoport, and Zunz shaped his turn to history. Still, Talmud study filled most of his days. He wrote pamphlets on rabbinic literature while living at home. His life's work traced how Jewish law developed over time. The entry honors a founder of that study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winternitz-mori:
Moriz Winternitz was an Austrian scholar of India. Joseph Jacobs and Louis H. Gray wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Horn on December 23, 1863. He entered the University of Vienna in 1880. He took his doctorate there in 1886. In 1888 he went to Oxford to work.

At Oxford, Winternitz assisted Max Müller for four years. They prepared the second edition of the Rig Veda. He also served as librarian of the Indian Institute. In 1899 he moved to Prague as a lecturer. In 1902 he became professor of Sanskrit there. Ethnology formed his second field of study. His books include an old Indian wedding ritual.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zerahiah-ha-yew:
Zerahiah ha-Yewani was a Greek moral writer of old times. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the 1200s or the 1300s by best guess. No facts of his life are known to men now.

His fame rests on one work of right acts and faith. That work bears the name Sefer ha-Yashar in Hebrew. It was long mixed with a law book of the same name. That law book was the work of Jacob Tam of France. A sage of Lonzano set the true sire of the work right. A fresh slip then gave the work to a like named man. That man was Zerahiah ha-Levi, of Maor fame in lore. The work holds eighteen short parts on man and God. It is a brief form of the great work of Bahya.
journals-of-expeditions-of-discovery-int:
Volume two of Edward John Eyre's Journals of Expeditions of Discovery continues his 1840-41 Australian travels. The work covers the overland route from Adelaide to King George's Sound. It was sent out by South Australian colonists with the sanction and support of their government. Like volume one, it includes Eyre's account of Aboriginal customs and relations with Europeans.

Eyre inscribes the volumes to Governor George Gawler with gratitude for his kindness. His preface answers why publication waited until after 1844. Peace work among the Murray River tribes, after their 1841 attacks on colonists, claimed those years. He believed his long experience among Aboriginal people fitted him for that duty. The journals preserve his observations exactly as the expeditions recorded them.
kerner-seeress-prevorst-1845:
Justinus Kerner tends a frail seer in The Seeress of Prevorst, in English from 1845. Kerner was a healer and poet in a small German town. His guest, Friederike Hauffe, lay ill for years, spoke in trance in strange tongues, drew rings of signs, and told of a world of souls in close touch with ours each day.

Kerner prints her words, draws, and cures with love and care. The book is part ward log, part hymn. It founds a whole kind of book: the seer as saint and case. Its glow still charms.
lawes-against-witches-1645:
