The chain of steps links insulin signals to control of vessel inflammation. That link may matter for diabetes, where both insulin problems and vessel damage are common.
plos-pone-0358545:
Chung-Fen Tsai leads a team of seven profiling brain bleeds in Taiwan and their effect on thinking, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Intracerebral hemorrhage strikes East Asian populations at high rates, and where the bleed sits changes its cause and outlook. The study recruited two hundred two patients from two large hospitals. It compared bleeds near the brain's surface with deep ones. It also compared cases tied to a vessel stiffening disease of aging with other causes.

Surface bleeds, a fifth of the total, came with older patients, worse consciousness, bigger bleeds, and higher death within a month. Those patients also showed more of the tiny surface bleeds and iron staining that mark the aging vessel disease, and their early thinking scores were worse. Deep bleed patients, by contrast, almost universally had high blood pressure. The comparison gives clinicians a sharper local picture of which bleed pattern threatens cognition most.
plos-pone-0358845:
Hongkun Liu leads a team of six studying how well cancer patients in China judge their own risk of falling, in PLOS ONE in 2026. People receiving radiation or chemotherapy are often weak and unsteady, and patients who underestimate the danger may skip precautions. The authors surveyed survivors at a large hospital in Zibo to find distinct patterns of awareness and what shapes them.

More than five hundred patients took part, rating fall risk perception alongside social support, health literacy, and confidence in managing chronic illness. Statistical grouping found three profiles: a low awareness group of about a quarter, a middle group of about half whose awareness depended on their condition, and a highly self aware quarter. Pinpointing which patients under judge risk helps nurses aim fall prevention teaching where it is most needed.
plos-pone-0358945:
Matthieu Coupet leads a team of eight building software to map brain aneurysms that reopen after treatment, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Aneurysms are often sealed from inside with metal coils, but blood sometimes finds its way back in, a problem called recanalization. Surgeons considering a follow up clipping operation need exact measurements of the reopened space, the coil mass, and the vessel neck, which are tedious to trace by hand.

Their framework trains a proven medical imaging network on three dimensional angiography scans to outline the vessel tree, the coils, and the reopened channel separately. Automated steps then compute planning numbers such as the distance from coils to neck and the volume of the recurrence. Early results across the evaluated cases were consistent and encouraging. The authors position the tool as preparation support for microsurgery, not a replacement for surgical judgment.
plos-pone-0359545: Kono and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on two friendly bacteria found in yogurt. The strains carry the codes OLL1073R-1 and OLS3059. The team reports that they switch on dendritic cells, both the common kind and the plasmacytoid kind. They also report a boost to anti-viral immune responses. If food bacteria can prime virus defenses, diet may play a small role in infection readiness.
plos-pone-0359645: Tanjila and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on women workers in Bangladesh. They searched for what shapes how engaged women feel in their jobs. Engagement means energy, pride, and focus at work. Knowing its drivers helps employers in Bangladesh keep skilled women and improve daily work life. The topic matters in a workforce where women's formal jobs have grown fast.
plos-pone-0360245:
Ambreen Gowani and colleagues adapted a heart failure questionnaire for use in Pakistan in 2026. The instrument, the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire, asks patients how their condition limits daily life, and it is used worldwide to judge treatment benefit from the patient's side. A questionnaire cannot simply be translated word for word; its questions must carry the same meaning in a new language and culture.

The team carried out the translation and cultural adaptation, the careful process of adjusting wording, examples, and response habits so Pakistani patients understand each item as intended. A validated local version lets Pakistani clinics and trials measure quality of life on the same scale as the rest of the world.
pmc-13192245:
Sila Usta is first author on a 2026 dental materials study of how root canal rinses affect two repair cements. Endodontic irrigants, the washing solutions used during root canal treatment, touch hydraulic cements such as PD MTA and Biodentine. Whether they dissolve, stain, or roughen these materials matters for sealing and appearance.

Cement cylinders soaked for a day in five solutions, including bleach-like sodium hypochlorite and a chitosan nanoparticle rinse. The two cements dissolved alike overall, but two solutions raised dissolving in both. Biodentine stained more than PD MTA in most solutions, with the bleach rinse worst. One rinse roughened both most. Rinse choice, the authors say, protects material integrity.
pmc-13197445:
Ozan Ahmet Cetin and colleagues studied home versus hospital chemotherapy for gut cancers in a 2026 Turkish cohort. Home infusion through an implanted port saves travel but may strain patients on long regimens. Proof on anxiety and quality of life in this setting was thin, so the team ran a forward-looking study.

They enrolled 190 patients set for add-on therapy after surgery. Patients chose home port infusion or hospital infusion through a vein. After six cycles, the home group reported higher anxiety and worse pain, fatigue, and nausea. Gaps shrank by twelve cycles. Urgent visits with no physical cause were more common at home early on. Living alone and low social activity also tied to high anxiety.
pmc-13198045:
Christine Frank and colleagues engineered a heat-loving bacterium to make an amino acid in 2026. The bacterium Bacillus methanolicus grows on methanol, a renewable feedstock, and naturally pours out glutamate. The team aimed to redirect it toward L-proline, an amino acid used in food and industry.

A borrowed gene set from a cousin species failed: it raised a related compound instead, likely because one enzyme wilts at high heat. A rebuilt gene set using the bacterium's own genes, freed from its natural brakes, worked better. Cells secreted L-proline while growing on methanol at high heat. Levels reached a set mark after forty hours in fed-batch culture. Salt buildup from glutamate slowed growth, a hurdle for scale-up.
pmc-13198645:
Thomas Beuchard and colleagues compared drainage tactics for double blockage by cancer in a 2026 multicenter study. Cancer can block both the bile duct and the stomach outlet. Scope-guided drainage offers several pairings, and the best pairing was unknown, so eleven centers pooled past cases.

The study covered 159 patients from 2017 to 2023, most with pancreatic cancer. Four pairings combined two bile drainage routes with two stomach outlet routes. The pairing of liver-linked bile drainage with a scope-made stomach bypass failed least, with blockage in twelve percent. At one year, its open-stent survival ran highest as well. Severe side effects clustered more with one bile route. End choice may trade durability against safety.
pmc-13199545:
Sneha Dwivedi and colleagues made zinc oxide nanoparticles with a fungus in a 2026 study. Nanoparticles are specks far smaller than a cell, with wide uses in farming and medicine. Green synthesis swaps harsh chemicals for living helpers; here a fungus living inside a medicinal plant did the work.

Lab checks confirmed pure particles of the right crystal form, about twenty-seven nanometers wide. Fungal molecules coated their surface. The particles fought free radicals, curbed several bacteria at low doses, and slowed a crop fungus. In water-grown rice seedlings, a low dose modestly raised fresh weight and leaf efficiency. Safety testing in cells is still needed before any field use.
pmc-13199645:
Kazuki Kai and colleagues built a tiny implanted radio controller for cyborg cockroaches in a 2026 study. Cyborg insects carry electronics that steer their motion, offering scouts for cluttered spots humans cannot reach. Back-mounted gear spoils the insect's natural body shape and climbing skill, so the team shrank the kit to fit inside.

Their controller measures about ten millimeters square and three millimeters thick. It radios steering signals to prompt movement. Implanted roaches kept natural gap-crossing skill, matching untouched insects. Back-mounted roaches performed worse on the same terrain. An automatic steering program guided implanted roaches to a target with about ninety-one percent success. Implants may unlock tougher terrain work.
pmc-13201345:
Estimating how many deaths are caused by excess weight sounds simple, but a 2026 systematic review led by Guadalupe García shows the methods vary widely. The review examines how researchers have calculated attributable mortality for overweight and obesity, and what should change so estimates can be compared fairly.

García and colleagues searched three major databases and included 23 studies from four continents. Studies differed in body mass index cut-offs, in the causes of death counted, and in where their risk figures came from. The authors recommend standard World Health Organization cut-offs, measured rather than self-reported body data, and clearer reporting of each study's limits.
pmc-13205645:
Finland told its wellbeing counties how to organize quitting support, and a 2026 survey authored by Tuija Ylitörmänen takes a baseline reading of what exists. The cross-sectional study asked professionals across the counties about structures for tobacco and nicotine cessation care, ahead of judging the 2024 national recommendations.

Twenty-one counties answered, yet only a minority had named a body responsible for cessation work or ran yearly staff training. Recording a patient's tobacco use in the medical record was the strongest area, reported by most counties in the survey. Digital services were also common, while early identification and brief advice lagged, leaving wide variation between counties.
pmc-13211945:
Sleep after a complicated pregnancy may echo into heart health, and a 2026 pilot study by Anais Hausvater checks how mothers actually sleep years later. Forty-nine women, three to seven years past childbirth, wore a smart ring for two weeks and completed questionnaires; twenty-eight had hypertensive pregnancy disorders and twenty-one did not.

Sleep quality scored suboptimal in both groups, and average nightly sleep fell short of seven hours regardless of pregnancy history. Nearly half the women showed poorly timed sleep by the study's midpoint definition in the wearable data. The pilot proves the wearable approach is feasible and frames larger studies of whether postpartum sleep shapes cardiovascular risk.
pmc-13213045:
Xiaoqiang Wang and colleagues reply in 2026 to a critique of their crystal structure of a plant enzyme that starts the making of isoflavonoids, compounds valued as dietary phytoestrogens and plant defences. A commentator had argued the enzyme's startling shape was an artefact caused by a sulfate ion.

The authors stand by their structure, saying its unusual shape may reflect the enzyme's double job, which couples adding oxygen with moving a ring between positions. Ions seen in the crystal, they argue, sit on the protein surface and should not affect its chemistry. With only one structure available, they agree more work is needed to settle how this singular enzyme really works.
pmc-13213145:
Benjamin W. King and colleagues survey in 2026 American college baseball pitchers about a hard trade-off. Faster pitches win attention, yet throwing hard strains the elbow ligament. Repair of that ligament is known as Tommy John surgery.

Among 169 pitchers, large majorities called velocity critical for game success, recruitment, and reaching professional baseball. Two thirds also accepted that velocity raises injury risk. On average, pitchers said they would accept a ten percent higher injury risk for one extra mile per hour. Harder throwers were more often top-division starters who rated themselves effective. The results show young pitchers knowingly gamble ligament health for speed.
pmc-13214645:
Lidija Šoher and a large team report in 2026 the first national picture of what older Croatians eat, drawn from a food consumption survey using European methods. Nearly eight hundred people aged sixty-five and over gave diet records, activity answers, and body measurements.

Only about a fifth sat in the normal weight range, while the rest were overweight or obese. The younger group, aged sixty-five to seventy-four, differed from those seventy-five and older in energy and nutrient intake. Body mass shaped intake in the younger group, while activity level mattered more in the older group. Both groups fell short on nutrient-rich foods and fluids, giving health planners clear targets for healthy-ageing programmes.
pmc-13216145:
Marina Romozzi and co-authors present a 2026 cohort study of headache that follows flow-diverter stent treatment for unruptured brain aneurysms. This 'post-pipeline headache' is noticed more often now but has lacked agreed rules for diagnosis.

Among 137 patients treated between 2021 and 2025, about one in five developed the headache, split between entirely new pain and worsening of existing pain. The team built a scoring system that matched separate neurologist judgements well, supporting a cut-off of nine points. A wider aneurysm neck predicted the headache on its own, which the authors link to vessel wall remodelling and inflammation. They argue the score can steady diagnosis and advice before treatment.
pmc-13216645:
Frederik E. Deiman and co-authors present a 2026 study of a heart muscle disease passed down in families, caused by a small deletion in the phospholamban gene, which regulates the heart's calcium pump. Mouse work hinted RNA therapy could help, but the human molecular picture was missing.

The team profiled proteins and their phosphorylation in heart tissue from six patients. Against other dilated cardiomyopathies, a distinctive signature stood out, centred on the contractile and cytoskeletal machinery, plus signs of fibrosis. Stem-cell-derived heart cells carrying the same deletion copied the signature. Antisense RNA therapy lowered phospholamban, reversed most of the shared phosphorylation changes, reduced protein aggregates, and sped calcium handling. The authors argue the approach merits clinical testing.
pmc-13218145:
Yue Chen and co-authors synthesize qualitative research on how people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease manage their own condition, in a 2026 meta-synthesis. COPD is a long-term lung disease, and day-to-day self-management at home shapes how well patients do. Knowing what that work feels like, and what patients say they need, can guide better support programs.

The team searched ten databases, in English and Chinese, through March 2025 and kept fifteen qualitative studies covering 251 patients. Fifty-two findings were grouped into thirteen categories and then four overarching themes. Symptom burden weighed heavily on psychological well-being, and patients faced many tangled barriers to managing well. Some patients built active coping strategies and personal resources despite the difficulties. Patients also voiced continuing, many-sided support needs. The authors argue that interventions should be designed around these stated needs rather than around clinical routines alone.
pmc-13218345:
Shengjian Kuang and co-authors test green manures for weed control in dragon fruit orchards, in a 2026 study from Guizhou Province, China. Dragon fruit farming expanded in China, and weeds in mountain orchards are hard to manage. Few green manures have been evaluated for this setting, where a cover crop could smother weeds while improving soil.

From March to June 2019, the team grew nine legume species in a mountainous orchard and compared them with grass cover. They scored them with a membership function analysis that blends traits. Common bean, rice bean, and bush bean earned the highest scores. Intercropping with legumes cut weed richness and diversity, and five species suppressed more than ninety percent of weeds, led by bush bean. Fast emergence, early growth, and fresh biomass predicted the best suppression. The authors recommend the three beans and call for longer, multi-site trials on ecological and economic effects.
pmc-13220845:
Sandra Sandria and Megan C. King present a 2026 review on how cells sense physical force. Their focus is the link between integrin adhesions, which anchor cells to the surrounding matrix, and the nucleus, which also responds to force. The authors ask whether these two sensing systems work apart or act as one connected pathway.

Inside, the review traces how matrix stiffness and stretch reach the cell surface, then move inward to alter gene activity. It weighs what is known about signals passing between adhesion sites and the nucleus. Readers gain a clear map of an open question in cell biology, with clues for future work on development, cancer, and tissue repair.
pmc-13221445:
Lee Sherry and colleagues publish a 2026 author correction to their study of a yeast-made three-strain polio vaccine candidate. The original article's Figure 6 reported immune response data in which the control vaccine, IPV, had also received adjuvant. That error affected how its performance was presented against its control.

The corrected figure now compares the virus-like particle versions with plain IPV. Its legend has also been revised to match the correct statistics for antibody titres in treated rats. The experiment tested three poliovirus types at several dose levels, with blood drawn three weeks after a single dose. The update keeps the published record accurate for readers judging the vaccine.
pmc-13222045:
Henry Nabeta and co-authors recount repeated bloodstream infections in a 51-year-old man on hemodialysis, in a 2026 case report. The patient had diabetes, hypertension, and end-stage kidney disease, with a tunneled chest catheter for dialysis. Cultures over successive admissions grew several drug-resistant organisms, including ESBL-producing Klebsiella and two Achromobacter species.

Care meant stronger antibiotics, pulling infected lines, and at last cutting out an infected arm graft where the same germ was growing. A gut illness with C. difficile struck during the middle stay. He went home after cultures turned negative, then came back a month later with the illness again. The case shows how dialysis access sites can seed stubborn, mixed infections.
pmc-13226145:
Néstor Jiménez-Cañete and colleagues trace a 2026 mechanism explaining why obesity makes acute pancreatitis deadlier. In the inflamed pancreas, incoming white blood cells normally release a metabolite called itaconate. Nearby pancreatic cells import it and use it to sustain defences that block ferroptosis, a form of iron-driven cell death.

Protein checks in pancreatic neutrophils from obese mice showed the itaconate-making enzyme sharply cut, plus other fuel-use enzymes. With less itaconate delivered, defences in pancreatic cells sagged and lipid damage rose. Supplying a cell-entering form of itaconate restored the defence chain and reduced injury, marking immune-cell fuel use as a lever on how severe the disease gets.
pmc-13230745:
Bappaditya Mandal and colleagues present in 2026 a wearable antenna that sends signals through body fat instead of air. The flexible U-shaped antenna sits in a skin-safe silicone coating and works in a common medical frequency band. Fat between skin and muscle loses less signal than other tissues, so it forms a natural channel.

Simulations, tissue models, torso phantoms of lean and obese builds, and human volunteers all tested the design. Against a standard Bluetooth chip antenna, the body channel version gave steadier and more efficient transmission across body types. Heating of tissue stayed well within safety limits in the checks. Sending health data through the body this way could power low-energy monitoring with fewer dropouts.
pmc-13231645:
Hanna Luetke Lanfer and colleagues follow in 2026 how people with disabilities in urban Sierra Leone move between kinds of care. In Freetown, hospital medicine sits beside traditional healers, spiritual care, and charity services. Six group discussions with forty-two disabled adults and caregivers rebuilt their care paths from first symptoms onward.

Early on, families bounced between care types, trying each in turn when results disappointed. Over time most settled on hospital or charity care, and traditional care largely dropped away, while many adults quit seeking care entirely. Hospital care won trust for diagnosis yet carried the worst barriers, from cost and travel to rude treatment. Charity services felt easier to use but were unknown at the start.
pmc-13232845:
Changwoo Lee and colleagues probe in 2026 why Korean herbal medicine claims under car insurance grew so much faster than conventional care claims. Herbal care took a sharply rising share of crash-injury spending in South Korea over five years. National panel data let the team split the usage gap into patient traits versus supply-side structure.

Herbal patients used more visits and longer hospital stays than comparable conventional patients. Patient traits explained little of that gap, and among the heaviest users structural factors explained all of it and more. That pattern fits provider-driven demand more than sicker patients, though direct severity measures were missing. Reimbursement design, the authors argue, is where oversight should aim.
pmc-13234045:
Jiaxuan Fang and colleagues published a 2026 cosmetic science study turning passion fruit peel into a sun-protection ingredient. Ultraviolet B light drives skin photoaging through oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage, and barrier breakdown. The team fermented Passiflora edulis peel to extract a polysaccharide, characterized its structure, then tested it on UVB-exposed skin cells and on the backs of mice.

The sugar polymer shielded cells on several fronts: it aided wound closure in a scratch test, cut reactive oxygen buildup, steadied mitochondrial voltage, and sharply reduced an inflammatory signal. Skin barrier proteins rose to roughly double their damaged levels. In the animal work it preserved epidermal thickness, suppressed a DNA damage marker, and halved two enzymes that chew up skin structure. The authors pitch the peel extract as upcycled skincare.
pmc-13234845:
Lanfang Ren and colleagues reported in 2026 a polymer carrier that both delivers cancer vaccine ingredients and wakes up innate immunity. Therapeutic vaccines often fail because antigens do not reach the right compartment inside dendritic cells. Screening a library of modified dendrimers identified a naphthyl-bearing polymer that formed stable complexes with antigens. The complexes escaped quickly from cellular compartments and released antigen into the cell interior.

The polymer also triggered a defence pathway called STING without needing its usual upstream sensor. Extra immune boosters could be loaded into the same particle for stronger effects. In mice with melanoma, vaccine versions raised strong anti-tumour responses. Pairing the vaccine with a checkpoint drug improved tumour control, killer cell entry, and survival. The authors propose the carrier for next-generation cancer nanovaccines.
pmc-13235245:
Sanyukta Mathur and co-authors spoke in 2026 with seventeen health care providers in Johannesburg about a daily pill still being tested. The Dual Prevention Pill combines a drug that prevents HIV with birth control in one tablet. Providers worked at family planning and HIV service sites across the city. Talks were grouped with an in-depth framework covering likely users, the product concept, and health system issues.

Providers said the single pill could meet client needs and make joined sexual and reproductive care work better. Daily dosing demands, maybe stronger side effects, and ethical questions about offering it to teens raised concern. They backed supply through public clinics, with local delivery as an added route for reach. Bias among staff toward teens needed tackling before launch, they warned. Local teaching and efforts to build demand should accompany any rollout.
pmc-13236245:
Jonathan A. Fridell and a large international group surveyed in 2026 how transplant centres handle pancreas transplantation for people with type 2 diabetes. The operation was long reserved for type 1 diabetes, yet selected type 2 patients now receive it successfully. Thirty-seven transplant professionals answered the electronic survey in mid-2025. Questions covered candidate selection, thresholds, and care before and after surgery.

Most programs offered the operation for type 2 diabetes only when a kidney transplant was also needed. Daily insulin dose and body mass index were the factors checked most often for eligibility. Programs differed widely on metabolic cutoffs, with many setting no threshold for a hormone marker of insulin production. Weight strategies before listing included lifestyle change, modern diabetes drugs, and bariatric surgery referrals. Surgical and immune-suppression practice otherwise matched type 1 care closely across centres.
pmc-13236545:
Himani Aggarwal and co-authors examined in 2026 how advanced small-cell lung cancer is actually treated in United States community oncology clinics. Electronic records covered nearly three thousand five hundred patients who started first systemic therapy between late 2018 and mid-2023. Treatment choices, time on therapy, time to next therapy, and survival were summarized from routine care data. Most patients had widespread disease at first presentation in the cohort.

Immunotherapy combined with platinum chemotherapy formed the first treatment for nearly three quarters of patients. Chemotherapy alone ranked second, matching guideline-era practice patterns overall. More than half of patients never received a second line of therapy after the first failed. Median survival after starting first treatment sat near ten months in the real-world data. Outcomes worsened with each later line, underlining the authors' call for better new options.
pmc-13236645:
Liuyue Wang and co-authors surveyed in 2026 nearly six hundred pregnant women in two Chinese cities to build a model predicting depressive symptoms late in pregnancy. Participants were in their second or third trimester and attending regular prenatal checkups. Questionnaires covered social support, coping style, personality vulnerability, and parenting confidence alongside a standard depression scale. Two modelling approaches were trained and compared on the same survey data.

More than two fifths of women screened positive for depressive symptoms in the survey. Strong social support and active coping went together with fewer symptoms in the correlations. Negative coping and a vulnerable personality pattern went together with more symptoms in the same analysis. A neural network model predicted symptom status more accurately than a traditional regression model. The authors offer the model to help nurses flag high-risk women early in prenatal care.
pmc-13236845:
Dirk De Craemer, Christiane Van den Branden, and Frank Roels traced the history of research on peroxisomes in the human liver in a 2026 review. Peroxisomes are small structures inside cells that handle fats and other chemistry, and the human liver versions differ from those in lab animals. The authors lean on electron microscopy and tissue studies gathered over decades.

Much of the knowledge comes from hundreds of patients, including children with inherited peroxisome diseases and adults with acquired illness. Odd findings include liver cells where some peroxisomes look normal and others do not. The review also covers newer work on contact sites between peroxisomes and other cell structures. The authors urge doctors to keep examining human liver tissue for full diagnosis.
pmc-13237245:
Diana W. Njuguna and a large Kenyan research team interviewed 130 men with prostate cancer across five counties in a 2026 qualitative study. The men, recruited from oncology clinics in Nairobi, Garissa, Meru, Machakos, and Kisii, described what diagnosis and treatment did to their identities, relationships, and daily lives. Interviews were analyzed thematically with software support.

Five themes stood out. They were shock and raw disruption at diagnosis, and treatment as both hope and hardship. Distance and money formed barriers, and masculine identity and dignity felt threatened. Family and community acted as both support and stigma. Many men felt shifted from strong providers to vulnerable patients. The authors call for care that adds psychosocial support from diagnosis onward and tackles structural barriers to access.
pmc-13238245:
Konstantinos Kodonas, Anastasia Fardi, and Hannah Wesley described in 2026 the conservative management of a broken root in a seven-year-old boy's front tooth. A fall on pavement fractured the root of an upper central incisor that had only just erupted, leaving an immature root with an open tip. The boy felt no pain, and three-dimensional imaging three months later confirmed the oblique fracture.

The tooth built its own dentin bridge across the fracture, sealing the upper pulp from the healthy lower pulp. When a small sinus tract appeared and the crown had erupted enough, the team cleaned the space above the bridge and sealed it with a calcium silicate cement. Two years on, the root kept developing and the boy stayed symptom-free. The case supports keeping the pulp alive in selected young teeth.
pmc-13239145:
María Alejandra Velásquez Peña and colleagues measured exposure to the roundworm Toxocara in 2026 among seventy dogs, one hundred forty cats, and one hundred eighteen owners in Villavicencio, Colombia. Blood tests checked antibodies in all three groups, and stool tests in the animals measured actual egg shedding. Owners also answered an allergy survey and took skin-prick tests.

Eighty percent of the pets carried antibodies, and about twenty-three percent of owners did too. Pets allowed outside more than three times a day were far likelier to be infected. Owners whose dog and cat were both positive were themselves over three times likelier to be positive. Sleeping in bed with pets also raised owner risk. No link appeared between owner exposure and allergy. The authors frame pet parasite control as a One Health duty.
pmc-13239345:
Gloria Chun Yan Lee and colleagues published a 2026 quality improvement study from a children's hospital in Singapore. Doctors there introduced a modified Step-by-Step rule to judge which febrile infants under three months might have a serious bacterial infection.

The team compared matched groups of infants seen before and after the rule arrived, drawn from more than three thousand admissions. Use of preventive intravenous antibiotics fell by about eleven percentage points, and lumbar punctures also became less common. Rates fell most clearly among infants who turned out not to have serious infections. The authors conclude the rule cut invasive care without missing sick babies.
pmc-13240145:
Venkatkiran Kanchustambham and Weston E Bowker describe a clever biopsy switch in a 2026 case report. Chest lipomas are benign fat tumours in the space between the lungs, and they are rare. The key task is to prove they are not a low-grade cancer called liposarcoma, which normally demands surgical sampling.

Their patient, a 61-year-old man who felt well, carried a huge fatty mass found by chance on a scan. A needle sample, taken through a bronchoscope with ultrasound guidance, brought back too little tissue. The team at once widened the same track and froze out several solid cores with a cryoprobe. Gene tests found no cancer marker, which confirmed a benign lipoma. Later surgery matched that call.
pmc-13241445:
Eid's team at Alexandria tracked airway change during the first orthodontic stage for deep-bite teens. Thirty patients with Class II division 2 bites, aged about fourteen, joined the trial. Only upper-arch leveling and straightening was done. Head X-rays before treatment and at six months measured airway and jaw place.

The airway widened sharply behind the nose and throat, but not lower down. Upper front teeth tipped forward and the lower jaw shifted ahead in use. Bone angles improved while face height shrank. Eid credits the jaw response, while granting natural growth may play a part.
pmc-13242145:
Siwat Chokpaisan, Charin Suwanwong, and Jakkrit Thavorn present a 2026 meta-analysis of why viewers send virtual gifts on live game streaming platforms. Gifting is a major income stream for streamers, yet earlier findings were scattered across psychology, social, and platform explanations. The authors pooled empirical studies from a decade of research.

Engagement, streamer attractiveness, usefulness, social acceptance, enjoyment-driven motivation, and awareness of streamer needs all linked positively to gifting. Passing time linked negatively. A close viewer-streamer bond showed a large average link, though results varied too much for firm conclusions. Findings differed somewhat between self-reported and recorded behavior data. The synthesis suggests gifting grows from active involvement, not idle viewing.
pmc-13242345:
Ullah's team in Harbin model a wobbling nanofluid sliding over a magnetized plate. The particles ride in water under mixed convection and heat rays. The equations were solved in full by finite steps. A neural network then learned the flow profiles. Heat and mass move through the fluid in waves.

The amplitude grew with radiation, fluid elasticity, and heat loss. Swinging heat and mass transfer grew as magnetic and buoyancy numbers rose. Skin friction climbed with the Maxwell and Eckert numbers. The network trained to very small error at the strongest magnetic setting tested.
pmc-13242945:
Andrew Carroll and co-authors tested whether a large language model can help run the support desk for REDCap, the research data platform. Their study appeared in JAMIA Open in 2026. They sampled ninety tickets from more than six thousand received in 2023 at a large academic medical center. Four GPT-4o setups, plain and fed with documentation from two universities, judged each ticket's complexity, assigned its category, and drafted a reply email.

The plain model matched human experts best on complexity, while documentation-fed versions tended to overrate difficulty. All four setups categorized tickets with high agreement to the human gold standard. The setup using Michigan documentation drafted the most correct replies, especially for simpler tickets. Experts still rated drafts rather than trusting them blindly. The authors see real workload relief ahead, provided human oversight stays and local documentation keeps growing.
pmc-13243045:
Huanyuan Wang and co-authors present a 2026 case report with a review of past reports on two blood disorders coexisting in one patient. A 74-year-old woman carried a quiet form of Waldenström macroglobulinemia, a slow lymphoma making an abnormal antibody, alongside myelodysplastic syndrome, a bone marrow failure condition. Their overlap is extremely rare.

Persisting low blood counts during lymphoma treatment prompted a second look, which blamed the counts on the marrow disorder progressing. Serial monitoring charted the clone growing from a small blast share to full acute leukemia. A new mutation appeared even after the marrow disorder reached remission and drove the final transformation. She died after the leukemia emerged. The authors stress a second look when counts misbehave.
pmc-13245045:
Agahan Hayta and colleagues compared reverse shoulder replacements done with augmented-reality guidance against the freehand technique. Their retrospective study appeared in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders in 2026. Of 203 operations, seventy-two used the headset system and the rest were done by eye and experience. The team measured complications, revisions, socket tilt, screw use, X-ray time, and surgical length.

Navigation did not significantly change the ninety-day complication, dislocation, or revision rates, which ran low in both groups. What it changed was precision: the baseplate sat much closer to neutral tilt, and badly tilted placements became far less common. Surgeons also fixed the plate with fewer but longer screws, used much less fluoroscopy, and finished faster. The authors read this as accuracy bought without early safety costs. Bigger studies with longer follow-up must now show whether better geometry today means fewer failures years out.
pmc-13245845:
Alami and colleagues reviewed how health systems should govern artificial intelligence, in this 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Hospitals are adopting AI tools fast, and many governance frameworks have appeared, but most cover only part of the problem. The team searched eight databases and other sources for frameworks meant to guide AI policy in health care.

Nineteen frameworks qualified, most published since 2022 and half from North American authors. They operated at international, national, regional, and local levels, yet few were built from primary research. The authors combine them into one integrative model with two dimensions and four linking mechanisms, and urge that it now be tested in practice.
pmc-13247145:
Asgari, Catrysse, and Yuan present metacrystals, printable panels designed to shape future wireless signals, in this 2026 Nature Communications paper. Sixth-generation networks will need help covering dead zones, and passive surfaces that redirect radio waves are attractive because they need no power. But ordinary flat metasurfaces typically work for only one polarization, band, or arrival angle at a time.

Metacrystals use modest thickness instead of a flat sheet, gaining the freedom to answer many different waves at once, independently. Designed by inverse topology optimization and made by low-cost three-dimensional printing, their all-dielectric panels simultaneously controlled reflection and absorption in both transmission and reflection. Simulations and experiments ran at frequencies up to one hundred gigahertz. The authors pitch them as structural, scalable building parts for smarter radio environments.
pmc-13247245:
Li, Zhang, Zhou, and co-authors studied signal bleed between microscopic light pixels in this 2026 Microsystems and Nanoengineering paper. Nanopixel displays promise sharper screens, and one promising design lights pixels without injecting carriers, the noncarrier injection mode. But neighboring pixels can disturb each other electrically, a crosstalk problem whose mechanism was unclear. The team paired computer simulation with bench experiments on nano-LED arrays.

Crosstalk changed with voltage size, driving frequency, insulation thickness, and pixel spacing, and circuit modeling exposed how it arises. Shallower etching of the array suppressed the effect, and the non-injection mode proved naturally better at containing crosstalk than the conventional injection mode. The authors offer design rules for building dense, high-quality nanopixel arrays for future displays.
pmc-13247545:
Jiwon Kim, Han Gyeol Kim, and Seung Hyeun Lee report a striking drug response in advanced lung cancer in a 2026 case. Their patient was a 52-year-old man with a rare EGFR mutation and cancer spread to liver and brain. Three prior treatment lines had failed in turn.

Fluid in his belly cleared, and his strength slowly returned. The response has held beyond nine months with only mild rash and mouth sores. The case is the first of its kind for this mutation.
pmc-13248645:
Pengfei Li and Zhen Liu survey machine learning for cancer diagnosis in a 2026 perspective. Early detection saves lives, yet building good diagnostic tests still leans on slow trial and error. Reading the flood of scan and molecular data also strains human interpretation.

The authors compare the main learning algorithms on data size, imbalance, and clarity of reasoning. They then gather recent wins, from tuning assay platforms to joining data across scales. Learning models can search design spaces far faster than manual tinkering. Hard problems remain, including skewed data and models that hide their logic. A roadmap closes the piece for builders of next-round tools.
pmc-13248745:
Peuranheimo and colleagues traced how melanoma returns after surgery, in a 2026 Acta Oncologica study from Helsinki. They followed three hundred fifty patients whose stage III skin melanoma had been fully removed between 2008 and 2017, before modern preventive drug therapy became standard. Records were checked for where and when the cancer came back.

More than half the patients relapsed, and risk climbed steeply with substage. Most first returns appeared within two years. Routine CT scans found about half of all recurrences and nearly two thirds of distant spread, which reached lungs, brain, and other organs. The authors back close scanning and examination in the early follow-up years.
pmc-13250045:
Xukun Huang and colleagues tackle a labelling problem in blood testing in this 2026 paper. Imaging flow cytometry photographs cells as they stream past, and software can sort white blood cells well, but teaching it needs hand-labelled images, and labelling loses cells, blocking a key count test.

Their fix teaches the system from unlabelled images first, using a method where the software learns by comparing views of the same cell. With only a simple sorting layer added, it then sorted cells in three separate datasets with accuracy between 92 and 97 percent, close to fully supervised systems. It also handled abnormal cells it had never been shown.
pmc-13250245:
Li, Yi, and Wu write a 2026 letter to the editor of the Journal of Pain Research about a cohort study linking metabolic index scores to new leg joint pain. The study under discussion, by Xue and colleagues, used China's national retirement and health survey to test triglyceride-glucose index variants. The letter writers praise the longitudinal design before raising doubts.

Their first concern is added value: combined scores that included body size predicted pain, while the glucose index alone did not, suggesting fatness rather than metabolism drives the result. They ask for direct comparisons against simple body measures, with discrimination and calibration checks. Second, they flag the loss of more than seventeen hundred participants during follow-up, which in an aging cohort is unlikely to be random and could bias the findings.
pmc-13250745:
Nakashima and co-authors describe a pregnant woman whose vomiting and black stools traced to a large tumor blocking her duodenum. Their 2026 Surgical Case Reports paper concerns a gastrointestinal stromal tumor near the head of the pancreas, found at thirty-seven weeks of pregnancy. She was severely anemic when she arrived for care.

Doctors performed an emergency cesarean section, delivering a healthy baby, then removed the tumor with a major pancreas operation one week later. Tissue tests confirmed a stromal tumor, and her recovery was smooth enough for discharge ten days after the operation. Lactation support began the day after surgery to shorten the separation of mother and baby. The authors praise flexible, team-based decisions in such rare emergencies.
pmc-13251245:
Arar and a large team ask whether emergency surgery still helps aortic dissection patients who arrive already intubated. Their 2026 Journal of Cardiothoracic Surgery study reviews four hundred thirty type A dissection repairs at one referral hospital between 2000 and 2018. A tear in the inner aorta is among surgery's deadliest emergencies.

Only about one in eight patients arrived intubated, but they carried far more tamponade, organ malperfusion, and resuscitation before surgery. Roughly thirty-eight percent of them died within thirty days, about double the rate of non-intubated patients. Even so, most intubated patients benefited from prompt repair, and survivors past the first year did acceptably well. The authors recommend offering emergency repair to these patients rather than withholding it.
pmc-13251545:
Zifu He and colleagues run a randomised trial of app-guided shoulder rehab in this 2026 study. Long-term rotator cuff injury causes pain and weak shoulders, and while guided injections ease pain fast, home exercise often fails through poor sticking power and sloppy form.

Sixty patients received an ultrasound-guided injection, then split into two groups for three months. One did standard exercises; the other trained with a digital system that corrects form and adapts the plan. Both improved, yet at three months the digital group had clearly better shoulder scores, less pain, and wider movement in every direction. The gains passed the bar for changes patients can feel.
pmc-13252945:
Yang and colleagues review water-swollen gel materials engineered to repair hearts and blood vessels. Their 2026 International Journal of Molecular Medicine paper notes that heart disease leads global deaths, while drugs, stents, and bypass surgery cannot truly rebuild damaged tissue. Hydrogels can carry cells and medicines and act as soft scaffolds.

Natural gels suit the body but are weak, synthetic gels tune well but lack biological activity, and composites trade simplicity for both strengths. Smart gels that answer body signals can release treatment on demand. Uses span heart attack repair, vessel regrowth, valve rebuilding, and heart failure support. Safety, durability, clotting risk, and manufacturing scale still block routine clinical use of these materials.
pmc-13254545:
Rebecca Quah and co-authors study the fungal diets of two bettong species in a 2026 Australian study. Boodies and woylies are threatened marsupials that eat fungi and spread them through digging and droppings. DNA testing of 90 scat samples from five sites, spanning Mediterranean-type to arid climates, traced what they ate.

Testing found 379 fungal sequence variants, of which 82 were macrofungi likely eaten on purpose. Both species had similar diet diversity, with one fungal family common at all sites. Small diet differences may cut competition and widen fungal dispersal, so the authors advise timing animal releases after rain.
pmc-13254845:
Haojun Duan, Junpeng Qi, and Xianwen Hu argue in a 2026 perspective that osteoporotic bone marrow shelters sleeping breast cancer cells and later wakes them. Longer survival after breast cancer has made late bone relapse a growing problem. The authors contend the driver is not thinning bone itself but a metabolic remodeling of the aging marrow.

In their account, fat expansion inside the marrow, an aging immune system, and garbled mechanical signaling together feed wandering tumor cells a private fuel supply. The same changes shield the cells from immune attack and therapy. That cocoon can hold cells dormant for years and then coax them back into growth. The framing, they suggest, helps explain why two large bone drug trials, D-CARE and ABCSG-18, diverged in outcome. Their prescription is a paradigm shift: preserving bone density alone may fail if the marrow's metabolic disorder is left in place.
pmc-13254945:
Abdullah Alnaqib and colleagues report a rare benign skull tumor that grew unchecked for fifteen years in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a sixty-seven-year-old woman with narrowing of the cervical spine, had a progressively enlarging mass on the back of her head. The lump arose from the left occipital bone and reached down toward the upper neck.

She had known about the mass for roughly fifteen years, but surgery had repeatedly been deferred because operating near her stenotic cervical spine was judged risky. In that time the lesion grew substantially. When she finally underwent resection, imaging and tissue analysis identified a protuberant fibro-osseous lesion, nicknamed the Bullough bump, an uncommon benign growth more often described in the temporal bone. The authors use it to discuss the diagnostic difficulty posed by skull masses, whose benign and malignant members overlap in appearance.
pmc-13255445:
Weiye Zhang and co-authors review how processing detoxifies toxic Chinese medicines in a 2026 systematic review. Some traditional medicines are potent yet risky, and processing aims to cut toxicity while keeping benefit. The team surveyed the toxic medicines in the 2025 Chinese Pharmacopoeia, their sources, toxic parts, and traditional processing methods.

They grouped the safety mechanisms into three levels: physical removal or change of toxic parts, chemical change of the toxic compounds, and shifts in how the body handles them. Patterns within plant families were traced at each level. The authors propose an integrated research strategy linking all three levels to guide safer processing.
pmc-13256545:
Seon-Chil Kim and co-authors present a 2026 pilot trial of an eye-tracking digital therapy for children with ADHD. Forty children aged six to eleven, all also on medication, used either gaze-adaptive learning content or a standard version for four weeks. The adaptive system watches where eyes wander and responds when attention drifts.

A composite attention score climbed significantly over the four weeks in the adaptive group. Gains concentrated in tasks tapping response inhibition and visual search, while basic processing speed measures barely moved. Improvement tracked with changes on a standardized attention test, supporting the gaze metrics as meaningful process measures. The authors caution that forty children in a pilot cannot settle efficacy. They frame real-time gaze feedback as a promising way to keep therapy honest about attention itself.
pmc-13256845:
Meza and co-authors review how targeted drugs have reshaped chronic lymphocytic leukemia care. Bruton tyrosine kinase blockers and BCL2 blockers now anchor both first-line treatment and care after relapse, pushing aside older chemo-centered approaches. The review weighs combined and triplet regimens, treatment guided by measurable leftover disease, and fixed-length strategies.

Past therapies and social factors also shape progression and outcomes, and the review folds them into its treatment maps. The authors frame modern management as choosing among time-limited and ongoing targeted options for each patient's biology and situation.
pmc-13257145:
Alice N. Mafe and Dietrich Büsselberg review in 2026 the use of lactic acid bacteria against toxin-producing fungi in food. Molds such as Aspergillus and Fusarium leave mycotoxins that can damage liver, nerves, and immunity. Heat and chemical preservatives cannot fully remove these stable toxins.

Studies from 2011 to 2025 were gathered from five databases, focusing on bacteria taken from local fermented foods. These bacteria fight fungi by making acids, secreting antimicrobial proteins, and competing for space. Some bind toxins on their cell walls or convert them into safer forms. Their by-products may also soften toxin effects on mammalian cells. Food safety researchers get a hopeful route that consumers may accept more readily. Trials in real foods and regulatory work are still required.
pmc-13257645:
Kamil Gałęziok and co-authors test whether time of day changes skin blood flow responses in a 2026 study. Thirty healthy volunteers, split evenly by sex, underwent a cuff occlusion test in the morning and again in the evening of the same day. Laser Doppler readings tracked resting flow and the flush after release.

Resting skin flow ran significantly higher in the evening, showing daily rhythm in baseline vessel tone. The reactive flush measures, including peak flow, time to peak, and recovery time, did not differ between sessions. A baseline offset measure also stayed stable. Reactive testing looks robust to timing, which simplifies protocols for clinics that cannot always test at dawn.
pmc-13258045:
Nafiye Busra Celik and co-authors review modern aortic arch surgery in a 2026 narrative article. The arch is among the hardest aortic segments to repair because brain and spinal cord blood flow must be protected throughout. Open replacement, hybrid graft hybrids, and fully internal branched repairs are compared against current American and European guidance.

The frozen elephant trunk technique enables one-stage treatment of arch and descending disease, with reintervention watchfulness required. Brain protection has shifted toward selective forward perfusion with moderate cooling for most open cases. Zone maps and entry-based schemes sharpen planning. Heart teams are urged to match method to patient anatomy and center skill, since no single route wins everywhere.
pmc-13258745:
Nooshin Sheidaei and co-authors wrote a 2026 cell biology study of how chromosomes meet the mitotic spindle during cell division. The spindle is the fiber structure that pulls chromosomes apart into new cells. Chromosomes stuck at the cell's edge or behind the spindle poles meet it slowly, raising the risk of faulty separation. Using human cell lines, the team studied a contracting network of actin and myosin proteins that forms around the nucleus before it breaks down.

After the nuclear envelope broke down, this network contracted and pushed edge and polar chromosomes toward the cell center. Tracking movement after light-based blocking of myosin showed this push helped chromosome tips make first contact with spindle fibers. It also sped the start of their gathering toward the spindle middle. The authors link missing networks in some cancer cells to chromosome number errors.
pmc-13260145:
Gianluca Castelnuovo wrote a 2026 grand challenge article on where clinical psychology and psychotherapy should head toward 2030. Newer challenges have also arisen since the earlier piece, and he compares the two sets for overlap and novelty. The article ranges across paired fields such as psycho-cardiology and psycho-oncology, where psychology meets a branch of medicine. Castelnuovo frames the piece as an agenda for researchers and services planning the next decade of care.
pmc-13263145:
Colwyn M Jones and James W Edwards report a decade of child dental surveys in the Falkland Islands in a 2026 journal article. Yearly surveys following World Health Organization methods counted decayed, missing, and filled teeth in five-year-olds, twelve-year-olds, and fifteen-year-olds.

Average tooth damage scores have trended down since 2013, the authors report. Since 2021, every age group has averaged below one affected tooth per child. Survey response rates ranged from 69 to 97 percent, which strengthens confidence in the trend. The authors credit preventive work for the improvement, while noting room to improve further and a need to survey the whole population.
pmc-13263245:

It can trigger Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, in which the tumor traps platelets and clotting factors, causing bleeding risk. This baby's tumor sat inside the abdomen with no skin signs.

The authors stress how hard such deep tumors are to spot and treat. They note care still leans on expert consensus and case experience, though sirolimus-based therapy is now first-line.
pmc-13263445:
Jiasun Su and colleagues examined in 2026 a rare extra copy of a chromosome segment, 19q13.42, in children with developmental disorders. pmc-13263945:

pmc-13264645:

pmc-13264745:

pmc-13264945:

pmc-13265845:

pmc-13266145:

pmc-13266845:

pmc-13267545:

Scans showed a small lesion, under two centimeters wide, and a biopsy confirmed the tumor.

pmc-13269145:

pmc-13269445:

pmc-13269545:

pmc-13269645:

The authors warn that earlier surgery might have limited this permanent damage.
pmc-13270745:
Zhen Yang led a 2026 journal article on Dachaihu decoction, a classic Chinese herbal formula, as a treatment for liver injury caused by sepsis, a life-threatening body-wide infection response. A weak gut barrier is a key driver of that liver harm, so the study tracked both organs in mice.

pmc-13271145:

Gaps, they say, include uneven evidence quality and no standard dosing, which block use in care and guide future formulation work.
pmc-13271545:
Jyotirmay Biswas and coauthors revisit in 2026 Eales' disease, a retinal blood vessel inflammation that mainly strikes young adults. pmc-13271745:

The underside carries unique finger-like structures under the surface that models predict amplify stress, sharpening touch without sacrificing durability. The authors offer this zoned design as a blueprint for robotic tactile skins.
pmc-13271945:
Lingyu Pang and coauthors describe in 2026 two children with febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome treated with the immune drug tocilizumab. pmc-13272345:
Kabelo N Mohlamonyane and coauthors demonstrate in 2026 a mass spectrometry imaging method that maps medicinal compounds inside South African plant tissues where they sit. pmc-13272445:

pmc-13272545:

pmc-13273845:

Higher scores were significantly tied to total coliform contamination. The test gave a p value of 0.006. Performance was moderate, the authors caution. Still, the tool can help target well testing after storms. It can transfer to other regions with similar data.
pmc-13275145:

pmc-13275545:
Ali Asilian and colleagues present a 2026 case report of giant porokeratosis, a rare skin disorder of ring-shaped plaques with raised borders, that resisted standard care. Their patient was a fifty-three-year-old woman with a twenty-one-year history of the condition. The giant form matters because it is linked to skin cancer, with malignancy reported in about seven and a half percent of porokeratosis cases.

No proven specific treatment exists. So the team combined fractional ablative carbon dioxide laser, which vaporizes thin skin layers, with methotrexate. That drug damps the immune system and is borrowed from psoriasis care, a disease with molecular similarities. The authors present the combination as a possible option for refractory cases, paired with firm biopsy confirmation of the diagnosis and ongoing surveillance for cancer.
pmc-13275745:
Pernille Emilie Hostrup and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on type 1 diabetes in adults. In this disease the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar. Some patients keep making a little insulin after diagnosis, and predicting who will matters for trials.

The team profiled lipids, the fats in blood plasma, from twenty-nine newly diagnosed adults. They tested which fats predicted later insulin output, measured through a marker called C-peptide after a test meal. One fat family, shortened to LPCs, stood out as the strongest predictor. Higher levels at diagnosis meant more insulin still being made a year later. Lower levels of another fat group, sphingolipids, pointed the other way. The pattern differed from earlier work in children.
pmc-13276045:
Anand Sojan and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a new way to build artificial lungs for premature babies. Babies born early often cannot breathe well and need machines, which can harm them. Small blood oxygenators, devices that add oxygen to blood outside the body, offer a gentler option but are hard to manufacture.

Their method prints a scaffold from isomalt, a sugar alcohol, then coats it with thin silicone membranes. The scaffold later dissolves, leaving open channels with no toxic solvents used. The team stacked eleven alternating blood and gas layers and got every channel open, with no rejects. Lab tests showed strong oxygen transfer. The device moved enough oxygen to support a one-kilogram baby while working without a pump.
pmc-13276145:
Vuong V Do and co-authors track unhealthy drinking among United States veterans from 2016 to 2024 in a 2026 study. Binge and heavy drinking carry known health risks in this population. The analysis used a national health survey and split trends by age and sex.

Binge drinking eased slightly overall, with clear drops in the youngest and older veteran groups. Heavy drinking held steady overall but rose among veterans aged thirty-five to forty-nine. Women cut heavy drinking notably and matched men's rates by 2024. Tobacco use, cost barriers to care, and poor mental health all matched higher heavy drinking, which points to linked support needs.
pmc-13276245:
Qiqi Lu and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a new way to measure how varied a tumor's ecosystem is. Tumors mix cancer cells with immune and support cells in shifting proportions. That variety drives growth and treatment resistance, but earlier measures mostly ignored the non-cancer cells.

Their framework, called QeITH, scores a tumor by the diversity and spread of its cell types and states. High scores came with a puzzle: worse long-term outlook, yet better responses to some therapies. Tumors scoring high also looked more aggressive, and the score varied across different spots inside one tumor. The authors released the tool as a free software package. They propose it can help predict how a cancer will progress and who may benefit from treatment.
pmc-13276445:
Xinhui Liang and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on brewing a prized antioxidant in one of the fastest-growing bacteria known. Ergothioneine, found in mushrooms and some bacteria, protects cells from damage but is costly to make. Vibrio natriegens grows extremely fast, yet editing its genes has been hard and fermentations expensive.

The team first built reliable DNA delivery and gene editing tools for the bacterium. They then installed the pathway that builds the antioxidant, tuned its controls, and deleted genes that wasted energy or made byproducts. Other genes boosting precursor supply were switched higher. Finally they ran fed-batch fermentation on cheap sugar, in salty broth that needs no sterilizing. The broth reached a solid yield of the product. The authors offer the strain as a platform for other valuable compounds.
pmc-13277645:
Huiting Yang and co-authors test physical methods for steering coconut oil crystallisation in a 2026 study. Crystal form decides texture and melting in foods such as margarine and frozen desserts. Chemical modification has limits, so ultrasound and stirring were tried alone and together.

Both virgin and refined coconut oils were treated under each condition. Every treatment sped nucleation and crystal growth, with the combined treatment strongest. The favoured beta-prime crystal form increased, producing thinner crystals in finer, more even clusters. Networks built this way showed lower melting temperature and greater hardness. The authors present paired ultrasound and stirring as a practical dial for designing structured fats.
pmc-13277745:
Rana Tabassum leads a 2026 case-control study of two gene variants and breast cancer risk in Bangladesh. The genes, HER1 and HER2, belong to a growth signal family long studied in cancer. The team tested 112 breast cancer patients from a national cancer hospital in Dhaka and 124 matched healthy controls from nearby communities.

One HER1 variant was strongly tied to higher cancer risk across several genetic models, with both mixed and double copies raising susceptibility. The HER2 variant showed little link, apart from a modest effect in one model. Genetic risk screening will need larger studies across many groups, the authors say, before such markers can guide care in Bangladesh or elsewhere.
pmc-13278945:
Yiting Liu and co-authors review vaccine-style treatment for allergic rhinitis in a 2026 article. Allergen immunotherapy retrains the immune system, yet benefits take years of treatment to arrive. Adding innate immune triggers called Toll-like receptor agonists may speed and strengthen that retraining.

These receptors sense microbial patterns and wake up dendritic cells, which steer the adaptive response. Properly aimed, that steering can shift allergy-driving Th2 responses toward tolerance. The review summarises agonists aimed at several receptor types and their trial progress so far. Safety and dosing questions remain open for many candidates. The authors offer the survey as design guidance for faster-acting allergy vaccines.
pmc-13280245:
Mohamed A. Daghash and colleagues report a 2026 study of eco friendly high performance concrete with basalt fibres. High performance concrete is prized for strength and long life. Yet its heavy use of made fibres and Portland cement raises green concerns. The team used hybrid basalt fibres at many scales, from macro to micro lengths. Ground mining materials part replaced cement: metakaolin, silica flour and ground feldspar.

Basalt fibres ran at one, two and three percent of binder weight, with four lengths from thirty to three millimetres. Hybrid levels mixed the lengths in set shares. Tests held compressive, split tensile and flexural strength, plus stiffness. More fibre hybridization and multi length mixes shifted strength traits in the results. Waste mineral powders cut cement demand at the same time. The design seeks strong concrete with a lighter earth cost.
pmc-13281345:
Maria Hofmann and colleagues tested a portfolio task in dental training in a 2026 study. Portfolios ask students to gather work and reflect on what they learn. The task ran through a third-term course on preventive dentistry, the care that stops tooth disease. Students built the portfolio across the term, tied to lectures and hands-on sessions. Sixty-four students from two terms took part and rated the task at the end.

More than nine in ten students rated the task good or very good. Its build, tasks, and workload all scored well. More than eight in ten said the reflection steps deepened their grip on the course. They also said the task made their growth in knowledge plain to them. The authors note such tasks are rare in dental studies so far. They back wider use to grow clear thinking.
pmc-13281645:
Yaxian Liu and colleagues described two enzymes that can remake milk sugar in a 2026 study. The enzymes turn lactose, the sugar in milk, into rarer sugars with health uses. Dairy work needs the change done cold, at fridge level, to keep germs out. Most known enzymes go sluggish in the cold. The team fished two new enzymes from sea and soil germs. Each was grown, cleaned, and tested across heat and acidity ranges.

Both enzymes worked well in mild warmth and stayed stable for months in the cold. One kept about two fifths of its strength at fridge level. The other kept about one fifth. One also held its strength across a wide acidity range. When lactose was packed dense, their sugar-swapping output soared many times over. The authors say such cold-tough enzymes could fit real dairy lines, where batches run long and cold.
pmc-13282845:
Mahan Sadjadi and co-authors present a 2026 multicentre study on how fully a kidney protection strategy is actually delivered to critically ill patients with acute kidney injury. International guidelines recommend the bundle: close monitoring, steady blood pressure, tracking kidney markers and urine, and avoiding high blood sugar, contrast dye, and kidney-toxic drugs where possible. Five European centres enrolled two hundred fifty-eight adults with moderate to severe injury, most on breathing machines or blood pressure drugs.

Only about thirty-one percent received the complete bundle within twelve hours, sustained for forty-eight hours. Blood pressure optimisation was the weakest element, at about thirty-three percent. Patients who got the full bundle fared better in exploratory analyses: less lingering kidney disease after day seven, far more kidney recovery by discharge, and less dialysis within thirty days. More bundle components meant better outcomes, a dose-response pattern.
pmc-13283945:
A heart rhythm burn procedure steadied a failing right heart in a 2026 case by Azmican Kaya and colleagues. The patient lived with a HeartMate 3 pump as a bridge to transplant. Typical flutter resistant to drugs was dragging down pump performance and right heart strength.

The 60-year-old man had non-ischemic heart muscle disease before pump placement. Shock conversion had failed to hold normal rhythm for long in his care. A 3D mapping study confirmed flutter circling a standard channel in the right atrium. Burning that channel blocked the circuit both ways and restored normal rhythm. One month later, right heart measures had improved substantially on repeat tests.
pmc-13284145:
Anne E Dawson and colleagues compared in 2026 children whose blood pressure runs high only in the clinic, called white coat hypertension, with children who have true hypertension. Both groups were referred to a kidney clinic and wore a day-long blood pressure monitor to sort them. Families filled in mental health screening surveys, and kidney, lipid, and heart scan results were gathered where available.

The study enrolled 552 patients, split fairly evenly between the two groups, and 472 completed the surveys. Metabolic risk factors did not differ clearly between groups. Mental health markers did not differ either, yet half of all screened patients flagged at least one concern, covering inattention, anxiety, or depression. The authors urge routine psychosocial screening in both groups.
pmc-13284545:
Maryam Hekmat and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a rare skin condition marked by mucin buildup in the dermis. Cutaneous focal mucinosis forms painless bumps or nodules, and treatment choices are few. Some cases fade alone, while drug options such as isotretinoin help unevenly and may not suit all patients.

The patient was a 19-year-old man with lasting bumps on both sides of the beard area, confirmed by biopsy. He did not want systemic drugs, so doctors used a superpulsed carbon dioxide laser. Lesions cleared well with no harmful effects, and results held at six months. The authors suggest laser care as a useful low-invasion option for local disease.
pmc-13285345:
Depression around birth falls into three patterns in a 2026 survey of more than ten thousand women in Fujian, China, by Chao Xue and co-authors. Mood trouble in pregnancy and after birth is common, yet its shapes and social links needed large-sample proof. Women from pregnancy to two months after birth answered the PHQ-9 scale between 2022 and 2023.

Most women, over four fifths, fit a no-depression pattern in the grouped results reported here. About fifteen percent fit a mild pattern and a small share a moderate one. Scores rose step by step across the groups. The team then tested how age, schooling, and marital state lined up with each pattern, to guide targeted support.
pmc-13285645:
One protein may both cool gum inflammation and spur bone growth, Huibing Lu and co-authors find in a 2026 study of gum ligament stem cells. Gum disease wrecks the tissues that hold teeth, driven by immune signals such as TNF-alpha and IL-1 beta. Gene reads of sore versus healthy gum tissue flagged the protein TRABD2A as raised in disease.

Adding the protein in lab dishes cut stem cell release of both flagged signals and sped cell growth. Bone marker Runx2 rose while a bone-eating signal fell, and dye tests showed more mineral laid down. Blocking the protein reversed the pattern. The authors pitch TRABD2A as a dual-action target for gum repair drugs.
pmc-13285745:
Chenyang Zhuang and co-authors build a fracture risk tool in a 2026 retrospective study of spine bone loss. Crushed vertebrae from weak bone cause much pain and disability in older adults. The team compared two scan-based scores, one from CT and one from MRI, and merged them into a simple chart that gauges risk.

Hospital records covered 385 patients seen between 2020 and 2024, of whom 127 had such a fracture. The fracture group showed lower CT density scores and higher MRI quality scores than the control group. The CT score proved the sharper single test of the two. A chart built on body mass index plus both scores sorted patients well in training and test sets. The authors see promise for spare-moment screening, pending checks at other centers.
pmc-13285845:
Ana Alice Pimenta-Pereira, Bailey Lubinski, and Rafael Kroon Campos review the alphavirus protein nsP3 in a 2026 overview of virus-host interplay. Alphaviruses, spread by mosquitoes, cause joint disease and brain infection in people and animals worldwide. One viral protein, nsP3, does many jobs at once, and much about its work remains murky.

Inside infected cells, nsP3 helps copy viral RNA and boost protein output from viral messages. It also grabs host proteins, binds RNA itself, strips chemical tags from other proteins, and bends cell pathways and immune defenses. Its chains fold into spiral scaffolds found in the factories where new virus copies form. Sorting out these roles could guide outbreak watch, risk forecasts, and new ways to block infection before it spreads.
pmc-13286145:
Zhi-qiang Zhang leads a 2026 mouse study on how a chemokine receptor steers allergy-linked blood cells from the bone marrow. In allergic rhinitis, eosinophils flood the nose lining and drive sneezing and swelling. The receptor CCR3 answers a signal that calls those cells out, and the team deleted it only in marrow cells to watch what changed upstream.

Data mining first flagged the stem cell marker CD34 as a hub gene tied to the missing receptor. Mice without marrow CCR3 scored lower on nose rubbing and sneezing in an allergy model, with cleaner nasal tissue as well. Their marrow, blood, and nose wash held fewer starter cells and fewer finished eosinophils than normal mice had. Blood levels of several allergy signals fell too, which paints CCR3 as a valve on eosinophil supply, not just a guide at the scene.
pmc-13286345:
Nathan J Robinson and colleagues teach computers to spot turtle breaths in animal-borne video in a 2026 methods study. Cameras strapped to sea turtles record hours of footage that no team can label by hand, and breath counts reveal diving habits and stress. Three image models, two builds of one network and a vision transformer, were trained on green turtle footage to flag frames where the animal breathes.

The transformer led the pack, tagging breath frames with the highest overall accuracy of the three. Every model caught nearly all true breaths, a recall above 99.9% across the board. False alarms stayed common, though, so breath rates came out somewhat inflated. The authors judge the tools unready for full automation but strong enough to slash the footage humans must still review.
pmc-13286545:
Natália de Castro Alves and a large team test whether adding resveratrol, an antioxidant from grapes, protects horse sperm during freezing. Published in 2026, the study addresses a weak point of semen freezing: removing seminal fluid leaves sperm exposed to damaging oxygen byproducts. Semen from ten stallions was frozen with several resveratrol doses or none.

After thawing, sperm given a mid-range dose swam better, kept stronger energy-producing structures, and bound more readily to oviduct tissue in a laboratory test. That dose also cut harmful oxygen compounds and quieted genes tied to cell death. Other doses helped less. The authors propose the supplement as a way to raise the fertility of frozen stallion semen used in breeding programs.
pmc-13286745:
Xiaoyu Tang and co-authors test whether artificially enlarging a small heart disease dataset makes machine learning risk models sturdier. Published in 2026, the study notes that small, uneven clinical datasets often produce fragile predictions. Five model types were trained after the training data were expanded by different amounts within safe feature limits.

Doubling the data gave the best compromise, cutting errors while improving fit. Under that setting, a random forest model reached about 94 percent accuracy after its continuous risk scores were converted into classes. Explanation tools highlighted a stress-test measure, the number of major vessels, chest pain type, and a heart imaging trait as the main drivers. The authors offer their recipe as a reusable pattern for small clinical datasets.
pmc-13287045:
Lili Tao and colleagues evaluate an AI-powered mobile system that screens older adults before vaccination and watches for reactions afterward. The 2026 study piloted the Medduo system at five vaccination centers with 2,609 people aged fifty and over, most with chronic diseases. Screening out people for whom a vaccine is unsafe normally consumes scarce staff time.

Nearly everyone completed the phone-based health check, and the system matched vaccine recommendations to their answers. Reported reaction rates ran near eight percent, highest in the fifty-to-fifty-nine group. Prior uptake was high for COVID-19 and flu shots but low for shingles vaccine. Combining active follow-up with passive reporting caught reactions sensitively. The authors present digital screening as a practical upgrade for immunization programs.
pmc-13287545:
Lan Yang and co-authors compare in 2026 four rare pituitary tumours that grew above the normal gland site, removed through the nose with a scope. Two grew inside the stalk that links gland and brain. Two grew mostly outside it, pressing on it from beside.

Scans before surgery could not show the stalk clearly in the inside cases, and the stalk ended up thinned to a film. In outside cases the stalk stayed visible and intact despite pressure. The authors warn that inside growth raises the risk of hormone failure after surgery. For patients without symptoms, watchful waiting may be wiser than early removal.
pmc-13287745:
Payas Arora and colleagues screened variants of the diabetes drug metformin in 2026 by computer, hunting for one that might block growth signals in head and neck cancer. Docking tests, movement simulations, and energy calculations were run against several cancer pathway targets, with the protein mTOR drawing the closest look.

One catalogue compound, listed as CID 222300, bound most strongly to mTOR. Over a 100 nanosecond simulation the pairing stayed compact and steady, with regular weak bonds holding it together. The authors name the compound a lead for lab follow-up. No cells or animals were tested, so any treatment promise rests on later bench work.
pmc-13287845:
Ye Yuan and colleagues built a fatigue detector for tennis serves, reported in 2026. The serve moves energy from the legs through the trunk to the racket in one fast chain. Tired muscles change that chain and raise injury risk, yet most wearables track motion alone. The team paired motion sensors with muscle activity sensors on 15 high-level players. Each player served until exhausted under a set protocol.

A graph neural network read the combined data, using the body skeleton as its map and muscle signals as node inputs. The system sorted fresh from fatigued serves with about 95 percent accuracy. It beat standard sequence and image-style networks by clear margins in the same tests. The analysis also found a lag between muscle drive and joint motion once fatigue set in. Because the model answers in a few milliseconds, the authors see on-court use as realistic.
pmc-13288045:
