Sahar Sadr Moharerpour and co-authors paired the antibiotic amikacin with two other drugs in 2026 against twenty hard-to-treat Escherichia coli strains taken from urinary infections. Pairing was tested on checkerboard plates that reveal whether drugs help, ignore, or fight each other.

Half the strains showed true synergy for amikacin with imipenem, and forty percent for amikacin with ciprofloxacin. No pairing backfired. All strains resisted ciprofloxacin alone, and over half resisted each of the other drugs alone. The authors propose planned drug pairs as a practical route when single drugs fail against resistant urinary infections, pending patient trials.
pmc-13288345:
Sung Woo Ko and co-authors describe a new bypass for a blocked bowel in a 2026 case report. A 47-year-old man with spread pancreatic cancer kept vomiting despite an earlier surgical bypass. Tumor growth had narrowed both his duodenum and the surgical connection itself. A standard stent attempt failed because the narrowing was too tight. The team chose an ultrasound-guided route to build a fresh channel.

Working through the old bypass, they filled a loop of small bowel with dyed fluid so it stood out on ultrasound. From inside the duodenum, they placed a short metal stent that joins the two walls, creating a duodenojejunostomy. Blue fluid flowed through at once, confirming the channel was open. The approach shows how endoscopic ultrasound can rescue patients when surgery and stents have already failed. Such rescues matter because blocked bowels cause severe suffering in advanced cancer.
pmc-13288545:
Maria J Rus leads a 2026 study of spit hormones and mouth germs in midlife women. The team enrolled 30 women. Ages ran from 40 to 65. Two estrogens were measured in saliva. Germ samples came from four mouth sites.

One estrogen, estrone, fell with age. It tied to dry mouths and worse oral scores. It also tied to richer germ mix on the tongue. Porphyromonas rose with it there. The other estrogen, estradiol, tied to friendly germs. Streptococcus and Lactobacillus were in that set. It tied against gum-linked germs instead. Site mattered for each pattern. The mouth may mirror body hormone change.
pmc-13289345:
Christopher McLaughlin and Lewis Kaplan authored a 2026 patient guide on surgical site infections for trauma and emergency surgery readers. Such infections grow where an operation was done and usually appear within 30 days. Rates run near 0.5 to 2 percent after planned surgery and 10 to 15 percent after emergency surgery, the guide notes.

Infections are grouped by depth: skin level, deep under skin to muscle, or inside the body space. Prevention spans skin cleansing, sterile covers, and antibiotics started before surgery, with longer courses when surgery treats an existing infection. Warning clues include redness, extra pain, oozing, bad smell, fever, low energy, poor appetite, and nausea. Readers are urged to report clues to the surgical team at any hour.
pmc-13289845:
Anushree Agarwal and a large team describe a 2026 co-designed digital tool to keep adults with congenital heart disease in lifelong specialist care. Gaps in such care lead to preventable harm and early death, yet scalable fixes are scarce. The team blended behavior theory, interviews with patients and clinicians, and community partnership to build the intervention from the ground up.

The target behavior was completing a specialist appointment for the heart condition. Interviews guided by a capability, opportunity, and motivation framework found barriers a digital tool could plausibly ease. Community partners helped set goals, shape the theory map, and define tool features with patients. Theory-driven design aims for lasting use, not just downloads.
pmc-13289945:
Daniel S. Berman led a 2026 proof-of-principle pipeline, called Fung-AI, that designs antifungal peptides with generative artificial intelligence. New fungal threats endanger health and food crops, and fresh antifungal scaffolds are urgently needed. A generative network learned to invent peptide strings, while classifier models ranked them for antifungal promise and low red cell harm before any lab testing began.

From about 10,000 candidates, thirteen peptides entered two rounds of lab testing. Five mildly blocked a wheat fungus, and four of those also blocked a human Candida pathogen at tested doses. Two leads showed low harm to human liver cells, marking them as optimization starting points. None strongly blocked the emerging Candida auris, urging species-specific selection.
pmc-13290145:
What helps applicants match into plastic surgery residency is sorted out in a 2026 systematic review by Jaina Eckert and colleagues. The specialty runs two routes, an integrated track entered from medical school and an independent track taken after other surgical training, and competition for both keeps tightening.

Reviewing the published evidence, the authors found strong grades and exam scores, heavy research output with first-author papers, and honor society membership all tied to success on both tracks. Letters of recommendation, leadership, and interview performance mattered too. The independent track weighed the pedigree of prior surgical training and interview counts more heavily. Eckert and colleagues offer the synthesis to applicants planning their strategy and to programs refining how they select.
pmc-13290245:
Which trauma patients end up needing a second, higher amputation is the question Jaquelyn Kakalecik and colleagues tackle in a 2026 retrospective study. They reviewed traumatic lower-extremity amputations closed definitively at a Level I academic trauma center between 2005 and 2024.

Eighty-six patients met the study criteria, many of them smokers with high injury severity. Over a third ultimately required an above-knee or through-knee amputation, and those patients arrived sicker, with worse injury grades. Needing further debridement after the stump was closed stood out: it came with higher body mass index and a much higher rate of revision amputation. Keeping a below-knee level, when possible, meant better walking rates and less need for assistive devices, which the authors tie to planning and infection control.
pmc-13290445:
Faster ways to build glycopeptides, and the habits of thought that blocked them, are the subject of a 2026 perspective by Dror Ben Abba Amiel and colleagues. Glycopeptides, protein fragments bearing sugar chains at defined sites, are prized tools for studying glycosylation, but standard solid-phase synthesis prepares them slowly and wastefully.

The authors recount how their lab developed a method using high-shear mixing at high temperature that finishes glycopeptides within minutes while using few building blocks. Diffusion, they argue, was the overlooked variable: understanding how molecules move through the reaction reshaped the protocol. They compare their approach with other speed-up techniques and credit the breakthrough to questioning settled assumptions about solid-phase synthesis. The piece closes with where the strategy might widen glycopeptide research next.
pmc-13290545:
A simple nutrition index forecasts death and heart events in people with diabetic foot ulcers, Yukun Tao and colleagues report in 2026. The prognostic nutritional index combines blood markers of nutrition and immunity, and this retrospective study tested it against hard outcomes.

The cohort held 1,225 patients admitted to the Air Force Medical Center between January 2015 and December 2022, followed for a median of 3.6 years across the group. In that time 378 patients died, 30.9% of the total. Each one-unit rise in the index came with about 5% lower all-cause mortality risk, with similar protection for cardiovascular death and major heart events. The relationship bent around a threshold near 39 in the data. Kidney function, measured by eGFR, carried roughly a ninth of the effect. Tao and colleagues back the index as a cheap risk marker in ulcer care.
pmc-13290845:
China's pathologists are multiplying, but tumor workloads are multiplying faster, Zhun Shu and colleagues report in a workforce study from 2026. Pathology underpins cancer diagnosis worldwide, and little was known about whether China's staffing kept pace with its rising cancer burden between 2010 and 2022.

Yearbook and registry data show the pathologist share of physicians held steady while absolute numbers grew about 84%. New cancer cases per pathologist actually fell, from roughly 332 in 2010 to 215 in 2018, as density improved. Yet oncology outpatients per pathologist jumped 131% and inpatients 47% over the full period, because patient volumes grew far faster than staffing. Shu and colleagues argue workforce planning and efficiency technology must close a demand gap that headcount growth alone has not.
pmc-13291245:
Steroid hormones can reshape how cells handle RNA messages. Victoria J. Nicolini and colleagues report this fresh effect in a 2026 letter. Dark granules called P-bodies store and sort RNA in cells. What body signals control their assembly was unclear.

The team screened more than fifteen hundred approved drugs. Steroid drugs stood out as strong granule builders. Common drugs like dexamethasone raised granule counts within two days. Blocking the steroid receptor stopped the effect fully. Removing the drug reversed it within a day. The receptor’s main form proved required for the change. This link adds a new layer to how steroid drugs act.
pmc-13291445:
A tubal pregnancy reached full term and a live birth in Tanzania. Charlotte M. Nelen and colleagues report this rare 2026 case. Most tubal pregnancies are caught and treated early. Rupture and bleeding make late cases deadly.

The woman had many prenatal visits before delivery. Three ultrasound scans also missed the true site. Signs were present but pointed the wrong way. The truth emerged only during a cesarean birth. The baby was born alive at 42 weeks. Such cases can mimic abdominal pregnancies closely. Careful belly checks and sharper scan skills are urged. Low-resource settings face the highest risk of a miss.
pmc-13292245:
Lila Jiangenuer and colleagues map how stress and growth symptoms intertwine in stoma patients, in a 2026 survey study. People living with an intestinal stoma after colorectal cancer often carry posttraumatic stress and posttraumatic growth side by side. The team surveyed 416 patients at three Chinese hospitals in early 2026. Standard checklists measured both symptom families, and network analysis hunted for central and bridging symptoms. Bootstrap checks tested the network's steadiness.

Self-blame for the stressful experience sat at the network's center on the stress side. Better understanding of spiritual matters anchored the growth side. Sleep trouble and changed life priorities bridged the two clusters, linking distress with growth. The model held up acceptably under resampling, though bridge estimates deserve caution. The authors suggest screening could target these hub symptoms first. Tailored support might ease distress while leaving room for growth. Confirming the pattern needs follow-up over time, not one snapshot.
pmc-13292445:
Nour M Zaki, Maya A Shehata, and Jana A Nasr study a 2026 parenting question inside Egypt: how discipline passes, or fails to pass, between generations. Using scales built from local meanings, they surveyed 490 parents of children aged two to twelve and a half. The questionnaire covered five kinds of discipline: physical, verbal, psychological, deprivation-based, and positive, with the first three combined as harsh discipline.

Parents did repeat much of what was done to them, yet the younger generation used harsh strategies less than the one before. Four things predicted harshness today: believing the culture approves it, remembering harsh treatment from one's own parents, having more children at home, and family income. The authors discuss social, legal, and cultural implications. They frame harsh discipline as a culturally rooted risk pattern rather than a private family habit.
pmc-13292545:
Yuru Tang and colleagues use genetic instruments to test whether aging itself raises infection risk, in a 2026 Mendelian randomization study. Older people suffer more COVID-19 and sepsis, but separating aging from its diseases is hard. Mendelian randomization uses inherited variants as natural experiments for exposures like telomere length and immune cell traits. The design also weighs body fat, blood pressure, lipids, and lifestyle factors such as smoking and healthy weight.

The study frames biological aging and aging-linked immune cell types as independent risk factors for both infections. Age-related immune change is explored as the mechanism connecting the two. Weight control and smoking behavior enter as possible mediators that people can actually change. If those pathways hold, prevention in older adults could target them directly. The authors pitch the work as guidance for protecting geriatric populations. Genetic designs sidestep much confounding, though assumptions still bind the claims.
pmc-13292945:
Jakyoung Lee and co-authors propose, in 2026, a three-stage system for spotting depression early with wearable sensors. Most devices only split people into well or ill, which gives little guidance on when to act for prevention.

Nine body, behavior, and biology signals were tracked over time to mark normal, pre-disease, and disease states, using warning signs that appear before a sharp shift. A computer agent sorted states with high accuracy, aided by soft neural probes that record with little harm, a result the authors report. A skin patch that stimulates the vagus nerve worked best when given in the pre-disease stage, with faster recovery than later care.
pmc-13293445:
Florence Gyembuzie Wongnaah and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, how often women in Ghana say they have had sexually transmitted infections or related symptoms. Such infections raise risks of HIV, infertility, and pelvic inflammation, above all where care is limited.

Data came from the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey, covering 12,997 women aged 15 to 49 with survey weights applied. About one in four women reported an infection or symptom, with discharge the most common complaint. Women in their forties reported less than teens did, as did women whose first sex came at age 17 or later. Partner counts also shaped the odds.
pmc-13293745:
Rayan Harari and colleagues build computer models that predict whether knee osteoarthritis will worsen, in a 2026 study using data from six hundred participants in a national research cohort. Predicting progression matters because some knees stay stable for years while others deteriorate quickly. The models combined personal details, X-ray grades, pain scores, and precise magnetic resonance measurements of cartilage, bone, and joint inflammation, taken at the start and again two years later.

Change over time predicted X-ray progression best, with the random forest model reaching strong accuracy. Starting measurements alone also performed well, while combined pain-plus-structure progression proved harder to forecast. Explanations built into the models highlighted cartilage loss on the inner femur and bone marrow lesions as leading signals. The authors present the approach as a transparent aid for spotting patients at risk.
pmc-13294045:
Dimitri Chubinidze heads a 2026 mixed-methods study on how cutlery feels to adults in intensive eating disorder care. Sensory sensitivity is common, even more so for neurodivergent patients, yet research has chased food texture and room design while ignoring utensils. In a specialist service using the autism-friendly PEACE Pathway, patients judged 31 items differing in material, weight, size, and shape.

Metal pieces were preferred most, while wood, paper, plastic, and hybrid sporks were widely rejected. Weight, balance, texture, mouth fit, and neutral feel shaped comfort and readiness to eat. Shared limits coexisted with strong personal variation, and tastes stayed stable across settings.
pmc-13294545:
Priya R. Baral and a large team report ultra-short magnetic spirals in a cobalt tellurium oxide crystal for a 2026 study. Twisted spin textures in insulators could run memory devices on far less power than metals, but spiral pitches usually span tens of nanometers. Neutron scattering, magnet checks, and first-principles math probed the chiral cubic material Co5TeO8 across temperature and field.

Spiral pitch tuned smoothly from 5.7 to 10 nm inside a phase map with eight distinct states in the reported count. Electrical capacitance quirks in every phase hint at electric control of magnetism. Single-ion anisotropy beat the usual twist force by about tenfold in calculations, offering a design rule for compact textures.
pmc-13295145:
Naokata Sumitomo and co-authors review progressive cardiac conduction disease in a 2026 article. In this rare inherited condition, the heart's electrical wiring slowly fails, risking complete block, fainting, or sudden death. Gene discoveries have greatly widened the list of linked disorders in recent years.

Faults span ion channel genes, gap junction genes, muscle disease genes, control genes, and metabolic and mitochondrial causes. The authors propose sorting cases into isolated forms and forms tied to wider illness. Pacemaker fitting remains first-line care, while some patients also need a defibrillator device. The grouping aims to guide diagnosis, risk judgement, and family screening in everyday cardiology practice.
pmc-13295445:
Chenbo Huang and colleagues run camera traps in a Chinese nature reserve in a 2026 survey. The Zhangjiajie reserve was created mainly for the giant salamander and its waters, yet its forests may shelter much more land wildlife. Cameras worked broad-leaved and coniferous woods from March 2024 to August 2025.

Recordings identified 59 species, split between 18 mammals and 41 ground-dwelling birds, including protected and China-only kinds. Most small and medium meat-eaters moved at night, while birds and squirrels kept daytime hours. One civet reliably shifted its peak activity between seasons, giving managers a baseline for habitat care and quieter sensitive hours.
pmc-13295545:
Fan Sheng and colleagues model future homes for the milu deer in Jiangsu wetlands in a 2026 study. The globally endangered deer holds its largest wild population along this Chinese coast. Climate shifts and human pressure threaten that ground, so managers need maps of where suitable habitat will persist.

Satellite tracking records and environmental layers fed a combined modelling package for present and future conditions. Good habitat now hugs the coastline and is expected to grow across central and northern shore areas. Distance from the sea, driest-month rain, temperature swings, and human density jointly shaped the map, informing corridor plans and disturbance control.
pmc-13295845:
Stephen Gerard Flynn and co-authors argue a middle path in a 2026 commentary on children's airway care. Trainees need practice placing breathing tubes, yet repeated attempts raise the risk of serious harm, and video scopes now beat direct viewing on success in many settings.

Rather than choosing one method, the authors favour video-assisted direct laryngoscopy, where a blade allows direct viewing while a camera lets a teacher watch and guide. They note direct viewing still gives a wide field and helps clear blood or secretions. Their point is that combining both views serves patients and training at once.
pmc-13295945:
Barbara J. Brunnick, Graysen D. Boehning and Stefan Harzen propose, in 2026, using facial pigment marks to help identify individual bottlenose dolphins. Researchers usually rely on nicks in dorsal fins, but calves lack such marks and fin damage can erase a known pattern.

Bridle marks, dark facial features that are distinctive and stable over time, can be photographed alongside fins. The authors argue these marks offer a backup check on identity, especially for clean-finned calves that leave their mothers before fin marks develop. Adding facial records could cut mistaken identity in long-term population studies.
pmc-13296345:
Joana B. Silva and colleagues test how external memory aids affect two kinds of remembering in a 2026 experiment. A total of 152 participants had to send an email two days later at a set time. Some set a reminder, some scheduled the email automatically, and some relied on memory alone. Participants also watched a news report that they later recalled.

Both aid groups performed better on the timed email task than the unaided group. Recall of the news report, by contrast, showed no clear difference between groups. Confidence in remembering also rose with the aids. The pattern separates remembering to act from remembering past content, a distinction that matters for designing reminders people actually use.
pmc-13296445:
Juan Pablo Bozo and co-authors probe, in 2026, how mitochondria help B cells grab and display fragments of germs to partner T cells. When a B cell meets its target it builds a contact zone, hauls digesting sacs there and extracts material, and the team test whether splitting mitochondria matters for that work.

A compound that disturbs the splitting machinery changed mitochondrial shape and activity, kept them from settling at the contact zone and held the digesting sacs back. Extraction and display to T cells both fell. The authors conclude mitochondrial reshaping supports the whole capture-and-present sequence.
pmc-13296645:
Hagar Tal, Winson F.Z. Yang and Matthew D. Sacchet map, in 2026, studies pairing meditation with neurofeedback, where brain signals are shown back to the meditator as a training aid. Interest is growing, but no full map of the young field existed.

Most studies prove the concept rather than test benefit, and designs, measures and practices vary widely. Brain activity does shift reliably under feedback, yet gains in behaviour, felt experience or lasting meditation skill stay thinly shown. The authors recommend tighter methods and ask whether feedback can ease common hurdles such as anxiety and self-doubt.
pmc-13296945:
Carlee D. Chezzi and colleagues report delayed links between geomagnetic activity and human brain waves in a 2026 study. Brain rhythms in the alpha and theta bands have been tied to environmental influences, but timing was unclear. Archival recordings from 238 people over four years were matched against daily geomagnetic indices.

Correlations in both bands peaked when geomagnetic activity nineteen days earlier was considered. A second experiment exposed twenty-two volunteers to a simulated geomagnetic storm. Their recordings nineteen days later showed reduced power in several bands over frontal and parietal areas. Two different designs pointing to the same lag is striking, and the authors call for work on mechanisms and behaviour.
pmc-13297045:
Ganbayar Batchuluun and co-authors train, in 2026, chest X-ray classifiers to look at lungs rather than picture frames. Models often cheat using borders, text marks and scanner quirks, so the team use heatmaps of model attention and an adversarial check against true lung masks.

The classifier learns to keep its labels while making its attention map mask-like, needing masks only in training. New test measures count prediction flips under rotation and attention spilling outside the lungs. Experiments show tighter lung focus and sturdier behaviour. The authors frame the method as bio-inspired attention discipline.
pmc-13297345:
Pekik Wiji Prasetyaningrum and Shinji Sakai ask how the added chemistry on gelatin, before it is ever set into a gel, affects living cells, in a 2026 study. Three tagged forms of gelatin serve as starting materials for tissue scaffolds, and cells meet the loose forms briefly during making and again where tags remain after setting. Four cell types were bathed in each soluble form at matched strength.

No form proved broadly toxic. What differences appeared were subtle and depended on the cell type. Skin-like fibroblasts shifted mainly under the methacrylate-tagged form. Stem cells shifted most under that same form, least under the norbornene form, which matched untreated cells. Makers of gelatin scaffolds should weigh these leftover effects, the authors say.
pmc-13299345:
Qi Sun and a team study how a moth pest finds its host, an ancient fern called a living fossil, in a 2026 entomology paper. Plant odours guide host-seeking in herbivorous insects, so the researchers collected and analysed volatiles released by the fern. Antenna tests identified five compounds that triggered electrical responses in the moth.

Behaviour experiments then singled out one compound, 4-ethylbenzaldehyde, which attracted both male and female moths clearly at the tested dose. The team proposes this compound as the core ingredient for developing attractant-based control tools against a pest that seriously damages a rare and protected fern species.
pmc-13299845:
Janusz Wiesław Błaszczyk argues that brain ageing and degeneration begin as energy failures rooted in glucose metabolism, in a 2026 theoretical paper. Brain cells cannot be replaced and depend almost entirely on glucose fuel, with a helper molecule called NAD in decline during ageing. High-demand regions such as the hypothalamus show the earliest changes.

Early signs often surface as body-wide metabolic problems, including insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, followed by neurological or psychiatric symptoms matching the affected regions. Trials suggest supplements that restore NAD precursors may slow early ageing changes, yet protection fades once disease is fully developed. Timing therefore defines the therapeutic window.
pmc-13300345:
Jeel Moya-Salazar and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of breath based tests for liver fibrosis. Diagnosis usually rests on biopsy, an invasive procedure often done late, so the authors compared studies that detect volatile organic compounds in exhaled breath instead. Searches across thirteen databases followed PRISMA guidelines, and study quality was graded with the PEDro scale.

Only seven investigations met the inclusion rules, all from Europe and all in adults. Gas chromatography with mass spectrometry was the most common technique, used in four studies, while electronic nose devices appeared in two. Sensitivity mostly ranged from 85 to 100 percent, and three studies passed ninety percent specificity. Isoprene emerged as the most consistent breath marker. The authors ask for more work in regions where liver fibrosis risk and prevalence run high.
pmc-13300645:
Could a common vitamin soften the cancer risk carried by BRCA1 mutations? Joanna Robaczyńska and colleagues weigh the evidence in a 2026 narrative review. Carriers face high lifetime risks of breast and ovarian cancer, and vitamin D touches cell growth, immune control, and the DNA repair paths that BRCA1 defects disrupt.

The review gathers molecular work on calcitriol signaling through its receptor, then turns to the sparse human data in carriers themselves. Findings so far remain thin and inconsistent, with no firm proof that raising vitamin D levels changes outcomes for this group. The authors mark out clear gaps and argue for targeted studies before any preventive advice is given.
pmc-13300945:
Two drug-resistant yeasts are rewriting hospital infection control, Sepinoud Raeisi and colleagues warn in a 2026 review of Candida auris and Candida glabrata. Drawing on surveillance from the CDC, ECDC, WHO, and regional networks, the authors track recent outbreaks, resistance shifts, and control practice across intensive care, neonatal, and long-term care units.

Azole resistance in C. auris already tops eighty percent in some regions, and multidrug patterns now reach the echinocandins too. C. glabrata shows rising dual resistance plus biofilm tolerance. Faster identification through MALDI-TOF, PCR, and genome tracking helps, the authors note, but access lags where resources are thin, leaving stewardship and surveillance as priorities.
pmc-13301145:
M I A Bistriceanu and co-authors pool the early prospective evidence on pulsed field ablation for ventricular tachycardia in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Six studies covering 186 patients, mostly men with scarred, weak ventricles and frequent earlier ablations, met the criteria. The team merged acute success, defined as the rhythm no longer being triggerable, with recurrence over roughly six months of follow-up.

Pooled acute success reached about eighty-six percent, with no statistical inconsistency between studies. Recurrence by follow-up, however, touched about thirty percent of patients. Complications stayed rare, led by conduction problems near four percent and vascular issues near three percent, with coronary spasm and stroke each under two percent. The authors position pulsed field energy as a promising complement to radiofrequency for deep scar targets, capable of non-thermal full thickness lesions, while noting how young the evidence base remains.
pmc-13301745:
J M Choi and co-authors link neighborhood deprivation to sudden cardiac death in a 2026 UK Biobank analysis. The cohort held 500,877 participants with no prior events or implanted defibrillators, sorted into thirds by the Townsend deprivation index of their home area. Over a mean follow-up of about thirteen and a half years, the team counted 3,041 sudden cardiac deaths and 2,203 ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation events, adjusting for demographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors.

Risk climbed in a graded staircase with deprivation. The most deprived third carried about twenty-four percent higher sudden death risk and eighteen percent higher arrhythmia risk than the least deprived third in the fully adjusted model. Deprivation bit hardest in adults under fifty. Smoking amplified the deprivation effect. The authors argue sudden death prevention frameworks should fold social determinants in directly, with targeted strategies for disadvantaged communities.
pmc-13302545:
A ringworm fungus jumps from pets to people with its genome nearly unchanged, Zebin Du and colleagues show in a 2026 study from Beijing. Thirty-eight isolates of the fungus, gathered from dogs and cats at two veterinary hospitals, underwent drug-susceptibility testing against six antifungals plus whole-genome sequencing. One human-derived strain was added for comparison.

Every isolate matched the reference genome at over 99.9 percent identity, and the human strain sat inside the pet family tree, genomic support for cross-host spread. Terbinafine worked best; eleven isolates showed high tolerance to several drugs at once. Extra copies of the CDR1 pump gene tracked with higher drug tolerance, a lead for resistance surveillance.
pmc-13302845:
Blood markers whisper what dialysis patients rarely say about their own resilience, Gloria María Zaragoza Fernández and colleagues explore in a 2026 exploratory study. Adults on maintenance hemodialysis completed the fourteen-item Resilience Scale while routine labs supplied beta2-microglobulin, albumin, calcium, and vitamin D values. Models adjusted for age, dialysis history, diabetes, and heart disease, with gender interactions tested head-on.

Higher beta2-microglobulin tracked with lower resilience in simple comparisons, though the link faded after adjustment. Albumin leaned the other way without reaching significance, and no gender-specific pattern survived the full models. The authors read the signals as preliminary and call for larger longitudinal work before biology claims a seat beside social support.
pmc-13302945:
Machine learning can predict how much a drawbead grips sheet metal, Tomasz Trzepieciński and colleagues show in a 2026 forming study. Drawbead simulator tests on DC04 low-carbon steel varied lubrication, bead height, sample size, and surface roughness, recording the friction coefficient each time. Three learning algorithms competed to model those results while importance analyses ranked the inputs.

A support vector machine with a cubic kernel won clearly, posting an error of 0.0085 and explaining the data with an R-squared of 0.9657. Friction conditions mattered most, then bead height; Shapley analysis showed low bead heights push friction sharply upward. The rankings give press shops a data-backed order for tuning their setups.
pmc-13303645:
Musa Ghufron, Sukardiman Sukardiman, and Muhammad Miftahussurur screen plant chemicals by computer, in a 2026 study, hunting for weapons against drug-resistant stomach bacteria. Indonesian Helicobacter pylori strains more and more shrug off levofloxacin and metronidazole, two standard antibiotics. The team built models with full 3-D shape of the bacterial proteins those drugs target.

Candidate plant compounds were docked into the modelled binding pockets, then checked for drug-like behaviour and run in motion. Curcumin, the yellow pigment in turmeric, gripped all three targets more tightly than the standard drugs in the computer runs. Its complex with one target also wobbled least in motion tests, suggesting a stable fit. The authors present curcumin as the front-runner, while noting that lab proof still lies ahead.
pmc-13304045:
Marvin C. Masalunga and a panel of specialists update, in a 2026 narrative review, what is known about salivary duct carcinoma, a fast and dangerous cancer of the saliva glands. The tumour resembles breast duct cancer under the microscope and spreads readily to neck nodes and distant sites. Knowledge has moved since the last world classification.

New shape-based subtypes and driver gene changes may help forecast behaviour and open drug targets. Staining profiles used by pathologists have sharpened, aiding diagnosis among look-alike gland tumours. The review also covers the immune surroundings of the tumour, which may steer treatment choices ahead. Prognosis remains poor overall, and the authors stress personalised care built on these refining markers.
pmc-13304245:
Daniel George Boicu leads a 2026 narrative review of ringing ears and hearing loss after injury. Loud blasts, explosions, and head knocks frequently damage hearing, yet reported rates and recovery odds vary wildly between studies.

Four databases were searched for work from 2010 to 2025 on adults exposed to sound, blast, or head trauma. The gathered evidence confirms that hearing problems commonly follow blast injury and sudden loud sound. Recovery patterns and warning signs for lasting damage differed by injury type. Early treatment timing drew special focus, since prompt care may protect long-term hearing for many patients.
pmc-13304545:
Mengxuan Dong and co-authors map where psilocin, the active form of the psychedelic psilocybin, travels in zebrafish in a 2026 imaging study. Safety and body distribution data lag behind interest in the drug for anxiety and depression care.

Fish swam in three dose levels for four hours while behavior was scored in a standard tank test. Treated fish moved restlessly with more zone crossings. A spray-based imaging method then charted the drug across organs with checked accuracy. Signal showed up in eye, brain, heart, liver, and kidney, piling up most in brain and parts of liver, and rose with dose.
pmc-13305445:
Maria de Jesus Xavier Aguirre heads a 2026 narrative review of how teen friendship networks shape weight. Friends share food habits and activity patterns, and those shared habits may push body weight in the same direction.

Five databases were searched for studies from 2009 to 2022 on teens aged twelve to nineteen using network analysis. Boys mirrored friends in unhealthy food intake, while girls mirrored friends in sitting-heavy pastimes. Network effects differed by gender across studies. Prevention plans that work through friendship groups, tuned by gender, may beat messages aimed at teens alone.
pmc-13307445:
Yuxin Guo and co-authors build in 2026 a low cost way to break hurdle clearance into phases using a single side view video and marker free pose tracking. Their group filmed 37 physical education students with mixed skill as they cleared hurdles in training.

The pipeline joins hurdle detection, pose tracking, rule based event spotting, and phase wise measures of body motion. Hurdle spotting proved highly accurate, and pose results matched hand labels well in the checks reported here. Phase timing error averaged well under one frame and beat two learning based rivals. Coaches could thus review technique in normal sessions without costly lab gear or sensors on the body.
pmc-13307645:
Erfan Pakatchian and co-authors report in 2026 a Phase III trial of Gardisun, a new four type HPV vaccine, against the licensed Gardasil vaccine in healthy volunteers aged 15 to 35 years. A total of 450 people got three doses on days 0, 60, and 180, and antibody levels were checked a month after the last dose.

Both vaccines raised antibodies and gave high conversion rates for all four HPV types covered here. The main test met its goal for HPV-6, and extra checks backed a like verdict for the other types as well. Harms were mostly mild and brief, with no serious event tied to a vaccine in either group.
pmc-13308945:
Shannon N Greenberg and co-authors report a 2026 case of cecal bascule, a rare fold block of the large bowel, in a woman aged 27 years whose organs sit in mirror place. She also had Kartagener syndrome and no past belly surgery, and she came in with one day of left upper belly pain.

Scans showed full mirror anatomy with the cecum swung to the left upper space and turned in a way that fit the fold. Urgent surgery found a swollen cecum with a clear block point at the fold site. The team cut out the join of small and large bowel and stitched a fresh link. Mirror anatomy makes even rare calls harder to spot in time.
pmc-13309345:
Ifrah Zawar comments in 2026 on a brain scan study of late onset unexplained epilepsy. In that state, seizures start past age 55 years with no clear cause. Zawar asks how it sits beside slow brain decay. The study set 59 such patients, mean age 71.2 years, against 53 matched healthy older adults with scans and thought tests.

Patients showed thin rinds in sense and inner time brain zones, plus shrunk deep grey hubs, and those losses tracked weak word fluency scores. Other spots ran thick or large, more so in those whose seizures spared awareness in the group. Zawar reads the pattern as a bridge state, part seizure state and part early decay.
pmc-13309445:
Anne Wienholz and co-authors present a 2026 eye-tracking study on how signers follow who is who in German Sign Language. Signers place people they mention at spots in the signing space and can point to those spots later. The team asked whether pointing makes a person easier to pick up again.

Deaf adult signers watched short signed stories that named two people, with pointing used for one person or for neither. Eye movements showed signers looked toward whoever the next sentence continued with. Pointing itself did not speed or guide those looks. The authors suggest pointing may serve another role, or that their story setup could not reveal the effect.
pmc-13309745:
Naif Taleb Ali and co-authors review artificial intelligence help for spotting carriers of inherited blood disorders in a 2026 article. The disorders covered include thalassemias and sickle cell disease, where carrier screening before marriage can prevent illness in children. Cheap blood tests exist, but human reading misses carriers, above all where staff are few.

Seven databases yielded 85 studies covering 133,498 people in 23 countries for the pooled analysis. Software-aided reading of blood counts, smears, and related tests reached pooled sensitivity of 92.8 percent and specificity of 91.5 percent in the combined results, beating standard reading on sensitivity. Gains varied by region. The authors back wider use with care for fairness and local setup.
pmc-13309845:
Kushani Shah and co-authors study how a long noncoding RNA drives melanoma through three-strand DNA structures in a 2026 article. The RNA, called SLNCR, was already known to aid melanoma growth by working with transcription factors. New work ties it to genomic sites where RNA can latch onto DNA as a third strand.

Four triplex-forming regions sit in the RNA sequence, echoing regions in three other known RNAs. Adding the full RNA to melanoma cells sped growth, movement, and invasion, with gene shifts in cell cycle and migration paths. Deleting any one region reversed those shifts and stiffened the RNA shape. The authors map target genes whose promoters host the matching sites.
pmc-13310645:
Yutaka Yoshida, Soshiro Kashio, and Masayuki Miura hunt in 2026 for blood-borne repair signals in fruit flies. Their tagging system sits in the Golgi apparatus, the cell's shipping department for secreted proteins. Their earlier work showed the fly fat body, an organ resembling liver and fat combined, aids repair of wing precursor tissue from a distance. The new tool labels fat-body secretions so their proteins can be fished from circulation.

Combining the labelling with blood proteomics and genetic tests pointed to two signal families. Innate immune regulators coming from the fat body influenced how well the damaged tissue repaired. Iron-handling mediators from the same organ also affected repair outcomes. Organs clearly talk during healing, yet the messenger proteins are rarely catalogued directly. A Golgi-specific tagging route, the authors argue, can systematically expose such inter-organ signals in other repair settings too.
pmc-13311145:
Jing Zhao and colleagues trace a receptor pair that drives ovarian cancer spread in a 2026 study. Ovarian cancer holds the highest death rate among women reproductive cancers, and most cases are found late with wide spread. Growth receptor drugs have disappointed despite high receptor levels, which hints at a hidden regulator.

A partner receptor called GPR107 was raised in tumors and boosted spread. Contact between the pair fired the growth receptor harder and woke a signal chain that freed the spread factor IL-6. Antibodies that block IL-6 curbed spread driven by the pair in models. Cutting the cross talk may open a fresh drug angle.
pmc-13311345:
Preeti Banerjee and colleagues search in 2026 for warning signs of heavy bleeding after repeat caesarean birth, looking back over two hundred women treated between 2020 and 2025. Records supplied body data, birth history, and surgery details. Bleeding counted as postpartum haemorrhage at a litre or more, or when transfusion or action was needed.

Seventy-two women, thirty-six percent, met the haemorrhage rule. They ran higher body mass, more previous caesareans, lower antenatal haemoglobin, and far longer surgeries. The fitted model kept placenta previa or placenta problems as the strongest warning sign, roughly tripling the odds. Scar adhesions, three or more previous caesarean births, and emergency surgery also raised risk on their own, with parity, body mass, surgery time, and haemoglobin. Repeat caesareans are rising worldwide, and scarred tissue clouds each next surgery. Flagging these signs before theatre, the authors argue, lets teams prepare blood, staff, and method in advance.
pmc-13311945:
Kristal Potter and co-authors argue, in a 2026 editorial, for placing pharmacists inside sports medicine teams. Athletes juggle drugs and supplements against anti-doping rules. They also travel across time zones and climates, and body makeup changes how drugs are absorbed. A sports pharmacist works much like an ambulatory care pharmacist but within the team. The role adds expertise on medicines, performance supplements, banned substances, and blood markers such as iron and vitamin D.

The role reaches well beyond anti-doping checks. These specialists can serve weekend, college, and elite athletes. They can work with clinicians, coaches, sporting bodies, and national governing boards. The editorial notes that academic medical centers have already begun embedding them this way. Its aim is to define the specialty clearly and encourage wider adoption. Drug decisions in sport, the authors argue, deserve the same expert attention as training and injury care.
pmc-13312245:
Kellie Arensman Hannan and co-authors study, in a 2026 retrospective review, how appropriately antibiotics were prescribed for acute sinusitis in outpatient care. National guidelines say antibiotics fit only when set symptom criteria are met, yet sinusitis remains one of the most common reasons for a prescription.

The team reviewed 1,000 randomly chosen adult encounters from emergency departments, urgent care centers, and clinics between January and March 2024. Prescribing criteria were met in 67.6 percent of visits, but antibiotics still went to 80.2 percent of patients who fell short of the criteria, and drug choice plus duration both matched local guidance in under half of all cases. Cough and symptoms lasting seven to nine days predicted inappropriate prescribing, while electronic visits carried far lower odds of an antibiotic.
pmc-13312445:
Kwang Hyun Cho, Seogjoo J Jang, and Young Min Rhee present a 2026 study of why natural light-harvesting complexes in purple bacteria have the size they do. The LH2 complex, a ring of pigment molecules with nine-fold symmetry, converts light to electronic energy with remarkable efficiency. The team used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations strengthened by a neural network approach. They compared the natural ring with artificial six-fold and twelve-fold versions built in the computer.

The unnatural rings showed markedly larger energetic disorder in their pigment excited states. They also had more broken hydrogen bonds, which the authors identify as a key stabilizer. Local motion nearby, by contrast, changed little between the designs. The calculations supply direct evidence that natural LH2 geometry is tuned to minimize disorder, which supports efficient energy transfer. That principle, the authors suggest, can guide engineers designing man-made light-harvesting systems.
pmc-13312545:
Barbara Šakić and co-authors explore, in a 2026 study, the shared genetics between psychiatric traits and insulin-related traits in the general population. Conditions such as ADHD, autism, and obsessive-compulsive disorder often travel with obesity and type 2 diabetes, yet comparing diagnosed cases blurs the picture because the conditions overlap so heavily.

Using summary data from huge genetic studies, the team applied genomic structural equation modeling across ADHD-, autism-, and OCD-linked traits plus five insulin measures. A three-factor model fit best, and two of its factors mixed psychiatric with insulin traits: one joined ADHD symptoms to body mass index, fasting glucose, and glycated hemoglobin. Another tied OCD symptoms to glycated hemoglobin. Follow-up scans flagged 57 genes for the ADHD factor and the gene MTNR1B for the OCD factor, with brain tissue expression prominent.
pmc-13312845:
Dan Wang and co-authors examine, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether measuring nitric oxide in exhaled breath at several flow rates can flag airway hyperresponsiveness in people with chronic cough. The link between airway inflammation and obstruction in this common, hard-to-diagnose complaint was unclear, so the team tested three breath measures against lung function and a provocation test.

Records covered 2,205 outpatients, with 582 also undergoing methacholine challenge. Two flow-based measures ran higher in patients with airflow obstruction and correlated weakly but significantly with worse lung function, a little more strongly in women. Each predicted hyperresponsiveness moderately well, while the alveolar measure predicted nothing. Pairing the standard breath measure with a small-airway function value lifted accuracy to an area under the curve of 0.895 in the reported analysis. The authors advise cautious, combined use.
pmc-13314745:
Adham do Amaral e Castro and co-workers present three cases of a rare cartilage tumor in the hand, in a 2026 journal article. Soft tissue chondroma grows from cartilage cells away from bone and is benign, but it can be mistaken for worse growths.

Imaging does the heavy lifting in spotting it, the authors note. A soft tissue mass with no tie to nearby bone is the key sign. Chalky or bony specks often show inside, though they are not required for the call. The three hand cases were worked up with X-ray, ultrasound, CT, and MRI, and checked under the microscope and by eye after removal. By setting out the shared clinical, scan, and tissue traits, the report helps doctors name this rare lump with more confidence.
pmc-13315345:
Mark R. Bauter and co-authors report safety testing in 2026 for TruCBN, a purified form of cannabinol made to be nearly free of THC. Cannabinol forms as CBD and THC break down, and it is being studied for sleep and other uses, so its oral safety needed checking in animals first.

Male and female rats got daily oral doses of 0, 100, 200, or 400 milligrams per kilogram for 14 days and for 90 days under good laboratory practice rules. No harmful effects appeared in signs, weight, food intake, behavior, blood tests, or tissue checks. The 90-day work supports a no-harm level of 400 milligrams per kilogram per day.
pmc-13316645:
Changsheng Chen and co-authors set out, in a 2026 food study, to improve chickpea protein isolate by attaching sugar groups with help from ultrasound. Chickpea protein is rich and well balanced, but it whips and holds emulsions poorly, which limits its use in factory foods.

The study design pairs an ultrasound pretreatment with the sugar-attachment reaction. It then reads the changed protein at several levels: chemical shape, everyday functions such as foaming and mixing, and behavior where oil meets water. The approach is green, since the reaction runs on heat alone without harsh solvents, though the team notes care is needed to limit unwanted browning products. Results guide makers of plant protein foods toward steadier, more useful ingredients.
pmc-13316845:
Nataleya Felix and Shweta Nagesh compared, in a 2026 bench study, clear teeth aligners made by direct 3D printing against the classic heat-formed kind. Thirteen planned treatment stages were turned into 39 aligners across three groups, then scanned and laid over the starting model.

Direct-printed aligners in TA-28 resin strayed least from the plan, beating both heat-formed polyurethane and PET-G versions at every one of nine landmarks checked. The two heat-formed groups barely differed from each other. Fit followed the same ranking. The authors say printed aligners could track planned tooth moves more faithfully, though bench precision still needs proof in real mouths, where saliva, wear, and cleaning all push back.
pmc-13317545:
Yuanqiang Li, Wenting Jiang, and Jingchen Liu ran a 2026 randomized trial on protecting the heart during keyhole colon cancer surgery in high-risk patients. Gas pressure inside the belly speeds the heart and strains it, causing silent heart injury after surgery in some patients.

A total of 270 patients split among usual care, a dexmedetomidine drip, and an esmolol drip, the last two tuned to keep heart rate between 50 and 70 beats per minute. Injury struck 20.0 percent of usual-care patients versus 7.8 percent on dexmedetomidine in the main count, a gap that just missed the strict adjusted bar, though a per-protocol check cleared it. Esmolol's dip was weaker and not significant. Heart control looked steadier on dexmedetomidine without extra low pressure.
pmc-13318245:
Souad Rebhi and colleagues report a 2026 training trial in adolescent female handball players, comparing two ways of adding work to plyometric practice over eight weeks. One group paired plyometrics with reactive agility, another with isometric exercise, and a third served as control, with twelve players in each arm.

Testing before and after covered sprinting, repeated direction changes, jumping, throwing speed, and knee extension force, plus estimates of muscle volume. The agility pairing produced the strongest gains in repeated direction change and the T-half test, while the isometric pairing improved lower limb muscle volume and maximal knee force more. Neither approach lifted sprint, throwing, or jump results beyond control, so coaches are advised to match the pairing to whether agility or maximal strength matters most.
pmc-13318545:
Giti Ghazi-Soltani leads a 2026 study of two kinase genes in Waddlia chondrophila. The bacterium lives inside host cells. It is linked to abortion in cattle and poor pregnancy outcomes in people. Most relatives in its phylum carry only one such gene.

Both genes switched on early in infection. Their protein levels peaked while the bacteria were multiplying. The first protein stayed bound to the compartment holding the bacteria. The second reached parts of the host cell. The drug AZT slowed bacterial growth and protected host cells from death. That sensitivity depended on the second gene. Its protein is therefore a likely functional target for future work.
pmc-13318645:
Yezhou Chen and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare weakness disorder. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome was the first sign of small cell lung cancer. The patient was a 73-year-old male smoker. Unusually, his tests lacked the standard calcium channel antibodies. They carried anti-SOX1 antibodies instead.

Muscle tests and symptoms supported the syndrome diagnosis. Chest scans then found a mass in the left upper lung. Doctors confirmed small cell cancer at stage T1cN3M0 (IIIB). Standard cancer treatment markedly improved his weakness. His survival has passed 36 months since diagnosis in this account. The authors urge SOX1 testing when similar weakness appears. They also back cancer risk scoring, even without the usual antibody.
pmc-13319745:
Theresa Lederer and co-authors hunt for a steady yardstick gene bit for stool tests in a 2026 study of tiny RNA marks. Such marks in stool may flag gut swelling or cancer, but results need a stable in house reference to compare against, and no agreed choice exists for stool. A three step search across separate groups was used to find one.

Early tests mixed blood and stool in set steps and screened RNA marks for those that stayed flat in all mixes. One mark held flat with near zero shift and stayed steady in groups with gut swelling and liver illness, with a large check group of 360 people in the last step. That mark may beat the older common choice for stool work.
pmc-13320245:
Marine Roux, Aurélie Miot and Damien Boutin present, in 2026, a diagnostic case of a 75-year-old woman whose migrating skin eruption revealed a pancreatic tumour. Over months she developed tiredness, weight loss and low mood alongside plaques that spread from one leg to the groin, buttocks, lower back and mouth area. The plaques expanded outward, crusted and eroded, then healed in the centre.

Skin biopsy showed dying upper skin cells, and blood tests found anaemia plus several nutrient deficiencies. Zinc and nutrition brought no improvement. Low blood sugar testing showed the body was making too much insulin, and glucagon was also raised. Scans found a large pancreatic head mass, confirmed as a neuroendocrine tumour. The eruption improved markedly within weeks of tumour-directed treatment, matching necrolytic migratory erythema.
pmc-13320345:
Jamie S. Myers wrote an editorial in 2026 on how nurses shape cancer trial work inside a national team network in the United States. Nurses fill many roles in running trials, and those with deep training also lead their own studies, chiefly on life after cancer. Group networks funded since the 1950s give those nurse leaders a shared stage across many hospitals, a role this piece spotlights.

A few leading cases show nurse scientists and advanced nurses setting study aims, lifting enrollment, and holding top posts in the network. Their work builds the proof base that guides daily survivor care, from symptom control to long term follow up. The list is a sample, not a full roll, and aims to make hidden labor visible.
pmc-13320445:
Denise AM Peeters and co-authors study missed cholesterol drugs at discharge after artery opening in a 2026 records study from the Netherlands. Fat lowering drugs are urged for all who get a heart artery stent, yet scripts still lapse, most of all in older patients. Two merged heart registries gave discharge drug lists and one year outcomes for heart attack patients with stents.

Of the large group tracked, about one in thirteen left hospital with no fat lowering drug on the list, and the share ran higher past age seventy. Those without the drugs carried more risk factors at the start and faced a far higher rate of major heart events at one year in the adjusted counts. Older patients showed the same link with higher raw rates.
pmc-13321045:
Zihan Wang and co-authors engineer yeast to make a scent compound inside its nucleus in a 2027 study. Myrcene is a valued terpene used in fragrance, flavour, and farm products, but making it in microbes is hard due to competing pathways and weak flow. The team treated the yeast nucleus as a separate workshop for the pathway.

Two strong myrcene making enzymes, from snapdragon and Norway spruce, were found by screening. Myrcene appeared only when the key enzymes sat together in the nucleus, not in the main cell body. Rebuilding the full mevalonate pathway in the nucleus and easing bottlenecks lifted the final yield to 23.4 milligrams per litre in flask culture.
pmc-13323145:
Thomas Roach, Linda de Bont and Haijun Liu introduce a journal collection on control of photosynthesis in a 2026 editorial. Light-driven electron flow must balance NADPH and ATP supply against shifting demand, so plants and algae carry layered systems to tune redox balance under changing conditions.

Four featured studies examine proton motive force, bicarbonate chemistry, redox-sensitive enzymes and carbon dioxide responsive respiration. Together they touch photoprotection, energy efficiency and carbon gain, and they expose limits in current models and measures. One review casts proton motive force as a central regulator linking energy and redox balance. The editors frame the set against the low efficiency ceiling seen in most crops.
pmc-13323245:
Xiaoli Zhang and co-authors map which pregnancy complications cluster together, in a 2026 study of women who gave birth at Shanghai First Maternity and Infant Hospital between January 2023 and November 2025. Their set held 15,773 women with a mean age near 31 years.

Anaemia in pregnancy was the most common pregnancy complication and postpartum haemorrhage the most common delivery complication in their counts. Network analysis placed gestational diabetes at the centre, with the strongest links in the web, and its pairing with gestational hypertension gave the strongest association rule. Networks for older and younger mothers did not differ significantly. The authors aim the map at prevention planning for linked conditions.
pmc-13324845:
Bo Yuan and co-authors build a smart implant coating to help weak osteoporotic bones heal in a 2026 study. Fracture sites in such bone are acidic, oxygen-poor, and full of reactive oxygen, which traps immune cells in an angry state.

Their coating, called CALM, pairs a calcium-aluminum layered mineral with manganese oxide. The mineral base dissolves to buffer acid, while the oxide mops up reactive oxygen and releases helpful oxygen. That reset let macrophages shift from the inflammatory M1 state to the reparative M2 state and restored their energy machinery. In rats with osteoporotic fractures, coated implants sped bone regrowth. Gene and protein checks point to the PI3K and Akt pathway at work.
pmc-13325145:
Hatice Asri and Serap Mert build alginate microcapsules that release the antioxidant quercetin slowly in a 2026 formulation study. Two protected amino acids, Fmoc-tyrosine and Fmoc-proline, were added to toughen the capsule walls.

Electrospraying plus calcium cross-linking gave beads averaging 187 micrometres for plain alginate, 154 with Fmoc-tyrosine, and 131 with Fmoc-proline. Spectra confirmed the additives inside the walls. At body-like pH, plain capsules finished release within 7 hours, while hybrids stretched release to 24 hours. The hybrids also kept their round shape for 16 hours where plain beads eroded by hour six. Electron images showed denser, less porous hybrid surfaces.
pmc-13325445:
Brendan T. Fuller and colleagues watch kinase signaling inside breast cancer cells as a growth factor drifts past in a 2026 study. Tumors bathe cells in uneven chemical gradients, yet most lab setups flood cells all at once.

A simple chip builds steady diffusion gradients with no pumps or pressure flow. Cells carrying a glowing Akt reporter lit up in staggered waves that matched the delivery rate of epidermal growth factor. A threshold dose was needed to switch Akt on, and crowded cells needed more. Modeling from measured values predicted single-cell patterns well. Both switch-on and switch-off speeds tracked how fast the dose changed, not just its level.
pmc-13325645:
Weixian Chen and co-authors show that blocking one enzyme speeds long bone growth and fracture repair in a 2026 study. The enzyme, soluble epoxide hydrolase, can be stalled by the drug TPPU.

In newborn mice, TPPU lengthened long bones and reshaped the growth plate cartilage layers. It also woke septoclasts, the cells that clear cartilage, raising their MMP9 and FABP5 signals near the plate. Cell pairing tests showed vessel cells passing a HIF-1α cue that switched on Notch signaling in stem cells. At fracture sites, treatment drew more septoclasts and sped healing. The enzyme joins the target list for bone repair drugs.
pmc-13326045:
Xiaowei Hao and a large team mine transplant registry data for urinary cancers after kidney transplant in a 2026 study. Cancer after transplant is a leading cause of death in recipients, and urinary tumors are rising.

United States registry records covered 268,606 recipients transplanted from 2000 to 2019. Kidney cancer appeared in 0.77 percent, prostate cancer in 1.20 percent of male recipients, and bladder cancer in 0.32 percent of the group. These cancers caused large shares of deaths, reaching 50.4 percent among bladder cancer cases. Five-year survival ranked prostate cancer best at 93.3 percent and bladder cancer worst at 81.0 percent. Tailored screening per cancer type is advised.
pmc-13327345:
Gyumin Kang and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on how hard aerobic exercise changes sugar handling in the blood. A small side route for glucose, the hexosamine pathway, can weaken insulin action when it runs too high. The team asked whether training set by each animal's peak oxygen use would calm that route.

Twelve male mice were split into a resting group and a training group that exercised for eight weeks at about 65.72 percent of peak oxygen use, with blood compounds profiled by mass spectrometry afterward. Eight N-acetyl compounds fell in trained mice, matching lower activity in amino sugar pathways. Results link intense training to a quieter hexosamine route, which may help protect insulin sensitivity.
pmc-13327545:
Tim Thomas and colleagues test what gene-regulating enzymes actually do in mouse embryos in a 2026 study. KAT6A and KAT6B add acetyl marks to histones and overlap heavily during development, and losing KAT6A causes bone pattern shifts, heart defects, and failure to form blood stem cells. The team asked whether the marking action itself explains those effects.

Mice whose enzymes kept their shape but lost marking power fared better than mice missing KAT6A outright. Mutants still showed heart wall defects and weaker blood stem cell activity, but bone pattern and the aortic arch formed normally, and hitting both enzymes worsened matters only partly. The proteins thus do work beyond their chemical marking role.
pmc-13327745:
Eva Lengyelova and colleagues work out the right dose for a new prostate cancer scan tracer in a 2026 phase I sub-study. The tracer, 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA, targets a prostate marker and lasts longer in the body than standard tracers, at 12.7 hours against under two hours, which may reveal smaller spots. Thirty men with untreated, confirmed prostate cancer took part.

Each man received 100, 150, or 200 MBq and had whole-body scans two to four hours later, and blinded readers graded image usefulness and quality. Rebuilt images let readers compare doses within the same person as well. The 200 MBq dose earned the highest mean usefulness score, guiding the activity level carried into clinical use.
pmc-13329245:
Yameng Xu and co-authors test whether common anaesthetic gases help nerve regrowth in rats in a 2026 study. Earlier work hinted that isoflurane at a higher dose aided repair after a cut sciatic nerve. Here 12-week-old male Lewis rats had nerve cut and repair, then joined control or gas groups.

Groups received isoflurane, sevoflurane, or desflurane for 1 hour on three days in a row, starting soon after surgery. Checks at 12 weeks covered muscle signals, force, muscle weight, and fibre counts. Desflurane stood out: fibre numbers and myelin width rose, and specific muscle force improved. The authors call for dose and mechanism studies to confirm whether desflurane can protect healing nerves.
pmc-13329545:
Menpara Krishna Kishorbhai and team systematically reviewed keyhole versus robot surgery across common procedures. Their 2026 review notes that keyhole surgery changed work by cutting surgery trauma, after-surgery pain, and healing time against open methods. Old-style keyhole limits in tool bend and sight drove robot help uptake. The review pulled together comparison studies from 2015 to 2025 in adults, ending with eleven studies in qualitative review.

Data pulled covered surgery-time results such as surgery time, blood loss, hospital stay, snags, switch, return, and reoperation. Cancer results covered edge status, lymph node haul, return, and survival. Function results spanned urinary, sexual, and bowel function, kidney keeping, and healing measures. The review aims to mark zones of edge, tie, and trade-off between robot and keyhole methods across fields. It gives surgeons and systems a comparison map for picking method by procedure and result priority, not tech alone.
pmc-13330545:
Mauricio G. Mateu reviews how mechanical force shapes virus biology in a 2026 article. Viruses are solid particles that bend, resist, and sometimes break under force, and those traits may aid survival. Atomic force microscopy now lets researchers probe virus stiffness and strength at fine scale.

Some viruses have evolved to withstand force in nature, while others use force during infection steps, the review notes. Force tools also reveal virus structure, motion, and function in ways other methods miss. Mateu argues that mechanical traits count as adaptive features shaped by selection, much like traits in larger organisms. Findings feed into medicine and nanotechnology design, from drug carriers to new materials.
pmc-13331645:
Nichola Cooper and colleagues present 2026 survey results on life with immune thrombocytopenia, a condition in which low platelets raise bleeding risk. The ITP World Impact Survey 2.0 asked 1018 patients and 431 doctors in fifteen countries about symptoms, daily life, and care. About one third of patients said the disease hit daily tasks and family or social life hard, and just over half said it hit emotional well-being hard. Nearly all patients had received treatment, most often steroids.

Patients and doctors largely agreed on symptoms and goals, yet fatigue stood out: far more patients than doctors called it common and troubling. About one quarter said they would have picked a different treatment, and two thirds wished to limit time on drugs or avoid lifelong use. The survey presses for shared choices that weigh quality of life alongside platelet counts.
pmc-13333345:
Misha M. Madhavan and a large team tested whether a large language model can help predict healthy eating scores, in a 2026 study of Indian college students. AI tools are spreading into nutrition research, but their worth for forecasting behavior from survey data was unproven.

The team surveyed 914 undergraduates at agricultural universities between December 2024 and February 2025 and scored their eating behavior with a standard scale. Inside a ChatGPT-4o assisted workflow, the model generated predicted scores under several training and test splits. Predictions drifted closer to the real survey scores as the training share grew, and with enough training data the predicted means no longer differed significantly from the observed ones. The drivers of healthy eating the model named also matched earlier literature. The authors judge such tools fit for exploratory prediction when data are plentiful, while urging larger and more varied datasets.
pmc-13334745:
Chen Sun and colleagues study 2026 how career assets shape future work self-salience among Chinese trade students. Future work self-salience is critical for trade college students navigating the school-to-work transition, yet research on distinct profiles of career resources shaping students' agency in envisioning professional identities has been limited. The study aimed to identify latent groups based on configurations of psychological, identity, and social career assets, and to examine differences in future work self-salience across groups.

The study involved 1,093 first- and second-year trade college students in China. Latent Profile Analysis in Mplus classified career asset groups, the BCH method examined differences in future work self-salience across subgroups, and relative mediation analysis tested the mediating role of personal growth initiative. The work gives educators a profile-based view of which asset mixes support a vivid future work self, and where growth initiative carries the effect.
pmc-13335945:
Siyuan Cai and co-authors built a stretchable wound zipper that closes injuries along several axes in a 2026 device study. Standard closure tools pull in one direction only and cannot adapt to awkward wound shapes, limiting personalized care.

The device is woven from electrothermally driven shape memory alloy lattices arranged hierarchically, giving six axes of stretch and smartphone-programmed contraction. Force adjusts from zero to 0.494 MPa with a response near 1.73 seconds, fitting varied wound geometries. In rats, it closed linear wounds almost instantly and improved circular wound healing by 35.91 percent over controls. Tissue analysis showed the programmed pulling encouraged blood vessel regrowth, surface re-covering, and collagen remodeling. The work points toward closures prescribed to the wound rather than the other way round.
pmc-13336445:
Gwangsik Kim and JinHyeok Cha looked at lithium fluoride's role in the protective skin of lithium metal batteries in a 2026 article. Lithium metal anodes promise top-tier storage, but the interphase where metal meets electrolyte keeps failing.

LiF-rich interphases are the popular fix because lithium fluoride blocks electrons and halts runaway electrolyte decay. The authors argue the field has fixated on how much LiF is present, when arrangement matters more: nanoscale structure, spatial spread, and the boundaries where LiF meets other interphase ingredients govern performance. They compare interphases grown in place from fluorinated salts, additives, and solvents with lab-made coatings applied beforehand. Reframing LiF as a nanostructured building block points designers toward shaping its grains and interfaces, not just its quantity.
pmc-13336545:
Febin Ashraf and Vivek K. Bharti describe a 2026 case report of a one-year-old boy born with tight bands around his fingers, missing digits, and a turned-in right foot. The child had fused fingers on one foot and no clear face, nerve, or fluid-swelling problems. Doctors sorted the limb changes using Patterson's classification system.

The diagnosis was amniotic band syndrome, also called the ADAM complex. In this rare, non-inherited condition, a torn sac in the womb is thought to wrap strands around the growing baby. Effects range from shallow rings to lost limbs. Reports like this one help doctors spot the pattern early and plan care for affected children.
pmc-13337445:
Yazi Zhao and co-authors hunt risk factors for breathlessness caused by the blood thinner ticagrelor in a 2026 study. The side effect troubles many heart patients on the drug after acute coronary syndrome. The team enrolled 102 patients on ticagrelor plus aspirin, 23 who developed the breathlessness and 79 who did not, and measured drug and metabolite levels by chromatography.

Patients with breathlessness had higher peak ticagrelor levels in their blood. Two other measures ran lower in that group: the lactate dehydrogenase level and the ratio of active metabolite to parent drug. Each factor held up as an independent risk signal in regression models. Blood testing could flag patients likely to struggle with this common, adherence-threatening side effect.
pmc-13339645:
Maria Izabel Muniz and colleagues calculate mismatch strength in DNA-RNA hybrids in a 2026 study. Such hybrids arise in transcription and gene editing, and a wrong pair that binds strongly can cause CRISPR off-target cuts. Melting data fed a mesoscopic model of bonds and stacking.

Only the dT-rG mismatch showed strong hydrogen bonding, even above a correct dT-rA pair in the reported estimates. Other mismatches gained modest support from stacking alone. That strength explains why dT-rG edits almost like a perfect match in CRISPR tests. Editors screening guide sequences should treat this single mismatch as a serious off-target risk.
pmc-13341545:
Water on the brain after head injury is reviewed by Bruno Splavski and Dario Muzevic in a 2026 narrative review paired with a case series. Post-traumatic hydrocephalus complicates recovery from brain injury, driven by disturbed spinal fluid flow, inflammation, bleeding, and sometimes skull-opening surgery.

In their center's year of cases, 20 of 95 injured patients (21.05%) developed the illness, often with enlarged ventricles and raised pressure. Acute subdural hematoma appeared in 14 of those 20. Care spans close testing, drainage or shunting, and watching for leaks, blockages, and infections, making follow-up as demanding as the first operation.
pmc-13342045:
A newer sedative looks gentler for gut endoscopy, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis by Yuxiao Kong and colleagues. Eight trials with 2,455 patients compared remimazolam against midazolam and propofol for gastrointestinal endoscopy sedation, from databases searched to January 2026.

Remimazolam cut low blood pressure risk (RR 0.59), slow heart rate (RR 0.42), apnea (RR 0.51), and oxygen desaturation (RR 0.20) relative to the older drugs. Injection pain also dropped sharply (RR 0.20). With rapid onset and brief action, the drug's profile suits busy endoscopy units, though the authors present it as favorable rather than definitively superior.
pmc-13343445:
Xinyu Du and colleagues talked in 2026 about bendable organic crystals for flexible light devices and tiny photonics. Ordered molecules give these crystals strong potential, and self bending plus controlled curvature have improved, yet many bend tricks still need hand work or outside triggers that are slow and imprecise. Bending by force often causes lasting structural harm and loss of light performance.

Those limits block real use and factory scale use in high end devices and joined systems. The talk maps bend routes, harm routes, and design routes toward crystals that bend back without losing light function. Bendable crystal devices could enable wearable photonics and compact light circuits.
pmc-13343845:
Lena Friebel and co-authors dissect cannibalism inside Bacillus subtilis biofilms in 2026. One cell group poisons siblings with three toxins, SDP, SKF, and EPE, eating the remains to delay spore formation, yet how the toxins divide that work across a colony stayed unclear.

Mutants missing each toxin or its self-protection were mapped with light reporters, flow cytometry, colony sampling, and mass spectrometry imaging. The toxins appear in distinct, partly overlapping zones and lean on each other's placement. Losing EPE or SDP immunity wrecked colony shape, and losing all three shrank colonies into wrinkled, over-sporulating mats. Ordered self-killing, the team shows, sculpts the whole biofilm.
pmc-13344045:
Tingting Xia and Andrea Cimarelli review interferon-induced transmembrane proteins in 2026, a family famous for blocking viruses at the cell membrane. These small proteins stiffen and reshape membranes so enveloped viruses cannot fuse, yet the same family keeps surfacing in cancer growth, survival, and spread.

The review gathers the scattered roles assigned to IFITM1, IFITM2, and IFITM3 across virology and tumor biology and offers one lens for all of them: control of membrane behavior. By remodeling the cell surface protein set and bending signaling pathways, one membrane trick may explain both virus blocking and cancer effects. The frame gives researchers a shared way to judge new claims about this family.
pmc-13345845:
Qianwen Joyce Yu and Si-Jia Sun study how small-animal veterinarians in China build professional identity around the clash between business and care in a 2026 Q-method study. Thirty employed vets sorted 42 statements about emotional labor, and interviews afterward explained their most extreme choices.

Three identity paths emerged, together explaining 58 percent of the sorting variance. Pragmatic service providers treat money calls as survival and detach to cope. Conflicted caregivers feel moral distress when budgets shrink care below their ideals. Resilient integrators treat limits as design constraints and keep learning while holding ethical lines. Training and support, the authors argue, should differ by path rather than assuming one struggling vet fits all.
pmc-13346045:
Agnieszka Jaff, Mia Folke, and Annica Kristoffersson study screen design for do-it-yourself physical ability tests in 2026. Digital self-assessment promises cheaper checks than clinic testing. It works only if people perform and grade movements correctly. The team iterated six prototypes with 24 working-age adults thinking aloud through a tempo-guided chair squat.

Recurring breakdowns piled up: tempo cues got misread, right-versus-wrong form boundaries stayed fuzzy, counters lost track of repetitions, visual guidance vanished mid-movement, and safety setup notes were skipped. Self-grades drifted from researcher grades as a result. The authors distill transferable design principles, framing self-assessment as a layered task taxing mind and body at once.
pmc-13346845:
Ha-Eun Choi and colleagues measure what keeps a milled plastic crown seated on a titanium abutment, in a two-phase lab study from 2026. The work varied blasting of the abutment, how fully the screw hole was filled, and treatment of the crown inner surface, then aged each sample before a pull-out test.

Blasting the abutment raised retention by a mean of 33.71 N over untreated pieces in the reported comparison, and partial hole filling beat full filling by a smaller margin. For the crown itself, blasting gave the highest hold while a primer with MDP gave the lowest. Microscope views matched that split, showing smooth primer surfaces and rough blasted ones.
pmc-13347245:
