Nabiha El Abdi and colleagues wrote in 2026 about limited access to blinatumomab in Morocco, a powerful immunotherapy for relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The drug, which directs T cells against CD19 on leukaemia cells, achieves high rates of deep remission and improves survival in trials, yet many Moroccan patients still receive older chemotherapy.

The editorial traces the gap to cost, restricted supply, and regulatory delays that slow adoption in middle-income countries. It argues that evidence alone does not change practice when procurement, pricing, and approval systems lag. Closing that gap, the authors urge, requires coordinated action by regulators, payers, and suppliers so that proven immunotherapy reaches patients beyond wealthy health systems.
pmc-13347345:
Basil Raju Karimadom and co-authors model a Fenton-like reaction on an iron surface with first-principles calculations, in a study from 2026. Such reactions clean polluted water by turning hydrogen peroxide into reactive hydroxyl groups. The team used spin-aware density methods on a clean Fe(110) face in water to follow each step.

Peroxide split on its own at the surface, and crowding the surface with hydroxyl groups weakened iron-oxygen bonds and partly oxidised deeper iron layers in the reported model. Surface hydroxyl proved far less reactive than free hydroxyl in water. The calculation gave a reduction value of only 0.15 V at high pH. That low value helps explain slower pollutant breakdown.
pmc-13347945:
Rebecca Signer and colleagues show how body weight changes the way gene variants steer gene activity, in a study from 2026. Genome scans link variants to disease but ignore setting. So weight was treated as a setting across tissues, hunting variants whose control of nearby genes strengthens or fades as body mass index rises, with brain and gut in focus.

Weight-linked control sites turned up across tissues, while weight alone acted mainly in hormone tissues. Cell type, enhancer marks, and inflammatory signals helped explain the pattern in the reported models. Adding weight-by-variant terms predicted gene activity better and surfaced more disease genes that held up on retest than variant-only models, arguing for context in gene hunting.
pmc-13348045:
Serena N. Gilmore and co-authors studied in 2026 blocks to healthy eating in adults with steatotic liver disease at a safety-net health system. Diet change is key to managing this liver illness. Yet it is hard to sustain. Low income shapes food access, cooking time, and knowledge in ways that bland advice often skips.

Surveying 344 adults from early 2020 to early 2024, the team scored unhealthy eating from food frequency. They tested which blocks, from cost and access to habits and support, tracked with higher scores. Age, sex, race, obesity, and exercise were allowed for. Median age was 53. Most faced real-world limits. The findings help clinics aim at the blocks that matter most for their own patients.
pmc-13348245:
Zihan Wei and co-authors built in 2026 scalable high-temperature superconducting diodes from natural Josephson junctions inside layered cuprate crystals. Such diodes let current flow with no resistance in one way only. They promise lossless electronics. Yet joining high-temperature use with workable making has proved hard.

Using Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8 crystals, the team set the number of stacked junctions to tune one-way flow. Single-surface junctions gave peak efficiency and programmable memory states at zero field. A model pins the effect to geometry-driven asymmetry in the current-phase link. The lithography-friendly platform brings lossless diodes closer to real circuits. It also aids tests on broken time-reversal symmetry.
pmc-13348445:
Shane Sinclair and colleagues test a compassion training program for care staff in Canada, in a feasibility study from 2026. The EnACT program ran nine months across two long-term care homes and two hospices from 2023 to 2024. A total of 163 providers took part. A total of 634 patients rated felt compassion on a set questionnaire.

Nearly all feasibility targets were met, learner satisfaction stayed high, and trained staff gained in fulfilment and confidence, with confidence holding nine months later in the reported results. Patients of trained staff reported more felt compassion one month after training than control patients, and power sums support a full randomised trial as the next step.
pmc-13348845:
Momoko Hamano and colleagues hunt heart failure risk variants in Japan. Their study appeared in 2026. It works through vessel gene switches. A trans-omics plan layered several data types. Genome scan hits from Japanese patients came first. Control elements from vessel lining cells came next. Factor binding maps joined the stack. Heart failure mechanisms stay thinly mapped in this group. Rising cases with ageing make the gap urgent.

Two candidate variants stood out from the stack. One sits in the promoter of CDKN1A. The other sits in an enhancer. That enhancer links to two downstream genes. Both genes are known birth heart disease genes. The flags are only starting points. Lab checks must follow them. Such checks can show how vessel control tilts hearts. Failure may be the end of that tilt.
pmc-13349945:
Shiyang Li and co-authors probed in 2026 how p62 protein complexes drive immune evasion in gastric cancer cells. They switch on PD-L1 through NF-kappaB signalling and spark T-cell death. Autophagy has been linked to PD-L1 control. Yet the adaptor complexes linking p62 to NF-kappaB and their functional impact on T cells were incompletely mapped.

In MKN45 gastric cancer cells, the team used autophagy and NF-kappaB blockers plus p62 knockdown. They measured PD-L1 and path molecules by PCR and protein assays. They then tested effects on T-cell growth, death, and cytokine release. Complexes of p62 with TRAF6 and RIP1 fired the path and raised PD-L1, weakening T-cell replies. Blocking this axis could restore immune attack against gastric tumours that now shield themselves.
pmc-13350045:
Brandon M. Chelette and colleagues studied a hormone signal behind cancer fatigue in a 2026 mouse experiment. Fatigue in cancer may arise as tumours and muscles compete for energy, a strain worsened when chemotherapy harms cell power plants.

The hormone FGF21 helps tissues adjust their fuel use under stress, working through a helper protein called beta-klotho. Blocking that helper with a peptide made male mice run less on their wheels, and it deepened the running drop caused by the chemotherapy drug cisplatin. Measuring the hormone in blood and liver of tumour-bearing and treated mice set the scene. The results tie this pathway to activity loss in cancer.
pmc-13350345:
Peiyu Lu and co-authors traced where the immune messenger interleukin-21 comes from inside colorectal tumours in a 2026 single-cell study. IL21 helps antitumour immunity, but its source and control programme in bowel cancer were murky.

Gene data from tumour-infiltrating T cells showed IL21 made mainly by a small CD4 T cell group marked by another messenger, CXCL13, a pattern confirmed in treated patient samples and tissue staining. Mouse tumour tissue grown with added IL21 revealed which genes it switches. Knowing exactly which cells supply this signal could help design immunotherapies that recruit or imitate them.
pmc-13350545:
Yoshiya Yamauchi and co-authors tested in 2026 whether the lactate dehydrogenase-to-albumin ratio at treatment start forecasts survival in metastatic or recurrent pancreatic cancer getting gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel. Forecast sorting matters when picking first-line therapy for unresectable disease. Yet plain, objective blood markers are scarce.

In a single-centre look-back cohort of patients treated from 2015 to 2024, base line ratio was tallied from labs drawn within seven days pre-therapy and linked to survival outcomes. The ratio joins tumour-linked activity, mirrored by lactate dehydrogenase, with host food and inflammation state, mirrored by albumin. A trustworthy ratio could help clinicians counsel patients and sort trials with no costly gene testing.
pmc-13350745:
Hua Wu and co-authors traced in 2026 how cultivated land evolved across terrain gradients in the Hehuang Valley. This valley sits on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. It is a typical agro-pastoral zone where land use shapes livelihoods and ecology. Rational land care needs to know not only how much farmland shifts, but where, on which slopes, and toward what new uses.

Long-term high-detail land use data were joined with terrain gradient work and kernel density mapping. A PLUS model and standard deviation ellipse theory were also used. Shifts from 1980 to 2020 were tracked. Cultivated land fell by a net 119 square kilometres. It mostly turned to grassland, water, and built-up areas, with higher density in river valleys.
pmc-13351645:
Jenny L Wales leads a 2026 systematic review of wearable tools for measuring sitting and low movement in people with mild memory loss or dementia. Time spent sedentary is a changeable health risk, and it may be higher in people with cognitive problems. Self-reports can mislead, so the review focused on device-based studies.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched five databases to January 2025 for studies of adults aged 50 years or older living at home or in care homes. Records were checked for how much sedentary time devices found, what patterns appeared, and how sound the methods were. The review maps gaps that future device studies in this group should address.
pmc-13351845:
Xiaoyue Li and colleagues tested in 2026 how dietary arginine shapes growth and testicular maturation at different life stages in male swimming crabs, an important aquaculture species. Arginine supports growth and reproduction, yet optimal levels for juvenile versus adult crabs were unclear.

Six diets with graded arginine from 1.89 to 3.80 percent were fed to 180 juvenile males for twenty weeks, with sampling at week thirteen for juveniles and week twenty for adults. At the juvenile stage, the 2.27 percent diet gave significantly higher final weight, weight-gain rate, and specific growth rate than control, with testicular development and apoptosis patterns also shifting by dose and stage. The results guide stage-specific feed formulation for crab farming.
pmc-13354445:
Raseel Almutairi and colleagues mapped the most-cited literature on colonic diverticular disease, in a 2026 bibliometric study. No earlier work had charted the papers that shaped diagnosis and care for this common gut condition. The team pulled the top 50 cited articles from the Web of Science Core Collection and coded each by citations, year, journal, country, design, and evidence level.

The leading papers span 1953 to 2020, clustering in 2010 to 2015, with the United States behind 58 percent and few papers from low- and middle-income countries. Retrospective cohorts, reviews, and guidelines dominate, at mostly level 5 and level 1 evidence. Keyword and collaboration maps show where the field has crowded and where global gaps remain.
pmc-13354945:
Stephanie Ji Chen and co-authors compared 12 large language models in 2026 on pulling clear facts from lung clinic notes. The notes covered 100 patients with interstitial lung disease, a group of illnesses that scar the lungs. Models answered ten yes-or-no questions per note, and three lung doctors set the standard answers by agreement.

Seven models matched the doctors, at about 96 percent correct, while five did far worse. Each note took one to two seconds per call, at a tiny cost next to human work. Sorting patients into disease classes proved harder, with lower scores. The authors see these tools as a fast aid for registries and study screening.
pmc-13355245:
Zhenzhen Yang and co-authors compared early versus delayed repair surgery in 2026 for boys whose urethra was torn in a pelvic fracture. Timing is debated, and long-term data are scarce. Their single-center study covered 48 boys treated between 2001 and 2023, with follow-up of about nine years on average.

Fifteen boys had repair within ten days and 33 after at least three months. Rates of narrowing, leakage, erection problems, and repeat surgery did not differ clearly between groups. Overall, more than half had some complication. Because the early group was small, real gains or harms cannot be ruled out, and the authors call for larger joint studies.
pmc-13355745:
Yuting Guo and co-authors combined several data types in 2026 to study inflammation in preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy illness marked by high blood pressure. Placental inflammation is central to the illness, but its triggers are unclear. The team paired single-cell placenta data with gut microbe and chemical profiles, and used machine learning across patient subgroups.

Bacteria-linked inflammation stood out in every subgroup, while twin, single, early, and late cases each added their own patterns, shaped also by fetal sex. Gut profiles showed more bacteria that make an inflammatory toxin and fewer helpful microbes. The authors link gut imbalance to the placental program and propose it as a research lead.
pmc-13356045:
Julian Arroyave and co-authors ran three pig feeding trials in 2026 on a new insoluble fiber source for nursery pigs. Fiber was long seen as a drawback in young pig diets, but firm stools matter for health after weaning. Nearly a thousand weaned pigs ate diets with varied fiber levels, durations, and formulation styles, then shared a common diet.

Fiber did not change overall growth in any trial, though high levels in one trial tended to trim daily gain and feed efficiency. Stool dry matter rose with fiber at day ten in all trials and at day twenty-four in one. The authors conclude the fiber firms stools without hurting overall growth.
pmc-13358745:
Mohammad Faraz Omair and co-authors present a 2026 review on how diabetes harms the heart and blood vessels. They argue the damage follows one linked path, which they call the gluco-vascular injury axis. High blood sugar is only the start: insulin resistance, unhealthy blood fats, and inflammation injure vessel walls, then the heart muscle itself.

The review joins lab, animal, and patient evidence into a single chain from vessel injury to heart failure. Steps along the chain include stiff arteries, harm to tiny vessels, and scarring of the heart. Laying the steps out in order aims to help doctors see where treatment can break the chain earliest.
pmc-13358845:
Tess Gillham and co-authors share lessons on skin side effects from a lung cancer drug pair in a 2026 paper. The pair, amivantamab plus lazertinib, beats the standard single drug for a mutated form of lung cancer, but it often causes harsh rashes and nail problems. The COCOON trial tested a skin care plan meant to blunt those effects.

Gillham and co-authors set the pair's gains against the older options and explain what the skin plan involved and how well it worked. Practical guidance like this matters because side effects that patients can see and feel often decide whether they stay on a treatment that is working.
pmc-13359945:
Roberto S. Accolla and co-authors review a viral protein behind a severe leukemia in a 2026 paper. HTLV-1 was the first human cancer-causing retrovirus found, and it leads to adult T-cell leukemia-lymphoma. Two viral products drive the disease. This review focuses on the quieter one, HBZ, a protein that works even when the virus hides from the immune system.

The authors trace HBZ's discovery and cell biology, and gather new findings on its tricks. Surprisingly, it reaches into basic machinery that governs how RNA messages are spliced and how long they survive. Understanding that reach may expose weak points for future drugs against this hard leukemia.
pmc-13360545:
Karnika Singh and others showed self-driven colloids in coatings, in 2026. Coatings rely on passive parts whose spatial spread cannot be guided, capping working traits. Active parts that move on their own could beat settling and chem gradients during film making.

By adding active Janus colloids into mixes, the team showed build-up at both top and bottom coating edges, weighing fuel depletion times against evaporation-driven assembly. The result is a coating whose parts position themselves rather than settling randomly. Items scientists gain a route to working coatings with built internal group.
pmc-13360745:
Zvonko Antunović and co-authors tracked blood changes in sheep across late pregnancy and nursing in a 2026 study. The flock held 30 healthy adult Lika Pramenka ewes, about five years old and in their fourth nursing season. Blood was drawn 20 days before lambing and again on days 40, 70, and 100 of nursing. The sheep ate meadow hay plus a daily oat ration.

Lab work covered blood cell counts, red cell measures, minerals, and enzyme activity in the blood serum. The team found that late pregnancy and nursing clearly shifted many of these blood indicators. Such profiles give vets reference values for judging whether a ewe in these demanding stages is healthy or in trouble. They also guide feeding care when the body's needs peak.
pmc-13361245:
Mustafa Çetiner and co-authors compare anesthesia choices for stroke clot removal in a 2026 study. The procedure, mechanical thrombectomy, pulls a clot from a brain artery to restore flow. Patients may get general anesthesia or lighter conscious sedation, and which is better is still debated. The team reviewed anterior circulation stroke cases treated from January 2021 to March 2025.

They sorted patients by anesthesia type and then matched the groups closely so the comparison stayed fair. Success meant reopening the artery well and, more importantly, patients living independently 90 days later. Stroke care races the clock, so any edge from anesthesia choice matters. Matched real-world data like this help stroke teams settle a long-running argument in daily practice.
pmc-13361445:
Vanessa Ruiz-Esparza-Palacios led a 2026 cell study of a hereditary disease that harms the brain and eyes. Spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 comes from a stretched repeat in the ATXN7 gene, which makes a faulty protein. The team used human Müller glial cells, support cells of the retina, carrying either a normal or stretched gene version. They asked whether the faulty protein destabilizes the genome and ages the cells early.

Cells with the stretched protein showed a disordered nuclear shell, marks of DNA damage response, small extra nuclei, and shortened chromosome ends. Each sign points to genomic instability, a known trigger of early cell aging. Aged cells were already seen in the brains of mice with this disease. The work ties the faulty protein to a chain from DNA harm to early senescence.
pmc-13361545:
Catarina Fragoso and co-authors reviewed nursing work that builds health literacy in the young in a 2026 paper. Health literacy means understanding health information well enough to act on it. It shapes habits and self-care across a whole life, so building it early matters. The team gathered studies of nurse-led programs for children and teens.

The approaches change with age. Storytelling suits small children, playful lessons suit older children, and group or digital tools suit teens. Most programs run in schools and focus on staying healthy, avoiding disease, and managing illness. The authors say nurses are key players in this work across clinics and communities. They call for standard measures and long-term studies to prove lasting impact.
pmc-13363045:
Liana Beresescu and colleagues report a 2026 survey of 202 practicing dentists on how well modern preventive dentistry reaches daily practice. Preventive care, from fluoride use to early, gentle repair methods, is well established in guidance, yet habits vary. The anonymous survey, run over eight months, asked about knowledge, chairside choices, and use of formal risk systems for tooth decay.

Most dentists knew the core ideas well, above all remineralization and fluoride, and used preventive steps often. Use was rarely structured, though: formal risk checks were routine for about seven in ten, but the standard CAMBRA system was routine for only about two in ten. Extra training went with more preventive tool use. The authors call for simple, structured systems that fit real clinic time.
pmc-13363445:
Jenny Nahman Sichin and colleagues report a 2026 records study on tube feeding in patients kept on breathing machines for the long term. Such patients face high malnutrition risk. The team grouped patients by feeding path: staying on a high-protein formula, switching to one, switching away, or moving to a calorie-dense formula. Weight, blood protein, and albumin were compared at the start and up to six months later.

Weight rose in every group, with the largest gain in patients who switched to the high-protein formula. Albumin, a blood marker of nutrition, rose clearly only in that switch group, while the dense formula showed a near gain in total protein. The authors call for planned trials with shared protocols to pin down the best feeding path.
pmc-13364745:
Jin Kim and co-workers put forth in 2026 a frame for liver care thought they call data fed gut feel. Liver ills shift over time and mix hard facts with soft signs. Pure score use can miss the tale a case tells, while pure gut feel can drift.

Their frame trains gut feel with fast feed back from data, so skill grows case by case. Eight axes, from time span to doubt, make the play of facts and feel plain to see. The pair of authors urge schools to teach this skill and smart tools to back it, not swap it out.
pmc-13367545:
Krishnapriya Kumar and co-workers ask in 2026 if years lived with sleep breath blocks raise heart and sugar risk. The link of the ill to such harms is known, but the role of span was not. They read 279 adults with mid to harsh ill, all with lab sleep proof.

A math guess puts mid span near nineteen years, with start near age 32. High blood press, the top harm, climbs with span tiers and stays tied in full checks. No clear tie shows for kin harms. The cross cut form makes the find a lead, not a proof.
pmc-13371545:
Paula von Spreckelsen and colleagues evaluate a large online gatekeeper training to prevent youth suicide in the Netherlands in a 2026 study. Gatekeepers learn to spot signs of suicidal thoughts, start supportive talks, and refer young people to care. The training ran online from October 2022 to March 2023, reaching 8,040 formal gatekeepers such as health and school staff, plus 1,142 informal gatekeepers such as family and friends.

Knowledge and confidence rose after training, and behaviour at three months was tracked to see whether learning turned into action. The study also explores what predicts real gatekeeper behaviour and what participants describe in their own accounts. The scale shows that online training can reach a wide network quickly when youth suicide risk is rising.
pmc-13371945:
Raphaela da Costa Miranda Barbosa and co-authors measured how people swallow after throat surgery in a 2026 study. The group held 100 patients in Brazil who had part of the voice box removed for cancer. X-ray films of thin liquid sips were scored with a set method, step by step.

Many scores were off the healthy range. About one in five had unsafe swallows, one in three had a weak seal at the voice box, and three in four had food left in the throat. The counts give speech and swallow teams a firm base. They can use it to plan therapy and to warn patients what to expect.
pmc-13373845:
David Sandoval and colleagues rework how photosynthesis efficiency is modelled across ecosystems in a 2026 study. Land models have long assigned each plant type a fixed maximum quantum yield, yet leaf experiments show that yield depends on temperature. The team fitted light-response curves to global eddy-covariance carbon flux data, correcting for photorespiration, to infer ecosystem-level yields.

The temperature response followed a universal bell-shaped curve across biomes. Its peak fell as aridity rose, its optimum temperature rose with growth temperature, and its sensitivity rose as growth temperature fell. The model aligns with theory on cytochrome b6f control of light reactions. If built into land models, it should improve forecasts of how ecosystems respond to warming.
pmc-13374145:
Abiola Adeniyi and others explore community views of a gender-responsive mother health programme in western Kenya in a 2026 study. Chamas for Change offers peer support, microfinance, and health education to pregnant women over three years, and a prior trial showed gains in mother and child health. This qualitative study asked how groups themselves experienced it.

Nine focus groups and four key informant interviews between late 2017 and mid 2019 gathered 75 people across four sub-counties in Trans Nzoia County. They included pregnant women, programme members, spouses, community health promoters, and nurses. The title quotes a spouse's view that the programme brought a new light to wives' lives. The study shows how peer groups, money, and learning together can shift household and community support for mothers.
pmc-13374745:
Rupali Fuldeore and colleagues tallied what metastatic pancreatic cancer costs the US health system, in a 2026 claims analysis. The team drew adult patients diagnosed between January 2020 and December 2022 from the Merative MarketScan database, covering commercial and Medicare plans. Visits and costs were counted per person per month for a year after diagnosis.

Among 2318 patients, mean monthly costs reached 34,215 dollars commercially and 15,158 dollars under Medicare. A quarter of commercial patients and 43.2 percent of Medicare patients received no first-line treatment within 90 days. The figures expose both the heavy price of advanced pancreatic cancer and a treatment gap for older patients.
pmc-13377145:
Marzano and colleagues report early outcomes of a branched stent graft for repairing the thoracic aorta where it arches past the left subclavian artery, in 2026 vascular surgery research. The Castor device seals the aorta in Ishimaru zone 2 while a built-in branch keeps blood flowing into that arm artery, avoiding open bypass surgery. The retrospective series covers 15 consecutive elective patients treated between July 2023 and December 2025 for aneurysm, aortic dissection, or penetrating ulcer at a single Western center.

Fourteen patients achieved technical and clinical success, a rate of 93 percent for the new device. One patient needed an extra covered stent where the branch had not fully expanded. There were no access complications and no deaths within 30 days of the procedure. Mean intensive care stay was 1.2 days and hospital stay 15.3 days across the cohort. Over a mean follow-up of 13.5 months, every left subclavian branch remained open on surveillance scans.
pmc-13378145:
Soheila Alyasin and others report a fatal case of febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha-Habermann disease in a toddler in a 2026 case report. This rare, severe form of pityriasis lichenoides presents rapidly with ulcerating, necrotic skin lesions, fever, and body-wide symptoms, possibly triggered by hypersensitivity. A 15-month-old Iranian boy got fast-spreading ulceronecrotic lesions with high fever and body-wide involvement.

Skin biopsy confirmed the finding. Despite methylprednisolone, intravenous immunoglobulin, and a TNF-alpha blocker, the disease proved fatal. The authors note this as the third reported fatal childhood case and the youngest documented to date. The report highlights diagnostic difficulty, illness risk, and limited treatment options, arguing for early immunosuppressive and antimicrobial therapy in aggressive cases.
pmc-13378645:
Subhra Sulipta Jena and co-authors introduce a 2026 test, called SAFE, for detecting heart injury from a blood sample in about ten minutes. Fast diagnosis of heart and vessel disease matters, but current tests often need hospital machines and lengthy preparation. Their test reads tiny RNA molecules carried inside small parcels released by cells, called extracellular vesicles.

The method fuses small fat bubbles carrying detector probes with those parcels in raw blood plasma, helped by brief sound treatment. No parcel isolation or RNA extraction is needed. In a small pilot with 20 patients and 15 healthy people, levels of two heart-linked RNAs were higher in patients, and the test sorted the groups with high accuracy.
pmc-13380045:
S C Lam and colleagues set out a 2026 study protocol for comparing ways of checking that an N95 mask fits a health worker's face. A tight fit is essential for filtering airborne particles, so workers must pass a fit test to choose the right mask. The long-standing test has eight steps, and a shorter four-step version appeared in 2019.

Regulators say the two are equal, but solid evidence is limited, and the repeatability of the older method is unstudied. The planned study will test three mask designs on Chinese health workers with both methods. Agreement between the methods will inform policy: strong agreement would let services use either test with confidence.
pmc-13382745:
Linghao Huang and co-authors ask where gallium sits in aluminium-rich coal from the Jungar Coalfield in China, in work published in 2026. Gallium is a key metal for chips, and such coals could serve as an added source. The team studied the Permian No. 4 seam with microscopes and fine-scale chemical mapping tools.

Bulk tests linked gallium closely to aluminium oxide in most samples from the mine. Close mapping told a different story, placing gallium mainly in the organic part of the coal rather than in clay minerals. That split view helps explain how the metal built up during peat growth and where recovery efforts should look.
pmc-13383145:
Valeria Gómez's team reviewed how protein-cutting enzymes worsen dentin erosion and whether blockers help, in a 2026 systematic review. Acid softens dentin, then matrix metalloproteinases and cathepsins chew the exposed collagen network. The team searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to January 2025 under PRISMA 2020 for inhibitor studies.

Twenty-two studies qualified, mostly lab-based with some in situ and combined designs. MMP-2, MMP-8, and MMP-9 plus cathepsin K emerged consistently as the key collagen-degrading enzymes after acid challenge. Synthetic and natural inhibitors preserved dentin in these models, pointing to anti-enzyme additives for toothpastes, rinses, and restorative materials.
pmc-13383245:
Vincenz Kohler's team made rare T-shaped platinum(0) compounds and caught their platinum(I) radical species, in a 2026 chemistry study. Low-valent Pt species are proposed in many group 10 metal reactions, yet Pt(I) species are hard to observe. The team reduced a Pt(II) chloride starting compound held by a bulky PNP ligand.

Reduction gave two anionic T-shaped Pt(0) compounds, isolated as sodium and Mg contact ion pairs. Reactions with organic bromides yielded coupled products plus Pt(II) bromide and alkyl species, with outcomes tracking radical stability. In situ EPR studies captured the transient 15-electron Pt(I) metal radical, grounding a stepwise single-charge transfer mechanism.
pmc-13383945:
Takahiro Hirayama and colleagues present an imaging protocol to find the lymph vessel behind skin backflow in swelling disorders in 2026 work. Backflow into the skin is a key sign in lymphedema, but the vessel feeding it is hard to locate. The team paired dye-based lymph imaging with contrast ultrasound in patients with the condition.

The first skin spot where dye appeared and then spread marked the target for ultrasound checks. Tiny bubble contrast then traced fine channels rising from a deeper collecting vessel, with some bubbles seen leaking back into the skin live. Tracing that vessel should help surgeons plan bypass operations more precisely.
pmc-13385345:
Yue-Xuan Mu and colleagues ask whether smart health devices close felt care gaps for older adults in China in 2026 work. Data pooled three survey waves, giving 34,482 observations from 18,292 respondents across 1,277 communities. A severe gap meant needing three or more community health services without getting them.

Family support alone showed no steady link to smaller gaps in their models. Devices helped most when family support was already strong, a pattern clearest in urban residents, women, and adults in their sixties. The authors conclude that gadgets work inside supportive family and community settings, not as stand-alone fixes.
pmc-13385445:
Samira Vera-Choqqueccota and a large team link cloud-connected stem cell labs to stronger science identity in underrepresented students in 2026 work. Stem cell research usually sits inside elite institutions, shutting out many learners. Their framework joins an inducible mouse stem cell system, cheap cloud microscopes, and a validated identity scale.

High school and community college students both gained in scientific identity during the program. Students who watched real stem cells change gained more than peers using a simpler cell line, especially in competence and readiness. Gains ran strongest for Hispanic and first-generation students, which supports the model for widening access.
pmc-13385945:
Sai Prathyusha Yarra and colleagues rebuild dentures and facial features for a teenager with cleft defects in a 2026 case report. The 17-year-old had repaired bilateral cleft lip and palate, no teeth in either jaw, missing ears on both sides, and an underformed nose. Such a combined presentation is exceedingly rare, the team notes.

Conventional acrylic dentures restored the mouth, while custom silicone pieces rebuilt both ears and the nose. The ear set clipped to a spectacle frame, and color matching used a systematic pigment method. Over twelve months of visits, chewing, speech, confidence, and satisfaction all improved, the patient and guardian reported.
pmc-13386945:
Chen-Tse Lee's team ran a small trial that assigned residents by chance to test whether airway models printed in three dimensions teach flexible bronchoscopic intubation better than a standard manikin. Twenty-eight anaesthesia residents in a single centre trained on one model. They then crossed over to the other model. Their skill was scored on a rating scale, a simulator, and a trainee survey.

Scores and intubation times rose after training with either model, and simulator results did not differ much between the two groups. Trainees still rated the printed models as more effective for learning, with a small edge in survey scores, and earlier hands-on experience seemed to shape how much each resident gained. The authors present printed airways as a useful training option rather than a proven leap ahead.
pmc-13388445:
Lopez and colleagues evaluate a fluorescent probe that lights up in the presence of cadmium, a toxic heavy metal, inside cells, in 2026 chemistry research. Monitoring cadmium in organisms usually requires destroying the sample for lab analysis. The probe, built on an HNBO dye scaffold, was tested in liquid and fixed to core-shell silica nanoparticles. Tests ran in cell lines and in mussel cells, mussels being pollution bioindicators whose tissues accumulate metals from seawater at contaminated sites.

Both probe forms detected cadmium without compromising cell viability in the assays. The free probe proved better at sensing cadmium dissolved in the cytoplasm, the cell's compartment. The nanoparticle conjugate instead suited detection in the organelles where cells store metals. Used together, the pair can track both the pollutant and the nanoparticle detector in real time. Lopez presents the system as a live-cell alternative to destructive testing for environmental monitoring.
pmc-13390745:
Archana Venkatesan and colleagues report, in 2026, a breast lump long proven benign that finally proved to be a malignant phyllodes tumour. Fibroadenomas are common harmless lumps usually watched rather than removed, while transformation into a malignant phyllodes tumour is rare but changes care completely.

Over several years, multiple core-needle biopsies all returned fibroadenoma, yet the mass kept growing past seven centimetres. Removal revealed a malignant phyllodes tumour with overgrown stroma, abnormal cells, fast division, and invasive edges. Breast clinicians gain a clear lesson on the limits of needle sampling in mixed fibroepithelial lumps: steady growth should override reassuring biopsies and prompt removal. A lump that keeps on growing needs a fresh look, not one more watch-and-wait plan. In the end, size told the truth.
pmc-13391445:
Philip D Tolley and co-authors describe, in 2026, a camera-guided method for expanding the back of an infant skull without the large ear-to-ear incision. Children with several fused skull sutures need posterior vault expansion to give the brain room, relieve pressure effects, and improve head shape.

Traditional open surgery leaves a large bicoronal scar that burdens families. The endoscopic distraction approach achieves substantial volume expansion with less blood loss, shorter hospital stay, and a smaller scar burden, while limiting relapse. Paediatric neurosurgeons gain a technique account for applying minimally invasive principles, proven in single-suture cases, to harder multi-suture disease.
pmc-13391745:
Larissa Claudino Ferreira and co-authors test, in 2026, whether a common synergist can restore the power of cattle tick treatments that resistance has blunted. Rhipicephalus microplus ticks resistant to macrocyclic lactone drugs cause major economic losses, driven by indiscriminate chemical use.

The team evaluated piperonyl butoxide combined with ivermectin, eprinomectin, and moxidectin against five tick populations from Brazil's semi-arid northeast. Laboratory bioassays showed widespread resistance to the lactones alone. Farm vets gain proof on a plain point. Does the booster save drugs that fail on their own? If it does, farms can keep old tick drugs in use for far more years. That would cut costs and slow the hunt for new drugs.
pmc-13392345:
Francesca Coppi and a large team investigate, in 2026, why men fare worse than women with pulmonary hypertension complicating systemic sclerosis. The lung artery condition is a severe, life-threatening complication, and although it affects more women, men often have poorer outcomes.

The one-centre records study held 61 firm cases: fifty-two women and nine men. It set heart events, right heart strength, and length of life side by side by sex. Past data of this kind, in this group, have been thin on the ground. Joint and heart doctors gain outcome proof split by sex. It backs closer checks on the small male group. The risk in that group is all too easy to miss at a glance.
pmc-13392645:
Gulmira Kalikhanovna Murzakayeva and colleagues charted canine transmissible venereal tumour, a contagious cancer passed between dogs during mating, at a diagnostic centre in Astana, Kazakhstan, over one year from February 2024. Data from Central Asia on this tumour are scarce. Of twenty-five hundred dogs screened, four hundred twenty-five had tumour-like growths examined in depth, and twenty-three proved to have this cancer.

Males made up nearly three quarters of cases, and most dogs were young to middle-aged adults, with mixed breeds the largest group. Every case showed a fragile genital mass with bloody discharge, and over half also carried pus-forming complications. Dogs with those complications ran faster hearts and breathing, with blood counts shifted toward infection and anaemia. Growths outside the genitals were uncommon. The authors supply a baseline picture for a region where the tumour had gone largely unmapped.
pmc-13393145:
Budoor Alqinai's team reports a seventy-six-year-old man with end-stage renal disease. His prior belly blood-cleaning, troubled by repeat belly ills, led to hardening wrapping belly ills, the abdominal cocoon syndrome. Progressive nausea, throwing up, and weight loss prompted imaging showing centre-clustered small bowel loops wrapped in a thick scarred membrane.

Look-see surgery found a frozen abdomen of densely wrapped intestine, requiring extensive scar cutting and membrane removal, and lab study proved dense fibre-membrane tissue. About two months later, nausea and throwing up had resolved, diet was regular, and bowel movements were daily and formed, with activity slowly returning to baseline.
pmc-13393445:
Fengze Wu and Xiaoyi Raymond Gao built an interpretable machine learning system to forecast who will develop primary open-angle glaucoma within ten years. The system blends genetics with features a deep learning model reads from retinal photographs. Participants were free of glaucoma at the start. The strict case definition yielded a few hundred cases against thousands of controls, while a broader definition widened both groups.

Ten algorithms were benchmarked, and gradient boosting won, separating future cases from controls with strong discrimination and excellent calibration of its risk estimates. Adding genetic risk scores and image-derived features each contributed predictive value beyond ordinary clinical measures. Explanation analysis ranked the photograph score, age, genetic score, and eye pressure as the strongest signals, and a slim model using only those four nearly matched the full system. The authors pitch the approach for targeted screening.
pmc-13394545:
Suvadeep Mal leads a 2026 team that built gold specks loaded with a plant compound to attack two threats at once. One threat is triple-negative breast cancer, a fast kind with few drug targets. The other is germs that shrug off antibiotics. The team coated gold particles with morin, then added folic acid as a homing tag and chitosan as a shell.

The specks were tiny, round, and stable in tests. They soaked up harmful oxygen radicals and killed germs at low doses. Breast cancer cells took them in fast, stalled, and died, while healthy cells were spared. Computer docking backed the broad action. The authors pitch the blend as a two-front therapy.
pmc-13394745:
Qian and co-authors profile, in 2026, the metabolites carried by plasma exosomes in elderly women at different stages of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risk factors for diabetes and heart disease. They compared 20 women with the syndrome, 23 with its precursor state, and 45 healthy controls. The precursor group already differed from controls in 27 metabolites, concentrated in histidine metabolism and the tricarboxylic acid cycle, the cell's central energy loop. pmc-13396645:

pmc-13397645:

pmc-13399945:

New boards release formaldehyde, a harmful gas, for years. Four catalyst colour families were mixed into a water based polyurethane coating and applied to four wood types.

Ratios were tuned so gas breakdown and coating toughness both met basic needs. Colour shift measures and eye tracking showed how each coating changed the look of each wood. A machine learning system then learned to propose recipes matching a desired appearance and performance. The framework links air cleaning design with furniture aesthetics.
pmc-13418545:
Xin Tong and colleagues find how a plant recycling receptor boosts a growth hormone signal in roots, in a 2026 study. The receptor is called VISP1. It was first known from plant virus work. Plants that made extra VISP1 grew shorter main roots and fewer side roots, with longer root hairs. Those traits point to a stronger cytokinin response. Plants with no VISP1 responded weakly.

Cytokinin turns the VISP1 gene on through a type B regulator. VISP1 then grabs type A regulators, which act as brakes on the signal. It sends those brakes to the cell's recycling system. With the brakes gone, the signal runs stronger and roots tune their growth.
pmc-13420145:
Xin Liu and colleagues describe a sponsor-proxy model that lets a central institute unit carry the regulatory load of clinical trials while investigators keep scientific control. Academic discoveries often stall before human testing because lone researchers lack the machinery to sponsor a trial legally. Their case study comes from a cancer institute serving a 28-county area of central Pennsylvania.

That catchment holds roughly four million residents, many in rural Appalachian communities far from research centers. Most investigator-led trials there are early phase studies, the foundation work for new treatments. Natural product therapies lean hardest on this route, since companies rarely fund them. The model offers other institutes a tested template for closing the gap between lab finds and first patient tests.
pmc-13420745: Cell Biology International retracted Yousif's 2014 article on fibronectin and ovarian cancer cell spread in 2026. Editor-in-Chief Xuebiao Yao, the International Federation for Cell Biology, and Wiley agreed to it after a third party raised concerns. An inquiry confirmed duplicated blot bands, the images used as protein evidence, within three figures and again between two more. Parts of the introduction were copied from an earlier article by a different group. Yousif promised the data, then sent nothing and stopped replying. The editors judged the results and conclusions compromised.
pmc-13420845:
Ingo J. Banke and colleagues pool comparative studies of needle arthroscopy, a hair-thin scope that can examine joints in an office rather than an operating room. Their review set the mini scope against conventional arthroscopy on function, diagnosis, and complications. Random-effects pooling with a conservative adjustment handled the gaps between studies.

Function scores favored the needle scope early, with advantages of 15.25 points at half a month and 7.25 points at six weeks in the pooled differences reported, while completion and diagnostic success ran even between methods. Detection accuracy showed no firm gap in exploratory analysis. The authors judge diagnosis promising yet treatment equivalence unproven. Clinics weighing office-based scoping get a clear line between what is shown and what is still hoped.
pmc-13421445:
Sehrish Sewyra and five colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, the rise of cobalt as a catalyst for building organic molecules. Cobalt is cheap and fairly low in toxicity. Chemists use it more and more in place of precious metals to build compounds of biological interest.

Covering work since 2020, the review ranges across reaction families: ring-forming cycloadditions, cross-couplings, multicomponent reactions, hydrogenation, hydroboration, amidation, annulation, isomerisation and carbonylation. Many products arrive in high yield with fine control of handedness, which matters for medicines. The authors expect cobalt catalysis to keep growing in scope. They present it as a greener path for synthesis.
pmc-13421745:
Won Seok Lee leads a nine-author team using Korean national records, in a 2026 study, to test whether newborn jaundice severe enough to need light therapy predicts developmental problems at school entry. Bilirubin, the pigment behind jaundice, can harm the developing brain at high levels, yet the long shadow of treated jaundice was uncertain.

From over three million births between 2009 and 2015, about one million children had screening data, and roughly 121,000 had received phototherapy. Treated jaundice carried modestly raised odds of abnormal results in gross motor skills, cognition and language at about five and a half years. Five or more days of therapy strengthened some associations. The authors adjusted for birth weight, prematurity and family income, among other factors.
pmc-13422245:
Reon Morioka leads a seven-author team reporting, in a 2026 case study, a rare melanoma inside the mouth — on the tongue — where it is rarer still. Two separate dark patches appeared on one patient's tongue, each looking harmless enough to pass for a benign mark.

Biopsy of the front lesion confirmed melanoma, and the rear patch, at the tongue's base, was suspected to be an in-transit metastasis, a spread pattern not well documented for this cancer. Wide removal followed, then the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab, borrowed from skin melanoma practice. A prosthesis preserved oral function. One year on there was no recurrence. The authors stress early biopsy of pigmented mouth lesions and team-based care.
pmc-13422345: Correction: Santoro and colleagues correct their 2026 paper on folate levels in Down syndrome regression disorder, a condition in which young people with Down syndrome lose skills. Two figures were wrong. The first used a dataset of 73 people instead of the final 67. It wrongly showed two spinal fluid folate values below normal, though both people had been excluded on eligibility grounds. The second figure had reversed axis labels. With the final group, every value sits within the normal range, and the paper's main conclusion stands unchanged.
pmc-13422645:
Samir Ghourab, Nada Alsahan, Osama Alomar and Reem Labani present, in a 2026 prospective study, a womb-saving operation for placenta accreta spectrum. In this condition the placenta grows too deeply into a scarred uterus. Delivery usually ends in hysterectomy. At Saudi Arabia's main tertiary centre, sixty-seven referred women with a previous caesarean scar and placenta previa underwent their targeted technique.

During caesarean delivery the surgeons shut down blood flow along the uterus's lateral walls, low near the cervix and below the round ligament. The womb was preserved in over ninety-five percent of cases. Average blood loss ran near one and a half litres, most women needed transfusion, and bladder injury in about a fifth was repaired on the spot. No mother died, and performance improved with practice.
pmc-13422845:
Alsufyani and colleagues automate a forensic judgment in this 2026 study: estimating whether a person is legally adult from dental X-rays. Wisdom teeth keep developing through the late teens, and the third molar index is a standard yardstick, but human scoring is operator-dependent. The team trained neural networks to segment the tooth and classifiers to call the eighteen-year threshold.

They worked from 597 panoramic radiographs of people aged 13 to 26, split nearly evenly by sex. An attention-equipped network segmented the molars best, and a nearest-neighbor classifier classified age best, reaching 77.77 percent sensitivity with 96 percent specificity in males and an AUC of 0.87 on that task, outperforming the human expert's sensitivity in both sexes. The authors suggest pixel-level machine perception catches developmental cues that the traditional index misses.
pmc-13422945:
Sun and colleagues report a 2026 study of neuroendocrine prostate cancer, an aggressive form that hides from the immune system and rewires its fuel use. A signal pathway, IL-8 acting through receptor CXCR2, is central to their account. They studied cell lines and patient samples, then blocked the pathway in two mouse tumor models.

Tumors rich in this signaling built up free fatty acids and very-long-chain fats in their surroundings. That fat pushed killer T cells into ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. Suppressor T cells and tumor-friendly macrophages then moved in, tilting the local immune mix toward protection of the tumor. The work links a single signal to both fuel and immune control, giving drug developers a target that might reopen these tumors to immune attack.
pmc-13423445:
Shunsuke Kasai heads the COLLAB pilot study, testing whether colorectal cancers can be sorted into consensus molecular subtypes from ordinary pre-surgery biopsy samples rather than the removed tumour. The four-subtype scheme, built on gene activity, promises better-matched therapy, but biopsy tissue is scant and may miss the tumour's mix.

Eight patients gave paired samples from two tumour spots, taken with standard and jumbo forceps. Both tools yielded ample, high-quality RNA, and every sample was classified successfully. Larger forceps gave somewhat more RNA. Worryingly, subtype calls disagreed between the two spots in three of eight patients, showing that one small biopsy may mislabel a tumour. Sampling caused no adverse events.
pmc-13423945:
Julian Scherer and eleven colleagues present AO Spine clinical practice recommendations for spinal tuberculosis, an infection that destroys vertebrae and can threaten the cord. An expert knowledge forum selected four influential studies covering the condition's key phases, then graded consensus advice using an established evidence framework.

For diagnosis, they conditionally back an FDG-PET/CT scan when magnetic resonance imaging is unclear, impossible, or marred by metal artefact. A seven-item routine blood-test model earned conditional support as an early screening aid while definitive tests are pending. For surgery on chest and lumbar disease, a back-only approach is conditionally preferred over front or combined routes. A fourth study addressed judging healed status by imaging, completing the care pathway.
pmc-13424645:
Sun-jin Nho and five colleagues chart heat-related illness across South Korea's capital region in the summer of 2025, using emergency department reports collected from mid-May to late September. The study area, Seoul, Incheon, Gyeonggi, and Gangwon, contributed 212 of the 516 hospitals in the national surveillance system, and cases were sorted by where symptoms began.

The region recorded 1,808 cases and 11 suspected deaths, about 40% of the national caseload. Growth outpaced the country as a whole: Seoul's cases jumped by 60.9% in a year, Incheon rose by 36.6% over the same span, and Gyeonggi climbed 27.5%, all against a national rise of about a fifth. Age patterns differed by province, with over-65s forming the largest share in Seoul at 37.6%, while working-age adults dominated in Gyeonggi.
pmc-13425845:
Pu and colleagues studied a paradox in cataract biology. Lens crystallin proteins carry many cysteines, sulfur-bearing units that can form harmful bonds with age. Yet those cysteines persist in healthy lenses. The team built human gammaD-crystallin variants with all four cysteines in the weak domain swapped out. They then tested how stable each variant was and how it clumped.

Removing the cysteines made the protein's N-terminal domain far less stable in both variants. One form suffered more than the other. On mild heating, both variants formed light-scattering clumps. Under the microscope the clumps looked shapeless. To the team's surprise, clumping started only from pairs of folded proteins linked by a single bridge between their tails. The lens's own guard molecule, myo-inositol, strongly held back the clumping. Clumping speed also rose in step with protein amount. That points to a slow shape change inside the pairs.
pmc-13425945:
Anan Al-Jabri and coauthors measured frailty, multiple conditions, and medication load in hospitalized older adults in Oman in a 2026 prospective multicenter cohort study. Patients aged sixty-five and over entered general internal medicine wards at two tertiary hospitals and were assessed consecutively. Frailty used the Clinical Frailty Scale, disease burden used the Charlson index plus a complex multimorbidity definition of three or more chronic conditions, and polypharmacy meant five or more medicines.

Regional data on how these overlapping problems affect hospital outcomes were scarce. Documenting prevalence together in one cohort helps Omani services plan geriatric staffing and medication review for admitted older patients. Charts from two large sites give the count more weight than a lone ward could, and the mix of old men and women was broad.
pmc-13426345:
Yoshiyo Oguchi wrote a 2026 letter distinguishing perception from evidence in psychiatrists' views of long-acting injectable antipsychotics. The letter discusses a study by Ifteni and colleagues in which 80 Romanian psychiatrists rated four second-generation injectable products across many domains. Aripiprazole scored most favorably on nearly every domain and in overall preference, while lack of patient trust, limited hospital supply, and inexperience were named as chief prescribing barriers.

Oguchi notes the survey captured what clinicians believed about effectiveness, safety, and cost rather than outcomes measured directly, a welcome but limited addition for Central and Eastern Europe. Three observations and future directions aim to frame how much weight such preference data should carry. What staff think a drug does and what trials show it does can sit far apart, and this gap is the heart of the note.
pmc-13426945:
Humphries and colleagues followed school-age children in rural Ghana in 2026 over two years to learn why hookworm infections persist or return after treatment. Hookworm infects hundreds of millions worldwide and drains children's growth and schooling. Mass deworming lowers rates, but infections bounce back, and the reasons mix nutrition, environment, and the worms' answer to the drug.

The cohort covered 274 children checked every six months, with stool and blood tests, body measures, and household surveys. Of those seen at every visit, over two in five were infected more than once. The standard drug cleared about seven in ten treated children, and worked better in older children and, oddly, in children from food-insecure homes. Past infection and treatment outcome were the strongest guides to later infection. The authors say deworming alone will not hold gains.
pmc-13427445:
Vera Stamenkovic and coauthors show that restoring a missing synaptic protein in young mice rebuilds disrupted interaction networks in a 2026 neurobiology study. SynGAP1 shortage, a cause linked with autism spectrum conditions, selectively reduced protein complexes containing SynGAP without broadly breaking NMDA-dependent signaling, as measured by quantitative multiplex co-immunoprecipitation across development. Protein interaction networks normally translate neural activity into biochemical signals shaping synapse structure.

Switching the gene back on at postnatal day 21 with tamoxifen fully restored both resting and activity-driven network organization in their measurements. Post-developmental rescue at the molecular level supports hope that some neurodevelopmental circuit defects remain reversible. Day 21 is well past birth, so a full fix then holds hope for late care. The fix held at a late age in these mice, which is the point that gives the work its punch for the field as a whole.
pmc-13427545:
Mert Keles and co-authors report a 2026 rat study on whether moringa leaf extract can ease gum disease. Forty male rats were split into five groups, including healthy controls and groups with induced gum disease around the lower molars. Diseased rats received moringa by mouth for four weeks at one of three daily doses. Blood tests measured inflammation signals and markers of cell damage from oxidation.

Rats on the two higher doses showed lower inflammation signals and stronger natural antioxidant defenses than untreated diseased rats. Tissue samples under the microscope also looked healthier in those groups. Kidney and liver blood tests showed no clear harm from the extract. Animal results do not prove benefit in people, but they support careful follow-up work on dose and safety.
pmc-13427845:
Ngoc Thuy Pham presents, in a 2026 engineering study, a smarter controller for induction motors, the workhorse motors of industry. Precise speed control gets hard when loads shift and motor values drift with heat. The design pairs a small neural network with a rugged sliding-mode controller, a method that forces the motor back on track despite disturbances. A further routine trims the magnetic field level in real time to save energy.

Settings were tuned by a swarm optimization method that mimics flocking search. Bench tests on a Texas Instruments processor chip showed tighter speed tracking and faster recovery from upsets than standard control. Energy use also fell under the flux-trimming routine. Factories running pumps and conveyors could gain efficiency from control software alone, with no new motor hardware required.
pmc-13428445:
Thomas kidanemariam Yewodiaw and co-authors map, in a 2026 study, anemia among young children across the Democratic Republic of Congo. Low blood hemoglobin slows growth and learning, and national figures hide local hotspots. The team used the 2023-24 national health survey, covering 11,393 children aged 6 to 59 months. Mapping tools searched for clusters, and layered models separated household factors from community ones.

Just over half the children were anemic, though severe cases were rare at about 1 percent. Babies in their first half year and boys ran slightly higher rates. Wasting, malaria infection, living where malaria risk is high, and low altitude each raised the odds. Wealthier households and overweight mothers were protective signs. Three provinces carried the heaviest burden, and the authors aim malaria and nutrition programs there first.
pmc-13429245:
Getman argues in a 2026 essay that Delaware, the fifth oldest state in the United States, should rethink aging by treating ageism as a public health problem. Ageist stereotypes and discrimination, she writes, damage the well-being of older adults, and a national poll found most older respondents met some form of ageism every day.

Getman draws on thirty years of work with older adults, after an earlier career in youth development. She describes how bias shows up in birthday card jokes, workplaces, and advertising. It appears even in health care, where older patients were treated as expendable during the pandemic. She calls for an integrated, cross-sector public health agenda that honors both the gains and the hardships of growing older. Her slogan aim is to make Delaware, the First State, first in aging well.
pmc-13429545:
Helene Marie Haug and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, results for a newer weight-loss operation called SASI bypass. The operation pairs a sleeve gastrectomy with a reroute that lets food split between the normal path and a shortcut. The review compared it with sleeve surgery alone and with two bypass standards across comparative studies. Twenty-six studies covering 1,603 patients qualified, most reporting one-year results.

Across single-arm pooling, average total weight loss reached about 36 kilograms at one year. Head-to-head comparisons were few: one randomized trial and a handful of non-randomized studies per rival operation. Confidence in the one-year evidence rated low to very low under standard grading. The authors stop short of ranking SASI against its rivals and call for proper randomized trials. Patients considering the newer operation get promise without proof, stated plainly.
pmc-13431945:
Suneeti R Madhavan and co-authors traced in 2026 how skin scarring wipes out fat under the skin, and they pinned the loss on a signal path that shuts down fat making. Fat loss in the deep skin layer marks an early sign of skin fibrosis, a state that later fills with stiff matrix. The same signal had to stay on for the loss, yet the link stayed dim.

Gene reads of ripe fat cells in living skin showed the path cut the fat-making chain within two days. One key fat-making enzyme fell in a drug-based mouse model and in human scar tissue of two kinds. Blocking that enzyme while the signal wound down kept fat from bouncing back and left the matrix in poor shape. The authors name the path a fresh drug target for skin scars.
pmc-13433345:
Shubham Tomar and co-authors opened a 2026 collection on neurocardiology, the science of how heart and brain shape each other. For decades the two fields grew apart, each locked on one organ. Fresh proof shows a two-way web that trades nerve, hormone, swelling, vessel, and spark signals to hold body balance.

Breaks in that web can start harm in either organ, then echo across the pair and swell the load. The collection spans crowd counts, vessel science, body function, thought, brain scans, genes, and nerve science. Shared paths, not lone organ faults, frame most pieces: vessel harm, tiny brain vessel disease, brain swelling, wall leaks, and pressure shapes. The editors mark a shift from noting links to hunting the gears that drive them.
pmc-13434545:
Lee and colleagues published a 2026 study on life quality in South Korean teens with eczema. Atopic dermatitis brings itchy, dry skin that can shadow the teen years. The team surveyed 97 adolescents aged 13 to 18 with the condition. They asked about symptoms, body image, friendships, and self-care habits.

Heavier symptoms tracked with clearly worse life quality in the data. Teens who managed their skin care actively reported better life quality. Body image and peer ties also rose alongside better scores overall. Allergy sensitivity, symptom load, and self-management together explained about 40 percent of differences. The authors urge nurses to coach teens toward confident self-care routines. Personal teaching plans, tuned to each teen, are their practical advice.
pmc-13434645:
Estela Caballero-Picazo's team asked in 2026 whether the way people act changes what their working memory holds onto, using immersive virtual reality. Working memory is the short-term store that links what we see to what we do, and past lab tasks often used only a simple button press. Here volunteers answered either with a button press or by moving an object in a lifelike way, while a cue marked the item most likely to be tested.

Lifelike moves beat button presses, but only for items the cue had marked as likely, showing that action context tunes the gain from cueing rather than lifting all recall. The study also shows virtual reality can test memory under lifelike yet controlled conditions. Memory teams get a neat result and a method that bridges lab tasks and real action.
pmc-13434745:
David Hollingworth and coauthors pinpoint where sleep gases grip nerve channels in 2026. These channels set how easily nerves fire, and sleep gases tune their shut off timing. Crystals of a bacterial twin channel show one gas, sevoflurane, at atomic detail.

The gas sits in a greasy pocket in the channel wall, pushing out fat. Swapping one key amino acid in the pocket erases both binding and effect. Human channel tests show the gas also slows the long shut off state. Twin sites likely exist in human channels. A shared pocket may explain how sleep gases calm the brain.
pmc-13436645:
Chigozie Chukwunyere, Jessica Heil, and Matthew Salzman survey emergency graduates on addiction training and waiver drills in 2026. An eight hour course joined the residency in 2018 at their hospital. Sixty three of eighty one graduates from 2016 to 2022 answered the survey.

Graduates after the course prescribed buprenorphine at 76.1 percent, versus 58.8 percent before it. Comfort in treating substance use disorder was the main gauge. Career path sway from the course was the second gauge. Early returns favor the training, though group sizes stay small. Residency programs weigh like courses as overdose care grows.
pmc-13437345:
Jesus Ramón-Llin and three co-editors introduce the third volume of a research collection on racket sports, spanning tennis, padel, badminton, pickleball, and table tennis. Their 2026 editorial argues that strong performance in these sports grows from many fields at once: body conditioning, movement science, mental skills, and food.

One featured study found that recreational tennis players who felt more involved in the sport planned more strongly to keep playing. Other work in the volume covers athlete growth, well-being, tactics, thinking skills, and smarter training across skill levels. The editors trace a shift in the field: older research leaned on physical demands and stroke mechanics, while newer work gives motivation, emotion control, and quick perception a central place. They present the collection as a current map of racket sport science, meant to help coaches and researchers build training that treats the whole athlete rather than the swing alone.
pmc-13438445:
Tshimanga Tshilumba Esperant and colleagues mapped bowel injuries in patients operated on for abdominal trauma at two Ugandan teaching hospitals. Where the gut is torn decides the repair, yet local pattern data were thin. Their 2026 study enrolled ninety-nine consecutive patients who underwent emergency abdominal surgery between late September and late December 2024. Surgeons recorded which bowel segment was hurt and how it was fixed.

Thirty-four patients had a bowel injury. The small bowel took most hits, and within it the jejunum, its middle stretch, was the commonest site. Penetrating trauma, from stabs or shots, more than tripled the odds of a bowel injury against blunt force. Complications ran far higher in the bowel group, about thirty-one percent against twelve, with belly infection and septic shock behind the group's one death. The authors press for stronger pre-hospital care and trauma training, so patients arrive with stable circulation.
pmc-13438545:
Xiaohan Yu and colleagues built a sunlight-driven system to pull valuable metals out of dead lithium-ion batteries. Standard recycling roasts or bathes the material in chemicals at heavy energy and pollution cost. Their 2026 study centers on a crafted polymer catalyst that, under light, brews hydrogen peroxide on the spot. That peroxide attacks the cathode material, freeing lithium and metals such as cobalt into solution.

Under tuned conditions the setup freed lithium fast and recovered over ninety percent of the transition metals, across several cathode chemistries. Left outdoors under real sun, it kept recycling a common cathode type for over thirty days, with steady daily yields. The authors frame the method as a loop-closer for the battery age: the sun that charges clean transport could refine its waste. Scale-up questions remain, yet a month of open-air stability gives the idea unusual weight.
pmc-13439345:
Jablonszky and colleagues test whether a songbird's song reveals its genes. Male collared flycatchers sing complex songs that females may use to judge mates, and song is partly learned, which clouds any genetic signal. Their 2026 study pairs fifteen years of song recordings from a wild population with genome wide markers from the same males. It then asks whether song likeness tracks genetic likeness, once place and year gaps are taken into account.

No link appeared. Males from the same genetic cluster sang no more alike than males from different clusters, and genetic distance matched neither distance in space nor in time. Song likeness did fade as the years between recordings grew, a pattern that fits cultural change, like drifting dialects. Song content in this species, the authors conclude, is shaped mainly by learning and culture, letting it shift fast as conditions change.
pmc-13440045:
H F Poulsen and colleagues present designs for a true neutron microscope, aiming to lift neutron imaging past its pinhole-camera limits, in a 2026 paper. Neutron sources are dim, so imaging usually parks a detector right behind the object and accepts a trade between sharpness, speed, and field size. Their instrument instead gathers neutrons with a nested Wolter-I mirror optic acting as a condenser, a set of curved mirrors that focus the beam onto the object.

Magnification comes from a two-dimensional bank of achromatic objectives that blend bending and focusing elements to stay sharp across neutron energies. Together the parts promise microscope-style imaging rather than shadow projection. Such an instrument could serve the many contrast modes neutron imaging already supports, from magnetism mapping to internal strain and grain studies, at far finer detail.
pmc-13440645:
Lizhi Hu and colleagues show that removing a single immune receptor protects the heart from a powerful cancer drug, reporting mouse work in 2026. Doxorubicin cures many cancers but damages the heart in proportion to dose. Inflammation was suspected, yet the part played by CCR2, a receptor that guides immune cells, stayed vague. Mice lacking CCR2 faced both sudden and drawn-out doxorubicin schedules, with bone marrow swaps to locate the protective cell type.

Hearts without CCR2 kept stronger pumping measures and lower injury markers in blood. Their heart cells also ran autophagy, the internal cleanup system, at a higher rate, clearing damaged parts faster. Protein profiling fingered interleukin-12B from heart macrophages as the messenger. Giving that protein copied the protection in normal mice, and blocking it erased the protection entirely. The authors name a CCR2 to IL12B to autophagy chain as a drug target.
pmc-13441245:
Raphael Mwezi and colleagues chart outcomes of pesticide poisoning across Tanzanian hospitals from 2017 to 2024, reporting in 2026. Poisoning by farm chemicals remains a heavy burden where highly hazardous products stay within easy reach. Records from regional and district hospitals in five regions yielded 635 cases. Most patients were men, and most were aged sixteen to thirty-five. Deliberate exposure accounted for about seven in ten cases.

Two thirds of patients recovered fully, while just under a fifth died. Fatality varied sharply by product, with paraquat the deadliest by a wide margin in the data. The authors place their findings beside Tanzania's recent regulatory moves against the most hazardous pesticides. They argue that product-specific fatality figures, not pooled poisoning counts, should guide which chemicals get restricted first and how hospitals prepare antidote and care pathways.
pmc-13442645:
Xiaodong Han and colleagues build a lab-made antibody that blocks Zika virus entry in a 2026 study. The virus harms unborn babies and nerves, yet no shots or drugs have full approval. Cells let the virus in through a door protein called ITGB4, so the team raised mouse antibodies against that door.

One antibody, named 7C3, gripped the door with very tight force, at a strength mark of 30.9 pM in their tests. Its grip spot did not overlap the spot of a known twin antibody, 13H10. Cells dosed with 7C3 before virus contact held far less virus RNA in all four cell lines tested. Brain-like cells in the set matter most, since Zika harms the growing brain. The pair of antibodies could team up for a stronger block, the authors say, after more safety work.
pmc-13442845:
Enrico Fornasa and colleagues build a fresh Monte Carlo scheme to untangle giant polymer melts in a 2026 paper. Melts are dense soups of long chains whose knots set how plastics flow and stretch. Old sampling stalls as chains grow, since each shift takes ages to settle.

Their scheme lets chain counts shift during runs, while strict local moves pass bond swaps across scales. Settle time grew in near-direct step with system size, far kinder than past tools. Packed lattice runs reached about 1.1 billion units in total size in the best case. Chains as long as 500,000 units showed knots and links held in small zones, not spread as global tangles. Link strength between neighbor chains grew as the fourth root of length, a slow climb the team flags for theory.
pmc-13443945:
Dongsuk Sung and colleagues build a physics model that predicts human brain temperature person by person in a 2026 paper. Direct brain heat reads are rare, so care teams lean on models. Their model guards mass, push, and energy at each scale, fed by each subject's own MR anatomy, heat output, and blood flow.

A bridge layer for mid-size vessels links big and small flow zones with push kept intact. Across 30 healthy subjects, map gaps against MR heat reads sat between 0.18 and 0.36 degrees in most spots. Zone checks tied model marks to real marks only when push was conserved. A fake artery block run showed why that guard matters. The authors eye clinic use for stroke and heat care.
pmc-13444145:
Ehsan Sedaghat-Rostami and coauthors compare a 2026 pig study of porcine coronavirus and H1N1 flu, two lung threats whose courses differ and may reveal how host defense shapes outcome. Using pigs as a large-animal model, the team tracked viral load, shedding, immune protein and T cell levels, B cell memory, and nasal germs.

The virus drove higher viral loads, longer shedding, stronger systemic and mucosal T cell firing, and memory B cell growth. Flu set off faster blocking antibodies, stronger follicular helper and germinal center action, and broader early nasal range. Shared interferon genes opened both cases before stromal and vessel pathways split. Pigs thus offer a strong side-by-side model for lung virus research.
pmc-13445145:
Sierra and colleagues map which brain areas a rat needs when it seeks a reward under threat of harm. Their 2026 study uses a conflict task that scores avoidance, risk checking, and reward approach in one session. The team briefly switches off eight candidate areas, one at a time, with a drug that quiets nerve cells. The areas span outer brain regions for control and inner regions for emotion and reward.

Switching off the prelimbic cortex or the rear insular cortex freed approach during conflict, but the two differed on risk checking, so they limit approach in distinct ways. Silencing the basolateral amygdala, an emotion hub, loosened restraint broadly, even without conflict. Silencing the nucleus accumbens, a reward hub, left approach fragmented and poorly timed. Four other areas changed nothing in this task. The result is a short, selective list of nodes that organize behavior when desire and danger collide.
pmc-13445845:
Petr Heneberg reviews a 2026 bird-focused roundup of how rapid outside change shifts trematode pests that cycle through birds, snails, and other hosts. The review spans fresh-water, coastal, man-made wetland, farm, and far-north systems, linking heat, water flow, dirt, and bird travel to spread.

Warming can speed pest output yet shorten lives or break timing with bird hosts, while altered waters reshuffle snail hosts into patchy spread mosaics. Shaken systems may lose rare kinds, flatten in function, or hide lineage swap behind stable species lists. Watch should fuse stage-set sampling, gene-based naming, travel data, and remote sensing, the author argues.
pmc-13446345:
Jie Chen and colleagues study demethoxycurcumin, a curcumin cousin from turmeric, as a brake on the blood vessel growth that feeds breast tumors, in a 2026 study. Tumors cannot thrive without new vessels, and their vessel nets grow wild and leaky, which helps spread. A safe plant compound that prunes that growth could slow the disease.

The compound curbed tumor growth and new vessel sprouting in their models. It dialed down a regulator named RGS5 in tumor vessels and in vessel lining cells grown in dishes. Tests that moved RGS5 up or down showed it carries much of the compound's anti-vessel effect, which marks it as the key target. The authors frame the pair as a lead for vessel-focused breast cancer care.
pmc-13447245:
Hanlei Yan and colleagues pool studies of keyhole liver surgery for children's liver tumours in a 2026 systematic review. Removing part of the liver can cure many of these rare tumours, yet open surgery means a large wound for a small patient. Whether the keyhole route is safe and truly beneficial in children needed a combined look.

Nine studies covering one hundred forty-four keyhole cases met the rules. Operations averaged about three and a half hours, hospital stays under a week, and complications in roughly one in six children, most often bile leaks. No cases of gas entering the blood or tumour seeding at entry sites were reported. Versus open surgery, keyhole cases took longer in theatre yet left hospital sooner, with similar blood loss. Limited, uneven evidence means careful patient choice still rules.
pmc-13447445:
