Dixon and Price describe a privacy-first web dashboard for drug-gene risk assessment in this 2026 paper. Pharmacogenomics uses a patient's genes to predict drug risks, including opioid and multi-drug risks, but high-performing models rarely reach the clinic in usable form. Their system runs entirely on serverless cloud functions. A static website fronts containerized backends. Those backends hold 56 ensemble models, spanning two cohorts, seven age bands, and four density groups.

The dashboard also generates patient cards that check gene-drug rules from the CPIC guidelines across 573 test cases, without storing any personal information. Warm predictions returned in about six milliseconds on average, while cold starts took about two seconds, meeting their speed targets. Predictions stayed reasonably stable when only a few inputs were supplied, shifting by about a tenth against the full-data baseline.
pmc-13447945:
Liheng Zhang and colleagues identify a 2026 blood biomarker, serum 5-prime tRF-Val, for early detection of esophageal cancer, a disease usually caught late for lack of non-invasive screening. Screening a small-RNA database and validating a PCR assay, the team studied 289 participants spanning early and advanced cancer, benign lesions, healthy controls, and postoperative patients.

Marker levels ran higher in cancer patients and tracked advanced stage and metastasis, with strong early-stage accuracy at 0.857 and solid separation from benign lesions at 0.824. Levels fell significantly after radical surgery, suggesting treatment monitoring value. Multicenter trials must confirm the marker before clinical adoption.
pmc-13448245:
Jacub Pandelaki leads a team reporting eye-saving artery chemotherapy for retinoblastoma, a childhood eye cancer, at a single Indonesian centre in 2026 work. Delivering chemotherapy through the eye artery can save eyes that systemic treatment cannot, yet the usual route through the internal carotid artery sometimes fails, forcing detours through external carotid branches. Whether detour routes save eyes as well was the practical question.

Twenty-four eyes in twenty-four toddlers received sixty-five treatment sessions between 2022 and 2025, split between the standard route and detour routes. About four in five eyes were saved at six months, falling to under three in five still eye-preserving by thirty-nine months. Detour access carried markedly worse eye survival and independently predicted eye removal in adjusted analysis. No severe blood-flow complications occurred, and the standard route is preferred whenever feasible.
pmc-13449345:
Mandy Meijer and colleagues test in 2026 how much a blood sample can reveal about the mix of cell types inside the brain, using DNA methylation patterns. Brain tissue is hard to obtain from living patients, so psychiatry research leans on blood, even though methylation is mostly tissue-specific. The team worked with matched frontal brain and blood samples from 104 donors and estimated the proportions of seven brain cell types in each.

About ten percent of the methylation sites tied to brain cell proportions showed matching levels in blood. Multivariate models trained on blood methylation predicted brain microglia proportions best, though still modestly. Blood immune cell proportions also tracked brain stromal proportions, a link that faded once age was removed. Brain epigenetic age acceleration showed no tie to cell mix in either tissue. The authors conclude blood methylation carries a partial, immune-flavored echo of brain composition.
pmc-13449645:
Ina Ejsing Hunnerup Jørgensen and colleagues compared cool versus standard dialysis fluid temperatures in a 2026 crossover study. Cooling the dialysate may steady blood pressure during dialysis, a common problem when fluid is removed. Fourteen patients each underwent a four-hour session at thirty-five degrees and at thirty-seven degrees, a week apart, with order randomized and patients blinded.

Fluid removal was similar at both temperatures, and body temperature stayed stable on cool fluid but rose on standard fluid. Blood pressure held steadier during cool sessions, while standard sessions saw a larger fall in systolic pressure, averaging about twenty millimeters of mercury from start to lowest point. The small study supports cool dialysate as a simple way to reduce intradialytic blood pressure drops.
pmc-13450345:
Ya-Nan Li and colleagues report in 2026 a flat vapor chamber cooler that sheds heat at rates modern power chips demand and conventional chambers cannot reach. Vapor chambers move heat by evaporating and condensing a working fluid, but under extreme load the returning liquid cannot keep up through a single wick. Their redesign pairs a two-scale porous wick, super-wettable, that pulls condensate back hard, with a condenser patterned at micro and nano scales so droplets bead and shed instead of filming over.

The chamber reached a total thermal resistance near 0.17 degrees per watt, with temperature uniformity resistance around 0.02. Its dissipation flux passed 600 watts per square centimeter, and it kept working tilted against gravity, the orientation that starves ordinary wicks. The authors offer the design as a serious candidate for the next generation of gallium nitride and silicon carbide power electronics, where heat flux is the binding constraint.
pmc-13450445:
Frank Lin and co-authors report in 2026 a cancer syndrome unmasked by a pattern in a patient's fingernails. During a skin check after treatment for a stage IIA melanoma of the forearm, their 43-year-old patient was found to carry longitudinal streaks on all ten fingernails. The changes had crept in painlessly over years. Single nail tumors of this kind, onychopapillomas, are benign and usually solitary; finding them across digits is a recognized flag for BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome.

His family history sharpened the suspicion: a grandfather with mesothelioma and maternal relatives with melanoma. Genetic testing confirmed a germline mutation in BAP1, a tumor suppressor whose inherited loss raises the risk of skin and eye melanomas, mesothelioma, and kidney cancer. The case argues that a nail finding most clinicians would wave past can be the cheapest test trigger in the room. It can redirect a family into surveillance.
pmc-13450645:
Ford and colleagues characterize a cat model of an inherited retinal disease in this 2026 study. Fundus albipunctatus causes night blindness and sometimes central vision loss, and it results from mutations in RDH5, a gene in the eye's vitamin A recycling pathway. Cats carrying such a mutation arose spontaneously, offering a large-animal model closer to humans than mice. The team examined them with retinal imaging, electrical response tests, and microscopy.

Beyond the known rod dysfunction, the cats' cones recovered slowly after intense light exposure, mirroring a second defect in patients. In cats that developed central degeneration, rod outer segments first lengthened and their tips disorganized, suggesting failed shedding and cleanup, before the light-sensing cells died. The authors present the model as a platform for understanding this disease family and testing future therapies.
pmc-13451645:
Thoma and colleagues develop a new model of care for rheumatoid arthritis in this 2026 study. Rehabilitation is seldom built into routine rheumatology, even though many patients struggle with daily activities. Their PREVAIL model adds a function-focused screening survey to regular visits, using the answers to trigger rehabilitation referrals. The team surveyed 309 adults with the disease and interviewed patients, rheumatologists, and physical therapists to test the idea.

The screening tool tracked established measures moderately well. Those measures covered function and disease activity. But its referral criteria flagged 90 percent of participants, far too many. The thresholds needed refinement before wider testing. Interviewees across all groups backed the model, praising its proactive focus on function and better communication. Suggested fixes included completing surveys remotely, adding educational materials, and inserting a triage call with a physical therapist.
pmc-13451945:
Engy Abdelhamed and Shajitha Thekke Veettil present in 2026 the first known case from Qatar of a rare gene disorder that lays glassy stuff in skin and organs. The disorder, lipoid proteinosis, stems from faults in a matrix gene and has fewer than 400 cases in print. Their patient, a woman aged 36, came with itchy eyelid beads and a hoarse voice held since youth.

Her tongue was broad with cobbled mouth plaques, and brain scans showed paired chalk spots deep in the brain. A scope found a child-like voice box, a fresh note for this disease. She declined gene tests and brain care despite a seizure and low mood. The case urges early, team-wide care.
pmc-13452145:
Gaowa and co-authors test in 2026 Mongolian warm needling in rats made sleepless by stress and a brain chemical. Poor sleep harms the gut wall and stirs immune strain, yet the needling's gut effects were unclear. Rats were split into plain, model, needling, drug, and sham needling groups.

Needled rats slept better, thought more clearly, and showed less anxiety-like acts, with less gut wall damage. Three seal proteins of the gut wall rose toward normal. Swelling signals fell while a calming one rose, and a key swelling path in the gut quieted. The authors offer warm needling as a drug-free aid worth human study.
pmc-13452245:
Anu Lahteenmaki-Uutela and co-authors test in 2026 whether boosting sea alkalinity with mine leftovers could work in the Baltic Sea. The method speeds rock weathering so seas soak up more carbon. Their case uses serpentinite gangue, a mine side product, and weighs carbon yield, law, and cost in one frame.

Each tonne of carbon removed would emit well under a tenth of a tonne on the way, by their count. Permits would hinge on care for sea life at the site. On cost, credits would need to fetch over a hundred euros per tonne to pay off. The authors say firm buyer pledges could tame market doubt if sea harms prove fair.
pmc-13452345:
Jiajie Tang and co-authors track in 2026 sore mouth lining damage during focused radiation for head and neck cancer. The harm, a raw and painful mouth, can stall care. The team watched 134 patients on intensity-shaped radiation and logged when damage rose, how hard it hit, and which of sixteen traits tracked it.

Damage struck four of five patients, most often at grade two, rising in week two and peaking in week three. Single-trait checks flagged tumor site, mouth cleanliness, and total mouth dose. When all traits ran together, only mouth dose stood as a lone driver, adding about a tenth of risk per unit. The team urges tight dose watch and early mouth care.
pmc-13453745:
Na Liu and six co-authors ask what helps or blocks patients with end stage heart failure from accepting advance care planning in China. Such planning lets patients state care wishes before a crisis, yet uptake stays low. Their 2026 study interviews 22 patients at a large hospital and sorts the answers with the COM-B model, which splits behavior into capability, opportunity, and motivation.

On capability, patients knew little about their disease or about planning itself and struggled to take in new facts. On opportunity, family led choices, filial duty, and a taboo on speaking of death squeezed the patient's own voice. On motivation, fear and a sense of duty to family dulled the wish to plan. The authors argue that plans built for this family centered culture could raise acceptance.
pmc-13454045:
Colin W Fuller and Aileen Taylor track match injuries at the women's Rugby World Cup across sixteen years, from 2010 to 2025. Team medical staff from eighteen national teams logged body measures and every injury under a shared elite rugby method. Their 2026 study spans five tournaments as the women's game turned professional.

The overall rate came to 45.2 injuries per 1,000 player match hours, with an average layoff of 48.4 days. Concussion led the list for backs at 21.7 percent, while knee ligament tears led for forwards at 17.2 percent. Knee ligament injuries also ate the largest share of lost time in both groups. Rates ran lower than in the men's tournament, yet each injury cost more days, so total burden matched. The authors urge prevention work aimed at knees and concussion.
pmc-13454145:
Zeng and colleagues identify a protein, TSC22D4, that clear cell kidney cancers exploit to protect their master antioxidant switch, NRF2, from destruction, helping the tumors resist oxidative stress and drug treatment. TSC22D4 binds KEAP1, the protein that normally tags NRF2 for disposal, using a conserved docking motif and thereby breaks the pair apart.

Freed from KEAP1, NRF2 accumulates and switches on antioxidant genes, including the cystine transporter SLC7A11 that blocks ferroptosis, the iron-driven cell death sorafenib tries to trigger in these tumors. TSC22D4 itself is markedly overexpressed in this cancer type, and forcing its levels up drove proliferation, invasion, and metastasis in the team's models. Clinically, high TSC22D4 tracked with advanced stage and poorer patient survival across the cohorts examined. The authors nominate TSC22D4 as a drug target for restoring treatment sensitivity.
pmc-13454445:
Lucia Linares and eight colleagues sum up, in a 2026 article, lessons from a workshop on health diplomacy held at the European Health Forum Gastein in 2025. The session, hosted by schools of public health from Europe and beyond, gathered early-career professionals. Health diplomacy means the talks and deals that let countries act together against health threats.

Speakers framed the field as vital in a time of political tension and fast-moving risks. Young professionals were cast as central players, not bystanders, in fair cross-border health work. Discussion stressed trust, open communication, and teamwork across sectors such as trade and security. The article closes by naming the skills future health diplomats need, from negotiation to cultural awareness. It also urges training programs to build those skills early in health careers.
pmc-13454645:
Chris Mathew Prince and six colleagues survey, in 2026, what the public in the United Arab Emirates knows about rheumatoid arthritis. The disease is a long-term autoimmune attack on the joints that can disable if caught late. The team handed a structured questionnaire to adults across the country, collecting 739 completed responses.

About 65 percent had heard of the disease, and a similar share showed adequate knowledge overall. Most knew it is autoimmune and targets joints, and about two thirds knew it cannot be fully cured. Recognition of whole-body symptoms lagged, with under half spotting fatigue and fewer still fever. Roughly three quarters said they would see a doctor for lasting joint symptoms. The internet was the top information source, chosen by about 77 percent. The authors call for campaigns that fill the symptom gaps they found.
pmc-13455145:
Kalaivanan and team scoped a decade of research on cognitive flexibility and creativity in children and adolescents aged 0 to 18. Flexibility is the mental skill of shifting angles and plans. The question was whether it supports creativity in youth. The link is well shown in adults, but youth evidence was scattered by wildly varied methods across studies.

Fourteen studies met their bar for the scoping synthesis of this developmental literature. Nine found a significant positive link between the two. The link was strongest when it was measured as a complex, many-sided capacity and creativity with traditional divergent thinking tools. Five reported null or inconsistent results, often using narrow task-switching tests or tasks contaminated by reasoning demands on the child participants. No consistent age differences appeared across preschoolers, school children, and adolescents. The authors conclude it leans on strategic flexibility, not simple rule switching.
pmc-13455345:
Yuan and a large team used droplet microfluidics, growing one bacterial cell per droplet, to fish a once unknown Corynebacterium species from vaginal swabs of a pregnant woman with preeclampsia. Standard growing misses much of this genus, a normal member of mucosal surfaces including the female reproductive tract.

The isolate, strain TJG_1T, is a Gram-positive, non-spore-forming short rod whose gene sequence matched its nearest relative, Corynebacterium coyleae, at only 97.39 percent identity in the taxonomic comparison. Its genome spans 2,481,283 base pairs with a guanine-cytosine content of 61.52 percent, and genome-wide match scores fell below species thresholds against all relatives tested. Gene annotation flagged metabolism, transport, possible resistance, and host-interaction traits for the new species. Neither its secretions nor live cells harmed placental trophoblast cells in vitro, though live bacteria altered their migration behavior.
pmc-13455445:
Imane Hamdane and colleagues review virtual reality distraction for children at the dentist in a 2026 systematic review. Dental fear often derails treatment in children, and immersive headsets promise to pull attention away from drills and needles, yet trials varied in design. The team searched five databases for work from 2013 to 2023, keeping 15 trials and interventional studies covering 1,168 children from age 4 to 15.

Most studies reported better behaviour, less anxiety and lower felt pain with virtual reality than with standard care. The authors still urge caution, since methods differed widely and overall evidence certainty was low. Dentists gain a safe, drug-free option worth trying for anxious children, while researchers must standardise headsets, content and measures before the benefit can be sized with confidence.
pmc-13457145:
Tiara Aninditha and six colleagues study, in a 2026 review of records, how meningioma position shapes symptoms and tumor grade. Meningiomas are the commonest primary brain tumors, and their behavior depends on where they sit. The team gathered 531 adults operated for a first meningioma over ten years at Indonesia's national hospital in Jakarta.

Women made up an overwhelming 92 percent of patients, with a median age of forty-five. Skull base tumors dominated, at about 77 percent. Those deep tumors paired more often with female sex, younger age, the mildest grade, and nerve and vision problems, yet they were also harder to remove fully. Tumors on the brain's outer surface announced themselves with headache, weakness, sensory loss, seizures, and clouded consciousness. The authors say the map of associations can prime surgeons and patients for what a given location is likely to bring.
pmc-13458645:
Lilly J Schmalbrock and colleagues asked whether vasectomy changes how middle-aged men see themselves sexually, a persistent worry among men considering the procedure. Their 2026 analysis drew on the Bavarian Men's Health Study and matched 1,140 men with and without vasectomy in pairs, balancing age, lifestyle, and background factors. The men averaged about 51 years old, and those with vasectomy had undergone it 8.5 years earlier on average before answering the survey.

Across all four dimensions of sexual self-concept — body image, perceived pressure, toughness, and sexual self-esteem — the two groups scored the same. Symptoms of depression and anxiety also did not differ between them. Vasectomized men instead reported more frequent sexual activity, greater sexual satisfaction, and a higher importance placed on sexuality, each a statistically significant difference. The authors say the results should reassure clinicians counseling men who fear the procedure will diminish them.
pmc-13459045:
Huihui Wang and Shixin Zhu model in 2026 how trust in government carries over to acceptance of artificial intelligence in Chinese public services. Agencies now use such systems to route questions, screen eligibility, and help caseworkers. Their design paired a simulation of 936 software agents with a scenario experiment and a small human pilot that retained 182 careful responses.

Across both the simulated and human data, trust in institutions lifted trust in the AI service, while feeling at risk pulled acceptance down. The fully automated, high-risk scenario scored lowest on trust and on willingness to use the service. Visible human review, the authors conclude, may be essential when automated decisions carry high stakes.
pmc-13459445:
Karnika Singh and colleagues combined in 2026 machine learning with plant chemistry to spot heat and drought stress in Acacia senegal, a hardy desert legume eaten in dry regions. Young plants grown in a greenhouse were split into control, heat, and drought groups after two months. The team photographed leaves, measured growth and leaf weight, and ran chemical assays on the tissue.

Their image set held 3,454 leaf photographs, and a hybrid model pairing a neural network with a support vector machine separated healthy from stressed leaves with accuracy near 87 percent. Chemical profiling found more than fifty plant compounds, letting the team watch how stress changes the leaf's nutritional value. Such automated scouting could help growers protect underused dryland crops.
pmc-13459645:
Wang, Zheng, and Que review the use of leech in treating diabetic foot ulcers in this 2026 paper. Diabetes slows wound healing. A core problem is pathological fibrosis, meaning excess scar-like tissue. It is driven by lingering inflammation, disordered metabolism, and poor blood flow under high blood sugar. Leech, used in traditional Chinese medicine, is known to thin blood, calm inflammation, and improve microcirculation in tiny vessels.

The review describes how leech treatment acts on several fronts at once: easing clotting, moderating inflammatory responses, and boosting flow in small vessels around the wound. It also reduces the transition of surface cells into scar-forming cells and the buildup of extracellular matrix by dampening multiple fibrosis signaling pathways together. The authors call for work pinpointing leech's active ingredients and how their effects combine.
pmc-13459845:
Kazuhiro Ito and co-authors report in 2026 a pilot study of keyhole chest surgery performed without a breathing tube for acute thoracic empyema, a pocket of infection around the lung. The mostly older cohort held 41 patients treated between 2019 and 2025, thirty-two as their first procedure and nine after chest drainage. Working through one small incision under local anesthesia with sedation, surgeons broke up internal partitions, washed the cavity, and placed a drain.

Every case finished through the single incision, though one patient needed conversion to general anesthesia. Operating time ran shorter when surgery came first rather than after drainage. No patient died in hospital or within six months, and fluid cultures turned negative quickly in nearly all cases. The team presents the approach as feasible early source control for frail patients.
pmc-13460045:
Kaho Mori and colleagues report in 2026 a set of 804 genomes reconstructed from microbes living in an artificial seawater aquarium tank in Nagoya, Japan. Water samples were gathered over four months in 2017 and 2018 while the SEA LIFE Nagoya conditioning tank was being established. Shotgun sequencing of twelve samples let the team assemble genomes directly from mixed DNA, without growing each microbe separately.

The reconstructed genomes span 27 phyla, almost all bacterial with one archaeal phylum represented. Microbes in such closed systems drive nitrogen cycling and keep water safe for the animals on display, yet their diversity was poorly charted at genome level. The collection gives researchers a reference for how artificial marine communities assemble and change over time.
pmc-13460145:
The International Journal of Clinical Practice retracted in 2026 a 2022 randomized trial by J. G. Zhang and co-authors comparing three nerve block techniques for pain after video-assisted chest surgery. The blocks studied were the rhomboid intercostal, erector spinae plane, and serratus plane approaches. Retraction followed a publisher inquiry run with the journal's editorial board and its publisher, Wiley.

Investigators found signs of organized tampering with the publishing process. They listed six possible warning signs. The signs cover mismatches in scope and in how the research was described, plus a gap between the data claimed and the research reported, poor citations, and a bent peer review. Editors state these problems end their trust in the article. The notice does not say whether the authors knew of any manipulation.
pmc-13460845:
McKenna Postles and colleagues scope plasma lido levels during IV lido therapy in children in a 2026 review. IV lido supports around-surgery multi-way pain relief in adults at 1 to 2 mcg per mL, yet child dose ranges and treatment levels were undefined. Searches of three databases found four studies covering 174 healthy children aged 1 to 18, with story-style round-up due to mixed reporting.

Peak levels ranged from 2.82 mcg per mL after a 1.5 mg per kg bolus plus 1 mg per kg per hour, up to just under 5 after a 2 mg per kg per hour drip. Levels stayed below presumed toxic thresholds, and only one brief sensory upset was reported. Sleep doctors gain comfort on safety but still lack dosing guidance, pending large multi-site drug-level trials.
pmc-13461545:
Nwobi, Loukil, and Jawahar built in 2026 a prototype chatbot to help Scottish health workers reach medication-assisted treatment standards for heroin addiction. Scotland's drug death rate is among the world's highest, yet staff must hunt across scattered websites for current standards. The team surveyed 39 treatment professionals and reviewed past chatbot studies, then built a system pairing a language model with retrieval from source texts and a knowledge graph.

Nwobi found only five of 39 staff rated current systems as exceptional, while most rated them average or worse, blaming scattered information and slow access. The prototype scored moderately on text quality measures, and its knowledge graph linked 227 nodes with 136 relationships drawn from official Scottish health sources. The review of 14 past studies confirmed no chatbot had targeted this treatment area. The authors present the tool as a first step toward faster clinical decisions.
pmc-13461645:
Zhou and a multicentre team ask whether some childhood bone tumours of immune origin can simply be watched. Their 2026 study covers 134 children with single-site bone Langerhans cell histiocytosis, a rare inflammatory growth disorder, treated at seven Chinese centres. Children with lesions near the central nervous system were excluded, and the rest were managed with observation alone.

Over a median follow-up of three years, 16 children had an event, giving a three-year event-free survival of about 88 percent. Nearly all events were new lesions, and almost all appeared within the first twelve months. Children staged with PET-CT scans at diagnosis fared notably better than those staged conventionally, with event-free survival near 98 percent against about 84 percent. Long-term quality of life was satisfactory, and the authors endorse watchful waiting for this group.
pmc-13461845:
Junling Zhu and co-authors search, in a 2026 study, for gene markers that sharpen outlook prediction in liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma). Standard staging sorts patients by tumor spread, yet people at the same stage fare differently. The team reasoned genes guiding body development might mark more aggressive disease. They mined a US cancer data set with gene activity and records, then checked findings in a Japanese cohort.

Screening weighed gene differences between tumor and normal tissue, links to traits, and ties to survival. Two genes stood out, HOXD9 and MESP2. In adjusted models only stage and HOXD9 stayed tied to overall survival. Adding HOXD9 improved how well the model sorted patients and predicted one-year survival. The gain was modest, and checks in the second cohort were part of the design. The authors present HOXD9 as a stage-adjusted marker worth further study, not a stand-alone test.
pmc-13461945:
Xiao Li, Yaqiong Song, and Jianhua Li pool randomized trials, in a 2026 review, on adding immune checkpoint drugs to chemotherapy with nab-paclitaxel across solid tumors. Checkpoint drugs release immune cell brakes so they can attack cancer. Whether the pairing helps across cancer types was unmeasured. The team searched four databases through the start of 2026 for trials comparing the pair against nab-paclitaxel-based care without immune drugs.

Twenty-four trials with 6,682 patients covered five tumor types: lung, breast, pancreatic, stomach, and throat. The pairing improved survival and time before growth, and more tumors vanished at surgery. Response and disease control rates rose. Survival gains held across all cancer types and both drug classes. One class, aimed at PD-1, beat the other on time before growth. Repeat checks confirmed stability. The authors back broad use of the pairing, with PD-1 favored for delaying growth.
pmc-13462845:
Josef Finsterer and Sinda Zarrouk write, in a 2026 letter, a critique of a case report about an 11-month-old boy whose mitochondrial disease struck only his liver. The boy carried two variants in the POLG1 gene, one from each parent, and suffered low blood sugar and acute liver failure. The letter writers raise three points of dispute.

First, they say both gene variants were described before, in patients with eye movement and nerve diseases, contrary to the report's claim of novelty. Second, calling the case a mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome needs proof: the gene can harm the liver without depleting mitochondrial DNA, so copy number should be measured precisely. Third, the child was not, in their view, screened for disease in other organs, though this gene often affects brain, nerves, and muscle. They ask whether brain scans and brain wave tests were done.
pmc-13463245:
Diana P. Reyes-Alata and colleagues tracked peak breathing flow in 2026 after abdominal surgery in a Peruvian hospital. Peak flow gauges how well patients can cough and clear airways, yet data from Latin American surgical wards is thin. Eighty-two adults due for planned abdominal surgery blew into a hand-held meter before surgery and again on day seven.

Average flow slipped from 367.9 to 346.0 litres per minute, with a typical drop of 20 litres per minute. Flow loss did not differ by sex or body mass, and age alone predicted a larger fall. Routine bedside flow checks may thus flag older patients who need closer breathing watch and early support in settings with few resources.
pmc-13463745:
Lu and colleagues survey intensive care nurses in China about stress and engagement at work in this 2026 study. They asked whether two personal resources, dispositional mindfulness, a habit of paying calm attention, and sleep quality, carry part of stress's effect on how engaged nurses feel. The survey covered 623 nurses at major hospitals using four validated questionnaires.

Stress was linked to lower engagement and lower mindfulness, and to worse sleep. Statistical modeling showed stress reduced engagement directly. It also acted indirectly through both pathways. The mindfulness route and the sleep route together accounted for about 22 percent of the total effect. A model treating the two pathways side by side fit the data better than one chaining them in sequence.
pmc-13463845:
Wardah S. Hasan and four co-authors turn date seed waste into a natural brown food colorant. Food makers want plant-based colors to replace synthetic dyes, and date pits are a cheap, thrown-away source. The team used water extraction and a Taguchi plan, a compact test grid, to tune the process.

Roasting heat drove most of the color strength, with best results at two hundred degrees for five minutes and a fifteen-minute extraction. Chemical reads confirmed the pigment groups behind the brown tone, plus helpful plant compounds such as catechin and gallic acid. Cold storage in dark amber bottles kept color and plant compounds best. The colorant also carries minerals such as potassium, calcium, and magnesium.
pmc-13463945:
Zixuan Ding and ten co-authors show how Webervirus phages pick two opposite doors into the germ Klebsiella pneumoniae. This germ often sheds its sugary capsule, which locks out phages that need the capsule to land. The team compared receptor use across a Webervirus collection to see how the other phages get in.

One phage group needs the capsule, while the other is blocked by it and lands on the O-antigen, a sugar chain in the cell wall coat. Grip proteins split into matching family lines for each door. Swapping a grip protein by gene editing flipped which door a phage used. Mixing both phage kinds suppressed a clinic strain better than either kind alone.
pmc-13464945:
Erin Hoover and three co-authors trace esophageal cancer surgery from open operations to robotic-assisted minimally invasive work. Removing the food pipe is among the hardest operations in surgery, with heavy complication risk. Robots promise finer control, yet proof of real advantage over standard keyhole surgery has lagged.

Robotic cases show less blood loss, fuller lymph node removal, and fewer lung complications across studies. Cancer control and long-term survival land on par with open and standard keyhole routes. The trade-offs are longer operating times, steep training demands, and high cost. Artificial intelligence tools, better imaging during surgery, and next robot generations close the review as the forces to watch.
pmc-13465045:
Jin and colleagues sequenced in 2026 the full genome of a virus pulled from caterpillars of Graphiphora augur. The moth's larvae defoliate forests across Eurasia and North America. The caterpillars were collected in Mongolia. The virus belongs to the granuloviruses, insect pathogens used as biological pest control. No baculovirus had ever been formally reported from this host before.

The genome is a circular strand of DNA 147,179 letters long. About 44 percent of its letters are G or C. It carries 167 predicted genes, including all 38 core genes shared across the family. Family-tree analysis placed it as a distinct species. Its closest relative is a granulovirus from the turnip moth, another crop pest. Microscopy confirmed the typical granular form that gives the group its name. A characterized new species adds a candidate weapon for forest protection and a data point for virus evolution.
pmc-13465145:
Carla S. Dos Santos and eleven colleagues published this 2026 study creating prostate cancer cell lines from sub-Saharan African patients. This group is hit harder by the disease yet has just one commercial cell model. Using conditional reprogramming, a technique that coaxes patient cells to grow in the lab, the team established three new lines from biopsies. They characterised them genetically, and screened them against a thousand compounds alongside European lines.

The three lines kept growing for up to 102 days. A fourth candidate was lost to cross-contamination. The drug screen exposed an ancestry-linked difference. The African-derived models were about nine times less sensitive to camptothecin, a topoisomerase I inhibitor, than the European lines. They responded the same to epirubicin, a topoisomerase II inhibitor. The authors argue that ancestry-diverse models can reveal ancestry-specific drug responses that a single-ancestry toolkit would miss, for fairer cancer research.
pmc-13465445:
Giap and co-authors assembled a chromosome-level genome of the Japanese cutlassfish in 2026 to settle long-running confusion in the hairtail family. These commercially important fishes have been repeatedly misclassified by appearance. The team paired the new genome with whole-genome resequencing of related species. Phylogenetic, demographic, and population genetic analyses were combined.

The assembly scored about 97 percent completeness on a standard gene check, with a GC content near 41 percent. The analysis confirmed Trichiurus japonicus and Trichiurus nanhaiensis as distinct species. It also exposed a cryptic, genetically distinct lineage, probably from the Indian Ocean. That lineage had been mislabeled as another species in earlier studies, likely through trade mixing. Within the Northwest Pacific, T. japonicus showed weak population structure and low local differences. Its numbers look stable through the ice-age swings of the Pleistocene, useful news for fishery planning.
pmc-13465545:
Fourie and Kempen explored in 2026 why South African shoppers so rarely buy pearl millet, a hardy native grain that could ease food insecurity. The grain is nutritious and grows with little input, yet stigma and low familiarity keep it off plates. The team asked consumers directly what they think of it and what might draw their eye in a store.

Small online focus groups revealed wide uncertainty: many shoppers had never cooked the grain, overlooked it on shelves, or held wrong ideas about it. Willingness to try it rose with clear price, appealing packaging, local origin, a trusted retailer, and quality cues on the pack. The authors argue that marketing and consumer education are the missing step if this climate-fit grain is to help feed the country.
pmc-13466745:
Guoqin Tao and colleagues report a fungal infection inside the eye of a man with severe liver failure, in a 2026 case report. The forty-four-year-old arrived with yellowed eyes lasting six weeks and steadily worsening vision. He carried long-standing hepatitis B that had tipped into acute liver failure, rated in the most severe class.

During his stay the left eye's vision dropped, and an eye exam suggested infection within the eyeball, possibly with the retina detached. Inflammation markers in his blood ran very high across several measures. The fungus blamed, Aspergillus fumigatus, can invade many body sites, and the authors focus on how their laboratory pinned down its identity.
pmc-13466845:
Lin and colleagues in China fed in 2026 mulberry leaf extract to grass carp, a top farm fish, to test if the plant add could firm the flesh. The team set 160 young carp in cages for eight weeks. One set ate plain feed, and three ate feed dosed at one, two, or four parts in a hundred. Growth, organ weights, flesh traits, and gene marks were read at the end.

Growth did not budge on any dose, but the fish trimmed fat round the gut and liver. Flesh grew firmer, springier, and paler on all dosed sets. Thaw drip loss and flesh fat fell, while the stretch protein that gives bite rose on the two high doses. Muscle strands packed tighter and thinner. The authors back the two high doses.
pmc-13466945:
Nguyen Quoc and colleagues guide doctors through gene testing for babies born with low thyroid hormone. The gland fault can be brief or can last for life. Gene finds can confirm the cause, shape care, and help advise the wider family.

Short case stories show when to test and how results change care. A gene result can set how long hormone pills are needed and at what dose. It can also flag linked health issues in other organs. Most cases of a missing or misplaced gland still show no gene fault. Testing thus aids some families much more than others.
pmc-13467245:
Shiqi Wang and colleagues identify a gene that marks cartilage turning fibrous in osteoarthritis, then show a common dietary compound dialing it down, in a 2026 study. The gene, RARRES1, surfaced from bulk and single-cell gene data as a signal of degeneration, and it ran high in patients' damaged cartilage regions. A lab fibrosis model in cartilage cells confirmed the pattern.

Silencing the gene relieved fibrosis in that model. The compound betaine lowered RARRES1 and encouraged repair toward smooth hyaline cartilage, the joint's proper surface. A second gene, RGS2, emerged as the channel through which betaine acts. Tests spanned dishes and animals, with protein checks, cell sorting, and tissue staining.
pmc-13467545:
Ibrahim Taha Albas and colleagues compare in 2026 three ways of stabilizing a worn lower spine: rigid fusion, flexible dynamic rods, and hybrid mixes of the two. Rigid fusion gives instant stability but loads the neighboring spinal segments, which can wear them out sooner. Dynamic and hybrid systems aim to keep more natural motion and reduce those fusion-related problems. The study reviewed 86 patients operated on between January 2017 and December 2021.

Patients fell into four groups by technique, covering titanium rods, flexible PEEK rods, and each combined with an interbody fusion cage. The team compared back and leg pain scores, motion at the treated and total spine level, disc and nerve opening heights, and fusion success. Their comparison speaks to a standing surgical question: how much stiffness a degenerating spine actually needs.
pmc-13467745:
Shinagawa and co-authors surveyed Japan's Paris 2024 Olympic delegation for this 2026 study. They asked how supplement use relates to professional nutrition guidance. Supplements are widespread in elite sport but risky. Tainted products can trigger anti-doping bans. The team asked whether athletes who had received dietitian support chose in other ways.

Eight hundred athletes, including Olympic candidates, reported their supplement intake over the past year. Overall, 92.3 percent of respondents used supplements. The share was much higher among athletes with nutrition support experience than among those without it. The supported group also used more proven sports foods. These foods sit in the Australian Institute of Sport classification. The pattern held after adjusting for age and sex. The authors recommend dietitians work within mixed teams when teaching supplement safety.
pmc-13467945:
Vasiliki Kaikiti and co-authors describe in 2026 a practical three-step route to hybrid molecules that join a cyclic monoterpene ring directly to an aromatic ring. Such natural hybrids show antimicrobial, anticancer, and cannabinoid-related activity, yet older syntheses lean on fragile organometallic intermediates and struggle to deliver certain three-dimensional shapes. The new method starts from terpene ketones taken from the chiral pool, so the shape information comes built in.

The route first converts the ketone into an enol triflate. It then links that intermediate to a range of aromatic building blocks through a Suzuki-Miyaura coupling. Finally, it hydrogenates the link with shape control to give the target hybrids. Computer screening then assessed how the products might fit the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2. A dependable route to these hybrids lets chemists make analogs that nature does not supply and test which shapes carry the useful biology.
pmc-13468445:
Prantika Datta and Rozalynne Samira review in 2026 how sorghum roots, microbes, and transporter proteins cooperate to feed the plant. Sorghum tolerates drought, heat, and lean inputs, yet its yields still suffer when nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium run short. The review starts with root shape and the sugary leaks from roots, which gather the root-zone microbiome, the community of microbes hugging the root.

It then details the membrane transporters that pull in nitrate, ammonium, phosphate, and potassium. It also profiles the microbe partners that help, from nitrogen fixers to fungi that trade nutrients with roots. The authors connect the chemical dialogue between root and microbe to the transporter genes each nutrient uses. For a crop grown where fertilizer is scarce, grasping this three-way partnership is the route to yields without heavy inputs.
pmc-13469645:
Zhang and colleagues feed young lambs D-serine, an amino acid supplement, in 2026 animal science research testing whether it speeds development of the rumen, the first stomach chamber where microbes ferment feed. Twenty healthy male Hu lambs were split into two groups of ten. The supplemented group received 2 grams of D-serine per kilogram of body weight daily from 7 to 48 days of age, while researchers tracked growth, feed intake, and gut development.

Supplemented lambs raised their average daily starter feed intake by 25.96 percent over the 30-day recording period compared with controls. Their rumens grew heavier and larger, with longer, wider, and denser papillae, the finger-like projections that absorb nutrients, while the muscle layer stayed unchanged. Fermentation strengthened too: propionate, an energy-rich acid, rose from 21.41 to 25.11 percent of total acids across the groups. Microbial diversity barely moved, though 248 metabolites differed between groups in the analysis.
pmc-13470245:
Li and colleagues compare two electrical treatments for acute shingles pain in a 2026 chart-review study from a single hospital. Shingles, caused by reactivated chickenpox virus, can leave lasting nerve pain called postherpetic neuralgia. The study covers 421 patients treated between 2020 and 2023 for acute or subacute zoster pain. Of these, 167 received short-term spinal cord stimulation, where a device sends pulses to the spine, and 254 received pulsed radiofrequency treatment near the nerve.

Both treatments cut pain sharply during follow-up, but stimulation worked faster. Responder rates at two weeks reached 80.2 percent with stimulation against 50.8 percent with radiofrequency treatment in the reported comparison. At one month the gap persisted, at 92.2 percent against 75.6 percent for the two groups. Lasting neuralgia developed in only 7.2 percent of stimulation patients, compared with 20.9 percent after radiofrequency treatment. Sleep improved more with stimulation, while daily functioning improved equally, and no permanent nerve damage occurred.
pmc-13470445:
Li and a team in China built in 2026 a tiny drug boat to calm ulcerative colitis, a chronic sore gut ill with no cure. Their mark was NETs, webs of DNA that white cells cast out to fan gut harm. An enzyme, DNase I, can chew those webs, but it breaks down fast in the body. The team packed it in a crystal cage. They then wrapped the cage in skins shed by germs, which home to sore spots.

In dishes and in sick mice, the wrapped pack found the sore gut and piled up there. It chewed the DNA webs down, curbed a stress path in gut cells tied to a gene called PTGS2, and helped the gut wall heal shut. Mouse guts showed less swelling and better form. The authors pitch the germ skin wrap as a soft way to land frail drugs on sore tissue.
pmc-13470545:
Liang and colleagues reported in 2026 that exposing father mice to polystyrene nanoplastics, tiny plastic particles, damaged the lungs of their offspring across generations. The lung harm resembled bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a chronic disease of early lung growth. Breeding exposed males gave three generations for study, and the team layered genome methylation, single-cell, and standard gene sequencing on offspring lungs.

Liang found first- and second-generation male offspring showed the typical lung damage pattern, while exposed fathers themselves had weaker sperm. The particles raised a methylation enzyme in fathers, spreading extra chemical tags across the sperm genome. One tag pattern, silencing a gene that guards mitochondria against iron overload, survived the usual wiping between generations. Offspring lungs thus ran low on that guard, free iron rose, and a form of iron-driven cell death injured the air sacs. Blocking the enzyme in fertilised eggs broke the chain.
pmc-13470745:
Juan Tarlera and co-authors investigate in 2026 why some charred wood materials strip lead from water far better than others. Biochar made from forest waste can clean heavy metals, and a mobile air curtain burner now produces it in the field with less smoke than open pile burning. Seven biochars from that burner showed lead removal ranging widely, from modest to very high per gram.

The team measured surface area, acidity, and mineral makeup, using X-ray pattern analysis to pin down calcium carbonate content. Carbonate content tracked removal capacity in a straight line, marking it as the main driver. After exposure, crystals of two lead carbonate minerals appeared in the used biochar. The picture points to chemical precipitation, lead locking into new minerals, as the cleanup mechanism.
pmc-13471945:
Cheng and colleagues present a 2026 water treatment design that cleans nanofiltration concentrate, the polluted leftover stream from advanced water filtering, using an electro-Fenton process. Standard versions struggle because oxygen supply is unstable and electrodes get wet through, especially in salty wastewater.

Their membrane cathode traps oxygen molecules in tiny wedge-shaped structures that boron nitride forms inside carbon nanotubes. This confinement keeps the surface from wetting and speeds the iron cycling that drives the chemistry, steering output toward singlet oxygen, a selective oxidant. Degradation ran five times faster than standard setups, and one test drug was fully removed within fifteen minutes. The system kept high efficiency through 48 hours of continuous running, including on real concentrate from a treatment plant.
pmc-13472145:
Jinlang Lyu and co-authors examine whether exposure to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons before birth changes how children grow in their first three years. These pollutants come from combustion and are widespread. Their 2026 study uses a prospective Chinese birth cohort and measures sixteen of the compounds in mothers' first-trimester blood.

Growth patterns were identified in 1,467 children, and exposure was measured in 333 mothers, alongside twenty maternal gene variants involved in processing these pollutants. Higher exposure raised the risk of a rapid, high growth pattern: slightly higher birth weight scores followed by fast infant growth that stayed high. Three compounds contributed most. The effect appeared only in mothers carrying certain versions of the AHR gene, a sensor for these pollutants. The authors argue for exposure reduction and targeted monitoring of susceptible mothers.
pmc-13472745:
Jia and colleagues report a 2026 study of a gene switch that worsens rheumatoid arthritis by driving a fiery cell death in joint lining cells. The switch, IRF1, was measured in patient joint tissue, arthritic mouse joints, and cultured lining cells stimulated with the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha. The team then blocked IRF1 and mapped which genes it controls.

IRF1 ran high in rheumatoid tissue and in stimulated cells. Suppressing it cut pyroptosis, the inflammatory bursting death, and lowered the inflammatory output of the lining cells. Gene mapping showed how the TNF signal, through its p65 relay, switches IRF1 on. Treating arthritic mice by modulating IRF1 eased disease severity. The chain gives drug hunters a defined axis to interrupt in a disease where lining cells act as aggressors, not victims.
pmc-13473145:
Yuyu Zhang and seven colleagues tested in 2026 whether cutting one amino acid from the diet could protect the kidneys of diabetic mice. Diabetic kidney disease is a leading complication of diabetes with few dietary treatments, and the role of gut microbes in kidney damage was unclear. Diabetic db/db mice ate a methionine-restricted diet for thirteen weeks, while the team tracked kidney function, gut bacteria, and short-chain fatty acids, the small molecules microbes make from fibre.

The restricted diet improved kidney function and tissue damage, restored gut barrier proteins, and lowered a bacterial toxin in the blood. Gut profiling showed more bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, with faecal propionate rising and its gut receptor recovering. Propionate tracked with stronger gut barriers and with lower kidney inflammation and oxidative stress. The authors present methionine restriction as promising, while noting mouse findings must be tested in people first.
pmc-13473245:
Nazli Begum Ozturk and co-authors review cases of acetaminophen overdose at a liver transplant center in 2026. Acetaminophen is a common pain drug that can cause sudden liver failure when taken in excess. Records covered 165 adults treated between 2011 and 2020. The team sorted cases by intent, mind health history, and need for transplant care.

About two thirds of patients had a known mental health condition alongside the overdose. Just over half of the overdoses were on purpose, while the rest came from error or overuse. Roughly half of all patients later needed inpatient mental health care. Eleven people died, and seven received a liver transplant. The findings press for joint liver and mental health care after overdose.
pmc-13473345:
Li and colleagues mapped in 2026 the kidney risk hidden inside mixed-type IgA vasculitis, a disease where inflamed small blood vessels harm several organs at once. Mixed-type cases are common but uneven, and which mixes threaten the kidneys most was unclear. The team reviewed patients treated at their hospital over seven years.

From about 2,800 records, 2,416 patients were kept, and about seven in ten had mixed-type disease. Kidney involvement varied sharply by mix, from about a quarter of one group to over three quarters of another. Mixes that included kidney signs at first visit carried the highest odds. Adding the mix type to a model built on routine data lifted its accuracy a great deal. The authors argue for sorting patients by mix early, so kidney checks match risk.
pmc-13473545:
Tengshen Jing and seven colleagues studied in 2026 how to stabilise bentonite, a swelling clay that weakens when wet and troubles roads and railways. Building on geopolymer methods, which bind soil with alkali-activated minerals, the team treated bentonite with fly ash and sodium hydroxide, varying fly ash, alkali concentration, and starting moisture. They then measured unconfined compressive strength. X-ray diffraction, infrared spectroscopy, and electron microscopy revealed the chemical and structural changes behind the strength gains.

Sodium hydroxide concentration mattered most, followed by moisture content and then fly ash content. Strength rose with alkali level up to an optimum, then fell. The authors explain this as competition between cation exchange and geopolymer gel formation, since too much alkali hinders gel growth. The work gives engineers a clearer recipe for treating expansive clay, with the optimum alkali dose as the key control, while noting laboratory mixes still need field validation.
pmc-13474145:
Lee and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how reactive oxygen species help drive high-grade serous ovarian cancer, the deadliest form of ovarian cancer. These species are unstable oxygen-based molecules that can damage cells, yet tumors also use them as signals. Ovarian cancer is often found late, returns after treatment, and learns to resist drugs, so each driver matters.

The review gathers 19 lab studies on cells grown outside the body. Pollutants that raise these species in ovarian surface cells also raised inflammation and DNA damage, priming cancer to start. In growing tumors, low oxygen and hormone signals used the species to switch on growth pathways. The species also helped cells spread and blunted platinum chemotherapy, partly by reshaping cell power plants. The authors point to antioxidants aimed at those power plants as a treatment idea.
pmc-13474245:
Stutts, Choe, and Fan drew in 2026 on a national health survey to show that fat children in the United States can still be short on key foods. Their set held 544 children aged three to eleven, from the 2021 to 2023 round of the NHANES survey, none on food pills. One in five met the mark for obesity. The team set food logs and blood vitamin D scores beside weight class.

Both groups ate near the same total food, protein, and fat each day. Set by body weight, though, the fat group took in far less protein. Their odds of falling short of the protein need ran more than five times higher. Blood vitamin D ran low in the same group, with odds of a low score more than three times higher. The authors call this hidden hunger inside full plates, and urge closer food checks.
pmc-13474545:
Hacer Eberlikose, Caner Ozturk, and Hakan Alpay Karasu gauge life quality after fixed implant teeth in 2026 for people with severe jaw shrinkage. Bone from the front hip was grafted into the upper jaw to hold implants steady. Twenty-eight patients answered two standard surveys before and after care, one on mouth-related life quality and one on general health. Scores were compared by sex and age as well.

Mouth-related life quality rose clearly after treatment, with women showing the largest gains. Men scored higher on some general health parts, such as physical role and overall health view. Age shaped general health scores but not mouth scores. Tailoring care to patient traits may lift gains further.
pmc-13474645:
Zhu and colleagues design an eco-efficient ultrasound treatment for toxic algal blooms in this 2026 study. Cyanobacterial blooms threaten drinking water because species such as Microcystis aeruginosa release potent liver toxins and organic matter when they die. Ultrasound alone can inactivate algae through cavitation, sound-driven bubble collapse, but it is energy-hungry. The team made an iron-modified bamboo biochar, a porous carbon, to amplify the ultrasound effect as a sonocatalyst.

Their best material, labeled BC-900-2, removed about 91 percent of the algae. The dose was 400 milligrams per liter. Treatment meant ten minutes of ultrasound, then thirty minutes of settling. Blocking experiments showed hydroxyl radicals were the dominant reactive species, since quenching them cut removal far more in the combined system than with ultrasound alone. The authors also discuss recovering value from the treated algal material.
pmc-13474745:
Lili Teng and five colleagues published this 2026 review on how gut microbes drive brain inflammation after stroke, and how that gut-brain loop might be treated. Stroke injures the gut as well as the brain: up to half of patients develop gut changes tied to slower recovery and higher mortality. The authors map the microbiota after stroke and the routes, immune, neural and hormonal, by which intestinal bacteria stoke or soothe inflammation in the brain.

They describe a feedback circuit: dysbiosis and leaky gut amplify inflammation that worsens brain injury. The stroke, through stress hormones and sympathetic activation, further disrupts the gut, closing a vicious cycle. Communication runs through immune cells, the vagus nerve, stress hormones and metabolites. Interventions aimed at the microbiota could damp inflammation and support neural repair. The review weighs strategies and their limits, and sets out what must be shown before clinic use.
pmc-13478045:
Bonilla and colleagues built a short homegrown survey for a busy private surgical practice in 2026, testing whether a brief form can track recovery as well as long standard questionnaires. Their survey asks about pain, function, and stress, plus a Net Promoter Score, the business metric asking whether patients would recommend the practice. Forms went out by email before surgery and again 120 days afterward, between 2021 and 2024.

The practice sent 2,908 surveys and received 439 matched pairs of before-and-after replies, with 101 patients across four high-volume operations forming the main analysis set. Pain scores improved significantly after every operation type, with test statistics above 3.4 in each group, and function and stress scores improved alongside pain. Patients rated the practice glowingly, giving a Net Promoter Score of 88.2 built from 400 promoters against only 13 detractors among respondents.
pmc-13478345:
Shafiqul Islam and colleagues report a 2026 study identifying loss of CDK10 as a marker that predicts response to drugs blocking its cousins CDK12 and CDK13. Those two kinases keep long genes, including DNA repair genes, fully transcribed, and blocking them can kill cancer cells. A genome-wide CRISPR screen across six breast and ovarian cancer models hunted for genes that change drug response.

CDK10 loss ranked at the top for boosting sensitivity to the blocker CTX-439. Follow-up tests in cell lines and mouse tumors confirmed stronger cell death and tumor control when CDK10 was missing. Without CDK10, drug-induced transcription shutdown lasted longer, and the transcription machinery returned to sensitive genes more slowly. The authors propose CDK10 testing to select patients, and possibly co-targeting it to deepen drug effects.
pmc-13478845:
Ye and colleagues in China traced in 2026 a gene chain that speeds clear cell kidney cancer, the most common and most deadly type of kidney tumor. Their hunt began with screens of tumor samples and gene banks. One switch gene, ETS1, stood far higher in tumor tissue than in sound kidney. The team then raised or cut the switch in cancer cells and in tumors grown in mice.

More ETS1 made cells grow, move, and spread with more force, and tumors in mice grew faster. The switch works by grabbing a brake gene, EGR2, and marking its protein for shredding. With the brake gone, a growth path called NOTCH runs free, since EGR2 once held it down through a partner switch. The authors name the three link chain a drug target: cut any link, and the growth path may stall.
pmc-13479545:
Águeda Molinos-Quintana and coauthors published a 2026 study tracking substance P, a nerve signaling molecule, during cytokine release syndrome after CAR-T cell therapy in children with leukemia. This inflammatory storm is the therapy's main toxicity, yet nerve-immune signals inside it were unexplored. Blood samples came from eighteen young patients with relapsed or resistant B-cell leukemia treated with tisagenlecleucel.

Substance P was measured before treatment and on days seven, fourteen, and twenty-eight, with extra draws during storm episodes when possible. The analysis follows how the molecule rises and falls against the timing and severity of the syndrome. Understanding neuropeptide behavior could reveal new ways to predict or calm this dangerous reaction. The work is set in real-world clinical care rather than a controlled trial.
pmc-13479945:
Zuyao Xiao and coauthors published a 2026 qualitative study of why patients with type 2 diabetes fail at home self-management before ending up in hospital. Good daily control of food, activity, and medication prevents complications, yet many patients arrive admitted after long lapses. Nineteen patients at a tertiary hospital in northeast China were interviewed between December 2025 and February 2026.

Analysis distilled 319 initial codes from the interview transcripts. The authors interpret the barriers through protection motivation theory, which weighs how people judge threats and their own coping ability. Fear without confidence, family habits that sabotage diets, and weak understanding of long-term risk all surfaced in the coding. The study aims to help discharge teams target the exact beliefs that undo home care.
pmc-13480245:
Sary Wedinly and co-authors present a 2026 series on clipping a leaky mitral valve in patients with very weak hearts, backed by a balloon pump. Five patients had severe leak from heart stretch rather than valve damage, with pumping strength ranging in the lowest band. All had been turned down for transplant or a mechanical heart pump, and landmark trials had shut out patients this ill.

A balloon pump in the main artery steadied blood flow during each clip procedure. Every placement succeeded, counting one patient who needed a second clip for a returning leak. All five left hospital in the top two symptom classes, and gains held at later checks. The pump may blunt the strain spike that follows clipping, the authors suggest, though five cases can only point the way for larger study.
pmc-13480345:
Ryskalin and a team in Italy probed in 2026 how shockwave care, sound pulses used to heal tissue, may spur muscle repair. One guess is that treated cells spew out exosomes, tiny bubbles that carry signals to their peers. The team zapped muscle starter cells, called myoblasts, in dishes and tracked the bubbles they shed. Counts were made at set hours, sizes were gauged, and fine photos checked the cells' insides.

Bubble counts spiked six hours after the pulse, then fell back to plain levels by twelve hours. Bubble size spread did not shift at all, so the dose changed how many were made, not their shape. Fine photos showed brisk bubble traffic and release in the zapped cells. The authors read the burst as a brief call to arms that could help explain how shockwave care aids muscle healing in the clinic.
pmc-13481945:
Sareh Yousefi and Mohammad Reza Daliri describe a 2026 method that reads brain wiring maps to spot multiple sclerosis during memory work. The team scanned 22 people, eight patients and fourteen peers, while they played a Persian letter memory game at three load levels. Brain maps across 116 regions fed six wiring measures into simple learning models, checked by leaving one person out at a time.

The hardest game level sorted patients from peers with accuracy above ninety-five percent using a support vector model. Three wiring measures carried the signal, covering how linked, how central, and how deep in the core each region sat. The cerebellum mattered at low load and a frontal region at high load, both fresh leads. Harder tasks exposed wiring gaps that rest scans miss, which may aid early checks.
pmc-13482645:
Nouf Ahmed Althumairi and co-authors present a 2026 study of zinc oxide particles boosted by two added metals. Zinc oxide serves sensors and electronics yet conducts modestly. The team baked powders with one percent aluminium and five percent calcium through a gel route with special drying, shrinking the crystal grains by nearly half as the lattice warped.

Tests showed heat-activated conduction in both pure and doped powders. Two ways of reading the energy barrier for charge hops landed close together, which points to one shared hopping route for conduction and relaxation. The doped powder cut resistance at grain borders, lifted charge mobility, and sharpened its response to electric fields. Dual doping thus tunes one cheap oxide for electronics, sensing, and energy parts without exotic steps.
pmc-13483545:
Yang and colleagues compared two testing strategies for Chinese patients with stable chest pain from narrowed heart arteries. One group went straight to angiography, an invasive camera procedure, while the other first had a perfusion scan that pictures blood flow to the heart muscle. Their 2026 study matched 130 patients in each group from an initial pool of over 7,000, then followed costs and heart events.

The scan-first group suffered 6 cardiac events against 16 in the direct-angiography group after matching. Fewer scan-first patients needed artery-opening procedures, with 5 against 12 in the comparison group. Heart attacks and deaths also ran lower in the scan-first group, though the counts were small. Total costs favored the scan-first route as well. Yang argues the scan acts as a gatekeeper, sparing low-risk patients an invasive procedure.
pmc-13483645:
Sana Hamidi and co-authors review two generations of laboratory-activated immune cell therapy for glioma, a deadly brain tumor family that includes glioblastoma. Their 2026 systematic review follows standard reporting guidance and searches four databases through August 2025. Earlier lymphokine-activated killer cells are compared with later cytokine-induced killer cells across survival, safety, and delivery routes.

Twenty-one studies qualified from 930 records, mostly small non-randomized designs, with glioblastoma the dominant tumor type. The earlier cell type was usually placed directly into the tumor cavity and lengthened survival, yet caused more complications, partly linked to a companion immune drug. The later cell type was usually given into a vein and acted without needing matched tissue types. The comparison helps clinicians judge where each approach still deserves testing.
pmc-13483845:
Nattapat Wongtirawit reports a 2026 randomized trial of blood filtering to strip inflammatory signals during septic shock in Thailand. Patients needing high-dose norepinephrine at two tertiary centers were assigned to standard care alone or standard care plus two three-hour sessions with the HA-330 adsorber. The main outcome was death within 28 days.

Recruitment stopped early at 128 of a planned 206 participants because enrollment ran slowly and funding ran short. Deaths by day 28 were 58 percent with standard care and 44 percent with added filtering, a gap that did not reach statistical significance. Organ support days, shock reversal, drug doses, and inflammatory markers also matched between groups. An adjusted exploratory model is reported in the full text, yet the early stop leaves the question genuinely open.
pmc-13483945:
Deng and colleagues designed a music teaching system that watches a learner's emotions and adapts lessons in real time. Ordinary music software follows a fixed script, ignoring frustration or boredom. Their 2026 system reads facial expressions, body signals, and interaction behavior, then picks teaching strategies meant to restore engagement and support emotional wellbeing. Three modern rival systems served as comparison benchmarks.

The adaptive system classified learner states with about 87 percent accuracy across the datasets used for testing. Its balanced error score and discrimination score also led the comparison systems in the reported results. The design loops emotion modeling, strategy choice, and personal feedback into one continuous cycle rather than grading at the end. Deng argues emotionally aware teaching tools can sustain motivation, while flagging fairness and accuracy risks when such systems judge real students.
pmc-13485345:
Minotti and colleagues laid out in 2026 a gap in trials of newborn sepsis, a severe infection in the first days of life. The trials lack a shared way to say who counts as a case. Adult and child sepsis care has agreed yardsticks that get updated over time. Newborn care has none that all sides accept. Signs in newborns are vague, blood tests find the germ in few cases, and risk shifts a lot by birth timing.

The authors trace 25 years of rival definitions and scores, and show how far apart they sit. Ward rules prize catching every case, so many babies with no infection get antibiotics anyway. That habit feeds drug resistance and stirs the young gut flora. For trials, entry rules must sit at one fixed check point, and weigh safety against sharp case picks made clear up front.
pmc-13486645:
Hiroki Furukawa and others hunt a weakness in cancer cells that survive KRAS-targeted drugs and later drive relapse. In 2026, the study studies pancreas and lung cancer cells carrying KRAS mutations, which enter a reversible tolerant state under drug treatment, halting division while rewiring their fuel use. Protein and metabolite profiling reveals broad changes linked to cell recyclers, the cell's recycling spaces.

Blocking glutamine fuel use and cell recycler function together selectively killed tolerant cells under KRAS blocking. Adding a metabolite called alpha-ketoglutarate rescued the cells, apparently by backing redox balance rather than by feeding the energy cycle. The authors propose co-targeting these two pathways during KRAS therapy to cut off the reservoir from which resistance grows.
pmc-13487345:
András Molnár and co-authors probe links among vertigo severity, sleep apnea, mood, and body weight in clinic patients. Published in 2026, the study enrolls 111 patients with sleep apnea accompanied by vertigo, using overnight breathing polygraphy plus dizziness handicap, depression, and broad symptom questionnaires. Sleep apnea severity is graded from the breathing recordings.

About one quarter ultimately showed no apnea, while two fifths were mild and one quarter severe on testing. Dizziness handicap tilted higher with severe apnea without reaching significance as a group difference. Regression flagged depression scores and obese body category as strong predictors of vertigo within the apnea group, albeit with very wide uncertainty ranges. Depression and anxiety symptom scores both correlated moderately with total dizziness handicap. Dizzy apnea patients deserve mood screening as routine.
pmc-13488145:
Zhan and colleagues built a mouse model of cervical cancer that spreads naturally to lymph nodes, then used it to find a helper cell that feeds metastasis. Many existing models lack a working immune system, distorting how cancers spread. Their 2026 study implanted glowing tumor cells into the cervix of immune-normal mice, tracked spread by light imaging, and profiled single cells in primary tumors and their lymph-node offspring.

A fibroblast subgroup marked C3-positive stood out in the metastatic tumors profiled by the team. Those support cells secreted a signal protein, GAS6, which switched on the AXL pathway in cancer cells, a known driver of invasion and drug resistance. Blocking that axis is a candidate strategy the model now makes testable. Zhan also offers the single-cell atlas as a resource for metastasis research.
pmc-13491645:
Federica Bevilacqua leads a twelve-author team reporting a 2026 survey of emotional distress in Italian women waiting for colposcopy after a positive cervical screening result. A closer examination follows an abnormal test, and the wait itself can be stressful even before any diagnosis. The team also asked whether trust within a woman's closest relationship softened that distress.

A total of 573 women at a Turin clinic completed questionnaires on depression, anxiety, stress, and relationship trust. Seven in ten reported at least mild stress symptoms, and higher trust in a partner was tied to lower risk across all three measures. Younger women and those with less education faced higher risk. The authors recommend screening support that is matched to each woman's risk and involves partners where helpful.
pmc-13491745:
Ernest Maya and seven co-authors adapt in 2026 three short questionnaires that measure whether health workers find an intervention acceptable, appropriate, and feasible. With midwives and family planning nurses in Ghana, they tested the adapted scales. The original scales were built in wealthy countries, and wording that fits one health system can misread another. The context was postpartum family planning counseling supported by a World Health Organization eligibility app.

Focus groups with eighteen providers reshaped the wording, and 150 midwives then completed the adapted survey. Reliability was strong across all three constructs, and the statistical structure held up after minor tweaks. Shorter versions of the scales, however, separated the three ideas more cleanly than the expanded ones. The authors advise balancing local adaptation against keeping the original measurement skeleton intact.
pmc-13491945:
Can Nacar and four colleagues trial in 2026 a nose-drop sedation method for yellow-legged gulls brought into wildlife clinics. Handling frightened wild birds for examinations and X-rays risks injury to bird and staff alike, and restraint itself is stressful. Sixteen gulls received a mix of diazepam and the pain reliever butorphanol, split between the nostrils, in this preliminary prospective evaluation.

Every gull reached adequate sedation, with deep sedation arriving at roughly eleven minutes in young birds and thirteen in adults. X-rays taken during that window were diagnostic quality and required no hands-on restraint or staff radiation exposure. Recovery and perching came back at around one hundred ten minutes. The authors call the protocol effective, gentle, and practical for routine wildlife diagnostics.
pmc-13492845:
Regena and colleagues report a 2026 study of antibiotic prescribing by community physicians in Chengalpattu, Tamil Nadu, India, . The World Health Organization's AWaRe system sorts antibiotics into groups by resistance risk. Phase one reviewed 680 prescriptions; phase two gave 28 physicians education plus audit and feedback on their own prescribing.

Audit and feedback means showing prescribers their own numbers against guidelines, a method known to shift habits better than lectures alone. The study gauged how far local prescribing matched the AWaRe framework before and after the intervention. Community practice is where most antibiotics are consumed in India, yet it is the least monitored setting. A low-cost loop of review, teaching, and personal feedback offers a practical lever against resistance that does not depend on new drugs or new laws.
pmc-13494045:
J. Swainson and colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of ketamine and esketamine used with psychotherapy for depression in adults. A scoping review maps what studies exist rather than pooling their results. The authors split the field into two models. Assisted therapy puts the drug's altered state and later talk-through of the experience at the center. Combined therapy runs standard talk therapy alongside the drug.

They found 47 studies, yet only four were randomized trials, and case reports made up a large share. Most work used the assisted model. The combined model had fewer but stronger studies, with three pointing to gains when ketamine was paired with cognitive behavioral therapy, a talk therapy that targets thought patterns. The review calls for better trials that describe the therapy model in full.
pmc-13494545:
Elena Kremneva and others develop a tumour-on-chip platform that tests drugs and immune cell giving under realistic vessel states. In 2026, the microfluidic system joins patient-derived tumour organoids with a working vessel lining barrier and liquid flow, recreating how drugs travel from blood vessels into tumour tissue. Tumour variety and resistance limit current therapies.

In pancreas cancer, the model captured resistance-linked cellular traits and pathway rewiring at one-cell detail, with drug responses trending toward patients' actual medical results in a small look-back exploratory analysis. The platform also assesses immune cell movement driven by tumour factors. Team gain a scalable tool for studying response mechanisms under physiologically constrained giving.
pmc-13495145:
Fuad A Abdu leads a 2026 cohort study comparing ten simple blood-based scores for insulin resistance as predictors of death in adults with high blood pressure. Insulin resistance, where the body answers insulin poorly, is tightly tied to hypertension. Some scores need a fasting insulin test and others do not, and no study had pitted them head to head across blood sugar levels.

The team used a national US health survey with 7,548 hypertensive adults grouped as normal sugar, prediabetes, or diabetes, and tracked deaths over about nine years. One insulin-based score predicted death across all three sugar groups. A non-insulin score called eGDR showed the strongest links overall, with top scorers far less likely to die. Another score, TyG, predicted death mainly in the diabetes group. The authors say cheap non-insulin scores can rival lab-heavy ones, which matters where insulin tests are hard to get.
pmc-13500345:
Pepper and colleagues tracked sales in 2026 of cigarettes containing WS-3, a lab-made cooling agent that chills the throat without a mint taste, after California banned menthol cigarette sales. Tobacco firms market such cigarettes as menthol stand-ins.
