Using retail scanner data for the Pacific division, which bundles California with Washington and Oregon, the team followed weekly sales from mid-2022 to early 2024.

WS-3 cigarettes appeared in the Pacific data about two weeks before the December 2022 ban took effect and were nearly absent elsewhere until the next spring. Most WS-3 sales, 87 percent, occurred in the Pacific division, peaking near nineteen thousand cartons a week. Menthol sales in the region fell by over a hundred thousand cartons a week within two months of the ban. The authors say the coolant cigarettes replaced only part of the menthol drop, leaving a net fall in flavored sales.
pmc-13500445:
Haimi Dang and colleagues test in 2026 a design trick for an African swine fever vaccine. An antibody tailpiece is attached to two viral proteins to make them more visible to the immune system. The disease devastates pig farming worldwide and still lacks an effective vaccine. Four lab-made proteins were produced in insect cells, pairing the two viral antigens in both orders, with and without the tailpiece borrowed from pig antibodies.

Tailpiece versions bound far more strongly to receptors on antigen-presenting cells, the sentries that display foreign material to the immune system. Mice immunised with those versions mounted stronger antibody and cellular responses than mice given plain antigens. Their blood serum also blocked a tagged version of the virus from infecting pig lung immune cells in dishes far more effectively, marking the fused designs as promising subunit vaccine candidates.
pmc-13500645:
Ben Ansbacher and others use information theory to connect gene levels shifts with growth stages in fruit flies. In 2026, the study applies entropy and tangle tests to public gene readouts data from whole Drosophila embryos across growth. It tests whether tiny gene action maps onto large form through a stats lens. Growth links time-tied reactions to likely body shape.

A measure called shuffle entropy of indexed groups tracked growth stages strongly and showed signs of one-way flow in gene readout tangle. The authors present this as a test case for linking marker numbers to growth shifts, hinting that information tangle can reveal how embryos are guided by chance through next body-form stages.
pmc-13500845:
Vandana Kumari and Susruta Samanta report a 2026 computational study of curcumin, the yellow compound from turmeric, and its possible direct interaction with NF-kappaB. That protein complex switches on genes involved in inflammation, and curcumin is known to dampen its signalling, mostly through indirect routes. The pair docked curcumin onto the p50 homodimer form of NF-kappaB, using a structure from the Protein Data Bank, and focused on the region that recognizes DNA.

Docking placed curcumin near the Rel homology domain with a score of minus 6.0 kilocalories per mole. A 100-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulation then showed the bound complex holding its local contacts and fluctuating less near the binding site than the unbound protein. The complex stayed compact, with a radius of gyration between 2.50 and 2.60 nanometres. Free-energy calculations using the MM-PBSA method indicated favourable binding driven mainly by van der Waals and electrostatic forces.
pmc-13501645:
Yong-Xiang Xie leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 methodological study that built a quality indicator system for newborn jaundice care. Jaundice affects most newborns, and badly managed cases can suffer permanent brain damage, yet care quality varies widely and no jaundice-specific nursing measure existed. The team followed Donabedian's structure-process-outcome model. A literature review and semi-structured interviews produced a draft, which 18 experts then refined through two Delphi rounds, a structured method for reaching expert consensus.

Response rates were 90.0 percent in the first round and 100.0 percent in the second. Expert authority coefficients, which grade how qualified the panel is, reached 0.851 and then 0.879 across the rounds. The finished system holds 3 first-level, 10 second-level, and 24 third-level indicators. The authors describe it as a standardized yardstick for auditing and improving jaundice care, while noting it still needs real-world testing before wide rollout.
pmc-13501845:
Gabrielle Pouilloux leads a four-author team with a 2026 review of whether people with high intellectual potential process sensations in extreme ways. Sharp senses are often claimed as a gifted trait, but no review had tested the claim. Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched six databases in December 2024 with terms joining sensory processing to high ability. Of 739 articles screened, twenty-one looked eligible and only five finally met the inclusion criteria.

Those five studies disagreed with one another. Their frameworks, constructs, and measuring tools differed so much that results could not be lined up, and none controlled properly for brain-development conditions that themselves alter sensation. Some reported reactivity differences, yet nothing converged. The authors conclude the literature does not support a generalized extreme sensory profile in high-potential people, and they ask future studies to standardize methods and characterize participants' thinking clearly.
pmc-13502845:
Cohen and colleagues review an unlikely tool for diseases of the gullet: ultrasound. The oesophagus hides behind air and bone along most of its length, so sonography was long dismissed for it, but the neck and upper abdominal stretches can be imaged. Point-of-care ultrasound is now widespread. Their 2026 review gathers what studies show across disorders, from the swallowing failure achalasia to reflux in infants.

Ultrasound separated achalasia patients from healthy people and from cancer patients in the cited work. Wall thickness tracked with dangerous swollen veins in patients with liver cirrhosis, hinting at a screening role that avoids endoscopy. It also spotted swallowed foreign bodies in adults and children. Infant reflux studies matched ultrasound findings against acid measurements, though adult reflux data are weaker. The authors blame slow adoption on missing standard protocols, reference values, and training rather than on the physics.
pmc-13503145:
Caroline Molins leads a five-author team describing a 2026 intervention that teaches emergency medicine residents the ultrasound-guided fascia iliaca block. The nerve block eases hip and femur fracture pain while sparing opioids. Formal teaching of the block lags its clinical value, so the team built a curriculum. It opens with a thirteen-minute video with pre- and post-tests. Then a workshop rotates residents through scanning stations and needle practice on ballistic gelatin models, closing with an examination and survey.

Fifteen residents at a university level I trauma centre completed the programme. Knowledge scores climbed from 58.9 percent before the intervention to 78.4 percent after it on the reported testing, a significant gain. Among the nine residents answering the survey, every one reported confidence and preparedness to perform the block. The authors present the low-resource, reproducible format as a way to fold regional anaesthesia into residency training.
pmc-13503445:
Wilhelm Haverkamp, Gerhard Hindricks, and Nils Strodthoff write a 2026 German-language commentary warning cardiologists not to be seduced by the headline scores of AI electrocardiogram tools. Modern algorithms read a standard twelve-lead ECG and claim to spot weak heart muscle, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, amyloidosis, and high potassium. Some even forecast rhythm disorders before they appear, all with sensitivity, specificity, and curve areas labelled excellent. The authors argue those numbers answer the wrong question.

What a test result means for one patient depends on pretest probability, the chance the disease was present before testing. Bayes' theorem shows the trap: applied where disease is rare, even superb algorithms mint false positives in bulk, with clinical, psychological, and economic fallout. Knowing your patient population's epidemiology is therefore part of reading the ECG. The piece closes by prescribing partnership: AI output weighed by clinical judgement, never adopted uncritically.
pmc-13503745:
Perez L Kemeni Kambiet leads a study of how traits of character shape worry about climate risk among grain farmers in Morocco, in a 2026 paper. Feeling at risk is a step toward acting on climate threats, yet its roots in character are little known outside rich Western settings.

The team linked survey data from farming households to the five broad traits used in psychology. Calm, steady character went with less climate worry. Outgoing and open character went with more worry. Broader trait blends showed the same split, and one blend tied to social harmony showed a U-shaped link, with worry lowest at mid levels. The authors stress the links are patterns, not proof of cause, and urge climate messages tuned to these gaps.
pmc-13503845:
Huaize Pan, Yuexia Lv, and Wenfeng Bai present a self-tuning fix for errors in computer-guided lathe work, in a 2026 paper. Heat, tool wear, and cutting force all bend parts out of shape as a lathe runs. Fixed corrections made ahead of time cannot keep up with those shifting faults.

Their setup pairs two smart tools in a loop. A genetic search tunes the broad settings, while a learning agent adjusts cuts in real time as it works. On a hard titanium alloy used in aircraft, the mean error fell to a few micrometers, with most of the fault removed. The pair learned faster than the agent alone and beat three rival methods on error scores. Accuracy faded when cut settings drifted far from training.
pmc-13504745:
Reda Rhellab leads a team laying out a method to estimate extra deaths in a disease group when only summary data exist, in a 2026 methods paper. Extra mortality compares deaths in the group with a matched general population. Standard models need patient-level records, which are often locked away.

Their method runs a microsimulation, a model that follows many fake patients over time, and tunes it until its survival curves match the observed ones. A golden section search, a smart interval-cutting method, finds the best fit fast. Applied to aortic valve repair in younger adults, the method gave an overall excess risk near 2.7, which rose across time bands. Code in R is shared with the paper.
pmc-13507245:
Lan Zhao leads a 2026 team that builds a layered nanovesicle, dubbed a nanoconcentrisome, to restore bone repair in aged female rats. Profiling of healing bone showed deep loss of SAM, a molecule that donates methyl tags controlling gene activity. Without it, aged tissue loses epigenetic order, meaning stable control of which genes stay on or off.

Their carrier wraps stem cell vesicles inside SAM-loaded shells that fuse directly with target cells, dodging waste compartments. In immune macrophages it calmed inflammation and improved debris clearance, while in aged stem cells it restored gene control, energy organelles, and bone building. Defect repair improved markedly in rats. Cell-free precision delivery may counter age-linked healing failure.
pmc-13507345:
Tingshuai Ma leads a 2026 team that captures the first detailed structures of the human receptor OXGR1 bound to its two natural activators. The receptor sits in kidney tubules and in airway lining, where it senses leftover products of cell metabolism and helps the airways mount an early defense against germs. Its activators are alpha-ketoglutarate, a key step in the cell energy cycle, and itaconate, a substance immune cells make.

Frozen electron microscopy shows both activators docked in the receptor pocket with its signaling partner attached, exposing the grip points and the shape shifts that turn the receptor on. Tests with related small acids mapped which chain lengths and chemical groups the pocket accepts or rejects. Activity peaked at the normal body pH of 7.4, which suits the kidney setting well. Drug designers gain a clear blueprint for compounds aimed at kidney stones and related disorders.
pmc-13508245:
Marie Martin leads a thirteen-author team describing a train-the-trainer program built to lift teaching quality at Liberia's health sciences university, in 2026 work. The university has faced turmoil, disease outbreaks, and staff shortages over past decades. Leaders picked faculty teaching skills as a top fix in 2018. The team created a teaching center and ran the course in three rounds. Unusually, trainers came from the same city and country, a South-South model that kept expertise local instead of importing it.

Surveys across the three rounds showed large gains in how participants rated their own teaching knowledge. Gains spanned eleven skill areas covering teaching, learning, and assessment. The authors read two lessons from the results. Local peer trainers can build skills effectively, and they also create a supportive culture that pushes change. The model offers a template for other low-resource schools that must grow their own trainers.
pmc-13508345:
LiLi Guo leads a ten-author team studying what pushes depressed teenagers who self-injure toward planning suicide, in 2026 work. Suicide planning marks a dangerous step in the path toward an attempt. The study covered 100 adolescents with depression and non-suicidal self-injury. A standard interview item recorded suicide planning in the past month. Surveys and interviews scored stressful life events, insomnia, depression, anxiety, and past attempts. Combined models then weighed which factors held an independent link to planning.

Fifty-seven of the teenagers reported planning within the past month. That group carried heavier stress exposure, worse sleep, and stronger depression and anxiety than the rest. Stressful events also tracked closely with insomnia burden. In the full model, stressful life events and depressive symptoms each stayed independently tied to planning. The findings argue for screening that weights life stress and mood depth heavily when judging risk in this group.
pmc-13508445:
Karli Gilbert, Amrita Cheema, Henry Kaminski, and Linda Kusner use blood protein reading plus machine learning to predict who will respond to myasthenia gravis treatment, in 2026 work. This autoimmune disease weakens muscles, and patients answer treatments unevenly. Blood came from a phase 3 trial that compared thymus surgery plus steroids against steroids alone, plus matched healthy controls. Proteins were read by a high-throughput method at trial entry. Learning models then linked starting protein patterns to clinical change six months later.

Enriched pathways covered complement attack, antibody production, and T cell signaling. Each treatment arm had its own predictive protein panel. The surgery arm's model leaned on tangled, non-linear protein links, while the steroid-only model was mostly additive. Predictive proteins clustered around T cell signaling and white cell movement. The authors say such panels could one day guide who should get surgery, pending outside validation.
pmc-13508545:
Ebru Ayman Kılıç, Abdullah Atli, and Funda Gümüş compare spiritual wellbeing, death anxiety, and life satisfaction in heart artery patients and the relatives who care for them, in 2026 work. The study ran at a cardiology clinic in Mardin, Türkiye, in late 2024 and early 2025. It enrolled 233 patients and 233 primary caregivers. Each person completed three standard scales covering the three themes. Patients averaged near fifty-seven years old, while caregivers averaged near thirty-nine.

Death anxiety tied weakly but clearly to lower life satisfaction in patients and caregivers alike. Caregivers, strikingly, carried higher death anxiety than the patients themselves. Being the patient or the caregiver mattered less for life satisfaction than the anxiety and spiritual scores did. The authors argue that clinics should screen and support caregivers' fears as part of heart care. Spiritual wellbeing support may also lift satisfaction for both sides of the care pair, they suggest.
pmc-13508745:
Lee and co-authors turn ordinary microneedle patches, the painless skin arrays, into devices that can read molecular handedness. Chirality, whether a molecule is left- or right-handed, decides how drugs behave, and microneedles sit at dimensions suited to terahertz light. Their 2026 team coated commercial needles with two gold layers sprayed at a glancing angle, giving each needle a twisted, non-symmetric cap that interacts with light in a handed way.

The arrays produced strong terahertz circular dichroism signals, the signature of chiral light response, and rotated polarisation by up to several degrees. When the team dusted the needles with left- and right-handed cystine crystals as stand-ins for chiral drugs, the crystals' internal vibrations coupled with the needles' own resonances. The spectra shifted in a handedness-dependent way. A modified coupled-mode theory reproduced the effect quantitatively.
pmc-13510045:
Zhenwei Song, Liujiang Song, and Hua Mei present a laboratory protocol paper, published in 2026. It covers peeling the corneal endothelium cleanly out of mouse eyes. This is the single cell layer that keeps the cornea clear. No established method existed. This limited mouse studies of corneal endothelial disease. The team refined a mechanical peeling technique. A dissecting microscope guided the work.

They worked from a small flap at the rim. The whole endothelial sheet was peeled away with its membrane. It was digested into single cells. Purity exceeded ninety-five percent. Yields ran to several thousand cells per eye. This held for young and old mice. Viability was high. The sheet can also be dried flat for spatial gene studies.
pmc-13511545:
Xue and colleagues examined in 2026 how brain network control differs across healthy ageing, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease. They built directed brain networks from multimodal scans, meaning networks where signals flow in set directions between regions. They then asked which regions drive the network and how easily it can be steered, a property called controllability.

Default-mode regions acted as common drivers across all groups. MCI added sensorimotor drivers, and Alzheimer's added frontoparietal drivers, giving each stage a distinct driving pattern. Controllability rose and fell in a non-monotonic pattern across the three stages at whole-brain scale. The authors suggest control architecture changes mark disease stage. They propose the framework for characterising decline and call for longitudinal studies to test whether the patterns predict who worsens.
pmc-13511645:
Ashraf Kakoo, Dara K. Mohammad, Ahmed Yassin, Taban K. Rasheed, and Mustafa Al-Attar study natural killer cell subsets and infections in people newly diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer, in 2026 work. Infection is the chief driver of illness and death in this disease. Blood from 47 patients was profiled for two killer cell subsets, one tuned for signal release and one tuned for direct killing, and patients were screened for infections.

Patients carried more killer cells overall than healthy controls, yet the balance had shifted toward the signaling subset and away from the killing subset. About a third of patients had infectious complications, split between viral and bacterial causes. Patients who developed infections showed lower killer cell shares, while those without infections sat at the high end. The authors advise close infection watch in this group and deeper study of the subset shift.
pmc-13512645:
Laura Amicone, Carla Cicchini, Fabio Petti, and Alessandra Marchetti review two partner proteins, YAP and TAZ, as the central hub steering a cell identity program called epithelial-mesenchymal transition, in 2026 work. In this program, sheet-like epithelial cells loosen into wandering mesenchymal forms, a shift now seen as a sliding scale with hybrid states rather than an on-off switch. The pair reads mechanical, chemical, and metabolic cues from the cell's surroundings.

Through loops that feed forward and back with transition pathways, the hub locks in flexible states and runs context-fit gene programs. The same machinery serves embryo growth and wound repair, yet it also drives organ scarring and cancer spread when misused. The authors propose the hub model as a guide for drugs that would tune cell plasticity, aiming to block harmful shifts while sparing healing ones.
pmc-13513045:
Ahmed and co-authors reported a 2026 field study on forecasting generations of the Egyptian cotton leafworm, a moth pest that strips leaves from cotton and many other crops. Farmers in Egypt often react after damage appears because adult flight timing is hard to predict. The team tested a degree-day model, which adds up daily heat to time insect development.

Over three seasons from 2017 to 2019 in Assiut, Ahmed set pheromone traps that lure male moths and compared catches with model predictions. Trap peaks closely matched the emergence times the heat sums forecast from earlier laboratory values. Six successive generations followed the overwintering generation each year. The authors conclude the degree-day model is reliable enough to time pest management before larvae surge.
pmc-13515645:
Adli and colleagues reported in 2026 that a protein called DCDC2C shows up far less in the tails of sperm from men whose sperm swim poorly. Weak sperm movement, named asthenozoospermia, is the most common known cause of male infertility. The protein helps steady the tiny tubes that give the sperm tail its shape and beat.

The team studied sperm samples from 60 men and stained them to see where the protein sits. In men with normal sperm, about four in five sperm carried the protein on the tail. In men with weak movement, fewer than one in five did. Other measures, such as DNA damage in sperm and the chemistry of semen fluid, did not differ between the groups. The authors propose the protein as a marker test for this cause of infertility.
pmc-13515745:
Amedeo Lonardo and Ralf Weiskirchen review, in a 2026 article, the staged metabolic rewiring that drives fatty liver disease tied to metabolism, known as MASLD. The disease runs from simple fat build-up to inflamed, scarred liver and, in some, cancer. The authors argue that each stage reflects a deeper rewiring: fat overflows the liver, disposal routes falter, mitochondria strain, and stress signals feed inflammation and scarring.

Chemical profiling of blood and tissue finds recurring signatures. Harmful fats such as diacylglycerols and ceramides pile up, while protective polyunsaturated fats and related lipids drain away. Bile acids, amino acids, and gut microbe products shift in step. Layering these maps with imaging and genetic data could sort patients into true biological subgroups and track treatment response without biopsy. The authors caution that standard methods and long, multi-centre validation must come before precision liver care is real.
pmc-13516845:
Mengxi Wang and six colleagues compare nine calcium supplements head to head in a 2026 study spanning lab dishes and animals. Products differ in chemical source, physical form, and added ingredients, and those choices may decide how much calcium the body keeps. The team measured release in fluids mimicking the stomach and gut. They tracked calcium through rat blood, urine, and faeces, and tested bone protection in mouse and rat models of bone loss and calcium shortage.

One product, coded CS-1, released its calcium fast and nearly fully in stomach-like fluid and kept a favourable profile through gut-like conditions. Rats retained more of its calcium, and its bone gains were the most consistent across strength and structure measures. A salmon-bone ingredient inside CS-1 showed activity of its own, which may explain part of the edge. The authors link the win to the liquid form plus that functional ingredient.
pmc-13519245:
Michael Marks-Hultström leads a ten-author reply in 2026 defending cystatin C-based staging of acute kidney injury in critically ill patients. Two commentators had raised methodological worries about the group's earlier study: possible selection bias, steroid effects on the marker, and risks of overmonitoring. The reply answers each point in turn.

Excluding patients whose markers were falling, the authors argue, defines the population where staging is a real clinical question rather than inflating risk. Steroid-driven false upstaging cannot explain why reclassification improved mortality prediction in both directions. Kidney guidelines, they note, never base dialysis decisions on stage alone. The authors agree a prospective trial with defined thresholds is the definitive test, which their study helps set up.
pmc-13520345:
Hisashi Ukawa and colleagues examine in 2026 how wide genetic testing changed inherited kidney cyst disease in cats across Japan. A known variant in the PKD1 gene is the main test target, and breeders have used kitten testing since 2019 to guide mating choices.

Datasets covered more than 110,000 insured cats and nearly 62,000 tested cats across 14 breeds. Most cats with cystic kidneys carried the known variant, though sequencing found other possible genes too. Carrier frequency fell by over two fifths between 2019 and 2022. The authors argue that testing curbed the variant without narrowing breeding so far as to cause inbreeding harm.
pmc-13520445:
Jing Chen and colleagues report in 2026 that a lipid kinase called PIK3C2A acts as a brake on liver cancer spread, contrary to a simple growth-promoter role. Liver cancer kills largely through metastasis, so brakes on spread are valuable drug clues.

Levels of the kinase were often low in human liver tumours, while low levels tracked with stronger growth signalling, worse survival and more aggressive features. Removing the kinase made cancer cells invade more in dishes and spread more in animals, while restoring it reversed those effects. Lipid shifts that activate a partner protein explain the chain. Blocking that partner curbed the extra invasion.
pmc-13521145:
Víctor Joaquín Escudero-Saiz and colleagues test in 2026 whether common drugs can knock protein-bound toxins off blood albumin during dialysis, freeing them for removal. Two toxins of this type resist standard dialysis and track with heart deaths in kidney patients.

Twelve chronic dialysis patients each underwent six session types in crossover fashion, covering standard treatment, high-flux dialysis, oral water pills, infused water pills and infused ibuprofen. Only infused ibuprofen clearly boosted toxin removal, reaching about two thirds for one toxin. Water pills by either route brought no significant gain. No acute harms appeared in the opening summary, though wider safety testing remains essential.
pmc-13521945:
Kiran Bharadwaj Vedula, Rajesh Arunachalam and Sumanth Venugopal mix in 2026 farm sensors, blockchain logs and a hybrid learning model. Jobs cover plant disease calls, pest finds and smart watering. Field data safety and call accuracy were joint design goals.

Sensor reads land on an Ethereum chain first. The tuned network then reads the data for each farm job. Disease call accuracy hit about 94 percent. Pest finds scored close on accuracy and catch rates. Watering error scores are listed with the main results. A bird-inspired search tuned the network settings. The full design targets small farms that need trusted auto advice.
pmc-13522345:
Mingming Wang and colleagues simulate in 2026 staged screw removal from external locking plates for shattered lower shin fractures, seeking fixation that starts rigid then loosens as healing callus matures. Computer models spanned four healing stages under body-weight-scale load.

Seven screw layouts plus fibula status were compared on movement, stress shielding and stresses in callus and plate. Early healing moved excessively even with full screws, arguing for protected weight bearing. By three months every layout held sub-millimetre movement, while dropping from four screws to two cut shielding and raised callus stress by about one seventh. An intact fibula cut movement and plate stress by half or more.
pmc-13522545:
Kshitiz Paudel, Sonika Patial, and Yogesh Saini test whether an earlier ozone injury changes later lung responses in mice in a 2026 study. Ground-level ozone is a common air pollutant that inflames airways. One group of mice received a single strong ozone exposure, recovered for three weeks, and then faced nine days of repeated lower exposures, while comparison groups received only part of that sequence.

Mice with only repeated exposure developed an allergic-type response, with more eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, and more mucus-producing cells. Mice with the earlier injury showed a blunted version of that response, with fewer eosinophils and lower levels of several signaling proteins. Prior injury therefore reshapes later inflammation, a point relevant to people facing repeated pollution peaks.
pmc-13523145:
Issey Agredano and colleagues report a severe heart complication during treatment with an allergy drug in a 2026 case report. A sixty-four-year-old man developed chest pain, breathlessness, very high levels of eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, and body-wide symptoms three months after starting dupilumab for a type 2 inflammatory condition. Heart imaging showed weakened pumping, and a heart muscle biopsy confirmed eosinophilic myocarditis, inflammation driven by those cells.

Treatment with high-dose steroids and a strong immune-suppressing drug brought rapid improvement. The authors discuss evidence that such biologic therapy may unmask an underlying vessel inflammation disease rather than directly cause it. They urge careful monitoring of eosinophil counts and prompt heart evaluation, including biopsy when needed, if new systemic or cardiac symptoms appear.
pmc-13523245:
Türkan Sezen Erhamza and colleagues compare three appliances that advance the lower jaw in growing patients in a 2026 orthodontic study. Forty-five young people with a class II bite pattern, where the lower jaw sits back, were treated in equal groups. Treatments were a twin block, a monoblock, or a clear aligner system with advancement features. X-ray measurements of skeleton, teeth, and soft tissue were taken before and after treatment.

All groups improved on bite and jaw measures, with no significant differences in soft tissue change. The aligner group showed less increase in vertical face measures and stronger correction of upper front tooth tilt. Lower front tooth tilting was greatest with the twin block. Jaw advancement itself was similar across groups, supporting the aligner as a comparable option with some distinct tooth effects.
pmc-13523345:
Hongzhao Wang, Yabing Jiang, Xiao Wang, and Tianyun Zhao compare doing both knees at once versus in stages in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Fifty-three cohort studies covering more than half a million patients with arthritis in both knees were pooled from five databases for studies published since 2000. All included evidence was observational, which shapes how the mortality comparison should be read.

Simultaneous surgery was linked to higher reported short-term mortality, more deep vein clots, and far greater transfusion needs. Hospital stay tended to be shorter with the one-stage approach, especially in Asian studies. Staged surgery, by contrast, carried higher rates of superficial and deep infection. Revision, lung clot, nerve, and heart outcomes did not differ clearly. The authors advise individualizing the choice around patient health and preferences.
pmc-13524745:
Kieran Dalton, Ciara Kenny, Maeve Culhane, and Robert Callaghan survey, in a 2026 study, Irish community pharmacists' views on prescription transfer through a national secure email system. A law in April 2020 allowed doctors to send prescriptions straight to pharmacies by Healthmail. The team asked how the change shaped care delivery and workflow.

An online survey went to all community pharmacists in November 2020 and drew 494 responses. About nine in ten agreed the method was quick and handy, most said it fit into dispensary work, and three quarters chose it over other routes. Almost all called it a positive step. Concerns included finding senders and handling patient expectations on timing. Most pharmacists felt patients lacked information about the system and seemed less part of decisions about their care.
pmc-13524945:
Sara Iftikhar and others extract and study, in a 2026 study, a natural dye from wild pomegranate peel from the Western Himalayas of Pakistan. Textile dyeing leaves heavy effluent, and plant dyes are a safer choice that breaks down in nature, unlike synthetic colorants. The peel of this wild fruit had not been studied for dye use before.

The extract went through screening plus ultraviolet, infrared, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis, which found 51 compounds with strong color promise. Dyed cotton was tested with three mordants, agents that fix color, against unmordanted fabric, and color values and fastness were taken. Infrared work showed dye compounds binding to cotton. Antioxidant testing was positive, and cell assays checked for harm. The authors propose uses across cloth, food, cosmetics, and medicines.
pmc-13525845:
Nabbout and co-authors test whether a tooth-development gene switches on as dental stem cells mature. Their 2026 paper grows from Lebanese family studies of inherited missing teeth, which flagged two candidate genes, CACNA2D2, a calcium channel subunit, and TRIO. The team cultured dental pulp stem cells and stem cells from shed baby teeth, then drove the pulp cells toward odontoblast-like cells, the dentine makers, over 21 days.

The channel gene rose about threefold during that maturation, a statistically clear increase across five replicate experiments. Its resting level was also about sevenfold higher in the baby-tooth stem cells than in pulp stem cells. TRIO, by contrast, showed no significant differences in either comparison. The authors conclude the calcium channel subunit, but not its fellow candidate, tracks with tooth-forming differentiation, strengthening its candidacy in the missing-teeth families.
pmc-13526145:
Mai Hatano leads a very large team in a 2026 PET imaging study mapping how AMPA receptor density in the living human brain changes with age and sex. These receptors carry fast excitatory signaling and support learning, yet their distribution across the lifespan was uncharted. The tracer used binds AMPA receptors and allows direct measurement.

The study imaged 143 healthy volunteers aged twenty to seventy-nine and related receptor density to scores on a standard neuropsychological battery. Age-related differences appeared across most brain regions. Women in their fifties showed a striking surge in receptor upregulation, and clustering revealed five distinct regional aging trajectories with marked sex dependence. Higher density tracked with better cognitive performance, and delayed memory correlated with whole-brain density in both sexes, while other domains showed sex-specific regional links.
pmc-13526845:
Du and colleagues report a 2026 study of how chronic liver fluke infection scars the liver, using the fluke Clonorchis sinensis in mice.  The team mapped immune cells in the liver over the course of chronic infection.

A population of resident memory CD8 T cells built up in the liver and drove the damage. These cells release chemokines, signal proteins that call in more immune cells and switch on scar-forming fibroblasts. Removing CD8 T cells at set phases clearly eased inflammation and scarring, proving their causal role. One chemokine, CCL4, mostly from these cells, tracked fibrosis severity in mice and in patient samples. A blood marker that mirrors liver scarring could let doctors monitor this infection without biopsies.
pmc-13527945:
Farhat Ul Ain and six colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of health workers in Pakistan and what shapes their willingness to deliver rehabilitation in primary care. Interviews held in mid-2024 covered 61 providers across five job types in Thatta and Swat, two districts in different provinces, and the analysis used the theory of planned behavior.

Many providers began skeptical, then warmed to rehabilitation after watching patients regain function. Peer encouragement, including through WhatsApp groups, kept motivation up, while cultural attitudes and gender stigma held wider uptake back. Training and job aids boosted confidence, yet heavy workloads, time pressure, and scarce assistive devices limited what providers felt able to sustain.
pmc-13528045:
Amin Taheri-Garavand and three colleagues fine-tune herbicide use in faba bean fields in western Iran in a 2026 study. They used a statistical method called response surface modeling. The herbicide imazethapyr was sprayed at rates from zero to 1,000 milliliters per hectare. Timing ranged from before planting to after sprouting. One season, 2024 to 2025, was studied.

Middle rates, 250 to 500 milliliters, worked best when applied near planting or just after sprouting. Those settings boosted canopy growth, pods, seed weight, and grain yield. Weed biomass fell at the same time. Higher rates or late spraying hurt the crop despite better weed control. The models predicted leaf area and seed weight very well. The authors present the method as a decision aid for precise spraying.
pmc-13528145:
Mengjia Yi and five colleagues survey nursing interns in Guangxi, China, about artificial intelligence in a 2026 study. The 259 interns were in final clinical placements at seven hospitals. Data came in mid-2025 through an online form. It scored views on AI, belief in one's creative power, and problem-solving skill. The three ideas were tested for links.

Average AI attitude sat mid-range at about forty-eight points. Creative self-belief averaged about twenty-nine. Problem solving averaged about eighty. All three measures rose and fell together. Sex, study program, creative belief, and problem solving each tied to AI views on their own. The authors stress these are links, not causes. They suggest training that builds creative confidence may warm interns to AI tools. Programs could also teach AI through problem-solving tasks.
pmc-13530145:
Wang and colleagues presented EmitGCL, a deep learning system that predicts whether a cancer will spread, in a 2026 multi-omics study. The study combines gene activity, protein, and other molecular data layers. Spread, or metastasis, causes most cancer deaths, yet clinicians lack tests to foresee it, partly because the responsible cells can hide below imaging detection.

Wang benchmarked the system against rival tools across six cancer types in seven patient cohorts and reports better sensitivity and specificity throughout. In one breast cancer patient declared disease-free by scans and lymph node checks, the system flagged metastatic cells that later proved real. It nominated heat-shock proteins HSP90AA1 and HSP90AB1 as markers. Tests showed blocking HSP90 slowed breast cancer cell migration, a result supported in five cohorts totaling 420 patients. A second candidate, the transcription factor YY1, was confirmed as a spread driver in cell and mouse experiments.
pmc-13530345:
Nádia Gonçalves Ferreira and co-authors compare in 2026 licensed artificial intelligence software with radiologists reading prostate MRI scans. The study drew on a referral center where cancer was unusually common among scanned men. Biopsy results, plus surgery findings for many, judged every reading.

Of 959 men, about 86 percent held significant cancer. The software gave fewer uncertain middle scores than radiologists, traded some sensitivity for higher specificity, and matched overall curve performance. Among men who later had surgery, the software missed more significant cancers. The authors present a close contest with a caution about missed disease.
pmc-13530745:
Chopra and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 207, early outcomes of split anconeus fascia transfer. This repair for chronic elbow instability uses the patient's own fascia rather than a harvested tendon graft. The condition, posterolateral rotatory instability, follows injury to the lateral ulnar collateral ligament.

The single-surgeon series compared 11 transfer patients with 30 patients who had conventional ligament reconstruction using donor or own tendon grafts between 2010 and 2023. The transfer group had one complication, nonspecific chronic pain, and no recurrent instability, and every patient returned to work. The reconstruction group had complications in about a quarter of patients, and four patients, about thirteen percent, suffered recurrent instability, though none in either group re-injured the elbow. Motion after surgery was similar and non-inferior in the transfer group.
pmc-13531745:
Nicholas Bakewell and co-authors follow in 2026 whether injecting the painkiller hydromorphone raises heart valve infection risk for people who inject drugs in Toronto. Health records linked to a supervised injection cohort of 514 people allowed one year of follow-up. Groups were set by which opioids participants reported injecting recently.

Infection rates stayed low in every group, between roughly two and three cases per hundred person-years. Adjusted comparisons found no clear excess for hydromorphone against other prescription opioids or other drugs. Wide uncertainty from few events limits the verdict, and the authors call for larger cohorts.
pmc-13531845:
Felister Apili and colleagues gather in 2026 the views of Ugandan mothers cared for at home by midwifery students through pregnancy, birth, and the weeks after. Eighteen postnatal women in Lira city gave in-depth interviews about the continuous care from one university program between April and August 2024.

Four themes organized their accounts: the care experience itself, empowerment through knowledge and skills, easier entry into the health system, and a fresh approach to care. Women praised steady information they had missed in earlier births and wished the program to continue. Stakeholder backing is needed for survival.
pmc-13533845:
Huang and co-authors identified a 2026 immune pathway fuelling drug refractory epilepsy, where seizures resist available medicines. About a third of people with epilepsy reach that state, including most with Dravet syndrome, a severe genetic form starting in infancy. The team examined brain tissue from patients with the refractory condition.

A DNA sensor called cGAS was switched on in patient brain tissue, and microglia, the brain's immune cells, carried a strong interferon signature. Huang showed overexcited neurons release DNA that activates this sensor in neighbouring microglia in their models. In Dravet model mice, reducing the sensor genetically or blocking it with a drug eased seizure features. Glial inflammation calmed and neuronal gene activity normalised under treatment, marking the pathway as a drug target.
pmc-13536545:
Ahmad Mohammad Al Zamel and colleagues survey in 2026 barriers to healthcare access for women in Sudan. Money limits, male decision power, and distance delay care and deepen health gaps. Face-to-face interviews covered 760 women aged 18 and older across urban and rural areas.

About one quarter reported rare or no financial ability to reach care, and about one third always needed male permission. Living over ten kilometres from a facility raised the odds of poor access sharply. The team urges cheaper, closer services plus stronger autonomy for women in daily health choices and household spending decisions.
pmc-13536845:
Xiangyu Ye and colleagues introduce a dual reading method that captures human genes and microbes together from nose swabs in a 2026 study of coronavirus infection. Seventy-six infected patients without symptoms at entry were swabbed at entry and again a week later, and about two thirds developed symptoms. Reads that did not match human genes were mapped to microbe genomes and checked against a standard microbe test.

Virus levels ran higher at entry in patients who later developed symptoms, then fell in both groups over the week. Microbe profiles matched the standard test closely for common groups. Dozens of bacterial species were less abundant in the group that became ill, and many linked to host genes tied to smell, skin cell growth, and chemical gene control. The authors present the method as a window on host-microbe links.
pmc-13538245:
A C Silva and co-authors review markers tied to Crohn disease fistulas near the anus in a 2026 systematic review. These tunnel-like wounds heal poorly and return often, so better markers could guide personal care. Searches through May 2025 in two databases narrowed thousands of records to thirty-three studies, split between formation markers and diagnostic markers. Two reviewers screened studies and judged bias separately.

Gene variants in immune and sensing pathways shaped fistula risk and severity, while altered gut microbes and resistance genes supported a bacterial role. Inflammatory signals and immune cells drove damage, with tissue change processes helping fistulas persist. Diagnostic options ranged from metabolic profiles and urine light tests to stool and tissue markers. Mixed study designs block direct guideline use for now.
pmc-13538645:
Cao and colleagues settle an argument in cross-linking mass spectrometry, a technique that glues proteins together at touching points so a mass spectrometer can map their architecture. Analysts must choose between DSS, a non-cleavable linker, and DSSO, which snaps apart inside the instrument to leave signature fragments. Their 2026 head-to-head ran both linkers across samples of rising complexity, from single purified complexes through bacterial lysates to human cell lysate.

DSS found more cross-links in simple and bacterial samples. The authors trace its edge to a longer, floppier spacer arm, which reaches across a spatial volume more than two fifths larger than its rival's. As complexity rose the advantage shrank, and in human lysate DSSO pulled ahead, because DSS identifications collapse faster when the search space explodes. Their advice is DSS up to bacterial complexity, DSSO beyond it.
pmc-13538745:
Huilin Tang and colleagues emulate a trial of diabetes drugs and skin cancer risk in a 2026 records study. Adults with type 2 diabetes starting a popular gut hormone drug class were matched against starters of two rival classes in a large health record network spanning a decade. Melanoma and other skin cancers were tracked over three years with bias checks including a calibration outcome.

Melanoma risk showed no increase against either rival class. Other skin cancer risk edged borderline higher against one rival class but not the other, and the signal faded after calibration for hidden bias. Results held across sensitivity checks including delayed counting and an obesity-only subset. The authors conclude the drug class looks reassuring for melanoma, with the mild signal likely artifactual.
pmc-13540845:
Gao and colleagues test a low-technology recipe for teaching dental anatomy: draw the tooth, identify the tooth, then carve the tooth. Dental students traditionally learn tooth shape by carving wax blocks alone, a slow route to recognising form. Their 2026 study compared three consecutive cohorts of Chinese undergraduates. One had carving only, one added supervised two-dimensional drawing plus an identification test, and one had drawing and identification woven through the whole course as scaffolding.

After adjusting for incoming grades, every measure improved along the sequence. Carving marks rose step by step across the three cohorts, and theory scores jumped clearly once drawing was added. The fully scaffolded cohort's accuracy at identifying extracted teeth leapt from the low sixties to around eighty percent in a year. Drawing marks also improved significantly, and students rated the training highly, with most agreeing it clarified how tooth form serves function.
pmc-13540945:
Anqi Liu leads a 2026 imaging study setting reference values for a magnetic resonance method that maps breathing and blood flow in the lungs without radiation or held breaths. The technique, called PREFUL-MRI, needs healthy baselines before it can judge patients.

Eighty-seven healthy adults were scanned while breathing normally and while breathing deeply and slowly. Deep breathing shifted the metrics in opposite directions depending on the measure, and individuals split between rising and falling blood flow responses. Men showed higher ventilation than women during normal breathing and more matched defects during deep breathing. Age comparisons add further reference detail for future patient studies.
pmc-13542245:
Yilin Yu and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study on why some colorectal cancers resist radiotherapy. Working with resistant cancer cell models, patient tissue, and mice, the team traced resistance to a protein called EFHD2. A small regulatory RNA that normally restrains EFHD2 was scarce in resistant cells, and restoring it weakened the cancer's ability to repair radiation damage to its DNA.

EFHD2, chemically tagged by lactate at one key site, partnered with another protein to raise lactate production and steady a low-oxygen response factor. The extra lactate pushed immune cells toward a suppressive state, raised a checkpoint protein that shields tumours, and reduced helpful T cell entry. Silencing EFHD2 while adding immune checkpoint treatment made tumours far more sensitive to radiation in the animal work. The findings point to the EFHD2 pathway as a drug target for resistant rectal and colon cancers.
pmc-13542745:
Abdulaziz Gul and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study comparing how much force different zirconia dental implant designs can withstand before breaking. Five designs were tested: a one-piece implant, plus bone-level and tissue-level two-piece implants fitted with either ceramic or titanium screws. Specimens were first loaded repeatedly in moist conditions to mimic chewing, then loaded once until they fractured, following an international testing standard. Fracture surfaces and crystal changes were examined microscopically.

Tissue-level two-piece implants were strongest, resisting about 775 newtons, ahead of one-piece implants near 606 newtons and bone-level designs near 498 newtons. Screw material made no significant difference overall. Where the implant sits relative to tissue and bone mattered far more than what the screw is made of. All designs passed levels the authors judge sufficient to justify further clinical study of ceramic implants.
pmc-13543345:
Ruining Jin and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study of how never-married Chinese women who studied abroad renegotiate marriage after coming home. Returning can unsettle life plans when family hopes, workplace treatment, and social norms pull in different directions. The team interviewed 22 single women who had come home after studying in Western countries, interpreting their accounts through ecological systems theory and the idea of patriarchal bargaining.

At family level, the women met pressure over marriage timing, filial duty, and respectable life choices. At work they described gendered assumptions and uneven chances to advance. Public talk about unmarried women, and about women with overseas experience, added a further layer of scrutiny. Many therefore approached marriage cautiously, weighing family wishes against housing, reproduction, and quality of life. Continued singlehood, the authors argue, is often an active negotiation rather than simple delay or personal preference.
pmc-13545045:
Harrington and colleagues report a 2026 eye study asking whether the dominant eye, the one a person sights with, differs in shape from the other eye. They pooled three cohorts, nearly two thousand people in all: children and teens in Ireland and young adults in Western Australia. Each person had a sighting test for dominance, a focusing measure, and an eye-length measure.

Simple right-versus-left differences were tiny in children and teens. The dominant eye, though, was slightly longer and slightly less long-sighted than its partner in every age group. Dominance explained most of the steady gap between the eyes. The gap shrank in short-sighted people and grew in those whose eyes differed most. Though small, the gaps near sizes that matter in short-sight research, so eye studies should record dominance.
pmc-13545345:
Awj Twam and a team of co-authors tested in 2026 a compact deep learning model that outlines gynecologic organs and cervical tumors on MRI scans for radiotherapy planning. Drawing such outlines by hand is slow and varies between clinicians. Their two-stage model, PocketNet, was trained on scans from 102 patients receiving definitive radiotherapy and checked against a second, external collection.

PocketNet overlapped expert outlines well, scoring above 70 percent for tumors and above 80 percent for organs on the home data, with similar results externally. A standard full-size model matched its accuracy yet needed roughly twice the training time and far more memory. The authors argue the lighter model suits time-pressured treatment planning.
pmc-13547345:
Tetsuya Tachibana and co-authors built in 2026 a two-stage learning system that measures hip and thigh muscle volume from CT scans taken before hip replacement surgery. Muscle strength predicts recovery, yet patients in severe pain cannot show their true strength in tests, so volume offers another route. The system first classifies slices, then outlines muscles, and was trained on scans from 107 patients.

Against hand-drawn outlines, its volume errors stayed between one and ten percent, with strong overlap scores for every muscle group. In a separate group of 58 patients, muscles on the painful side were smaller, and larger volumes in several muscles predicted better hip strength and faster sit-to-walk performance after surgery. The authors support automated volumetry for objective assessment.
pmc-13548545:
Ting Pan and colleagues test whether amyloid buildup in one smell-related brain region can by itself cause smell loss, in a 2026 mouse study tied to Alzheimer's disease. Poor smell is among the earliest signs of the disease, and the lateral entorhinal cortex, a hub for odor processing, is hit early. Direct proof that damage there drives the symptom was missing, so the team injected amyloid-beta oligomers into that region alone.

Treated mice became worse at detecting and telling apart odors. Recordings showed the region's neurons firing too much at rest and during smells, with stronger rhythm activity, while the population code for odors broke down. Synapses also looked damaged and signaled poorly. The authors read this as direct evidence that a hyperactive, disordered entorhinal cortex helps explain early smell failure in Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-13548945:
Aiza A. Butt and Joseph M. Ready survey the chemistry of borylcyclopropanes, three-membered carbon rings carrying a boron group, in a 2026 review. The carbon and boron bond is one of synthesis's most flexible handles. Planting it on a strained ring unlocks reactions plain rings cannot do. Those range from cross-coupling and oxidation to ring openings that yield precisely arranged boron compounds for building larger molecules.

The review sorts the many ways to make these compounds by mechanism. Routes include metal and enzyme catalyzed carbene transfers, light-driven radical paths, direct borylation of ring carbon and hydrogen bonds, and additions to related strained systems. Boron-stabilized radicals, anions, and cations enable cyclopropanation tricks with no classical equivalent. Applications run from drug discovery scaffolds to natural product synthesis, and the authors map where each strategy shines.
pmc-13550345:
Juan Fang and colleagues sift gene data for signals of how radiotherapy reshapes the immune surroundings of rectal cancer, in a 2026 bioinformatics study. Radiation is a backbone of rectal cancer care, yet its effects on infiltrating immune cells and their genes are incompletely charted. Combining public expression databases with immune analysis tools, the team compared treated and untreated tumors and linked candidate genes to cell infiltration and patient outcomes.

Eleven genes shifted with radiation, seven up and four down. Two stood out. MASP1, part of an ancient immune alarm system, tracked with broad immune infiltration and with better benefit from checkpoint immunotherapy. SLC9A3R2 related to response against two major checkpoint drug classes. Both inversely or directly tracked suppressor cell levels in telling patterns. The authors propose the pair as biomarkers for pairing radiation with immunotherapy.
pmc-13550645:
Hyoungchul Ham and four colleagues probe the excited anion state behind plasmon-driven reduction of 4-nitrobenzenethiol. Experiments link the reaction to short-lived negative ions and unusual vibrational excitation, but the molecular nature of the excited anion state stayed unclear. Their 2026 paper uses time-dependent density functional theory on a gold-4-NBT complex. It asks how hot-electron injection reaches a low-lying excited anion manifold and how those states couple to vibration.

The team identifies a low-lying quartet excited anion state, called Q1, that gold coordination makes reachable under plasmon-driven electron attachment. Q1 mixes local excitation with charge-transfer character. Its access hinges on the NO2 symmetric stretch, which also shapes a possible radiative decay path from Q1. Low-energy crossing regions along that coordinate fit vibronically assisted access to the excited manifold.
pmc-13550745:
Carlos Antonio Godoy Junior, leading ten colleagues, published a 2026 choice study asking caregivers what they want from telemedicine for children receiving palliative care at home. Asynchronous messaging with artificial intelligence support could widen access, yet family priorities were unclear. Thirty-one primary caregivers in a tertiary program completed twelve tasks, each forcing trade-offs among service type, reply time, and fewer hospital visits.

Caregivers preferred joining a service over opting out, and reply time drove about 60 percent of decisions. They modestly favored doctor and nurse supported care over AI-supported care, while fewer hospital visits did not consistently sway choices. Predicted uptake stayed high only when replies came quickly, so the authors urge designs that speed human response rather than replace clinicians.
pmc-13551545:
Lucas M Seuren, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 qualitative study of service providers who supported people released from custody in Ontario, Canada during the COVID-19 pandemic. Twenty in-depth interviews explored how mental health and substance use services coped with disruption. Providers described public health rules that were not tailored to their clients, who often had to isolate just as outreach became hardest.

The resulting domino effects raised risks of substance use, overdose, and suicide, while providers felt pressure to help under policies that blocked them. Collaboration and more person-centered care counted as silver linings. The authors urge future emergency planners to weigh blanket policies' fallout on underserved groups and to involve those communities in research.
pmc-13551845:
Dahlia Foo, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 tracking study of young southern elephant seals on their first foraging trip from Macquarie Island. Weaned pups receive no guidance on where to feed, only fat reserves from their mothers. Satellite tags followed pups on their post-weaning migration, and their routes were compared with adult females' winter journeys and with ocean current patterns.

Pups mostly traveled east to south-east, aligned with the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, while adults headed south toward Antarctic waters, a difference the authors attribute to learned experience. Pup survival probability rose with current-following in the reported models. The authors propose that currents widen the feeding area reachable by energy-limited pups, a framework they suggest may fit other marine species with naive young.
pmc-13551945:
Edy Quizhpe and Miguel San Sebastián published a 2026 study of ethnic gaps in child dental care in Ecuador. They used a national survey from 2018. The study compared Indigenous children with non-Indigenous children and teens. Two outcomes were tracked. One was skipping dental care in the past year. The other was brushing less than twice a day. Models adjusted for sex, place, and region.

Skipping care was far more common in Indigenous children. The adjusted gap sat near nine points. Weak brushing was also higher in Indigenous children and teens. Adjusted gaps ran from about eleven to thirteen points. The authors call for fair, culturally apt dental policies for Indigenous groups. They frame the gaps as a matter of equity, not habit alone.
pmc-13554145:
Illias Alhassane leads a six-author team testing drinking wells in Agadez, Niger, for three harmful substances at once in a 2026 study. Groundwater there carries uranium, fluoride, and nitrate, each able to harm health over time. The team sampled every public well plus a cross-section of private ones. Roughly two thirds of wells broke world guidance lines for uranium and for fluoride, while fewer broke the nitrate line.

Combined risk scores passed the safe mark in most wells, for children even more often than adults. Uranium moved freely through local sandstone in carbonate-rich water. Fluoride built up under alkaline conditions as calcium drained away. Nitrate came from poor sanitation, with one well at an extreme level. About 124,000 residents face this daily exposure.
pmc-13554245:
Yuchen Han leads a fourteen-author team attacking drug resistance in osteosarcoma, a bone cancer of the young, in a 2026 study. The standard drug doxorubicin often stops working as tumours adapt. The team traced resistance to how mitochondria, the cell's power plants, split and merge. A gene switched on by a partner protein pushed that splitting, stirring up harmful oxygen species that kill cancer cells.

A drug that activates the partner protein restored sensitivity in dishes and in animals. A second drug blocking a related signal path did the same. Given together with doxorubicin, the pair multiplied the killing effect beyond either boost alone. The authors propose this combined attack as a fresh strategy for resistant bone tumours.
pmc-13554845:
Mohit Pahuja leads a seven-author team reporting a heart-lung machine rescue during a periviable pregnancy in a 2026 case report. A thirty-two-year-old woman at nearly twenty-five weeks arrived in severe heart shock, and her baby had just died in the womb. Her heart rhythm raced, drugs failed, and her heart stopped with no pulse. Emergency delivery was not feasible in the catheter room where she lay.

A heart pump already in place gave large-bore access, letting the team start full machine support quickly. She stabilised, came off the machine on day seven, and delivered on day eleven. Sixty days after arrival she went home with much-improved heart function. The authors say fast machine support can save the mother when delivery cannot happen first.
pmc-13555145:
Chih-Yuan Chang leads a six-author team studying melanoma return in Taiwanese patients whose sentinel node test was clear in a 2026 study. Melanoma in Asian populations often grows on hands and feet, unlike Western patterns. Records from a Taipei hospital covered 181 patients treated between 2005 and 2025. Ninety-two had clear sentinel nodes, the first node draining the tumour.

A quarter of the clear-node group saw cancer return within a median follow-up of about twenty-nine months. Spread to nodes was the most common first pattern and tended to arrive earliest. Lower body mass, diabetes, and surface ulceration each tied to faster return. Older age, lower body mass, and thicker tumours tied to worse survival. The authors urge careful follow-up for such patients.
pmc-13558345:
Mrunal Pradeep Desai and four colleagues probed in 2026 whether common heart drugs change how the body handles lapatinib, a breast cancer pill that can itself strain the heart. Calcium channel blockers are often prescribed alongside it, and both drug families share the same gut pumps and liver enzymes. The team combined gut tissue experiments, liver cell metabolism assays, and dosing studies in rats to map the interactions.

Two blockers, verapamil and nicardipine, let more lapatinib cross gut tissue, while nicardipine and diltiazem slowed its breakdown in liver preparations sharply. In living rats, diltiazem and nicardipine raised peak lapatinib levels by roughly a third, whereas verapamil lowered the peak by a similar share. Directions differ by drug, so the authors urge clinical studies before assuming any blocker pairing with lapatinib is harmless.
pmc-13558745:
Moldir Yermagambetova and five colleagues sequenced in 2026 the complete chloroplast genomes of twelve onion relatives native to Kazakhstan. The genus Allium is one of the largest and most tangled among flowering plants, and Central Asia is a heartland of its diversity, yet genomic records for Kazakh species were thin. The team assembled each genome and compared structure, gene content, and variable regions across the dozen.

Every genome kept the classic four-part layout and the same 137 genes, with sizes differing by barely one percent. Most variation sat between genes rather than inside them, and four fast-changing regions were flagged as ready-made markers for identification work. Family trees built two ways agreed on three major lineages, matching earlier studies, and dating placed the group's main chloroplast splits in the early Eocene. The dataset anchors future taxonomy in the region.
pmc-13559045:
Malwina Molendowska and colleagues report a technical study testing whether a specialized MRI approach can produce trustworthy intravoxel incoherent motion imaging of the prostate. IVIM is a scan method that maps how water moves in tissue and how blood flows through tiny vessels, without contrast dye. Weak repeatability has held the method back in prostate cancer care, so the team built a new acquisition framework.

Their setup pairs velocity-compensated diffusion encoding, which separates blood flow from pure diffusion, with a spiral readout on a 3 T scanner fitted with very strong gradients. Five men, with and without prostate cancer, were scanned. Signal stayed above the noise floor in 91 percent of voxels at the strongest diffusion weighting. The resulting maps showed fine detail, and parameter values repeated well across tissue zones and cancer. The authors present the framework as a step toward IVIM measures reliable enough to guide detection and monitoring.
pmc-13560145:
Jaya Chakravarty and colleagues test symptom-directed antinuclear antibody screening as a route to diagnosing lupus in people living with HIV. Their 2026 study screened 129 patients whose symptoms fell inside the clinical domains of the 2019 lupus classification criteria. Positive screens led to finer antibody testing, and diagnoses followed those same criteria.

Antibodies showed up in 54 patients, yet only four carried anti-dsDNA antibodies, and each of those four proved to have lupus. Joint inflammation was their commonest showing, with protein in the urine next. Three other autoimmune diseases surfaced once each in the screened group. The authors argue that aiming the test at symptoms, rather than screening everyone, avoids the false positives that HIV itself can provoke.
pmc-13560245:
Fan and colleagues study a small control molecule, microRNA-345-3p, that appears to restrain colorectal cancer's spread to the liver, in 2026 cancer research. The team collected blood from 110 colorectal cancer patients and 90 healthy people, measuring the microRNA and a target gene. They then raised the molecule's levels in cancer cells in the lab to watch growth and the shape-shifting process, called epithelial-mesenchymal transition, that helps cancers invade new organs.

Low levels tracked with advanced tumor stage, deeper invasion, lymph node spread, and poorer outlook. Restoring the molecule in cells slowed growth and reversed transition-linked changes. pmc-13560345:
Yunhan Nie and colleagues sift a decade of fertility treatment records to learn why women with high body mass index repeatedly fail to reach live birth, and what might change the odds. Mixed models separated risk factors for repeated failure from strategies after a first failed transfer.

Switching to a progestin-primed stimulation protocol after failure lowered the risk of failing again, as did transferring a blastocyst-stage embryo. The authors distinguish fixed risks from adjustable ones and suggest risk-stratified adjustments for lower-risk patients.
pmc-13560445:
Weiwei Pan and three colleagues test microRNA-21 as a driver of the abnormal bone formation that stiffens the spine in ankylosing spondylitis. Their 2026 study works in synovial fibroblasts taken from patients, the cells blamed for turning inflammation into bone, plus a proteoglycan-induced arthritis mouse model. A MAPK and NF-κB signaling pathway is the suspected conduit.

Adding the microRNA to fibroblasts boosted their growth and bone-forming differentiation while switching the pathway on; blocking it reversed each effect. In mice, an inhibitor of the microRNA eased spinal cartilage damage and cooled the blood's inflammatory signals. It also normalized bone metabolism markers and quieted the same pathway in spinal tissue. The authors read microRNA-21 as a promoter of fibroblast bone transformation tied to that pathway. They nominate it for further study as a treatment target.
pmc-13562145:
Emanuel Mastrangelo and three colleagues audit how well Canadian emergency training programs teach ECG reading, a core emergency skill. pmc-13562345:
Joon-suk Bom and three colleagues test whether long-term beta-blocker treatment distorts a monitor score used to judge pain during surgery. The score, drawn from heart rate variation, falls when a painful stimulus reaches a patient under anaesthesia. Twenty-four patients took beta-blockers and 25 did not. Four set stimuli were applied to each person, and the lowest score after each one was recorded. Scores fell after stimulation in both groups by similar amounts and with similar timing. No real group difference appeared. The authors conclude the monitor stays readable, as a within-patient signal, in people on chronic beta-blocker therapy.
pmc-13562645:
Maya M. Polovitskaya leads an international team reporting fifteen people with variants in CLCN3, a gene for an ion exchanger inside cells, plus fresh details on five earlier cases. Faults in the cell's internal sorting compartments hit the nervous system hardest. The patients showed problems, from developmental delay and intellectual disability to epilepsy. The 2026 team studied how twenty of the gene's spelling changes alter the exchanger, which swaps chloride for protons inside endosomes, and how a partner protein, TMEM9, brakes it.

Others widened the range over which the exchanger conducts, and those escaped the brake's control. Both groups produced a toxic gain of function, swelling internal compartments when overproduced. The authors say the work firms up counselling for affected families and reveals a link between the exchanger's shape changes and its braking system.
pmc-13562945:
Gavin R. Broad and a Darwin Tree of Life consortium publish the genome of Ophion crassicornis, a night-flying parasitic wasp described from British specimens in 1982. pmc-13569445:
Kristina Aagaard and colleagues used genetics to test whether a mother's pregnancy diet truly affects her child's ADHD risk, publishing the trio study in 2026. Observational studies link unhealthy pregnancy diets to higher ADHD odds, but shared genes could inflate that link, since mothers pass both genes and eating habits to children. The team built polygenic scores for healthy dietary patterns in mother, father, and child trios.

That pattern did not replicate in the far larger MoBa and ALSPAC cohorts, where direct genetic effects pointed to confounding. The authors find no robust evidence for a causal diet pathway and warn that genetic confounding likely inflates observed associations.
pmc-13569645:
Kento Yumita and colleagues tested whether combining two MRI sequences sharpens facial-nerve mapping before parotid surgery, publishing the study in 2026. Facial nerve palsy is a major risk of parotid gland operations, and risk hinges on whether a tumour sits superficial or deep to the nerve. Direct MRI visualisation of the nerve promises better prediction than indirect landmarks, but the two candidate sequences had rarely been compared head to head.

In 36 patients, the nerve's main trunk appeared in every case, and its split into upper and lower divisions showed in 81 percent with either sequence alone but 94 percent combined. Tumour position was judged correctly in 83 percent combined, versus 75 and 67 percent singly. The authors recommend pairing the sequences for surgical planning.
pmc-13570345:
X. J. Li and colleagues profile, in a 2026 study of Wanxi white geese, how the pituitary gland rewires its hormone signals as birds move from first birth into the laying period. Blood hormones, gene activity, and small regulatory RNAs were measured in pituitary tissue at both stages, with laboratory assays confirming one predicted gene target.

Hundreds of genes and dozens of small RNAs changed, gathering around pathways for hormone release and tissue signaling, coordinated by two small RNAs at the network center. Poultry scientists get a molecular map of the switch that turns on sustained egg laying.
pmc-13571545:
Maryam Muhammad Ali Majeed-Saidan and colleagues propose a new pressure measure to judge mitral valve repair while the patient is still on the table. Mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair clips the valve leaflets together, and leftover leakage predicts outcomes, yet echo and pressure readings sometimes disagree. Their 2026 study examined 231 patients treated between 2019 and 2022, defining V-prime as the V-wave height minus mean left-atrial pressure.

Repair lowered atrial pressures in both primary and secondary leakage, and V-prime ran higher in patients left with more than mild residual leakage. Patients whose post-repair V-prime exceeded 13 millimetres of mercury faced about triple the risk of heart-failure admission or death. The authors offer V-prime as a practical intraprocedural guide to whether the repair is good enough.
pmc-13572345:
Kala Baskar, Vishnu Prasad J, and Guhan Jayaraman engineer, in a 2026 study, E. coli bacteria that make 3-hydroxypropionic acid, a building-block chemical for acrylics and biodegradable plastics, more efficiently by fixing a redox traffic jam. Making the product from glycerol floods the cells with a spent carrier molecule and starves the pathway of its fresh form.

The team crippled the bacteria's own glycerol burning so glycerol flowed only into product, then fed a second sugar purely for growth and carrier recycling. Six sugars were tried, and sucrose and ordinary sugar sources such as molasses performed best, roughly doubling output over glycerol alone. Waste plant liquors also worked, pointing toward cheaper, greener production of a versatile chemical.
pmc-13572445:
Yasin Altinişik, with four colleagues, presents a 2026 forecast method for solar power data that hold long runs of zeros. Panels make no power at night and little under thick cloud, so zero values pile up by design. Most past tools treat those zeros as a side issue, which can skew forecasts.

The method splits the task in two: first call whether power is zero, then gauge how much flows when it is not. Three tools tried the first task and six tried the second, for 18 paired models in all. Data came from a real plant in Zonguldak, Türkiye, rated near 110 kilowatts. Tree-based tools for the second task gave the lowest errors and the best fit scores. The top pairs scored near 0.899 on the fit measure used.
pmc-13572545:
Mylena Maria Guedes de Almeida and colleagues describe a community of practice built to put low- and middle-income countries in charge of health AI, publishing the case study in 2026. AI for global health has been fragmented, with poorer countries often reduced to data suppliers while solutions are designed elsewhere. The AI4GH community, founded in 2023, links scientists, field workers, and officials across the Global South.

Using a structured community roadmap, the authors trace how the group co-creates and scales responsible AI for public-health priorities, sharing ethical, regulatory, and operational know-how. The model strengthens local expertise and context-specific learning rather than importing ready-made tools. Other fields can adapt the blueprint to build their own communities of practice.
pmc-13573345:
Chengyao Li, with 13 colleagues, reports a 2026 case of a rare skin cancer in a giant panda, the first of its kind on record. The tumour, trichilemmal carcinoma, grows from the outer sheath of hair roots and is scarce even in people. The patient was a 23-year-old male panda in captivity with a sore, swollen patch on the scrotum.

The lesion had grown for four weeks and measured about four centimetres across. Tissue study showed invasive nests of clear cells and cysts of the hair root sheath. Marker stains matched the human pattern for this tumour and ruled out two close look-alikes. Surgeons cut the tumour out with a slim margin under full anaesthesia. The wound healed in two weeks with anti-infection care. At three months, no return showed and the panda acted normally.
pmc-13573445:
Lijun Deng, with ten colleagues, carried out a 2026 study of how plum pistils answer pollen from varied sources. Cross-pollination drives commercial plum crops, since the pollen source shapes tube growth down the pistil and the fruit that sets. The fine chemistry of that match was little known for the Fengtang plum.

That three-way watch can show why some pollen races ahead while other pollen stalls, and which signals mark a good match early. Growers could use such marks to pick polliniser trees with data, not habit. The study builds a base for orchard plans that raise fruit set in this cultivar.
pmc-13574145:
Arno Smid, with 13 colleagues, reports a 2026 mouse study of tiny clots that guide blood flow in the early placenta. Before the placenta matures, maternal blood bathes the embryo, and its flow must be metered with care. The team found small clots, stocked with platelets, clotting factors, and complement proteins, at the heart of that metering.
