The work shows the two systems must be balanced, not just active.
pmc-13574345:
Christopher X. Hong, with four colleagues, reports a case series on custom vaginal pessaries for pelvic organ prolapse after standard ones fell short. A pessary is a support device worn in the vagina, and stock shapes fail about one in four who try them. Discomfort and poor hold drive many to quit within a year.

The series covers patients fitted with a patient-specific device, shaped by digital modelling to their own anatomy, between February 2024 and September 2025. Care ran at 18 sites across Canada, and outcomes were logged on one secure platform. The outcome of note was still using the device four weeks after the final fitting. The authors report high fitting success and continuation in this hard group. Such data test whether custom design keeps its pilot promise in daily practice.
pmc-13574845:

Spine height held at first, then shrank by late follow-up. The authors urge using scans already on file to flag weak bones early, when guard steps help most.
pmc-13578045: Łajczak and colleagues published a correction in 2026. It amends their review of deep learning used to outline vestibular schwannoma, a benign growth near the inner ear. The note is a correction, and it adds a short statement that was left out. The added text says the team used Gemini to help with writing and grammar checks. It also says no large language model was used for data work, and the team stands by the final text.
pmc-13582745:

Flipped classrooms need strong pre-class videos, but traditional lectures often ignore multimedia learning principles, and AI output quality hinges on prompt design. Their 2026 paper describes IMPACT: iterative refinement, meta-prompting, prompt chaining, theory alignment, contextual examples, and tiered validation, arranged as a six-stage video pipeline.

The authors present IMPACT as a way to let trainees with little instructional-design experience build sound videos alongside faculty, while keeping human review between stages to guard quality.
pmc-13589945:

pmc-13591345:

pmc-13591645:

pmc-13593545:
Shabnam Madadi and colleagues report a patient with dextrocardia, a heart positioned on the right side with organs mirrored. Published in 2026, the case describes a de-networking procedure that ablated the faulty fiber network after standard care failed to stop the dangerous rhythm.

They caution that a long QT interval seen after resuscitation does not by itself prove an inherited long QT condition. pmc-13593745:

pmc-13594045:
Carla Rognoni and colleagues weighed the hospital costs of vacuum removal versus cutting removal for unclear breast lesions in Italy. Their budget-impact analysis over five years drew problem rates from papers and review, and costs from detailed counting across five Italian clinics.

With uptake rising from 20 to 80 percent, five-year hospital savings reached about 11 to 14 million euros. The authors present vacuum removal as a cost-saving, barely invasive option that can improve hospital output.
pmc-13595845:
Kuang Kuay Lim and co-authors compared two national adolescent health surveys in Malaysia, from 2017 and 2022. The two surveys used the same sampling design and self-completed questionnaires, giving the comparison a firm footing.

Vaping-only use climbed from about six percent to over eight, and dual use eased down slightly. Boys, older students, and teenagers whose parents used tobacco carried higher odds in every category, and patterns differed by ethnicity. pmc-13598045:
Amy N.S. Webb and co-authors interviewed ten fertility professionals and regulators and ten patients in Australian clinics about machine learning systems that grade and select embryos. Their 2026 qualitative study explored the ethical pressure points of handing part of this intimate decision to an algorithm.

Both groups voiced mistrust and insisted on human oversight. Nobody could quite say how the systems produce their knowledge, and that opacity raised hard questions about who answers for a machine-assisted choice. Professionals added fears of badly trained models, biased scoring, and a deskilled workforce leaning too hard on the machine. The authors frame embryo selection AI as contested territory needing transparency before trust.
pmc-13598845:
Juliana Carvalho Ferreira and Cecilia María Patino say lung research oft scores what is easy, not what sick people prize. Their case tracks ICU folks on breathing machines where double-trigger bursts foretold more machine days, fewer free days, and worse 28-day life odds. Those scores are plain to count but mute on how people feel or fare after ICU.

pmc-13599245:

Patients were scored on daily-living and sports function, and eight X-ray measures of foot alignment were compared before surgery and at final follow-up. The authors set their results beside published series using grafts or augmentation and found the direct repair competitive. pmc-13600645:
Dragana Žuvić and colleagues weighed four LDL fat-score math rules in people with high blood fats in Vojvodina. Straight LDL tests are not always at hand or cheap, so clinics lean on math from total fat, blood fats, and HDL fat. Old rules were built for blood fats under 4.5 millimoles per litre, which leaves a gap for high-fat cases.

The look-back work held 272 people whose fats were read from June 2022 to June 2023, all with blood fats from 4.5 to 9.0 millimoles per litre. Straight LDL from an Abbott Alinity test stood as the gold gauge. Friedewald, Sampson, Anandaraja, and Martin-Hopkins math were each set beside that gauge to judge which rule holds when blood fats run high.
pmc-13602745:

The team collected clinical data on patients hospitalized with severe or critical COVID-19 at a Jinzhou hospital during the December 2022 to February 2023 wave. Statistical selection found the risk factors, which were shaped into a nomogram, a chart turning patient values into a personal risk estimate.

In the development group, 60.3 percent of patients developed long COVID. A separate Panjin Central Hospital group showed a similar 62.3 percent and tested the model on outside data. The nomogram is a practical aid for flagging high-risk patients early, the authors say, so support can be planned before symptoms settle in. Building the model in one hospital and checking it in another is meant to make the tool credible elsewhere.
pmc-13605745:

The team searched for studies whose systems handled at least three standard measures or planes during the second and third trimesters, the combination real practice requires.

Nineteen studies covering more than 730,000 ultrasound images qualified, and eighteen compared machine readings against manual ones. Systems performed favorably on head size, abdominal circumference, and thigh bone length. Beyond that headline, the studies diverged widely in design, model design, checking method, and the metrics reported, which blocked clean comparison between them. The authors judge the tools promising for consistency and speed. They require standard reporting and forward testing across hospitals, machines, operators, and pregnancy stages before recommending routine use.
pmc-13607645:

Most vesicle research has chased protein and microRNA cargo, but newer tools now expose the lipid side. The review gathers five years of work beyond cholesterol and triglycerides, covering sphingolipids, phospholipids, and sugar-bearing lipids in vessels and vesicles. Ceramides stand out in artery plaque formation. The authors say the open question is causal: how much do changed vesicle lipid loads alter the cardiovascular system? Answering it could open new routes to treatment and early detection.
pmc-13613245:

RNA-based sprays can target one pest and then break down safely, but the RNA needs a coating to survive the trip onto the leaf.

Mixing the parts with a microfluidic device gave tiny charged droplets under 200 nanometres wide that shield the RNA from enzymes that would destroy it. pmc-13616245:

Aptamers bind their targets with antibody-like precision yet are smaller and easier to make.

It also faces the hard parts: keeping aptamers stable in blood and getting enough of them through the barrier. For a disease where survival gains have crept for decades, a guidance system this exact is one of the more hopeful routes open.
pmc-13616845:
Manuel Friedrich, Leonard Kreutz, and Ulisse Stefanelli present a mathematics paper on crystallization, the process by which particles settle into ordered lattice patterns. Their setting is two-dimensional: a finite set of particles rests on a flat crystalline substrate, much like a crystal growing layer by layer on a surface. A parameter called beta measures how strongly the particles bind to that substrate.

The authors prove crystallization for every positive value of beta, the first such result with a prescribed substrate in two dimensions. They also prove sharp laws for how far competing lowest-energy arrangements can differ from each other. The gap follows one scaling when beta is rational and a smaller one when it is irrational and algebraic. Those bounds yield convergence toward the Winterbottom equilibrium shape as particle numbers grow.
pmc-13617345:

These proteins are part of the immune system's attack machinery. Tissue came from 55 revision surgery patients.

Two central complement factors stood out. They were C3 and C5. They distinguished infection from aseptic loosening with high accuracy. This held across high-grade and low-grade cases. They beat blood markers and another complement factor. Infection types also differed in culprit bacteria. The authors propose tissue C3 and C5 testing for inconclusive cases. Further validation is pending.
pmc-13618045:

The equations keep the tidy gradient-dynamics form of older models, with the free energy widened to include polarization contributions. A generalized surface tension emerges that depends on orientation as well as concentration, derived in a thermodynamically consistent way. The framework should better predict when surfactant films stay smooth or break into flows.
pmc-13618945:

Publication has grown over twenty-five years, but two thirds of studies are one-off cross-sectional surveys with small samples, focused narrowly on sleep quantity and quality. Short weekday sleep was common, partly repaid by longer weekend sleep. Bedtime screen use, sleeping environment, school schedules, and chronic illness were the major risk factors, and poor sleep tracked with worse school performance, depression, anxiety, and cardiometabolic risk. The authors call for objective sleep measurement and larger longitudinal and mixed-method studies to guide interventions.
pmc-13619645:

They examined 396 joints from 198 people and sorted each joint as normal, uncertain, or clearly affected. Statistical models then weighed patient traits and twenty joint measurements against those categories.

About a quarter of joints fell into the uncertain group and a similar share showed clear disease at the joint level. Missing teeth was the one strong marker for the uncertain stage. Clear disease tied to older age, missing teeth, jaw shape, and several size measures of the joint socket and knob. The authors treat uncertain scans, often showing flattening or hardening, as a middle stage worth watching rather than ignoring.
pmc-13619845:
