Their idea places a thin measurement strip, a navigator, before the first echo instead of after the last one, catching field changes with less error buildup.

Scans covered two stretches of the thoracic cord in twenty healthy volunteers and three people with multiple sclerosis. Corrected images showed higher signal and contrast, less ghosting behind the cord, and clearer structure in blinded ratings. The three patients' scans also improved, with lesions standing out better. The authors offer the approach as proof of concept that needs no separate breathing monitor.
pmc-13620145:
Mengqin Wu and four colleagues review how traditional fermented foods might be made to industrial standards without losing their character, in a 2026 paper. Foods like kefir, sauerkraut, vinegar, and Chinese liquor rely on open, spontaneous microbial communities, which gives them distinctive flavors yet makes quality and safety swing from batch to batch. Modern buyers increasingly expect consistency.

The review shows how multi-omics tools, which read genes, proteins, and metabolites together, can map which microbes are present, how they interact, and what they produce, including the viruses that infect them. Control strategies follow from that map: choosing functional strains, building synthetic communities, managing those bacterial viruses, and tuning physical and chemical conditions. The authors close with the hurdles between today's craft practice and a predictable, scalable fermentation industry.
pmc-13621945:
Yshoner Antonio Silva-Diaz leads a cross-sectional study of teeth and quality of life among older adults in two Indigenous communities of the Peruvian Amazon, Imacita and Yamayakat. Losing all natural teeth, called edentulism, is common in old age and can affect eating, speaking, and confidence. The team counted natural teeth and asked residents how they rated their lives.

Ninety-five adults over sixty took part, fifty-four in Imacita and forty-one in Yamayakat. Complete tooth loss was more common in Yamayakat, though the gap between villages was not firm in statistical terms. Keeping more natural teeth tracked closely with better ratings of general health, overall life quality, and the physical and social parts of the survey. The authors call for programmes that prevent tooth loss in Indigenous older adults, where dental care is hard to reach.
pmc-13622445:
Nickita Dutta and three co-authors study a fungus that lives inside the leaves of a mangrove tree, Avicennia officinalis, collected in Goa, India. Fungi of this kind, called endophytes, often make chemicals that protect their host. The team tested whether extracts from this fungus, a Daldinia species, could kill bacteria and stop them forming biofilms, the sticky layers that shield germs from drugs.

An extract made with ethyl acetate slowed two harmful gut bacteria, Escherichia coli and a Shigella species, at low doses. Tests showed the extract damaged bacterial membranes and raised harmful oxygen chemicals inside the cells. It blocked biofilm formation by roughly nine tenths for both bacteria, and microscope images confirmed thinner films and battered cells. Chemical profiling found several compounds known for germ-fighting effects. The authors present the fungus as a promising source for new antibacterial leads, though testing stays in the lab.
pmc-13623145:
Kurban Kotan, Serdar Kırışoğlu, and Hiroyuki Maruyama test a technique for filling gaps in health data, a step called imputation. Missing values plague medical records, and different filling methods fail in different ways depending on why data went missing. Their technique, named CHIT, was compared with two methods under three missing-data patterns.

The team worked with three health data sets, on kidney disease, heart disease, and mouse protein measures, deleting a fifth to a quarter of values in planned patterns. Eight classification programs were trained on the filled data. CHIT held near-perfect accuracy across patterns, while rival methods lost ground in the hardest pattern, where missingness depends on the unseen values. The authors credit two design choices: the training pool grows as records are completed, and the scarcest fields per record are filled first. They offer the results as guidance for data teams.
pmc-13623945:
You Wang and colleagues published a 2026 deep learning study of HPV vaccine discussion on Weibo, China's large social media platform. China has piloted free HPV vaccination since 2020 to lift low coverage of a vaccine that prevents cervical cancer. The team wanted a live read on public attitudes, barriers, and misinformation.

They collected every relevant Weibo post from 2018 to 2023, close to two million posts. Human coders labelled a sample of 6,600 posts against behaviour-change theory, and deep learning models trained on those labels sorted the rest with good accuracy. Positive posts far outnumbered negative ones, and the positive share climbed steeply across the period while misinformation fell by more than two thirds. Attitudes varied by region and by vaccine type, with the two-valent vaccine liked least. The authors propose social listening as a cheap, fast surveillance tool for vaccine policy.
pmc-13624045:
Michael N K Muturi leads a scientific note reporting beetles of the genus Aethina living inside wild stingless bee nests for the first time. A relative, the small hive beetle, is a pest of honey bee colonies and managed stingless bees, yet nobody knew whether any Aethina species used wild stingless bee colonies. The note fills that gap from Kakamega Forest in Kenya.

In February 2024, during the local dry season, the team opened four underground nests of the stingless bee Meliponula lendliana. Every nest held beetles, seventy-one in total, while no eggs or larvae appeared, a pattern that raises questions about whether the beetles breed there or shelter. Samples went to labs in Switzerland and South Korea for examination and DNA work to identify the species, which looks new to science. The authors present the find as a first record that widens the host range of the genus.
pmc-13624245:
Faizan-e-Mustaffa, Muhammad Shahbaz Aslam, and Muhammad Junaid review the next generation of CAR-T cell therapy, where a patient's immune cells are engineered to hunt cancer. The first versions transformed blood cancer care, yet they struggle with tumours that shed their markers, cells that wear out, side effects, and prices and methods that limit reach.

The review sorts engineering ideas by how proven they are, weighing clinical, regulatory, and laboratory evidence from 2022 to 2026. Covered designs include armoured cells carrying payloads, dual-target and logic-gated systems that demand two signals before attacking. Also covered: universal off-the-shelf cells, gene editing by CRISPR and base and prime editors, and methods building the cells inside the body using fat-particle delivery. Combinations with checkpoint drugs, radiation, and cancer-killing viruses aim at solid tumours. The authors close with manufacturing, safety, and durability hurdles that gate wider use.
pmc-13624545:
Esmé Jansen van Vuren and colleagues follow young South African adults to see whether what they eat tracks with depression. Their African-PREDICT group covered ages twenty to thirty in North West Province, a group rarely studied for diet and mood. Diet came from three day-long food recalls, and mood was scored with a standard health questionnaire at the start and again five years later.

About three in ten participants met the cutoff for depression at the start. Over time, higher milk intake went with a lower chance of new depression in one adjusted model. Sugary drinks went with higher odds in snapshot checks, while calcium and vegetables went with lower odds, which argues for food-aware mental health work in similar settings.
pmc-13625345:
Şengül Akdeniz and Karin Wolf-Ostermann explore whether older adults who understand health information also age more actively and successfully. Successful aging stresses health and avoiding disease, while active aging adds social participation and security. At a city-run active aging center in Antalya, Türkiye, they surveyed 306 adults aged sixty-five and over between October 2024 and May 2025, scoring health literacy alongside both aging scales.

Most participants were women, most held university degrees, and two-thirds lived with a chronic illness, yet many exercised body and mind regularly. Higher schooling, income, exercise, and mental activity all tracked with stronger literacy and aging scores. Health literacy itself rose and fell together with both aging measures, which supports teaching health skills as part of aging programs.
pmc-13625645:
Aysu Yildiz Karaahmet studies what shapes sexual attitudes inside arranged marriages, a setting where custom, gender roles, and couple dynamics pull at once. Her online survey reached 520 married adults, 280 women and 240 men, who rated their attitudes on a standard scale. Statistical modeling then tested which traits linked to warmer attitudes and whether how often couples have sex carries part of the effect.

Men, younger respondents, and the better educated reported more positive attitudes, while age pulled the other way. The fitted model explained a bit over a third of the differences between people. Regular sexual contact sits inside the pathway the model describes, so the author suggests support for couple intimacy, especially as long marriages and parenthood reshape desire, may help keep attitudes healthy.
pmc-13626345:
Huawei Tan and co-authors read the headlines of China's CCTV News on WeChat, the country's dominant social platform, for the values hidden in their wording. Using a method called discursive news values analysis, they examined 218 of the account's most-read headlines posted between 2014 and 2024. The account, a flagship of state media, draws tens of millions of weekly readers, so its headline craft shows how official news competes for attention.

Five values dominated: personalization, eliteness, negativity, proximity, and positivity. Headlines leaned on named people, elite figures, bad news, closeness to the reader, and upbeat framing, a mix that balances the outlet's political mandate with the hunger of a feed. The study carries a Western-born framework into a Chinese state media setting and finds it travels well.
pmc-13628845:
Zehao Zhao and colleagues tested whether a combined cholesterol, good-cholesterol, and glucose index predicts heart-kidney-metabolic syndrome. The CHG index sums metabolic burden, yet its power over syndrome onset, staging, and prognosis was unclear. Their 2026 study tracked 370,916 UK Biobank volunteers free of syndrome diseases for a median 16.5 years, plus 8,494 Beijing hospital patients with advanced disease.

Each standard-deviation rise in CHG raised diabetes risk by about 47 percent, heart and kidney disease risks by about 7 percent each, and sped stage progression. In advanced patients, the same rise raised major heart-brain event risk by about 12 percent, sharpest with low inflammation and high HbA1c. Zhao and colleagues present CHG as a practical risk gauge.
pmc-13629345:
Nurfitri, Amrullah, and Rachmayani publish in 2026 an oceanographic dataset from Buli Bay, a semi-enclosed bay in East Halmahera, Indonesia. It records how near-surface currents and sea level behaved over two weeks in late summer 2022. Baseline data for such remote Indonesian waters are scarce.

A bottom-mounted acoustic profiler looked upward from its mooring, sampling the water column every ten minutes and logging 2,160 current profiles in total. The published series focuses on the current 4.5 meters below the surface, averaged to hourly values. It splits that current into the astronomical tide and a leftover residual current using harmonic analysis software. Synchronized sea level records keep their original ten-minute spacing. The authors intend the data for studying local hydrodynamics and validating coastal models of the bay.
pmc-13629845:
Helen Clarke and nine colleagues followed forty-seven premenopausal women with obesity and raised risk of breast or womb cancer through a year-long total diet replacement programme in British secondary care. The plan opened with twelve weeks of full meal replacement and tissue biopsies, then reintroduced food and moved into a maintenance phase.

Four in five women finished the programme, meeting dietitians a median of twenty-eight times. Weight fell sharply by three months and, despite partial regain, remained well below baseline at one year. Quality of life improved and binge eating scores dropped, while mental health and activity measures held steady. The authors call the approach promising for high-risk clinics, pending controlled trials with longer follow-up.
pmc-13631545:
JW Macgregor and six colleagues published this 2026 study describing ultrasound views of the platypus abdomen. Platypus organs sit in unusual places compared with common domestic mammals, which makes clinical scanning hard to interpret. The team scanned fifty-four wild adult platypuses in northwest Tasmania. All scans used one small window on the left side of the belly, between the ribs and the epipubic bone.

The right lower lobe of the spleen lay right under that window in almost every animal, so it works as a reliable starting landmark. The left kidney always sat behind that spleen lobe and partly in front of it in most animals. The left testis or left ovary lay behind the kidney area. The paper gives sizes and positions for each organ, giving vets a reference for examining sick or injured platypuses.
pmc-13633245:
Kimberly C. Olney and colleagues published this 2026 study of how sepsis reaches the brain, using pigs instead of the usual rodents. Sepsis is a runaway immune response to infection that can cloud the brain, a complication tied to lasting thinking problems. Pig brains resemble human brains more than rodent brains do. The team infected Yorkshire pigs with a urine-tract strain of E. coli bacteria and examined the cortex at an early stage.

Gene readings showed sweeping shifts toward inflammation and vessel dysfunction. Zooming into single cell nuclei, the strongest changes sat in vessel-lining cells and in glial support cells, not in neurons. Cells talked to each other far more than in healthy controls, and the talk turned inflammatory. Signals that maintain the blood-brain barrier faded. The picture is a coordinated vessel-and-glia response that flips the brain's support unit from calm housekeeping to alarm mode.
pmc-13633345:
Jochumsen and co-authors prospectively evaluated a 2026 scoring system for guiding second prostate biopsies with a PSMA PET/MRI scan tracer called [18F]PSMA-1007. Men with a negative MRI but raised PSA density still hide significant cancers at times. The PRIMARY score grades the tracer pattern inside the prostate from one to five.

Ninety-one patients were enrolled, and eighty-six went forward for biopsy guidance after negative scans or non-significant earlier biopsies. Significant cancer, grade group two or higher, was found in about twenty-three percent of patients overall. Jochumsen found lesion level cancer rates climbed steeply with score, reaching sixty percent at scores four and five but zero at scores one and two. Score three lesions with cancer often sat at the front of the gland.
pmc-13636245:
Simple rocking motion can tune the size of lab-grown liver cell clusters, Megaly and colleagues show. Hepatic spheroids are small three-dimensional balls of liver cells. They work better than flat cell layers in artificial liver devices, drug-toxicity testing, and pharmacology, but many ways of making them need special equipment or static setups that resist scaling. The team grew rat liver cells on a rocker system, varying rocking speed and starting cell density, and tracked cluster shape and function over ten days.

Faster rocking made smaller clusters, with average diameter falling from about two hundred micrometres at the slowest speed to about eighty at the fastest. Function matured over time, with urea and albumin output rising across the study. Urea production peaked at a middle rocking speed. Megaly and colleagues present the rocker method as a cheap, scalable way to produce liver clusters of chosen size.
pmc-13638845:
Anamika Patel and three colleagues present a 2026 case series on eye damage from cytomegalovirus infection inside the eye. The virus is best known for attacking the retina in people with weak immune systems, but these patients showed a different pattern.

Five patients with six affected eyes had widespread bleeding in the retina and blocked small blood vessels, shown clearly on wide-field dye scans. Three eyes had raised pressure without classic retinitis, and bleeding into the eye's gel occurred in three eyes. Antiviral treatment helped at first, yet the authors stress that long monitoring remains essential.
pmc-13642945:
Zhiwei Zhong and ten colleagues present a 2026 drug study of SGI-7079, a new inhibitor aimed at FLT3, a growth switch often mutated in acute myeloid leukemia. Current FLT3 drugs lose ground when second mutations appear in the same gene.

In cell tests the compound blocked growth across the main mutation and several resistant variants, shut down downstream signals, and pushed cells into arrest and death. In mouse leukemia models it reduced disease burden without major toxicity and beat two approved drugs against their resistant forms. It also outperformed them in patient leukemia cells, marking it as a translation candidate.
pmc-13643445:
Raman Baweja led a 2026 real-world study of treatment patterns and outcomes for youth with ADHD, comparing those with and without co-occurring autism spectrum disorder. The combination is common and hard to treat, yet how it shifts prescribing and outcomes at scale was unclear. The team analyzed health records for 869,510 children and teens aged three to eighteen with ADHD, of whom 155,543, or 17.9 percent, also had autism, matching groups and tracking outcomes over one year.

Youth with both conditions carried more mental health problems and used more health care. They received fewer stimulant drugs but more non-stimulants than peers without autism. Within the combined group, those drugs tracked with the most favorable outcomes, including fewer hospital stays, emergency visits, suicidal behaviors, and later antipsychotic or mood drug starts. Atomoxetine looked best among the other drugs.
pmc-13645545:
Müjdat Kara and five colleagues review records from 285 adults who had pituitary gland surgery through the nose between 2004 and 2025. Their topic is delayed low blood sodium, a known risk in the days after this operation. Reported rates vary widely in past work. The team asks how much of that spread comes from how often sodium is checked.

In the full group, about one in six patients showed delayed low sodium, but the share rose sharply among patients tested on days five to seven. Most of the rise seen over twenty years faded once testing habits were held steady. Early low sodium and female sex marked higher risk. The study warns that recorded rates may say as much about blood test routines as about patients themselves.
pmc-13648145:
Hee-Tae Kang and co-authors project in this 2026 study how many occupational and environmental medicine specialists Korea will need and have between 2025 and 2035. These doctors run special health exams for exposed workers and staff workplace health programs.

Demand was estimated from 2024 workloads applied to expected exam and management volumes under four growth scenarios. Supply was modeled from just over one thousand certified specialists, training pipelines, and retirement ages. The workforce under ninety grows from under a thousand to about twelve hundred fifty by 2035. Supply beats demand in three scenarios but falls about thirty-three doctors short in the fastest growth case. The authors advise steady training numbers and new roles for the coming surplus.
pmc-13649445:
Kaio Cezar Rodrigues Salum and colleagues scanned the full gene set of 93 adults with severe obesity that began in youth, hunting for rare changes in the endocannabinoid system. This body system helps steer hunger and energy balance, yet its role in early, severe weight gain is unclear.

Nine rare changes turned up in 12 people, and most remain of uncertain effect. One change in a gene called FAAH stood out: three computer tools agreed it likely weakens the protein's fold, and it sits near, but not on, the active site. Body and blood measures did not differ between carriers and others once strict checks were applied. The authors frame the finds as leads for lab follow-up.
pmc-13649745:
Andrés Carrazco-Montalvo and eleven colleagues read the genomes of a deadly bird flu virus found in wild seabirds on the coast of Ecuador. The strain, a fast-spreading H5N1 type, has swept South America, yet its entries into Ecuador were poorly mapped. Samples came in 2023 from two frigatebirds and two blue-footed boobies.

All four viruses fell in one genotype, but they split into two clusters, each close to viruses seen earlier in Peru. That split points to at least two entries into Ecuador, apart from cases in farm birds. A screen flagged 29 gene changes tied in past work to virulence, host range, or drug resistance. The authors back joint watch work across wildlife, farm, and health teams.
pmc-13650545:
Timur Yurttas and three colleagues review flow-controlled ventilation, a newer way to run a breathing machine during chest surgery, where often only one lung is ventilated. Squeezing all airflow into a reduced lung area strains tissue and mismatches air and blood flow, and lung complications after such surgery remain common despite protective settings.

Unlike standard machines that push air in and let it drift out, this method controls both directions with constant flow. It produces smooth pressure changes and lets clinicians read pressure inside the windpipe directly and tune settings to lung stretchiness. Bench and animal studies report better lung mechanics, aeration, oxygen levels, and lower mechanical energy delivered to tissue. Small clinical studies during one-lung ventilation hint at better oxygen and carbon dioxide handling with less total airflow. The authors caution that patient-centered outcomes remain unproven and call for large multicenter trials.
pmc-13650745:
Miłosz Pietrus and six co-authors argue that endometrial cancer, the commonest gynecological cancer in wealthy countries, needs a wider lens than its four famous molecular subtypes. That classification transformed care and lately enabled combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy as a first-line standard, yet survival for aggressive disease still lags and tumors differ in far more than their mutations.

The review layers in misrouted developmental signaling, proteins found in the wrong cell compartments, chemical gene marks, stem-cell traits, and the immune landscape inside tumors. It surveys small regulatory RNAs in tissue and blood that separate grades and forecast outcomes, counts of infiltrating immune cells, and the pattern of immune receptors as a newer marker. Emerging tools include tumor DNA in blood for spotting leftover disease, single-cell and spatial mapping, and AI-assisted pathology. Their integrated model is meant to sharpen prognosis and treatment matching.
pmc-13650945:
Wen-Yueh Ho and seven colleagues create a family of recyclable catalysts for click chemistry, the copper-catalyzed reaction that snaps azides and alkynes into triazole rings for uses from drug discovery to materials. Their catalysts are aryl imidazolium salts carrying both kinds of acidity at once, proton-donating and electron-accepting sites in one framework.

The dual character raised the reaction's efficiency and selectivity, and the salts removed the need for extra phase-transfer helpers or cosolvents, simplifying the setup. The catalyst stayed stable in water and open air, which suits greener laboratory practice, and its top activity survived four reuse cycles. Because the aryl framework is tunable, chemists can adjust its properties for different jobs. The authors present the salts as a sustainable platform for running a cornerstone reaction with less waste and simpler workup.
pmc-13651445:
Alexander Muacevic and thirteen colleagues survey breast cancer screening knowledge among women studying non-medical subjects at a university in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. There, early detection drives survival yet awareness often stops at good intentions. The cross-sectional study ran in mid-2025 across four universities.

A bilingual questionnaire reached 679 students. Attitudes toward screening were broadly sufficient, but fewer than half showed adequate general awareness, under a fifth knew risk factors and warning signs well, and under a quarter practiced screening adequately. A breast lump was widely recognized as a sign, while family history and age were the best-known risks and early puberty among the least known. Self-examination and clinical examination uptake both ran low, though many students sit below the age for routine mammography. One university's affiliation strongly predicted both knowledge and practice, and family history of the disease also helped, pointing to where education campaigns should aim.
pmc-13651545:
Lucas Joel and ten colleagues demonstrate practical control methods that push a standard amine carbon capture plant to roughly total capture. The methods remove essentially all the carbon dioxide beyond what entered with the combustion air. Amine scrubbing dominates commercial capture projects, and early plants will still be running when net zero deadlines bite, so their achievable rate matters.

The strategy has two loops. The regeneration column is tuned, using simple temperature readings, to produce the leanest solvent possible without wasting energy. The absorber's liquid-to-gas ratio is held at the minimum that hits the target rate. Modeling explained the principles, and a pilot plant then ran seventy-five continuous hours at the near-total rate at a thirty-tonne daily scale. Operators needed little training, and standard instruments plus one better exhaust analyzer sufficed. The authors offer design and permitting guidance, noting each plant's hardware caps its ceiling.
pmc-13651745:
Othman Al-Dossary and seven co-authors review engineered carbon-based fertilizers, materials that promise to feed crops while healing the soil that synthetic fertilizers have degraded. Made from crop residues, manure, and organic waste through charring, wet carbonization, composting, or digestion, these products have evolved from simple soil amendments into built nutrient couriers.

The review dissects how pore architecture, surface area, charge, and oxygen-bearing surface groups govern the capture and slow release of nutrients through adsorption, ion exchange, and diffusion. Advanced tweaks include chemical activation, co-charring with minerals, and blending in nano-carbons such as graphene offshoots and carbon dots. Interactions among the carbon matrix, nutrients, and root-zone microbes receive careful separation into proven mechanisms versus speculative responsive-delivery ideas. A closing critique confronts the lab-to-field gap: real soils transform these materials unpredictably, and the authors set priorities for reproducible, field-proven designs.
pmc-2824145:
Thabane, Ma, Chu, and co-authors offer a tutorial on pilot studies: what they are, why they matter, and how to run them. Pilot studies precede large phase three trials, which compare treatments to give early proof that a drug or intervention works. Pilots are also called feasibility or vanguard studies.

The authors explain that a pilot tests whether the big trial can be done well, not whether the treatment works. Recruitment, procedures, and follow-up are all rehearsed. Clear guidance helps teams avoid a common error: treating small pilot results as proof of benefit.
pmc-3179345:
Bonewald reviews the osteocyte, a bone cell once dismissed as a passive placeholder. Osteocytes sit embedded inside bone, surrounded by hard matrix, and were long thought to do little. The previous decade brought an explosion of data on their molecular biology and function, she writes.

Far from passive, osteocytes orchestrate bone remodelling, signalling where old bone should be removed and new bone laid down. They also sense strain and help control minerals. Recognising their central role changed bone research and opened new ideas for treating thinning bones and fractures.  Signals from osteocytes also reach distant organs, widening their role beyond bone itself.
pmc-3463245:
Peakall and Smouse present GenAlEx 6.5, an update to their population genetics software that runs inside Microsoft Excel. The package offers analysis of genetic data from diploid, haploid, and binary markers, plus DNA sequences. Both teaching and research users can run it without specialist computing setups.

GenAlEx provides frequency-based statistics such as F-statistics and heterozygosity, which summarise how variation splits within and between populations. Running inside a familiar spreadsheet made population genetics accessible to field biologists and students. The update kept a long-used teaching tool current with new data types.
pmc-4233345:
Petoukhov, Franke, Shkumatov, and their team reported updates to the ATSAS software in 2012. ATSAS is a program package for small-angle scattering, a method that probes the shape of molecules in solution. The data are isotropic, meaning they average over all directions, and need careful handling.

Version 2.4 added new tools and revised older ones for processing and analyzing such data. From raw scattering curves, users can estimate size, shape, and flexibility of proteins and complexes. The package is a standard in structural biology labs that lack crystals for X-ray work. Its updates kept pace with faster detectors and larger data sets.
pmc-4915045:
Ondov, Treangen, Melsted, and their colleagues introduced Mash in 2016. Comparing whole genomes and metagenomes normally takes heavy computation. Mash extends the MinHash technique, which reduces large sequences to small representative sketches, to estimate how far apart two genomes are.

From those small sketches, Mash gives a pairwise mutation distance plus a significance test. That enables efficient clustering and search across massive sequence collections. A lab can ask which known genome a new sample matches in seconds rather than hours. Mash made it practical to search and cluster the flood of genomes produced by modern sequencers.
pmc-5408845:
McCarthy, Campbell, Lun, and their co-authors presented Scater in 2017, an R package for single-cell RNA sequencing. More and more labs use single-cell RNA-seq to read gene activity cell by cell. Getting raw data ready for analysis, though, is far from simple.

Bias, artifacts, and other unwanted variation all lurk in these data. Scater handles pre-processing, quality control, normalization, and visualization in one workflow. Good quality control removes failed cells before they distort results. Visualization lets researchers see cell groups and outliers at a glance. A shared, careful pipeline helps single-cell studies produce results other labs can trust and reproduce.
pmc-5480145:
Atkins, Francis, Islam, and their team wrote a guide in 2017 on the Theoretical Domains Framework. Putting new practice in place means changing what people do. Change is far more likely when teams first learn what drives current habits and what the new habits need.

The framework was built by a group of behavior scientists and health researchers. It sorts the many forces on behavior into a set of clear domains, such as skills, beliefs, and social pressure. The guide shows how to use those domains to find why a new practice stalls in a clinic or ward. A sharp diagnosis of the block leads to a fix aimed at the right cause.
pmc-5688245:
Trisha Greenhalgh and colleagues published this framework paper in 2017. Many health and care technologies that look promising are never taken up, or are dropped after a short trial. Others fail when teams try to spread them to new sites or keep them running.

The authors built the NASSS framework to explain why adoption succeeds or fails. It looks at the condition, the technology, the users, the organization, and the wider system over time. Planners can use it before launch to spot weak points early. The framework has become a common reference for teams rolling out digital health tools.
pmc-6323945:
The Gene Ontology Consortium marked twenty years of its resource in this 2019 paper. The Gene Ontology gives genes structured, machine-readable descriptions of their functions. It began in the late nineteen nineties and spread across the life sciences.

Terms cover molecular jobs, cell locations, and wider biological processes. Curators keep adding terms and annotations as knowledge grows, and software across the field consumes them. Enrichment tests built on the ontology are a daily ritual in genomics. The paper reviews growth, quality work, and plans to keep the vocabulary current. The consortium also maintains training material that teaches new users how the terms fit together.
pmc-6796845:
Daolin Tang, Rui Kang, Tom Vanden Berghe, and coauthors reviewed the machinery of regulated cell death in 2019. Cells can die by accident or by controlled programs. Regulated death follows tight signaling chains with defined molecular steps.

Beyond apoptosis, new forms such as necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis have joined the list. Each has its own triggers, executioners, and disease links. The review organizes this fast-growing cast and the crosstalk between paths. Cancer and inflammation researchers use it to pick which death program a treatment might exploit or need to avoid.
pmc-7566045:
The Global Burden of Disease 2019 Demographics Collaborators produced in 2020 a sweeping account of how the world's population changed across seven decades. Their analysis covers more than two hundred countries and territories from 1950 to 2019. It tracks fertility, deaths, healthy life expectancy, and total population in one consistent framework.

The authors stress that sound decisions on health, pensions, and development all depend on knowing how many people there are and how old they are. Their estimates show populations aging in most regions, with fertility falling below replacement level in many countries. Because the same methods are applied everywhere, governments and researchers can compare countries fairly and plan against shared numbers.
poe-facts-case-m-valdemar-1845:
Edgar Allan Poe wrote The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar in 1845. The tale is told as a true case from the mesmeric art. A man near death from lung rot grants a test of his friend's art. The friend holds him in a trance at the point of death.

Valdemar's tongue speaks from the trance: I am dead, it says, week by week. The flesh stays fresh while the voice begs for release at last. When the trance breaks, the corpse falls to rot in a flash. The tale was read as fact by some and is Poe's most grim art work.
poe-the-raven-1845:
Edgar Allan Poe published The Raven in 1845, and the poem made him famous at once. Many call it the most famous American poem of the nineteenth century in the world. Its music of loss and dread has been parodied and quoted ever since its debut.

A student, grieving his lost Lenore, sits at midnight in his chamber of books. A raven taps, enters, and perches on a bust of Pallas above his door. To each fond question the bird croaks one word, Nevermore, and will not leave. The student sinks from hope to despair as the refrain tolls like a bell. Poe's craft of sound and rhythm makes the short poem hard to forget.
potsdam-declaration-1945:
The Potsdam Declaration went out in 1945, as the Pacific war neared its end. America, Britain, and China speak with one voice in its terms. Japan must surrender at once or face prompt and utter ruin.

The text lists fair terms: occupation, disarming, and a free new order. It warns that the alternative is total destruction of Japan's forces. Tokyo's leaders first met the ultimatum with contempt and delay. Days later, atomic bombs fell, and the Soviet Union joined the war. The Pacific war's final demand still anchors debate on how the war ended. Its silence on the Emperor's fate left room for the surrender that followed.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol3-1845:
Witnesses carry Quicherat's third volume, printed in 1845. It holds the testimony given in 1455 and 1456, when a new court re-tried Joan of Arc's name. Men and women who knew her spoke a full twenty-five years after her death.

Friends from her village, soldiers from her campaigns, and townsfolk from Orléans tell what they saw. Their words rebuild her early life, her battles, and her time in prison from the ground up. The inquiry cleared her name on the strength of this proof. The volume is the most human of the five, full of living voices.
reinaud-fave-feu-gregeois-1845:
Joseph Toussaint Reinaud and Ildefonse Fave wrote in French on Greek fire in 1845. Their book traces the lost fire weapon of Byzantium and the start of gunpowder. Greek fire could burn on water and sank many fleets. Its mix was a state secret for ages.

Old texts in Greek, Latin, and Arabic give the proof the pair work from. They tell how the fire was shot from tubes on ships and walls. Long notes weigh claims for the first use of powder in war. The book set the base for all later study of Greek fire.
sarmiento-facundo-1845:
Domingo Faustino Sarmiento published Facundo in 1845, his great essay on Argentina's soul in the Rosas years. The life of the caudillo Facundo Quiroga becomes an argument about civilization and barbarism in the young republic. Sarmiento wrote it in Chilean exile, in haste, as a blow against the dictator Rosas and his gaucho armies.

Quiroga, a tiger of the plains, rises by horsemanship, terror, and a genius for the pampas' rough democracy of force. Sarmiento reads the land itself, its emptiness and distances, as the mother of caudillos and the enemy of cities. Biography, geography, and political pamphlet fuse in prose of famous energy, haste, and rhetorical fire. He dreams of schools, immigrants, and railways civilizing the desert that bred the men he fought in exile. The book founded Argentine letters and still frames its national argument about itself.
select-speeches-of-daniel-webster-1817-1:
A. J. George, a rhetoric teacher in Newton, Massachusetts, edited this choice of Daniel Webster's speeches from 1817 to 1845. D. C. Heath issued the school edition in Boston in 1903, with a preface, opening essay, and notes. George dedicated the book to Senator George F. Hoar.

A preface pairs Webster with Burke as models of public speech for students. The speeches show Webster at work in court and Senate across three decades of national debate. Students of rhetoric could study how a great speaker built an argument, held a hall, and shaped the young republic's sense of itself.
she-and-allan-pg5745:
H. Rider Haggard first published this African adventure in 1921, and a note in Allan Quatermain's name opens the book. Quatermain says he set down the events for his own satisfaction, since memory fails with age. Chapter heads name the stakes: a talisman, messengers, and Umslopogaas of the axe.

A lion fight, a sea-cow hunt, and a swamp pursuit lead Allan through a mountain wall to a white witch. Ayesha herself appears, with a midnight battle and the slaying of Rezu. Haggard joins his hunter hero to the deathless queen in a tale of oaths, spells, and the gate of death.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5045:
Jimmy Carter gives four yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from January 19, 1978, to January 16, 1981. Three stars part each address from the next. The first opens with dates from his own road. Two years ago today came the first caucus in Iowa. One year ago tomorrow he walked to the White House. That walk began his duties as president. He jokes that he has saved energy ever since.

In arms, in rule, in trade, and in spirit, the Union stands sound. America is a great and strong country, Carter says. A sure and hard-working folk keep it so. Each wave of Americans faces states not of its choosing. Character is weighed by such states of affairs. Times of crisis ask for all of a nation's force. Leaders must bring their strength to one pressing task then.
thackeray-pg18645: Anthony Trollope wrote Thackeray for the English Men of Letters set. John Morley shaped that set. Macmillan and Co. printed the book in London in 1879. The right of translation and reproduction was reserved. Charles Dickens and Evans printed it at the Crystal Palace Press. Chapters open with Thackeray's life story. His work for Fraser's Magazine and Punch comes next. Vanity Fair gains its own chapter. Pendennis and The Newcomes share the part that follows.
the-american-phrenological-journal-and-m: The American Phrenological Journal and Miscellany, volume 7, 1845. Another volume. This book preserves that periodical. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, September 20, 1828, No. 332, visits Anne Hathaway's Cottage at Shottery. The view belongs to Mr. Rider's series illustrating the life of Shakespeare. The cottage, a mile from Stratford-upon-Avon, is where the poet's wife is said to have lived with her parents before her marriage. Neither exterior nor interior, Rider reports, has suffered any renovating process.

In July 1827 the occupier was a widow, the last of the Hathaway name there. She showed Rider the old carved bedstead and recalled the furniture long called Shakespeare's Courting-Chair. A woodcut of the chair from Ireland's Views on the Avon supplies a vignette of the interior. The article treats the chair as a throne for the sighing lover of the sonnets. Readers get Shakespeare biography built from furniture, tenancy, and a widow's memory.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, December 27, 1828, No. 348, illustrates Barber's Barn in Hackney. The ancient mansion in Mare Street was built about 1591 on ground called Barbour Berns. Colonel John Okey, one of the regicides charged with compassing Charles I's death, resided there and held the premises at his attainder in October 1660. His forfeited interest passed to the Duke of York, who in 1663 granted it back to Okey's widow.

Okey was seized in Holland in 1662 with Berkestead and Corbett, sent to England, and executed at Tyburn, among the last regicides punished capitally. The grounds later turned to peaceful pursuits as a nursery under John Busch. Catherine II of Russia engaged Busch to lay out her garden, and in 1771 he handed the Hackney nursery to the Loddiges firm. Readers follow one house from treason trials to imperial gardening.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, October 10, 1829, No. 393, illustrates Glamis Castle in the valley of Strathmore. The castellated palace stands in a park of 160 acres near the village of Glamis in Angus. Malcolm II was assassinated there in 1034, and the chamber where he expired is still shown. Two obelisks mark where he was attacked, one near the manse and one in a neighbouring field.

Some historians also place Macbeth's murder of Duncan at Glamis. The article notes Scott's recently published version instead puts it at a great castle near Inverness, with Boethius agreeing. Fordun says Elgin, others Cawdor Castle. The castle's fabric joins two rectangular towers with fifteen-foot walls into a Z-like plan of mutual defence. A spiral staircase of 143 steps climbs from bottom to top. Readers get a murder scene argued over by chroniclers, inside a working stronghold.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, April 2, 1831, No. 483, illustrates the grotto at Ascot Place in Surrey. The estate stands five miles south-east of Windsor, by Ascot Heath near Winkfield. Andrew Lindergreen built the residence; Daniel Agace, its later owner, showed considerable taste in arranging the grounds. A circular Corinthian temple ornaments the adjoining lawn, but the grotto is the estate's gem.

The grotto sits at the end of a canal through the grounds and holds four rooms, one finished for the refreshing pastime of tea drinking. It is covered almost entirely with white spar, polished pebbles, and petrifactions, with pendant ornaments on the ceiling. Under a strong sun the effect is almost magical, the article says. A workman named Turnbull executed the decorations over several years. The view is copied from Hakewill's engravings for his History of Windsor. Readers are invited to share the cool retreat's repose.
the-oxford-movement-twelve-years-1833-18:
R. W. Church, sometime Dean of St. Paul's and Fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, wrote papers on the Oxford Movement of 1833 to 1845. An advertisement explains that Church revised the papers in the last months of his life. Fourteen reached the form he wanted, one was nearly ready, and the last four were finished from his pencilled notes after his death.

A fragment of his letter to Lord Acton states his aim. He did not claim to write a full history of the movement. He wanted to preserve a memorial of a noble effort he had watched himself, by men he calls the salt of their generation. The papers record religious earnestness fifty years gone.
the-taming-of-the-shrew-pg2245: Christopher Sly, drunk in the Induction, frames this edition: the Lord's players perform Kate and Petruchio's battle for the tinker. The shrew is tamed, or seems to be, in a whirl of farce. The Induction's trick makes the whole play a play-within-a-play.
tob-0045:
Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara ordered a private history of how the United States slid into the Vietnam War. The study, leaked in 1971, became famous as the Pentagon Papers. Volume one of the edition entered into the record by Senator Mike Gravel covers the years from Truman through Johnson.

Inside, memos and cables show leaders doubting the war in private while pressing it in public. The leak fed a landmark fight over press freedom and helped turn opinion against the war. Gravel's edition put the documents themselves before ordinary readers. The volume remains the paper trail behind the headlines of a generation.
tob-13145:
Swami Vivekananda crossed the world in the 1890s to teach Hindu thought to Western audiences. Seven of his lectures on Jnana Yoga, the path of knowledge, form Part Two of that course. Vivekananda was trained in Advaita Vedanta, the teaching that the self and the divine are one.

Lecture by lecture he argues that the soul is already divine and that fear and weakness come from forgetting it. Reason, he says, pushed honestly to its end, leads past itself into direct realization. His forceful, plain speech made abstract doctrine feel urgent. The lectures helped plant Indian philosophy firmly in the West.
tob-4145:
Julius Jolly translated the Vishnu Smriti for volume seven of the Sacred Books of the East in 1882. The Hindu law-book speaks in Vishnu's name and orders life by dharma. It sets the duties of the four castes and the stages of a man's life. It also gives penances for faults, and rules of gift and purity.

Kings learn how to judge cases and set punishments. Householders learn debts, inheritance, and the rites owed to ancestors. Jolly, a fine scholar of Indian law, keeps the dense rules clear. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Smriti shows ancient India's legal mind at work on daily life.
tob-4245:
Arthur Middleton Reeves weighed the evidence for Norse America in The Finding of Wineland the Good, published in 1890. His subject is the Icelandic sagas of voyages west: Bjarni's sighting, Leif Eriksson's landing, and the farms raised in a land of vines and timber. Reeves, an American scholar of Icelandic, sorts saga from saga.

He compares the accounts, maps the likely coasts, and judges what the tales can prove. Five centuries before Columbus, on his showing, Norsemen wintered in the New World. Verified from the 1919 edition, the study remains a careful, readable brief for the Vinland voyages and their sources.
ulrich-lanzelet-hahn-1845:
Ulrich von Zatzikhoven told the Lancelot story his own way in Lanzelet, a German poem of some 9,440 verses. Karl Hahn's 1845 edition prints the medieval text complete. His hero is raised far from court, by a fairy in a lake land.

Lanzelet grows up not knowing his own name or kin, then rides out to learn both by deeds. Tournaments, rescues, and strange hosts test him until he wins his place at the Round Table. The poem is an early, free branch of the Lancelot legend, apart from the French line. Hahn's edition keeps that branch within reach.
un-charter-1945:
Fifty nations signed the Charter of the United Nations at San Francisco in 1945, as the Second World War was ending. The Charter founded the United Nations and remains the basic law of the world body. It grew out of the failure of the League of Nations and a shared resolve that great wars must not happen again.

The text sets up the Security Council, the General Assembly, and the other main organs, and states the members' core promises. Nations pledge to keep peace, respect the equal rights of peoples large and small, and settle disputes without force. Every member state since has accepted the Charter, making it the closest thing the world has to a constitution.
un-ga-res-45:
Food stayed short long after the guns fell silent, and Resolution 45 of the General Assembly, passed on 11 December 1946, takes stock of the crisis. In February the Assembly had urged swift action on a feared lack of bread grains and rice. By year's end, the joint effort had paid off. The grain state of 1946 was far better than feared. Millions of lives had been saved in the hard months before harvest.

Yet the text warns that the food state stays poor. Many lands had not yet shaken off the ruin of enemy rule and still needed forced imports of grains, fats, and other staples. A sharp lack of such foods held on in much of Europe, even in lands that once sold food abroad.
un-ga-res-a-69-45:
Regions are urged to cut arms on their own doorstep in Resolution A/69/45, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The vote stands in a chain that reaches back to 1990. Its faith is stated at the start. The drive of states toward full disarmament grows from a plain human wish. That wish is for true peace and safety, and for an end to the threat of war.

Peace kept in one region, the text argues, frees funds, minds, and goods for peaceful work. The call asks states to take up regional arms steps that fit their own ground. Trust built near home, in this view, is the base on which wider arms deals can stand.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 45, adopted on 11 December 1946, kept up the fight against the world food shortage. Joint effort before the 1946 harvest had saved millions of lives. But the Assembly found the food state still poor. Famine had struck parts of Asia. Bread was newly rationed in some lands. Supplies for 1947 looked well short of the least people needed.

Food-growing countries were urged to raise output and exports. They were urged to keep grain land in use, move crops faster, and curb price gouging. Industrial lands were asked to send farm machines, fertilizer, and seed. All lands were asked to stretch supplies by milling rules and curbs on feeding bread grain to animals.

General Assembly resolution 69/45 (2014) is the annual statement on regional disarmament. The Assembly affirms that global and regional work fits together and should go forward side by side. Regional arrangements made to fit each area's conditions can cut arms. They can do so while keeping every state's security at full strength. It calls on states to conclude regional and subregional agreements on non-proliferation, disarmament, and confidence-building where they can. It is glad to see the regional work already under way.
un-sc-res-1245:
Sierra Leone stood before the Council as it adopted Resolution 1245 on Sierra Leone on 11 June 1999. Government and rebel envoys were talking in Lomé, Togo, about ending the war. The talks offered the first real hope of a settlement in years. The observer mission in the country, called UNOMSIL, was due to expire within days.

The Council extends UNOMSIL until 13 December 1999. It urges both sides to stay at the table and bend where they can. If the Lomé talks succeed, the Secretary-General will propose a bigger mission with a fresh mandate. Any wider deployment must match the safety on the ground. The Council stresses that only a political settlement can bring lasting peace.
un-sc-res-1345: At number 1345 in its series, the Security Council decision is catalogued here as a 1999 record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1445:
Congo is the subject of Resolution 1445 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 4 December 2002. Congo and Rwanda had signed the Pretoria Agreement, and Congo and Uganda the Luanda Agreement. Foreign troops were pulling out; over twenty-three thousand Rwandan soldiers had left. Ethnic violence in Ituri was growing worse.

The Council backs the new plan for the United Nations mission, MONUC, and lets it grow to 8,700 troops in two task forces. The mission should help verify the withdrawals and support voluntary disarmament of foreign armed groups. Kisangani must be demilitarized, and the Congo River reopened to free movement. Uganda is held to its pledge to finish pulling out by 15 December 2002.
un-sc-res-145:
Resolution 145, adopted without dissent on 22 July 1960, follows up the Council's first Congo decision a week earlier. It rests on the Secretary-General's first report on how Resolution 143 was being carried out. The text notes that UN troops had already reached Leopoldville and that their arrival had a calming effect.

The Council calls on Belgium to carry out the withdrawal of its troops quickly, and it authorizes the Secretary-General to take all action needed for that end. It asks all states to avoid any act that could block the return of law and order or weaken the Congolese government's authority. The Congo operation was becoming a test of what UN forces could do.
un-sc-res-1545:
Resolution 1545 was the Council's answer on Burundi, adopted on 21 May 2004. The Arusha peace deal had set the country on a path to elections. An African Union force was already on the ground guarding the truce. The Council judged that a United Nations mission should now take over.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates the United Nations Operation in Burundi, called ONUB, from 1 June 2004. It starts with up to 5,650 troops and 120 police. Most first troops come from the African force already deployed. The mission watches the ceasefire, disarms fighters, and guards arms collection sites. It also helps refugees go home and backs the planned elections.
un-sc-res-1645:
Resolution 1645 created the United Nations Peacebuilding Commission in 2005, acting together with a matching vote in the General Assembly. The new body was meant to help countries coming out of war, when peace often fails within a few years. Its focus was recovery, not fighting.

The text lays out who sits on the commission, how it picks countries to help, and how it should raise money and attention for them. It advises on rebuilding courts, police, and services after conflict. For readers, the text serves as the charter of the UN's main attempt to make peace last after the guns stop.
un-sc-res-1745:
For Timor-Leste, the Council's answer came in Resolution 1745, adopted on 22 February 2007. The young country was still shaky after the unrest of April and May 2006. Presidential and parliamentary elections were due within months. The United Nations Integrated Mission there, called UNMIT, backed the police and the courts.

The text extends the mandate of UNMIT until 26 February 2008. It adds up to 140 more police for an extra formed unit around the elections. All parties are told to shun violence and respect the vote timetable. The Council also presses for justice over the 2006 unrest and for a full review of the security forces.
un-sc-res-1845: Security Council Resolution 1845 is preserved here as a transcription of the United Nations official record. The act belongs to the Council's numbered series, the running file of its decisions on peace and security. Its text follows the standard internal order, and the entry preserves that order whole, from first finding to final instruction.
un-sc-res-1945:
Sudan's Darfur expert panel was renewed on 14 October 2010. The final phase of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement was under way, with the South's referendum near. Darfur's violence had risen, with more tribal fighting and sexual violence. Chad and Sudan had agreed in January to normalize their ties. The Council restated its support for the Doha peace talks.

The Council extended the Panel of Experts on Sudan, first named under resolution 1591 (2005), until 19 October 2011. A midterm briefing was due by 31 March 2011, with a first report within ninety days. The panel had to coordinate its work with the African Union–United Nations force in Darfur. All states and bodies were urged to cooperate with the sanctions committee and the panel in full. States in the region had to report the steps they took under resolutions 1591 (2005) and 1556 (2004).
un-sc-res-245: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 245, catalogued for 1968 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-345: Chinese became a working language of the Security Council on 17 January 1974. The General Assembly had made Chinese a working language of its own in December 1973, noting that the other four official languages already held that status in both bodies. The Council agreed without a vote. It amended its provisional rules of procedure as set out in the annex. Speeches in any of the five would now be interpreted into the other four, and resolutions published in all five.
un-sc-res-445: An official UN record text, Resolution 445 is catalogued in this library with a 1979 date. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-45: The Union of Burma applied to join the United Nations in 1948. A committee on new members reviewed its case. The Council's members had approved the application without dissent. On 10 April 1948 the Security Council recommended to the General Assembly that Burma be admitted. The vote was ten to none, with Argentina abstaining. The text is a single short paragraph. Burma had won independence from Britain that January. It took its United Nations seat the same month as the recommendation.
un-sc-res-745:
Resolution 745 was the Council's answer on Cambodia, adopted on 28 February 1992. The Paris agreements of October 1991 had ended the country's long conflict on paper. The United Nations now had to run much of the country until its people could vote.

The text sets up the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia for up to eighteen months. The Authority would oversee the peace plan and prepare free elections, due by May 1993. Cambodian parties had to disarm before voter registration ended. The Council also asked states to fund the return of refugees and the rebuilding of the country.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sierra Leone's observer mission is extended while peace talks run in Resolution 1245, adopted on 11 June 1999. The situation stayed fragile despite ECOMOG's cooperation, the sixth Secretary-General's report on UNOMSIL had just landed, and the government and rebel representatives were negotiating in Lomé under ECOWAS auspices.

The Council extends the mandate of the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, until 13 December 1999. It stresses that only an overall political settlement and national reconciliation can end the conflict peacefully, welcomes the Lomé talks, and calls on all sides to stay committed and flexible. It notes the Secretary-General's plan to recommend an expanded UNOMSIL with a revised mandate and concept of operations if the talks succeed, and says any further deployment must weigh security conditions. The Secretary-General must keep the Council closely informed.

Armed ethnic Albanian groups fighting in Macedonia and southern Serbia draw the Council's attention on 21 March 2001. Their violence risked spreading the Kosovo crisis across new borders. The Council backed the multiethnic plans put forward by both governments, and the work of NATO, the European Union, and others in the region.

Everyone taking up arms against those states was told to stop at once, lay down their weapons, and go home. Albanian political leaders were called on to condemn violence and ethnic hatred in public and to use their influence for peace. States were also asked to help build democratic, multiethnic societies and to help displaced people return home.

Foreign troops leave Congo as Resolution 1445 is adopted on 4 December 2002. The Pretoria Agreement between Congo and Rwanda and the Luanda Agreement with Uganda had set withdrawal terms; 23,400 Rwandan troops had already left, verified by the Third Party Verification Mechanism. Voluntary disarmament and repatriation of foreign armed groups was the next test, while violence flared in Ituri.

The Council authorizes MONUC to expand to up to 8,700 military personnel in two task forces, deployed in phases. It stresses that disarmament of the groups named in the Lusaka Agreement must stay voluntary and match the pace of withdrawals. It demands a full halt to fighting, an end to all support for the eastern armed groups, demilitarization of Kisangani, and full access for MONUC and verification teams. Uganda is held to its pledge to finish withdrawing by 15 December 2002.

United Nations troops had reached Leopoldville and their arrival was already calming the capital when this Congo text passed on 22 July 1960. It follows up the operation created days earlier. The Secretary-General's first report described the work begun, though much more help was still needed.

Belgium is called on to carry out the earlier resolution quickly and withdraw its troops, and the Secretary-General is empowered to take all needed steps toward that end. All states are asked to do nothing that would block the return of law and order or weaken Congo's authority over its own land. Further reports are requested as the crisis develops.

Burundi gets a UN peacekeeping operation in Resolution 1545, adopted on 21 May 2004. The Arusha Agreement's transition was due to end on 31 October 2004. Ceasefires covered most armed movements, though one fought on. Burundi's transitional authorities and the African Union asked that AMIB, the African Mission in Burundi, become a UN operation.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes the United Nations Operation in Burundi, ONUB, for an initial six months from 1 June 2004. It is built from AMIB's forces and capped at 5,650 military personnel and 120 civilian police. ONUB may use all necessary means to monitor ceasefires, secure pre-disarmament sites, run disarmament and demobilization, and watch arms flows across borders including Lake Tanganyika. It may protect civilians under imminent threat and create secure conditions for aid, refugee return, and elections. It must also advise on police, judicial, and institutional reform and monitor human rights.

A new body, the United Nations Peacebuilding Commission, is created on 20 December 2005. The 2005 World Summit had called for a body devoted to countries coming out of war. The Council acted together with the General Assembly, each passing the same founding text on the same day.

The Commission is an advisory body meant to keep world attention on post-war countries, marshal aid, and join up recovery, reintegration, and rebuilding work. It meets in different groupings, including country-specific meetings for states under review. An Organizational Committee drawn from Council members, Assembly members, and top financial contributors runs its agenda, and a support office and fund were created alongside it.

Timor-Leste's 2007 elections dominate Resolution 1745, adopted on 22 February 2007. The country was fragile after the April-May 2006 crisis, with judicial cases under way and a commission of inquiry's findings accepted by parliament. The UN Integrated Mission, UNMIT, was in place, backed by an international security force. Timor-Leste's leaders had asked for one more formed police unit for the election period.

The Council extends UNMIT until 26 February 2008 and raises its strength by up to 140 police for the extra unit. It calls on all parties to shun violence and respect the election timetable set by the National Commission on Elections, so the polls unite rather than divide the country. It backs use of the December 2006 security arrangement on rebuilding the national police, and a joint forum linking the government, UNMIT, and the international force. A report is due within 60 days after the elections.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's European Union force is renewed for a further twelve months on 20 November 2008. The annual authorization follows the line of the 2004, 2005, 2006, and 2007 texts. Full support is again voiced for the High Representative and for completing the 1995 peace agreement.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to maintain EUFOR under unified command. The force may take all necessary measures to carry out the peace agreement's military terms and defend itself. Bosnia's progress toward European integration is welcomed, while domestic leaders are noted to still bear the main duty for reforms the peace required.

Sudan's arms embargo and the Darfur conflict stand behind Resolution 1945, adopted on 14 October 2010. A Panel of Experts watched the embargo set by Resolutions 1556 and 1591. Its reports noted blocks on its work, including limits on its movement. Violence in Darfur was rising, with tribal fighting, attacks on aid workers and peacekeepers, and talks in Doha still incomplete.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the Panel of Experts until 19 October 2011. It sets dates for an interim report, a midterm briefing, and a final report with findings and advice. States must tell the sanctions committee in advance before sending allowed supplies into Darfur in support of the peace deal. Any sale of arms to Sudan that is not banned must come with end-user papers so its lawfulness can be checked.

South West Africa, the territory South Africa ruled under an old League of Nations mandate, is the subject of Resolution 245. The General Assembly had voted in 1966 to end that mandate. South Africa had ignored the decision. It was putting more than thirty South West Africans on trial in Pretoria. The Council adopted the resolution unanimously on 25 January 1968.

The Council condemned South Africa's refusal to stop the trial, which the General Assembly had already declared illegal. South Africa was called on to end the trial at once. The South West Africans involved had to be released and sent home. All states were asked to use their influence to press South Africa to comply. A report on the matter was requested as soon as possible.

Chinese joins the working tongues of the Security Council in Resolution 345. It passed with no vote on 17 January 1974. The Assembly had made Chinese a working tongue of its own in December 1973. Four of the UN's five formal tongues held that rank in both halls. The Assembly judged it right for the Council to match, for the sake of swift work.

The Council agreed. It changed its own draft rules as set out in a note tied to the text. From then on, Chinese stood with English, French, Russian, and Spanish. All five were both formal and working tongues of the Council. A speech in one would be rendered in the rest.

Rhodesian forces struck across their borders in the spring of 1979, raiding Angola, Mozambique, and Zambia. Those countries backed the liberation struggle in Zimbabwe. At home, executions continued, and the regime prepared its own elections for April. Resolution 445 was adopted on 8 March 1979.

The Council strongly condemned the invasions. They were clear violations of the sovereignty of the three countries. The front-line states were praised for their support and for their restraint. All states were asked to give them substantial material help to strengthen their defenses. The regime's planned April elections were condemned as well. They were a device to keep minority rule, the Council said. The elections and their results were declared null and void, and states were urged to send no observers.

Burma won independence from Britain in January 1948. The Southeast Asian nation applied for UN membership within months. Its admissions committee report reached the Council that spring. Resolution 45 was adopted on 10 April 1948. Ten members voted in favor. Argentina alone abstained. The text notes the application had already won unanimous approval in committee.

The Council recommended the Union of Burma for admission. The General Assembly seated Burma days later. The country, now called Myanmar, kept that seat through monarchy, democracy, and military rule. Its UN journey began with this calm vote. Few then foresaw the civil wars that would trouble Burma for generations after independence.

Cambodia's transition under UN care is launched by Resolution 745, adopted in 1992. The Paris agreements of 23 October 1991 had set a full settlement of the Cambodia conflict. The UN Advance Mission was already helping keep the ceasefire and clear mines. The Council said free and fair elections were the key to a just and lasting peace and vowed that the abuses of Cambodia's recent past would not return.

The Council approves the Secretary-General's plan and sets up the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia for no more than eighteen months. It rules that elections must be held by May 1993 at the latest. It urges the Cambodian sides to fully disarm before voter registration ends and to hand surplus weapons to the Authority. States are asked to fund the work, including refugee return, and reports are set for June and September 1992 and January and April 1993.
vietnamese-declaration-independence-1945:
Ho Chi Minh issued Vietnam's Declaration of Independence on September 2, 1945. He opens by quoting the American declaration of 1776 on men created equal, with rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. In a broader sense, he says, all peoples are equal from birth. All hold the right to live, be happy, and be free. He quotes the French declaration of 1791 to the same effect, and calls both statements truths no one can deny.

Then the charge turns. For more than eighty years, he says, French rulers abused the banner of liberty, equality, and fraternity. They violated his land and crushed its people. They stripped away free government and split the country into three regimes to break its unity. They built more prisons than schools. Patriots were slain and uprisings drowned in blood. The document builds its case count by count toward a single end: Vietnam's claim to stand free.
williford-cariden-examination-1645:
Joane Williford and Joan Cariden of Kent went through charge, trial, and death in 1645, and a pamphlet keeps each stage. The Examination, Confession, Triall, and Execution prints the whole course of their case. The year places them in the Hopkins panic, when eastern courts sat full of such work.

Readers get the first questions, the words taken as confession, the verdict, and the end. Few prints hold all four stages of a witch case in so small a space. The record shows the speed with which a life could pass through the machine of the law. It is grim, plain, and complete.
williford-examination-execution-1645:
Three Kent dames go to the gallows in the Examination pamphlet of 1645, a state tale from Faversham. Joan Williford, Joan Cariden, and Jane Hott were charged as witches in the year the great hunt gripped the east. The town's mayor took down their quiz, their words of guilt, their trial, and their deaths on September 29, all in one brief, grim print for the crowd to buy.

Such tales were oft loose and wild. This one is prim and full, which gives it rare worth. It is one day of a panic, kept whole. Its plain tone chills.
zoist-vol-03-1845:
April 1845 to January 1846 is the span of The Zoist's third volume. Elliotson edits a journal now settled into its combative routine. Mesmeric surgery reports continue, each with witnesses and outcomes. Cerebral physiology, the era's study of brain and character, shares the pages.

Readers meet somnambulist cases that strain belief and invite tests. Country doctors write in with cures of pain, fits, and locked limbs. London critics answer, and the journal answers back. The thirteen volume run, from 1843 to 1856, holds the movement's whole record. Volume three is its sturdy middle beginning. It preserves a medical underground in its own words.
